A) Tibialis posterior tendon
B) Superficial peroneal nerve
C) Flexor digitorum longus
D) Gastrocnemius muscle
questions.answer:
B)
The superficial peroneal nerve courses along the lateral compartment of the leg in close proximity to the fibula. It innervates the peroneus longus and brevis muscles (foot eversion) and provides cutaneous sensation to the dorsum of the foot. A fibular fracture can injure this nerve, explaining the patient's eversion weakness.

A is incorrect because the tibialis posterior tendon runs along the medial aspect of the ankle, posterior to the medial malleolus, and is not closely associated with the fibula. C is incorrect because the flexor digitorum longus is a deep posterior compartment muscle located on the medial side of the leg and ankle, far from the fibula. D is incorrect because the gastrocnemius muscle is a superficial posterior compartment muscle that originates from the femoral condyles and is not in close anatomic proximity to the fibula at the level of a typical fibular fracture.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a fall onto an outstretched hand. He complains of pain in the proximal forearm and difficulty pronating his wrist. On examination, he has tenderness over the anterior proximal forearm and is unable to flex the interphalangeal joint of the thumb or the distal interphalangeal joint of the index finger. There is no sensory deficit. Which of the following structures is most likely affected in this case?
A) Anterior interosseous nerve
B) Radial nerve
C) Ulnar nerve
D) Median nerve (main trunk)
questions.answer:
A)
The anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) is a pure motor branch of the median nerve that innervates the flexor pollicis longus, the lateral part of the flexor digitorum profundus (to the index and middle fingers), and the pronator quadratus. Injury produces inability to flex the thumb IP joint and index DIP joint (loss of the "OK" sign), weakness of forearm pronation, and no sensory loss — classic AIN syndrome.

B is incorrect because the radial nerve innervates wrist and finger extensors; its injury causes wrist drop, not loss of thumb/index flexion.
C is incorrect because the ulnar nerve innervates the medial FDP (ring/small fingers), interossei, and hypothenar muscles; its injury would not explain loss of thumb IP or index DIP flexion.
D is incorrect because a main trunk median nerve injury would produce sensory loss in the radial 3½ digits and weakness of thenar (opposition) and forearm flexor muscles, unlike the isolated motor deficit without sensory loss seen here.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male presents to the clinic with a painful, swollen knee after falling from a height. Physical examination demonstrates a prominent bony ridge on the lateral aspect of the knee, and x-rays show a fracture of the lateral tibial plateau. Which bony landmark is likely involved in this fracture and is significant for surgical fixation techniques?
A) Medial condyle
B) Bifurcate ridge
C) Lateral spine
D) Intercondylar eminence
questions.answer:
B)
Explanation: The bifurcate ridge is a key anatomical landmark on the tibial plateau that separates the ACL and PCL bundles. It is important in surgical planning for fixation techniques in tibial plateau fractures, as it influences the stability and alignment of reconstructive procedures.

questions.question:
A 63-year-old male presents with knee pain and has difficulty performing activities such as stair climbing and standing up from a seated position. He has a history of diabetes and peripheral vascular disease. A thorough examination reveals a diminished posterior tibial pulse. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
A) MRI of the knee
B) Ultrasound of the lower extremity
C) Referral for vascular surgery
D) Physical therapy
questions.answer:
C)
Explanation: Given the patient's age, history of diabetes, and diminished posterior tibial pulse, there is a concern for significant vascular insufficiency. Referral for vascular surgery is warranted to assess and potentially address any underlying vascular issues that might be contributing to his knee pain and functional limitations.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old female presents with bilateral wrist pain and stiffness, particularly in the morning. Laboratory tests are positive for rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies. Which of the following findings would you expect on her wrist x-rays?
A) Osteophyte formation at the distal radius
B) Joint space narrowing and erosions
C) Increased bone density
D) Normal findings
questions.answer:
B)
In rheumatoid arthritis, wrist imaging characteristically demonstrates joint space narrowing due to cartilage destruction and periarticular erosions caused by pannus formation. These findings, along with periarticular osteopenia, are hallmarks of inflammatory arthritis affecting the small joints of the hands and wrists.

A is incorrect because osteophyte formation is a hallmark of osteoarthritis (a degenerative process), not rheumatoid arthritis, which is an erosive inflammatory arthropathy.
C is incorrect because rheumatoid arthritis causes periarticular osteopenia (decreased bone density), not increased bone density.
D is incorrect because a patient with established RA who is seropositive for both RF and anti-CCP would be expected to have imaging abnormalities; normal findings would be inconsistent with symptomatic, serologically confirmed disease.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male presents with chronic joint pain and swelling. Magnetic resonance imaging reveals damage to the articular cartilage, including loss of chondrocytes and proteoglycans. What is the primary role of chondrocytes in cartilage health?
A) Production of synovial fluid
B) Maintenance of the extracellular matrix
C) Promotion of bone resorption
D) Generation of new cartilage tissue
questions.answer:
B)
Chondrocytes are the sole resident cells of articular cartilage and are responsible for maintaining the extracellular matrix by synthesizing and turning over type II collagen, proteoglycans (primarily aggrecan), and other matrix components. Loss of chondrocytes leads to progressive matrix degradation and is a hallmark of osteoarthritis and other cartilage disorders.

A is incorrect because synovial fluid is produced by type B synoviocytes (fibroblast-like cells) in the synovial membrane, not by chondrocytes.
C is incorrect because bone resorption is carried out by osteoclasts, not chondrocytes.
D is incorrect because while chondrocytes do participate in limited cartilage repair, their primary role is maintenance of the existing extracellular matrix rather than generation of new cartilage tissue; articular cartilage has very limited regenerative capacity.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old man presents with progressive thigh pain. He has been on long-term bisphosphonate therapy for osteoporosis. An x-ray of the femur shows lateral cortical thickening of the femoral diaphysis with a transverse lucent line. What underlying condition is most likely contributing to his fracture?
A) Osteoporosis
B) Osteogenesis imperfecta
C) Paget's disease
D) Osteomalacia
questions.answer:
A)
Atypical femur fractures (AFFs) are strongly associated with prolonged bisphosphonate use. Bisphosphonates are prescribed for osteoporosis, and their long-term suppression of bone remodeling leads to accumulation of micro-damage and stress fractures with characteristic lateral cortical thickening. Osteoporosis is the underlying condition for which the patient was being treated and is therefore the most likely contributor.

B is incorrect because osteogenesis imperfecta is a genetic collagen disorder presenting in childhood with multiple fractures, blue sclerae, and hearing loss — it does not produce the lateral cortical thickening pattern seen in AFFs. C is incorrect because Paget's disease causes disorganized bone remodeling with cortical thickening and bowing but typically shows a mixed lytic-sclerotic pattern and elevated alkaline phosphatase, not the transverse stress-fracture pattern of AFFs. D is incorrect because osteomalacia (deficient mineralization) leads to Looser zones (pseudofractures) on the medial/compression side of bone and generalized osteopenia, not lateral cortical thickening.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman sustains a subtrochanteric femur fracture due to a high-energy trauma. After initial assessment and stabilization, you decide to perform a surgical intervention. Which surgical approach would best facilitate access to the subtrochanteric region of the femur?
A) Lateral approach
B) Anterior approach
C) Posterior approach
D) Medial approach
questions.answer:
A)
The lateral approach is best suited for subtrochanteric femur fractures as it provides direct access to the lateral cortex of the femur between the lesser trochanter and the femoral shaft, facilitating accurate reduction and application of fixation devices such as cephalomedullary nails or plate constructs.

B is incorrect because the anterior approach to the hip (e.g., Smith-Petersen or direct anterior) is designed for access to the hip joint itself, not the subtrochanteric region of the femur. C is incorrect because the posterior approach provides access to the posterior hip joint and acetabulum but does not offer optimal exposure of the subtrochanteric femur for fracture fixation. D is incorrect because the medial approach risks injury to critical neurovascular structures (femoral artery, vein, and nerve) and does not provide practical surgical access for subtrochanteric fracture fixation.

questions.question:
A young male athlete sustains a neck injury during a football game. An x-ray reveals a clay shoveler’s fracture at the C7 level. Which of the following best describes this type of injury?
A) Fracture of the anterior and middle columns
B) Avulsion fracture of the spinous process
C) Fracture through the pars interarticularis
D) Fracture-dislocation of the facet joint
E) Burst fracture of the vertebral body
questions.answer:
B)
A clay shoveler's fracture is an avulsion fracture of the spinous process, most commonly occurring at C6, C7, or T1. It results from sudden forceful muscular contraction of the trapezius and rhomboid muscles against the intact supraspinous ligament, or from direct trauma. It is a stable injury involving only the posterior elements and is typically managed conservatively.

A is incorrect because a clay shoveler's fracture involves only the spinous process (posterior column); the anterior and middle columns are intact.
C is incorrect because a fracture through the pars interarticularis describes a hangman's fracture (C2) or spondylolysis in the lumbar spine, not a clay shoveler's fracture.
D is incorrect because a fracture-dislocation of the facet joint (e.g., unilateral or bilateral facet dislocation) is a distinct, more unstable injury pattern unrelated to spinous process avulsion.
E is incorrect because a burst fracture involves failure of the vertebral body under axial load with retropulsion of fragments into the canal, which is an entirely different mechanism and injury pattern.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman presents with pain and swelling in her wrist after a fall. An MRI reveals a die-punch fracture involving the lunate fossa of the distal radius. What is the recommended initial management for this type of fracture?
A) Immobilization in a splint
B) Immediate surgical intervention
C) Observation for 4 weeks
D) Corticosteroid injection
questions.answer:
B)
A die-punch fracture involves a depressed fracture of the lunate fossa of the distal radius, which often requires surgical intervention to restore the normal anatomy and prevent complications such as joint incongruity.
A is incorrect because immobilization in a splint is insufficient for a depressed intra-articular fracture that requires anatomical reduction. C is incorrect because observation would not address the displaced fracture and could lead to poor outcomes. D is incorrect because corticosteroid injection is not a treatment for fractures and would not address the structural deformity.

questions.question:
During a surgical procedure to harvest iliac crest bone graft, the surgeon approaches from a posterior direction. Which muscle is primarily responsible for the laterally directed force during this approach, aiding in the access to the iliac crest?
A) Gluteus maximus
B) Latissimus dorsi
C) iliopsoas
D) Obturator externus
questions.answer:
A)
The gluteus maximus is primarily responsible for providing lateral stability and force during a posterior approach to the iliac crest for bone graft harvesting. Understanding the anatomical relationships of surrounding muscles is crucial for minimizing complications.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man with a history of chronic elbow pain now presents with sudden worsening of symptoms after lifting a heavy object. On examination, there is a palpable defect over the lateral epicondyle and weakness in wrist extension. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Lateral epicondylitis
B) Olecranon fracture
C) Radial head fracture
D) Extensor tendon rupture
questions.answer:
D)
A palpable defect over the lateral epicondyle combined with acute weakness in wrist extension after a sudden loading event in a patient with chronic elbow pain is consistent with rupture of the common extensor origin (extensor tendon rupture). Chronic lateral epicondylitis weakens the tendon, predisposing it to acute rupture with a forceful contraction.

A is incorrect because lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) causes pain at the lateral epicondyle but does not produce a palpable defect or sudden loss of wrist extension strength; it is a tendinopathy, not a complete rupture. B is incorrect because an olecranon fracture presents with posterior elbow pain, swelling, and inability to extend the elbow against gravity, not a defect over the lateral epicondyle with wrist extension weakness. C is incorrect because a radial head fracture typically follows a fall on an outstretched hand, presents with lateral elbow pain and limited forearm rotation, and does not cause a palpable defect over the lateral epicondyle.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents with shoulder pain after a fall onto her shoulder while skiing. She is unable to lift her arm above her head. Physical examination reveals a positive cross-body adduction test and tenderness over the AC joint. An x-ray shows a clear separation of the clavicle from the acromion. What is the best initial management for this injury?
A) Immediate surgical fixation
B) Acromioclavicular joint injection
C) Conservative management with a sling
D) Referral for physical therapy
questions.answer:
C)
For most acromioclavicular (AC) joint separations, including Type III injuries, the best initial management is conservative treatment with a sling for comfort, ice, and early range-of-motion exercises as tolerated. The majority of Type III AC separations do well with nonoperative management, and surgery is generally reserved for higher-grade injuries (Types IV–VI) or for patients who fail conservative treatment.

A is incorrect because immediate surgical fixation is not first-line for a Type III AC separation; surgery is typically reserved for Types IV–VI or for failed conservative management, particularly in high-demand overhead athletes or laborers.
B is incorrect because an AC joint injection (e.g., corticosteroid) does not address the underlying ligamentous disruption and is not standard initial management for an acute AC separation.
D is incorrect because while physical therapy is an important component of rehabilitation, the immediate priority is pain control and immobilization with a sling; formal physical therapy is initiated after the acute phase has subsided.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman presents after a fall with severe neck pain. An X-ray reveals a Jefferson fracture of the C1 vertebra with less than 6.9 mm of combined lateral mass overhang. Given the potential complications, which of the following is the most critical next step in management?
A) Immediate surgical fixation
B) Cervical traction
C) Halo-vest immobilization
D) Observation and follow-up
questions.answer:
C)
A Jefferson fracture is a burst fracture of the C1 ring. When the transverse ligament is intact (indicated by combined lateral mass overhang <6.9 mm on open-mouth odontoid view), the fracture is considered stable and is best managed with halo-vest immobilization for 8–12 weeks, providing rigid external stabilization while the fracture heals.

A is incorrect because immediate surgical fixation (e.g., C1-C2 fusion) is reserved for unstable Jefferson fractures with transverse ligament disruption (lateral mass overhang >6.9 mm) or those that fail conservative management. B is incorrect because cervical traction may be used as a temporizing measure but is not definitive management; halo-vest immobilization is the standard treatment for stable Jefferson fractures. D is incorrect because simple observation without immobilization risks displacement and neurological compromise given the inherent instability of a C1 burst fracture.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old man with a history of multiple shoulder dislocations presents with difficulty raising his arm overhead. Physical examination reveals weakness in external rotation. An MRI shows a full-thickness tear of the infraspinatus tendon. Which of the following clinical tests would best assess the integrity of the infraspinatus?
A) Neer test
B) Empty can test
C) Lateral rotation lag sign
D) Lift-off test
questions.answer:
C)
The lateral rotation (external rotation) lag sign is specifically designed to assess the integrity of the infraspinatus. The examiner passively externally rotates the patient's arm and then releases it; if the arm drops back into internal rotation (a positive lag), it indicates a significant infraspinatus tear. This correlates with the MRI findings described in the stem.

A is incorrect because the Neer test is an impingement provocation maneuver (passive forward flexion with the scapula stabilized) and does not isolate a specific rotator cuff tendon. B is incorrect because the empty can (Jobe) test primarily evaluates the supraspinatus, not the infraspinatus. D is incorrect because the lift-off test (Gerber test) assesses the subscapularis by asking the patient to lift the dorsum of the hand off the lower back against resistance.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old man presents with lateral foot pain, especially on the base of the fifth metatarsal after stepping off a curb. Physical examination reveals tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal. What is the most likely mechanism of injury leading to his condition?
A) Direct trauma to the fifth metatarsal
B) Inversion ankle sprain
C) Stress fracture from overuse
D) Avulsion fracture from muscle contraction
questions.answer:
D)
An avulsion fracture at the base of the fifth metatarsal can occur due to the pull of the peroneus brevis muscle during an ankle inversion injury. This mechanism is common in individuals who experience a sudden twist or step off a curb.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old man presents with pain in the upper back and shoulder area. On examination, he has weakness in the scapular movement and has difficulty raising his arms. Which muscle is primarily responsible for this function and may be implicated in his symptoms?
A) Serratus anterior
B) Rhomboid major
C) Trapezius
D) Latissimus dorsi
questions.answer:
C)
The trapezius muscle, innervated by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), is a major stabilizer of the scapula responsible for elevation, retraction, and upward rotation. Weakness of the trapezius leads to difficulty raising the arms overhead, shoulder droop, and upper back pain due to loss of scapular stability.

A is incorrect because while the serratus anterior (long thoracic nerve) is critical for scapular protraction and upward rotation, its dysfunction classically presents with medial scapular winging that worsens with forward flexion or wall push-ups, rather than the upper back and shoulder pain pattern described here.
B is incorrect because the rhomboid major functions primarily in scapular retraction and downward rotation; its weakness would not be the primary cause of difficulty raising the arms.
D is incorrect because the latissimus dorsi is a powerful arm adductor, extensor, and internal rotator; it does not play a primary role in scapular elevation or arm raising.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman presenting with a paronychia on her left thumb is advised to seek surgical intervention. During the procedure, the surgeon is careful to drain the collection at the nail fold. Which of the following is the most appropriate location for drainage in this situation?
A) At the midpoint of the nail
B) At the base of the nail fold
C) At one or both corners of the nail fold
D) At the distal tip of the nail
questions.answer:
C)
The most appropriate drainage site for a paronychia is at one or both corners of the nail fold. Paronychia involves infection along the lateral (and sometimes proximal) nail fold, and incision at the corners of the nail fold directly accesses the abscess cavity while preserving the nail matrix and minimizing tissue damage.

A is incorrect because the midpoint of the nail is not the site of pus collection in a paronychia; incising here would unnecessarily damage the nail plate without adequately draining the paronychial abscess.
B is incorrect because the base (proximal aspect) of the nail fold is not the primary site of drainage; incising here risks injury to the germinal matrix and is only considered when infection extends beneath the proximal nail fold (eponychia), not as a first-line approach.
D is incorrect because the distal tip of the nail is remote from the nail fold infection and would not provide access to the paronychial collection.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male athlete presents with a painful sensation in his knee following a football game where he twisted his knee during a tackle. On examination, he has tenderness over the medial joint line and a positive McMurray test. Which of the following physical exam tests would most likely help confirm a suspicion of a meniscus tear?
A) Anterior Drawer Test
B) Apley Compression Test
C) Lachman Test
D) Lift Off Test
questions.answer:
B)
The Apley Compression (Grinding) Test is performed with the patient prone and the knee flexed to 90°. The examiner applies a downward compressive force while rotating the tibia. Pain with compression and rotation suggests a meniscal tear, making it a useful confirmatory test alongside the already-positive McMurray test.

A is incorrect because the Anterior Drawer Test evaluates anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) integrity, not the meniscus. C is incorrect because the Lachman Test is the most sensitive clinical test for ACL rupture, not meniscal pathology. D is incorrect because the Lift Off Test (Gerber test) assesses subscapularis function in the shoulder and is unrelated to knee pathology.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old female athlete reports persistent pain along the outside of her ankle, exacerbated during sports activities. On examination, she has tenderness over the lateral malleolus and reproduction of pain with resisted eversion. What condition is most likely affecting the peroneal tendons in this scenario?
A) Tendon rupture
B) Tendonitis
C) Dislocation
D) Tenosynovitis
questions.answer:
B)
Peroneal tendonitis is characterized by chronic lateral ankle pain worsened by activity, tenderness over the peroneal tendons posterior to the lateral malleolus, and pain with resisted eversion. This is a common overuse condition in athletes, particularly those involved in running and cutting sports.

A is incorrect because tendon rupture typically presents with acute weakness of eversion, a palpable defect, and often a history of a sudden pop or acute traumatic event, rather than persistent activity-related pain.
C is incorrect because peroneal tendon dislocation presents with a snapping sensation over the lateral malleolus, often with visible subluxation of the tendons anterior to the fibula, and is associated with a torn or attenuated superior peroneal retinaculum rather than simple tenderness with resisted eversion.
D is incorrect because tenosynovitis specifically involves inflammation of the tendon sheath and classically presents with swelling, crepitus along the tendon sheath, and fluid within the sheath on imaging; the stem does not describe these findings, making simple tendonitis more likely.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old male construction worker presents with pain in his wrist after lifting heavy materials. An MRI shows edema in the pronator quadratus muscle. What is the primary action of the pronator quadratus muscle?
A) Wrist flexion
B) Wrist extension
C) Forearm pronation
D) Forearm supination
questions.answer:
C)
The pronator quadratus is a flat, quadrilateral muscle spanning the distal forearm between the distal ulna and radius. Its primary action is forearm pronation; it is the chief pronator for slow, unresisted pronation. It also plays an important role in stabilizing the distal radioulnar joint. Edema in this muscle on MRI is consistent with overuse or strain from repetitive heavy lifting.

A is incorrect because wrist flexion is primarily performed by the flexor carpi radialis and flexor carpi ulnaris, not the pronator quadratus.
B is incorrect because wrist extension is performed by the extensor carpi radialis longus/brevis and extensor carpi ulnaris; the pronator quadratus has no role in wrist extension.
D is incorrect because forearm supination is performed by the supinator and biceps brachii; the pronator quadratus is an antagonist to supination, acting as a pronator.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman presents with chronic pain and swelling around her ankle, particularly during activities such as walking. An MRI reveals degenerative changes in the posterior tibialis tendon. Which of the following motions is primarily affected by dysfunction of this tendon?
A) Dorsiflexion and eversion
B) Inversion and plantarflexion
C) Eversion and flexion
D) Dorsiflexion and abduction
questions.answer:
B)
The posterior tibialis tendon is the primary inverter of the foot and also assists with plantarflexion. Dysfunction leads to loss of the medial longitudinal arch (acquired flatfoot deformity) and inability to perform a single-limb heel rise, reflecting loss of inversion and plantarflexion power.

A is incorrect because dorsiflexion and eversion are functions of muscles in the anterior and lateral compartments (tibialis anterior for dorsiflexion, peroneus brevis/longus for eversion), not the posterior tibialis. C is incorrect because eversion is the opposite action of the posterior tibialis; eversion is performed by the peroneal tendons. D is incorrect because dorsiflexion is primarily performed by the tibialis anterior, and abduction is not a primary motion of the posterior tibialis tendon.

questions.question:
A 3-month-old infant is diagnosed with developmental dysplasia of the hip after a routine screening. The orthopedic surgeon decides to proceed with closed reduction and spica casting. What is the primary goal of this intervention?
A) Immediate relief of symptoms
B) Restoration of normal walking patterns
C) Stable reduction of the hip joint
D) Prevention of osteoarthritis
E) Improvement of muscle strength
questions.answer:
C)
The primary goal of closed reduction and spica casting in developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) is to achieve a stable, concentric reduction of the femoral head within the acetabulum. Maintaining this anatomic relationship allows the acetabulum and femoral head to remodel and develop normally during growth, preventing long-term complications such as subluxation, dislocation, and early degenerative changes.

A is incorrect because a 3-month-old with DDH is typically asymptomatic; the intervention is not directed at symptom relief but at restoring hip joint congruency.
B is incorrect because a 3-month-old is not yet walking; restoration of normal walking patterns is not the immediate goal of treatment at this age.
D is incorrect because prevention of osteoarthritis is a downstream benefit of achieving stable reduction, but it is not the primary, immediate goal of the procedure.
E is incorrect because improvement of muscle strength is not a goal of closed reduction and spica casting; muscle strengthening is not relevant to the treatment of DDH in an infant.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old male presents with a painful, swollen left hand after falling on an outstretched hand. X-rays reveal an oblique fracture of the index metacarpal. During the exam, his index finger appears shortened and rotated. What is the most likely reason for this clinical presentation?
A) Intra-articular involvement of the fracture
B) Malunion of the fracture
C) Muscle imbalance due to injury
D) Shortening and rotation caused by the fracture pattern
questions.answer:
D)
Oblique metacarpal fractures are inherently unstable and prone to shortening (due to intrinsic muscle pull collapsing the fracture) and rotational deformity (due to the oblique fracture geometry allowing rotational displacement). This directly explains the acute clinical findings of a shortened, rotated index finger.

A is incorrect because intra-articular involvement would present with joint incongruity and effusion but does not specifically explain the combination of shortening and rotation seen with a diaphyseal oblique fracture pattern.
B is incorrect because malunion is a late complication occurring after healing in a malaligned position; this is an acute presentation, so the deformity is due to fracture displacement, not malunion.
C is incorrect because muscle imbalance implies a neurological or tendon injury causing dysfunction; while interosseous and lumbrical muscles do exert deforming forces, the primary reason for the clinical presentation is the inherent instability of the oblique fracture pattern itself, not a discrete muscle injury.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male complains of chronic lateral foot pain and instability, which worsens with activity. He has failed 6 months of structured physical therapy and bracing. Physical examination reveals a positive anterior drawer test of the ankle. An MRI shows a complete tear of the anterior talofibular ligament. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Ankle brace and physical therapy
B) Surgical reconstruction of the anterior talofibular ligament
C) Corticosteroid injection
D) Conservative management with ice and rest
E) Ankle arthrodesis
questions.answer:
B)
For chronic lateral ankle instability due to a complete tear of the anterior talofibular ligament that has failed an adequate trial of conservative management (bracing and physical therapy), surgical reconstruction (e.g., modified Broström procedure) is indicated to restore mechanical stability and allow return to normal activities.

A is incorrect because the patient has already failed a structured rehabilitation and bracing program, making continued conservative therapy unlikely to succeed. C is incorrect because corticosteroid injection does not address the underlying mechanical instability from a torn ligament and may weaken remaining soft tissues. D is incorrect because ice and rest are acute injury measures and are insufficient for chronic ligamentous instability. E is incorrect because ankle arthrodesis is reserved for end-stage ankle arthritis or salvage situations, not for ligamentous instability with a preserved joint.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old man presents with a laceration to the medial aspect of his wrist sustained while working with a table saw. Upon examination, he has weakness in grip strength, loss of sensation over the small finger and ulnar half of the ring finger, and clawing of the ring and small fingers. A nerve conduction study reveals an injury to the ulnar nerve at the wrist. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Splinting the wrist in extension
B) Surgical exploration and repair of the ulnar nerve
C) Occupational therapy for wrist function
D) Analgesics and follow-up in 6 weeks
questions.answer:
B)
Surgical exploration and repair of the ulnar nerve is indicated for a sharp laceration causing complete ulnar nerve deficit. Sharp nerve lacerations have the best prognosis with early primary repair, and delay leads to motor endplate degeneration and poorer outcomes. The mechanism (table saw laceration) implies a clean transection amenable to direct repair.

A is incorrect because splinting alone does not address the underlying nerve transection and will not restore nerve function.
C is incorrect because occupational therapy is an adjunct to recovery after nerve repair but cannot restore continuity of a severed nerve.
D is incorrect because a sharp laceration causing complete nerve deficit warrants urgent surgical exploration; observation for 6 weeks is appropriate for closed injuries (e.g., neurapraxia) but not for open lacerations with nerve transection.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a fall from a height. He complains of severe pain in his elbow with limited flexion and a mechanical block. An x-ray reveals a fracture of the capitellum. Which classification system is most appropriate to assess the severity of this fracture?
A) Mason Classification
B) Bryan and Morrey Classification
C) Neer Classification
D) AO Classification
questions.answer:
B)
The Bryan and Morrey Classification is the most widely used system specifically designed for capitellum fractures. It categorizes them into three types: Type I (Hahn-Steinthal) — a large osseous fragment of the capitellum, Type II (Kocher-Lorenz) — a superficial osteochondral shear fragment, and Type III — a comminuted capitellum fracture. This classification guides surgical decision-making and prognosis.

A is incorrect because the Mason Classification is used for radial head fractures, not capitellum fractures. C is incorrect because the Neer Classification is used for proximal humerus fractures. D is incorrect because while the AO Classification can be applied broadly to distal humerus fractures, it is not the most specific or commonly referenced system for isolated capitellum fractures; the Bryan and Morrey system is the standard.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old male presents with left arm pain and has undergone multiple imaging studies that demonstrate a well-defined lytic bone lesion. Biopsy results confirm fibrous dysplasia. Which of the following genetic mutations is most commonly associated with this condition?
A) TP53
B) GNAS
C) EXT1
D) APC
questions.answer:
B)
Fibrous dysplasia is caused by a post-zygotic activating mutation in the GNAS gene, which encodes the Gsα subunit of the stimulatory G-protein. This leads to constitutive activation of adenylyl cyclase and increased cAMP, resulting in abnormal proliferation of medullary bone-forming mesenchymal cells and replacement of normal bone with fibrous tissue and woven bone.

A is incorrect because TP53 mutations are associated with Li-Fraumeni syndrome and various malignancies (e.g., osteosarcoma), not fibrous dysplasia. C is incorrect because EXT1 mutations are associated with hereditary multiple exostoses (osteochondromas), not fibrous dysplasia. D is incorrect because APC mutations are associated with familial adenomatous polyposis and Gardner syndrome, not fibrous dysplasia.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old man presents with knee pain and swelling after a twisting injury during a recreational activity. MRI findings reveal a complex tear of the medial meniscus and damage to the anterior horn of the medial meniscus. What is the most effective minimally invasive surgical approach to address these injuries?
A) Lateral meniscectomy
B) Medial meniscectomy
C) Arthroscopic repair
D) Open meniscal repair
questions.answer:
C)
Arthroscopic repair is the preferred minimally invasive surgical approach when feasible, as it preserves meniscal tissue and maintains the biomechanical function of the knee. Meniscal preservation is associated with better long-term outcomes including reduced risk of osteoarthritis compared to meniscectomy.

A is incorrect because the injury involves the medial meniscus, not the lateral meniscus; a lateral meniscectomy would not address the pathology described in the stem.

B is incorrect because while arthroscopic partial medial meniscectomy is commonly performed for complex degenerative tears, it removes meniscal tissue rather than preserving it, and the question asks for the most effective approach — meniscal preservation is preferred when repair is possible.

D is incorrect because open meniscal repair is a more invasive procedure with greater surgical morbidity compared to arthroscopic repair; the stem specifically asks for the most effective minimally invasive approach, making arthroscopy the superior choice.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman presents with persistent pain and swelling on the lateral aspect of her ankle after a recent inversion injury. A CT scan reveals a fracture of the distal fibula with a posterior dislocation of the fibula. What is this type of injury commonly referred to as?
A) Maisonneuve fracture
B) Bosworth fracture-dislocation
C) Pott's fracture
D) Trimalleolar fracture
questions.answer:
B)
A Bosworth fracture-dislocation is a fracture of the distal fibula in which the proximal fibular fragment becomes entrapped (locked) behind the posterior tubercle (posterolateral ridge) of the tibia, resulting in a fixed posterior dislocation that is typically irreducible by closed means. It is an important injury to recognize because failure to identify it leads to unsuccessful closed reduction and necessitates open reduction.

A is incorrect because a Maisonneuve fracture involves a proximal fibula fracture associated with disruption of the interosseous membrane and injury to the ankle syndesmosis/deltoid ligament — not a distal fibula fracture with posterior dislocation. C is incorrect because Pott's fracture is a historical term for a bimalleolar-type ankle fracture (medial and lateral malleolus involvement) and does not describe posterior fibular dislocation. D is incorrect because a trimalleolar fracture involves fractures of the medial malleolus, lateral malleolus, and posterior malleolus — it is not characterized by posterior dislocation of the fibula behind the tibia.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old female presents with pain and swelling around her heel. On examination, there is tenderness at the calcaneal tuberosity. She reports that the pain worsens with standing and decreases with rest. Which of the following muscles originates from the calcaneal tuberosity and could be involved in her condition?
A) Abductor hallucis
B) Flexor hallucis longus
C) Extensor digitorum brevis
D) Tibialis posterior
questions.answer:
A)
The abductor hallucis originates from the medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity and is one of the first-layer intrinsic muscles of the plantar foot. It lies directly deep to the plantar fascia at its origin and is commonly implicated in plantar heel pain syndromes such as plantar fasciitis, which classically presents with weight-bearing heel pain that improves with rest.

B is incorrect because the flexor hallucis longus originates from the posterior fibula and interosseous membrane, not the calcaneal tuberosity. C is incorrect because the extensor digitorum brevis originates from the dorsolateral calcaneus (sinus tarsi region), not the calcaneal tuberosity. D is incorrect because the tibialis posterior originates from the posterior tibia, fibula, and interosseous membrane, not the calcaneal tuberosity.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male presents with acute shoulder pain following a fall onto his shoulder while skiing. He demonstrates limited active and passive range of motion due to pain. An x-ray reveals a greater tuberosity fracture of the humerus. Given this injury, which of the following complications is the greatest concern?
A) Brachial plexus injury
B) Rotator cuff tear
C) Hemarthrosis
D) Glenohumeral dislocation
questions.answer:
D)
A greater tuberosity fracture is strongly associated with anterior glenohumeral dislocation; up to 15–30% of anterior dislocations have an accompanying greater tuberosity fracture. When an isolated greater tuberosity fracture is identified, an occult or spontaneously reduced glenohumeral dislocation must be excluded, making this the greatest immediate concern.

A is incorrect because brachial plexus injury (particularly axillary nerve) is more commonly a concern with glenohumeral dislocation itself rather than an isolated greater tuberosity fracture. B is incorrect because while the rotator cuff (supraspinatus) inserts on the greater tuberosity and may be injured, a rotator cuff tear is a secondary concern compared to the possibility of joint instability/dislocation. C is incorrect because hemarthrosis, while it may occur with any intra-articular fracture, is typically self-limited and not the greatest clinical concern in this setting.

questions.question:
A 6-year-old boy presents with pain in his lower back that worsens with extension and is relieved by flexion. Upon examination, he shows a positive lumbar extension test. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
A) Spondylolisthesis
B) Lumbar disc herniation
C) Muscle strain
D) Osteoid osteoma
questions.answer:
A)
The positive lumbar extension test suggests a condition that causes pain on extension, typically seen in spondylolisthesis, where the vertebra slips forward and can lead to pain during extension movements. B is incorrect because lumbar disc herniation usually causes pain with flexion, not extension. C is incorrect because muscle strain would not typically cause pain specifically with extension in this age group. D is incorrect because osteoid osteoma pain is typically worse at night and not specifically related to extension movements.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old woman with osteoporosis is prescribed bisphosphonates for fracture prevention. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of bisphosphonates? 
A) Increase osteoblast activity
B) Prevent osteoclast formation
C) Stimulate collagen synthesis
D) Promote bone resorption
questions.answer:
B)
Bisphosphonates primarily work by inhibiting osteoclast formation and promoting their apoptosis, thereby reducing bone resorption. This action is essential in managing osteoporosis and preventing fractures. A is incorrect because bisphosphonates do not increase osteoblast activity. C is incorrect because bisphosphonates do not stimulate collagen synthesis. D is incorrect because bisphosphonates reduce, not promote, bone resorption.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman presents with a painful hip after a fall. Imaging reveals an acetabular fracture involving both the posterior wall and the posterior column. According to the Judet-Letournel classification, which of the following best differentiates an associated (complex) acetabular fracture pattern from an elementary (simple) pattern?
A) The presence of soft tissue injury
B) Involvement of more than one elementary fracture pattern
C) Patient's age
D) Degree of fracture displacement
questions.answer:
B)
In the Judet-Letournel classification, elementary (simple) acetabular fracture patterns involve a single wall or column (e.g., isolated posterior wall, anterior column, transverse). Associated (complex) patterns are defined by the combination of two or more elementary patterns (e.g., posterior column + posterior wall, transverse + posterior wall, both-column). This distinction is critical for surgical planning, approach selection, and prognosis.

A is incorrect because soft tissue injury can accompany both simple and complex acetabular fractures and is not the defining criterion in the Letournel classification.
C is incorrect because patient age affects treatment decisions (e.g., THA vs. ORIF) but does not define the fracture pattern classification.
D is incorrect because displacement can occur in both elementary and associated fracture patterns; it influences surgical indication but does not differentiate the two categories.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old man presents after a fall with severe pain in the hip and an inability to move his leg. An x-ray shows a posterior dislocation of the hip joint. Which of the following is the most critical initial management step?
A) Immediate closed reduction
B) Administration of analgesics
C) Surgical exploration
D) Obtain a CT scan for better visualization
questions.answer:
A)
Immediate closed reduction is the most critical initial step in managing a posterior hip dislocation. Delay beyond 6 hours significantly increases the risk of avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head. Prompt reduction also reduces the risk of ongoing sciatic nerve compression and further cartilage damage.

B is incorrect because while analgesics are important for patient comfort, they do not address the underlying pathology; delaying reduction to manage pain increases the risk of AVN. C is incorrect because surgical exploration is not the initial step — closed reduction under sedation should be attempted first; open reduction is reserved for irreducible dislocations or associated fractures requiring fixation. D is incorrect because obtaining a CT scan before reduction would cause unnecessary delay; CT is appropriately obtained after successful closed reduction to evaluate for associated acetabular fractures, femoral head fractures, or incarcerated fragments.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old male is evaluated for chronic knee pain following a sports-related injury two years ago. He has difficulty with lateral movements and reports a sensation of instability. Examination reveals tenderness over the lateral aspect of the knee and a palpable defect over the lateral joint line. Which ligament is most likely compromised in this scenario?
A) Anterior cruciate ligament
B) Medial collateral ligament
C) Lateral collateral ligament
D) Posterior cruciate ligament
questions.answer:
C)
The chronic lateral knee pain, lateral instability with difficulty in lateral movements, tenderness over the lateral aspect, and a palpable defect over the lateral joint line are classic findings of a lateral collateral ligament (LCL) injury. The LCL resists varus stress and its disruption leads to lateral compartment instability.

A is incorrect because an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury typically presents with anteroposterior instability (positive Lachman and anterior drawer tests), not isolated lateral tenderness with a palpable lateral defect.
B is incorrect because a medial collateral ligament (MCL) injury would produce tenderness and instability on the medial aspect of the knee, not the lateral side.
D is incorrect because a posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injury presents with posterior sag and a positive posterior drawer test, not lateral joint line tenderness or a palpable lateral defect.

questions.question:
Which nerve is at greatest risk during percutaneous Achilles tendon repair?
A) Tibial nerve
B) Sural nerve
C) Saphenous nerve
D) Deep peroneal nerve
E) Superficial peroneal nerve
questions.answer:
B)
The sural nerve crosses the lateral border of the Achilles tendon approximately 10 cm proximal to its insertion and is the structure most commonly injured during percutaneous and minimally invasive Achilles tendon repairs. Careful technique and mini-open approaches with limited-open jigs reduce this risk.

A is incorrect because the tibial nerve lies deep in the posterior compartment, medial to the Achilles tendon and within the tarsal tunnel; it is not typically at risk during percutaneous repair unless dissection is carried far medially and deep.
C is incorrect because the saphenous nerve runs along the medial leg with the great saphenous vein and is not in proximity to the Achilles tendon repair site.
D is incorrect because the deep peroneal nerve courses in the anterior compartment of the leg and is not at risk during posterior Achilles tendon procedures.
E is incorrect because the superficial peroneal nerve travels in the lateral compartment and pierces the fascia anterolaterally in the distal leg; it is not in the operative field of a percutaneous Achilles repair.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male presents to the emergency department with severe throbbing pain and swelling in his right index fingertip that has progressively worsened over the past 4 days after sustaining a small puncture wound from a thorn. On examination, the fingertip pulp is tense, erythematous, and exquisitely tender. There is no fluctuance at the nail bed and no evidence of flexor tendon sheath involvement. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Splinting the finger in extension
B) Incision and drainage of the pulp space
C) Immediate referral to a hand surgeon
D) Prescribing antibiotics and analgesics
questions.answer:
B)
A felon is a closed-space infection of the fingertip pulp, typically following a penetrating injury. The tense, erythematous, tender pulp compartment requires incision and drainage to decompress the septated pulp space, prevent osteomyelitis of the distal phalanx, and allow culture-directed antibiotic therapy.

A is incorrect because splinting in extension is the treatment for a mallet finger (terminal extensor tendon disruption) and does not address a pulp space infection. C is incorrect because a felon is a straightforward surgical emergency that can be managed in the emergency department with a unilateral longitudinal or fish-mouth incision; immediate hand surgery referral is not required for uncomplicated cases. D is incorrect because antibiotics alone without surgical drainage cannot adequately decompress the septated pulp space, and failure to drain risks osteomyelitis and tissue necrosis.

questions.question:
During a surgical approach to the medial side of the knee, the surgeon identifies the semitendinosus tendon. What is the most appropriate step in relation to this tendon during the procedure?
A) Transect the tendon completely
B) Retract the tendon medially
C) Preserve the tendon for potential autograft use
D) Expose the tendon for direct repair
questions.answer:
C)
Preserving the semitendinosus tendon is important as it can be used as an autograft for reconstructive procedures, especially in cases of ligamentous injuries like ACL reconstruction.
A is incorrect because transecting the tendon would prevent its use as an autograft. B is incorrect because retracting the tendon medially is not a standard step and could damage the tendon. D is incorrect because exposing the tendon for direct repair is not typically necessary unless there is a specific injury to the tendon itself.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old woman presents with persistent lateral hip pain and a mass felt over the greater trochanter following a metal-on-metal hip arthroplasty performed three years ago. MRI reveals a periprosthetic soft tissue mass consistent with a pseudotumor. What likely caused this complication?
A) Excessive wear of the polyethylene liner
B) Metal ions released from the bearing surfaces
C) Infection due to surgical contamination
D) Fracture of the femoral neck
questions.answer:
B)
Pseudotumors (also termed adverse local tissue reactions or ALTR) associated with metal-on-metal hip arthroplasties are caused by the release of cobalt and chromium metal ions from the bearing surfaces. These ions trigger an adverse immune-mediated inflammatory response (type IV hypersensitivity), leading to the formation of destructive periprosthetic soft tissue masses. This is a well-documented complication of metal-on-metal bearings.

A is incorrect because there is no polyethylene liner in a metal-on-metal bearing; polyethylene wear produces osteolysis rather than pseudotumors. C is incorrect because while periprosthetic infection can cause soft tissue swelling, the MRI finding of a pseudotumor in the setting of a metal-on-metal bearing is characteristic of an adverse reaction to metal debris, not infection. D is incorrect because a femoral neck fracture would present with acute pain and implant instability rather than a chronic soft tissue mass.

questions.question:
A 10-year-old girl presents with a history of a right femur fracture treated non-operatively. After 6 months, her leg shows signs of shortening and deformity. She is experiencing pain during activity. What is the most likely complication of her fracture treatment?
A) Growth arrest
B) Osteomyelitis
C) Nonunion
D) Malunion
questions.answer:
D)
Malunion is the most likely complication of a pediatric femoral shaft fracture treated non-operatively. Inadequate reduction or loss of alignment during conservative management can result in angular deformity, rotational malalignment, and limb-length discrepancy, all of which match this patient's presentation at 6 months.

A is incorrect because growth arrest requires damage to the physis; a diaphyseal femur fracture does not typically involve the growth plate, making growth arrest unlikely as the primary complication here. B is incorrect because osteomyelitis would present with signs of infection (fever, erythema, elevated inflammatory markers) rather than isolated shortening and deformity. C is incorrect because nonunion of the femoral shaft is exceedingly rare in children due to their robust healing potential and periosteal activity; the presence of deformity implies the fracture did heal, albeit in a poor position.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male presents with a fracture of the anterior column of the acetabulum after a fall. A CT scan reveals involvement of the anterior wall, superior pubic ramus, and iliac crest. Which of the following surgical approaches would be most appropriate for optimal visualization of this fracture?
A) Kocher-Langenbeck approach
B) Anterolateral approach
C) Medial approach
D) Ilioinguinal approach
questions.answer:
D)
The ilioinguinal approach is the standard surgical approach for anterior column acetabular fractures. It provides excellent visualization of the entire anterior column from the iliac crest to the symphysis pubis, including the anterior wall and superior pubic ramus, through three surgical windows (lateral, middle, and medial). This is the classic Letournel approach for anterior column and anterior column–posterior hemitransverse fracture patterns.

A is incorrect because the Kocher-Langenbeck approach is a posterior approach used for posterior wall and posterior column acetabular fractures; it does not provide adequate visualization of anterior column structures.
B is incorrect because the anterolateral approach is not a standard named approach for acetabular fracture surgery in the Letournel classification and does not provide the necessary exposure of the entire anterior column.
C is incorrect because a medial approach does not provide adequate access to the iliac wing or the full extent of the anterior column; it is not a recognized approach for acetabular fracture fixation.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old female presents with a mid-shaft humeral fracture after a motor vehicle accident. The fracture is assessed with a CT scan, which shows a well-preserved medial calcar. How much intact medial calcar is generally considered to be a good prognostic factor in these injuries?
A) 5mm
B) 8mm
C) 1cm
D) 1.5cm
questions.answer:
B)
Explanation: An intact medial calcar of at least 8mm is associated with better functional outcomes in humeral shaft fractures. This preservation indicates a lower risk of complications and suggests that surgical intervention may not be necessary. The other measurements do not reflect the same prognostic implication.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a fall while playing basketball. He complains of severe shoulder pain and is unable to move his arm. Physical examination reveals a prominent acromion, loss of the normal deltoid contour, and the arm held in slight abduction and external rotation. X-rays confirm an anterior dislocation of the shoulder without associated fracture. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Apply a shoulder immobilizer and schedule for outpatient follow-up
B) Attempt closed reduction of the shoulder
C) Refer for surgical intervention immediately
D) Obtain an MRI to assess for associated injuries
questions.answer:
B)
In an acute anterior shoulder dislocation confirmed on X-ray without associated fracture, the most appropriate immediate management is closed reduction in the emergency department. Prompt reduction relieves pain, prevents neurovascular compromise, and restores normal joint alignment. After successful reduction, post-reduction films should be obtained and the patient placed in a sling with appropriate follow-up.

A is incorrect because applying a shoulder immobilizer without first reducing the dislocation leaves the joint displaced, which can cause ongoing neurovascular injury and increasing soft tissue damage.
C is incorrect because surgical intervention is not indicated acutely for an uncomplicated anterior shoulder dislocation; closed reduction is the first-line treatment, and surgery may be considered later for recurrent instability or associated injuries.
D is incorrect because while MRI may be useful after reduction to evaluate for labral tears, rotator cuff injuries, or Hill-Sachs lesions, it is not the immediate priority; restoring joint alignment takes precedence.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old male presents with a painful bunion on his left foot, exacerbated by wearing narrow-toed shoes. Physical examination reveals a lateral deviation of the great toe. Which of the following factors is most likely contributing to his condition?
A) Genetic predisposition
B) Tight footwear
C) Flatfoot deformity
D) High arches
questions.answer:
B)
Tight and narrow-toed shoes are commonly associated with the development of hallux valgus (bunions) as they can cause increased pressure on the great toe, leading to its lateral deviation. This patient’s history supports the role of footwear in his condition.

questions.question:
A 9-year-old boy presents with a bowing deformity of the tibia. Imaging shows that the tibial bow is directed laterally, and the apex of the deformity is located at the mid-shaft. Which of the following terms best describes this type of bowing?
A) Varus bowing
B) Valgus bowing
C) Tibial torsion
D) Bowing associated with rickets
E) Congenital bowing
questions.answer:
B)
A laterally directed tibial bow means the apex of the deformity points laterally (away from the midline). An apex-lateral angulation of the tibia is termed valgus bowing. This can be seen in various conditions and should be distinguished from physiologic valgus alignment seen in younger children.

A is incorrect because varus bowing has an apex-medial deformity (the tibia bows medially, producing a bowleg appearance), which is the opposite of what is described in the stem. C is incorrect because tibial torsion refers to rotational malalignment of the tibia along its longitudinal axis, not angular bowing in the coronal plane. D is incorrect because while rickets can cause bowing deformities, the question asks for the descriptive term for the direction of the bow, not its etiology. E is incorrect because congenital bowing is an etiologic classification (e.g., anterolateral or posteromedial congenital bowing), not a directional descriptor of the deformity.

questions.question:
A trauma patient presents with a high-energy femur fracture requiring external fixation. The decision is made to place the half pins in a lateral-to-medial direction. What is the primary clinical rationale for this pin orientation?
A) To minimize the risk of neurovascular injury
B) To enhance fracture stabilization
C) To allow for easier pin placement
D) To facilitate early mobilization
questions.answer:
A)
The primary rationale for placing femoral external fixation half pins in a lateral-to-medial direction is to minimize the risk of neurovascular injury. The femoral artery, vein, and deep femoral (profunda femoris) vessels lie medially and posteriorly; by inserting pins from the lateral cortex, the surgeon directs the pin away from these critical structures, reducing the chance of vascular or nerve damage.

B is incorrect because pin orientation (lateral-to-medial vs. other directions) does not significantly enhance fracture stabilization compared to the overall frame construct and pin number/spread.
C is incorrect because ease of placement is not the primary driver; safe corridors are chosen based on anatomy, not convenience.
D is incorrect because early mobilization depends on the overall fixation construct stability and patient factors, not specifically on the direction of pin insertion.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with a 'duck bill' deformity of her thumb. She reports pain and difficulty gripping objects. What is the underlying biomechanical issue contributing to this deformity?
A) Extensor tendon rupture
B) Flexor tendon contracture
C) Joint hyperextension
D) Dislocation of the first carpometacarpal joint
E) Ligamentous laxity
questions.answer:
C)
The 'duck bill' deformity of the rheumatoid thumb (Nalebuff Type III / swan-neck type) involves CMC joint subluxation with compensatory MCP joint hyperextension and IP joint flexion. The underlying biomechanical issue is progressive joint hyperextension at the MCP, driven by CMC joint destruction and adduction contracture, which shifts the extensor mechanism dorsally and causes the characteristic deformity with loss of pinch grip.

A is incorrect because extensor tendon rupture would cause a lag in extension (e.g., mallet or dropped finger) rather than the hyperextension pattern seen in this deformity.
B is incorrect because flexor tendon contracture would produce a fixed flexion deformity rather than the hyperextension component that defines the 'duck bill' appearance.
D is incorrect because while CMC joint disease contributes to the overall pathomechanics, the primary biomechanical abnormality producing the visible deformity is the compensatory MCP hyperextension, not CMC dislocation itself.
E is incorrect because although ligamentous laxity may be present in RA, the specific deformity pattern is driven by joint hyperextension secondary to altered biomechanics rather than generalized ligamentous laxity alone.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman is diagnosed with a bicondylar tibial plateau fracture following a fall from a height. She is scheduled for surgical intervention but requires temporary stabilization. Which of the following is the most appropriate form of external fixation for this type of fracture?
A) A long leg cast.
B) A hinged knee brace.
C) A circular external fixator.
D) An external fixator with pins placed above and below the fracture site.
questions.answer:
D)
For temporary stabilization of a bicondylar (Schatzker V/VI) tibial plateau fracture prior to definitive fixation, a spanning external fixator with pins placed in the femur (above) and tibia (below the fracture) is the standard approach. This maintains limb length, alignment, and allows soft-tissue recovery before definitive ORIF or definitive circular fixator application.

A is incorrect because a long leg cast does not provide adequate stability for a high-energy bicondylar fracture, cannot maintain reduction, and does not allow wound/soft-tissue monitoring.
B is incorrect because a hinged knee brace does not provide sufficient skeletal stabilization for an unstable bicondylar fracture pattern.
C is incorrect because a circular (Ilizarov-type) external fixator can be used as definitive fixation for select tibial plateau fractures, but it is not the standard choice for temporary stabilization; a simple spanning frame is faster and easier to apply in the acute setting.

questions.question:
A young athlete presents with hip pain after an intense training session. Imaging reveals a stress fracture of the femoral neck. To improve recovery and prevent future fractures, which of the following factors should be addressed in her treatment plan?
A) Increasing calcium intake
B) Reducing training intensity
C) Implementing a cross-training program
D) All of the above
questions.answer:
D)
Management of a femoral neck stress fracture in a young athlete is multifactorial. Adequate calcium (and vitamin D) intake supports bone mineralization, reducing training intensity prevents continued mechanical overload at the fracture site, and cross-training maintains cardiovascular fitness while off-loading the injured bone. All three interventions together optimize recovery and reduce recurrence risk.

A is incorrect because increasing calcium intake alone, while beneficial for bone health, does not address the mechanical overload from training or the need to maintain fitness through alternative activities.
B is incorrect because reducing training intensity alone does not correct potential nutritional deficiencies that contributed to the stress fracture.
C is incorrect because cross-training alone maintains fitness but does not reduce the specific mechanical stress on the femoral neck or address nutritional factors.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old man with a history of osteoarthritis in both hips presents with worsening pain on the right side, especially with weight-bearing activities. During the physical examination, you note significant pain on internal rotation of the hip. Which of the following findings would most likely confirm your suspicion of hip arthritis?
A) Decreased range of motion in all directions
B) Palpable tenderness over the greater trochanter
C) Joint effusion on ultrasound
D) Crepitus during hip flexion
questions.answer:
A)
In hip osteoarthritis, progressive cartilage loss and osteophyte formation lead to a global decrease in range of motion in all planes (flexion, extension, internal/external rotation, abduction/adduction). Internal rotation is typically the first and most limited motion. A globally restricted hip is the most reliable clinical finding to confirm hip arthritis in this setting.

B is incorrect because tenderness over the greater trochanter is characteristic of greater trochanteric bursitis or abductor tendinopathy, not intra-articular hip arthritis.
C is incorrect because a joint effusion on ultrasound is a nonspecific finding that can be seen in inflammatory arthritis, infection, or trauma and does not specifically confirm osteoarthritis.
D is incorrect because crepitus during hip flexion can occur in many conditions (e.g., labral tears, loose bodies, snapping hip) and is not specific enough to confirm osteoarthritis.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old male sustains a femoral shaft fracture after falling from a height. The orthopedic surgeon plans to use a retrograde intramedullary nail for fixation. Which of the following is a critical consideration to avoid complications during this procedure? 
A) Maintain proximal perfusion 
B) Ensure complete fracture reduction 
C) Avoid injury to the femoral nerve 
D) Use a lateral approach to access the femur 
E) Secure the distal fragment only
questions.answer:
B)
During retrograde intramedullary nailing of the femur, ensuring complete fracture reduction is a critical step to avoid complications such as malunion, nonunion, and limb-length discrepancy. Adequate reduction must be achieved before and during nail passage to restore alignment and allow uneventful healing.

A is incorrect because while maintaining perfusion is generally important, it is not a specific technical consideration unique to retrograde nailing of the femur. C is incorrect because the femoral nerve lies in the anterior thigh and is not at particular risk during a retrograde nail inserted through the knee; the popliteal artery and articular cartilage are the structures most at risk at the entry site. D is incorrect because retrograde nailing uses a medial parapatellar or midline knee approach through the intercondylar notch, not a lateral approach to the femoral shaft. E is incorrect because both proximal and distal fragments must be secured with interlocking screws to maintain rotational and axial stability.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old male presents with persistent neck pain and limited range of motion following a sports injury. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the upper cervical region, and muscle spasm is palpated in the trapezius and levator scapulae. Which structure is most likely involved in this case?
A) Alar ligament
B) Levator scapulae
C) Posterior longitudinal ligament
D) Intertransverse ligament
questions.answer:
B)
The levator scapulae muscle is likely involved due to its anatomical location and function, which aligns with the symptoms of muscle spasm and tenderness in the upper cervical region. A is incorrect because the alar ligament is more associated with stability of the atlantoaxial joint and not typically involved in muscle spasm. C is incorrect because the posterior longitudinal ligament is more involved in spinal stability and not directly related to muscle spasm. D is incorrect because the intertransverse ligament is not typically associated with the symptoms described.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old man falls from a height and presents with back pain and difficulty walking. Imaging shows a burst fracture of the L2 vertebra. Which of the following findings would most likely be present on examination?
A) Saddle anesthesia
B) Hyperreflexia in the lower extremities
C) Intact anal sphincter tone
D) Upper extremity weakness
questions.answer:
A)
Explanation: A burst fracture can lead to spinal cord injury, and in this case, saddle anesthesia (loss of sensation in the perineal region) is a common finding associated with such injuries, indicating possible involvement of the cauda equina or conus medullaris.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old woman with a prior history of corticosteroid use for rheumatoid arthritis is scheduled for total hip arthroplasty due to severe pain and limited mobility. What consideration should be taken into account regarding her surgical management?
A) Increased risk of thromboembolism
B) Potential for increased wound healing complications
C) Higher likelihood of requiring cementless components
D) Decreased need for postoperative rehabilitation
questions.answer:
B)
Chronic corticosteroid use impairs wound healing by suppressing the inflammatory phase of tissue repair, inhibiting collagen synthesis, and compromising immune function. In patients with rheumatoid arthritis on long-term steroids, the surgeon must anticipate increased risk of wound dehiscence, delayed healing, and periprosthetic infection, and plan perioperative wound management accordingly.

A is incorrect because while thromboembolism is a general risk of THA, corticosteroid use is not a primary independent risk factor for venous thromboembolism; the most important consideration specific to steroid use is wound healing. C is incorrect because chronic corticosteroid use is associated with osteoporosis and poor bone quality, which would actually favor cemented (not cementless) fixation to achieve adequate initial stability. D is incorrect because corticosteroid-related muscle weakness, osteoporosis, and joint deconditioning in rheumatoid arthritis patients typically increase (not decrease) the need for structured postoperative rehabilitation.

questions.question:
During a total hip arthroplasty, the surgeon notes that the femoral stem has been placed with excessive anteversion. What is the most likely consequence of this surgical error?
A) Posterior dislocation of the hip
B) Increased polyethylene wear
C) Anterior dislocation of the hip
D) Leg-length discrepancy
questions.answer:
C)
Excessive femoral stem anteversion increases the combined anteversion of the hip construct, predisposing to anterior dislocation, particularly with external rotation and extension. This is a well-recognized cause of instability after total hip arthroplasty.

A is incorrect because posterior dislocation is associated with insufficient anteversion (retroversion) of the femoral or acetabular component, not excessive anteversion. B is incorrect because while malalignment can theoretically affect wear patterns, the primary and most clinically significant consequence of excessive anteversion is instability/dislocation, not accelerated polyethylene wear. D is incorrect because leg-length discrepancy results from errors in femoral neck cut level or stem seating depth, not from rotational malalignment of the stem.

questions.question:
An orthopedic surgeon is preparing to perform an intramedullary nailing of a femoral shaft fracture. Which of the following advantages does this technique provide regarding the reduction of fracture fragments?
A) Allows anterior exposure of the fracture site
B) Provides superior stability compared to plates
C) Facilitates easier reduction of fracture fragments
D) Eliminates the need for anesthesia
questions.answer:
C)
Intramedullary nailing facilitates reduction of femoral shaft fracture fragments by using the intact intramedullary canal as a guide for alignment. The nail acts as an internal splint, allowing indirect (closed) reduction without the need for direct fracture exposure, thereby preserving the periosteal blood supply and fracture biology.

A is incorrect because intramedullary nailing is performed through a closed or semi-closed technique and does not require anterior exposure of the fracture site; avoiding direct fracture exposure is one of its key advantages.
B is incorrect because, while IM nails provide excellent load-sharing fixation for femoral shaft fractures, the question specifically asks about reduction of fracture fragments, not stability; furthermore, plates can provide comparable or superior rigidity in certain fracture patterns.
D is incorrect because intramedullary nailing still requires anesthesia (general or regional); no surgical fixation technique eliminates the need for anesthesia.

questions.question:
During an anterior approach to the hip, a surgeon needs to make an incision at a specific anatomical landmark. Which of the following landmarks is crucial for accurately orienting the incision?
A) Greater sciatic notch
B) Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)
C) Femoral neck
D) Pubic symphysis
questions.answer:
B)
The anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) is the critical surface landmark for orienting the incision in the direct anterior approach (Smith-Petersen / Hueter) to the hip. The skin incision typically begins at or just distal and lateral to the ASIS and extends distally toward the lateral aspect of the patella. Accurate identification of the ASIS ensures proper internervous interval exposure while minimizing soft-tissue damage.

A is incorrect because the greater sciatic notch is a posterior pelvic landmark relevant to posterior approaches and is not used to orient an anterior hip incision.
C is incorrect because the femoral neck is a deep intra-articular structure that is not palpable and therefore cannot serve as a surface landmark for incision planning.
D is incorrect because the pubic symphysis, while a palpable anterior landmark, is medial and does not guide the incision for the standard anterior approach to the hip.

questions.question:
During a surgical procedure for a laceration to the flexor tendons of the ring finger, the surgeon notes that the tendons for the middle and ring fingers are positioned superficially to those of the index and small fingers. What is the clinical significance of this anatomical relationship?
A) It affects the function of the flexor digitorum profundus
B) It influences the choice of surgical approach
C) It alters the risk of tendon rupture
D) It increases the likelihood of nerve injury
questions.answer:
B)
The flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) tendons to the middle and ring fingers lie superficial to those of the index and small fingers within the carpal tunnel and distal forearm. This layered arrangement is clinically significant because it directly influences the surgical approach: the surgeon must recognize which tendons are encountered first during dissection to correctly identify and repair the injured structure and avoid iatrogenic damage to deeper tendons.

A is incorrect because this anatomical relationship describes the flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) arrangement, not the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP); FDP function is not directly affected by the superficial layering of FDS tendons.
C is incorrect because the relative superficial or deep position of the FDS tendons does not inherently alter the risk of tendon rupture; rupture risk depends on tendon loading, degeneration, and trauma rather than layering order.
D is incorrect because the superficial positioning of the middle and ring finger FDS tendons does not increase the likelihood of nerve injury; nerve injury risk is related to the proximity of the median and ulnar nerves, not to the relative depth of the FDS tendons.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman undergoes a shoulder surgery to repair her torn rotator cuff. During the procedure, the surgeon needs to ensure the axillary nerve is protected. Which anatomical structure should the surgeon be cautious of during a posterior approach to the shoulder?
A) Teres major
B) Long head of the triceps
C) Supraspinatus
D) Teres minor
questions.answer:
D)
During a posterior approach to the shoulder, the axillary nerve is at risk as it traverses the quadrilateral space and courses along the inferior border of the teres minor muscle. The interval between the teres minor and the infraspinatus is commonly used, and the axillary nerve lies approximately 5–7 cm inferior to the acromion, making the teres minor the critical structure to identify and protect.

A is incorrect because the teres major forms the inferior border of the quadrilateral space and is more distal; while it is a landmark, the nerve is most intimately related to the teres minor during a posterior approach. B is incorrect because the long head of the triceps forms the medial border of the quadrilateral space but is not the structure most closely associated with axillary nerve risk during the posterior surgical approach to the rotator cuff. C is incorrect because the supraspinatus is located superiorly and is innervated by the suprascapular nerve, not the axillary nerve; it is not the structure that places the axillary nerve at risk during a posterior approach.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman undergoes arthroscopy for a meniscal tear. During the procedure, the surgeon notes that the screw used for fixation sits proud of the bone surface. What technique can be employed to ensure the screw sits flush with the surface of the bone?
A) Increasing the screw diameter
B) Countersinking the screw
C) Using a longer screw
D) Reducing the torque during insertion
questions.answer:
B)
Countersinking involves creating a conical recess at the surface of the bone so that the screw head sits flush with or slightly below the bone surface. This technique prevents hardware prominence, reduces soft-tissue irritation, and can improve the compression profile of the construct.
