Raising the arms above the head (the shoulder abduction relief sign / Bakody sign) reduces tension on the inflamed cervical nerve roots by shortening the course of the nerve root from the foramen to the brachial plexus. This positional change decreases traction on the compressed C6 nerve root, thereby alleviating radicular pain. It is a well-recognized clinical sign of cervical radiculopathy caused by disc herniation.

A is incorrect because increased intrathoracic pressure (e.g., with Valsalva) typically worsens radicular symptoms by increasing epidural venous pressure, not alleviates them.
B is incorrect because raising the arms overhead does not significantly reduce cervical lordosis, and a change in lordosis alone would not reliably explain selective relief of radicular symptoms.
D is incorrect because activation of the trapezius muscle during arm elevation is incidental and does not directly relieve nerve root tension; the mechanism is positional unloading of the nerve root, not muscular contraction.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. He has severe pain in his right knee and is unable to bear weight on that leg. Physical examination reveals an effusion and significant tenderness along the medial joint line. An x-ray shows a tibial plateau fracture. Which of the following classifications best describes this type of fracture?
A) AO classification
B) Schatzker classification
C) Gustilo-Anderson classification
D) Neer classification
questions.answer:
B)
The Schatzker classification is specifically used to classify tibial plateau fractures based on the fracture type and involvement of the articular surface. This classification system helps guide treatment decisions and prognosis. A is incorrect because the AO classification is a comprehensive system for all fractures, not specific to tibial plateau fractures. C is incorrect because the Gustilo-Anderson classification is used for open fractures, not closed tibial plateau fractures. D is incorrect because the Neer classification is used for proximal humerus fractures, not tibial plateau fractures.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman with a history of chronic back pain reports new-onset bowel incontinence. On examination, there is notable loss of perianal sensation and decreased anal sphincter tone. What syndrome should be suspected in this patient?
A) Cauda equina syndrome
B) Conus medullaris syndrome
C) Lumbar radiculopathy
D) Spinal stenosis
questions.answer:
A)
Cauda equina syndrome (CES) is characterized by compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus medullaris, producing bowel/bladder incontinence, saddle (perianal) anesthesia, and decreased anal sphincter tone. It is a surgical emergency requiring urgent decompression, typically within 48 hours, to maximize neurologic recovery.

B is incorrect because conus medullaris syndrome involves injury to the terminal spinal cord (typically at L1–L2) and tends to present with more symmetric, upper-motor-neuron findings (hyperreflexia, Babinski sign) along with early and prominent bladder dysfunction; the clinical picture described here — loss of perianal sensation with lower-motor-neuron sphincter hypotonia — is more consistent with a cauda equina lesion.

C is incorrect because lumbar radiculopathy typically causes dermatomal pain, sensory changes, and weakness in a single nerve-root distribution; it does not produce bilateral saddle anesthesia or sphincter dysfunction.

D is incorrect because lumbar spinal stenosis classically presents with neurogenic claudication (bilateral leg pain/heaviness worsened by walking and relieved by flexion); while severe stenosis can rarely progress to CES, stenosis alone does not explain the acute sphincter and perianal findings described.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male athlete sustains a traumatic injury to his left thigh while playing soccer. He notices pain and swelling over the mid-thigh region. On examination, he has weakness in extension of the knee. Which muscle's injury is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
A) Vastus lateralis
B) Semitendinosus
C) Rectus femoris
D) Vastus medialis
questions.answer:
C)
The rectus femoris is the most commonly injured quadriceps muscle in soccer players due to its biarticular nature (crossing both hip and knee). It originates from the anterior inferior iliac spine and is heavily loaded during kicking. A mid-thigh injury causing weakness in knee extension in a soccer player is classic for a rectus femoris strain or rupture.

A is incorrect because the vastus lateralis, while a knee extensor, is less commonly injured in athletic kicking injuries; it is a single-joint muscle and not as susceptible to the eccentric overload that affects the biarticular rectus femoris.
B is incorrect because the semitendinosus is a hamstring muscle located in the posterior thigh; its injury would cause weakness in knee flexion, not extension.
D is incorrect because the vastus medialis, like the vastus lateralis, is a single-joint knee extensor and is less commonly injured in traumatic sporting injuries compared to the rectus femoris.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old female presents with pain in her heel and ankle after stepping off a curb awkwardly. An MRI reveals a partial tear of the Achilles tendon. You note the location is approximately 6 cm proximal to its insertion. Why is this area a common site for Achilles tendon injuries?
A) Poor blood supply
B) High mechanical load
C) Increased flexibility
D) Chronic overuse
questions.answer:
A)
The area approximately 2–6 cm proximal to the Achilles tendon insertion is known as a "watershed zone" with relatively poor blood supply. This hypovascularity makes the tendon vulnerable to degenerative changes and subsequent rupture, especially in active individuals.

B is incorrect because, while the Achilles tendon does bear high mechanical loads, high load alone does not explain why this specific zone is preferentially injured; the critical factor is its relative hypovascularity.
C is incorrect because increased flexibility is not a characteristic of this region and does not predispose to tendon rupture.
D is incorrect because chronic overuse can contribute to tendinopathy anywhere along the tendon, but the reason this particular zone is most commonly affected is its poor blood supply, not overuse per se.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old female athlete presents with a mallet finger after attempting to catch a ball. Physical examination reveals an inability to extend the distal phalanx of the ring finger. Which classification system is used to categorize her injury?
A) Eaton and Littler Classification
B) Doane Classification
C) Doyle's Classification
D) Taitz Classification
E) Green Classification
questions.answer:
C)
Doyle's Classification is the standard system used to categorize mallet finger injuries. It divides mallet fingers into four types: Type I (closed, with or without small avulsion fracture), Type II (open, laceration at or proximal to the DIP joint), Type III (open, deep abrasion with loss of skin and tendon substance), and Type IV (subdivided into IVa–c involving epiphyseal plate fractures in children, hyperflexion injuries with >50% articular surface fracture, and hyperextension injuries with DIP joint subluxation). This classification guides treatment decisions and helps predict outcomes.

A is incorrect because the Eaton and Littler Classification is used for thumb CMC (basal joint) osteoarthritis staging, not mallet finger injuries.
B is incorrect because the 'Doane Classification' is not a recognized or validated classification system for mallet finger injuries in the orthopaedic literature.
D is incorrect because the 'Taitz Classification' is not a standard classification used for mallet finger injuries.
E is incorrect because the 'Green Classification' is not the accepted classification for mallet finger; Green's Operative Hand Surgery references Doyle's classification for mallet fingers.

questions.question:
A 14-year-old girl presents to the clinic for a routine check-up. Her mother reports that she has noticed a cosmetic concern related to her back, particularly an asymmetry in her shoulder height. On examination, there is a noticeable right thoracic curve. An x-ray confirms a 30-degree right thoracic scoliosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Observation with repeat x-rays in 6 months
B) Referral for bracing therapy
C) Surgical intervention
D) Physical therapy
E) MRI of the spine
questions.answer:
B)
For adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis exhibiting a curve between 20 and 40 degrees and with significant growth remaining, bracing is the most appropriate next step. Observation may be warranted for curves less than 20 degrees, while surgical intervention is typically reserved for curves over 40 degrees or if progression is noted. A is incorrect because observation is appropriate for curves less than 20 degrees. C is incorrect because surgical intervention is typically for curves over 40 degrees. D is incorrect because physical therapy does not address curve progression. E is incorrect because MRI is not routinely indicated unless there are neurological symptoms or atypical features.

questions.question:
A child falls off a swing and lands on their outstretched hand. Subsequently, they present with pain and swelling at the wrist, particularly over the anatomical snuffbox. Initial x-rays are negative. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Immobilize in a thumb spica splint and repeat x-ray in 10–14 days
B) MRI of the wrist
C) CT scan of the wrist
D) No treatment needed — reassure and discharge
questions.answer:
A)
When a scaphoid fracture is clinically suspected (snuffbox tenderness, pain with axial loading of the thumb) but initial radiographs are negative, the standard of care is to immobilize the wrist in a thumb spica splint and obtain repeat imaging in 10–14 days. Bone resorption at the fracture site during healing makes occult fractures more visible on follow-up films.

B is incorrect because although MRI has high sensitivity for occult scaphoid fractures and can be used early, the classic board-answer first-line approach remains immobilization with repeat radiographs; MRI is typically reserved when early definitive diagnosis is needed (e.g., high-level athlete). C is incorrect because CT is useful for characterizing known fractures (displacement, comminution) but is less sensitive than MRI for occult fractures and is not the standard initial next step. D is incorrect because clinical findings of snuffbox tenderness after a fall on an outstretched hand warrant presumptive treatment for a scaphoid fracture even with negative initial films; failure to immobilize risks nonunion and avascular necrosis.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old female presents with low back pain and left leg weakness after a fall while skiing. An MRI reveals a Grade II isthmic spondylolisthesis at L5-S1. Which of the following factors is most likely correlated with the severity of her spinal slip?
A) Lumbar lordosis
B) Pelvic incidence
C) Anterior pelvic tilt
D) Sacral inclination
questions.answer:
B)
Pelvic incidence (PI) is a fixed morphologic parameter (PI = sacral slope + pelvic tilt) that does not change with posture. In isthmic spondylolisthesis, a higher pelvic incidence is strongly correlated with greater slip grade and progression. It reflects the inherent sagittal pelvic anatomy that predisposes to anterior shear forces at L5-S1, making it the most reliable predictor of slip severity and an essential factor in surgical planning.

A is incorrect because lumbar lordosis is a positional (compensatory) parameter that changes with posture and degeneration; it is a consequence of pelvic morphology rather than an independent predictor of slip severity.
C is incorrect because anterior pelvic tilt is a dynamic, compensatory postural parameter and is not as directly correlated with the degree of spondylolisthesis as pelvic incidence.
D is incorrect because sacral inclination (sacral slope) is a positional parameter that varies with standing posture and pelvic compensation; while related to PI, it is not the fixed parameter most strongly correlated with slip severity.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old man presents with severe anterior neck pain and hoarseness following a car accident. Upon examination, he demonstrates an inability to raise his voice. Which structure is most likely compromised due to trauma in this case?
A) Recurrent laryngeal nerve
B) Vagus nerve
C) Phrenic nerve
D) Longus colli muscle
questions.answer:
A)
The recurrent laryngeal nerve innervates all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid. Injury to this nerve results in vocal cord paralysis, leading to hoarseness and inability to raise the voice. In anterior neck trauma from a motor vehicle accident, the recurrent laryngeal nerve is vulnerable due to its course along the tracheoesophageal groove.

B is incorrect because while the vagus nerve gives rise to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, isolated vagus nerve injury would produce additional findings beyond hoarseness, including palatal and pharyngeal dysfunction; the more specific and likely injury given isolated hoarseness is to the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
C is incorrect because the phrenic nerve (C3-C5) innervates the diaphragm; its injury would cause respiratory compromise (hemidiaphragm paralysis), not hoarseness.
D is incorrect because the longus colli is a prevertebral flexor muscle; injury to it would cause neck pain and difficulty with flexion but would not explain hoarseness or vocal cord dysfunction.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male presents with persistent shoulder pain following a dislocated shoulder that was reduced in the emergency department. He now has limited range of motion and weakness. On examination, you suspect an injury to the deltoid muscle. Which of the following is the most likely function that may be affected?
A) Flexion of the elbow
B) Abduction of the arm
C) Internal rotation of the shoulder
D) Extension of the wrist
questions.answer:
B)
The deltoid muscle is the primary abductor of the arm, particularly from 15 to 90 degrees. Following shoulder dislocation, axillary nerve injury is common, which denervates the deltoid and impairs abduction. This leads to significant functional limitation in raising the arm laterally.

A is incorrect because flexion of the elbow is primarily performed by the biceps brachii and brachialis, not the deltoid. C is incorrect because internal rotation of the shoulder is primarily performed by the subscapularis, pectoralis major, and latissimus dorsi, not the deltoid. D is incorrect because extension of the wrist is performed by the extensor carpi radialis longus/brevis and extensor carpi ulnaris, which are innervated by the radial nerve and unrelated to deltoid function.

questions.question:
A patient undergoes an exam under anesthesia (EUA) to evaluate hip stability after sustaining an acetabular fracture. What is the primary goal of this procedure?
A) To determine the need for surgical fixation
B) To assess for chondral injury
C) To evaluate joint congruency
D) To identify associated ligamentous injuries
questions.answer:
C)
The primary goal of an exam under anesthesia after an acetabular fracture is to evaluate joint congruency — specifically, whether the femoral head remains concentrically reduced within the acetabulum through a range of motion and under stress. This directly guides treatment decisions by identifying dynamic instability or incongruency that may not be apparent on static imaging.

A is incorrect because the decision for surgical fixation is primarily based on fracture pattern, displacement criteria, and imaging findings (e.g., roof-arc measurements, CT assessment), not the EUA alone.
B is incorrect because chondral injury assessment requires direct visualization (arthroscopy or arthrotomy) or advanced imaging, not an EUA.
D is incorrect because the hip joint relies on bony and labral constraints rather than discrete ligaments (unlike the knee); ligamentous injury evaluation is not the primary purpose of a hip EUA after acetabular fracture.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male football player reports persistent pain in his left elbow after a tackle. He has difficulty fully extending his arm and experiences tingling in his ring and little fingers. Examination reveals tenderness along the medial aspect of the elbow. An x-ray is unremarkable. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
A) Ulnar nerve entrapment
B) Lateral epicondylitis
C) Medial collateral ligament injury
D) Elbow fracture
questions.answer:
A)
Ulnar nerve entrapment is suggested by the patient's symptoms of tingling in the ring and little fingers, coupled with the history of trauma. The medial aspect of the elbow is a common site for ulnar nerve issues, especially in athletes.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old female presents with a painful, swollen ankle after a basketball injury. An MRI of the ankle is performed and shows extensive bone marrow edema and a fracture line. The radiologist mentions that the bone healing observed is classified as primary. Which of the following best characterizes this type of bone healing?
A) Involves significant callus formation
B) Occurs with rigid fixation of the fracture fragments
C) Requires a longer healing time
D) Is characterized by an inflammatory response
questions.answer:
B)
Primary (direct) bone healing occurs when fracture fragments are rigidly stabilized and in close apposition, allowing direct osteonal remodeling (cutting cones) across the fracture site without significant callus formation. This is classically seen with anatomic reduction and rigid internal fixation such as compression plating.

A is incorrect because significant callus formation is characteristic of secondary (indirect) bone healing, not primary healing. Primary healing proceeds via intramembranous ossification without a cartilaginous callus intermediate.

C is incorrect because primary bone healing does not inherently require a longer healing time compared to secondary healing; in fact, with rigid fixation and direct remodeling, healing progresses in an orderly fashion without the prolonged callus maturation phase.

D is incorrect because while a minimal inflammatory response may occur, primary bone healing is specifically characterized by the absence of a prominent inflammatory and reparative phase; the hallmark inflammatory response with hematoma formation and granulation tissue is a feature of secondary bone healing.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old male with a history of osteoporosis falls at home and presents with severe pain and swelling around the hip. An x-ray reveals a fracture through the quadrilateral plate of the acetabulum. What is the most significant concern related to this type of injury?
A) Nerve injury
B) Hip joint instability
C) Avascular necrosis
D) Infection risk from open fracture
questions.answer:
B)
A quadrilateral plate fracture involves the thin medial wall of the acetabulum. The primary concern is medial displacement (protrusio) of the femoral head into the pelvis, resulting in hip joint instability and loss of articular congruity. This often necessitates surgical fixation with buttress plating to restore the medial wall and prevent further central subluxation.

A is incorrect because while neurovascular structures (obturator nerve/vessels, sciatic nerve) can be injured with acetabular fractures, nerve injury is not the most significant concern specific to quadrilateral plate fractures. C is incorrect because avascular necrosis of the femoral head is more commonly associated with femoral neck fractures or hip dislocations rather than isolated quadrilateral plate fractures. D is incorrect because quadrilateral plate fractures are typically closed injuries; open fracture and infection risk are not a primary concern with this fracture pattern.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old male golfer presents with pain over the anterior knee, particularly when climbing stairs or kneeling. He reports that the pain began gradually and has worsened over the past few months. On examination, there is tenderness at the inferior pole of the patella. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Patellar tendinopathy
B) Patellofemoral pain syndrome
C) Quadriceps strain
D) Iliotibial band syndrome
questions.answer:
A)
The symptoms and examination findings are indicative of patellar tendinopathy (jumper's knee). This condition is characterized by activity-related anterior knee pain localized to the inferior pole of the patella, worsened by loading activities such as stair climbing and kneeling. It is common in athletes who perform repetitive knee extension.

B is incorrect because patellofemoral pain syndrome typically presents with diffuse or peripatellar pain, often worse with prolonged sitting or squatting, and tenderness is usually along the medial/lateral patellar facets rather than precisely at the inferior pole of the patella.
C is incorrect because a quadriceps strain would present with pain and tenderness in the quadriceps muscle belly or its proximal attachment, not at the inferior pole of the patella, and is usually associated with an acute injury event.
D is incorrect because iliotibial band syndrome causes pain over the lateral aspect of the knee at the lateral femoral epicondyle, not at the inferior patellar pole.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old woman who underwent reverse shoulder arthroplasty presents with new-onset shoulder pain and tenderness. Imaging studies show a stress fracture of the acromion. What is the most likely contributing factor to this complication?
A) Excessive postoperative activity
B) Infection
C) Improper surgical technique
D) Inherent bone quality
questions.answer:
D)
Acromial stress fractures after reverse shoulder arthroplasty are most commonly associated with inherent poor bone quality (osteoporosis/osteopenia). The reverse prosthesis design increases deltoid tension and shifts mechanical loads to the acromion; when the acromion is osteoporotic, it is predisposed to insufficiency-type stress fractures. This is the most frequently cited risk factor in the orthopaedic literature.

A is incorrect because while excessive postoperative activity can theoretically contribute, it is not the most commonly identified factor; many acromial fractures occur even with appropriate activity restrictions.
B is incorrect because infection typically presents with warmth, erythema, elevated inflammatory markers, and does not characteristically cause acromial stress fractures.
C is incorrect because although component positioning (excessive lateralization) can increase acromial stress, the stem asks about the most likely contributing factor, which is the patient's inherent bone quality rather than surgical technique error.

questions.question:
A 26-year-old male soccer player presents with complaints of burning pain on the lateral aspect of his thigh after a recent training session. On physical examination, sensory testing reveals decreased sensation over the anterolateral thigh with no motor deficits and no tenderness over the greater trochanter. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Meralgia paresthetica
B) Femoral nerve injury
C) L4 radiculopathy
D) Greater trochanteric bursitis
questions.answer:
A)
Meralgia paresthetica is caused by compression or irritation of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (LFCN) as it passes near or through the inguinal ligament. It classically presents with burning pain and decreased sensation over the anterolateral thigh without motor deficits, which matches this presentation.

B is incorrect because femoral nerve injury would produce quadriceps weakness and diminished patellar reflex in addition to sensory changes, primarily in the anterior thigh and medial leg (saphenous distribution). C is incorrect because L4 radiculopathy would typically include back or buttock pain, dermatomal sensory changes in the medial leg, quadriceps weakness, and a diminished knee-jerk reflex. D is incorrect because greater trochanteric bursitis presents with point tenderness over the greater trochanter and pain with resisted hip abduction, not with a purely sensory deficit over the lateral thigh.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman presents with chronic pain and swelling at the thumb metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint. She has a history of repetitive pinching activities. Examination reveals laxity of the ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) of the thumb MCP joint with valgus stress testing. Which of the following conditions is she most likely experiencing?
A) Gamekeeper's thumb
B) Bennett's fracture
C) CMC joint osteoarthritis
D) Scapholunate dissociation
questions.answer:
A)
Gamekeeper's thumb refers to chronic attenuation or rupture of the ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) at the thumb metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint, resulting from repetitive valgus stress. The clinical findings of UCL laxity at the MCP joint with pain and swelling are classic for this diagnosis.

B is incorrect because a Bennett's fracture is an intra-articular fracture-dislocation at the base of the first metacarpal (CMC joint), typically caused by an axial load, and would be identified on imaging rather than by UCL laxity.
C is incorrect because CMC joint osteoarthritis involves the trapeziometacarpal joint at the base of the thumb, presenting with a positive grind test, not UCL instability at the MCP joint.
D is incorrect because scapholunate dissociation is a carpal ligament injury presenting with dorsal wrist pain, a positive Watson (scaphoid shift) test, and widening of the scapholunate interval — unrelated to the thumb MCP joint.

questions.question:
During a posterior approach to the lumbar spine, a surgeon must navigate around the spinal nerves. Which of the following anatomical landmarks is most critical for avoiding injury to the L4 nerve root during dissection?
A) Lamina of L4 vertebra
B) Transverse process of L4 vertebra
C) Pedicle of L4 vertebra
D) Ligamentum flavum
questions.answer:
C)
The pedicle of L4 is the most critical landmark for avoiding injury to the L4 nerve root during a posterior lumbar approach. The L4 nerve root exits the spinal canal beneath the L4 pedicle, and the pedicle serves as the consistent bony reference point to identify the nerve root's location. Dissection that strays too far laterally near the pedicle risks direct nerve root injury.

A is incorrect because the lamina of L4 is a midline/paramedian structure that is typically removed during laminectomy; while important for exposure, it does not directly mark the location of the exiting nerve root.
B is incorrect because the transverse process of L4 is located more laterally and posteriorly and, while useful for fusion or instrumentation landmarks, does not directly indicate the path of the L4 nerve root in the spinal canal.
D is incorrect because the ligamentum flavum is a midline soft-tissue structure connecting adjacent laminae; it is incised during decompression but does not serve as a landmark for localizing a specific nerve root.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old male athlete is evaluated for shoulder instability after multiple anterior dislocations. An MRI reveals a Bankart lesion. Which additional associated bony injury should you most expect to find in this patient?
A) Glenoid rim fracture (bony Bankart)
B) Rotator cuff tear
C) Hill-Sachs lesion
D) Acromioclavicular separation
questions.answer:
C)
A Hill-Sachs lesion is a compression fracture of the posterolateral humeral head caused by impaction against the anterior-inferior glenoid rim during anterior shoulder dislocation. It is the most commonly associated bony injury found alongside a Bankart lesion, particularly in young patients with recurrent anterior instability.

A is incorrect because a bony Bankart (glenoid rim fracture) can coexist but is a variant of the labral pathology already identified, not a separate associated injury in the way the question intends; the Hill-Sachs lesion is the classic paired finding.
B is incorrect because rotator cuff tears are more commonly associated with anterior dislocations in patients older than 40, not in a 22-year-old athlete.
D is incorrect because acromioclavicular separation results from a direct blow to the acromion or a fall onto the shoulder and is not a consequence of glenohumeral dislocation.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old woman presents with lateral wrist pain that has gradually worsened over the past few months. She reports pain when she attempts to grip objects or perform wrist movements, especially when pushing her thumb against her index finger. A Finkelstein's test is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) De Quervain's tenosynovitis
B) Intersection syndrome
C) Scaphoid fracture
D) Wrist sprain
questions.answer:
A)
De Quervain's tenosynovitis involves inflammation of the first dorsal compartment tendons (abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis). The hallmark findings are radial-sided (lateral) wrist pain exacerbated by thumb use and a positive Finkelstein's test, both of which are described in this stem.

B is incorrect because intersection syndrome involves pain and swelling more dorsally and proximally on the forearm (approximately 4–6 cm proximal to the wrist joint), where the first dorsal compartment tendons cross over the second dorsal compartment tendons; Finkelstein's test is not its defining clinical test.

C is incorrect because a scaphoid fracture typically presents with anatomic snuffbox tenderness after a fall on an outstretched hand, not with a positive Finkelstein's test or gradual onset of symptoms.

D is incorrect because a wrist sprain is a ligamentous injury usually following acute trauma; it would not produce a positive Finkelstein's test or pain specifically with thumb opposition against the index finger.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old female runner reports persistent pain in the midfoot, exacerbated by activity. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the cuboid and 4th/5th metatarsals. She has a cavovarus foot deformity. Which of the following conditions is she most likely experiencing?
A) Freiberg's disease
B) Stress fracture of the metatarsals
C) Tarsal coalition
D) Lisfranc injury
E) Plantar fasciitis
questions.answer:
B)
Stress fractures of the metatarsals are the most likely diagnosis in a runner with persistent activity-related midfoot pain, tenderness over the cuboid and 4th/5th metatarsals, and a cavovarus foot deformity. Cavovarus alignment causes lateral column overload, predisposing to stress fractures of the 4th and 5th metatarsals. The insidious onset with activity-related pain in a runner is classic for a stress injury.

A is incorrect because Freiberg's disease (avascular necrosis of a metatarsal head, usually the 2nd) typically presents in adolescents with pain at the metatarsal head, not the midfoot. C is incorrect because tarsal coalition presents with rigid flatfoot (not cavovarus), peroneal spasm, and hindfoot stiffness, usually in adolescents. D is incorrect because Lisfranc injury involves the tarsometatarsal joint complex (primarily the 1st-2nd ray) and typically results from an acute axial load or crush mechanism, not from overuse; tenderness would be at the TMT joints, not the cuboid. E is incorrect because plantar fasciitis causes plantar heel pain at the calcaneal origin of the fascia, not lateral midfoot pain.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman with a history of hip osteoarthritis presents with increased pain and limited range of motion in her left hip. Upon examination, you note weakness in her ability to externally rotate her thigh. Which muscle, originating from the ischial tuberosity and inserting into the greater trochanter, is likely affected?
A) Quadratus femoris
B) Superior gemellus
C) Inferior gemellus
D) Piriformis
questions.answer:
A)
The quadratus femoris originates from the lateral border of the ischial tuberosity and inserts on the intertrochanteric crest of the greater trochanter. It is a powerful external rotator of the hip. In the setting of hip osteoarthritis, weakness or dysfunction of this muscle can contribute to diminished external rotation strength.

B is incorrect because the superior gemellus originates from the ischial spine (not the ischial tuberosity). C is incorrect because, although the inferior gemellus does originate from the ischial tuberosity, it inserts into the medial surface of the greater trochanter via the obturator internus tendon rather than directly into the greater trochanter. D is incorrect because the piriformis originates from the anterior surface of the sacrum and inserts on the superior aspect of the greater trochanter — it does not originate from the ischial tuberosity.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old man complains of persistent neck pain and intermittent headaches following a motor vehicle accident. An MRI reveals a herniated disc at the C6-C7 level causing spinal cord compression. Which surgical procedure is most appropriate for immediate decompression?
A) Posterior cervical laminectomy
B) Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion
C) Foraminotomy
D) Spinal fusion without decompression
questions.answer:
B)
Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) is the most appropriate surgical procedure for a single-level herniated disc at C6-C7 causing spinal cord compression. ACDF provides direct anterior access to the pathology, allows complete removal of the offending disc, and restores stability with fusion. It is the gold-standard approach for single-level ventral cervical cord compression from a herniated disc.

A is incorrect because posterior cervical laminectomy addresses dorsal compression and does not directly remove a ventrally located herniated disc; it may also lead to post-laminectomy kyphosis, especially at a single level.
C is incorrect because foraminotomy is used to decompress a nerve root within the neural foramen (radiculopathy) and does not adequately address central spinal cord compression from a herniated disc.
D is incorrect because spinal fusion without decompression would stabilize the segment but would not relieve the spinal cord compression caused by the herniated disc.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old male presents with insidious onset of knee pain, and imaging reveals a discoid meniscus. Which of the following symptoms would most likely be associated with this condition?
A) Locking and catching of the knee
B) Swelling exclusively on the medial side
C) Complete range of motion without pain
D) Acute pain after a recent injury
questions.answer:
A)
A discoid meniscus has an abnormal broad, disc-like shape that predisposes it to tears, instability, and mechanical symptoms such as locking, catching, and a classic "snapping knee" (Wrisberg variant). These symptoms arise from the meniscus displacing or interposing within the joint during motion.

B is incorrect because swelling from a discoid meniscus is typically a generalized joint effusion, not exclusively medial-sided; moreover, discoid menisci are far more common on the lateral side.
C is incorrect because a symptomatic discoid meniscus characteristically causes pain and mechanical limitation of motion, not painless full range of motion.
D is incorrect because the hallmark of a discoid meniscus is insidious, chronic mechanical symptoms rather than acute pain from a single traumatic event; the stem itself describes insidious onset.

questions.question:
A 15-year-old girl presents with right hip pain after falling from a skateboard. Initial x-rays reveal a femoral neck fracture. Given her skeletal maturity, which of the following factors would most likely indicate a higher risk of avascular necrosis related to this injury?
A) Female sex
B) Delayed presentation beyond 24 hours
C) Absence of weight-bearing ability
D) Presence of knee pain
questions.answer:
B)
Delayed presentation and treatment beyond 24 hours is a well-established risk factor for avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head following femoral neck fractures. Prolonged delay allows ongoing compromise of the already disrupted blood supply (medial femoral circumflex artery branches), increasing the likelihood of femoral head ischemia. Early anatomic reduction and stable fixation are critical to restoring or preserving perfusion.

A is incorrect because female sex is not an independent risk factor for AVN after femoral neck fracture; fracture displacement, time to reduction, and quality of reduction are far more important determinants.

C is incorrect because inability to bear weight reflects pain and fracture severity but is not itself a predictor of AVN; it is the degree of fracture displacement and delay in treatment that drive AVN risk.

D is incorrect because knee pain in the setting of a hip fracture is a well-known pattern of referred pain (obturator nerve) and has no bearing on the vascular status of the femoral head or AVN risk.

questions.question:
A 36-year-old male construction worker presents with lateral ankle pain after stepping off a curb. Examination reveals tenderness over the anterior talofibular ligament and an obvious ankle effusion. X-rays show no fracture, and the Bohler's angle is measured at 35 degrees. What does this angle indicate?
A) Pathological condition
B) Normal calcaneal anatomy
C) Risk for peroneal tendon injury
D) Sprain severity
questions.answer:
A)
Explanation: A Bohler's angle less than 20 degrees is indicative of a pathological condition, typically associated with calcaneal fractures. In this case, although there is no fracture, the low angle suggests potential underlying issues that may need further investigation, particularly if the patient presents with chronic pain.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male presents with increasing left hip pain over the past two weeks. He has a history of chronic osteomyelitis. MRI reveals a lytic lesion in the femoral head with surrounding edema. Given the imaging findings, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Initiate bisphosphonate therapy
B) Perform a biopsy of the lesion
C) Schedule for orthopedic surgical intervention
D) Obtain a follow-up MRI in one month
questions.answer:
B)
A biopsy is critical in this scenario to establish a definitive diagnosis of the lytic lesion in the femoral head. In a 28-year-old with chronic osteomyelitis, the differential diagnosis includes infection (Brodie abscess), benign tumors, and malignancy (e.g., sarcoma arising in chronic osteomyelitis — Marjolin-type transformation). Histological confirmation is essential before committing to a treatment plan.

A is incorrect because bisphosphonate therapy is used for osteoporosis or certain metastatic bone diseases and has no role before a tissue diagnosis is established. B is the correct answer. C is incorrect because surgical intervention (curettage, resection) should not be performed without a tissue diagnosis, as the surgical approach differs significantly depending on whether the lesion is infectious, benign, or malignant. D is incorrect because delaying diagnosis with a follow-up MRI in one month risks progression of a potentially aggressive or malignant process; a tissue diagnosis should be obtained promptly.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old chef presents with pain in her thumb after repetitive gripping activities. She reports that her thumb feels weak, and she has difficulty pinching. On examination, there is tenderness over the base of the thumb and a positive Finkelstein test. What is the likely diagnosis? 
A) De Quervain's tenosynovitis 
B) Trigger finger 
C) Osteoarthritis 
D) Avascular necrosis
questions.answer:
A)
De Quervain's tenosynovitis is characterized by pain with repetitive thumb/wrist use, tenderness over the first dorsal compartment (radial styloid area), and a positive Finkelstein test (pain reproduced by ulnar deviation of the wrist with the thumb flexed into the palm). This condition involves inflammation of the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons and is common in individuals performing repetitive gripping or thumb movements.

B is incorrect because trigger finger involves stenosing tenosynovitis of the A1 pulley, presenting with catching, locking, or clicking of the affected digit — not a positive Finkelstein test.
C is incorrect because osteoarthritis of the thumb (CMC joint) can cause base-of-thumb pain and weakness with pinching, but the hallmark exam finding is a positive grind test (axial compression with rotation), not a positive Finkelstein test.
D is incorrect because avascular necrosis at the wrist (e.g., Kienböck disease of the lunate or Preiser disease of the scaphoid) would not produce a positive Finkelstein test and presents with different localization of tenderness.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old woman presents with persistent pain and swelling in her ankle after a fall. An x-ray shows a calcaneus fracture treated non-operatively. What is the most common long-term complication associated with non-surgical management of this injury?
A) Subtalar arthritis
B) Osteonecrosis
C) Chronic instability
D) Joint stiffness
questions.answer:
A)
Subtalar arthritis is the most common long-term complication following non-operative management of calcaneal fractures. Residual incongruity of the posterior facet and loss of calcaneal height/width lead to progressive degenerative changes in the subtalar joint.

B is incorrect because osteonecrosis of the calcaneus is rare; the calcaneus has a robust blood supply and avascular necrosis is not a typical sequela of calcaneal fractures.
C is incorrect because chronic instability is more commonly associated with lateral ankle ligament injuries (e.g., recurrent sprains) rather than calcaneal fractures.
D is incorrect because while some stiffness may occur, the hallmark long-term complication of calcaneal fractures is subtalar arthritis from articular incongruity, not simple joint stiffness.

questions.question:
A 15-year-old male presents with a painless mass on the lateral aspect of his knee. Physical examination reveals a hard bony mass, and an X-ray shows a well-circumscribed lesion arising from the metaphysis of the femur. Given the typical presentation of this condition, what is the most appropriate management option?
A) Immediate excision
B) Observation with periodic follow-up
C) Curettage and bone grafting
D) Referral for radiation therapy
questions.answer:
B)
Observation with periodic follow-up is the standard management for an asymptomatic osteochondroma in a skeletally immature patient. These are the most common benign bone tumors, typically arising from the metaphysis and growing away from the joint. They tend to stabilize or stop growing after skeletal maturity, and routine monitoring is sufficient unless the lesion becomes symptomatic, causes mechanical problems, or shows features concerning for malignant transformation (e.g., rapid growth, cartilage cap >2 cm in adults).

A is incorrect because immediate excision is not warranted for an asymptomatic, benign-appearing osteochondroma; surgery is reserved for symptomatic lesions, neurovascular compromise, or concern for malignant transformation.
C is incorrect because curettage and bone grafting is used for intramedullary benign lesions such as unicameral bone cysts or enchondromas, not for pedunculated surface lesions like osteochondromas.
D is incorrect because osteochondromas are benign cartilage-capped bony growths that do not respond to radiation therapy; radiation is not indicated and carries risks of radiation-induced sarcoma.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old male presents to the clinic with chronic hip pain. His history reveals that he suffered a fall three months ago but did not seek immediate medical attention. On examination, significant tenderness is noted over the anterior aspect of the hip. An MRI is ordered, which shows edema around the anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS). What structure is primarily affected in this patient?
A) Iliopsoas tendon
B) Rectus femoris tendon
C) Adductor longus muscle
D) Pectineus muscle
questions.answer:
B)
The rectus femoris muscle originates from the anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) via its direct head (and from the superior acetabular rim via its indirect/reflected head). MRI showing edema around the AIIS in the setting of a remote fall is consistent with a chronic strain or tendinopathy of the rectus femoris origin. This is the structure primarily affected.

A is incorrect because the iliopsoas tendon inserts on the lesser trochanter of the femur, not the AIIS. Pathology of the iliopsoas would produce tenderness more medially and distally.
C is incorrect because the adductor longus originates from the body of the pubis near the pubic symphysis, not the AIIS. It would present with medial groin/adductor tenderness.
D is incorrect because the pectineus originates from the pectineal line of the pubis (superior pubic ramus), not the AIIS. Tenderness would be located more medially.

questions.question:
A newborn infant is referred to the orthopedic clinic for evaluation of potential hip dysplasia. The ultrasound shows an abnormality in the left hip, but the right hip appears normal. Which of the following findings is most commonly associated with this condition?
A) Left-sided dislocation of the hip
B) Right-sided hip dislocation
C) Bilateral hip dysplasia
D) Acetabular dysplasia on the left
E) Femoral head necrosis on the right
questions.answer:
A)
Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) most commonly affects the left hip. This is because the most common fetal position is left occiput anterior (LOA), which places the left hip against the mother's sacrum, limiting abduction and predisposing to instability or dislocation. When a newborn ultrasound shows a unilateral abnormality, left-sided involvement is the expected finding.

B is incorrect because right-sided hip dislocation, while possible, is less common than left-sided involvement in DDH due to the typical fetal positioning.
C is incorrect because although bilateral DDH occurs in approximately 20% of cases, unilateral left-sided involvement is more common overall.
D is incorrect because while acetabular dysplasia on the left can be part of the DDH spectrum, the question asks about the finding most commonly associated with the condition, and left-sided dislocation/instability is the classic board-level association for unilateral DDH.
E is incorrect because femoral head necrosis on the right is not a presenting feature of DDH; avascular necrosis is a complication of treatment (e.g., prolonged casting or surgical reduction), not a finding at initial screening.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents with a history of recurrent episodes of her knee 'locking' and 'catching'. On examination, there is tenderness over the medial joint line, and an MRI reveals a displaced meniscal tear. Which of the following best describes the likely mechanism of her symptoms?
A) Chronic synovial irritation
B) Loose body formation
C) Ligamentous instability
D) Joint effusion
E) Osteophyte formation
questions.answer:
B)
In a displaced meniscal tear (e.g., a bucket-handle tear), the torn meniscal fragment flips into the intercondylar notch and acts as a mechanical block to full knee extension, producing true locking and catching. This displaced fragment functionally behaves like a loose body within the joint, intermittently obstructing normal joint motion. This is the classic mechanism for the episodic mechanical symptoms described.

A is incorrect because chronic synovial irritation causes pain and effusion but does not produce true mechanical locking or catching.
C is incorrect because ligamentous instability causes giving way or a sense of the knee buckling, not true locking episodes.
D is incorrect because joint effusion causes stiffness and limited range of motion but does not cause the intermittent mechanical locking and catching described.
E is incorrect because osteophyte formation is associated with osteoarthritis and can limit motion, but it does not cause episodic locking and catching in a 45-year-old with a confirmed displaced meniscal tear on MRI.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old woman who had an ORIF for a distal humeral fracture presents with limited range of motion in her elbow. Physical examination reveals a hard end-feel at 90 degrees of flexion. Which of the following surgical options would be most appropriate to improve her range of motion?
A) Open release of the posterior bundle of the MCL
B) Arthroscopic debridement of the joint
C) Excise osteophytes
D) Perform a radial head resection
questions.answer:
C)
After ORIF of a distal humeral fracture, a hard end-feel at 90° of flexion suggests a mechanical bony block, most commonly from osteophyte formation or heterotopic ossification. Excising these osteophytes removes the mechanical barrier and is the most appropriate surgical option among the choices listed to restore range of motion.

A is incorrect because open release of the posterior bundle of the MCL addresses valgus instability or contracture of the medial collateral ligament, not a bony mechanical block. There is no indication of ligamentous instability in this scenario.
B is incorrect because arthroscopic debridement can address soft-tissue contractures and loose bodies, but a hard end-feel after ORIF with hardware in place is best managed with open excision of bony impediments; arthroscopy around prior hardware is technically challenging and less effective for significant bony blocks.
D is incorrect because radial head resection is indicated for comminuted radial head fractures or radiocapitellar arthritis, not for post-ORIF bony blocks of the distal humerus causing limited flexion.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old male presents with chronic lower back pain that worsens with extension of the spine. He has difficulty standing for prolonged periods and experiences relief when bending forward. What physical exam finding would most likely indicate spinal stenosis in this patient?
A) Increased pain with coughing
B) Decreased strength in hip flexion
C) Pain relieved with lumbar flexion
D) Pain with straight leg raise
questions.answer:
C)
Lumbar spinal stenosis classically produces neurogenic claudication that worsens with spinal extension (which narrows the spinal canal) and is relieved with lumbar flexion (which opens the canal). A positive "shopping cart sign" — the patient leaning forward for relief — is a hallmark exam finding.

A is incorrect because increased pain with coughing raises intrathecal pressure and is more suggestive of a disc herniation causing radiculopathy, not specifically spinal stenosis. B is incorrect because decreased hip flexion strength suggests an upper lumbar radiculopathy (L2-L3) and is not a characteristic finding of lumbar spinal stenosis on exam. D is incorrect because a positive straight leg raise test is the classic provocative maneuver for a lumbar disc herniation with nerve root tension, not for spinal stenosis.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer is experiencing debilitating bone pain despite analgesic therapy. The orthopedic team is considering non-invasive options for pain control. Which treatment modality is most appropriate for this patient's symptom management?
A) Chemotherapy
B) Radiation therapy
C) Surgical intervention
D) Increased opioids
questions.answer:
B)
Radiation therapy is an effective and non-invasive option for the management of bone pain caused by metastatic lesions. External beam radiation can significantly reduce pain and improve quality of life in patients with advanced cancer, and is the most appropriate non-invasive modality for localized symptomatic bone metastases.

A is incorrect because chemotherapy is a systemic treatment that may be used for disease control but is not primarily a non-invasive pain management modality for focal bone pain and carries significant systemic side effects.
C is incorrect because surgical intervention is invasive, not non-invasive, and is typically reserved for impending or completed pathologic fractures or spinal cord compression rather than pain control alone.
D is incorrect because simply increasing opioids does not address the underlying cause of pain, carries risks of tolerance, dependence, and side effects, and the stem specifies the patient already has debilitating pain despite analgesic therapy.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman presents with flatfoot deformity and is unable to perform a single-heel rise. This raises suspicion for posterior tibial tendon insufficiency. Which of the following stages best describes her condition?
A) Stage I
B) Stage II
C) Stage III
D) Stage IV
questions.answer:
B)
Stage II posterior tibial tendon insufficiency is characterized by a flexible flatfoot deformity with an elongated or dysfunctional posterior tibial tendon, resulting in inability to perform a single-heel rise. The deformity is still passively correctable at this stage. Early recognition allows for tendon-sparing reconstructive procedures such as FDL transfer with medializing calcaneal osteotomy.

A is incorrect because Stage I PTTD presents with tenosynovitis, medial ankle pain, and mild swelling but the tendon length is normal, the arch is maintained, and the patient can typically still perform a single-heel rise. C is incorrect because Stage III PTTD is defined by a rigid (fixed) flatfoot deformity; the stem does not specify rigidity, making Stage II more appropriate. D is incorrect because Stage IV PTTD includes a rigid flatfoot with associated valgus tilt of the talus in the ankle mortise (deltoid ligament insufficiency), which is not described in this stem.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old male athlete sustains a right femur fracture during a football game. On examination, there is significant swelling and tenderness over the mid-femoral shaft. A CT scan reveals a comminuted fracture. Which of the following surgical approaches would provide adequate exposure for fixation while minimizing damage to the surrounding musculature?
A) Anterolateral approach
B) Posterolateral approach
C) Medial approach
D) Lateral approach
questions.answer:
D)
The lateral approach is commonly used for femoral shaft fractures as it provides good exposure while minimizing damage to the surrounding musculature. It is particularly suitable for midshaft fractures and allows for straightforward fixation.
A is incorrect because the anterolateral approach is more commonly used for proximal femur exposure and may not provide optimal access to the midshaft.
B is incorrect because the posterolateral approach is not typically used for femoral shaft fractures and may involve more muscle dissection.
C is incorrect because the medial approach is not suitable for femoral shaft fractures and does not provide adequate exposure.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with progressive pain and deformity at the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Upon examination, she has significant lateral deviation of the great toe, and a palpable bony prominence is noted at the medial aspect. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Hallux rigidus
B) Morton's neuroma
C) Hallux valgus
D) Sesamoiditis
questions.answer:
C)
Hallux valgus (bunion) is characterized by lateral deviation of the great toe at the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint with a medial bony prominence. Rheumatoid arthritis accelerates this deformity through synovitis-driven capsular and ligamentous attenuation. The clinical findings described—progressive lateral deviation and a medial eminence—are classic for hallux valgus.

A is incorrect because hallux rigidus refers to degenerative arthritis of the first MTP joint with loss of dorsiflexion range of motion and osteophyte formation; the hallmark is stiffness rather than angular deviation. B is incorrect because Morton's neuroma is an interdigital nerve entrapment (typically between the 3rd and 4th metatarsal heads) presenting with burning pain and a positive Mulder's click, not great-toe deviation. D is incorrect because sesamoiditis involves inflammation of the sesamoid bones beneath the first metatarsal head, causing plantar pain under the great toe, without lateral deviation or a medial bony prominence.

questions.question:
A 6-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department after falling while playing on the playground. She cannot extend her elbow and exhibits wrist drop. An X-ray shows a mid-shaft humeral fracture. Which of the following is the most likely associated injury?
A) Ulnar nerve injury
B) Median nerve injury
C) Radial nerve palsy
D) Brachial plexus injury
questions.answer:
C)
A mid-shaft humeral fracture is the classic fracture associated with radial nerve palsy because the radial nerve courses along the spiral groove on the posterior aspect of the humeral shaft and is vulnerable to injury at this level. Wrist drop (inability to extend the wrist and fingers at the MCP joints) confirms radial nerve involvement. Most cases are neuropraxias that recover spontaneously; initial management includes wrist splinting and serial clinical examinations.

A is incorrect because the ulnar nerve is most commonly injured with fractures around the medial epicondyle or distal humerus (e.g., supracondylar fractures), not mid-shaft fractures, and would present with clawing or intrinsic weakness rather than wrist drop.
B is incorrect because the median nerve is typically at risk in supracondylar fractures or distal humeral injuries; its injury would present with loss of thumb opposition, forearm pronation, and wrist/finger flexion weakness, not wrist drop.
D is incorrect because brachial plexus injuries are associated with traction mechanisms (e.g., birth injuries, shoulder dislocations, high-energy trauma to the neck/shoulder) rather than isolated mid-shaft humeral fractures, and would produce a broader pattern of upper-extremity weakness.

questions.question:
A 6-year-old girl is evaluated for a limp that has persisted for several weeks. She has a history of recurrent fevers and joint pain. On examination, there is swelling in the hip region and limited range of motion. An MRI is performed and shows effusion in the hip joint. What is the most likely underlying condition?
A) Septic arthritis
B) Perthes disease
C) Osteomyelitis
D) Juvenile idiopathic arthritis
questions.answer:
A)
Explanation: The combination of fever, joint pain, and hip effusion raises concern for septic arthritis, which is a surgical emergency requiring prompt intervention to prevent joint destruction.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a skiing accident. He complains of severe shoulder pain and weakness in internal rotation. Physical examination reveals a positive lift-off test and a positive belly-press test, with tenderness over the anterior shoulder. An MRI confirms a full-thickness tear of the subscapularis tendon. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in managing his condition?
A) Physical therapy
B) Surgical repair of the subscapularis tendon
C) Corticosteroid injection
D) Activity modification
questions.answer:
B)
In a young, active patient with an acute, traumatic full-thickness subscapularis tendon tear confirmed on MRI, early surgical repair is the most appropriate management. The subscapularis is the largest and strongest rotator cuff muscle and is critical for internal rotation and anterior stability of the glenohumeral joint. Delay in repair can lead to tendon retraction, fatty infiltration, and poorer surgical outcomes.

A is incorrect because physical therapy alone is insufficient for a full-thickness traumatic subscapularis tear in a young active patient; it cannot restore the structural integrity of the tendon. C is incorrect because corticosteroid injection may provide temporary pain relief but does not address the underlying tendon disruption and may impair healing. D is incorrect because activity modification is a conservative measure that would be inadequate for a complete traumatic tear in a young patient and risks progressive muscle atrophy and tendon retraction.

questions.question:
A 14-year-old girl presents for a routine check-up, and her parents express concern about her noticeable spinal curvature. An examination reveals a 25-degree right thoracic scoliosis. The physician suggests a management plan. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of her scoliosis?
A) Surgical intervention
B) Observation and follow-up
C) Physical therapy
D) Custom bracing
questions.answer:
D)
For adolescent idiopathic scoliosis in a skeletally immature patient (age 14), a 25-degree curve falls within the 25–40° range for which bracing is the standard of care to prevent progression during remaining growth. The BrAIST trial demonstrated that bracing significantly reduces the likelihood of curve progression to a surgical threshold.

A is incorrect because surgical intervention (typically posterior spinal fusion) is generally reserved for curves exceeding 40–50° or those that progress despite bracing; a 25-degree curve does not meet surgical criteria.
B is incorrect because observation alone is appropriate for curves less than 25° in a growing adolescent; at 25° with remaining growth, the risk of progression warrants active treatment with bracing.
C is incorrect because physical therapy (e.g., Schroth exercises) may serve as an adjunct but has not been shown to be as effective as bracing in preventing curve progression and is not the standard first-line management for a 25-degree curve in a growing adolescent.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents after falling onto her outstretched hand. X-rays reveal a distal radius fracture consistent with a Frykman Type II fracture. Which of the following findings is expected?
A) Ulnar styloid fracture
B) Scaphoid fracture
C) Radial styloid fracture
D) Lunate dislocation
questions.answer:
A)
The Frykman classification of distal radius fractures is based on articular involvement and the presence or absence of an ulnar styloid fracture. Odd-numbered types (I, III, V, VII) lack an ulnar styloid fracture; even-numbered types (II, IV, VI, VIII) include one. Frykman Type II is an extra-articular distal radius fracture accompanied by an ulnar styloid fracture, making an ulnar styloid fracture the expected finding.

B is incorrect because a scaphoid fracture is not a component of the Frykman classification; it is a separate carpal bone injury typically associated with a fall on an outstretched hand but is classified independently.
C is incorrect because a radial styloid fracture (chauffeur's fracture) is an intra-articular injury pattern not described by Frykman Type II, which is extra-articular.
D is incorrect because a lunate dislocation is a perilunate/lunate ligamentous injury pattern, not part of the Frykman distal radius fracture classification.

questions.question:
During a surgical procedure for a trochanteric fracture, the surgeon contemplates the importance of the piriformis fossa. What is the significance of this anatomical location regarding intramedullary nailing?
A) It houses the femoral artery
B) It is the entry point for antegrade nailing
C) It is where the sciatic nerve is located
D) It contains the vastus lateralis muscle
questions.answer:
B)
The piriformis fossa is a critical anatomical landmark that serves as the traditional entry point for antegrade intramedullary nailing of the femur. Accurate identification of this site ensures proper nail alignment along the femoral canal and reduces the risk of iatrogenic fracture or malalignment. Modern trochanteric-entry nails use the tip of the greater trochanter, but the piriformis fossa remains the classic described entry point for standard antegrade femoral nails.

A is incorrect because the femoral artery lies anteromedially in the femoral triangle, not in the piriformis fossa. B is the correct answer. C is incorrect because the sciatic nerve exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic notch and courses posterior to the hip joint deep to the piriformis muscle — it is not located within the piriformis fossa of the femur. D is incorrect because the vastus lateralis muscle originates from the lateral aspect of the proximal femur (intertrochanteric line and linea aspera), not from the piriformis fossa.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old pitcher reports increasing shoulder pain and a feeling of instability. MRI reveals a tear in the subscapularis, which is causing difficulty with internal rotation. Which of the following physical examination findings would most likely correlate with this injury?
A) Increased internal rotation
B) Decreased external rotation
C) Positive apprehension test
D) Decreased internal rotation
questions.answer:
D)
The subscapularis is the primary internal rotator of the shoulder. A tear in this muscle leads to decreased internal rotation strength and range of motion. Physical examination findings consistent with subscapularis tears include a positive lift-off test (Gerber test), positive belly-press test, and increased passive external rotation due to loss of the subscapularis's restraining effect.

A is incorrect because a subscapularis tear causes weakness and loss of internal rotation, not increased internal rotation.
B is incorrect because decreased external rotation would suggest pathology of the infraspinatus or teres minor (external rotators), not the subscapularis. In fact, passive external rotation may be increased with a subscapularis tear due to loss of its anterior restraint.
C is incorrect because a positive apprehension test is associated with anterior glenohumeral instability (e.g., Bankart lesion or capsular laxity), not specifically with a subscapularis tear. While the subscapularis contributes to anterior stability, the apprehension test is not the most direct correlate of a subscapularis tear—loss of internal rotation is.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male presents with acute pain and swelling in the foot after sustaining a fall. An x-ray reveals a fracture in the lateral malleolus. Given the mechanism of injury and fracture type, what is the most likely associated compartment that could develop compartment syndrome?
A) Anterior compartment
B) Lateral compartment
C) Superficial posterior compartment
D) Deep posterior compartment
questions.answer:
B)
Explanation: The lateral compartment of the leg is where the peroneal muscles reside, which can be affected by lateral malleolus fractures. This compartment is at risk for developing compartment syndrome due to swelling and increased pressures following the injury.

questions.question:
A 14-year-old male presents with knee pain after falling while playing soccer. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the medial aspect of the knee and limited range of motion. An x-ray shows a Salter-Harris Type II fracture at the distal femur growth plate. Which of the following is the most critical concern in the management of this injury?
A) Risk of malunion
B) Risk of premature closure of the growth plate
C) Risk of avascular necrosis
D) Risk of fracture nonunion
questions.answer:
B)
Salter-Harris Type II fractures extend through the growth plate (physis) and into the metaphysis. In a 14-year-old with significant remaining growth, the most critical concern is premature physeal closure, which can lead to limb length discrepancy or angular deformity. The distal femoral physis contributes approximately 70% of femoral longitudinal growth, making growth disturbance here particularly consequential.

A is incorrect because while malunion can occur, it is a lesser concern compared to growth disturbance in a skeletally immature patient, and remodeling potential remains.
C is incorrect because avascular necrosis is not a typical complication of distal femoral Salter-Harris II fractures; AVN is more commonly associated with femoral neck fractures or Salter-Harris injuries about the proximal femur or talus.
D is incorrect because nonunion is uncommon in physeal fractures of the distal femur, as the metaphyseal fragment and rich blood supply promote healing.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old female presents with knee pain and instability after a fall while skiing. She has a history of patellar dislocations and now reports that her kneecap feels loose. Physical examination reveals apprehension with lateral tracking of the patella. What is the most appropriate surgical procedure to address her recurrent patellar instability?
A) Lateral release
B) Medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction
C) Patellar realignment
D) Patellar tendon repair
questions.answer:
B)
Medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) reconstruction is the gold-standard surgical treatment for recurrent patellar instability. The MPFL is the primary soft-tissue restraint to lateral patellar translation and is torn in virtually all traumatic patellar dislocations. Reconstruction restores this restraint and significantly reduces redislocation rates.

A is incorrect because isolated lateral release does not address the fundamental pathology (a deficient MPFL) and, performed alone, can paradoxically worsen medial instability. It may be used as an adjunct but is not the primary procedure for recurrent instability.

C is incorrect because "patellar realignment" (e.g., tibial tubercle osteotomy) is considered when there is a significant bony malalignment such as an elevated TT-TG distance. The stem does not describe such malalignment, making MPFL reconstruction the first-line procedure.

D is incorrect because patellar tendon repair addresses a ruptured patellar tendon (loss of the extensor mechanism), not recurrent patellar instability/dislocation. There is no indication of patellar tendon pathology in this scenario.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman is undergoing a surgical procedure to address her herniated lumbar disc. The surgeon plans to use an anterolateral approach to the lumbar spine. Which anatomical landmark is crucial for identifying the proper incision site during this procedure?
A) Iliac crest
B) Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)
C) Greater trochanter
D) Pubic symphysis
questions.answer:
B)
Explanation: The anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) serves as a key landmark for accessing the lumbar spine via an anterolateral approach. It helps guide the incision to avoid injury to surrounding structures and provides optimal access to the lumbar vertebrae.

questions.question:
A 4-year-old boy presents with an in-toeing gait. On examination, his foot posture reveals a significant internal rotation of the tibia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to evaluate the underlying cause?
A) MRI of the knee
B) Thigh-foot angle measurement
C) Hip X-ray
D) CT scan of the pelvis
questions.answer:
B)
The thigh-foot angle measurement is a useful clinical tool to assess tibial torsion, which is a common cause of in-toeing gait in children. This non-invasive assessment can help determine if the internal rotation is due to tibial torsion or other factors. A is incorrect because an MRI of the knee is not typically used to assess tibial torsion. C is incorrect because a hip X-ray is not necessary for evaluating tibial torsion. D is incorrect because a CT scan of the pelvis is not indicated for assessing tibial torsion in a child with in-toeing gait.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female with a suspected osteosarcoma undergoes a biopsy to confirm the diagnosis. Which principle should be prioritized to ensure the biopsy does not compromise future surgical options?
A) Use fine needle aspiration for a quick diagnosis
B) Ensure the biopsy tract is within the planned resection area
C) Perform an open biopsy to collect a larger sample
D) Conduct multiple biopsies to increase diagnostic yield
questions.answer:
B)
A fundamental principle of musculoskeletal oncology biopsy is that the biopsy tract must lie within the planned surgical resection field. This ensures that any potentially contaminated tissue along the tract is excised en bloc with the tumor, preventing local recurrence and preserving limb-salvage options.

A is incorrect because fine needle aspiration (FNA) often yields insufficient tissue for the histologic subtyping, grading, and special studies required to diagnose osteosarcoma; core needle biopsy or open biopsy is preferred.
C is incorrect because while an open (incisional) biopsy can provide adequate tissue, the question asks about the overriding principle — tract placement — not the biopsy technique. An open biopsy performed outside the planned resection field would compromise future surgery.
D is incorrect because performing multiple biopsies through separate tracts increases the number of contaminated tissue planes, potentially making limb-salvage surgery impossible or requiring a wider resection.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man presents with pain and swelling over the dorsum of his hand after a punch injury. On examination, there is tenderness at the neck of the 5th metacarpal with a depressed knuckle and rotational deformity of the small finger. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Boxer's fracture
B) Bennett's fracture
C) Mallet finger
D) Scaphoid fracture
questions.answer:
A)
A Boxer's fracture is a fracture of the 5th metacarpal neck, the most common metacarpal fracture, typically caused by a closed-fist punch injury. It presents with pain, swelling, a depressed ("lost") small-finger knuckle, and possible rotational malalignment.

B is incorrect because a Bennett's fracture is an intra-articular fracture-dislocation at the base of the 1st metacarpal (thumb CMC joint), not related to a punch mechanism at the 5th metacarpal. C is incorrect because a mallet finger is a disruption of the terminal extensor tendon at the DIP joint, typically from a forced-flexion injury to the fingertip, not a punch injury to the metacarpal. D is incorrect because a scaphoid fracture occurs at the radial side of the wrist (anatomical snuffbox tenderness) from a fall on an outstretched hand, not from a direct punch mechanism at the metacarpal.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman falls and presents with wrist and elbow pain. X-rays show a fracture of the distal humerus. She also reports tingling in her hand and weakness in wrist extension. Upon physical examination, which nerve is most likely compromised due to this fracture?
A) Ulnar nerve
B) Median nerve
C) Radial nerve
D) Musculocutaneous nerve
questions.answer:
C)
The radial nerve is the most likely nerve compromised based on the clinical findings of weakness in wrist extension (wrist drop) and tingling in the hand. The radial nerve courses along the posterior aspect of the humerus and can be injured by distal humeral fracture fragments, particularly supracondylar or distal-third shaft fractures. Injury results in loss of wrist and finger extension and sensory deficit over the dorsal first web space.

A is incorrect because the ulnar nerve, while at risk in distal humerus fractures (especially medial epicondyle), would present with numbness in the ring and small fingers and weakness of intrinsic hand muscles, not wrist drop.
B is incorrect because the median nerve is not commonly injured in distal humeral fractures; its injury would cause weakness of forearm pronation, wrist flexion, and thumb opposition, with sensory loss over the palmar aspect of the lateral 3½ digits.
D is incorrect because the musculocutaneous nerve innervates the anterior arm compartment (biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis) and provides lateral forearm sensation; it is not at risk in distal humeral fractures and its injury would not cause wrist drop.

questions.question:
A 13-year-old girl presents with knee pain and a noticeable deformity of her left leg. Upon examination, her left knee appears hyperextended and her tibial tubercle is prominent. She has a history of rapid growth in the past year. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Osgood-Schlatter disease
B) Tibial tubercle avulsion fracture
C) Tibial recurvatum deformity
D) Patellar tendinopathy
E) Anterior cruciate ligament injury
questions.answer:
A)
Osgood-Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle caused by repetitive stress from the patellar tendon on the developing apophysis, most commonly seen in active adolescents during periods of rapid growth. The hallmark findings are anterior knee pain localized to a prominent, tender tibial tubercle — exactly as described in this stem.

B is incorrect because a tibial tubercle avulsion fracture presents acutely (often with a "pop" during jumping), inability to actively extend the knee, and hemarthrosis, none of which are described here.
C is incorrect because tibial recurvatum deformity refers to a fixed hyperextension deformity of the proximal tibia (e.g., from premature physeal arrest), not the activity-related pain with a prominent tubercle seen here.
D is incorrect because patellar tendinopathy ("jumper's knee") causes pain at the inferior pole of the patella, not at the tibial tubercle.
E is incorrect because an ACL injury would present with joint effusion, instability (positive Lachman/pivot shift), and a history of a pivoting or deceleration injury, not a prominent tibial tubercle.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman sustains an injury during a fall where her knee struck the ground at an awkward angle. She presents with swelling and pain over the anterior aspect of her knee. X-rays reveal a fracture of the proximal tibia. Which surgical approach is most appropriate for addressing a fracture in this location with minimal soft tissue disruption?
A) Posterior approach
B) Lateral approach
C) Anterolateral approach
D) Anterior approach
questions.answer:
C)
The anterolateral approach to the proximal tibia provides excellent exposure of the lateral tibial plateau while minimizing soft tissue disruption. It utilizes the interval between the tibialis anterior and the lateral compartment musculature, preserving the anterior soft tissue envelope and blood supply critical for fracture healing. This is the most commonly used approach for lateral tibial plateau fractures.

A is incorrect because the posterior approach to the proximal tibia is reserved for posterior column or posterior shear fractures (e.g., posterior tibial plateau fractures) and involves more complex dissection around neurovascular structures; it is not the first-line approach for a typical proximal tibial fracture.

B is incorrect because a direct lateral approach risks injury to the common peroneal nerve and does not provide the same versatile exposure of the articular surface as the anterolateral approach.

D is incorrect because a direct anterior approach (e.g., a midline incision) places the skin and soft tissue envelope at higher risk of wound complications due to the subcutaneous nature of the proximal tibia anteriorly, and it does not provide optimal access to the lateral plateau.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man undergoes radial shaft fracture fixation through a volar (Henry) approach. Postoperatively, he reports numbness and paresthesias over the dorsolateral aspect of the hand and the dorsum of the first web space. Motor function of the wrist and fingers is intact. Which nerve is most likely injured?
A) Median nerve
B) Ulnar nerve
C) Superficial radial nerve
D) Posterior interosseous nerve
questions.answer:
C)
