B) Direct tendon repair using suture anchors
C) Reconstruction using a graft from the palmaris longus
D) Non-operative management with splinting
questions.answer:
A)
FPL rupture in the setting of a distal radius fracture is most commonly an attritional rupture (Mannerfelt lesion) caused by bony prominences or hardware. The tendon ends are typically frayed and retracted, precluding direct repair. Tendon transfer is the standard surgical treatment. Transfer of the extensor indicis proprius (EIP) or, more classically, the FDS of the ring finger to the FPL stump is the accepted reconstructive technique to restore thumb IP flexion.

B is incorrect because direct tendon repair with suture anchors is not feasible in attritional ruptures where the tendon ends are degenerated and retracted; suture anchors are used for bony avulsions, not mid-substance tendon failures.
C is incorrect because palmaris longus graft reconstruction (intercalary grafting) is a secondary option when tendon transfer is not available, and it requires an intact proximal muscle-tendon unit with adequate excursion, which is often compromised in attritional ruptures.
D is incorrect because non-operative management of a complete FPL rupture will result in permanent loss of thumb interphalangeal flexion and significant functional impairment; surgical reconstruction is indicated.

questions.question:
A 20-year-old female athlete reports chronic knee pain and a feeling of instability during sports. MRI shows damage to the patellar retinaculum and patellofemoral ligament. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Rest and physical therapy
B) Surgical reconstruction of the retinaculum
C) Knee arthroscopy for debridement
D) Patellar brace application
questions.answer:
B)
Surgical reconstruction of the patellar retinaculum and patellofemoral ligament is indicated to restore stability and function in an athlete with chronic symptoms and structural damage. A is incorrect because rest and physical therapy alone are unlikely to address structural instability. C is incorrect because knee arthroscopy for debridement does not address ligamentous instability. D is incorrect because a patellar brace may provide temporary support but does not correct the underlying structural damage.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman complains of pain and limited range of motion in her shoulder after a fall. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the anterolateral shoulder, and imaging shows a large subacromial bursa. Which surgical approach would be most relevant for addressing this condition while preserving surrounding structures?
A) Anterior approach to the glenohumeral joint
B) Posterior approach to the shoulder
C) Anterolateral approach
D) Subscapular approach
questions.answer:
C)
The anterolateral (deltoid-splitting) approach provides direct access to the subacromial space and is the standard approach for subacromial bursectomy or decompression. It splits the deltoid in line with its fibers, preserving the deltoid origin and the axillary nerve (which must not be violated beyond ~5 cm distal to the acromion).

A is incorrect because the anterior approach (deltopectoral) targets the glenohumeral joint and is not designed for subacromial pathology; it would not provide direct access to the subacromial bursa.
B is incorrect because the posterior approach accesses the posterior glenohumeral joint or infraspinatus fossa and does not address subacromial pathology.
D is incorrect because a subscapular approach targets the anterior glenohumeral joint/subscapularis and is not relevant to subacromial bursal disease.

questions.question:
A 10-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after a skateboard accident. His left arm is painful and held in a position of flexion and adduction. An x-ray shows a type III supracondylar humerus fracture. What is the most appropriate definitive treatment for this injury?
A) Closed reduction and splinting
B) Open reduction and internal fixation
C) Closed reduction and percutaneous pinning
D) Functional bracing
questions.answer:
C)
A type III (Gartland III) supracondylar humerus fracture is a completely displaced fracture and represents the most common indication for surgical intervention in pediatric elbow fractures. The standard of care is closed reduction and percutaneous pinning (typically with lateral-entry or crossed K-wires) performed urgently to restore alignment, maintain reduction, and minimize the risk of neurovascular complications and malunion.

A is incorrect because closed reduction and splinting alone cannot reliably maintain reduction of a completely displaced (type III) fracture; redisplacement is expected without pin fixation. B is incorrect because open reduction and internal fixation is reserved for cases where closed reduction fails (irreducible fractures) or when there is vascular compromise requiring open exploration; it is not the first-line definitive treatment. D is incorrect because functional bracing is used for certain adult humeral shaft fractures and has no role in the management of displaced pediatric supracondylar fractures.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female patient with chronic ankle instability has undergone a peroneal tendon repair. During rehabilitation, she begins to experience posterior ankle pain after activities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
A) Achilles tendon rupture
B) Flexor hallucis longus tendinitis
C) Anterior talofibular ligament tear
D) Peroneal tendon subluxation
questions.answer:
B)
Following peroneal tendon repair, altered hindfoot biomechanics and compensatory overuse can lead to flexor hallucis longus (FHL) tendinitis. The FHL runs through a fibro-osseous tunnel posterior to the ankle between the medial and lateral talar tubercles, and its irritation classically produces posterior ankle pain with activity, particularly with push-off. This is consistent with the described presentation.

A is incorrect because Achilles tendon rupture presents with acute inability to plantarflex, a palpable gap, and a positive Thompson test, rather than insidious posterior ankle pain with activity.

C is incorrect because an anterior talofibular ligament tear would cause anterolateral ankle pain and instability (positive anterior drawer), not posterior ankle pain.

D is incorrect because peroneal tendon subluxation presents with lateral (retromalleolar) snapping or pain behind the lateral malleolus, not posterior ankle pain. Although it is a recognized complication after peroneal surgery, the location of symptoms described in the stem is more consistent with FHL pathology.

questions.question:
During a total hip arthroplasty, a 65-year-old male experiences an intraoperative fracture of the femur while utilizing an anterior Smith-Petersen approach. Which of the following techniques is most likely to help prevent this complication in future cases?
A) Increase the depth of the acetabular reaming
B) Use a larger femoral head
C) Avoid excessive retraction on the femur
D) Pre-drill the femoral canal
questions.answer:
C)
Avoiding excessive retraction on the femur is the most effective technique to prevent intraoperative femoral fractures during the direct anterior (Smith-Petersen) approach. The proximal femur is at risk because it must be elevated and externally rotated for canal preparation and stem insertion; excessive force or aggressive retraction creates a fulcrum that can cause a calcar or greater trochanter fracture. Gentle handling, adequate soft-tissue release, and proper patient positioning on a specialized table all reduce this risk.

A is incorrect because increasing the depth of acetabular reaming addresses the acetabular side and does not reduce stress on the femur during stem preparation.
B is incorrect because using a larger femoral head affects stability and range of motion but does not mitigate the mechanical forces on the proximal femur that lead to intraoperative fracture.
D is incorrect because pre-drilling the femoral canal is not a standard technique in cementless THA; sequential broaching is used, and the fracture risk is related to retraction forces on the femur rather than canal preparation method.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male presents with a wrist injury after falling onto an outstretched hand. On examination, there is localized tenderness over the snuffbox, and an x-ray shows no visible fracture. Which of the following imaging studies is most appropriate to definitively rule out a scaphoid fracture?
A) MRI of the wrist
B) CT scan of the wrist
C) Ultrasound of the wrist
D) Repeat x-ray in 2 weeks
questions.answer:
A)
MRI of the wrist is the most sensitive and specific imaging modality for detecting an occult scaphoid fracture when initial plain films are negative. MRI can identify bone-marrow edema, non-displaced cortical fractures, and associated soft-tissue injuries, making it the definitive study to rule out a scaphoid fracture.

B is incorrect because CT scan, while excellent for characterizing known fractures and surgical planning, has lower sensitivity than MRI for detecting occult, non-displaced fractures (it cannot reliably detect bone-marrow edema). C is incorrect because ultrasound has limited sensitivity and specificity for scaphoid fractures and is not a standard diagnostic tool for this purpose. D is incorrect because repeat x-rays in 2 weeks may show a fracture line due to bone resorption, but this delays diagnosis and is not definitive — up to 20% of scaphoid fractures may remain occult on plain films even at follow-up.

questions.question:
A 16-year-old girl diagnosed with osteosarcoma reports that she has experienced pain in her knee for several months, and imaging reveals a primary tumor in the femur along with a second lesion in the proximal tibia. What is the term used to describe this finding?
A) Skip lesions
B) Multifocal disease
C) Metastatic spread
D) Local recurrence
questions.answer:
A)
Skip lesions in osteosarcoma are defined as additional foci of tumor within the same bone or across an adjacent joint, separated by intervening normal marrow from the primary lesion. A primary osteosarcoma in the distal femur with a separate lesion in the proximal tibia (transarticular skip) fits this definition and is a well-recognized pattern that worsens prognosis and must be identified for surgical planning.

B is incorrect because multifocal osteosarcoma (also called multifocal sclerotic osteosarcoma or osteosarcomatosis) refers to synchronous lesions in multiple, non-contiguous skeletal sites (e.g., femur and humerus), not two lesions in the same limb separated by a joint. C is incorrect because metastatic spread implies hematogenous dissemination to distant organs (typically lungs) or distant bones; a second lesion in the ipsilateral proximal tibia adjacent to a distal femoral primary is classified as a skip lesion, not a distant metastasis. D is incorrect because local recurrence refers to tumor regrowth at the site of a previously treated lesion; this patient has a newly diagnosed primary tumor with a synchronous second focus, not a recurrence.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old male with a history of osteoarthritis in his first metatarsophalangeal joint is experiencing increasing pain and decreased range of motion. Upon examination, there is significant stiffness and bone spur formation. After discussing treatment options, which procedure would be most appropriate for addressing the symptoms of hallux rigidus in this patient?
A) Cheilectomy
B) Arthrodesis
C) Osteotomy
D) Arthroplasty
questions.answer:
B)
Arthrodesis (first MTP fusion) is the gold-standard treatment for advanced hallux rigidus with significant joint stiffness, decreased range of motion, and extensive osteophyte formation. In a 62-year-old with these findings, fusion reliably eliminates pain and provides a stable, durable result.

A is incorrect because cheilectomy is indicated for early-stage (Grade 1–2) hallux rigidus where symptoms are primarily due to dorsal impingement and the joint still has reasonable cartilage preservation; it would be insufficient for the advanced disease described in this stem. C is incorrect because osteotomy (e.g., Moberg dorsal closing-wedge) is used as an adjunct in mild-to-moderate disease to improve dorsiflexion and is not appropriate as a standalone procedure for advanced hallux rigidus. D is incorrect because first MTP arthroplasty (implant or interpositional) has historically shown inferior long-term outcomes compared to arthrodesis for advanced hallux rigidus and is not considered the standard of care, particularly in an active patient.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old athlete presents with acute low back pain after lifting a heavy weight. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the lumbar spine, and MRI shows a herniated disc at L4-L5. After conservative management fails, what is the most appropriate surgical intervention?
A) Spinal fusion
B) Microdiscectomy
C) Laminectomy
D) Artificial disc replacement
questions.answer:
B)
Microdiscectomy is the gold-standard first-line surgical intervention for a lumbar disc herniation that has failed adequate conservative management. It involves removal of the herniated disc fragment through a small incision with minimal disruption of surrounding structures, providing reliable relief of radiculopathy with a high success rate and low morbidity.

A is incorrect because spinal fusion is not indicated for a simple disc herniation without instability, spondylolisthesis, or recurrent herniations; it is a more invasive procedure with greater morbidity and loss of motion.
C is incorrect because a laminectomy alone removes the lamina to decompress the canal but does not specifically address the herniated disc fragment; it is more commonly used for spinal stenosis rather than a focal disc herniation.
D is incorrect because artificial disc replacement is primarily considered in the cervical spine or in highly selected lumbar cases; it is not the standard first-line surgical treatment for a typical lumbar disc herniation.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a fall from a ladder. He complains of severe lower back pain and difficulty moving his legs. Physical examination reveals bilateral lower extremity weakness and diminished reflexes. An MRI shows a central disc herniation at the L3-L4 level. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Immediate surgical intervention
B) Conservative management with physical therapy
C) Epidural steroid injection
D) Lumbar laminectomy
questions.answer:
A)
Immediate surgical intervention is the most appropriate next step. This patient presents with bilateral lower extremity weakness, diminished reflexes, and a central disc herniation at L3-L4 — a classic presentation of cauda equina syndrome. Cauda equina syndrome is a surgical emergency requiring urgent decompression (typically within 24–48 hours) to prevent permanent neurological deficits including paralysis and bowel/bladder dysfunction.

B is incorrect because conservative management with physical therapy is inappropriate when there are signs of cauda equina syndrome with progressive bilateral neurological deficits; delay risks permanent damage. C is incorrect because epidural steroid injections are used for chronic radiculopathy without red-flag neurological findings and have no role in acute cauda equina syndrome. D is incorrect because while lumbar laminectomy is a specific surgical technique that may be used during the decompression, the question asks about the next step in management — the correct concept is immediate surgical intervention (emergent decompression), not a specific elective procedure choice; additionally, 'lumbar laminectomy' as listed here is a distractor meant to differentiate urgency from a named procedure.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old male presents to the emergency department after falling from a ladder while trimming a tree. He complains of severe pain and swelling in his right foot. On examination, there is tenderness over the first and second tarsometatarsal (TMT) joints, and an x-ray reveals a fracture at the base of the second metatarsal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Conservative treatment with a walking boot
B) 1st and 2nd TMT arthrodesis
C) Open reduction and internal fixation of the fracture
D) Referral for physical therapy
E) Application of a short leg cast
questions.answer:
C)
A fracture at the base of the second metatarsal with tenderness over the first and second TMT joints after a high-energy fall is the hallmark of a Lisfranc (tarsometatarsal) injury. The second metatarsal base is the "keystone" of the Lisfranc joint complex, and fracture here implies ligamentous disruption and joint instability. Open reduction and internal fixation is the standard of care for displaced or unstable Lisfranc injuries to restore anatomic alignment and prevent post-traumatic arthritis.

A is incorrect because conservative treatment with a walking boot does not provide adequate stability for a displaced Lisfranc injury and risks malunion, chronic instability, and painful arthritis. B is incorrect because primary arthrodesis of the 1st and 2nd TMT joints may be considered in purely ligamentous Lisfranc injuries or revision settings, but ORIF is the most appropriate initial surgical step for an acute fracture-dislocation pattern. D is incorrect because physical therapy alone cannot address the bony and ligamentous instability of a Lisfranc injury. E is incorrect because a short leg cast does not provide sufficient reduction or fixation for a displaced Lisfranc fracture-dislocation and risks loss of alignment.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old woman presents after a fall with severe pain in her right hip. X-rays reveal a periprosthetic fracture around her total hip arthroplasty implant. The surgical team plans to revise the implant. Which of the following is the most appropriate first step in the management of her fracture?
A) Immediate reimplantation of the same prosthesis
B) Application of a hip brace for stabilization
C) Removal of the existing implant
D) Placement of cerclage wires and immediate reimplantation
questions.answer:
C)
In the setting of a periprosthetic fracture requiring revision arthroplasty (e.g., Vancouver B2 or B3 with a loose stem), the first intraoperative step is removal of the existing implant. This allows full assessment of fracture pattern, bone stock, and canal geometry to guide selection of the appropriate revision construct.

A is incorrect because immediate reimplantation of the same prosthesis without first removing it and assessing the fracture and bone quality is not appropriate; the original implant is likely loose and the same implant may not provide adequate fixation.
B is incorrect because a hip brace does not provide sufficient stabilization for a periprosthetic fracture around a loose implant and would not address the underlying implant loosening.
D is incorrect because placing cerclage wires and immediately reimplanting without first removing the existing implant and thoroughly evaluating the fracture and bone stock does not allow proper surgical planning and risks inadequate fixation.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male presents with a traumatic injury to the lower leg after a motorcycle accident. The initial x-ray shows a spiral fracture of the fibula, but the patient also exhibits significant swelling and tenderness around the knee joint. Which of the following factors would be most important to predict the extent of soft tissue injury and potential need for amputation?
A) The location of the fibula fracture
B) The degree of fracture displacement
C) The presence of any vascular compromise
D) The patient's age and comorbid conditions
questions.answer:
C)
Vascular compromise is the single most important factor in predicting the extent of soft tissue injury and the potential need for amputation after a high-energy lower extremity injury. Validated scoring systems such as the Mangled Extremity Severity Score (MESS) heavily weight limb ischemia and warm ischemia time. Absence of distal pulses or prolonged ischemia markedly increases the likelihood of amputation.

A is incorrect because while fracture location contributes to overall injury assessment, it is not the most critical predictor of amputation risk compared to vascular status. B is incorrect because fracture displacement alone does not reliably predict the need for amputation; many displaced fractures are successfully reconstructed when perfusion is intact. D is incorrect because although age and comorbidities influence outcomes and are included in scoring systems, they are secondary to vascular status in determining limb salvageability.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman presents with a non-healing fracture of the radius after a fall. She reports no significant medical history and denies any smoking or alcohol use. A workup for non-union is initiated. Which of the following laboratory tests would be most informative in assessing for potential infection?
A) Serum calcium levels
B) Complete blood count with differential
C) Serum vitamin D levels
D) Bone density scan
questions.answer:
B)
When evaluating a non-healing fracture for potential infection (septic non-union), laboratory markers of infection are essential. Among the listed options, a complete blood count (CBC) with differential is the most informative for assessing infection, as leukocytosis with a left shift (elevated neutrophils) can suggest an infectious etiology. Although ESR and CRP are more sensitive markers for infection in non-union workups, they are not offered as choices here.

A is incorrect because serum calcium levels assess metabolic bone health and calcium homeostasis (e.g., hyperparathyroidism) but do not evaluate for infection. C is incorrect because serum vitamin D levels help identify metabolic deficiency contributing to impaired bone healing but are not informative for detecting infection. D is incorrect because a bone density scan (DEXA) measures bone mineral density to assess osteoporosis risk and does not provide information about infection.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man sustains an injury to his right ring finger while playing football. He grabbed an opponent's jersey and felt a sudden pop. On examination, there is swelling at the volar fingertip, the DIP joint rests in extension, and the patient cannot actively flex the distal interphalangeal joint. Which of the following classifications should be applied to assess this injury?
A) Lichtman Classification
B) Leddy and Packer Classification
C) Salter-Harris Classification
D) Gustilo Classification
questions.answer:
B)
The Leddy and Packer Classification is used to classify closed avulsion injuries of the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon, known as jersey finger. It categorizes injuries into types based on the level of tendon retraction and the presence of a bony fragment, which directly guides the urgency and type of surgical repair. This patient's mechanism (grabbing a jersey) and inability to flex the DIP joint are classic for jersey finger.

A is incorrect because the Lichtman Classification is used for Kienböck disease (avascular necrosis of the lunate), not flexor tendon injuries. C is incorrect because the Salter-Harris Classification is used for physeal (growth plate) fractures in skeletally immature patients and is not applicable here. D is incorrect because the Gustilo Classification is used for open fractures to grade the severity of soft-tissue injury, not for closed tendon avulsions.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a fall on an outstretched hand. He reports pain and swelling in his wrist and has difficulty moving his thumb. An x-ray reveals a fracture at the base of the first metacarpal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Splinting and referral for follow-up in two weeks
B) Closed reduction and casting if stable
C) Surgical fixation due to potential for CMC joint instability
D) Initiate physical therapy for range of motion
E) MRI to assess for ligamentous injury
questions.answer:
C)
Surgical fixation is often indicated for fractures at the base of the first metacarpal due to the risk of carpometacarpal joint instability, especially with significant displacement or angulation. Proper surgical management prevents long-term functional impairment.
A is incorrect because splinting and delayed follow-up may not address potential instability. B is incorrect because closed reduction and casting may not stabilize the joint adequately if there is significant displacement. D is incorrect because initiating physical therapy without addressing the fracture stability is inappropriate. E is incorrect because MRI is not the immediate next step for fracture management.

questions.question:
A young soccer player sustains a direct blow to the lateral knee during a game. Following the injury, he reports persistent pain and swelling, and physical examination reveals a tense compartment. Which condition should be urgently assessed to prevent further complications?
A) Medial meniscus tear
B) Compartment syndrome
C) Anterior cruciate ligament tear
D) Popliteal artery injury
questions.answer:
B)
The finding of a tense compartment on physical examination after a direct blow to the lateral knee raises urgent concern for compartment syndrome, a surgical emergency. If not promptly treated with fasciotomy, elevated intracompartmental pressures can lead to irreversible ischemic damage to muscles and nerves (Volkmann-type contracture equivalent in the leg).

A is incorrect because a medial meniscus tear presents with joint-line tenderness, effusion, and mechanical symptoms (locking, catching), not a tense compartment. C is incorrect because an anterior cruciate ligament tear causes knee instability and hemarthrosis but does not produce a tense compartment requiring emergent intervention. D is incorrect because while popliteal artery injury is a vascular emergency that should also be considered with knee trauma, the stem specifically describes a tense compartment on examination, which points directly to compartment syndrome as the most urgent diagnosis to assess.

questions.question:
A 68-year-old male with a history of osteoarthritis presents with hip pain that worsens with activity. During the physical exam, the patient exhibits pain with internal rotation of the hip. What does this finding suggest about the underlying pathology?
A) Trochanteric bursitis
B) Labral tear
C) Osteonecrosis
D) Advanced hip osteoarthritis
questions.answer:
D)
Pain with internal rotation of the hip is a classic physical examination finding in advanced hip osteoarthritis. Internal rotation compresses the degenerative articular surfaces and narrows the already-compromised joint space, reproducing the patient's symptoms. Combined with the history of known OA and activity-related pain, this finding strongly suggests progressive intra-articular cartilage loss.

A is incorrect because trochanteric bursitis presents with lateral hip/greater trochanter tenderness and pain with resisted abduction or direct palpation, not primarily with internal rotation of the hip joint.
B is incorrect because a labral tear can cause pain with provocative maneuvers (e.g., FADIR), but in a 68-year-old with established osteoarthritis and activity-related pain, advanced OA is the far more likely diagnosis; labral tears are more commonly a consideration in younger patients with mechanical symptoms such as clicking or catching.
C is incorrect because osteonecrosis (AVN) can cause hip pain and limited internal rotation, but it typically presents with groin pain at rest or night pain and is associated with risk factors such as corticosteroid use or alcohol abuse, none of which are described here; the clinical picture is most consistent with OA.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male sustains a high-energy injury from a motorcycle accident and presents with severe thigh pain and swelling. Imaging reveals a comminuted femur fracture in the mid-shaft region. Which of the following muscles is likely to be most affected by this type of injury?
A) Gluteus maximus
B) Quadriceps femoris
C) Adductor magnus
D) Biceps femoris
questions.answer:
B)
The quadriceps femoris — particularly the vastus intermedius, which originates directly from the anterior and lateral surfaces of the femoral shaft — is the muscle group most likely affected by a comminuted mid-shaft femur fracture. Its intimate apposition to the femoral diaphysis makes it vulnerable to direct injury, hemorrhage, and subsequent functional impairment of knee extension.

A is incorrect because the gluteus maximus inserts on the gluteal tuberosity of the proximal femur and the iliotibial band; it is not in close proximity to the mid-shaft region. C is incorrect because the adductor magnus originates from the ischium/pubis and inserts along the linea aspera and adductor tubercle; while it has some femoral attachment, it is more medial/posterior and less directly involved than the quadriceps overlying the mid-shaft. D is incorrect because the biceps femoris (long head) originates from the ischial tuberosity and only its short head arises from the lateral lip of the linea aspera in the distal third of the femur, making it less affected by a mid-shaft fracture than the quadriceps.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male presents to the emergency department after falling from a height while rock climbing. He complains of severe pain in his left shoulder and has difficulty raising his arm. On examination, there is swelling over the lateral shoulder and tenderness over the clavicle. X-rays reveal a displaced fracture of the midclavicle. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for this injury?
A) Immediate surgical fixation
B) Sling immobilization and analgesia
C) Physical therapy
D) Open reduction and internal fixation
E) Observation without intervention
questions.answer:
B)
For a displaced midshaft clavicle fracture, initial management in the emergency department consists of sling immobilization and analgesia to provide comfort and protect the limb. Definitive treatment decisions—including possible operative fixation for significantly displaced or shortened fractures—are made after appropriate outpatient follow-up, but the most appropriate *initial* step is non-operative stabilization.

A is incorrect because immediate surgical fixation is not performed emergently for isolated clavicle fractures; surgery, when indicated, is scheduled electively after swelling subsides and the patient is optimized. C is incorrect because physical therapy is not appropriate as initial management of an acute displaced fracture; it is introduced later during rehabilitation. D is incorrect because, while ORIF may ultimately be indicated for a displaced midshaft clavicle fracture, it is not the initial management step in the emergency setting. E is incorrect because observation without any intervention (no sling, no analgesia) would leave the patient in unnecessary pain and without limb support, which is substandard acute care.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman presents with a humeral shaft fracture after a motor vehicle accident. An x-ray shows the fracture with 15 degrees of anterior angulation and 1.5 cm of displacement. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Surgical fixation
B) Non-operative management with a brace
C) Immediate orthopedic consultation
D) Repeat x-ray in 2 weeks
questions.answer:
B)
Humeral shaft fractures are well-managed non-operatively with a functional brace (Sarmiento brace). Accepted non-operative parameters include up to 20° of anterior-posterior angulation, 30° of varus/valgus angulation, and up to 3 cm of shortening. This fracture with 15° of anterior angulation and 1.5 cm of displacement falls within those limits, so functional bracing is the most appropriate treatment.

A is incorrect because surgical fixation is reserved for humeral shaft fractures that exceed acceptable alignment parameters, are open, have associated vascular injury, are bilateral, or involve a floating elbow — none of which apply here. C is incorrect because while orthopedic follow-up is appropriate, the question asks for the next step in management, which is initiating treatment with a brace; an urgent orthopedic consultation is not necessary for a fracture within acceptable alignment. D is incorrect because simply repeating imaging without initiating any treatment (bracing) is not appropriate management; the fracture should be immobilized in a functional brace with scheduled follow-up.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with weakness in the flexor pollicis longus and the flexor digitorum profundus to the index finger. She is unable to make an "OK" sign. There is no sensory loss in the hand. Which nerve is primarily affected, and what condition does this presentation suggest?
A) Ulnar nerve; ulnar neuropathy
B) Median nerve; anterior interosseous syndrome
C) Median nerve; carpal tunnel syndrome
D) Radial nerve; posterior interosseous syndrome
questions.answer:
B)
The anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) is a pure motor branch of the median nerve that innervates the flexor pollicis longus, the flexor digitorum profundus to the index (and sometimes middle) finger, and the pronator quadratus. Weakness of FPL and FDP with inability to form an "OK" sign and absence of sensory loss is the hallmark of anterior interosseous syndrome. Rheumatoid arthritis can cause AIN compression through synovitis or structural changes in the proximal forearm.

A is incorrect because the ulnar nerve innervates the FDP to the ring and small fingers and the intrinsic muscles of the hand (interossei, hypothenar muscles); it does not supply FPL or FDP to the index finger. C is incorrect because carpal tunnel syndrome involves compression of the median nerve at the wrist, causing sensory loss in the radial 3½ digits and thenar (APB/opponens pollicis) weakness — it does not affect FPL or FDP, which are innervated proximal to the carpal tunnel. D is incorrect because the posterior interosseous nerve is a branch of the radial nerve supplying wrist and finger extensors; its compression causes weakness of finger/wrist extension, not flexor weakness.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old woman is diagnosed with a femoral neck fracture after falling at home. After discussing treatment options with her, the orthopedic surgeon mentions the importance of minimizing postoperative complications. Which of the following factors should be prioritized during the surgical approach to optimize recovery?
A) Preservation of the gluteus medius
B) Extensive dissection of surrounding muscles
C) Aggressive manipulation of the fracture
D) Using a posterior approach for better visualization
questions.answer:
A)
Preservation of the gluteus medius is critical during hip surgery because it is the primary hip abductor and stabilizer. Damage to the gluteus medius leads to a Trendelenburg gait, impaired mobility, and increased fall risk, all of which significantly compromise postoperative recovery in elderly patients.

B is incorrect because extensive dissection of surrounding muscles increases blood loss, soft-tissue damage, and the risk of postoperative weakness and dislocation; minimizing dissection is a fundamental principle of optimizing recovery.
C is incorrect because aggressive manipulation of the fracture can further compromise the already tenuous blood supply to the femoral head and damage surrounding soft tissues, worsening outcomes.
D is incorrect because while the posterior approach provides good visualization, it is associated with a higher dislocation rate compared to anterior or anterolateral approaches; the question asks about prioritizing factors to optimize recovery, and preserving the gluteus medius (relevant to lateral/anterolateral approaches) is the best answer among the choices listed.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old patient presents with a suspected compartment syndrome following a tibial fracture. The intra-compartmental pressure is measured, and the reading indicates a value of 35 mmHg. What does this value suggest regarding the patient's condition?
A) Normal compartment pressure
B) Mild compartment syndrome
C) Severe compartment syndrome
D) Compartment syndrome is unlikely
questions.answer:
C)
An intra-compartmental pressure of 35 mmHg in the setting of a tibial fracture with clinical suspicion of compartment syndrome is highly concerning. Absolute pressures greater than 30 mmHg (or a delta pressure [diastolic BP − compartment pressure] ≤ 30 mmHg) are widely accepted thresholds for fasciotomy. This reading, combined with the clinical scenario, is consistent with compartment syndrome requiring emergent surgical intervention.

A is incorrect because normal resting compartment pressure is typically 0–8 mmHg; 35 mmHg is far above normal.
B is incorrect because a pressure of 35 mmHg exceeds the 30 mmHg threshold and, in the context of a tibial fracture with suspected compartment syndrome, represents a surgical emergency rather than a mild or equivocal finding.
D is incorrect because 35 mmHg in a symptomatic patient after a tibial fracture strongly supports the diagnosis of compartment syndrome; it cannot be dismissed as unlikely.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman presents with pain and swelling over her thenar eminence after repetitive use of her hand as a factory worker. On examination, there is tenderness in the thenar crease, and she has difficulty opposing her thumb. Which of the following interventions would be most appropriate to manage her condition?
A) Corticosteroid injection
B) Surgical release of the flexor pollicis brevis
C) Splinting and activity modification
D) Physical therapy focused on strengthening exercises
questions.answer:
C)
In cases of overuse-related thenar muscle strain or flexor pollicis brevis tenosynovitis from repetitive hand use, initial management is conservative: splinting (thumb spica) and activity modification to reduce mechanical stress on the inflamed structures. This approach is first-line and is effective in the majority of occupational overuse injuries.

A is incorrect because corticosteroid injection may be considered if conservative measures fail, but it is not the most appropriate initial intervention for an overuse injury without a confirmed diagnosis requiring injection.
B is incorrect because surgical release of the flexor pollicis brevis is not a standard procedure for overuse tendinopathy and would only be considered after failure of prolonged conservative treatment, if at all.
D is incorrect because strengthening exercises during the acute inflammatory phase can worsen symptoms; initial management should focus on rest and offloading before progressing to rehabilitation.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old boy presents to the clinic with bowing of his legs. X-rays show widening of the growth plates. According to the Heuter-Volkmann law, what is the most likely effect on the growth plates due to mechanical compression?
A) Increased growth rate
B) Decreased growth rate
C) No effect on growth
D) Irregular bone formation
questions.answer:
B)
The Heuter-Volkmann law states that increased compressive forces across a physis inhibit (decrease) longitudinal growth, while reduced compression (or tension) stimulates growth. In this child with leg bowing, asymmetric mechanical compression on the growth plates leads to decreased growth on the compressed side, perpetuating or worsening the deformity.

A is incorrect because increased compression suppresses, rather than stimulates, physeal growth according to the Heuter-Volkmann law; it is reduced compression (or tension) that accelerates growth.
C is incorrect because the Heuter-Volkmann law specifically describes a direct relationship between mechanical loading and physeal growth rate — mechanical forces do have an effect.
D is incorrect because while irregular bone formation can occur in various pathologic conditions, the Heuter-Volkmann law specifically addresses the rate of longitudinal growth in response to compressive forces, not irregular ossification patterns.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male presents with a suspected hip dislocation after a sports injury. Physical examination reveals his hip in an externally rotated position. Which of the following muscles forms a conjoined tendon with the superior and inferior gemelli and inserts into the greater trochanter to externally rotate the hip?
A) Gluteus maximus
B) Superior gemellus
C) Obturator internus
D) Inferior gemellus
questions.answer:
C)
The obturator internus forms a conjoined tendon (the triceps coxae) with the superior and inferior gemelli muscles. It originates from the obturator membrane and surrounding pelvic bones, exits through the lesser sciatic foramen, and inserts on the medial surface of the greater trochanter. Together these three muscles are important short external rotators of the hip.

A is incorrect because the gluteus maximus is a powerful external rotator but does not form a conjoined tendon with the gemelli; it inserts on the iliotibial band and gluteal tuberosity.
B is incorrect because the superior gemellus is one of the flanking muscles that joins the obturator internus tendon — it does not independently form the central tendon described in the stem.
D is incorrect because the inferior gemellus similarly blends into the obturator internus tendon rather than being the primary muscle of the conjoined unit; the stem asks for the central muscle around which the gemelli are organized.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female presents with chronic groin pain and difficulty with activities such as walking and climbing stairs. She reports a history of pubic symphysis pain after running marathons. Physical examination reveals tenderness in the anterior pelvic region. Which of the following conditions is she most likely suffering from?
A) Osteitis pubis
B) Hip flexor strain
C) Labral tear
D) Femoroacetabular impingement
questions.answer:
A)
Osteitis pubis is characterized by inflammation of the pubic symphysis, commonly seen in athletes and individuals with repetitive stress to the pelvic region. The history of chronic groin pain localized to the anterior pelvis with pubic symphysis tenderness after marathon running strongly supports this diagnosis.

B is incorrect because a hip flexor strain typically presents with pain on resisted hip flexion and tenderness over the iliopsoas or rectus femoris, not over the pubic symphysis itself.
C is incorrect because a labral tear usually presents with deep groin or hip joint pain, mechanical symptoms (clicking/catching), and a positive anterior impingement test, rather than isolated pubic symphysis tenderness.
D is incorrect because femoroacetabular impingement presents with groin pain worsened by hip flexion and internal rotation (positive impingement test) and is localized to the hip joint, not the pubic symphysis.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old male is involved in a high-energy motor vehicle collision and presents to the emergency department with pelvic pain and instability. Upon examination, he exhibits a 2 cm diastasis of the pubic symphysis and fractures of both pubic rami. Using the Tile classification of pelvic ring injuries, which type does this scenario best represent?
A) Type A
B) Type B
C) Type C
D) None of the above
questions.answer:
B)
In the Tile classification, Type B injuries are rotationally unstable but vertically stable. A 2 cm pubic symphysis diastasis with bilateral pubic rami fractures indicates disruption of the anterior pelvic ring with partial posterior ring involvement, consistent with a Type B ("open-book" or external rotation) injury pattern. The posterior ligamentous structures (sacroiliac ligaments, pelvic floor) remain partially intact, preserving vertical stability.

A is incorrect because Type A injuries are stable injuries (e.g., avulsion fractures, undisplaced iliac wing fractures) with no disruption of the pelvic ring integrity. C is incorrect because Type C injuries are both rotationally and vertically unstable, implying complete disruption of the posterior sacroiliac complex, which is not described in this stem. D is incorrect because this injury pattern clearly fits the Tile Type B category.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female athlete sustains an inversion injury to her ankle while landing from a jump. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the lateral aspect of her ankle and positive anterior drawer and talar tilt tests. Which ligament is primarily injured in this type of injury?
A) Anterior talofibular ligament
B) Calcaneofibular ligament
C) Posterior talofibular ligament
D) Deltoid ligament
questions.answer:
A)
The anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) is the most commonly injured ligament in lateral ankle sprains caused by inversion. It is the weakest of the lateral ankle ligaments and the primary restraint to anterior translation of the talus; it is the first ligament to fail during an inversion injury. A positive anterior drawer test specifically indicates ATFL insufficiency. The positive talar tilt test suggests additional injury to the calcaneofibular ligament, but the ATFL remains the primarily injured structure.

B is incorrect because the calcaneofibular ligament (CFL) is the secondary restraint to inversion and is typically injured after the ATFL has already been disrupted (grade II or III sprains). It is not the primary ligament injured.
C is incorrect because the posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL) is the strongest of the lateral ankle ligaments and is rarely injured except in severe ankle dislocations.
D is incorrect because the deltoid ligament is on the medial side of the ankle and resists eversion forces; it would not be injured in an inversion mechanism.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a fall from standing height, complaining of hip pain. An x-ray reveals an intertrochanteric fracture with standard obliquity. Which of the following is the most appropriate surgical intervention for this type of fracture?
A) Hemiarthroplasty
B) Sliding hip screw
C) Intramedullary nail
D) Total hip arthroplasty
questions.answer:
B)
A sliding hip screw (SHS) is the gold-standard implant for stable (standard-obliquity) intertrochanteric hip fractures. It provides controlled, dynamic compression across the fracture site via the sliding mechanism, promotes healing, and allows early weight-bearing. Multiple studies and OITE teaching confirm the SHS as the preferred device for stable intertrochanteric fracture patterns.

A is incorrect because hemiarthroplasty is indicated for displaced femoral neck fractures in elderly patients, not for intertrochanteric fractures where internal fixation is the standard of care.
C is incorrect because an intramedullary nail (e.g., cephalomedullary nail) is preferred for unstable or reverse-obliquity intertrochanteric fractures and subtrochanteric fractures; for a standard-obliquity (stable) pattern, the SHS is equally effective and more cost-efficient.
D is incorrect because total hip arthroplasty is reserved for femoral neck fractures in active elderly patients with pre-existing arthritis, not for intertrochanteric fractures.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male construction worker sustains a fall from height and presents with severe mid-back pain and difficulty breathing. Examination reveals paradoxical movement of the left shoulder blade during arm elevation. Which muscle is most likely impaired due to potential thoracic spine injury?
A) Rhomboid major
B) Serratus anterior
C) Trapezius
D) Levator scapulae
questions.answer:
B)
The serratus anterior muscle, innervated by the long thoracic nerve (C5-C7), anchors the scapula to the thoracic wall. Injury to this nerve — which can occur with thoracic trauma or traction — causes medial winging of the scapula and paradoxical scapular movement during arm elevation, exactly as described in this stem.

A is incorrect because rhomboid major dysfunction (dorsal scapular nerve, C5) causes lateral winging of the scapula, not the classic medial winging with paradoxical movement described here. B is incorrect — skip (correct answer). C is incorrect because trapezius palsy (spinal accessory nerve, CN XI) causes lateral scapular winging and shoulder droop, but does not produce the paradoxical scapular movement pattern described. D is incorrect because levator scapulae dysfunction would impair scapular elevation but does not cause scapular winging or paradoxical movement during arm elevation.

questions.question:
A patient comes to the clinic with complaints of pain and swelling in the base of the thumb, especially during pinch and grip activities. An MRI reveals joint degeneration. What is the most appropriate surgical intervention for this condition?
A) Total wrist arthroplasty
B) Scaphoidectomy
C) Trapeziectomy with ligament reconstruction
D) Arthroscopy with debridement
questions.answer:
C)
Trapeziectomy with ligament reconstruction and tendon interposition (LRTI) is the most well-established surgical treatment for symptomatic basal joint (first carpometacarpal / trapeziometacarpal) arthritis of the thumb that has failed conservative management. Removing the trapezium eliminates the arthritic bone-on-bone contact, and ligament reconstruction provides stability to prevent proximal migration of the first metacarpal, resulting in reliable pain relief and improved pinch and grip function.

A is incorrect because total wrist arthroplasty addresses the radiocarpal joint, not the first CMC joint, and is indicated for conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis affecting the wrist. B is incorrect because scaphoidectomy (often combined with four-corner fusion) is used for scapholunate advanced collapse (SLAC) or scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse (SNAC) wrist arthritis, not thumb basal joint arthritis. D is incorrect because arthroscopy with debridement may provide temporary symptomatic relief in early-stage disease but is not the most appropriate definitive surgical intervention for established joint degeneration with significant symptoms during pinch and grip.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old female presents with a swollen and painful right finger after a recent puncture wound from a fish bone. On examination, the finger is held flexed, and there is tenderness along the flexor tendon sheath. Kanavel's signs are noted. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Initiate a course of antibiotics
B) Immediate surgical intervention for drainage
C) Apply a splint and observe
D) Refer for hand therapy
questions.answer:
B)
Immediate surgical intervention for drainage is the most appropriate next step when Kanavel's signs (fusiform swelling, flexed posture, tenderness along the flexor sheath, and pain with passive extension) are present, indicating purulent flexor tenosynovitis. Delay in surgical drainage can lead to tendon necrosis, digital stiffness, and potential amputation. A fish bone puncture wound is a classic mechanism for inoculation of the flexor sheath.

A is incorrect because antibiotics alone are insufficient to treat established purulent flexor tenosynovitis; while antibiotics are given as an adjunct, they cannot adequately penetrate the closed tendon sheath space without surgical drainage.
C is incorrect because splinting and observation would allow the infection to progress, risking tendon destruction and spread of infection.
D is incorrect because hand therapy is appropriate during the recovery phase after treatment but does not address the acute surgical emergency of purulent tenosynovitis.

questions.question:
A patient with an intertrochanteric fracture of the femur is scheduled for surgical fixation. During the anterolateral approach to the hip, which neurovascular structure is at the highest risk for injury? 
A) Femoral artery 
B) Obturator nerve 
C) Sciatic nerve 
D) Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve 
E) Inferior gluteal artery
questions.answer:
D)
The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (LFCN) is at highest risk among the listed structures during the anterolateral (Watson-Jones) approach to the hip. The LFCN emerges medial to the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS), crosses the sartorius, and runs within or near the interval between the tensor fasciae latae (TFL) and sartorius. Retraction of the TFL during the anterolateral approach can stretch or transect the nerve, causing meralgia paresthetica (numbness/dysesthesia over the anterolateral thigh).

A is incorrect because the femoral artery lies medially in the femoral triangle and is not in the surgical field of the anterolateral approach.
B is incorrect because the obturator nerve exits the pelvis through the obturator foramen and innervates the medial compartment of the thigh; it is not at risk in a lateral-based approach.
C is incorrect because the sciatic nerve lies posteriorly, deep to the short external rotators; it is at risk in posterior approaches, not the anterolateral approach.
E is incorrect because the inferior gluteal artery exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis and is at risk in posterior approaches, not the anterolateral approach.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic knee pain suddenly experiences a tear in his quadriceps tendon after an awkward landing while playing basketball. What is the most common mechanism of injury associated with quadriceps tendon ruptures?
A) Direct trauma
B) Sudden eccentric loading
C) Overuse
D) Chronic degenerative changes
questions.answer:
B)
Quadriceps tendon ruptures most commonly occur through sudden eccentric loading of the extensor mechanism, such as an awkward landing with the knee flexing against a contracted quadriceps. Pre-existing tendinopathy or degenerative changes lower the threshold for rupture but the acute event is the eccentric overload.

A is incorrect because direct trauma (e.g., a blow to the anterior thigh) can cause quadriceps contusion or even fracture but is not the most common mechanism for tendon rupture.
C is incorrect because overuse typically leads to tendinopathy or tendinosis rather than acute complete tendon rupture.
D is incorrect because chronic degenerative changes are a predisposing risk factor that weakens the tendon, but they represent the underlying condition, not the mechanism of the acute rupture event itself.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with severe back pain. She has limited mobility and on examination shows signs of instability in the cervical spine. Which of the following conditions should be most concerning for this patient due to her underlying disease?
A) Atlantoaxial subluxation
B) Lumbar disc degeneration
C) Spondylolisthesis
D) Osteoporotic vertebral fracture
questions.answer:
A)
Atlantoaxial subluxation is the most concerning cervical spine condition in rheumatoid arthritis. RA causes pannus formation and erosion of the transverse ligament of the atlas, leading to C1-C2 instability. This can result in spinal cord compression and is a well-recognized, potentially life-threatening complication of RA.

B is incorrect because lumbar disc degeneration is a common age-related finding and is not specifically associated with rheumatoid arthritis or cervical spine instability.
C is incorrect because spondylolisthesis is typically a degenerative or developmental condition of the lumbar spine and is not a hallmark complication of rheumatoid arthritis.
D is incorrect because while RA patients may have osteoporosis (often steroid-related), the stem specifically describes cervical spine instability, which points to atlantoaxial subluxation rather than an osteoporotic vertebral fracture.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents with pain and swelling at the base of her thumb after falling on an outstretched hand. X-rays reveal a fracture at the base of the first metacarpal. Considering the fracture's location, which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
A) Nonoperative management with a thumb spica splint
B) Open reduction and internal fixation
C) Percutaneous pinning
D) Referral for occupational therapy
questions.answer:
A)
A non-displaced, extra-articular fracture at the base of the first metacarpal is appropriately managed initially with a thumb spica splint or cast. These fractures are generally stable and heal well with immobilization for 4–6 weeks. Surgical intervention is reserved for displaced or intra-articular fractures (e.g., Bennett or Rolando fractures) that cannot be adequately reduced by closed means.

B is incorrect because open reduction and internal fixation is indicated for significantly displaced or intra-articular fractures (Bennett, Rolando), not as initial management of a non-displaced base fracture.
C is incorrect because percutaneous pinning is used when closed reduction is achieved but the fracture is unstable (e.g., Bennett fracture); it is not first-line for a non-displaced fracture.
D is incorrect because referral for occupational therapy is part of rehabilitation after fracture healing, not the initial management of an acute fracture.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old male complains of persistent pain in his ankle after suffering an injury several months ago. MRI shows an anteromedial impaction of the talus. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Corticosteroid injection
B) Ankle arthroscopy
C) Physical therapy
D) Conservative management with rest and ice
questions.answer:
B)
An anteromedial talar impaction lesion on MRI in the setting of persistent post-traumatic ankle pain several months after injury is consistent with an osteochondral lesion of the talus (OLT). Given the chronicity of symptoms (implying failure of conservative management), ankle arthroscopy with debridement and marrow-stimulation (microfracture) is the most appropriate next step for diagnosis and treatment.

A is incorrect because corticosteroid injection may provide temporary symptomatic relief but does not address the underlying osteochondral pathology and may impair cartilage healing.
C is incorrect because physical therapy alone is unlikely to resolve a symptomatic osteochondral lesion that has already persisted for several months.
D is incorrect because rest and ice represent initial conservative measures; the prolonged duration of symptoms in this scenario suggests these have already been attempted without success, warranting surgical intervention.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male presents to the clinic with pain and swelling over his right elbow following a direct blow while playing rugby. He has tenderness over the lateral epicondyle and difficulty flexing his forearm against resistance. Physical examination reveals weakness in forearm flexion. Which muscle is primarily involved, and what is its nerve supply?
A) Biceps brachii; musculocutaneous nerve
B) Brachialis; radial nerve
C) Coracobrachialis; median nerve
D) Flexor carpi ulnaris; ulnar nerve
questions.answer:
A)
The biceps brachii is the primary muscle responsible for forearm flexion against resistance and is innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6). A direct blow to the lateral aspect of the elbow can injure the biceps tendon or its insertion area, resulting in pain and weakness of forearm flexion. The biceps is the most clinically relevant forearm flexor tested against resistance.

B is incorrect because while the brachialis contributes to forearm flexion, its primary innervation is the musculocutaneous nerve (not the radial nerve as listed), and it is a deeper muscle less commonly tested in isolation clinically.
C is incorrect because the coracobrachialis is a shoulder flexor and adductor innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve; it does not contribute to forearm flexion.
D is incorrect because the flexor carpi ulnaris is a wrist flexor and ulnar deviator innervated by the ulnar nerve; it has no role in forearm (elbow) flexion.

questions.question:
A 16-year-old male soccer player presents with a history of left knee pain following a twisting injury while pivoting. On examination, he has joint effusion and a positive McMurray test. An MRI reveals a discoid meniscus with a characteristic bow-tie sign. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this condition?
A) Arthroscopic partial meniscectomy
B) Conservative management with physiotherapy
C) Open meniscus repair
D) Observation only
E) Corticosteroid injection
questions.answer:
A)
In a symptomatic discoid meniscus with mechanical symptoms (effusion, positive McMurray test), the standard treatment is arthroscopic partial meniscectomy (saucerization) to reshape the abnormally wide meniscus to a more anatomic contour, with repair of any peripheral instability if present. The bow-tie sign on MRI (the meniscal body bow-tie seen on more than two consecutive sagittal slices) is characteristic of a discoid meniscus.

B is incorrect because conservative management with physiotherapy is appropriate for asymptomatic discoid menisci, but this patient has mechanical symptoms (effusion, positive McMurray) that warrant surgical intervention. C is incorrect because open meniscus repair is not the standard approach; arthroscopic techniques are preferred, and the primary goal is saucerization rather than isolated repair. D is incorrect because observation alone is insufficient in a symptomatic patient with mechanical symptoms and effusion. E is incorrect because corticosteroid injection does not address the underlying structural abnormality of a discoid meniscus and would not resolve mechanical symptoms.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old male presents with a painful mass on the dorsum of his right foot that has gradually increased in size, particularly worsening with activity. On examination, the mass is pulsatile and there is associated swelling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Osteosarcoma
B) Aneurysmal bone cyst
C) Arteriovenous malformation
D) Liposarcoma
questions.answer:
C)
The pulsatile nature of the mass and its activity-related worsening are hallmarks of an arteriovenous malformation (AVM). AVMs consist of abnormal direct connections between arteries and veins without an intervening capillary bed, producing a pulsatile, compressible soft-tissue mass that enlarges with increased blood flow during activity.

A is incorrect because osteosarcoma is a primary malignant bone tumor that typically presents as a firm, non-pulsatile mass, most commonly around the knee in adolescents/young adults, and would show characteristic osseous destruction and periosteal reaction on imaging.

B is incorrect because an aneurysmal bone cyst is a benign, expansile, blood-filled cystic lesion of bone; while it can be pulsatile on rare occasions, it is an intraosseous lesion that would be identified on imaging as a lytic, "blown-out" bony lesion rather than a soft-tissue dorsal foot mass worsening with activity.

D is incorrect because liposarcoma is a malignant soft-tissue tumor composed of adipocytes; it typically presents as a painless, non-pulsatile deep soft-tissue mass, most commonly in the thigh or retroperitoneum, and would not exhibit pulsatility.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man presents with chronic low back pain and stiffness, especially in the morning. His symptoms improve with activity, and imaging reveals bilateral sacroiliitis. Which condition is most likely causing these findings?
A) Osteoarthritis
B) Ankylosing spondylitis
C) Degenerative disc disease
D) Osteoporosis
questions.answer:
B)
Ankylosing spondylitis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy characterized by inflammatory back pain (morning stiffness improving with activity) and bilateral sacroiliitis on imaging. It typically presents in young to middle-aged adults and is strongly associated with HLA-B27.

A is incorrect because osteoarthritis causes mechanical pain that worsens with activity and improves with rest, and it does not characteristically cause bilateral sacroiliitis. C is incorrect because degenerative disc disease produces mechanical back pain without the inflammatory pattern of morning stiffness improving with activity, and it does not cause sacroiliitis. D is incorrect because osteoporosis is a metabolic bone disease that leads to decreased bone density and fragility fractures; it does not cause sacroiliitis or inflammatory symptoms.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old boy is diagnosed with Blount's disease after presenting with bowing of the legs. The orthopaedic surgeon explains that the condition arises from abnormal development of a specific area of the tibia. Which part of the tibia is primarily affected in Blount's disease?
A) Distal anterior metaphysis
B) Proximal posterior medial physis
C) Distal fibular physis
D) Proximal anterior metaphysis
E) Distal posterior medial physis
questions.answer:
B)
Blount's disease (tibia vara) is caused by a growth disturbance of the proximal medial (posteromedial) tibial physis and adjacent metaphysis, resulting in progressive varus angulation of the lower extremity. The medial physis undergoes abnormal endochondral ossification, leading to the characteristic beaking and irregularity seen on imaging. Early recognition and treatment are essential to prevent progressive deformity.

A is incorrect because the distal anterior metaphysis of the tibia is not involved in Blount's disease; the pathology is localized to the proximal tibia.
C is incorrect because the distal fibular physis is unrelated to Blount's disease, which is a tibial disorder.
D is incorrect because while the proximal tibia is involved, the pathology is on the medial (posteromedial) side, not the anterior aspect.
E is incorrect because the distal posterior medial physis of the tibia is not the site of pathology in Blount's disease; the disease affects the proximal tibia.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old female runner presents with sudden onset of calf pain and difficulty plantar flexing her foot after a sprint. Physical examination reveals a palpable gap in the Achilles tendon. Considering her activity level, what is the most appropriate surgical approach for her Achilles tendon rupture?
A) Open repair
B) Percutaneous repair
C) Conservative management with immobilization
D) Delayed repair after 6 weeks
questions.answer:
A)
In a young, active individual with a complete Achilles tendon rupture, open surgical repair is the most commonly recommended approach on board examinations. It allows direct visualization of the ruptured tendon ends, secure suture fixation, and reliable restoration of tendon length and tension, which is critical for return to high-level athletics.

B is incorrect because percutaneous repair, while a valid technique with lower wound complication rates, provides less direct visualization and may result in a less secure repair, particularly for a complete rupture in a high-demand athlete. C is incorrect because conservative management with immobilization carries a higher re-rupture rate compared to surgical repair in young, active patients and is generally reserved for lower-demand individuals or those with surgical contraindications. D is incorrect because delayed repair after 6 weeks allows tendon retraction and degeneration of the stumps, making direct repair more difficult and often necessitating reconstruction with tendon transfer (e.g., FHL), leading to inferior outcomes.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman presents with a painful mass in her wrist, and imaging reveals a subarticular lytic lesion consistent with a giant cell tumor of bone (GCT). Based on the Campanacci classification, which grade indicates the most aggressive lesion with the highest risk of local recurrence?
A) Grade I
B) Grade II
C) Grade III
D) None of the above
questions.answer:
C)
Campanacci Grade III indicates an aggressive giant cell tumor with cortical destruction and soft-tissue extension, carrying the highest risk of local recurrence. These lesions often require wide resection or en bloc excision rather than intralesional curettage alone.

A is incorrect because Grade I describes a latent, well-marginated intraosseous lesion with an intact cortex and the lowest recurrence risk. B is incorrect because Grade II describes an active lesion with cortical thinning/expansion but an intact cortex; while it has moderate recurrence risk, it does not carry the most significant risk. D is incorrect because Grade III directly addresses the question.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old male basketball player experiences a knee injury while landing from a jump. He reports an immediate sensation of instability and difficulty bearing weight. On examination, there is a positive pivot shift test. An MRI shows a complete ACL tear and associated bone contusions. What mechanism of injury is most consistent with this presentation?
A) Direct blow to the knee
B) Hyperextension of the knee
C) Valgus force with internal rotation
D) Lateral force during landing
questions.answer:
C)
The classic non-contact ACL injury mechanism involves a valgus force combined with internal tibial rotation (or external femoral rotation) while the foot is planted, often during deceleration, cutting, or landing from a jump. This produces the pivot-shift phenomenon and is consistent with the bone-contusion pattern typically seen on MRI (lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau). A positive pivot shift test on examination further confirms this rotational mechanism.

A is incorrect because a direct blow to the knee (contact mechanism) more commonly causes ligamentous injuries such as MCL or PCL tears depending on the direction of force, and does not typically produce the classic pivot-shift pattern of ACL disruption.

B is incorrect because hyperextension can cause ACL tears, but the associated bone-contusion pattern is typically anterior (anterior tibial plateau and anterior femoral condyle), and the clinical presentation differs from the rotational instability described here.

D is incorrect because a pure lateral force during landing would more likely produce an MCL injury (valgus stress) without the rotational component necessary to generate the pivot-shift mechanism and the characteristic posterolateral bone-contusion pattern seen in this case.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old football player presents with pain at the base of his big toe after a game on artificial turf. He is unable to push off without significant pain. Examination reveals swelling and tenderness at the first metatarsophalangeal joint, and imaging suggests a plantar plate injury. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this turf toe injury?
A) Rigid taping
B) Surgical repair
C) Corticosteroid injection
D) Immobilization in a walking boot
questions.answer:
D)
Immobilization in a walking boot is the most appropriate initial treatment for a turf toe (plantar plate) injury. This allows the injured plantar plate to rest and heal by limiting dorsiflexion at the first MTP joint. Conservative management with immobilization is the standard first-line approach for most turf toe injuries (Grades I–III), with surgery reserved for refractory or severe cases.

A is incorrect because rigid taping alone does not provide sufficient immobilization for a symptomatic plantar plate injury with significant swelling; it may be used as an adjunct or for return-to-play after initial healing, but is insufficient as primary treatment. B is incorrect because surgical repair is reserved for Grade III injuries that fail conservative management or involve large capsular avulsions, sesamoid fractures, or traumatic hallux valgus — it is not the initial treatment. C is incorrect because corticosteroid injection is not indicated for acute turf toe; it can weaken the already-injured plantar plate and delay healing.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman presents with pain at the dorsal aspect of her foot after a fall. X-rays reveal a fracture at the base of the 5th metatarsal. She is concerned about long-term complications. Which of the following best describes the potential complication associated with this type of fracture?
A) Nonunion
B) Osteomyelitis
C) Hallux valgus
D) Tarsal tunnel syndrome
questions.answer:
A)
Nonunion is the most clinically significant long-term complication of fractures at the base of the 5th metatarsal, especially Jones fractures (meta-diaphyseal junction, Zone 2). This area has a watershed blood supply between the nutrient artery and metaphyseal perforators, predisposing to delayed union or nonunion.

B is incorrect because osteomyelitis is a complication of open fractures or post-surgical infection, not a characteristic complication of a closed 5th metatarsal base fracture. C is incorrect because hallux valgus is a deformity of the first ray (great toe MTP joint) and is unrelated to 5th metatarsal fractures. D is incorrect because tarsal tunnel syndrome involves compression of the posterior tibial nerve at the medial ankle and has no association with 5th metatarsal base fractures.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male presents with gradual onset of pain and weakness in his right shoulder over the past few months. On examination, he has difficulty abducting his arm and exhibits atrophy of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. MRI findings suggest a massive rotator cuff tear. What syndrome might be associated with this condition if it remains untreated?
A) Impingement syndrome
B) Quadrilateral space syndrome
C) Frozen shoulder syndrome
D) Subacromial bursitis
E) Glenohumeral osteoarthritis
questions.answer:
B)
Explanation: If a massive rotator cuff tear is left untreated, it can lead to conditions such as quadrilateral space syndrome due to muscle atrophy and altered shoulder mechanics, which may compromise the axillary nerve and lead to further weakness in arm abduction.

questions.question:
A surgeon is planning a total knee arthroplasty and wishes to ensure proper rotational alignment of the femoral component. Which anatomical relationship should the surgeon ensure is respected to achieve optimal rotational alignment?
A) The transepicondylar axis should be parallel to the posterior condylar axis
B) The transepicondylar axis should be perpendicular to Whiteside's line
C) The femoral component should be externally rotated 10° relative to the posterior condylar axis
D) Whiteside's line should be parallel to the posterior condylar axis
questions.answer:
B)
Whiteside's line (the anteroposterior axis of the distal femur, drawn from the deepest point of the trochlear groove to the center of the intercondylar notch) is perpendicular to the surgical transepicondylar axis in the axial plane. Using both landmarks together helps the surgeon confirm proper femoral component rotation during total knee arthroplasty, typically resulting in approximately 3° of external rotation relative to the posterior condylar axis.

A is incorrect because the transepicondylar axis is NOT parallel to the posterior condylar axis; it is externally rotated approximately 3° relative to the posterior condylar line. Aligning to the posterior condylar axis alone risks internal rotation of the component.
C is incorrect because the standard external rotation of the femoral component relative to the posterior condylar axis is approximately 3° (not 10°). Excessive external rotation leads to lateral patellar tracking problems and flexion gap asymmetry.
D is incorrect because Whiteside's line runs in the anteroposterior direction while the posterior condylar axis runs in the mediolateral direction; they are roughly perpendicular, not parallel.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman complains of persistent mid-back pain and tingling sensations down her left arm for several weeks. She has a history of repetitive overhead activities at work. A CT scan reveals a paracentral disc herniation at the C6-C7 level. Which nerve root is most likely affected by this condition?
A) C5
B) C6
C) C7
D) C8
questions.answer:
C)
In the cervical spine, nerve roots exit above their same-numbered vertebra. A paracentral disc herniation at C6-C7 compresses the C7 nerve root as it traverses toward the C6-C7 neural foramen. C7 radiculopathy classically causes triceps weakness, decreased triceps reflex, and numbness in the middle finger, consistent with arm tingling.

A is incorrect because the C5 nerve root exits at the C4-C5 level and would not be affected by a C6-C7 disc herniation.
B is incorrect because the C6 nerve root exits at the C5-C6 level; a paracentral herniation at C6-C7 compresses the traversing C7 root, not the exiting C6 root.
D is incorrect because the C8 nerve root exits at the C7-T1 level and would be affected by a C7-T1 disc herniation, not a C6-C7 herniation.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old female presents with lateral foot pain and discomfort over the fifth metatarsal head. Examination reveals a prominent bony prominence on the lateral aspect of her foot. What type of bunionette is she most likely experiencing based on her symptoms?
A) Type I
B) Type II
C) Type III
D) Type IV
questions.answer:
C)
A Type III bunionette, also known as a tailor's bunion, is characterized by a prominent fifth metatarsal head with associated pain and deformity. This condition often requires surgical intervention when conservative measures fail.

questions.question:
A patient with a suspected femoral neck fracture undergoes an MRI, which shows an impacted fracture. Considering this type of fracture, what is the most appropriate management strategy?
A) Immediate total hip replacement
B) Internal fixation with screws
C) Conservative management with weight bearing as tolerated
D) Observation with repeat imaging in 2 weeks
questions.answer:
B)
An impacted (valgus) femoral neck fracture is a stable fracture pattern in which the fracture fragments remain in contact. Internal fixation with parallel cannulated screws is the standard treatment, as it maintains the reduction, allows early mobilization, and preserves the native femoral head.

A is incorrect because total hip replacement is reserved for displaced femoral neck fractures in elderly or low-demand patients, not for stable impacted fractures where the femoral head can be preserved. C is incorrect because even though the fracture is impacted and relatively stable, non-operative management with weight bearing carries a significant risk of fracture displacement; internal fixation is recommended to prevent this. D is incorrect because observation with delayed imaging risks fracture displacement and avascular necrosis; definitive fixation should not be delayed when the diagnosis is confirmed on MRI.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old male soccer player presents with pain and swelling around his ankle following a fall where he landed awkwardly on his foot. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the anterolateral ankle and positive anterior drawer test. Which of the following structures is most likely injured in this scenario?
A) Anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament
B) Anterior talofibular ligament
C) Calcaneofibular ligament
D) Deltoid ligament
questions.answer:
B)
The anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) is the most commonly injured ligament in lateral ankle sprains, particularly with a plantarflexion-inversion mechanism.
