B is incorrect because hyperextension of the wrist is more likely to cause ligamentous injuries or fractures at the distal radius, not the base of the second metacarpal. D is incorrect because radial deviation of the wrist is more likely to cause injuries to the radial styloid or scaphoid, not the base of the second metacarpal.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male presents with an anterior shoulder dislocation after a fall while playing soccer. The dislocation has been reduced in the emergency department, and now he complains of persistent shoulder pain and instability. Which classification system is used to describe the pattern of associated fractures in the context of shoulder dislocations?
A) Neer classification
B) Milch classification
C) Rowe classification
D) AO classification
questions.answer:
A)
The Neer classification is used to categorize the patterns of associated fractures in the context of shoulder dislocations, particularly focusing on the anatomical implications of the humeral head and glenoid involvement. Understanding these classifications helps in planning for potential surgical interventions if instability persists.

questions.question:
A 12-year-old boy is noted to have a bipartite patella on imaging after a fall. This condition is characterized by failure of which structure to fuse?
A) Femoral condyles
B) Superolateral corner of the patella
C) Quadriceps tendon
D) Patellar tendon
E) Tibial tuberosity
questions.answer:
B)
Bipartite patella results from the failure of the superolateral accessory ossification center of the patella to fuse with the main body during skeletal maturation. It is most commonly found at the superolateral pole (Saupe type III, ~75% of cases) and is often an incidental finding that must be distinguished from an acute fracture.

A is incorrect because the femoral condyles are part of the distal femur and are unrelated to patellar ossification or bipartite patella. C is incorrect because the quadriceps tendon is a soft-tissue structure that inserts on the superior pole of the patella; it does not contain an ossification center that fails to fuse. D is incorrect because the patellar tendon connects the inferior pole of the patella to the tibial tuberosity and is not involved in the pathogenesis of bipartite patella. E is incorrect because the tibial tuberosity is the site of patellar tendon insertion on the tibia and is associated with Osgood-Schlatter disease, not bipartite patella.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old woman undergoes a posterior approach hip arthroplasty. During the procedure, the surgeon is careful to identify the superior gluteal vessels. Which anatomical feature is true regarding the superior gluteal artery?
A) It exits the pelvis below the piriformis muscle
B) It crosses the hip joint posteriorly
C) It exits the greater sciatic notch above the piriformis muscle
D) It primarily supplies the medial thigh muscles
questions.answer:
C)
The superior gluteal artery exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen above the piriformis muscle. It supplies the gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae. During posterior approach hip arthroplasty, awareness of its location is critical to avoid iatrogenic vascular injury.

A is incorrect because the structure that exits below the piriformis is the inferior gluteal artery (along with the sciatic nerve, pudendal nerve, and inferior gluteal nerve); the superior gluteal artery passes above the piriformis.
B is incorrect because the superior gluteal artery does not cross the hip joint posteriorly; it courses between the gluteus medius and minimus after exiting the sciatic notch, supplying the abductor musculature.
D is incorrect because the superior gluteal artery primarily supplies the gluteal (abductor) muscles, not the medial thigh muscles; the medial thigh is supplied by branches of the obturator and profunda femoris arteries.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old female has a history of chronic back pain and recent hip pain. Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scanning shows a T-score of -2.5. Which of the following statements about the T-score and Z-score in assessing her bone health is accurate?
A) The T-score compares her bone density to that of age-matched controls
B) The Z-score indicates her bone density relative to a healthy population
C) The T-score is more relevant for diagnosing osteoporosis in older adults
D) The Z-score is used primarily for diagnosing osteopenia in post-menopausal women
questions.answer:
C)
The T-score compares a patient's bone mineral density (BMD) to that of a young, healthy reference population (peak bone mass). A T-score of −2.5 or below defines osteoporosis per WHO criteria, and the T-score is the standard metric used for diagnosing osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and men ≥50 years old.

A is incorrect because the T-score compares BMD to a young healthy reference population, not age-matched controls — that description applies to the Z-score.
B is incorrect because the Z-score compares BMD to age- and sex-matched peers, not to a healthy young population; it is used mainly in premenopausal women, men <50, and children to identify whether bone loss is worse than expected for age.
D is incorrect because the Z-score is not used to diagnose osteopenia in postmenopausal women; the T-score is the standard for that purpose. The Z-score is primarily used in younger patients and when secondary causes of bone loss are suspected.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old recreational runner complains of chronic anterior knee pain, especially with running, squatting, and prolonged sitting. Physical examination reveals lateral patellar tilt and apprehension with lateral patellar displacement. An MRI shows lateral patellar tilt with lateral facet chondromalacia. The treating physician discusses treatment options, including the potential for a lateral retinacular release. Which of the following is the primary rationale for this procedure in this context?
A) To enhance blood flow to the menisci
B) To relieve lateral compartment pressure
C) To improve patellar tracking
D) To promote chondral healing
questions.answer:
C)
The primary rationale for a lateral retinacular release is to improve patellar tracking. In patients with lateral patellar tilt or excessive lateral pressure syndrome, a tight lateral retinaculum pulls the patella laterally, causing abnormal patellofemoral contact pressures and anterior knee pain. Releasing the lateral retinaculum allows the patella to track more centrally within the trochlear groove.

A is incorrect because lateral retinacular release does not enhance blood flow to the menisci; the menisci receive their blood supply from the perimeniscal capillary plexus, which is unrelated to the lateral retinaculum.
B is incorrect because the procedure addresses the patellofemoral compartment (lateral patellar facet pressure), not the lateral tibiofemoral compartment.
D is incorrect because lateral retinacular release does not directly promote chondral healing; it reduces abnormal contact pressures but does not regenerate articular cartilage.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman presents with an enlarging mass on her right arm. She has a family history of familial adenomatous polyposis. An imaging study shows a well-defined subcutaneous mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Lipoma
B) Desmoid tumor
C) Fibroma
D) Malignant fibrous histiocytoma
E) Osteosarcoma
questions.answer:
B)
Desmoid tumors (aggressive fibromatosis) are strongly associated with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), particularly the Gardner syndrome variant. They are locally aggressive, non-metastasizing fibrous neoplasms that commonly arise in the abdominal wall or extremities in FAP patients. The combination of a young patient, family history of FAP, and an enlarging soft-tissue mass makes desmoid tumor the most likely diagnosis.

A is incorrect because lipomas are the most common soft-tissue tumor but have no specific association with FAP; they are typically soft, mobile, and non-enlarging.
C is incorrect because fibromas are benign, small, slow-growing lesions without a recognized association with FAP.
D is incorrect because malignant fibrous histiocytoma (undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma) is a high-grade malignancy typically seen in older adults and is not associated with FAP.
E is incorrect because osteosarcoma is a primary bone malignancy, not a subcutaneous soft-tissue mass, and has no association with FAP.

questions.question:
A 15-year-old boy presents with knee pain and a palpable lump below the patella. He is active in soccer and basketball. X-rays show fragmentation of the tibial tuberosity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Osgood-Schlatter disease
B) Patellar tendinopathy
C) Jumper's knee
D) Patellar dislocation
questions.answer:
A)
Osgood-Schlatter disease is an apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity caused by repetitive traction of the patellar tendon on the immature apophysis. The classic presentation is an active adolescent with anterior knee pain, a prominent tibial tubercle, and imaging showing fragmentation of the tibial tuberosity.

B is incorrect because patellar tendinopathy (tendinosis of the patellar tendon proper) presents with infrapatellar tendon pain and MRI signal changes within the tendon substance, not fragmentation of the tibial tuberosity on X-ray.
C is incorrect because "jumper's knee" is a synonym for patellar tendinopathy and involves the tendon itself rather than the apophysis; it does not produce tibial tuberosity fragmentation.
D is incorrect because patellar dislocation presents with lateral patellar displacement, apprehension, and possible osteochondral injury — not a lump at the tibial tuberosity or tuberosity fragmentation.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old man complains of chronic low back pain that radiates to his left hip and thigh, worsened by bending and lifting. He has a history of osteoarthritis and is concerned about a herniated disc. An x-ray shows moderate degenerative changes without acute bony abnormalities. What is the most likely underlying mechanism for his symptoms?
A) Nerve root compression from disc herniation
B) Facet joint osteoarthritis
C) Sacroiliac joint dysfunction
D) Spinal stenosis
questions.answer:
B)
Facet joint osteoarthritis is the most likely mechanism given the patient's age, history of osteoarthritis, and x-ray findings of moderate degenerative changes without evidence of acute disc herniation. Facet arthropathy can produce referred pain to the hip and thigh that mimics radiculopathy, and degenerative facet changes are a common source of chronic low back pain in this population.

A is incorrect because although disc herniation can cause radicular symptoms, the imaging shows no acute disc pathology, and the x-ray demonstrates degenerative changes more consistent with facet arthropathy.
C is incorrect because sacroiliac joint dysfunction typically presents with pain localized to the buttock and posterior thigh, often provoked by specific SI joint provocative maneuvers, and is not suggested by the degenerative lumbar x-ray findings.
D is incorrect because spinal stenosis typically presents with neurogenic claudication (pain with walking/standing relieved by sitting or flexion), and the plain x-ray description does not indicate canal narrowing or stenotic features.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male presents with persistent knee pain and swelling after an injury while playing basketball. MRI reveals damage to the articular cartilage. What is the primary function of articular cartilage in the joint?
A) Transmit nerve signals
B) Provide tensile strength to bone
C) Allow smooth gliding of bones at joints
D) Store calcium and phosphate
E) Facilitate muscle attachment
questions.answer:
C)
Articular (hyaline) cartilage covers the ends of bones at synovial joints and provides a near-frictionless surface that allows smooth gliding during movement, distributing loads and minimizing wear. Damage to articular cartilage can lead to progressive joint pain and osteoarthritis because of its limited intrinsic healing capacity.

A is incorrect because articular cartilage is aneural and does not transmit nerve signals. B is incorrect because tensile strength of bone is provided by the collagen and mineral content of bone itself, not by articular cartilage. D is incorrect because calcium and phosphate are stored in bone (hydroxyapatite), not in cartilage. E is incorrect because muscle attachment occurs at tendons inserting onto bone (periosteum/entheses), not at articular cartilage.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male presents with a mallet finger after a basketball injury. He has complete extension lag of the distal phalanx of his ring finger. If there is no fracture identified, what is the most appropriate treatment for this acute injury?
A) Surgical repair of the tendon
B) Continuous extension splinting
C) Buddy taping to the adjacent finger
D) Corticosteroid injection
questions.answer:
B)
Continuous extension splinting of the DIP joint for 6–8 weeks is the standard first-line treatment for acute closed mallet finger without fracture. The splint maintains the distal phalanx in full extension (or slight hyperextension), allowing the disrupted terminal extensor tendon to heal. Outcomes with compliant splinting are generally good.

A is incorrect because surgical repair is not indicated for a closed soft-tissue mallet finger; operative treatment is reserved for cases with large bony fragments involving >30% of the articular surface with volar subluxation, or for failed conservative management.
C is incorrect because buddy taping does not maintain the DIP joint in extension and therefore does not allow the terminal extensor tendon to heal in the appropriate position.
D is incorrect because corticosteroid injection has no role in the treatment of mallet finger; it does not address the tendon discontinuity and could impair tendon healing.

questions.question:
A 75-year-old woman undergoes a total hip arthroplasty. The surgeon places the femoral component at an angle of 15 degrees. What is the significance of this angle in relation to the implant?
A) It reduces the risk of fracture
B) It ensures proper alignment with the transepicondylar axis
C) It promotes optimal range of motion and stability
D) It minimizes the risk of nerve injury
questions.answer:
C)
Explanation: Placing the femoral component at an angle of 15 degrees is significant as it promotes optimal range of motion and stability of the hip joint. Proper alignment is crucial for the overall function of the implant and to avoid complications.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old man with a history of gout presents with sudden onset of severe pain, swelling, and redness around his left ankle. An X-ray shows no fractures but reveals a soft tissue swelling. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Joint aspiration and analysis of synovial fluid
B) Initiation of allopurinol therapy
C) Application of a cast for immobilization
D) Referral to a rheumatologist
questions.answer:
A)
In a patient presenting with acute monoarticular joint pain, swelling, and erythema—even with a known history of gout—joint aspiration with synovial fluid analysis is the most appropriate next step. Identification of negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals under polarized microscopy confirms the diagnosis and, critically, rules out septic arthritis, which can present identically.

B is incorrect because allopurinol is a urate-lowering agent used for chronic gout prophylaxis; initiating it during an acute flare can worsen or prolong the attack and should not be started until the acute episode has resolved.
C is incorrect because cast immobilization is not indicated for an acute gout flare; treatment involves anti-inflammatory medications (NSAIDs, colchicine, or corticosteroids), not rigid immobilization.
D is incorrect because while rheumatology referral may be appropriate for refractory or chronic gout management, the immediate priority in an acute presentation is to aspirate the joint to confirm the diagnosis and exclude infection before any other management steps.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female recreational runner presents with recurrent episodes of her knee 'giving way' during running. Physical examination reveals a positive apprehension test and the patella is noted to track laterally during active range of motion. Given her symptoms and findings, what is the most appropriate initial management strategy?
A) Immediate surgical stabilization
B) Strengthening exercises for the quadriceps
C) Knee brace for lateral support
D) Corticosteroid injection
questions.answer:
B)
Strengthening exercises for the quadriceps — particularly the vastus medialis obliquus (VMO) — are the most appropriate initial management for patellar instability with lateral tracking. Rehabilitation-based dynamic stabilization is the cornerstone of first-line treatment and is effective in the majority of patients with recurrent patellar subluxation.

A is incorrect because immediate surgical stabilization (e.g., MPFL reconstruction) is reserved for patients who fail an adequate course of conservative management or who have significant structural abnormalities (e.g., trochlear dysplasia, patella alta). Surgery is not first-line for a recreational athlete without prior failed rehab.

C is incorrect because a knee brace may provide temporary symptomatic relief but does not address the underlying muscular imbalance and is not a definitive management strategy.

D is incorrect because corticosteroid injection does not treat the mechanical cause of patellar instability and is not indicated for recurrent subluxation/giving way episodes.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old construction worker sustains a laceration to the volar aspect of his hand while using a power tool. Examination shows a complete laceration of the flexor pollicis longus tendon. What is the most appropriate surgical approach for repair of this tendon?
A) Zigzag incision over the wrist
B) Dorsal approach through the wrist
C) Volar approach to the palm
D) Lateral approach to the thenar eminence
E) Transverse incision at the MCP joint level
questions.answer:
C)
A volar approach to the palm is the most appropriate for repairing a lacerated flexor pollicis longus tendon, as it allows direct access to the tendon while minimizing damage to surrounding structures. A is incorrect because a zigzag incision over the wrist does not provide adequate access to the flexor pollicis longus tendon in the palm. B is incorrect because a dorsal approach through the wrist does not allow access to the volar structures. D is incorrect because a lateral approach to the thenar eminence does not provide direct access to the tendon. E is incorrect because a transverse incision at the MCP joint level is not appropriate for accessing the tendon in the palm.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old athlete reports knee instability and pain after a tackle during a football game. Physical examination shows a positive varus stress test and tenderness along the lateral aspect of the knee. MRI results confirm a grade II partial tear of the lateral collateral ligament (LCL). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Surgical repair of the LCL
B) Bracing and rehabilitation
C) Intra-articular steroid injection
D) Complete immobilization for 6 weeks
E) NSAIDs and rest
questions.answer:
B)
Bracing and rehabilitation are the appropriate management for an isolated grade II (partial) tear of the lateral collateral ligament. This conservative approach allows ligament healing while maintaining range of motion and restoring strength and proprioception through structured physical therapy.

A is incorrect because surgical repair is generally reserved for grade III (complete) LCL tears, multi-ligament knee injuries, or cases with persistent instability after adequate conservative treatment. C is incorrect because intra-articular steroid injection does not address ligamentous healing and is not indicated for an acute LCL injury. D is incorrect because complete immobilization for 6 weeks leads to unnecessary stiffness, quadriceps atrophy, and delayed recovery; controlled motion with bracing produces superior outcomes. E is incorrect because while NSAIDs and rest may provide symptomatic relief, they alone are insufficient — structured bracing and rehabilitation are needed to protect the ligament, restore stability, and prevent re-injury.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old female presents to the clinic with wrist pain after falling onto an outstretched hand. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the distal radius and limited range of motion. An x-ray shows a fracture of the distal radius with dorsal angulation. What is the most likely mechanism of injury for this type of fracture?
A) Direct blow to the wrist
B) Compression from a fall
C) Extension of the wrist during a fall
D) Flexion of the wrist during a fall
questions.answer:
C)
The mechanism of injury for a distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation, commonly known as a Colles' fracture, typically occurs when the wrist is extended during a fall onto an outstretched hand. This causes the distal radius to fracture and angulate dorsally. A is incorrect because a direct blow to the wrist would more likely cause a different fracture pattern. B is incorrect because compression from a fall does not specifically explain the dorsal angulation. D is incorrect because flexion of the wrist during a fall would more likely result in a Smith's fracture, with volar angulation.

questions.question:
A 3-year-old boy is evaluated for a forearm fracture sustained during a fall. The treating physician notes that both forearm bones were fractured. Which of the following statements regarding pediatric forearm fractures is most accurate?
A) They require surgical intervention in all cases
B) They heal slower than adult fractures
C) They typically involve both the radius and ulna
D) They are more common in boys than girls
questions.answer:
D)
Pediatric forearm fractures are approximately twice as common in boys as in girls, a well-established epidemiologic finding supported by multiple large studies. This makes D the most accurate statement among the choices.

A is incorrect because the vast majority of pediatric forearm fractures are treated nonoperatively with closed reduction and casting; surgical intervention is reserved for unstable, irreducible, or open fractures. B is incorrect because pediatric fractures heal faster than adult fractures owing to the thicker, more metabolically active periosteum and greater remodeling potential in children. C is incorrect because, although both-bone forearm fractures are common, many pediatric forearm fractures involve only one bone (e.g., distal radius buckle/torus fractures, isolated greenstick fractures), so it is inaccurate to say they 'typically' involve both bones.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old woman undergoes total knee arthroplasty (TKA) and during the procedure, it is noted that the flexion gap is inadequate. What is the most appropriate surgical adjustment to correct this issue?
A) Increase the size of the femoral component
B) Resection of more bone from the anterior femur
C) Resection of more bone from the posterior femur
D) Add a thicker insert to the tibial component
questions.answer:
C)
Resecting more bone from the posterior femoral condyles directly enlarges the flexion gap by creating additional space when the knee is in flexion. The posterior condyles are the primary determinant of the flexion gap, so additional posterior resection is the appropriate correction.

A is incorrect because increasing the size of the femoral component would effectively shift the posterior condylar surface more posteriorly, which would tighten (decrease) the flexion gap rather than open it.

B is incorrect because resecting more bone from the anterior femur affects the extension gap (and patellar tracking), not the flexion gap.

D is incorrect because adding a thicker tibial insert would tighten both the flexion and extension gaps equally, worsening the already inadequate flexion gap.

questions.question:
During a total hip arthroplasty, the surgeon decides to use the posterior approach. After incising the skin and subcutaneous tissue, which of the following steps is essential in order to detach the external rotators from the femur?
A) Incise the gluteus medius
B) Elevate the gluteus maximus
C) Identify and retract the sciatic nerve
D) Carefully dissect the piriformis muscle
questions.answer:
D)
In the posterior approach to the hip, after splitting the gluteus maximus and incising the fascia, the short external rotators (piriformis, obturator internus, superior and inferior gemelli, and quadratus femoris) must be identified and detached from their femoral insertions. The piriformis is the key landmark — it is identified first and its tendon is tagged and divided, followed by the remaining short external rotators. This step is essential for adequate exposure of the posterior hip capsule.

A is incorrect because the gluteus medius is not incised in the posterior approach; it is the key muscle in the anterolateral (Hardinge) approach. Incising it posteriorly would risk damage to the superior gluteal nerve.
B is incorrect because the gluteus maximus is split along its fibers (not elevated as a flap) to gain access to the deeper structures; this step alone does not detach the external rotators.
C is incorrect because while identifying and protecting the sciatic nerve is an important safety step during the posterior approach, it is done to prevent nerve injury — it is not the step that detaches the external rotators from the femur.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old man, an offensive lineman, presents with persistent pain and weakness in his right shoulder after a tackle. The patient reports a sensation of instability and occasional clicking. MRI reveals a posterior labral tear. What is the most likely mechanism of injury that led to this condition?
A) Overhead throwing
B) Direct trauma from a tackle
C) Repetitive overhead lifting
D) Fall onto an outstretched arm
questions.answer:
B)
Posterior labral tears often occur due to direct trauma, such as a tackle, which can cause posterior shoulder instability and labral injury. This is common in contact sports.
A is incorrect because overhead throwing is more associated with anterior labral tears. C is incorrect because repetitive overhead lifting is not typically associated with posterior labral tears. D is incorrect because a fall onto an outstretched arm is more likely to cause anterior shoulder injuries.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old male presents with wrist pain and decreased grip strength. His examination shows tenderness over the extensor compartments of the wrist. You suspect involvement of the extensor digitorum and extensor indicis. Which compartment of the wrist contains these tendons?
A) First extensor compartment
B) Second extensor compartment
C) Fourth extensor compartment
D) Third extensor compartment
questions.answer:
C)
The extensor digitorum and extensor indicis tendons are located in the fourth extensor compartment of the wrist, which is responsible for extending the fingers. A is incorrect because the first extensor compartment contains the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis. B is incorrect because the second extensor compartment contains the extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis. D is incorrect because the third extensor compartment contains the extensor pollicis longus.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman presents with foot deformities characterized by a high arch and clawing of the toes. She reports a family history of similar conditions. What is the most likely underlying condition causing her symptoms?
A) Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
B) Rheumatoid arthritis
C) Osteoarthritis
D) Gout
questions.answer:
A)
Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease is a hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy that classically presents with cavovarus foot deformity and claw toes due to progressive muscle imbalance (peroneus brevis weakness with unopposed tibialis posterior, and intrinsic muscle wasting). A positive family history of similar deformities strongly supports this diagnosis.

B is incorrect because rheumatoid arthritis typically causes forefoot valgus, hallux valgus, and lesser-toe subluxation/dislocation with synovitis rather than a cavus foot; it is an inflammatory polyarthropathy, not a hereditary neuropathy.
C is incorrect because osteoarthritis causes joint-space narrowing and osteophyte formation but does not produce the combination of cavus foot and claw toes with a hereditary pattern.
D is incorrect because gout presents with acute monoarticular inflammation (classically the first MTP joint) due to urate crystal deposition; it does not cause cavovarus deformity or claw toes.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male has sustained an ankle disarticulation following a severe crush injury. During the pre-operative assessment, you note his intact tibialis posterior function. Which of the following is likely true regarding his potential for a Syme amputation?
A) It will be less energy-efficient for ambulation
B) The heel pad is stable and will provide cushioning
C) He will experience significant post-operative complications
D) His ankle motion will be preserved post-amputation
questions.answer:
B)
In a Syme amputation, a stable heel pad is crucial as it provides end-bearing cushioning in the absence of the foot. An intact tibialis posterior helps maintain the heel pad in a centered position beneath the distal tibia, supporting effective weight-bearing and ambulation.

A is incorrect because a Syme amputation is actually more energy-efficient than a below-knee amputation; preserving limb length and a functional heel pad reduces the metabolic cost of walking.
C is incorrect because Syme amputation, when properly indicated, has a reliable complication profile; stating he "will experience significant post-operative complications" is not an expected outcome and is not supported by the clinical scenario.
D is incorrect because ankle motion is not preserved after a Syme amputation — the ankle joint is completely disarticulated and removed as part of the procedure.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old male presents after a fall, complaining of severe neck pain and difficulty turning his head. X-rays reveal a type II odontoid fracture. Given his age and the nature of the fracture, what is the most appropriate treatment option?
A) Halo vest immobilization
B) Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion
C) Posterior cervical fusion
D) Surgical decompression
questions.answer:
C)
Posterior cervical fusion (typically C1-C2 posterior fixation) is the most appropriate treatment for a type II odontoid fracture in an elderly patient. Type II fractures occur through the base of the dens and have the highest nonunion rate of all odontoid fractures. In elderly patients, halo vest immobilization carries unacceptably high complication and mortality rates, and nonunion rates exceed 40%. Posterior C1-C2 fusion provides rigid fixation and high union rates with an acceptable surgical risk profile in this population.

A is incorrect because halo vest immobilization in elderly patients is associated with very high complication rates (respiratory compromise, aspiration pneumonia, pin-site infections, pressure sores) and mortality rates up to 21-42%, as well as high nonunion rates for type II fractures. B is incorrect because anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) is a procedure for cervical disc pathology, not for odontoid fractures; an anterior odontoid screw could be considered but is a different procedure and is less favored in the elderly due to osteoporotic bone and frequent fracture comminution. D is incorrect because surgical decompression alone does not address fracture stability and is not indicated for an odontoid fracture without evidence of spinal cord compression requiring decompression.

questions.question:
A 12-year-old boy suffers a fracture of the femoral neck. Imaging reveals no displacement, but there is concern for potential avascular necrosis. What is the most appropriate initial management of this fracture?
A) Observation with non-weight-bearing and serial imaging
B) In situ percutaneous screw fixation
C) Immediate total hip arthroplasty
D) Closed reduction and hip spica casting alone
questions.answer:
B)
In a 12-year-old with a non-displaced femoral neck fracture, in situ percutaneous screw fixation is the recommended treatment. Even non-displaced pediatric femoral neck fractures carry a significant risk of avascular necrosis (AVN) and displacement, and internal fixation provides stability to minimize further compromise of the femoral head blood supply. Urgent surgical stabilization is the standard of care.

A is incorrect because observation alone risks secondary displacement, which dramatically increases the rate of AVN; non-displaced pediatric femoral neck fractures are generally treated with internal fixation rather than observation. C is incorrect because total hip arthroplasty is not appropriate in a 12-year-old child; joint-preserving strategies are always preferred. D is incorrect because spica casting alone does not provide adequate stability for a femoral neck fracture and does not protect against displacement or AVN as reliably as internal fixation.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman undergoes total knee arthroplasty and subsequently develops swelling and redness around the incision site. An aspiration of the knee joint reveals 3,500 white blood cells per microliter. What does this finding suggest about the condition of the joint?
A) Inflammatory response
B) Infection
C) Normal post-operative response
D) Gouty arthritis
questions.answer:
B)
In the setting of a total knee arthroplasty, a synovial fluid white blood cell count of 3,500/μL is above the commonly accepted thresholds for periprosthetic joint infection (PJI). The Musculoskeletal Infection Society (MSIS) criteria use a cutoff of approximately 3,000 WBC/μL (some guidelines cite >1,760 for chronic PJI), and when combined with clinical signs of swelling and erythema around the incision, this finding is highly suggestive of infection requiring further workup (differential count, cultures, inflammatory markers) and likely surgical intervention.

A is incorrect because while an inflammatory response can elevate WBC counts, a count of 3,500/μL in a prosthetic joint with local signs of infection exceeds the PJI diagnostic threshold and should not be attributed to a benign inflammatory process.
C is incorrect because normal post-operative synovial fluid after TKA does not typically have WBC counts this high, especially when accompanied by erythema and swelling suggestive of infection.
D is incorrect because gouty arthritis, while it can cause elevated synovial WBC counts, would typically show monosodium urate crystals on polarized microscopy and is not the most likely diagnosis in a recently operated prosthetic joint with periincisional erythema.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male motorcyclist sustains a femoral neck fracture after a collision. During surgical planning for internal fixation, it is crucial to understand the anatomy of the acetabulum. If a transacetabular screw is to be placed, which of the following landmarks is most commonly used to define the quadrants of the acetabulum?
A) Anterior inferior iliac spine
B) Center of the femoral head
C) ASIS
D) Center of the acetabulum
questions.answer:
D)
The quadrant system for safe transacetabular screw placement (described by Wasielewski and others) uses the center of the acetabulum as the reference point. Two perpendicular lines through this center divide the acetabulum into posterosuperior, posteroinferior, anterosuperior, and anteroinferior quadrants, guiding safe screw trajectory to avoid neurovascular injury.

A is incorrect because the anterior inferior iliac spine is an extra-articular landmark used for other surgical approaches but is not the reference point for defining acetabular quadrants.
B is incorrect because the center of the femoral head is an intra-articular landmark of the proximal femur, not the acetabulum; it does not serve as the reference for the acetabular quadrant system.
C is incorrect because the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) is a pelvic landmark used for surgical approaches and clinical measurements but is not used to define the acetabular quadrants for screw placement.

questions.question:
A patient is suspected to have an anteromedial impaction injury of the ankle following a fall from a height. To confirm the diagnosis, which imaging modality would be the most appropriate next step?
A) X-ray
B) MRI
C) CT scan
D) Ultrasound
questions.answer:
C)
A CT scan is the most appropriate imaging modality for confirming an anteromedial impaction injury of the ankle. CT provides excellent bony detail, allowing precise characterization of impaction fractures, comminution, and articular surface depression that may be occult on plain films. It is the standard next step when an impaction fracture is suspected.

A is incorrect because plain X-rays may miss subtle impaction injuries due to overlapping bony structures and limited sensitivity for non-displaced or impacted fractures. B is incorrect because MRI is superior for soft-tissue and osteochondral lesion evaluation but is less precise than CT for defining bony impaction geometry and fracture lines. D is incorrect because ultrasound is useful for soft-tissue pathology (tendons, ligaments, effusions) but cannot adequately assess cortical impaction or intra-articular fracture detail.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old construction worker falls from a height and sustains a mid-shaft humeral fracture. During the evaluation, he exhibits wrist drop and inability to extend the fingers and thumb at the metacarpophalangeal joints. Sensation is diminished over the dorsal first web space. What is the most likely nerve injury associated with this type of fracture?
A) Ulnar nerve
B) Median nerve
C) Radial nerve
D) Axillary nerve
questions.answer:
C)
The radial nerve is most commonly injured in mid-shaft humeral fractures because it courses along the spiral groove on the posterior aspect of the humerus. Injury at this level produces wrist drop (loss of wrist extension), inability to extend the fingers at the MCP joints, and sensory loss over the dorsal first web space. Elbow extension (triceps) is typically preserved because the branches to the triceps arise proximal to the spiral groove.

A is incorrect because the ulnar nerve is not closely associated with the mid-shaft humerus; it is more vulnerable at the medial epicondyle and would present with clawing of the ring and small fingers and sensory loss in the ulnar 1½ digits. B is incorrect because the median nerve runs anteriorly in the arm and is not at risk in mid-shaft humeral fractures; its injury would cause loss of forearm pronation, wrist flexion, and thenar function. D is incorrect because the axillary nerve is associated with proximal humerus fractures or shoulder dislocations and would present with deltoid weakness and a sensory deficit over the lateral deltoid (regimental badge area).

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male rock climber presents with pain and swelling over the dorsum of his wrist after an intense climbing session. He reports that his pain worsens with wrist flexion and extension. Physical examination reveals tenderness along the second extensor compartment. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A) De Quervain's tenosynovitis
B) Intersection syndrome
C) Extensor tendinosis
D) Radiocarpal joint arthritis
questions.answer:
B)
Intersection syndrome involves inflammation where the muscle bellies of the first extensor compartment (APL, EPB) cross over the tendons of the second extensor compartment (ECRL, ECRB), approximately 4–6 cm proximal to Lister's tubercle on the dorsal forearm/wrist. It is common in athletes performing repetitive wrist motions such as rock climbing, and pain worsens with wrist flexion and extension.

A is incorrect because De Quervain's tenosynovitis involves the first extensor compartment (APL, EPB) at the radial styloid, not the second compartment. Tenderness would be at the radial styloid with a positive Finkelstein test. C is incorrect because extensor tendinosis is a degenerative condition of the extensor tendons (commonly at the lateral epicondyle) rather than an inflammatory condition at the intersection of the first and second compartments. D is incorrect because radiocarpal joint arthritis would present with joint-line tenderness, stiffness, and typically occurs in older patients or those with prior trauma, not as an overuse syndrome in a young climber with tenderness along the second extensor compartment.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old male athlete sustains a knee injury while pivoting during a soccer game. MRI results confirm a partial tear of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). The ACL attaches to the tibial footprint in a specific area. Where does the ACL primarily insert on the tibia?
A) Anteromedial aspect of the tibial plateau
B) Posterolateral aspect of the tibial plateau
C) Lateral aspect of the tibial plateau
D) Medial aspect of the tibial plateau
questions.answer:
A)
The ACL inserts on the tibia at the anterior intercondylar area, which is located on the anteromedial aspect of the tibial plateau between the tibial eminences. Understanding the precise tibial footprint is essential for anatomic ACL reconstruction to restore native knee kinematics.

B is incorrect because the posterolateral tibial plateau is the attachment site of the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL), not the ACL. C is incorrect because the lateral aspect of the tibial plateau is not the primary ACL insertion site; the ACL footprint is more anterior and medial within the intercondylar region. D is incorrect because while the ACL footprint has a medial component, it is specifically anteromedial and within the intercondylar area, not on the medial tibial plateau proper (which is associated with the medial meniscus and MCL attachment).

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man presents with a traumatic injury to his left hand, resulting in a bony avulsion at the distal interphalangeal joint (DIPJ) involving more than 50% of the joint surface. What is the most appropriate management for this injury?
A) Conservative management with splinting
B) Surgical repair of the avulsed fragment
C) Immediate arthrodesis of the DIPJ
D) Corticosteroid injection for inflammation control
questions.answer:
B)
Surgical repair (open reduction and internal fixation) of the avulsed fragment is indicated when a bony avulsion at the DIP joint involves more than 50% of the articular surface. Large fragments compromise joint congruity and volar stability; anatomic reduction and fixation restore the joint surface and prevent chronic subluxation or arthritis.

A is incorrect because conservative splinting is appropriate for mallet fractures involving less than one-third of the articular surface without joint subluxation. A fragment exceeding 50% of the joint surface risks volar subluxation and joint incongruity that splinting alone cannot address.

C is incorrect because immediate arthrodesis sacrifices DIP motion and is reserved for salvage situations such as failed prior repair, severe comminution precluding reconstruction, or established post-traumatic arthritis—not as a primary treatment when the fragment is amenable to fixation.

D is incorrect because corticosteroid injection does not address the mechanical problem of a large intra-articular fracture and joint instability; it plays no role in the acute management of bony avulsions.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with acute right hip pain after slipping on ice. She has a history of osteoporosis and is currently on bisphosphonates. An x-ray reveals a non-displaced femoral neck fracture. She undergoes percutaneous cannulated screw fixation. Which of the following best describes the predominant process involved in her fracture healing?
A) Endochondral ossification with external callus formation
B) Primary (direct) bone healing
C) Secondary bone healing with large periosteal callus
D) Intramembranous ossification alone
questions.answer:
B)
Primary (direct) bone healing occurs when fracture fragments are rigidly fixed with minimal interfragmentary gap and motion, as with cannulated screw fixation of a non-displaced femoral neck fracture. Intracapsular femoral neck fractures also lack a significant periosteal layer, further limiting callus formation. Healing proceeds via direct osteonal (Haversian) remodeling across the fracture site without a cartilaginous callus intermediate.

A is incorrect because endochondral ossification with external callus formation is characteristic of secondary bone healing, which requires interfragmentary motion and an intact periosteum — conditions not present with rigid fixation of an intracapsular fracture. C is incorrect because secondary bone healing with a large periosteal callus occurs when there is relative motion at the fracture site (e.g., intramedullary nailing, cast immobilization); rigid screw fixation of a non-displaced intracapsular fracture does not produce this pattern. D is incorrect because intramembranous ossification alone does not describe typical long-bone fracture healing; while some intramembranous bone formation occurs at fracture sites, it is not the predominant mechanism in this scenario.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old male sustains a mid-shaft clavicle fracture from a motorcycle accident. During surgical fixation, the surgeon must be cautious of which vital structure that lies posterior-medially to the clavicle?
A) Brachial plexus
B) Subclavian vessels
C) Axillary nerve
D) Long thoracic nerve
questions.answer:
B)
The subclavian vessels course directly posterior and inferior to the mid-shaft clavicle, separated only by the subclavius muscle and clavipectoral fascia. During plate fixation of a mid-shaft clavicle fracture, over-penetration of drill bits or screws posteriorly risks catastrophic vascular injury to these vessels.

A is incorrect because the brachial plexus, while also posterior to the clavicle, lies more lateral (at the level of the lateral third/first rib junction) and is not the structure classically described as 'posterior-medial' to the mid-shaft clavicle.
C is incorrect because the axillary nerve is located well distal to the clavicle, coursing around the surgical neck of the humerus through the quadrilateral space.
D is incorrect because the long thoracic nerve runs along the lateral chest wall on the serratus anterior and is not in the immediate posterior-medial vicinity of the mid-shaft clavicle.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old female with a hip fracture undergoes surgery using a cephalomedullary nail. During the procedure, the surgeon must ensure proper alignment of the device. Which anatomical landmark is typically used as a reference for the placement of the nail?
A) Greater trochanter
B) Center of the intercondylar notch
C) Tip of the femoral head
D) Lateral cortex of the femur
questions.answer:
A)
The greater trochanter is the primary anatomical landmark used as the entry point and reference for placement of a cephalomedullary nail. Modern trochanteric-entry nails use the tip of the greater trochanter (or slightly medial to it) as the starting point, and proper alignment of the nail in the intramedullary canal is confirmed relative to this landmark on both AP and lateral fluoroscopic views.

B is incorrect because the center of the intercondylar notch is the reference point for antegrade femoral nailing via a retrograde approach or for retrograde nails, not for cephalomedullary nails inserted proximally.
C is incorrect because the tip of the femoral head is the target for the cephalic lag screw component, not the reference landmark for placement of the nail itself.
D is incorrect because the lateral cortex of the femur is not a standard reference landmark for cephalomedullary nail insertion; the nail enters through the proximal trochanteric region, not the lateral cortex of the shaft.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man with a history of chronic osteoarthritis presents for follow-up after a recent knee arthroscopy. He is advised to avoid NSAIDs due to their potential effects on healing. What is the primary reason for avoiding NSAIDs in the context of fracture healing?
A) They increase inflammation
B) They impair osteoblast function
C) They stimulate chondrocyte activity
D) They enhance bone mineralization
questions.answer:
B)
NSAIDs can impair osteoblast function, which is crucial for bone healing after fractures. By inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, NSAIDs may delay the healing process, making it important to use them cautiously in patients recovering from fractures or surgeries involving bone. A is incorrect because NSAIDs decrease inflammation, not increase it. C is incorrect because NSAIDs do not stimulate chondrocyte activity; they inhibit it. D is incorrect because NSAIDs do not enhance bone mineralization; they can potentially impair it.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old male presents to the emergency department after experiencing a seizure. Upon examination, he is found to have a posterior shoulder dislocation. Which of the following mechanisms is most likely associated with this type of dislocation?
A) Direct trauma
B) Seizures or electrocution
C) Sports injury
D) Fall onto an outstretched hand
questions.answer:
B)
Posterior shoulder dislocations are often associated with seizures or electrocution due to the violent muscle contractions that can force the humeral head posteriorly. Recognizing these mechanisms is crucial for timely diagnosis and management. A is incorrect because direct trauma more commonly causes anterior dislocations. C is incorrect because sports injuries typically result in anterior dislocations. D is incorrect because a fall onto an outstretched hand is more likely to cause an anterior dislocation or a fracture.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male construction worker falls from a height and presents with severe back pain and inability to move his legs. Imaging reveals a burst fracture at L1 with involvement of the anterior and middle columns. What is the most appropriate management for this injury?
A) Conservative management with bed rest
B) Immediate surgical decompression and stabilization
C) Partial weight-bearing with a brace
D) Physical therapy for rehabilitation
questions.answer:
B)
A burst fracture at L1 involving the anterior and middle columns with associated neurological deficit (inability to move the legs) constitutes an unstable injury with spinal cord/conus medullaris compromise. Immediate surgical decompression and stabilization are indicated to relieve neural compression, restore spinal alignment, and prevent further neurological deterioration.

A is incorrect because conservative management with bed rest alone is insufficient for an unstable burst fracture with neurological deficit; it does not address canal compromise or spinal instability.
C is incorrect because partial weight-bearing with a brace is appropriate for stable compression fractures without neurological involvement, not for unstable burst fractures with paralysis.
D is incorrect because physical therapy is part of the rehabilitation phase after definitive treatment but does not address the acute need for decompression and stabilization in a patient with an unstable fracture and neurological deficit.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old female is involved in a sports collision and presents with acute neck pain. Initial CT imaging shows a dislocated C5-C6 facet joint. Neurological examination reveals weakness in the right upper extremity. What is the most likely mechanism of injury?
A) Hyperextension
B) Flexion-distraction
C) Axial loading
D) Hyperflexion
E) Rotation
questions.answer:
D)
A dislocated facet joint at C5-C6 is often associated with a hyperflexion mechanism of injury, where the neck is forced into excessive forward bending. This can lead to neurological deficits due to spinal cord compression. A is incorrect because hyperextension typically causes posterior element injuries. B is incorrect because flexion-distraction injuries usually involve ligamentous disruption without facet dislocation. C is incorrect because axial loading is more likely to cause burst fractures. E is incorrect because rotation alone is less likely to cause facet dislocation without accompanying flexion.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old man presents with shoulder pain and a history of trauma. An X-ray reveals a 'light bulb sign', suggesting a specific dislocation. Which type of dislocation is most consistent with this finding?
A) Anterior shoulder dislocation
B) Posterior shoulder dislocation
C) Inferior shoulder dislocation
D) Superior shoulder dislocation
questions.answer:
B)
The 'light bulb sign' is pathognomonic for a posterior shoulder dislocation. It occurs because the humeral head is locked in internal rotation behind the glenoid, causing the greater and lesser tuberosities to overlap on the AP radiograph, giving the humeral head a symmetric, rounded ('light bulb') appearance. This sign is critical because posterior dislocations are frequently missed on initial imaging.

A is incorrect because anterior shoulder dislocation typically shows the humeral head displaced medially and inferiorly relative to the glenoid on an AP view; the normal asymmetric humeral head contour is preserved, and no light bulb sign is seen.
C is incorrect because inferior shoulder dislocation (luxatio erecta) presents with the humeral head displaced below the glenoid and the arm locked in abduction, not with a light bulb sign.
D is incorrect because superior shoulder dislocation is exceedingly rare and is associated with massive rotator cuff and capsular disruption; it does not produce a light bulb sign.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old boy presents to the clinic with a history of right leg pain and limping over the past month. The mother reports that the child has been increasingly reluctant to participate in sports. On examination, there is tenderness over the right greater trochanter, and the child holds the hip in slight flexion and external rotation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Perthes disease
B) Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
C) Osteomyelitis
D) Greater trochanteric bursitis
questions.answer:
A)
Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease is avascular necrosis of the femoral head that typically presents in children aged 4–8 years with insidious hip or referred knee pain, an antalgic gait, and the hip held in flexion with limited abduction and internal rotation. This 7-year-old's age, gradual onset of pain, limping, and reluctance to participate in sports are classic for Perthes disease.

B is incorrect because slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) characteristically occurs in adolescents aged 10–16, often in obese children, and presents with obligate external rotation during hip flexion (Drehmann sign); a 7-year-old is outside the typical age range.
C is incorrect because osteomyelitis usually presents with acute onset of pain, fever, elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP, WBC), and focal bony tenderness rather than a chronic, insidious limp without systemic signs.
D is incorrect because greater trochanteric bursitis is exceedingly rare in children and is a diagnosis of adults, typically presenting with lateral hip pain exacerbated by direct pressure or repetitive activity.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old man presents with chronic groin pain and limited range of motion in his left hip. X-rays show subchondral sclerosis and joint space narrowing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Osteoarthritis
B) Avascular necrosis
C) Femoral neck fracture
D) Labral tear
questions.answer:
A)
The presence of subchondral sclerosis and joint space narrowing on x-ray is characteristic of osteoarthritis. This diagnosis is consistent with the patient's symptoms and imaging findings, indicating degenerative changes in the hip joint. B is incorrect because avascular necrosis would typically show a crescent sign or collapse of the femoral head. C is incorrect because a femoral neck fracture would present with acute pain and possibly displacement on imaging. D is incorrect because a labral tear would not typically show subchondral sclerosis or joint space narrowing on x-ray.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old boy with a history of hypothyroidism presents with hip pain and limping. X-rays show a slight displacement of the femoral head. What underlying condition might be causing this presentation?
A) Osteoarthritis
B) Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
C) Perthes disease
D) Osteochondritis dissecans
questions.answer:
B)
Hypothyroidism is a well-recognized endocrinopathy associated with slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE). Thyroid hormone is essential for normal physeal maturation and endochondral ossification; its deficiency weakens the physis and predisposes to slippage. A 7-year-old with hypothyroidism presenting with hip pain, limping, and femoral head displacement on X-ray is a classic atypical (young age) SCFE presentation warranting endocrine workup.

A is incorrect because osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease of adults and is not associated with hypothyroidism in a 7-year-old child. C is incorrect because Perthes disease (avascular necrosis of the femoral head) presents with fragmentation and sclerosis of the femoral epiphysis rather than displacement of the femoral head relative to the neck, and it is not specifically linked to hypothyroidism. D is incorrect because osteochondritis dissecans typically affects the knee (lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle) rather than the hip, and the described X-ray finding of femoral head displacement is characteristic of SCFE, not OCD.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents with persistent pain and swelling in the midfoot region after a fall. She has difficulty bearing weight on her right foot. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the tarsometatarsal joint. An X-ray shows a fracture of the second metatarsal with disruption of the tarsometatarsal joint. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Jones fracture
B) Lisfranc injury
C) Stress fracture
D) Morton's neuroma
E) Plantar fasciitis
questions.answer:
B)
A Lisfranc injury involves a fracture and/or dislocation at the tarsometatarsal (TMT) joint, most commonly affecting the second metatarsal base. The mechanism of injury often involves axial loading on a plantarflexed foot (e.g., a fall), and the presentation includes midfoot pain, swelling, and inability to bear weight, which aligns with this patient's history and imaging.

A is incorrect because a Jones fracture is a fracture at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction of the fifth metatarsal, not the second metatarsal or the tarsometatarsal joint. C is incorrect because stress fractures develop from repetitive microtrauma rather than an acute fall, and they do not cause tarsometatarsal joint disruption. D is incorrect because Morton's neuroma is an interdigital nerve entrapment causing forefoot pain and paresthesias in the web space, not midfoot tenderness or joint disruption. E is incorrect because plantar fasciitis presents with plantar heel pain, typically worst with the first steps in the morning, and is unrelated to tarsometatarsal joint pathology or acute trauma.

questions.question:
During a pelvic surgery, the surgeon needs to navigate between the external iliac vessels and iliopsoas muscle. What anatomical approach is best suited for this maneuver?
A) Posterior approach
B) Lateral approach
C) Medial window of the ilioinguinal approach
D) Anterior approach to the iliac crest
questions.answer:
C)
The medial window of the ilioinguinal approach provides access between the external iliac vessels and the iliopsoas muscle. This window is created by retracting the external iliac vessels laterally and the spermatic cord/round ligament medially, allowing direct visualization of the quadrilateral surface and pelvic brim — essential for acetabular and pelvic fracture fixation.

A is incorrect because the posterior approach (e.g., Kocher-Langenbeck) accesses the posterior column and wall of the acetabulum and does not provide exposure of the external iliac vessels or iliopsoas in this region. B is incorrect because a lateral approach does not provide access to the intrapelvic structures between the external iliac vessels and iliopsoas. D is incorrect because the anterior approach to the iliac crest exposes the iliac wing and anterior column but does not navigate between the external iliac vessels and iliopsoas muscle — that interval is specific to the medial window of the ilioinguinal approach.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman presents with numbness and tingling in the sole of her foot, particularly when standing or walking. Upon examination, compression of the tarsal tunnel elicits symptoms. Which condition is most likely affecting her tibial nerve?
A) Tarsal tunnel syndrome
B) Plantar fasciitis
C) Achilles tendinitis
D) Peripheral neuropathy
questions.answer:
A)
Tarsal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the posterior tibial nerve as it passes beneath the flexor retinaculum (laciniate ligament) posterior and inferior to the medial malleolus. It classically presents with numbness, tingling, and burning in the plantar aspect of the foot, reproduced by percussion or compression over the tarsal tunnel (positive Tinel sign).

B is incorrect because plantar fasciitis causes heel pain (especially with the first steps in the morning) due to inflammation of the plantar fascia origin at the calcaneal tuberosity; it does not cause numbness/tingling or reproduce symptoms with tarsal tunnel compression.
C is incorrect because Achilles tendinitis presents with posterior heel and Achilles tendon pain, not plantar numbness or tingling, and is unrelated to tibial nerve compression.
D is incorrect because peripheral neuropathy (e.g., diabetic) typically causes a symmetric stocking-glove distribution of sensory loss in both feet and would not be specifically reproduced by focal compression of the tarsal tunnel.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman sustains an ankle injury after rolling her ankle during a basketball game. She presents with pain along the medial aspect of the ankle and tenderness over the proximal fibula. An x-ray of the ankle shows widening of the medial clear space but no distal fibula fracture. What fracture pattern should be suspected?
A) Lateral malleolus fracture
B) Maisonneuve fracture
C) Pilon fracture
D) Bimalleolar fracture
E) Talar dome lesion
questions.answer:
B)
A Maisonneuve fracture is a proximal fibula fracture associated with disruption of the interosseous membrane, the syndesmosis (tibiofibular ligaments), and the deltoid ligament (or medial malleolus fracture). The key clue is medial ankle pain with widening of the medial clear space on ankle films but no distal fibula fracture — a full-length leg film will reveal the proximal fibula fracture. This pattern indicates significant ankle instability requiring surgical stabilization.

A is incorrect because a lateral malleolus fracture would be visible on the ankle x-ray and does not explain proximal fibula tenderness or isolated medial clear-space widening. C is incorrect because a pilon (tibial plafond) fracture results from axial loading mechanisms (e.g., fall from height), not a rotational ankle injury, and would show distal tibial articular comminution. D is incorrect because a bimalleolar fracture involves fractures of both the lateral and medial malleoli, which would be apparent on the ankle x-ray. E is incorrect because a talar dome lesion (osteochondral defect) is a cartilage/subchondral bone injury of the talus, not associated with proximal fibula tenderness or medial clear-space widening.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old diabetic patient presents with increasing pain and swelling in the knee joint. An MRI shows evidence of septic arthritis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Start oral antibiotics
B) Joint aspiration
C) Surgical debridement
D) MRI re-evaluation
E) Refer to rheumatology
questions.answer:
B)
Joint aspiration is the most appropriate next step when septic arthritis is suspected or suggested by imaging. Synovial fluid analysis (cell count, Gram stain, crystal analysis, and culture) is essential to confirm the diagnosis, identify the causative organism, and guide targeted antibiotic therapy. Aspiration also provides therapeutic benefit by decompressing the joint.

A is incorrect because starting oral antibiotics without first obtaining a synovial fluid sample for culture and sensitivity would be premature and could mask the organism, making definitive treatment more difficult; furthermore, septic arthritis typically requires IV antibiotics, not oral.
C is incorrect because surgical debridement (arthroscopic or open washout) may ultimately be needed, but it is not the immediate next step before confirming the diagnosis and identifying the organism via aspiration.
D is incorrect because MRI re-evaluation adds no further useful information when septic arthritis is already suspected; the priority is obtaining synovial fluid for analysis.
E is incorrect because septic arthritis is an orthopaedic emergency requiring urgent aspiration and treatment, not a routine rheumatology referral.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old male collegiate baseball pitcher presents with persistent medial elbow pain and instability during throwing. Physical examination reveals positive valgus stress test findings. An MRI shows a torn ulnar collateral ligament. Which of the following surgical techniques is most appropriate for this injury?
A) Open repair of the ulnar collateral ligament using a medial approach
B) Arthroscopic repair of the anterior oblique bundle
C) Lateral epicondyle release
D) Corticosteroid injection into the elbow
questions.answer:
A)
The standard surgical treatment for a torn ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) in a competitive throwing athlete is UCL reconstruction (Tommy John procedure) performed through a medial approach, typically using a palmaris longus or gracilis tendon autograft. While the answer choice states "open repair," among the options listed it is the best answer, as the procedure is performed open via a medial approach. Primary repair alone is reserved for select acute proximal avulsion injuries; most cases require reconstruction with a graft.

B is incorrect because arthroscopic repair of the anterior oblique bundle is not the standard of care for UCL injuries in throwing athletes; reliable arthroscopic UCL reconstruction techniques have not been established as standard practice. C is incorrect because lateral epicondyle release is used for recalcitrant lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow), which is a completely different pathology from UCL insufficiency. D is incorrect because corticosteroid injection is not a definitive treatment for a complete UCL tear causing instability in a throwing athlete and does not restore ligament integrity or stability.

questions.question:
During a surgical procedure on the lumbar spine, a surgeon must be cautious of the risk of damaging the inferior aspect of the vertebrae. Which structure is located inferiorly and could potentially be injured during retraction?
A) Dura mater
B) Cauda equina
C) Intervertebral disc
D) Spinal nerve root
questions.answer:
C)
Explanation: The intervertebral disc is located inferiorly to the vertebral body and is at risk during posterior surgical approaches. Careful retraction is required to avoid injury to the disc, which can lead to complications such as disc herniation or instability. The dura mater and cauda equina are typically posterior and lateral, respectively, while spinal nerve roots exit laterally.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman who recently started a new job requiring repetitive gripping and wringing motions presents with pain and swelling along the radial aspect of her wrist. On examination, tenderness is noted over the radial styloid and first dorsal compartment. The Finkelstein test reproduces her pain. Which of the following structures is most likely affected?
A) Abductor pollicis longus tendon
B) Opponens pollicis muscle
C) Flexor pollicis longus tendon
D) Extensor pollicis brevis tendon
questions.answer:
A)
De Quervain tenosynovitis is a stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal compartment, which contains the abductor pollicis longus (APL) and extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) tendons. A positive Finkelstein test (pain with ulnar deviation of the wrist while the thumb is clasped in the fist) is the hallmark finding. The APL is the larger and more consistently symptomatic tendon in this compartment and is the best single answer.

B is incorrect because the opponens pollicis is a thenar intrinsic muscle innervated by the median nerve; it is not part of the first dorsal compartment and is not implicated in de Quervain tenosynovitis. C is incorrect because the flexor pollicis longus travels in its own synovial sheath on the volar side of the wrist and would not produce radial-sided dorsal compartment pain or a positive Finkelstein test. D is incorrect because, although the EPB is also within the first dorsal compartment and is involved in de Quervain disease, the APL is the primary and larger tendon of this compartment; when only one structure can be selected, APL is the preferred board answer.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old male soccer player presents with a drooping distal phalanx of his right index finger following a direct blow during a match. Examination reveals an inability to actively extend the finger at the distal interphalangeal joint. There is no bony injury noted on the x-ray. What is the best initial treatment for this condition?
A) Surgical repair of the extensor tendon
B) Splinting the finger in extension for 6-8 weeks
C) Injection of a corticosteroid
D) Buddy taping to the adjacent finger
questions.answer:
B)
The patient has a mallet finger — a disruption of the terminal extensor tendon at the DIP joint — evidenced by a drooping distal phalanx and inability to actively extend the DIP joint. With no bony avulsion on x-ray, this is a closed tendinous mallet finger. The standard initial treatment is continuous splinting of the DIP joint in full extension (or slight hyperextension) for 6–8 weeks to allow tendon healing.

A is incorrect because surgical repair is not first-line for a closed tendinous mallet finger; it is considered for open injuries, failed splinting, or large bony avulsion fragments with joint subluxation.
C is incorrect because corticosteroid injection has no role in treating an acute extensor tendon disruption and could impair tendon healing.
D is incorrect because buddy taping does not maintain the DIP joint in extension and therefore cannot facilitate healing of the terminal extensor tendon.

questions.question:
During a surgical procedure for hip replacement, the gluteus maximus muscle is encountered and reflected. Which of the following structures must also be carefully handled to avoid compromising the surrounding tissues as the surgery approaches the posterior aspect of the acetabulum?
A) Tensor fasciae latae
B) Gluteus medius
C) Fascia lata
D) Piriformis
questions.answer:
C)
The fascia lata covers the gluteus medius and plays a protective role in the surgical approach to the acetabulum. Care must be taken to preserve this structure to maintain the integrity of the surrounding muscles and soft tissues, especially during posterior approaches.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician due to bowing of his legs and delayed walking. His family history reveals a cousin with rickets. Examination shows tenderness at the costochondral junctions. Which of the following is the underlying mechanism responsible for his condition?
A) Defective collagen synthesis
B) Impaired phosphate metabolism
C) Overproduction of calcitonin
D) Increased vitamin D absorption
questions.answer:
B)
X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets is characterized by impaired phosphate metabolism due to mutations (commonly in the PHEX gene) that lead to elevated FGF-23 and renal phosphate wasting. This results in inadequate mineralization of the growth plate, producing rickets with leg bowing, delayed walking, and rachitic rosary (costochondral junction tenderness). The family history of a cousin with rickets is consistent with X-linked inheritance.

A is incorrect because defective collagen synthesis underlies osteogenesis imperfecta, which presents with fragile bones and fractures rather than classic rickets with growth-plate widening and bowing.
C is incorrect because overproduction of calcitonin does not cause rickets; calcitonin inhibits osteoclastic resorption and is not a recognized mechanism for impaired mineralization of the growth plate.
D is incorrect because increased vitamin D absorption would enhance calcium and phosphate availability and would not cause rickets; rickets results from deficiency or resistance to vitamin D, or from phosphate wasting, not from excess absorption.

questions.question:
A 18-year-old girl presents with a persistent, painful mass on her mid-tibia that has not improved over the past 8 months. Despite being treated with conservative measures, her symptoms have worsened, and imaging reveals a small, cortically based lesion. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Start analgesics and observe
B) Consider radiofrequency ablation
C) Perform curettage of the lesion
D) Refer for surgical fixation
questions.answer:
B)
Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is the most appropriate next step for a symptomatic osteoid osteoma that has failed conservative management. Osteoid osteoma is a small (<1.5 cm), cortically based benign bone tumor classically presenting in adolescents/young adults with pain (often nocturnal) that responds to NSAIDs. When conservative measures fail, CT-guided RFA is the current first-line interventional treatment, offering high success rates (>90%) with minimal morbidity.

A is incorrect because analgesics and observation constitute continued conservative management, which has already failed over 8 months with worsening symptoms, making further observation inappropriate.
C is incorrect because curettage (open surgical excision) is a valid treatment for osteoid osteoma but is more invasive than RFA and is generally reserved for lesions in locations not amenable to RFA or after RFA failure; RFA is preferred as the first-line interventional approach.
D is incorrect because surgical fixation is not indicated; osteoid osteoma does not cause structural instability requiring fixation, and the lesion is a small cortical-based tumor, not a fracture.

questions.question:
A patient presents with acute shoulder pain and a palpable defect over the anterior shoulder following a weightlifting injury. Physical examination reveals weakness in flexion and adduction of the arm. Which structure is most likely involved in this injury?
A) Subscapularis tendon
B) Pectoralis major tendon
C) Supraspinatus tendon
D) Coracobrachialis tendon
questions.answer:
B)
The pectoralis major tendon is responsible for flexion and adduction of the shoulder. A rupture or tear of this tendon is commonly seen in weightlifting injuries, particularly when excessive weight is lifted during bench press exercises. A is incorrect because the subscapularis tendon is primarily involved in internal rotation and adduction, not flexion. C is incorrect because the supraspinatus tendon is involved in abduction, not flexion or adduction. D is incorrect because the coracobrachialis assists in flexion and adduction but is less commonly injured in weightlifting compared to the pectoralis major.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old male presents with difficulty in lifting his right arm and localized pain in the thoracic region. A CT scan reveals a herniated disc at the T7-T8 level. Which nerve root is most likely affected, causing weakness in the serratus posterior superior muscle?
A) T3
B) T4
C) T5
D) T6
questions.answer:
B)
Explanation: The serratus posterior superior muscle is primarily innervated by the intercostal nerves, particularly T2 to T5. A herniated disc at T7-T8 could lead to the involvement of T6, but the weakness in the muscle would be primarily due to the T4 nerve root being affected, as it is the closest to the herniation and innervates the muscle.

questions.question:
A 14-year-old boy sustains a fracture to the distal radius during a basketball game. An X-ray reveals a fracture line through the physis with a triangular metaphyseal fragment (Thurston-Holland fragment) but no epiphyseal involvement. Which type of Salter-Harris fracture classification is most likely represented in this case?
A) Type I
B) Type II
C) Type III
D) Type IV
questions.answer:
B)
A Salter-Harris Type II fracture extends through the physis and exits through the metaphysis, producing a characteristic triangular metaphyseal fragment (Thurston-Holland fragment). It is the most common physeal fracture pattern (~75% of all Salter-Harris injuries) and is the most frequent type seen in distal radius physeal fractures in adolescents.

A is incorrect because a Type I fracture involves separation purely through the physis without a visible fracture line on plain films (no metaphyseal or epiphyseal fragment). C is incorrect because a Type III fracture extends from the physis into the epiphysis without metaphyseal involvement; this pattern is less common and typically seen at the distal tibia. D is incorrect because a Type IV fracture crosses the metaphysis, physis, and epiphysis — a more complex injury pattern not described by this stem.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old woman presents with numbness and tingling in her little finger and half of her ring finger after a fall while rock climbing. She notes that the symptoms worsen when she performs gripping activities. Physical examination reveals atrophy of the hypothenar muscles. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
A) Cubital tunnel syndrome
B) Guyon's canal syndrome
C) Carpal tunnel syndrome
D) Median nerve compression
questions.answer:
B)
The numbness in the little finger and ulnar half of the ring finger combined with hypothenar muscle atrophy localizes the lesion to the ulnar nerve at or distal to the wrist — specifically Guyon's canal. A fall on an outstretched hand during rock climbing can directly compress the ulnar nerve within Guyon's canal. Hypothenar atrophy without dorsal hand sensory loss (which is supplied by the dorsal cutaneous branch arising proximal to Guyon's canal) further supports a distal ulnar nerve lesion at the wrist.

A is incorrect because cubital tunnel syndrome involves ulnar nerve compression at the elbow. While it produces similar sensory symptoms in the ring and little fingers, it typically also causes intrinsic hand muscle weakness (interossei, lumbricals to ring/little fingers) and may include decreased sensation on the dorsal ulnar hand (dorsal cutaneous branch). The mechanism of a wrist-level fall and isolated hypothenar atrophy favor a more distal lesion.
