C is incorrect because carpal tunnel syndrome involves median nerve compression, which causes numbness in the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger — not the little finger or ulnar half of the ring finger.

D is incorrect because median nerve compression produces symptoms in the median nerve distribution (thumb through radial half of ring finger) and thenar muscle atrophy, not hypothenar atrophy or little finger numbness.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male construction worker presents with shoulder pain and weakness after lifting heavy materials. Upon examination, he has a positive drop arm test and marked weakness in abducting the arm. An MRI reveals a full-thickness tear of the rotator cuff. Which surgical approach is most commonly used for rotator cuff repair in such cases?
A) Anterior deltoid approach
B) Lateral approach
C) Posterior approach
D) Deltopectoral approach
questions.answer:
B)
The lateral (deltoid-splitting) approach is the most commonly used open/mini-open surgical approach for rotator cuff repair. It provides direct access to the supraspinatus and infraspinatus tendons at the greater tuberosity while preserving the deltoid origin. In current practice, arthroscopic repair is most common overall, but among the listed open approaches, the lateral deltoid-splitting technique is standard.

A is incorrect because the anterior deltoid approach does not provide optimal exposure of the superior rotator cuff footprint and risks detaching the deltoid origin. C is incorrect because the posterior approach is used for procedures such as posterior instability surgery or infraspinatus-specific pathology, not for routine rotator cuff repair. D is incorrect because the deltopectoral approach is the workhorse for shoulder arthroplasty, proximal humerus fracture fixation, and anterior stabilization procedures; it does not provide adequate direct access to the superior rotator cuff insertion on the greater tuberosity.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old man sustains a wrist injury after falling onto an outstretched hand. He is unable to extend his little finger at the metacarpophalangeal joint. On examination, you find a laceration at the base of the little finger. Which of the following injuries is most likely responsible for this presentation?
A) Mallet finger
B) Jersey finger
C) Dupuytren's contracture
D) Extensor digiti minimi rupture
questions.answer:
D)
The inability to extend the little finger at the metacarpophalangeal joint, coupled with a laceration, suggests an extensor digiti minimi rupture. This injury results in the loss of extension at the MCP joint due to disruption of the extensor mechanism. A is incorrect because mallet finger affects the distal interphalangeal joint, not the MCP joint. B is incorrect because jersey finger involves the flexor tendon, leading to inability to flex, not extend. C is incorrect because Dupuytren's contracture causes flexion contractures, not inability to extend.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman complains of pain and a popping sensation in her right middle finger when gripping objects. On physical examination, her finger locks intermittently, and there is palpable tenderness over the A1 pulley. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Surgical release of the A1 pulley
B) Corticosteroid injection into the A1 pulley
C) Occupational therapy and splinting
D) Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications
questions.answer:
B)
Corticosteroid injection into the A1 pulley is the most appropriate first-line treatment for trigger finger (stenosing tenosynovitis) presenting with intermittent locking and tenderness over the A1 pulley. Injection has a high success rate (up to 60–90% resolution) and is the standard initial intervention before considering surgery.

A is incorrect because surgical release of the A1 pulley is reserved for cases that fail conservative management, including corticosteroid injections (typically after 2–3 failed injections or in recalcitrant cases). It is not the first-line treatment.
C is incorrect because while occupational therapy and splinting (e.g., MCP joint extension splint) may be used as adjuncts, they are less effective than corticosteroid injection for symptomatic trigger finger with intermittent locking and are not the most appropriate next step.
D is incorrect because NSAIDs alone provide limited relief for trigger finger and do not address the mechanical stenosis at the A1 pulley. They are inferior to corticosteroid injection as a primary treatment.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma presents with metastatic lesions in his lungs and bones. He is experiencing significant pain, and the orthopedic team is considering embolization for palliation. What is the primary benefit of renal cell embolization in this patient?
A) Cure of the renal cancer
B) Reduction of bone pain due to metastases
C) Prevention of new metastatic lesions
D) Improvement in renal function
questions.answer:
B)
Renal cell carcinoma metastases are characteristically hypervascular. Embolization — whether of the primary renal tumor or of hypervascular bone metastases — reduces blood flow, promotes tumor necrosis, and can significantly decrease pain. It is a palliative intervention, not curative, and is particularly useful for painful, hypervascular skeletal metastases from RCC.

A is incorrect because embolization is a palliative procedure; it does not cure renal cell carcinoma.
C is incorrect because embolization does not prevent the development of new metastatic lesions; it addresses existing tumor burden and symptoms.
D is incorrect because embolization causes tumor necrosis and ischemia — it does not improve renal function and may in fact reduce it if the renal primary is embolized.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old male basketball player presents to the clinic complaining of knee pain after landing awkwardly during a jump. Physical examination reveals a positive Lachman test and swelling around the knee joint. MRI shows an ACL tear. Which of the following graft options has the highest load to failure for ACL reconstruction in this patient?
A) Patellar tendon autograft
B) Quadriceps tendon autograft
C) Hamstring tendon autograft
D) Allograft tissue
questions.answer:
C)
A quadrupled (4-strand) hamstring tendon autograft has the highest ultimate load to failure among commonly used ACL graft options, reported at approximately 4108 N in biomechanical studies. This makes it the strongest graft in terms of load to failure, which is an important consideration in a young, high-demand athlete.

A is incorrect because the bone-patellar tendon-bone autograft, while an excellent graft with reliable bone-to-bone healing, has a lower ultimate load to failure (~2977 N) compared to a 4-strand hamstring graft.
B is incorrect because the quadriceps tendon autograft, although increasingly popular and a viable option, has a lower ultimate load to failure (~2352 N) than the 4-strand hamstring graft.
D is incorrect because allograft tissue generally has lower mechanical properties than autograft options due to processing (irradiation, freeze-drying) and is associated with higher re-tear rates in young, active patients.

questions.question:
During a surgical procedure to address a fracture of the distal radius, the surgeon must access the anterior aspect of the radius. They plan to make an extensile incision over the radial styloid. Which of the following describes the potential complications of this approach?
A) Damage to the ulnar nerve
B) Injury to the superficial radial nerve
C) Compromise of the median nerve
D) Impairment of the flexor pollicis longus
E) Fracture of the scaphoid
questions.answer:
B)
The superficial branch of the radial nerve (SBRN) courses along the lateral forearm deep to brachioradialis and emerges subcutaneously near the radial styloid. An extensile incision over the radial styloid places this nerve at significant risk; injury results in numbness or painful neuroma over the dorsoradial hand. Careful identification and protection of the SBRN is essential during this approach.

A is incorrect because the ulnar nerve lies on the medial (ulnar) side of the wrist and forearm and is not at risk during a radial-sided approach.
C is incorrect because the median nerve travels through the carpal tunnel on the central-volar aspect of the wrist; it is not in the direct surgical field of an incision over the radial styloid.
D is incorrect because the flexor pollicis longus (FPL) lies deep on the volar aspect of the radius; while it can be encountered during a volar (Henry) approach, it is not the structure most at risk from an incision specifically over the radial styloid — the SBRN is the classic at-risk structure.
E is incorrect because scaphoid fracture is not a recognized complication of this surgical approach; it is a traumatic injury, not a surgical complication of the incision.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for evaluation of his gait. His mother notes that he often sits in a 'W' position and has increased internal rotation of the legs. Physical examination confirms increased femoral anteversion. What is the most likely long-term outcome of this condition?
A) Increased risk of hip dislocation in adulthood
B) Resolution of symptoms without intervention
C) Development of osteoarthritis in the knee
D) Persistent in-toeing into adulthood
E) Increased risk of patellofemoral pain syndrome
questions.answer:
B)
Increased femoral anteversion in young children typically resolves naturally as they grow, with most children not requiring intervention. Symptoms usually improve without treatment.
A is incorrect because increased femoral anteversion does not increase the risk of hip dislocation in adulthood. C is incorrect because there is no direct link between femoral anteversion and knee osteoarthritis. D is incorrect because in-toeing usually resolves as the child grows. E is incorrect because increased femoral anteversion does not directly lead to patellofemoral pain syndrome.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female presents with shoulder pain after a fall from a bicycle. Physical examination reveals a prominent distal clavicle and pain on palpation over the acromioclavicular joint. An x-ray shows a disruption at the acromioclavicular joint but the coracoclavicular ligaments appear intact. Based on this presentation, which Rockwood classification does this injury fall under?
A) Grade I
B) Grade II
C) Grade III
D) Grade IV
questions.answer:
B)
A Grade II acromioclavicular (AC) joint injury is characterized by complete disruption of the AC ligaments with intact coracoclavicular (CC) ligaments. Clinically this presents with a prominent distal clavicle and pain at the AC joint, and imaging shows widening or subluxation at the AC joint without increased coracoclavicular distance.

A is incorrect because a Grade I injury is a sprain of the AC ligament without joint disruption or displacement on imaging; this patient has visible disruption at the AC joint.
C is incorrect because a Grade III injury involves complete disruption of both the AC and CC ligaments, resulting in superior displacement of the clavicle with increased coracoclavicular distance; here the CC ligaments are intact.
D is incorrect because a Grade IV injury involves complete disruption of both AC and CC ligaments with posterior displacement of the distal clavicle into or through the trapezius, which is not described in this presentation.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male soccer player presents with posterior knee pain and instability after a tackle. On examination, he has a positive posterior drawer test. An MRI reveals a tear of the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL). If surgical intervention is chosen, what complication might arise if the tibial tunnel is positioned improperly during reconstruction?
A) Graft impingement
B) Excessive laxity in the knee
C) Accelerated degenerative changes
D) Nonunion of the graft
questions.answer:
B)
Improper positioning of the tibial tunnel during PCL reconstruction can result in a non-anatomic graft orientation, leading to excessive residual laxity and persistent posterior instability. Accurate tunnel placement—particularly avoiding a tunnel that is too lateral or too distal on the tibial side—is critical for restoring normal knee kinematics and achieving adequate graft tension throughout the range of motion.

A is incorrect because graft impingement is more classically associated with ACL reconstruction when the tibial tunnel is placed too anteriorly, causing the graft to impinge against the intercondylar roof in extension; while it can occur in PCL reconstruction, it is not the most characteristic complication of tibial tunnel malposition in this context.
C is incorrect because accelerated degenerative changes are a long-term sequela of persistent instability rather than a direct, immediate complication of tunnel malposition itself.
D is incorrect because nonunion of the graft (failure of graft-to-bone healing) is related to biological incorporation factors and fixation method rather than tunnel positioning per se.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male presents with pain and weakness in his forearm after falling onto an outstretched hand while playing basketball. On examination, he has difficulty flexing the wrist and fingers. An x-ray reveals a fracture of the medial epicondyle. Which muscle primarily affected by this injury is responsible for wrist flexion and originates from the medial epicondyle?
A) Flexor digitorum profundus
B) Flexor carpi radialis
C) Flexor carpi ulnaris
D) Pronator teres
questions.answer:
B)
The flexor carpi radialis (FCR) originates from the medial epicondyle of the humerus and is a primary wrist flexor. Unlike the FCU, which has a dual origin (humeral head from the medial epicondyle and ulnar head from the olecranon), the FCR originates solely from the medial epicondyle, making it more directly compromised by a medial epicondyle fracture.

A is incorrect because the flexor digitorum profundus originates primarily from the proximal ulna and interosseous membrane, not the medial epicondyle. C is incorrect because while the flexor carpi ulnaris does have a humeral head from the medial epicondyle, it also has an ulnar head origin and its primary action is wrist adduction (ulnar deviation) rather than pure wrist flexion. D is incorrect because the pronator teres, although it originates from the medial epicondyle, is primarily a forearm pronator, not a wrist flexor.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old woman with a long-standing history of diabetes presents with a swollen, warm foot and a foot drop. Physical exam reveals a rocker-bottom deformity of the foot. X-rays show bone resorption in the midfoot. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
B) Charcot neuroarthropathy
C) Cavus foot deformity
D) Tarsal coalition
questions.answer:
B)
Charcot neuroarthropathy is a progressive, destructive arthropathy most commonly seen in patients with long-standing diabetes and peripheral neuropathy. The classic presentation includes a swollen, warm, erythematous foot with rocker-bottom deformity due to midfoot collapse, and imaging demonstrates bone resorption, fragmentation, and joint destruction. Foot drop may result from associated peripheral neuropathy.

A is incorrect because Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is a hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy that typically presents with cavus foot deformity and progressive distal muscle weakness, not rocker-bottom deformity or midfoot bone resorption. C is incorrect because cavus foot deformity is characterized by an abnormally high arch, often associated with neuromuscular conditions such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, and does not present with a rocker-bottom foot or midfoot bone destruction. D is incorrect because tarsal coalition is a congenital condition involving abnormal bridging (fibrous, cartilaginous, or osseous) between tarsal bones, typically presenting in adolescence with a rigid flatfoot and peroneal spasm, not with the destructive changes and rocker-bottom deformity seen here.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old male presents with acute neck pain following a fall. His CT scan shows a C6 vertebral body fracture with posterior displacement. Which of the following complications should the clinician be most concerned about?
A) Intra-abdominal hemorrhage
B) Spinal cord injury
C) Pneumothorax
D) Hematoma formation
questions.answer:
B)
A C6 vertebral body fracture with posterior displacement of the fracture fragment narrows the spinal canal and places the spinal cord at significant risk for compression or direct injury. This can result in devastating neurological deficits including quadriparesis, making spinal cord injury the most concerning complication in this clinical scenario.

A is incorrect because intra-abdominal hemorrhage is not a direct consequence of a cervical spine fracture; it would be associated with abdominal or pelvic trauma.
C is incorrect because pneumothorax is typically associated with thoracic trauma (e.g., rib fractures, penetrating chest injury) rather than a cervical vertebral body fracture.
D is incorrect because while epidural or soft-tissue hematoma can occur with cervical fractures, it is a far less immediately concerning complication compared to direct spinal cord compression from a posteriorly displaced fracture fragment.

questions.question:
A 2-year-old child is brought to the clinic for evaluation of a thumb fracture after a fall. The child has a stable fracture with no displacement. How many pins would be appropriate for internal fixation of this type of fracture in this age group?
A) One pin
B) Two pins
C) Three pins
D) Four pins
questions.answer:
B)
Explanation: In a 2-year-old with a stable thumb fracture, two pins are typically sufficient for internal fixation. This allows for adequate stabilization while minimizing the risk of complications associated with excess hardware in a young child.

questions.question:
A five-year-old child falls from a swing and lands on their outstretched arm. The child presents with elbow pain and swelling. On examination, the carrying angle is measured to be 15 degrees. Which of the following findings would most likely indicate a need for further imaging?
A) Increased range of motion in elbow extension
B) Tenderness over the lateral epicondyle
C) Inability to fully extend the elbow
D) Pain relief with rest
E) Normal forearm rotation
questions.answer:
C)
Inability to fully extend the elbow after a fall onto an outstretched hand in a child is a classic red-flag finding for a supracondylar humeral fracture. Loss of full extension suggests an effusion or bony block, and further imaging (radiographs) is warranted. The carrying angle of 15 degrees described in the stem is within the normal range (5–15 degrees) and is not itself concerning.

A is incorrect because increased range of motion in elbow extension is not a typical post-injury finding and would not raise concern for fracture.
B is incorrect because isolated lateral epicondyle tenderness in a 5-year-old is more suggestive of soft-tissue contusion; it is less specific for fracture than loss of extension, and lateral epicondyle fractures are uncommon at this age.
D is incorrect because pain relief with rest is a reassuring sign and would not prompt further imaging.
E is incorrect because normal forearm rotation suggests intact proximal radioulnar joint and radial head, which is a reassuring finding rather than one that warrants further workup.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old male sustained a complex pilon fracture of the ankle during a fall from height. After initial stabilization, external fixation is considered for his management. Which of the following statements about external fixation in this situation is MOST accurate?
A) It is contraindicated in closed fractures.
B) It is only effective for low-energy injuries.
C) It helps maintain limb length and alignment.
D) It is not useful in the presence of compartment syndrome.
questions.answer:
C)
External fixation in complex pilon fractures helps maintain limb length and alignment while allowing for soft tissue recovery before definitive fixation. This is a well-established damage-control strategy in high-energy injuries where immediate internal fixation is precluded by soft tissue swelling and compromise.

A is incorrect because external fixation is commonly used in both open and closed fractures, particularly high-energy closed pilon fractures where soft tissue swelling precludes early internal fixation.
B is incorrect because external fixation is especially valuable in high-energy injuries (not only low-energy ones), serving as a temporizing or definitive stabilization method.
D is incorrect because external fixation is actually useful in the setting of compartment syndrome; it stabilizes the fracture while allowing access for fasciotomies and ongoing soft tissue monitoring.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old man presents with severe knee pain and swelling after a fall. An x-ray shows joint effusion, and the treating physician suspects septic arthritis. Which imaging finding would most likely indicate the need for immediate arthrocentesis?
A) Subchondral bone cysts
B) Presence of a joint effusion
C) Osteophyte formation
D) Periarticular edema
questions.answer:
B)
A joint effusion in the setting of clinical suspicion for septic arthritis is the primary indication for immediate arthrocentesis. Aspiration allows analysis of synovial fluid (cell count, Gram stain, culture, crystal analysis) to confirm or exclude infection, and also provides therapeutic decompression of the joint.

A is incorrect because subchondral bone cysts are a feature of chronic degenerative or inflammatory arthropathy, not an acute finding that prompts emergent aspiration.
C is incorrect because osteophyte formation is a hallmark of osteoarthritis and reflects chronic joint remodeling, not an acute infectious process requiring arthrocentesis.
D is incorrect because periarticular edema (soft-tissue swelling around the joint) is a nonspecific finding; while it may accompany infection, it does not by itself confirm an intra-articular collection that can be aspirated, unlike a true joint effusion.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old man presents with a painful flexor tendon injury of the ring finger after a fall. Physical examination reveals an inability to flex the distal phalanx. The injury is suspected to be a jersey finger. Why is this type of injury particularly concerning?
A) It involves a complete rupture of the flexor tendon
B) It damages the vinculae, which supply blood to the tendon
C) It may lead to a fixed flexion deformity
D) It is associated with carpal tunnel syndrome
questions.answer:
A)
Jersey finger is defined by a complete avulsion of the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon from its insertion on the distal phalanx. This is particularly concerning because the ruptured tendon can retract proximally (sometimes into the palm), making delayed repair difficult or impossible. Early surgical reattachment is essential for restoring active DIP flexion.

B is incorrect because while the vinculae do provide segmental blood supply to the flexor tendons and may be disrupted during tendon retraction, vincular damage is a secondary consequence rather than the defining reason jersey finger is concerning. The primary concern is the complete tendon avulsion itself.
C is incorrect because jersey finger results in loss of active DIP flexion (an extension posture at the DIP), not a fixed flexion deformity. Fixed flexion deformity is more characteristic of Dupuytren contracture or other conditions.
D is incorrect because jersey finger (FDP avulsion at the distal phalanx) is not associated with carpal tunnel syndrome; these are distinct pathologies involving different anatomical sites.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old male presents to the clinic with left arm pain that has persisted for several months. He has a history of recurrent bone cysts. Recent imaging reveals a lytic lesion in the proximal humerus with a ground-glass appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Osteosarcoma
B) Aneurysmal bone cyst
C) Fibrous dysplasia
D) Enchondroma
questions.answer:
C)
The imaging findings of a lytic bone lesion with a ground-glass appearance in a young male suggest fibrous dysplasia, which is often associated with GNAS mutations. A is incorrect because osteosarcoma typically presents with more aggressive features, such as periosteal reaction and soft tissue mass, and does not have a ground-glass appearance. B is incorrect because aneurysmal bone cysts are expansile and have fluid-fluid levels on imaging. D is incorrect because enchondromas typically present as well-defined, lytic lesions with chondroid calcifications, not a ground-glass appearance.

questions.question:
A 12-year-old boy is diagnosed with a Tillaux fracture after an ankle injury from a fall. What is the best surgical approach for this fracture?
A) Closed reduction and casting
B) Open reduction and internal fixation
C) Arthroscopic repair
D) Conservative management with a brace
questions.answer:
B)
A Tillaux fracture is a Salter-Harris III fracture of the anterolateral distal tibial epiphysis, occurring in adolescents as the lateral physis is the last portion to close. Because it is an intra-articular fracture, open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) is indicated when articular displacement is ≥2 mm to restore joint congruity and prevent post-traumatic arthritis.

A is incorrect because closed reduction and casting may be appropriate only for non-displaced Tillaux fractures; the classic board teaching emphasizes ORIF for displaced intra-articular fractures to ensure anatomic reduction. C is incorrect because while arthroscopy can be used as an adjunct to confirm reduction, it is not the primary surgical approach for fixation of a Tillaux fracture. D is incorrect because conservative management with a brace does not provide adequate immobilization or reduction for a displaced intra-articular fracture of the distal tibial epiphysis.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man presents with complaints of numbness in the dorsal aspect of his foot and between the first and second toes. Neurological examination reveals an absence of deep touch, proprioception, and vibratory sense in these areas. Given this presentation, which sensory tract is likely affected?
A) Spinothalamic tract
B) Corticospinal tract
C) Dorsal columns
D) Lateral corticospinal tract
questions.answer:
C)
The dorsal columns (posterior columns) carry proprioception, deep touch, and vibratory sense. Loss of these modalities, as described in this patient, localizes the lesion to the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway.

A is incorrect because the spinothalamic tract carries pain, temperature, and crude (light) touch — not proprioception or vibratory sense. B is incorrect because the corticospinal tract is a motor (descending) pathway; damage produces upper motor neuron weakness, not sensory loss. D is incorrect because the lateral corticospinal tract is the major descending motor tract for voluntary limb movement; its disruption causes contralateral (above the decussation) or ipsilateral (below the decussation) motor deficits, not the sensory deficits described here.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old recreational golfer has been experiencing medial elbow pain for several months, worsened by his swing. On examination, there is tenderness over the medial epicondyle and pain with resisted wrist flexion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Lateral epicondylitis
B) Medial epicondylitis
C) Ulnar collateral ligament tear
D) Medial collateral ligament strain
questions.answer:
B)
Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) is caused by overuse and microtearing of the flexor-pronator mass origin at the medial epicondyle. It classically presents with medial elbow pain worsened by gripping and wrist flexion activities (e.g., a golf swing), tenderness directly over the medial epicondyle, and pain with resisted wrist flexion.

A is incorrect because lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) involves the extensor tendon origin at the lateral epicondyle and produces lateral elbow pain with resisted wrist extension, not medial pain with resisted wrist flexion.
C is incorrect because an ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) tear typically presents with medial elbow pain during valgus stress (e.g., overhead throwing), a positive moving valgus stress test, and instability rather than isolated pain with resisted wrist flexion.
D is incorrect because medial collateral ligament strain is essentially the same entity as a UCL injury; it would present with valgus instability and pain on valgus stress testing, not with pain localized to the medial epicondyle reproduced by resisted wrist flexion.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old male undergoes a total hip arthroplasty using a posterior approach. During the procedure, the surgical team needs to ensure proper exposure of the acetabulum. Which of the following steps is crucial for retracting the gluteus medius anteriorly during the posterior Southern-Moore approach?
A) Incising the gluteus maximus
B) Mobilizing the sciatic nerve
C) Identifying the trochanteric bursa
D) Using a blunt retractor on the gluteus medius
questions.answer:
D)
During the posterior (Southern/Moore) approach to the hip, the gluteus medius must be retracted anteriorly to expose the acetabulum. A blunt retractor (e.g., a Hohmann or cobra retractor) is placed on the anterior aspect of the gluteus medius to achieve this exposure while minimizing muscle trauma.

A is incorrect because the gluteus maximus is split (not incised/transected) along its fibers in the posterior approach; this step provides superficial exposure but does not specifically retract the gluteus medius anteriorly for acetabular visualization.
B is incorrect because the sciatic nerve is identified and protected during the posterior approach, but mobilizing it is not a step for retracting the gluteus medius; rather, it is a safety measure to prevent nerve injury.
C is incorrect because while the trochanteric bursa may be encountered and incised during dissection, identifying it is not the crucial step for anterior retraction of the gluteus medius to expose the acetabulum.

questions.question:
After performing a retroperitoneal approach to access the lumbar spine in a 50-year-old male, a surgeon notes a need to understand the applied surgical anatomy of this approach. Which structure should be avoided to prevent postoperative complications?
A) Aorta
B) Ureters
C) Lumbar plexus
D) Diaphragm
questions.answer:
A)
Explanation: When accessing the lumbar spine via a retroperitoneal approach, it is crucial to avoid the aorta, which can be injured during dissection. Understanding the anatomy in this region is vital for minimizing complications during surgical procedures.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old female soccer player sustains a direct blow to the knee during a game and presents with localized swelling and pain. MRI shows a fracture through the superolateral portion of her patella, which raises concern for a bipartite patella. What is the most appropriate management for her injury?
A) Conservative with rest and ice
B) Surgical fixation of the patella
C) Intra-articular corticosteroid injection
D) Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) only if displaced
questions.answer:
A)
A fracture through a bipartite patella (stress fracture through the synchondrosis) in the setting of a direct blow, presenting with localized swelling and pain without mention of displacement, is best managed initially with conservative treatment including rest, ice, activity modification, and a period of immobilization. Most symptomatic bipartite patella injuries and non-displaced patellar fractures heal with conservative care.

B is incorrect because surgical fixation is not indicated as first-line treatment for a non-displaced fracture or symptomatic bipartite patella; it is reserved for cases that fail conservative management or have significant displacement.
C is incorrect because intra-articular corticosteroid injection does not address a fracture and is not appropriate management for an acute bony injury.
D is incorrect because ORIF is reserved for displaced patellar fractures with loss of the extensor mechanism or significant articular incongruity; the stem does not describe displacement, so conservative management is the most appropriate initial step.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man presents with lateral elbow pain after lifting a heavy object. On examination, there is tenderness over the lateral epicondyle and pain with resisted wrist extension. An MRI shows tendinopathy with a partial tear at the common extensor origin. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Immediate surgery to repair the tendon
B) Activity modification and physical therapy
C) Intra-articular corticosteroid injection
D) Application of a counterforce brace alone without physical therapy
questions.answer:
B)
Partial tears and tendinopathy at the common extensor origin (lateral epicondylitis) are initially managed conservatively with activity modification, physical therapy focusing on eccentric strengthening, and possibly bracing. The majority of patients improve with 6–12 months of nonoperative treatment.

A is incorrect because immediate surgical repair is not indicated for a partial tear; surgery is reserved for patients who fail an adequate trial (typically 6–12 months) of conservative management.
C is incorrect because although corticosteroid injections may provide short-term relief, they are not the most appropriate next step as first-line management; they do not address the underlying pathology and may weaken the tendon with repeated use.
D is incorrect because a counterforce brace alone, without a structured physical therapy program including eccentric exercises, is insufficient treatment for a partial tear at the common extensor origin.

questions.question:
A 16-year-old male presents with a progressive thoracic kyphosis, measured at 75 degrees on standing x-ray. He reports no associated neurological symptoms but has noticeable difficulty maintaining an upright posture. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Initiate physical therapy
B) Monitor with annual x-rays
C) Refer for a spinal brace
D) Consider surgical intervention
questions.answer:
D)
In Scheuermann kyphosis exceeding 70–75 degrees, surgical correction is the most appropriate consideration, as bracing becomes less effective at this magnitude and the deformity carries risk of progression, chronic pain, and cardiopulmonary compromise. This patient's 75-degree kyphosis with postural difficulty meets the threshold for surgical intervention.

A is incorrect because physical therapy alone cannot correct a structural kyphosis of this magnitude; it may serve as an adjunct but is insufficient as primary treatment.
B is incorrect because annual monitoring without intervention is appropriate for mild kyphosis (typically <50–60 degrees); a 75-degree curve warrants active treatment rather than observation.
C is incorrect because bracing is generally indicated for Scheuermann kyphosis in the 55–70 degree range in skeletally immature patients; at 75 degrees, bracing is unlikely to achieve meaningful correction.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman with a history of cavovarus foot deformity presents with pain and weakness in her calf muscles. Physical exam reveals tightness in the gastrocnemius muscle with limited ankle dorsiflexion. Which surgical procedure would be most appropriate for addressing her condition?
A) Achilles tendon repair
B) Gastrocnemius recession
C) Ankle arthrodesis
D) Calcaneal osteotomy
questions.answer:
B)
Gastrocnemius recession (Strayer procedure) is the most appropriate surgical intervention when the primary problem is isolated gastrocnemius tightness causing limited ankle dorsiflexion. By lengthening the gastrocnemius aponeurosis, the procedure restores dorsiflexion and reduces forefoot overload, addressing the patient's functional limitations.

A is incorrect because Achilles tendon repair is indicated for acute Achilles tendon rupture, not for contracture or tightness of the gastrocnemius. C is incorrect because ankle arthrodesis is reserved for end-stage ankle arthritis with pain refractory to conservative measures, not for isolated gastrocnemius contracture. D is incorrect because calcaneal osteotomy (e.g., lateralizing or Dwyer) addresses hindfoot varus malalignment rather than isolated gastrocnemius tightness; while it may be part of a comprehensive cavovarus correction, it does not directly treat the dorsiflexion limitation described in this stem.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a motorcycle accident. He complains of severe knee pain and exhibits a deformity at the lateral aspect of the knee. On examination, there is a loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of his neurological deficit?
A) Direct trauma to the knee
B) Compression from hematoma formation
C) Stretching of the nerve during dislocation
D) Ischemia due to popliteal artery injury
questions.answer:
C)
The common peroneal nerve courses around the fibular neck and is tethered at this location, making it highly susceptible to traction injury during knee dislocation. In this scenario, the lateral deformity and dorsal foot sensory loss are consistent with a posterolateral knee dislocation with associated common peroneal nerve palsy. The nerve is stretched beyond its elastic limit as the tibia displaces, producing a neurapraxia or axonotmesis.

A is incorrect because direct trauma to the knee (e.g., a blow to the fibular head) can injure the peroneal nerve, but the clinical picture here — knee deformity consistent with dislocation — points to a traction mechanism rather than a direct blow. B is incorrect because while hematoma-related compression can cause nerve palsy, it typically presents in a delayed fashion rather than immediately after injury, and it is not the most common mechanism in knee dislocations. D is incorrect because popliteal artery injury can cause ischemia to the leg and foot, but ischemic nerve injury would present with more diffuse findings (motor and sensory loss in multiple nerve distributions, pallor, pulselessness) rather than an isolated common peroneal nerve deficit.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old male weightlifter experiences sudden shoulder pain while bench pressing. Examination shows a palpable defect in the anterior chest wall, and imaging confirms a rupture of the pectoralis major tendon. What is the recommended treatment?
A) Conservative management with ice and rest
B) Corticosteroid injection
C) Surgical repair of the tendon
D) Physical therapy alone
questions.answer:
C)
Surgical repair of the pectoralis major tendon is recommended for complete ruptures in young, active patients, particularly athletes who require upper body strength. Acute repair yields superior outcomes compared to delayed repair, restoring near-normal strength and cosmesis.

A is incorrect because conservative management alone for a complete tendon rupture in a young athlete leads to persistent weakness and cosmetic deformity, with significantly inferior functional outcomes compared to surgical repair.
B is incorrect because corticosteroid injection has no role in treating a complete tendon rupture; it does not restore structural continuity and may impair tissue healing.
D is incorrect because physical therapy alone cannot restore the mechanical continuity of a completely ruptured tendon and will result in residual weakness, especially with heavy lifting activities.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old athlete experiences a hip pointer after a direct blow to the lateral aspect of the hip during a soccer game. He presents with localized tenderness and swelling over the iliac crest. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for this condition?
A) Surgical intervention
B) Rest and ice application
C) Immediate MRI for assessment
D) Corticosteroid injection
questions.answer:
B)
A hip pointer is a contusion of the iliac crest and overlying soft tissues resulting from a direct blow. Initial management consists of rest, ice application, compression, and analgesics to reduce pain and swelling. This conservative approach allows gradual symptom resolution and return to activity.

A is incorrect because surgical intervention is not indicated for a hip pointer, which is a self-limited soft-tissue contusion without structural disruption requiring operative repair.
C is incorrect because an immediate MRI is unnecessary; the diagnosis is clinical, and imaging is reserved only if a fracture or other significant pathology is suspected and not confirmed on plain films.
D is incorrect because corticosteroid injection is not part of the standard initial management of a hip pointer and carries risks of tissue atrophy and delayed healing without meaningful benefit in this acute contusion.

questions.question:
A 37-year-old athlete undergoes ACL reconstruction utilizing a tendon graft. The surgeon harvests a tendon that is known to have a dual function in both knee flexion and hip extension. Which tendon is most likely used for this purpose?
A) Gracilis
B) Semitendinosus
C) Quadriceps tendon
D) Sartorius
questions.answer:
B)
The semitendinosus tendon is a hamstring muscle that functions in both knee flexion and hip extension, matching the stem description. It is one of the most commonly harvested tendons for ACL reconstruction (often as part of a hamstring autograft). Its expendability and adequate graft properties make it a suitable choice.

A is incorrect because the gracilis contributes to knee flexion and hip adduction (not hip extension); although it is also commonly harvested for ACL reconstruction, it does not match the dual function described in the stem.
C is incorrect because the quadriceps tendon is a knee extensor (not a knee flexor) and does not contribute to hip extension.
D is incorrect because the sartorius functions in hip flexion, abduction, and external rotation as well as knee flexion; it does not serve as a hip extensor.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old woman presents with knee pain after a skiing accident. Imaging shows a tear of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus and evidence of an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) deficiency. Which structure primarily restrains anterior translation of the tibia in the setting of an ACL-deficient knee?
A) Lateral meniscus
B) Posterior horn of the medial meniscus
C) Medial collateral ligament
D) Posterior cruciate ligament
questions.answer:
B)
In an ACL-deficient knee, the posterior horn of the medial meniscus serves as the most important secondary restraint to anterior tibial translation. This is why chronic ACL deficiency leads to increased stress on the medial meniscus, predisposing it to tears, and why ACL reconstruction outcomes are worse when the medial meniscus is deficient.

A is incorrect because the lateral meniscus contributes less to anteroposterior stability than the medial meniscus; it is more of a secondary restraint to rotation.
C is incorrect because the medial collateral ligament (MCL) primarily resists valgus stress and external rotation, not anterior tibial translation.
D is incorrect because the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) is the primary restraint to posterior tibial translation, not anterior translation.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old female basketball player suffers a left shoulder injury during a game. She reports pain localized to the lateral aspect of her shoulder and difficulty raising her arm above her head. X-rays reveal a fracture of the lateral third of the clavicle, where both the conoid and trapezoid ligaments remain intact. Which type of clavicular fracture does she have?
A) Type I
B) Type II
C) Type III
D) Type IV
questions.answer:
A)
In the Neer classification of distal (lateral) clavicle fractures, a Type I fracture occurs lateral to the coracoclavicular (conoid and trapezoid) ligaments, which remain intact and attached to the medial fragment. Because the CC ligaments are undisrupted, the fracture is typically stable and minimally displaced, and most are treated nonoperatively.

B is incorrect because a Type II fracture involves disruption of the coracoclavicular ligaments (the conoid ligament detaches from the medial fragment), resulting in instability and superior displacement of the proximal fragment — the stem specifically states both ligaments are intact. C is incorrect because a Type III fracture involves an intra-articular extension into the acromioclavicular joint without CC ligament disruption, which is not described here. D is incorrect because a Type IV fracture (described in pediatric patients) involves a periosteal sleeve avulsion with displacement of the clavicle superiorly through the periosteum, which does not match this presentation.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman with a history of chronic hip pain undergoes a total hip arthroplasty. During the procedure, the surgeon utilizes a medial approach to gain access to the hip joint. Which two muscles are primarily affected during this approach?
A) Gluteus maximus and iliopsoas
B) Iliopsoas and pectineus
C) Rectus femoris and sartorius
D) Gluteus medius and tensor fascia lata
E) Iliacus and psoas major
questions.answer:
B)
The medial (Ludloff) approach to the hip involves dissection in the interval near the adductor longus, pectineus, and iliopsoas. Among the listed choices, the iliopsoas and pectineus are the two muscles most directly encountered and affected during this approach, as they form the deep muscular floor of the medial dissection to the hip joint.

A is incorrect because the gluteus maximus is a posterior structure and is not primarily involved in a medial approach; it is encountered in posterior approaches to the hip.
C is incorrect because the rectus femoris and sartorius are anterior thigh muscles encountered in anterior or anterolateral approaches (e.g., Smith-Petersen), not the medial approach.
D is incorrect because the gluteus medius and tensor fascia lata are lateral hip abductors encountered in lateral or anterolateral approaches (e.g., Hardinge), not the medial approach.
E is incorrect because the iliacus and psoas major together form the iliopsoas; listing them as a separate pair is redundant and does not include the pectineus, which is a key muscle in the medial approach.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old football player presents with elbow instability after a fall during practice. He reports a sensation of the elbow 'giving way' during quick directional changes. Physical examination reveals a positive posterolateral drawer test. Which condition does this suggest?
A) UCL injury
B) Posterolateral rotatory instability
C) Medial epicondylitis
D) Lateral epicondylitis
questions.answer:
B)
Posterolateral rotatory instability (PLRI) is the most common pattern of recurrent elbow instability and results from insufficiency of the lateral ulnar collateral ligament (LUCL). The posterolateral rotatory drawer test (or pivot-shift test of the elbow) reproduces subluxation of the radial head posterolaterally relative to the humerus, which is pathognomonic for PLRI. This mechanism is consistent with a fall on an outstretched hand and the sensation of the elbow 'giving way.'

A is incorrect because UCL (medial collateral ligament) injury causes medial-sided instability and valgus laxity, not posterolateral instability; it would be assessed with a valgus stress test, not a posterolateral drawer test.
C is incorrect because medial epicondylitis is an overuse tendinopathy of the flexor-pronator mass causing medial elbow pain, not mechanical instability or a positive posterolateral drawer test.
D is incorrect because lateral epicondylitis is an overuse tendinopathy of the common extensor origin causing lateral elbow pain with gripping; it does not produce instability or a positive posterolateral drawer test.

questions.question:
During a routine examination, a pediatrician assesses a 2-month-old infant who is noted to have a left hip that is adducted and internally rotated. The Barlow test is performed, and a clunk is felt with posterior force applied. What does this finding indicate?
A) Normal hip development
B) Hip dislocation
C) Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
D) Femoral neck fracture
questions.answer:
B)
A positive Barlow test—elicited by adducting and applying a posteriorly directed force to the flexed hip, producing a palpable clunk—indicates that the femoral head can be subluxated or dislocated out of the acetabulum. This signifies hip instability consistent with developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH). Early detection and treatment (e.g., Pavlik harness) are critical to promote normal acetabular development.

A is incorrect because a normal hip would remain stable during the Barlow maneuver without any clunk or sensation of subluxation. C is incorrect because avascular necrosis of the femoral head is not a clinical finding in a 2-month-old on routine exam and would not produce a clunk on provocative testing. D is incorrect because a femoral neck fracture would present with acute pain, swelling, and limb shortening after trauma, not as a provocable clunk on the Barlow test.

questions.question:
A 12-year-old boy falls off his bike and lands on his outstretched arm. He presents with elbow pain and limited range of motion. An x-ray shows a minimally displaced (<2 mm) fracture of the lateral condyle of the humerus with an intact cartilage hinge. Which statement regarding the management of this fracture is true?
A) Surgical intervention is always indicated for lateral condyle fractures
B) Immobilization in a long-arm cast with close follow-up and serial imaging is appropriate initial management
C) The fracture will heal without any treatment due to its incomplete nature
D) Open reduction is required due to the child's age
questions.answer:
B)
Minimally displaced (<2 mm) lateral condyle fractures with an intact cartilage hinge can be managed nonoperatively with long-arm cast immobilization. However, close follow-up with serial imaging (typically at 1 week) is essential because these fractures are prone to late displacement, which would then require surgical fixation.

A is incorrect because surgical intervention is reserved for lateral condyle fractures with ≥2 mm displacement or those that displace during follow-up; minimally displaced fractures can be managed conservatively. C is incorrect because even incomplete lateral condyle fractures require immobilization and close monitoring — they do not simply heal without intervention, and neglected fractures can lead to nonunion, cubitus valgus, and tardy ulnar nerve palsy. D is incorrect because the child's age alone is not an indication for open reduction; the decision for surgery is based on fracture displacement, not patient age.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old athlete presents with pain and swelling in the anterior compartment of his leg after participating in an intense training session. His physical exam reveals tightness and diminished sensation in the foot. What is the most appropriate next step in management to prevent complications?
A) Rest and ice
B) Immediate fasciotomy
C) Physical therapy
D) Analgesics
questions.answer:
B)
Acute compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency. The combination of anterior compartment pain, tightness, and diminished sensation (suggesting deep peroneal nerve compromise) after intense exertion is consistent with acute compartment syndrome. Emergent fasciotomy is the definitive treatment to decompress the compartment and prevent irreversible muscle necrosis, nerve injury, and Volkmann-type contracture.

A is incorrect because rest and ice are appropriate for minor soft-tissue injuries or chronic exertional compartment syndrome after activity, but they will not relieve the elevated intracompartmental pressure in acute compartment syndrome and delay definitive treatment risks permanent damage.
C is incorrect because physical therapy has no role in the acute management of compartment syndrome; it may be useful in rehabilitation after surgical decompression but does not address the emergent elevated pressures.
D is incorrect because analgesics only mask pain without treating the underlying pathology; they may actually be harmful by obscuring worsening clinical signs and delaying fasciotomy.

questions.question:
An 80-year-old female presents after a low-energy fall. Imaging reveals a displaced 4-part proximal humerus fracture with disruption of the medial calcar. Given her age and low-demand lifestyle, what is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
A) Humeral head replacement (hemiarthroplasty)
B) Total elbow arthroplasty
C) Open reduction and internal fixation with locking plate
D) Conservative management with a sling
questions.answer:
A)
In elderly, low-demand patients with a displaced 4-part proximal humerus fracture, hemiarthroplasty (humeral head replacement) is the preferred treatment. Fixation of 4-part fractures in osteoporotic bone carries high failure rates (screw cut-out, avascular necrosis), and hemiarthroplasty reliably provides pain relief and acceptable function with lower reoperation rates in this population.

B is incorrect because total elbow arthroplasty addresses pathology of the elbow joint, not the proximal humerus; it has no role in proximal humerus fracture management.
C is incorrect because open reduction and internal fixation of a 4-part proximal humerus fracture in an 80-year-old with osteoporotic bone has high complication rates including fixation failure, AVN of the humeral head, and malunion; it is better suited for younger, higher-demand patients with adequate bone quality.
D is incorrect because a displaced 4-part fracture with calcar disruption in an elderly patient will result in significant pain, loss of function, and malunion if treated non-operatively; conservative management is more appropriate for non-displaced or minimally displaced fractures.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old female athlete experiences a twisting injury to her right knee while playing volleyball. Following the injury, she reports a sensation of her knee giving way and is unable to fully extend it. An MRI scan reveals a complete tear of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) with associated damage to the medial meniscus. Which of the following is the best initial management step for this injury?
A) Immediate surgical intervention
B) RICE protocol followed by rehabilitation
C) Bracing and activity modification
D) A follow-up MRI in 6 weeks
questions.answer:
B)
For an acute ACL tear with associated meniscal damage, the best initial management step is the RICE protocol (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) followed by a structured rehabilitation program to restore range of motion, reduce swelling, and regain quadriceps strength before proceeding to surgical reconstruction. Operating on an acutely swollen, stiff knee increases the risk of arthrofibrosis and poor outcomes. Once the knee has been optimized (typically 2–6 weeks), ACL reconstruction with concurrent meniscal repair can be planned.

A is incorrect because immediate surgical intervention on an acutely injured, swollen knee is associated with higher rates of arthrofibrosis and inferior outcomes; a period of prehabilitation is recommended before reconstruction.
C is incorrect because bracing and activity modification alone may be appropriate for low-demand patients, but this young athlete with a complete ACL tear and meniscal damage will ultimately need surgical reconstruction; however, the initial step is still to control swelling and restore motion first.
D is incorrect because a follow-up MRI in 6 weeks is unnecessary when the diagnosis has already been established; delaying treatment without initiating rehabilitation is not appropriate management.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male is evaluated for cervical radiculopathy. Physical examination reveals a diminished triceps reflex and weakness of wrist extension and finger extension. An MRI shows a herniated disc at the C6-C7 level. Which spinal nerve root is most likely affected in this patient?
A) C5
B) C6
C) C7
D) C8
questions.answer:
C)
A C6-C7 disc herniation compresses the exiting C7 nerve root. C7 radiculopathy classically presents with a diminished triceps reflex, weakness of wrist extension (extensor carpi radialis brevis, extensor carpi ulnaris) and finger extension, and sensory changes over the middle finger. The examination findings in this stem are consistent with C7 involvement.

A is incorrect because the C5 nerve root exits at the C4-C5 foramen and is compressed by a C4-C5 disc herniation; C5 radiculopathy causes deltoid and biceps weakness with a diminished biceps reflex. B is incorrect because the C6 nerve root exits at the C5-C6 foramen and is compressed by a C5-C6 disc herniation; C6 radiculopathy causes diminished brachioradialis reflex, biceps weakness, and sensory changes in the thumb and lateral forearm. D is incorrect because the C8 nerve root exits at the C7-T1 foramen and is compressed by a C7-T1 disc herniation; C8 radiculopathy causes intrinsic hand muscle weakness and sensory changes along the medial forearm and ring/small fingers.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old female basketball player reports a 'pop' in her knee followed by immediate swelling and inability to bear weight after landing awkwardly. Physical examination reveals a positive Lachman's test. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Immediate arthroscopy
B) MRI to confirm diagnosis
C) Knee immobilization and crutches
D) Corticosteroid injection
questions.answer:
B)
In a young athlete with a mechanism consistent with ACL injury (landing awkwardly, audible pop, immediate effusion) and a positive Lachman's test, the most appropriate next step is MRI to confirm the ACL tear and evaluate for commonly associated injuries such as meniscal tears, bone bruises, and other ligamentous damage. This information is essential for surgical planning and counseling.

A is incorrect because immediate arthroscopy is not indicated as a diagnostic step; MRI is noninvasive and provides comprehensive evaluation of intra-articular pathology. C is incorrect because while knee immobilization and crutches are part of initial symptomatic management, they do not constitute the most important next step — confirming the diagnosis and identifying associated injuries with MRI takes priority in guiding definitive management. D is incorrect because corticosteroid injection has no role in the acute management of a suspected ACL tear and could mask symptoms or potentially impair tissue healing.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male presents with a large, painful mass in the right thigh. Imaging reveals a large soft tissue mass with aggressive features. During the surgical approach, what is the most important consideration when planning for excision?
A) Avoiding neurovascular structures
B) Ensuring clear margins
C) Minimizing blood loss
D) Preserving muscle function
questions.answer:
B)
Ensuring clear (wide) surgical margins is the single most important factor in the surgical management of soft tissue sarcomas. Inadequate margins are the strongest modifiable predictor of local recurrence. The goal is a wide excision with a cuff of normal tissue around the tumor in every plane.

A is incorrect because while protecting neurovascular structures is desirable, it is secondary to obtaining adequate oncologic margins; if a major vessel or nerve is encased by tumor, it must be sacrificed to achieve a clear margin.
C is incorrect because minimizing blood loss is a general surgical principle but does not take priority over margin adequacy in oncologic resection.
D is incorrect because preserving muscle function is a goal of limb-salvage surgery, but function is subordinate to achieving tumor-free margins; muscle compartments involved by tumor must be resected as needed.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman with chronic wrist pain presents for evaluation. She describes pain that worsens with activity and is relieved by rest. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the first extensor compartment. Which tendon is most likely involved in her condition?
A) Extensor pollicis longus
B) Extensor pollicis brevis
C) Abductor pollicis longus
D) Extensor indicis
E) Extensor digitorum
questions.answer:
C)
De Quervain's tenosynovitis involves the first dorsal (extensor) compartment, which contains both the abductor pollicis longus (APL) and the extensor pollicis brevis (EPB). The APL is the primary and most consistently involved tendon. The clinical presentation of radial-sided wrist pain worsened by activity and tenderness over the first extensor compartment is classic for this condition.

A is incorrect because the extensor pollicis longus (EPL) travels through the third dorsal compartment (Lister's tubercle), not the first extensor compartment.
B is incorrect because the extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) does reside in the first dorsal compartment and is also involved in de Quervain's tenosynovitis; however, the APL is considered the primary tendon involved and is always present in the compartment, whereas the EPB may occasionally have a separate sub-compartment.
D is incorrect because the extensor indicis is located in the fourth dorsal compartment and is not associated with first compartment pathology.
E is incorrect because the extensor digitorum is located in the fourth dorsal compartment and does not contribute to first extensor compartment pathology.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male cyclist presents with a history of recurrent anterior shoulder dislocations. He has undergone a course of physical therapy and activity modification but continues to experience instability. During examination, the patient demonstrates significant apprehension with the arm in abduction and external rotation. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Continued physical therapy
B) Arthroscopic stabilization
C) Corticosteroid injection
D) Open reduction and internal fixation
questions.answer:
B)
In a young, active patient with recurrent anterior shoulder instability that has failed conservative management, arthroscopic stabilization (e.g., Bankart repair) is the most appropriate surgical intervention. It addresses the underlying capsulolabral pathology responsible for the recurrent dislocations and has excellent outcomes in this population.

A is incorrect because conservative management with physical therapy has already failed, and recurrent instability in a young active patient is unlikely to resolve with continued therapy alone. C is incorrect because corticosteroid injection does not address the structural cause of glenohumeral instability and provides no stabilizing benefit. D is incorrect because open reduction and internal fixation is used for acute fracture management, not for recurrent soft-tissue-based shoulder instability without fracture.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old female presents for evaluation of worsening hip pain and limited mobility. She has a history of osteoarthritis and is now considering hip arthroplasty. Upon examination, her hip range of motion is significantly diminished, and x-rays reveal advanced joint space narrowing and osteophyte formation. Which of the following factors is most likely to increase her risk of perioperative complications, including proximal femur fractures?
A) Younger age
B) Osteoporosis
C) Obesity
D) Smoking
questions.answer:
B)
Osteoporosis is the most significant risk factor for perioperative proximal femur fractures during hip arthroplasty in elderly patients. Diminished bone mineral density compromises the structural integrity of the proximal femur, making it susceptible to fracture during broaching, stem insertion, or impaction. This is well supported in the orthopaedic literature as a leading modifiable risk factor for intraoperative periprosthetic fractures.

A is incorrect because younger age is generally associated with better bone quality and lower fracture risk during arthroplasty, not higher risk.
C is incorrect because while obesity increases general surgical risks (wound complications, infection, VTE), it is not the factor most directly linked to perioperative proximal femur fractures; in fact, higher BMI may be associated with greater bone density.
D is incorrect because smoking impairs wound healing and increases infection and medical complication risk, but it is not the primary risk factor for intraoperative periprosthetic fracture compared to osteoporosis.

questions.question:
A 75-year-old woman with osteoporosis falls and sustains a hip fracture. Upon examination, she exhibits a shortened and externally rotated right leg. Which type of fracture is most consistent with these clinical findings?
A) Femoral neck fracture
B) Intertrochanteric fracture
C) Subtrochanteric fracture
D) Femoral head fracture
questions.answer:
B)
The clinical presentation of shortened and externally rotated leg, along with her age and mechanism of injury, strongly suggests an intertrochanteric fracture. This type of fracture is common in the elderly population and typically results from low-energy falls.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a motorcycle accident. He has weakness in his lower extremities and loss of sensation below the level of L1. What is the most likely diagnosis based on his neurological examination?
A) Complete spinal cord injury
B) Cauda equina syndrome
C) Transverse myelitis
D) Brown-Séquard syndrome
questions.answer:
A)
Explanation: Loss of sensation and weakness below the level of L1 suggests a complete spinal cord injury, as the spinal cord terminates around L1-L2 in adults. This indicates significant neurological compromise, leading to the symptoms described. Cauda equina syndrome would typically present with lower motor neuron signs and variable sensory loss, while transverse myelitis and Brown-Séquard syndrome involve different clinical presentations.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old female presents to the emergency department after a fall from standing height. On examination, her right leg is positioned in a flexed and adducted posture. An x-ray reveals a posterior hip dislocation. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management step?
A) Immediate reduction under general anesthesia
B) Closed reduction in the emergency department
C) Application of a hip spica cast
D) Observation and follow-up with outpatient orthopedics
questions.answer:
B)
Closed reduction in the emergency department under procedural sedation is the most appropriate initial management for a posterior hip dislocation. Reduction should be performed emergently (ideally within 6 hours) to minimize the risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head and sciatic nerve injury. Post-reduction imaging (CT scan) should be obtained to assess for associated acetabular fractures and confirm concentric reduction.

A is incorrect because while reduction under general anesthesia in the operating room may ultimately be needed, it is not the initial step; closed reduction with procedural sedation in the ED should be attempted first to minimize time to reduction.
C is incorrect because a hip spica cast is not used in the management of hip dislocations in adults; it does not address the dislocation and would delay definitive treatment.
D is incorrect because a posterior hip dislocation is an orthopedic emergency requiring urgent reduction; observation and outpatient follow-up would risk avascular necrosis, sciatic nerve damage, and other serious complications.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male presents with an open fracture of the tibia after a motorcycle accident. Which type of antibiotic is most appropriate for initial management of this open fracture?
A) Clindamycin
B) Vancomycin
C) 1st generation cephalosporin
D) Aminoglycoside
questions.answer:
C)
A 1st generation cephalosporin (e.g., cefazolin/Ancef) is the standard initial antibiotic for open fractures (Gustilo types I–IIIA) because it provides excellent coverage against gram-positive organisms, particularly Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species, which are the most common pathogens in open fracture wound infections. This is supported by EAST and OTA guidelines.

A is incorrect because clindamycin is reserved as an alternative for patients with a true penicillin/cephalosporin allergy; it is not first-line therapy.
B is incorrect because vancomycin is used when MRSA coverage is specifically needed (e.g., known colonization or nosocomial settings) and is not the standard empiric first-line agent for open fractures.
D is incorrect because an aminoglycoside (e.g., gentamicin) is added for additional gram-negative coverage in higher-grade open fractures (Gustilo type III), but it is not used alone and is not the initial single-agent recommendation for open fracture management.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman is evaluated for hip pain that radiates down her leg. MRI reveals a tear of the obturator internus muscle. Which of the following actions is primarily affected due to this injury? 
A) Hip flexion 
B) Hip adduction 
C) Hip external rotation 
D) Hip internal rotation
questions.answer:
C)
The obturator internus is one of the short external rotators of the hip. A tear of this muscle would primarily impair hip external rotation. It also contributes to hip abduction when the hip is flexed, but its principal action tested on boards is external rotation.

A is incorrect because hip flexion is primarily performed by the iliopsoas, rectus femoris, and sartorius, not the obturator internus.
B is incorrect because hip adduction is performed by the adductor group (adductor longus, brevis, magnus) and the gracilis, not the obturator internus.
D is incorrect because hip internal rotation is performed by the anterior fibers of the gluteus medius and minimus and the tensor fasciae latae; the obturator internus is an external rotator, essentially the opposite action.

questions.question:
A 12-year-old boy is referred for evaluation of scoliosis after a school screening identifies a 20-degree lateral curvature of the spine. His physical exam reveals no significant abnormalities, but he has a family history of scoliosis. What is the most important factor to monitor in this patient over the next several years?
A) Progression of the curvature
B) Pain management strategies
C) Neurological deficits
D) Limb length discrepancies
E) Impact on athletic ability
questions.answer:
A)
In adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS), the most critical factor to monitor is progression of the curvature, especially during the adolescent growth spurt when curves are most likely to worsen. A 12-year-old boy with significant remaining growth and a 20-degree curve requires serial clinical and imaging follow-up (typically every 4–6 months) to detect progression that may warrant bracing (25–40°) or surgical intervention (>45–50°).

B is incorrect because pain is uncommon in typical AIS; its presence should prompt evaluation for other diagnoses (e.g., tumor, infection, spondylolisthesis) rather than being a routine monitoring focus.
C is incorrect because neurological deficits are not expected in idiopathic scoliosis; their presence would suggest an atypical etiology (e.g., syringomyelia, tethered cord) requiring further workup, but routine neurological monitoring is not the primary concern.
D is incorrect because limb length discrepancy can cause a compensatory postural curve but is not the primary monitoring concern in true structural scoliosis.
E is incorrect because while scoliosis may affect athletic performance, impact on athletic ability is not a standard clinical monitoring parameter and does not guide treatment decisions.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old male presents with a cavovarus foot deformity noted since childhood. Physical examination reveals a high arch and a tendency for the toes to claw. Which neurologic condition is most likely associated with this presentation?
A) Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
B) Multiple sclerosis
C) Spinal muscular atrophy
D) Cerebral palsy
questions.answer:
A)
Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease is the most common hereditary sensorimotor neuropathy and is the classic neurological cause of cavovarus foot deformity. Progressive peroneal muscle weakness (especially peroneus brevis) with a relatively preserved peroneus longus and tibialis posterior leads to forefoot-driven cavus, hindfoot varus, and claw toes. A childhood onset with slow progression is typical.

B is incorrect because multiple sclerosis is a central demyelinating disease that typically presents in young adults with upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia) and is not classically associated with cavovarus foot deformity.
C is incorrect because spinal muscular atrophy causes progressive proximal (not distal-predominant) weakness and is more commonly associated with flaccid paralysis and scoliosis rather than cavovarus feet.
D is incorrect because cerebral palsy is an upper motor neuron disorder that more commonly produces spastic equinovalgus or equinovarus deformities rather than the progressive cavovarus pattern seen with peripheral neuropathies like CMT.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents with persistent bone pain and weakness. Laboratory tests show elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone levels. An MRI reveals multiple lytic bone lesions. Which of the following best explains the mechanism behind the formation of these lesions?
A) Increased activity of osteoblasts
B) Inhibition of osteoclast function
C) Activation of osteoclasts by parathyroid hormone
D) Decreased production of calcitonin
questions.answer:
C)
In primary hyperparathyroidism, chronically elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) stimulates osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. PTH acts on osteoblasts/stromal cells to upregulate RANKL, which in turn activates osteoclasts, leading to increased bone resorption and the formation of lytic lesions (brown tumors/osteitis fibrosa cystica).

A is incorrect because increased osteoblast activity would lead to bone formation, not lytic lesions. While PTH does stimulate osteoblasts, the net effect of sustained elevated PTH is predominantly catabolic.
B is incorrect because PTH promotes, rather than inhibits, osteoclast function; inhibition of osteoclasts would protect against lytic lesion formation.
D is incorrect because although calcitonin opposes bone resorption, decreased calcitonin production is not the primary mechanism driving lytic lesions in hyperparathyroidism; the dominant pathology is PTH-driven osteoclast activation.

questions.question:
A 75-year-old male sustains a periprosthetic fracture around his femoral stem following a low-energy fall. The fracture is located in the mid-shaft region and the implant is well-fixed. Which Vancouver classification type best describes this fracture?
A) Type A
B) Type B1
C) Type B2
D) Type C
questions.answer:
B)
Type B1 fractures in the Vancouver classification are periprosthetic femoral fractures located around or just distal to the stem with a well-fixed implant. This matches the stem's description of a mid-shaft fracture around a well-fixed femoral component.

A is incorrect because Type A fractures occur in the trochanteric region (AG = greater trochanter, AL = lesser trochanter), not the mid-shaft.
C is incorrect because Type B2 fractures also occur around the stem but are characterized by a loose implant, which is not the case here.
D is incorrect because Type C fractures occur well distal to the tip of the femoral stem and are essentially standard femoral shaft fractures unrelated to the implant fixation.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old female with a history of diabetes presents with foot drop and difficulty dorsiflexing her ankle. Examination reveals weakness in the anterior compartment of her leg. Which of the following muscles is primarily responsible for dorsiflexion of the ankle?
A) Gastrocnemius
B) Soleus
C) Tibialis anterior
D) Peroneus longus
questions.answer:
C)
The tibialis anterior is the primary muscle responsible for dorsiflexion of the ankle. It is innervated by the deep peroneal nerve (L4–L5), and weakness or paralysis of this muscle results in foot drop, as described in this patient with diabetic neuropathy affecting the anterior compartment.

A is incorrect because the gastrocnemius is a primary plantarflexor of the ankle and knee flexor; it does not contribute to dorsiflexion.
B is incorrect because the soleus is a plantarflexor of the ankle that acts primarily during stance phase; it opposes dorsiflexion rather than producing it.
D is incorrect because the peroneus (fibularis) longus is primarily an evertor and plantarflexor of the foot; while innervated by the superficial peroneal nerve, it does not dorsiflex the ankle.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man presents with knee pain after slipping on ice. He has a history of osteoarthritis and is concerned about his knee's stability. Physical examination reveals joint effusion and a positive Lachman test. X-rays demonstrate no fracture but show significant joint space narrowing. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Intra-articular steroid injection
B) Immediate surgical intervention
C) Referral to physical therapy
D) Joint aspiration
questions.answer:
D)
Explanation: Given the presence of joint effusion, joint aspiration is a reasonable next step to relieve pain and potentially analyze the joint fluid for any signs of inflammation or infection. This can also provide temporary relief of symptoms.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old male presents with gradual shoulder pain after years of competitive weightlifting. MRI reveals a partial tear of the acromioclavicular ligament. He is concerned about surgery impacting his performance. What is the most appropriate management strategy?
A) Immediate surgical intervention
B) Conservative management with activity modification
C) Complete rest from all physical activities
D) Corticosteroid injections
questions.answer:
B)
Conservative management with activity modification is the first-line approach for a partial acromioclavicular (AC) ligament tear. Rehabilitation, relative rest from aggravating movements, and gradual return to activity allow ligament healing while preserving long-term athletic performance.

A is incorrect because immediate surgical intervention is not indicated for a partial AC ligament tear without significant instability or failed conservative treatment; surgery carries unnecessary risks and recovery time in this setting.
C is incorrect because complete rest from all physical activities is overly restrictive; maintaining general conditioning and performing non-aggravating exercises promotes healing and prevents deconditioning.
D is incorrect because corticosteroid injections may provide short-term pain relief but do not address the underlying ligament pathology, can weaken soft tissues with repeated use, and are not considered definitive management for a partial AC ligament tear.

questions.question:
A patient arrives at the clinic with complaints of persistent pain and swelling in the knee following an injury where she landed awkwardly on her knee.
