A 35-year-old woman presents with pain in her thumb after an injury while playing volleyball. On examination, there is a significant laxity with valgus stress at the metacarpophalangeal joint of the thumb. Which of the following injuries is most likely present?
A) Complete rupture of the flexor pollicis longus
B) Avulsion of the proper ulnar collateral ligament
C) Fracture of the base of the proximal phalanx
D) Stener lesion of the ulnar collateral ligament
E) Incomplete tear of the abductor pollicis brevis
questions.answer:
D)
Significant laxity (loss of a firm endpoint) with valgus stress at the thumb MCP joint indicates a complete rupture of the ulnar collateral ligament (UCL). When the torn UCL displaces superficial to the adductor pollicis aponeurosis, it is termed a Stener lesion. This is the most important diagnosis to identify because the interposed aponeurosis prevents ligament healing, making surgical repair mandatory. On boards, marked instability at the thumb MCP joint after a forced abduction injury (e.g., volleyball, skiing) should raise suspicion for a Stener lesion.

A is incorrect because rupture of the flexor pollicis longus would present with inability to flex the interphalangeal joint of the thumb, not MCP joint laxity with valgus stress.
B is incorrect because while a simple UCL avulsion can cause laxity, the degree of instability described (significant laxity) and the clinical scenario favor a Stener lesion, which is the more critical diagnosis to identify as it changes management from possible conservative treatment to obligatory surgery.
C is incorrect because a fracture at the base of the proximal phalanx would present with bony tenderness and would be identified on radiographs; it does not typically produce isolated ligamentous laxity on valgus stress.
E is incorrect because the abductor pollicis brevis is on the radial side of the thumb and is not tested by valgus (ulnar-directed) stress at the MCP joint; injury to this structure would not explain the findings described.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old man presents after a fall with severe pain in his left shoulder. X-rays show a greater tuberosity fracture of the humerus with displacement. In order to prevent complications such as rotator cuff tear and loss of function, what is the most important structure to evaluate for involvement?
A) Subscapularis tendon
B) Supraspinatus tendon
C) Infraspinatus tendon
D) Teres minor tendon
questions.answer:
B)
The supraspinatus tendon inserts on the superior facet of the greater tuberosity and is the rotator cuff tendon most commonly disrupted in displaced greater tuberosity fractures. Displacement of the fragment reflects pull by the supraspinatus (and often the infraspinatus), and failure to recognize this involvement can lead to persistent rotator cuff dysfunction, subacromial impingement, and loss of active elevation.

A is incorrect because the subscapularis tendon inserts on the lesser tuberosity, not the greater tuberosity, so it is not directly at risk in this fracture pattern.
C is incorrect because, although the infraspinatus also inserts on the greater tuberosity (middle facet), the supraspinatus is the most important and most commonly evaluated tendon in this clinical scenario.
D is incorrect because the teres minor inserts on the inferior facet of the greater tuberosity and is less commonly the primary structure of concern compared with the supraspinatus in displaced greater tuberosity fractures.

questions.question:
A patient undergoes surgical fixation of a humeral shaft fracture and presents with weakness of wrist extension following the procedure. The surgical approach utilized was a lateral approach to the distal humerus. Which of the following is the most likely complication of this surgical approach?
A) Ulnar nerve entrapment
B) Median nerve injury
C) Radial nerve injury
D) Axillary nerve injury
questions.answer:
C)
The lateral approach to the distal humerus places the radial nerve at significant risk because the nerve courses along the lateral aspect of the humerus, piercing the lateral intermuscular septum approximately 10 cm proximal to the lateral epicondyle. During dissection, the radial nerve can be stretched, compressed, or transected, resulting in weakness of wrist and finger extension as described in this patient.

A is incorrect because the ulnar nerve runs along the medial aspect of the elbow (posterior to the medial epicondyle) and is at risk during medial or posterior approaches, not a lateral approach. B is incorrect because the median nerve travels anteromedially in the arm and is not in the surgical field of a lateral approach to the distal humerus. D is incorrect because the axillary nerve is located proximally around the surgical neck of the humerus and the quadrilateral space; it is not at risk during a distal lateral humeral approach.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old athlete presents with pain along the lateral aspect of his forearm after a fall. He describes difficulty in supinating his forearm. Which muscle is primarily responsible for this action and is likely injured?
A) Biceps brachii
B) Supinator
C) Brachialis
D) Pronator teres
questions.answer:
A)
The biceps brachii is the most powerful supinator of the forearm, particularly when the elbow is flexed or during forceful supination. In an athlete who has difficulty supinating after a fall, injury to the biceps brachii (or its distal tendon/musculotendinous junction) is the most likely cause of significant supination weakness.

B is incorrect because the supinator muscle acts as the primary supinator only during slow, unresisted supination with the elbow extended; it is not the most powerful supinator overall and its isolated injury rarely causes clinically significant supination weakness in an athlete. C is incorrect because the brachialis is an elbow flexor and does not contribute to forearm supination. D is incorrect because the pronator teres is a forearm pronator, not a supinator.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male football player experiences severe knee pain and instability after being tackled. On examination, there is significant swelling and a positive pivot shift test. An MRI reveals a tear of the anterolateral ligament (ALL). What is the most likely associated injury in this scenario?
A) Medial meniscus tear
B) Lateral collateral ligament sprain
C) Posterior cruciate ligament tear
D) Anterior cruciate ligament tear
questions.answer:
D)
The anterolateral ligament (ALL) is a lateral capsular structure that acts as a secondary restraint to internal rotation and anterior tibial translation. ALL tears are strongly associated with ACL ruptures; the pivot shift test specifically evaluates rotatory instability caused by ACL deficiency, and a positive pivot shift in the setting of an ALL tear is highly indicative of a concurrent ACL tear.

A is incorrect because while medial meniscus tears can accompany ACL injuries (the "unhappy triad"), the stem specifically highlights a positive pivot shift and ALL tear, which are most directly linked to ACL disruption rather than primarily to a medial meniscus tear.
B is incorrect because lateral collateral ligament (LCL) sprains result from varus forces and are not the typical associated injury with an ALL tear and positive pivot shift mechanism.
C is incorrect because posterior cruciate ligament tears result from posterior-directed forces (e.g., dashboard injury) and are not associated with the rotational/valgus mechanism that produces ALL and ACL injuries.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old woman with knee osteoarthritis is being evaluated for total knee arthroplasty. She has a well-preserved posterior cruciate ligament (PCL). The surgeon discusses the options of PCL-retaining versus PCL-substituting prostheses. Which statement is most accurate concerning PCL-retaining prostheses?
A) They always result in better postoperative knee stability.
B) They require more extensive soft tissue release during surgery.
C) They may provide a more natural knee kinematics if the PCL is intact.
D) They are contraindicated in all cases of severe arthritis.
questions.answer:
C)
PCL-retaining (CR) prostheses preserve the native posterior cruciate ligament, which can help maintain femoral rollback during flexion and provide more natural knee kinematics. This benefit is most reliably achieved when the PCL is well-preserved and functionally competent, as in this patient.

A is incorrect because PCL-retaining designs do not "always" result in better stability; outcomes depend on the quality and balance of the retained PCL. A deficient or attenuated PCL can lead to instability or abnormal kinematics, making a PCL-substituting (PS) design preferable in those cases.
B is incorrect because PCL-retaining designs generally require less bone resection (no intercondylar box cut) and do not inherently require more extensive soft tissue release compared to PS designs.
D is incorrect because PCL-retaining prostheses are not contraindicated in all cases of severe arthritis; they can be used when the PCL remains intact and balanced, though in cases with significant deformity or PCL insufficiency, a PS design may be more appropriate.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male presents with recurrent shoulder instability after a traumatic anterior dislocation. On examination, he exhibits a positive apprehension test and a positive relocation test. Which of the following classification patterns best describes his instability?
A) AMBRI
B) TUBS
C) Multidirectional instability (MDI)
D) Voluntary instability
questions.answer:
B)
TUBS stands for Traumatic, Unidirectional, Bankart lesion, requiring Surgery. This patient's history of a traumatic dislocation event followed by recurrent unidirectional (anterior) instability with a positive apprehension and relocation test is the classic TUBS pattern, which is typically associated with a Bankart lesion and often requires surgical stabilization.

A is incorrect because AMBRI (Atraumatic, Multidirectional, Bilateral, Rehabilitation, Inferior capsular shift) describes atraumatic multidirectional instability; this patient had a clear traumatic onset with unidirectional instability. C is incorrect because multidirectional instability (MDI) involves symptomatic instability in two or more directions (anterior, posterior, inferior) and is typically atraumatic, which does not match this presentation. D is incorrect because voluntary instability refers to patients who can willfully subluxate or dislocate their shoulder, often related to psychological or habitual factors, not a traumatic mechanism.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old male football player presents with pain in the forearm after being tackled. On examination, he has weakness in wrist extension and numbness along the dorsal aspect of the hand. An MRI reveals an injury to the radial nerve. Given the anatomy of the radial nerve, where is it likely injured?
A) At the elbow
B) In the mid-forearm
C) At the wrist
D) At the shoulder
E) In the axilla
questions.answer:
D)
The radial nerve is most vulnerable to injury as it courses through the spiral groove of the humerus in the arm. A direct blow or tackle to the arm can compress the nerve at this location, resulting in wrist drop (weakness of wrist and finger extension) and numbness over the dorsal hand — exactly matching this patient's presentation. Among the available choices, 'at the shoulder' best approximates the proximal arm/spiral groove region.

A is incorrect because injury at the elbow (posterior interosseous nerve syndrome) typically spares wrist extension (ECRL is innervated proximal to the elbow) and does not cause dorsal hand sensory loss (the superficial branch of the radial nerve is not affected at that level). B is incorrect because the radial nerve has already divided into its terminal branches in the mid-forearm; injury here would not produce wrist drop. C is incorrect because at the wrist only the superficial sensory branch is present; injury would cause sensory loss only, not motor weakness. E is incorrect because axillary injury (e.g., crutch palsy) would affect the radial nerve more proximally and would also involve triceps weakness, which is not described in this stem.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old male athlete complains of increasing hip pain and stiffness, which worsens with activity. An x-ray reveals a pistol-grip deformity of the femoral head, and the clinical suspicion is for femoroacetabular impingement. Which of the following imaging modalities would best confirm the diagnosis and provide further assessment of the joint morphology?
A) Standard x-ray
B) MRI with contrast
C) CT scan of the hip
D) Bone scan
questions.answer:
B)
MRI with contrast (MR arthrography) is the preferred imaging modality to confirm femoroacetabular impingement and provide comprehensive assessment of joint morphology. While CT provides excellent bony detail, MR arthrography not only delineates the cam or pincer bony morphology but also evaluates the labrum, articular cartilage, and other intra-articular soft-tissue pathology that is critical for surgical planning and confirming the clinical significance of FAI.

A is incorrect because standard x-rays (AP pelvis, Dunn lateral) are useful for initial screening and may demonstrate the pistol-grip deformity or crossover sign, but they cannot assess labral tears or cartilage damage and thus do not fully confirm the diagnosis or assess joint morphology. C is incorrect because CT scan provides excellent osseous detail and can quantify the alpha angle and version, but it does not evaluate the labrum or articular cartilage, which are essential components of the FAI diagnosis and treatment planning. D is incorrect because a bone scan is a nonspecific study that may show increased uptake in areas of stress or inflammation but provides no anatomic detail of the femoral head-neck junction or intra-articular structures.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old man presents with shoulder pain and weakness after lifting a heavy object. During the physical examination, you perform the Yergason and Speed tests. Which of the following conditions are these tests primarily used to evaluate?
A) Rotator cuff tear
B) Biceps tendinitis
C) Glenohumeral instability
D) Shoulder impingement syndrome
questions.answer:
B)
The Yergason and Speed tests are specifically designed to evaluate biceps tendon pathology, including biceps tendinitis and biceps tendon instability. The Yergason test involves resisted supination with the elbow flexed to 90°, stressing the biceps tendon in the bicipital groove. The Speed test involves resisted forward flexion of the shoulder with the elbow extended and forearm supinated; pain in the bicipital groove is a positive result.

A is incorrect because rotator cuff tears are evaluated with tests such as the empty-can (Jobe) test, drop-arm test, and external rotation lag sign, not the Yergason or Speed tests.
C is incorrect because glenohumeral instability is assessed with the apprehension, relocation, and load-and-shift tests.
D is incorrect because shoulder impingement syndrome is evaluated with the Neer and Hawkins-Kennedy impingement signs, not the Yergason or Speed tests.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old male presents with a history of progressive knee pain and swelling, particularly after prolonged activity. X-rays reveal joint space narrowing and osteophyte formation. He has significant tenderness on the medial aspect of his knee. What would be the best initial treatment option for this patient's condition?
A) Knee arthroscopy
B) Weight loss and physical therapy
C) Total knee arthroplasty
D) Intra-articular hyaluronic acid injection
E) Opioid analgesics
questions.answer:
B)
Weight loss and physical therapy are the best initial treatment options for osteoarthritis of the knee. This conservative approach addresses modifiable risk factors (obesity, deconditioning) and is supported by all major guidelines (AAOS, ACR) as first-line management before invasive or pharmacologic escalation.

A is incorrect because knee arthroscopy has not been shown to provide benefit over sham surgery or physical therapy for osteoarthritis and is not recommended as an initial treatment. C is incorrect because total knee arthroplasty is reserved for patients who have failed adequate conservative management, including activity modification, weight loss, physical therapy, and pharmacologic measures. D is incorrect because intra-articular hyaluronic acid injection is a secondary treatment option considered after failure of first-line conservative measures; moreover, AAOS clinical practice guidelines do not strongly recommend its use. E is incorrect because opioid analgesics are not appropriate initial management for osteoarthritis due to risks of dependence, side effects, and the availability of safer, more effective first-line options.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male presents with severe thigh pain after a motorcycle accident. An x-ray shows a four-part intertrochanteric femoral fracture. What is the most important aspect of management for this injury?
A) Immediate weight-bearing as tolerated
B) Surgical fixation to restore stability
C) Non-operative management with rest
D) Referral to physical therapy for rehabilitation
questions.answer:
B)
A four-part (unstable) intertrochanteric femoral fracture requires surgical fixation to restore mechanical stability, allow early mobilization, and reduce the morbidity and mortality associated with prolonged immobilization. Depending on fracture pattern stability, options include a sliding hip screw (SHS) or a cephalomedullary nail (e.g., trochanteric femoral nail).

A is incorrect because immediate weight-bearing as tolerated without surgical stabilization would lead to fracture displacement, varus collapse, and loss of function in an unstable fracture pattern.
C is incorrect because non-operative management of an unstable intertrochanteric fracture results in prolonged recumbency with high rates of pneumonia, DVT/PE, pressure ulcers, and mortality, and is reserved only for patients who are non-ambulatory or have prohibitive surgical risk.
D is incorrect because while physical therapy is an important component of postoperative rehabilitation, it alone cannot address the underlying mechanical instability of the fracture and is not a substitute for surgical fixation.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male presents with persistent ankle instability after an inversion injury sustained while playing basketball. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the lateral malleolus. A cotton test is performed to assess for syndesmotic injury. What does a positive result indicate?
A) Medial ligament injury
B) Anterior talofibular ligament tear
C) Syndesmotic instability
D) Deltoid ligament injury
questions.answer:
C)
A positive cotton test indicates syndesmotic instability. The test is performed by laterally translating the talus within the ankle mortise; increased lateral shift compared to the contralateral side indicates disruption of the syndesmotic ligaments (anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament, posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament, and interosseous membrane) that bind the distal tibia and fibula.

A is incorrect because medial (deltoid) ligament injury is assessed by eversion stress testing, not the cotton test. B is incorrect because an anterior talofibular ligament tear is evaluated with the anterior drawer test, which assesses anterolateral translation of the talus relative to the tibia. D is incorrect because deltoid ligament injury is essentially the same concept as medial ligament injury and is assessed with eversion stress or external rotation stress tests, not the cotton test.

questions.question:
A pediatric patient is diagnosed with camptodactyly, presenting with a flexion deformity of the finger. Which of the following statements best describes the pathophysiology of this condition?
A) It is caused by a rupture of the flexor tendons
B) It results from a developmental abnormality affecting the extensor mechanism
C) It typically occurs due to a fracture of the proximal phalanx
D) It is associated with an imbalance of flexor and extensor muscle forces in the hand
questions.answer:
D)
Camptodactyly is a congenital or developmental flexion contracture of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint, most commonly of the small finger. The underlying pathophysiology involves an imbalance between the flexor and extensor forces across the PIP joint, which may result from anomalous lumbrical or FDS insertion, fibrosis of the superficialis, or deficiency of the extensor mechanism. This imbalance leads to a progressive flexion deformity.

A is incorrect because camptodactyly is not caused by a rupture of the flexor tendons; the tendons are intact, and the problem is a developmental imbalance rather than a traumatic disruption. B is incorrect because, although the extensor mechanism may be relatively deficient, the primary pathophysiology is an imbalance between flexor and extensor forces rather than a primary developmental abnormality of the extensor mechanism alone. C is incorrect because camptodactyly is a soft-tissue condition and is not caused by a fracture of the proximal phalanx.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male with a history of recurrent shoulder dislocations undergoes an MRI after a recent incident. The imaging reveals a Bankart lesion. Which imaging technique is often used to assess this type of injury in detail?
A) Zanca view
B) West Point view
C) CT scan
D) Arthrogram
questions.answer:
D)
An MR arthrogram (arthrogram) is the gold-standard imaging technique for detailed evaluation of a Bankart lesion. Intra-articular contrast distends the joint, improving visualization of labral tears, capsular stripping, and associated soft-tissue pathology that may be missed on standard MRI.

A is incorrect because the Zanca view is a plain radiograph used to evaluate the acromioclavicular joint, not the glenoid labrum. B is incorrect because the West Point view is a plain radiographic projection that can show bony defects of the anteroinferior glenoid rim but does not provide the soft-tissue detail needed to fully characterize a Bankart lesion. C is incorrect because a CT scan is excellent for evaluating bony anatomy (e.g., glenoid bone loss or a bony Bankart) but is inferior to MR arthrography for assessing the fibrocartilaginous labrum and associated soft-tissue injuries.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old male presents with persistent pain and tingling in the ring and little fingers after a traumatic elbow dislocation. The physical exam suggests ulnar nerve compression at the cubital tunnel. Which surgical intervention is most appropriate for relieving his symptoms?
A) Ulnar nerve transposition
B) Medial epicondylectomy
C) Ulnar nerve decompression
D) Elbow arthroplasty
questions.answer:
C)
In-situ ulnar nerve decompression is the first-line surgical treatment for cubital tunnel syndrome when conservative management fails. Simple decompression releases the compressive structures around the ulnar nerve at the elbow and has equivalent outcomes to transposition with lower complication rates in most primary presentations.

A is incorrect because ulnar nerve transposition (subcutaneous or submuscular) is generally reserved for cases with ulnar nerve subluxation, significant cubitus valgus deformity, recurrent compression after prior decompression, or when local anatomy precludes a safe in-situ release. It is not the first-line surgical option.

B is incorrect because medial epicondylectomy is an alternative procedure that removes the medial epicondyle to reduce pressure on the nerve, but it is not the standard first-line surgical treatment and carries risks of medial instability and flexor-pronator weakness.

D is incorrect because elbow arthroplasty is indicated for severe articular destruction (e.g., end-stage arthritis, comminuted distal humerus fractures in elderly patients) and has no role in the primary management of ulnar nerve compression.

questions.question:
A patient presents with an open tibia fracture. The orthopedic surgeon notes that timing for intravenous antibiotics is crucial. What is the most important factor to prevent post-operative infection in this scenario?
A) Type of antibiotic chosen
B) Timing of antibiotic administration
C) Duration of antibiotic therapy
D) Route of antibiotic administration
questions.answer:
B)
The timing of intravenous antibiotic administration is the most important modifiable factor in preventing infection in open fractures. Multiple studies (including Patzakis and Wilkins) have demonstrated that administering antibiotics within one hour of injury significantly reduces infection rates, making early administration the single most critical intervention.

A is incorrect because while appropriate antibiotic selection matters (e.g., first-generation cephalosporin ± aminoglycoside depending on Gustilo-Anderson grade), the choice of agent is secondary to the timeliness of administration. B is incorrect — skip (correct answer). C is incorrect because prolonged antibiotic courses beyond 24–72 hours post-wound closure have not been shown to further reduce infection and may promote resistance; duration is less impactful than prompt initiation. D is incorrect because intravenous administration is the standard route for open fractures, but the route itself is not the most important factor — it is the speed with which antibiotics are given that drives outcomes.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male sustains a high-energy injury to the hip and is diagnosed with a femoral head fracture. What is the most critical factor influencing the decision between surgical fixation and arthroplasty in this case?
A) Age of the patient
B) Degree of displacement of the fracture
C) Presence of osteoarthritis
D) Mechanism of injury
questions.answer:
B)
In femoral head fractures (Pipkin classification), the degree of displacement and size/location of the fracture fragment is the most critical factor influencing the choice between open reduction–internal fixation and arthroplasty. Large, displaced fragments (especially those involving the weight-bearing dome) are more likely to lead to avascular necrosis, post-traumatic arthritis, and poor outcomes with fixation alone, potentially necessitating arthroplasty.

A is incorrect because while age influences implant choice in some hip fractures (e.g., femoral neck fractures in the elderly), in a 45-year-old it is not the most critical determinant — fracture characteristics take precedence.
C is incorrect because pre-existing osteoarthritis may favor arthroplasty in general, but in an acute traumatic femoral head fracture the fracture displacement pattern is the primary surgical decision driver.
D is incorrect because the mechanism of injury (e.g., dashboard injury) helps explain the fracture pattern but does not directly dictate the choice between fixation and arthroplasty — the resulting fracture displacement does.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old male construction worker complains of persistent neck pain radiating to his left arm, accompanied by numbness and tingling in his fingers. Upon examination, he shows a positive finger escape sign. What is the most likely underlying condition causing his symptoms?
A) C6-C7 herniated disc
B) Cervical radiculopathy
C) Thoracic outlet syndrome
D) Cervical myelopathy
questions.answer:
D)
The finger escape sign (Ono's sign) is a hallmark physical examination finding of cervical myelopathy, in which the patient is unable to maintain the small fingers in an adducted, extended position — the ulnar digits drift into abduction and flexion due to upper motor neuron dysfunction from spinal cord compression. Although this patient also has radicular symptoms (arm pain, numbness/tingling), the presence of the finger escape sign indicates spinal cord involvement (myelopathy), which takes diagnostic and therapeutic priority.

A is incorrect because a C6-C7 herniated disc describes a specific anatomical lesion that could cause radiculopathy, but the finger escape sign points to cord compression (myelopathy) rather than isolated nerve root pathology.

B is incorrect because cervical radiculopathy involves compression of a nerve root and presents with dermatomal pain, sensory changes, and possible weakness in a myotomal distribution, but does NOT produce the finger escape sign, which is an upper motor neuron (myelopathic) finding.

C is incorrect because thoracic outlet syndrome involves compression of the brachial plexus or subclavian vessels at the thoracic outlet and typically presents with vascular symptoms or lower trunk plexopathy (medial arm/hand), not a positive finger escape sign.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents with a painful bunion on her right foot. Upon examination, there is a prominent medial bony bump at the first metatarsophalangeal joint, and the first toe is deviated laterally. Which of the following describes the condition affecting her foot?
A) Hallux rigidus
B) Hallux valgus
C) Metatarsalgia
D) Morton's neuroma
questions.answer:
B)
The presence of a prominent medial bony bump at the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint with lateral deviation of the great toe is the hallmark of hallux valgus, commonly referred to as a bunion. This condition results from progressive lateral deviation of the great toe and medial deviation of the first metatarsal, creating the characteristic medial eminence.

A is incorrect because hallux rigidus refers to degenerative arthritis of the first MTP joint, characterized by pain and loss of motion (especially dorsiflexion), not lateral deviation of the toe. C is incorrect because metatarsalgia refers to pain under the lesser metatarsal heads, typically in the forefoot, and is not associated with a medial bony prominence or lateral toe deviation. D is incorrect because Morton's neuroma is an interdigital neuroma (most commonly between the third and fourth metatarsals) causing burning pain and numbness in the affected web space, unrelated to a medial bony bump or hallux deviation.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man is involved in a high-energy motor vehicle collision and sustains a posterior wall acetabular fracture with displacement. Which surgical approach provides access to the posterior aspect of the acetabulum while minimizing damage to the gluteus maximus?
A) Ilioinguinal approach
B) Extended iliofemoral approach
C) Kocher-Langenbeck approach
D) Anterior approach to the hip
questions.answer:
C)
The Kocher-Langenbeck approach is the standard posterior approach to the acetabulum, providing excellent access to the posterior wall and posterior column. It utilizes the interval between the gluteus maximus (splitting its fibers) and the short external rotators, thereby minimizing damage to the gluteus maximus muscle and its innervation.

A is incorrect because the ilioinguinal approach provides access to the anterior column and inner (medial) wall of the acetabulum, not the posterior/lateral acetabulum.
B is incorrect because the extended iliofemoral approach, while providing extensile exposure of both columns, requires detachment of the gluteus maximus origin from the ilium and is associated with significant soft tissue morbidity including devascularization of the abductors.
D is incorrect because the anterior approach (Smith-Petersen) accesses the anterior hip joint and anterior column of the acetabulum, not the posterior/lateral acetabulum.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman presents with weakness in her thumb and index finger along with atrophy of the thenar eminence. She reports numbness in the first three digits of her right hand. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for her symptoms?
A) Ulnar nerve entrapment at the elbow
B) Carpal tunnel syndrome
C) De Quervain's tenosynovitis
D) Posterior interosseous nerve syndrome
E) Trigger finger
questions.answer:
B)
The combination of thenar eminence atrophy, weakness of the thumb and index finger, and numbness in the first three digits is classic for carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve compression at the wrist). Thenar atrophy indicates chronic, severe compression of the recurrent motor branch of the median nerve.

A is incorrect because ulnar nerve entrapment causes numbness in the ring and small fingers and weakness/atrophy of the hypothenar and intrinsic muscles, not the thenar eminence. C is incorrect because De Quervain's tenosynovitis causes pain over the radial styloid with thumb use but does not cause numbness or thenar atrophy. D is incorrect because posterior interosseous nerve syndrome causes weakness of finger and wrist extension without sensory loss, as the PIN is a pure motor nerve. E is incorrect because trigger finger causes mechanical catching or locking of a digit during flexion/extension and does not cause numbness or thenar atrophy.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old male with a history of diabetes and prior total knee arthroplasty presents for evaluation of implant failure. The orthopedic surgeon notes that the implant surface is coated with hydroxyapatite. What is the intended purpose of this coating?
A) To increase the weight of the implant
B) To enhance osseointegration
C) To reduce wear rates
D) To provide a smoother surface finish
questions.answer:
B)
Hydroxyapatite (HA) coating on orthopaedic implants is specifically designed to enhance osseointegration. HA is chemically similar to the mineral component of bone and promotes direct bonding between the implant surface and host bone, thereby improving biological fixation, initial stability, and long-term implant longevity.

A is incorrect because increasing implant weight is not a goal of any coating; HA coatings are extremely thin (typically 50–150 µm) and add negligible mass.
C is incorrect because HA coating is applied to non-articulating surfaces to promote bone ingrowth, not to articulating surfaces to reduce wear; wear reduction is achieved through bearing surface material selection (e.g., highly cross-linked polyethylene, ceramic).
D is incorrect because HA coatings actually create a rougher, porous surface to facilitate bone ongrowth/ingrowth, not a smoother finish.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male presents with forefoot pain and difficulty wearing shoes. Clinical examination reveals a claw toe deformity with hyperextension at the metatarsophalangeal joints and flexion at the proximal interphalangeal joints. What is the most likely underlying cause of this deformity?
A) Neurological condition
B) Rheumatoid arthritis
C) Plantar fasciitis
D) Osteoarthritis
questions.answer:
A)
Claw toe deformity in a 25-year-old male is most commonly caused by an underlying neurological condition such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, which produces intrinsic muscle weakness and imbalance between the extrinsic extensors and flexors. This leads to MTP hyperextension and IP flexion — the hallmark claw toe pattern. Any young patient presenting with bilateral claw toes should be evaluated for a neuromuscular disorder.

B is incorrect because rheumatoid arthritis can cause MTP subluxation and lesser toe deformities, but it typically presents with synovitis, joint swelling, and other systemic inflammatory features; it is uncommon in a 25-year-old male without mention of inflammatory signs. C is incorrect because plantar fasciitis causes heel pain and does not produce claw toe deformity. D is incorrect because osteoarthritis is a degenerative condition of articular cartilage that does not cause the intrinsic-minus muscle imbalance responsible for claw toes, and it is unusual in a 25-year-old.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a fall while playing football. He is unable to abduct his arm and has significant pain with any shoulder movement. Physical examination reveals a noticeable deformity of the shoulder. X-rays indicate an anterior dislocation of the shoulder. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Immediate surgical intervention
B) Closed reduction of the dislocation
C) Application of a sling and rest
D) MRI to assess for associated injuries
questions.answer:
B)
The most appropriate next step for an acute anterior shoulder dislocation confirmed on X-ray is closed reduction to restore the humeral head into the glenoid fossa. This is typically performed in the emergency department using techniques such as external rotation, traction-countertraction, or Stimson's method, ideally with procedural sedation and analgesia.

A is incorrect because immediate surgical intervention is not indicated for a first-time anterior shoulder dislocation; surgery is reserved for failed closed reduction, associated displaced fractures (e.g., large greater tuberosity fragments), or recurrent instability.
C is incorrect because applying a sling without first reducing the dislocation does not address the underlying pathology; the joint must be reduced before immobilization.
D is incorrect because obtaining an MRI prior to reduction unnecessarily delays treatment; MRI may be considered after successful reduction to evaluate for labral tears (Bankart lesion), rotator cuff tears, or Hill-Sachs lesions, but it is not the immediate next step.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old woman presents with chronic back pain and a history of spinal surgery for scoliosis correction performed in her teens. MRI shows degenerative changes at the adjacent levels above the fusion. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her current symptoms?
A) Pseudoarthrosis at the fusion site
B) Adjacent segment disease
C) Infection at the surgical site
D) Hardware failure
E) New onset scoliosis
questions.answer:
B)
Adjacent segment disease is a well-recognized long-term complication following spinal fusion for scoliosis. The fused segments transfer increased mechanical stress to the mobile levels above and below the construct, accelerating degenerative changes at those levels. This patient's MRI findings of degeneration at the levels adjacent to her prior fusion are classic for this diagnosis.

A is incorrect because pseudoarthrosis (nonunion at the fusion site) would present with pain localized to the fusion mass and motion on dynamic imaging, not degenerative changes at adjacent levels. C is incorrect because surgical site infection years after surgery is uncommon and would typically present with constitutional symptoms, elevated inflammatory markers, or abscess formation rather than adjacent-level degenerative changes on MRI. D is incorrect because hardware failure (rod breakage, screw loosening) would be identified on imaging at the instrumented levels, not as degenerative changes at adjacent segments. E is incorrect because new-onset scoliosis (de novo degenerative scoliosis) is a consideration in older adults but does not explain the specific finding of adjacent-level degeneration above a prior fusion construct in a 38-year-old.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman with a long history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with severe pain and deformity of her fingers. Examination reveals a swan neck deformity with hyperextension of the PIP joint and flexion of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option for her condition?
A) PIP joint arthrodesis
B) Joint replacement of the PIP joint
C) Splinting and corticosteroid injections
D) Osteotomy of the proximal phalanx
questions.answer:
A)
In a patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis and severe, fixed swan neck deformity causing significant pain and functional impairment, PIP joint arthrodesis provides reliable pain relief and a stable, functional position. It is especially favored for the index finger and when joint destruction is advanced.

B is incorrect because PIP joint replacement (arthroplasty) is better suited for flexible deformities with preserved bone stock and is more commonly used in the ulnar digits; in severe fixed deformity with significant joint destruction, implant survival and outcomes are less predictable.
C is incorrect because splinting and corticosteroid injections are conservative measures appropriate for early or mild disease; they are insufficient for severe, fixed deformity with joint destruction.
D is incorrect because osteotomy of the proximal phalanx does not address the articular destruction or the soft-tissue imbalance responsible for swan neck deformity in rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.question:
A 75-year-old woman presents with worsening back pain and difficulty walking for the past six months. She has a history of osteoporosis. MRI shows significant spinal stenosis at L3-L4 with no evidence of neurological compromise. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in her management?
A) Physical therapy
B) Lumbar decompression surgery
C) Epidural steroid injections
D) Observation and lifestyle modifications
questions.answer:
A)
For spinal stenosis without neurological compromise, evidence-based guidelines recommend a trial of structured physical therapy as the first-line conservative treatment. Physical therapy focuses on core stabilization, flexion-based exercises, and aerobic conditioning, which can improve functional capacity and reduce symptoms in neurogenic claudication.

B is incorrect because lumbar decompression surgery is reserved for patients who have failed an adequate trial of conservative management or who have progressive neurological deficits; this patient has no neurological compromise and has not yet undergone structured conservative care.
C is incorrect because while epidural steroid injections may provide short-term symptomatic relief, they do not address the underlying functional deficits and are generally considered adjunctive rather than the primary initial treatment.
D is incorrect because observation alone with lifestyle modifications is too passive for a patient with worsening symptoms and difficulty walking; active structured physical therapy is preferred over watchful waiting in symptomatic spinal stenosis.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after a fall from standing height. She is unable to bear weight on her right leg, and imaging reveals a fracture of the tibial plateau. Which of the following factors is most critical in determining the need for surgical intervention?
A) Age of the patient
B) The presence of associated ligamentous injury
C) The degree of articular surface depression
D) The mechanism of injury
questions.answer:
C)
The degree of articular surface depression is the most critical factor in determining the need for surgical intervention in tibial plateau fractures. Board-level teaching holds that articular depression greater than approximately 5–10 mm (depending on the compartment involved and patient factors) is the primary indication for operative fixation, as it directly affects joint congruity, load distribution, and long-term risk of post-traumatic arthritis.

A is incorrect because while age may influence overall surgical risk and rehabilitation potential, it is not the primary determinant of operative need for a tibial plateau fracture.
B is incorrect because associated ligamentous injury is important in the overall management plan and may influence surgical approach, but it is not the most critical factor in deciding whether the fracture itself requires operative fixation.
D is incorrect because the mechanism of injury helps classify the fracture pattern but does not directly determine the threshold for surgical intervention.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents with right elbow pain following a fall onto an outstretched hand. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the lateral aspect of the elbow and limited range of motion. X-rays demonstrate a non-displaced fracture of the radial head (Mason type I). There is no associated dislocation or mechanical block to motion. What is the best next step in management?
A) Immediate surgical intervention
B) Brief immobilization for comfort followed by early functional range of motion
C) Provide a corticosteroid injection
D) Refer for a physical therapy evaluation
E) Immobilization with a splint for 6 weeks
questions.answer:
B)
A non-displaced (Mason type I) radial head fracture without mechanical block or instability is managed conservatively with brief immobilization for comfort (sling or posterior splint for a few days) followed by early active range of motion. This approach prevents elbow stiffness while allowing fracture healing.

A is incorrect because immediate surgical intervention is reserved for displaced fractures (Mason type II with significant displacement or Mason type III comminuted fractures) or those with mechanical block to motion or associated instability.
C is incorrect because corticosteroid injection has no role in acute fracture management and may impair bone healing.
D is incorrect because while physical therapy may be helpful later, the best initial step is appropriate immobilization for comfort and initiation of early motion, not a therapy referral as the first management step.
E is incorrect because prolonged immobilization for 6 weeks leads to significant elbow stiffness and is not recommended for non-displaced radial head fractures; early motion is the standard of care.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old female volleyball player presents with pain in the front of her knee that worsens with stair climbing and jumping. She notes discomfort when sitting with her knee bent for extended periods. Examination shows tenderness along the patellar tendon. Which condition is she most likely experiencing?
A) Patellofemoral pain syndrome
B) Iliotibial band syndrome
C) Patellar tendonitis
D) Quadriceps tendinopathy
questions.answer:
C)
Patellar tendonitis (jumper's knee) is characterized by activity-related anterior knee pain localized to the patellar tendon, particularly in athletes who perform repetitive jumping such as volleyball players. The hallmark finding is point tenderness at the patellar tendon (typically at its proximal insertion on the inferior pole of the patella), which is consistent with this patient's examination.

A is incorrect because patellofemoral pain syndrome typically presents with peripatellar or retropatellar pain and tenderness around or behind the patella rather than along the patellar tendon itself; although prolonged sitting discomfort (theater sign) can occur in both conditions, the localized tendon tenderness points to patellar tendonitis.
B is incorrect because iliotibial band syndrome causes lateral knee pain, typically at the lateral femoral epicondyle, and is more common in runners; it does not present with patellar tendon tenderness.
D is incorrect because quadriceps tendinopathy causes pain and tenderness at the superior pole of the patella where the quadriceps tendon inserts, not along the patellar tendon inferior to the patella.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man is evaluated for a hip injury sustained while playing soccer. Clinical examination reveals pain localized to the groin and lateral thigh. An MRI confirms a partial thickness tear of the gluteus medius. Which anatomical structure is critical to consider during surgical repair to preserve hip function?
A) Femoral neck
B) Trochanteric bursa
C) Vastus lateralis
D) Gluteus minimus
questions.answer:
D)
During surgical repair of a gluteus medius tear, the gluteus minimus is the most critical adjacent structure to consider. The gluteus minimus lies deep to the gluteus medius and inserts on the anterior facet of the greater trochanter; it is frequently involved in abductor pathology and must be assessed and preserved to maintain hip abductor strength and stability.

A is incorrect because the femoral neck, while an important anatomical landmark, is not at direct surgical risk during abductor repair at the greater trochanter footprint. B is incorrect because the trochanteric bursa is routinely debrided during gluteus medius repair and is not a structure whose preservation is critical for hip function. C is incorrect because the vastus lateralis lies distal and lateral to the surgical field of the abductor footprint and, while it may be encountered, it is not the critical structure that determines preservation of hip abductor function.

questions.question:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after falling from a swing. His left arm is held in a flexed position, and he exhibits significant pain when the arm is moved. On examination, there is a prominent swelling over the elbow and tenderness upon palpation. An X-ray reveals a displaced supracondylar humeral fracture classified as Gartland type III. What is the most appropriate treatment for this fracture?
A) Observation
B) Closed reduction and percutaneous pinning
C) Splinting in a flexed position
D) Surgical excision of the fracture fragment
questions.answer:
B)
Closed reduction and percutaneous pinning is the standard treatment for a Gartland type III (completely displaced) supracondylar humeral fracture in children. This approach restores anatomic alignment and provides stable fixation, minimizing the risk of neurovascular complications (e.g., anterior interosseous nerve injury, brachial artery compromise) and malunion (cubitus varus).

A is incorrect because observation alone is inappropriate for a completely displaced fracture, which requires reduction and stabilization to prevent neurovascular compromise and malunion.
C is incorrect because splinting in a flexed position without reduction does not address the displacement; furthermore, excessive flexion in a swollen elbow risks compartment syndrome by compromising vascular flow.
D is incorrect because surgical excision of the fracture fragment is not a recognized treatment for supracondylar fractures; the goal is anatomic reduction and fixation, not fragment removal.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male is seen in the clinic after experiencing pain in the anterior aspect of his elbow following a weightlifting injury. Physical examination reveals tenderness and swelling over the distal biceps tendon, and he is unable to flex his elbow against resistance. MRI confirms a complete rupture of the distal biceps tendon. Which of the following is the most common mechanism of injury for this type of rupture?
A) Eccentric loading of the elbow during flexion
B) Direct trauma to the elbow
C) Concentric loading during extension
D) Repetitive overhead lifting
questions.answer:
A)
Distal biceps tendon ruptures most commonly occur due to eccentric loading — the biceps is actively contracting in flexion while an unexpected extension force is applied to the elbow (e.g., catching a heavy weight). This creates excessive tensile strain on the distal biceps tendon at its insertion on the radial tuberosity, leading to failure. The typical patient is a male in his 40s–50s, and the dominant arm is most often affected.

B is incorrect because direct trauma to the elbow may cause contusion or fracture but is not the typical mechanism for distal biceps tendon rupture. C is incorrect because concentric loading during extension does not place significant tension on the biceps tendon; the biceps is a flexor and supinator, so it is not actively loaded during elbow extension. D is incorrect because repetitive overhead lifting may contribute to chronic tendinopathy (e.g., proximal biceps or rotator cuff pathology) but is not the classic acute mechanism for distal biceps rupture.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male is involved in a motorcycle accident and presents with severe right hip pain and difficulty bearing weight. On examination, there is a notable external rotation of the right leg, and imaging shows an acetabular fracture. Which of the following associated injuries should be suspected in this scenario?
A) Femoral head avascular necrosis
B) Common peroneal nerve injury
C) Posterior hip dislocation
D) Iliac wing fracture
questions.answer:
C)
A posterior hip dislocation is the most commonly associated injury with acetabular fractures sustained in high-energy mechanisms such as motorcycle accidents. The classic 'dashboard mechanism' drives the femoral head posteriorly, fracturing the acetabulum. External rotation of the leg can occur when the acetabular wall fracture allows the femoral head to displace. Posterior dislocation must be recognized and reduced emergently to minimize the risk of sciatic nerve injury and femoral head avascular necrosis.

A is incorrect because femoral head avascular necrosis is a potential complication (especially with delayed reduction of a dislocation), not an acute associated injury to suspect at presentation.
B is incorrect because the common peroneal nerve wraps around the fibular neck and is at risk with knee dislocations or proximal fibula fractures, not acetabular fractures. The nerve at risk with posterior hip dislocation is the sciatic nerve.
D is incorrect because an iliac wing fracture (Duverney fracture) is a separate injury pattern and is not the classic association with an acetabular fracture presenting with external rotation after a high-energy mechanism.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man presents with chronic hip pain and mobility issues. Imaging shows degeneration of the acetabulum with associated changes in the femoral head. Which of the following is the best initial non-surgical management option for this patient's condition?
A) Corticosteroid injection
B) Physical therapy
C) Hip arthroscopy
D) Total hip arthroplasty
questions.answer:
B)
Physical therapy is the recommended first-line non-surgical management for hip osteoarthritis with acetabular degeneration. It improves periarticular muscle strength, joint flexibility, and overall function, and is supported by major guidelines (AAOS, ACR) as initial conservative treatment before escalating to injections or surgery.

A is incorrect because corticosteroid injection is an adjunctive measure typically reserved for patients who have failed first-line conservative treatments such as physical therapy and activity modification; it is not the best *initial* option.
C is incorrect because hip arthroscopy is a surgical intervention, not a non-surgical management option, and is generally indicated for intra-articular pathology (e.g., labral tears, loose bodies) rather than diffuse degenerative disease.
D is incorrect because total hip arthroplasty is a definitive surgical treatment reserved for end-stage disease refractory to conservative management; it is not an initial management strategy.

questions.question:
A 75-year-old female patient with advanced osteoarthritis of the hip is scheduled for total hip arthroplasty. During the procedure, the surgeon notes significant damage to the lateral compartment of the joint. Which of the following is most likely to have contributed to the severity of disease in this compartment?
A) Excessive internal rotation of the hip
B) Previous hip dislocation
C) Valgus alignment of the knee
D) History of acetabular fractures
questions.answer:
B)
Explanation: Previous hip dislocation can lead to damage to the hip joint and contribute to the severity of osteoarthritis in the lateral compartment. This history is significant in understanding the progression of degenerative changes in the hip.

questions.question:
A patient with a fracture of the acetabulum is being evaluated for surgical intervention. The surgical team plans to use the Kocher-Langenbeck approach. What is the primary advantage of this surgical approach in acetalular fractures? 
A) Provides direct access to the anterior column 
B) Minimally invasive with less soft tissue dissection 
C) Allows for better visualization of the posterior wall 
D) Reduces the risk of deep vein thrombosis postoperatively
questions.answer:
C)
The Kocher-Langenbeck approach is a posterior approach to the acetabulum that provides excellent visualization of the posterior wall and posterior column, making it the preferred approach for posterior wall, posterior column, and transverse fractures of the acetabulum. It allows direct reduction and fixation of posterior wall fragments under direct vision.

A is incorrect because the Kocher-Langenbeck approach accesses the posterior column and wall; direct access to the anterior column requires an ilioinguinal or anterior intrapelvic (modified Stoppa) approach.
B is incorrect because the Kocher-Langenbeck approach involves significant soft tissue dissection including splitting or detaching the short external rotators and is not considered minimally invasive.
D is incorrect because the Kocher-Langenbeck approach does not inherently reduce the risk of deep vein thrombosis; DVT prophylaxis is required regardless of surgical approach, and the prone or lateral positioning used may not confer any DVT advantage.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old female is diagnosed with a pelvic fracture after a low-energy fall. Her imaging reveals a transverse fracture of the acetabulum. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for this type of fracture to prevent complications?
A) Immediate surgical fixation
B) Non-weight bearing for 6 weeks
C) Early mobilization with partial weight bearing
D) Bed rest and analgesics
questions.answer:
C)
Explanation: Early mobilization with partial weight bearing is recommended to prevent complications such as stiffness and loss of muscle strength while allowing the fracture to heal properly. Non-weight bearing for extended periods is not favored unless there are specific concerns about stability.

questions.question:
During a weekend basketball game, a 22-year-old male experiences a sudden onset of knee pain after landing awkwardly. He reports feeling a pop and has difficulty walking afterward. On examination, he has significant swelling and tenderness along the medial joint line. An MRI reveals a complete tear of the medial collateral ligament (MCL). What grading classification does this injury most likely correspond to?
A) Grade I
B) Grade II
C) Grade III
D) Grade IV
questions.answer:
C)
A complete tear of the MCL is classified as a Grade III injury. Grade III MCL injuries involve full-thickness disruption of the ligament, resulting in significant valgus instability with no firm endpoint on valgus stress testing. The clinical presentation of a pop, significant swelling, and difficulty walking is consistent with this severe grade of injury.

A is incorrect because a Grade I MCL injury represents a mild sprain with microscopic fiber disruption; the ligament remains intact, there is localized tenderness but no instability on valgus stress testing. B is incorrect because a Grade II MCL injury is a partial tear with some valgus laxity but a definite endpoint; MRI would show a partial rather than complete tear. D is incorrect because the standard MCL grading system uses Grades I through III; there is no Grade IV classification for MCL injuries.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male experiences sudden onset of severe, localized low back pain followed by bilateral leg weakness after lifting a heavy object. MRI reveals a massive central herniated disc at L5-S1. Which condition is he most likely experiencing?
A) Cauda equina syndrome
B) Spinal stenosis
C) Lumbosacral strain
D) Spondylolisthesis
questions.answer:
A)
Cauda equina syndrome is caused by compression of the cauda equina nerve roots, classically from a massive central disc herniation. It presents with bilateral leg weakness, saddle anesthesia, and bowel/bladder dysfunction, and requires emergent surgical decompression.

B is incorrect because spinal stenosis is a chronic, progressive narrowing of the spinal canal that typically causes neurogenic claudication rather than acute bilateral weakness from a single lifting event.
C is incorrect because a lumbosacral strain causes localized musculoskeletal pain without neurological deficits such as bilateral leg weakness.
D is incorrect because spondylolisthesis is a vertebral slip that may cause radiculopathy but does not typically present as acute bilateral leg weakness from a single lifting episode, and MRI here shows a massive central disc herniation, not vertebral translation.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old female presents with chronic back pain and stiffness, particularly in the lumbar region. Upon imaging, you notice a characteristic appearance of the vertebrae resembling 'flowing candle wax'. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Osteoporosis
B) Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis
C) Ankylosing Spondylitis
D) Paget's Disease
questions.answer:
B)
Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis (DISH) is characterized by flowing calcification and ossification along the anterolateral aspect of at least four contiguous vertebral bodies, often described as having a 'dripping' or 'flowing candle wax' appearance on imaging. It typically affects the thoracolumbar spine and causes stiffness and pain, consistent with this patient's presentation.

A is incorrect because osteoporosis causes decreased bone density and vertebral compression fractures but does not produce flowing ossification along the spine. C is incorrect because ankylosing spondylitis classically shows a 'bamboo spine' appearance with syndesmophytes (thin, vertical bridging ossifications) and sacroiliac joint fusion, not the bulky flowing ossification seen in DISH. D is incorrect because Paget's disease produces enlarged, sclerotic vertebrae sometimes described as 'picture frame' vertebrae or an 'ivory vertebra,' not flowing anterolateral ossification.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old male presents with acute posterior ankle pain after a fall from a height. Physical examination reveals tenderness along the posterior aspect of the ankle and inability to plantarflex the great toe. An MRI shows disruption of the flexor hallucis longus tendon. What is the most appropriate surgical treatment option for this injury?
A) Tendon repair only
B) Flexor hallucis longus transfer with V-Y advancement
C) Achilles tendon repair
D) Ankle arthrodesis
E) Conservative management with a boot
questions.answer:
A)
In an acute flexor hallucis longus (FHL) tendon rupture, primary tendon repair is the most appropriate surgical treatment. Acute injuries allow direct end-to-end repair before tendon retraction and degeneration occur, yielding the best functional outcomes.

B is incorrect because FHL transfer with V-Y advancement is reserved for chronic ruptures or cases where the tendon ends cannot be approximated due to retraction or tissue degeneration. C is incorrect because the Achilles tendon is a separate structure; the stem describes FHL disruption, not Achilles pathology. D is incorrect because ankle arthrodesis is used for end-stage arthritis or severe joint destruction, not isolated tendon injuries. E is incorrect because a complete FHL tendon rupture in an active patient warrants surgical repair to restore great toe plantarflexion and push-off function; conservative management alone would result in persistent functional deficit.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male presents with lateral ankle pain and a prominent bump over the lateral aspect of his foot. Upon examination, you suspect a cuboid fracture due to a history of a fall. Which of the following is a common associated injury with a cuboid fracture?
A) Medial malleolus fracture
B) Lateral talar dome fracture
C) Fracture of the fifth metatarsal
D) Navicular fracture
questions.answer:
C)
Cuboid fractures can be associated with fifth metatarsal fractures because both structures lie along the lateral column of the foot and share common injury mechanisms involving lateral compression or direct lateral foot impact. Recognizing associated injuries is important for complete evaluation and treatment planning.

A is incorrect because medial malleolus fractures are associated with ankle-level injuries (e.g., bimalleolar or trimalleolar fracture patterns) rather than midfoot cuboid fractures. B is incorrect because lateral talar dome fractures (osteochondral lesions) are typically associated with inversion ankle sprains and are not a common association with cuboid fractures. D is incorrect because although navicular fractures can occur with midfoot injuries (e.g., nutcracker fracture of the cuboid with navicular involvement), the more direct lateral column association with a cuboid fracture from lateral foot impact is a fifth metatarsal fracture.

questions.question:
A 66-year-old male with a long-standing history of hip osteoarthritis is being evaluated for total hip arthroplasty. The surgeon notes an abnormal alignment of the femoral component during preoperative planning. Which of the following is considered the most appropriate degree of anteversion for the femoral component to optimize stability and range of motion?
A) 5°
B) 10°
C) 15°
D) 20°
questions.answer:
C)
The ideal femoral component anteversion during total hip arthroplasty is approximately 10–15°, with 15° being the most commonly cited target. This degree of anteversion optimizes hip stability by reducing the risk of both anterior and posterior dislocation while allowing a functional range of motion. Combined with approximately 40° of acetabular anteversion (Lewinnek safe zone), it contributes to a stable construct.

A is incorrect because 5° of anteversion is too little and increases the risk of posterior dislocation by not adequately directing the femoral head anteriorly. B is incorrect because while 10° is within an acceptable range, 15° is the most commonly cited ideal target on board examinations. D is incorrect because 20° of anteversion is excessive and increases the risk of anterior dislocation and impingement.

questions.question:
A 10-year-old boy is evaluated for hip pain. The physician notes that the center-edge angle (CEA) on his x-ray is 18 degrees. Which of the following would be the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Surgical intervention
B) Physical therapy
C) Reassurance and observation
D) MRI of the hip
E) Referral to a pediatric orthopedist
questions.answer:
C)
Explanation: A center-edge angle of less than 20 degrees indicates acetabular dysplasia, but in a 10-year-old, the most appropriate management is typically reassurance and observation, especially if there are no significant symptoms or instability.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old male presents with an isolated ankle injury after a sports accident. Imaging reveals a Weber C fibula fracture. Which of the following complications is most commonly associated with this type of fracture?
A) Syndesmotic injury
B) Osteochondral defect
C) Achilles tendon rupture
D) Tibial shaft fracture
questions.answer:
A)
A Weber C fracture occurs above the level of the syndesmosis. By definition, the fracture line is proximal to the tibiofibular syndesmotic ligaments, and the energy required to produce this fracture pattern almost always disrupts the syndesmosis. Syndesmotic injury is therefore the most commonly associated complication and must be evaluated and treated to restore ankle stability.

B is incorrect because osteochondral defects of the talus are more commonly associated with inversion/rotational injuries to the talar dome and are not a characteristic complication of Weber C fractures. C is incorrect because Achilles tendon rupture is a separate injury mechanism (eccentric loading of the gastrocnemius-soleus complex) and is not associated with fibula fracture patterns. D is incorrect because tibial shaft fractures are a distinct injury; while a Maisonneuve fracture (a variant of Weber C) involves a proximal fibula fracture with interosseous membrane disruption, an associated tibial shaft fracture is not a typical complication of a Weber C pattern.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old mason presents with finger deformities after a fall, with specific concern about the function of his lumbricals. On examination, he demonstrates an inability to flex his metacarpophalangeal joints while extending his interphalangeal joints. What is the underlying mechanism of this dysfunction?
A) Damage to the flexor tendons
B) Injury to the extensor tendons
C) Disruption of the intrinsic hand muscles
D) Fracture of the metacarpals
questions.answer:
C)
The lumbricals are intrinsic hand muscles that flex the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and extend the interphalangeal (IP) joints via their insertion into the lateral bands of the extensor expansion. Disruption of these intrinsic muscles eliminates this coordinated action, producing the described deficit.

A is incorrect because damage to the flexor tendons (FDP/FDS) would impair IP joint flexion, not the combined MCP flexion with IP extension pattern characteristic of lumbrical function.
B is incorrect because injury to the extensor tendons would impair MCP extension and/or IP extension, not the lumbrical-specific action of MCP flexion with simultaneous IP extension.
D is incorrect because a metacarpal fracture could impair grip or cause pain but would not specifically abolish the coordinated MCP flexion with IP extension that is the hallmark of intrinsic (lumbrical) muscle function.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male comes to the clinic with pain in his lateral knee following a skiing accident. Physical examination reveals tenderness over Gerdy's tubercle and pain with resisted hip abduction. An MRI is ordered, and findings are consistent with iliotibial band syndrome. Which of the following management strategies is most appropriate for this condition?
A) Surgical release of the iliotibial band
B) Corticosteroid injection into the lateral knee
C) Stretching and strengthening exercises
D) Apply a knee brace
E) Modify skiing technique
questions.answer:
C)
Stretching and strengthening exercises are the first-line treatment for iliotibial band syndrome. They address the underlying biomechanical contributors such as hip abductor weakness and IT band tightness, improving flexibility and muscular balance to resolve symptoms without invasive intervention.

A is incorrect because surgical release of the iliotibial band is reserved for refractory cases that have failed prolonged conservative management (typically 6+ months), not as initial treatment.
B is incorrect because corticosteroid injection may provide short-term symptomatic relief but does not address the underlying biomechanical cause and is not considered first-line management.
D is incorrect because a knee brace does not correct the underlying muscle imbalance or tightness responsible for IT band syndrome and is not a primary treatment strategy.
E is incorrect because while activity modification can be a helpful adjunct, modifying skiing technique alone does not address the core pathology of IT band tightness and hip abductor weakness that drives the condition.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male farmer presents with a laceration to the palm of his hand after a fall onto a sharp object. On examination, there are deep lacerations and a loss of sensation in the index and middle fingers. What is the most critical structure to assess for injury in this scenario?
A) Flexor tendons
B) Ulnar nerve
C) Radial artery
D) Digital nerves
E) Superficial palmar arch
questions.answer:
D)
Loss of sensation in the index and middle fingers following a deep palmar laceration indicates injury to the digital nerves (common and/or proper digital nerves) arising from the median nerve, which supplies sensation to the radial 3½ digits. Assessing digital nerve integrity is critical because unrepaired nerve lacerations lead to permanent sensory loss and impaired hand function.

A is incorrect because while flexor tendon injury should also be evaluated, the stem specifically highlights sensory loss, making nerve assessment the most critical priority. B is incorrect because the ulnar nerve supplies sensation to the small finger and ulnar half of the ring finger, not the index and middle fingers. C is incorrect because the radial artery runs on the radial side of the wrist/hand and is not the primary structure at risk in a palmar laceration presenting with sensory deficits. E is incorrect because the superficial palmar arch is a vascular structure; its injury would present with bleeding rather than sensory loss.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old diabetic male presents with heel pain that has progressively worsened over the past few months. He reports pain during the first steps in the morning that improves with activity. On examination, there is tenderness at the medial calcaneal tuberosity. Which structure attaches here and is likely contributing to his symptoms?
A) Plantar fascia
B) Achilles tendon
C) Flexor digitorum brevis
D) Abductor hallucis
questions.answer:
A)
The plantar fascia originates from the medial calcaneal tuberosity and is the structure most commonly implicated in plantar fasciitis. The classic presentation of pain with the first steps in the morning that improves with activity, combined with point tenderness at the medial calcaneal tuberosity, is pathognomonic for plantar fasciitis. Diabetic patients are at increased risk due to altered biomechanics and tissue quality.

B is incorrect because the Achilles tendon inserts on the posterior calcaneal tuberosity, not the medial calcaneal tuberosity, and Achilles pathology presents with posterior heel pain and tenderness proximal to or at the posterior insertion. C is incorrect because although the flexor digitorum brevis also originates from the medial calcaneal tuberosity, it is not the primary structure implicated in the classic plantar fasciitis presentation; the plantar fascia is the most commonly cited culprit. D is incorrect because although the abductor hallucis also originates from the medial calcaneal tuberosity, plantar fasciitis specifically refers to pathology of the plantar fascia (plantar aponeurosis), which is the board-standard answer for this clinical scenario.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old woman with hip osteoarthritis is being considered for a hip arthroplasty procedure. The Smith-Petersen interval is chosen for exposure. What anatomical landmark is important for identifying this interval?
A) Greater trochanter
B) Iliopsoas tendon
C) Femoral head
D) Pubic symphysis
questions.answer:
B)
The iliopsoas tendon is critical for identifying the Smith-Petersen interval, as this interval is located between the iliopsoas and the anterior capsule of the hip joint, allowing for effective access during hip procedures. A is incorrect because the greater trochanter is not directly involved in identifying the Smith-Petersen interval. C is incorrect because the femoral head is not a landmark for this interval. D is incorrect because the pubic symphysis is not related to the Smith-Petersen interval.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old female presents with acute shoulder pain after a car accident. She exhibits weakness with adduction and internal rotation of the arm. Upon examination, there is tenderness over the anterior shoulder region, and she has difficulty lifting her arm overhead. Which muscle is primarily responsible for these actions, and what is its innervation?
A) Teres major; axillary nerve
B) Pectoralis major; lateral and medial pectoral nerves
C) Coracobrachialis; musculocutaneous nerve
D) Subscapularis; upper and lower subscapular nerves
questions.answer:
B)
The pectoralis major is the primary muscle responsible for adduction and internal rotation of the arm and also assists with forward flexion (lifting the arm overhead via its clavicular head). It is innervated by the lateral pectoral nerve (clavicular head) and medial pectoral nerve (sternocostal head). Tenderness over the anterior shoulder region is consistent with a pectoralis major injury.

A is incorrect because the teres major contributes to adduction and internal rotation but is innervated by the lower subscapular nerve, not the axillary nerve, making the pairing in this choice factually wrong. C is incorrect because the coracobrachialis primarily flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder but is not a significant internal rotator; it does not match the full clinical picture described. D is incorrect because the subscapularis is a primary internal rotator but is not a primary adductor of the arm, and it is located posteriorly on the scapula rather than in the anterior shoulder region described in the stem.

questions.question:
A 12-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after falling from his bicycle. He has significant tenderness and swelling over the lateral aspect of his knee, and x-rays reveal a fracture through the tibial tubercle. Which classification would best describe this injury?
A) O'Brien Classification
B) Ogden Classification
C) Salter-Harris Classification
D) Pandya Classification
questions.answer:
B)
The Ogden Classification is specifically used for tibial tubercle fractures, which include variations based on the fracture pattern and displacement. Understanding this classification helps guide appropriate management strategies for these common injuries in children.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old female presents with persistent pain in her hip following a total hip arthroplasty. During revision surgery, the orthopedic surgeon notes notching of the stem. What is the most serious implication of this finding?
A) Decreased wear of the acetabular component
B) Increased risk of stem fatigue failure
C) Difficulty in removing the implant
D) Higher likelihood of infection
questions.answer:
B)
Notching of the femoral stem creates a stress riser at the site of the cortical defect. Under cyclic loading, this focal stress concentration markedly increases the risk of fatigue failure of the stem, which is the most serious mechanical complication associated with stem notching.

A is incorrect because notching of the stem does not decrease acetabular component wear; stem notching is a stem-side mechanical issue unrelated to polyethylene or bearing-surface wear.
C is incorrect because while notching may theoretically complicate implant removal, difficulty of extraction is not the most serious implication — catastrophic fatigue fracture of the stem is far more consequential.
D is incorrect because stem notching is a mechanical phenomenon that does not directly increase the risk of periprosthetic infection.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old man presents with chronic elbow pain and decreased range of motion following a fall three months ago. He describes mechanical catching and is unable to fully extend his elbow. Imaging reveals osteophyte formation at the olecranon tip and several loose bodies within the joint. After conservative management with NSAIDs and physical therapy fails, he is referred for possible surgery. What is the most appropriate surgical procedure for this patient?
A) Open reduction and internal fixation
B) Arthroscopic debridement
C) Ulnar nerve transposition
D) Total elbow arthroplasty
questions.answer:
B)
Arthroscopic debridement (including removal of loose bodies and osteophyte excision) is the most appropriate procedure for a patient with post-traumatic elbow stiffness, mechanical symptoms, and imaging evidence of loose bodies and osteophytes after failure of conservative management. It is minimally invasive, preserves the native joint, and effectively addresses the mechanical block to extension.

A is incorrect because open reduction and internal fixation is indicated for acute fractures requiring anatomic reduction, not for chronic post-traumatic degenerative changes with loose bodies. C is incorrect because ulnar nerve transposition addresses ulnar neuropathy at the cubital tunnel and does not treat intra-articular mechanical pathology.
