A 15-year-old female basketball player complains of knee pain and swelling after a fall during practice. Physical examination reveals tenderness along the medial aspect of the knee and positive McMurray's test. An MRI is ordered, revealing a medial meniscus tear. Given her age and activity level, what is the most appropriate next step in the management of her injury?
A) Immediate surgical intervention
B) Conservative management with rest and rehabilitation
C) Arthroscopic meniscectomy
D) Perform a cortisone injection
questions.answer:
B)
In a young athlete with an acute meniscal tear and no mechanical symptoms such as locking or a displaced bucket-handle fragment, initial conservative management with rest, ice, anti-inflammatory medication, and structured rehabilitation is the appropriate first step. If symptoms persist or mechanical symptoms develop, arthroscopic evaluation with meniscal repair (preferred over meniscectomy in this age group) should be pursued.

A is incorrect because immediate surgical intervention is not warranted without a trial of conservative management, unless there is a locked knee or displaced bucket-handle tear causing mechanical block to motion.
C is incorrect because arthroscopic meniscectomy removes meniscal tissue and should be avoided in a 15-year-old whenever possible; meniscal preservation (repair) is strongly preferred in young patients to prevent premature degenerative changes.
D is incorrect because cortisone injection does not treat the underlying meniscal pathology, carries risks of cartilage damage with repeated use, and is not a standard treatment for acute meniscal tears in adolescents.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old female athlete undergoes open rotator cuff repair through a lateral deltoid-splitting approach. During the procedure, the surgeon is careful to limit the split to avoid injury to a nearby neurovascular structure. Which structure is at greatest risk of being damaged with this approach?
A) Radial nerve
B) Brachial plexus
C) Axillary nerve
D) Thoracodorsal nerve
questions.answer:
C)
The axillary nerve crosses the deep surface of the deltoid approximately 5–7 cm distal to the lateral edge of the acromion. During a lateral deltoid-splitting approach, extending the split beyond this safe zone places the axillary nerve at greatest risk of injury, which would result in deltoid denervation and loss of shoulder abduction, as well as sensory loss over the regimental badge area.

A is incorrect because the radial nerve courses in the spiral groove of the humerus and is at risk during approaches to the humeral shaft (e.g., posterior or anterolateral), not during a proximal deltoid-splitting approach.

B is incorrect because the brachial plexus lies medially in the axilla and is not directly at risk during a lateral deltoid split.

D is incorrect because the thoracodorsal nerve innervates the latissimus dorsi and runs along the posterior axillary wall; it is not in the surgical field of a lateral deltoid-splitting approach.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male sustains a fall from a height and lands directly on his heel. He reports immediate severe pain in his ankle. A CT scan shows a fracture of the talus with the talus driven down into the calcaneus. What mechanism of injury best explains this situation?
A) Supination-inversion
B) Plantarflexion with axial load
C) Dorsiflexion with external rotation
D) Hyperdorsiflexion
questions.answer:
B)
A fall from a height with the foot in plantarflexion subjects the talar neck to a shearing force as the posterior lip of the tibia acts as a fulcrum against the talar neck under axial load. This mechanism classically produces talar neck fractures and can drive the talus into the calcaneus.

A is incorrect because supination-inversion typically causes lateral ankle ligament injuries or lateral malleolus fractures, not axial talar fractures driven into the calcaneus.
C is incorrect because dorsiflexion with external rotation is the mechanism for Weber-type (Lauge-Hansen supination–external rotation or pronation–external rotation) ankle fractures involving the malleoli, not talar body/neck fractures.
D is incorrect because hyperdorsiflexion can cause anterior tibial lip fractures or anterior ankle impingement injuries, but does not produce the pattern of the talus being driven into the calcaneus as described in this stem.

questions.question:
A 12-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after a fall from his skateboard. He complains of severe pain in his right wrist and refuses to move it. X-rays reveal a fracture through the growth plate of the distal radius with a triangular metaphyseal fragment (Thurston-Holland fragment) visible on the lateral view. Which Salter-Harris classification does this injury most likely represent?
A) Type I
B) Type II
C) Type III
D) Type IV
questions.answer:
B)
A Salter-Harris Type II fracture extends through the physis and exits through the metaphysis, producing the characteristic triangular Thurston-Holland metaphyseal fragment seen on imaging. It is the most common Salter-Harris fracture type and frequently occurs at the distal radius in adolescents.

A is incorrect because a Type I fracture involves only the physis without any metaphyseal or epiphyseal fracture fragment; imaging may appear normal or show only physeal widening.
C is incorrect because a Type III fracture extends through the physis and into the epiphysis (intra-articular) without metaphyseal involvement.
D is incorrect because a Type IV fracture crosses the metaphysis, physis, and epiphysis — it is an intra-articular injury that typically requires surgical fixation to restore the articular surface and growth plate alignment.

questions.question:
A patient is undergoing rehabilitation 6 weeks after a total shoulder arthroplasty. He is being educated about the importance of shoulder mechanics. Which of the following best describes the role of the supraspinatus in shoulder function?
A) It primarily stabilizes the elbow joint
B) It assists in the internal rotation of the shoulder
C) It initiates abduction of the shoulder
D) It is responsible for forearm pronation
E) It prevents superior translation of the humeral head
questions.answer:
E)
The supraspinatus is a critical dynamic stabilizer of the glenohumeral joint. Its primary biomechanical role is to compress the humeral head into the glenoid and prevent superior translation during shoulder elevation, which is especially important after total shoulder arthroplasty. While it does contribute to initiating abduction, its role as a humeral head depressor and stabilizer is considered its most important function in shoulder mechanics.

A is incorrect because the supraspinatus acts at the shoulder, not the elbow joint.
B is incorrect because internal rotation is primarily performed by the subscapularis, pectoralis major, and latissimus dorsi, not the supraspinatus.
C is incorrect because although the supraspinatus assists in initiating abduction, its primary and most critical role in shoulder mechanics is preventing superior migration of the humeral head — this is the function most relevant to shoulder arthroplasty rehabilitation.
D is incorrect because forearm pronation is performed by the pronator teres and pronator quadratus, not the supraspinatus.

questions.question:
A patient with a recent high-energy ankle fracture undergoes evaluation in the trauma bay. After splinting, the orthopedic team decides to stabilize his fracture with an ankle spanning external fixator. What is the primary reason for using this type of fixation?
A) To allow for early weight-bearing
B) To maintain alignment during soft tissue healing
C) To facilitate immediate surgical intervention
D) To minimize blood loss during surgery
E) To prevent infection at the fracture site
questions.answer:
B)
An ankle spanning external fixator is primarily used to maintain fracture alignment and restore length while allowing the soft tissue envelope to recover from the initial high-energy injury. This temporizing measure ("damage control orthopaedics") reduces further soft tissue insult and permits definitive internal fixation once swelling subsides, typically when the "wrinkle sign" returns.

A is incorrect because an ankle spanning external fixator does not permit early weight-bearing; patients are kept non-weight-bearing on the affected extremity.
C is incorrect because the purpose of the external fixator is to delay, not facilitate, immediate definitive surgical intervention until soft tissues are ready.
D is incorrect because minimizing blood loss is not the primary rationale; the fixator is applied to protect soft tissues and maintain alignment, not to control hemorrhage.
E is incorrect because while maintaining soft tissue health may indirectly reduce wound complications, the primary goal is alignment and soft tissue rest, not direct infection prevention.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old female runner presents with anterior knee pain that worsens with climbing stairs and prolonged sitting. Physical examination reveals peripatellar tenderness and a positive patellar grind test. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for her condition?
A) Corticosteroid injection
B) Physical therapy focusing on quadriceps strengthening
C) Surgical intervention with lateral retinacular release
D) Bracing with a patellar stabilizing brace
questions.answer:
B)
This presentation — anterior knee pain worsened by stairs and prolonged sitting ("theater sign") with a positive patellar grind test — is classic for patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS). The most appropriate initial treatment is physical therapy focusing on quadriceps strengthening, particularly the vastus medialis obliquus (VMO), along with hip abductor and external rotator strengthening. This is the standard first-line, evidence-based treatment for PFPS.

A is incorrect because corticosteroid injections are not standard treatment for PFPS; they do not address the underlying biomechanical cause and carry risks of cartilage damage and tendon weakening. C is incorrect because surgical intervention (e.g., lateral retinacular release) is reserved for refractory cases that have failed prolonged conservative management and is not an initial treatment. D is incorrect because while a patellar stabilizing brace may provide some symptomatic relief, it does not address the underlying muscular imbalance and is considered an adjunct rather than the primary treatment.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old male presents with an open fracture of the tibia sustained during a motorcycle accident. Upon evaluation, you find significant contamination. Which of the following is the most critical initial management step in the trauma bay?
A) Immediate casting of the fracture
B) Administration of IV antibiotics
C) Irrigating the wound and removing gross debris
D) Early orthopedic consultation
questions.answer:
B)
Administration of IV antibiotics is the most critical initial management step for open fractures in the trauma bay. Per EAST and OTA guidelines, early antibiotic administration (ideally within one hour of injury) has been shown to significantly reduce infection rates. A first-generation cephalosporin (e.g., cefazolin) is standard for Gustilo type I/II injuries, with the addition of an aminoglycoside for type III injuries.

A is incorrect because immediate casting is not appropriate for an open fracture; the wound must be managed, and definitive fixation planning is required. C is incorrect because while irrigation and debridement are essential components of open fracture management, formal irrigation and debridement is performed in the operating room; in the trauma bay, the wound should be covered with a sterile saline-moistened dressing, but IV antibiotics take priority as the first intervention. D is incorrect because while early orthopedic consultation is important, it is not the most critical initial step — antibiotic administration should not be delayed while awaiting consultation.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male undergoes total hip arthroplasty for degenerative joint disease. Postoperatively, he develops pain and limited range of motion in the hip joint. Imaging shows signs of joint degeneration. Which of the following mechanisms is most likely responsible for his condition?
A) Intra-articular infection
B) Post-traumatic arthritis
C) Osteolysis due to wear debris
D) Mechanical loosening of the prosthesis
questions.answer:
C)
Osteolysis due to wear debris is the most common mechanism of late periprosthetic joint degeneration following total hip arthroplasty. Polyethylene (or other bearing surface) wear particles incite a macrophage-mediated inflammatory response that leads to progressive bone resorption around the implant, causing pain, limited motion, and eventual implant failure.

A is incorrect because intra-articular infection (periprosthetic joint infection) typically presents with systemic signs of infection (fever, elevated inflammatory markers, purulent aspirate) rather than simply imaging signs of joint degeneration.

B is incorrect because post-traumatic arthritis refers to degenerative changes following a fracture or joint injury, not a complication of prosthetic joint wear.

D is incorrect because mechanical loosening is often a consequence of osteolysis (i.e., downstream of wear-debris-induced bone loss) rather than the primary underlying mechanism itself; the stem asks for the mechanism responsible for the degeneration.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male presents with lateral elbow pain after a fall. On examination, he has tenderness over the lateral aspect of the elbow, and a provocative test reveals increased pain with varus stress. An MRI demonstrates a partial tear of the lateral collateral ligament complex. Which of the following structures is primarily responsible for providing stability to the lateral aspect of the elbow?
A) Medial collateral ligament
B) Lateral ulnar collateral ligament
C) Annular ligament
D) Radial collateral ligament
E) Biceps brachii tendon
questions.answer:
B)
The lateral ulnar collateral ligament (LUCL) is the primary stabilizer of the lateral elbow against varus and posterolateral rotatory instability. It originates from the lateral epicondyle and inserts on the supinator crest of the ulna. Deficiency of the LUCL is the essential lesion in posterolateral rotatory instability (PLRI), and a partial tear explains this patient's lateral pain and positive varus stress test.

A is incorrect because the medial collateral ligament (specifically the anterior bundle) is the primary restraint to valgus stress on the medial side of the elbow, not the lateral side. C is incorrect because the annular ligament stabilizes the proximal radioulnar joint by holding the radial head in the radial notch of the ulna; it does not primarily resist varus stress. D is incorrect because the radial collateral ligament (proper) originates from the lateral epicondyle and blends into the annular ligament; while it contributes to lateral stability, the LUCL is the primary restraint to varus and posterolateral rotatory instability. E is incorrect because the biceps brachii tendon is an elbow flexor and forearm supinator and does not serve as a primary lateral stabilizer of the elbow.

questions.question:
A 10-year-old boy presents with a painful ankle after a fall while playing basketball. X-rays reveal a displaced oblique fracture of the distal fibula with mild shortening. Considering his age and the fracture type, what is the most appropriate management option?
A) Surgical intervention with ORIF
B) Immediate casting without reduction
C) Observation with follow-up x-ray
D) Closed reduction and casting
questions.answer:
D)
A displaced oblique distal fibula fracture in a child is best managed with closed reduction and casting. This approach restores alignment, provides fracture stabilization, and takes advantage of the child's remodeling potential, avoiding unnecessary surgical intervention.

A is incorrect because ORIF is generally reserved for fractures that are irreducible by closed means, involve the physis with significant displacement (Salter-Harris types), or are associated with ankle joint instability not correctable with closed methods.
B is incorrect because casting without reduction would not address the displacement and shortening, risking malunion and functional impairment.
C is incorrect because observation alone is insufficient for a displaced fracture; without immobilization and reduction, the fracture may displace further and heal in a malposition.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old woman presents with pain and swelling around her wrist after falling on her outstretched hand. Examination reveals a positive press test and the wrist shows dorsal subluxation with instability. Which ligament is primarily responsible for the stability of the distal radioulnar joint in this scenario?
A) Palmar ulnocarpal ligament
B) Dorsoradial ligament
C) Triangular fibrocartilage complex
D) Dorsal interosseous ligaments
E) Volar radioulnar ligament
questions.answer:
C)
The triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) is the primary stabilizer of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ). It comprises the articular disc, the dorsal and volar radioulnar ligaments, the meniscus homologue, and the ulnocarpal ligaments. In this scenario with dorsal subluxation after a fall on an outstretched hand, disruption of the TFCC (particularly its dorsal radioulnar ligament component) allows the ulna to subluxate dorsally, producing a positive press test and DRUJ instability.

A is incorrect because the palmar ulnocarpal ligament (ulnolunate and ulnotriquetral) contributes to ulnocarpal stability but is not the primary restraint of the DRUJ. B is incorrect because the dorsoradial ligament is a term associated with the thumb CMC joint (trapezium), not a primary DRUJ stabilizer. D is incorrect because the dorsal interosseous ligaments refer to intercarpal or intermetacarpal structures and do not primarily stabilize the DRUJ. E is incorrect because the volar radioulnar ligament is actually a component of the TFCC; while it contributes to DRUJ stability (particularly resisting dorsal translation in supination), the question asks about the overall complex responsible, which is the TFCC as a whole.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man presents with severe shoulder pain and limited range of motion following a fall. An MRI is performed, revealing a massive rotator cuff tear. In the evaluation of this injury, which imaging technique is most effective for assessing the integrity of the shoulder joint?
A) X-ray
B) Computed Tomography (CT)
C) Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
D) Ultrasound
questions.answer:
C)
MRI is the most effective imaging modality for evaluating soft tissue structures of the shoulder, including the rotator cuff tendons, labrum, and surrounding musculature. It provides high-resolution, multiplanar images that allow precise characterization of tear size, retraction, and muscle quality (fatty infiltration), all of which are critical for surgical planning.

A is incorrect because plain radiographs are useful for evaluating bony anatomy (e.g., acromial morphology, glenohumeral arthritis, superior humeral head migration) but cannot directly visualize soft tissue structures such as the rotator cuff tendons.

B is incorrect because CT provides excellent bony detail and is useful for fracture characterization or preoperative planning for arthroplasty, but it has limited ability to assess soft tissue integrity compared with MRI.

D is incorrect because ultrasound can detect rotator cuff tears and is operator-dependent; while it is a useful and cost-effective screening tool, it is less comprehensive than MRI for evaluating the full extent of a massive tear, associated muscle atrophy/fatty infiltration, and intra-articular pathology.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman presents with persistent pain in the buttocks, especially when sitting for prolonged periods. Upon examination, tenderness is noted over the ischial tuberosity. Which condition is most likely responsible for her symptoms? 
A) Ischial bursitis 
B) Hamstring strain 
C) Piriformis syndrome 
D) Sciatica
questions.answer:
A)
The symptoms and location of tenderness suggest ischial bursitis, commonly presenting as pain around the ischial tuberosity, particularly aggravated by sitting. The other conditions listed may have overlapping symptoms but typically involve different mechanisms or locations.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman complains of numbness and tingling in her right hand, particularly affecting her thumb, index, and middle fingers. History reveals a repetitive wrist motion from her job as a seamstress. Physical examination shows a positive Phalen's test. Which of the following interventions is most appropriate for initial management of her condition?
A) Surgical decompression of the median nerve
B) Wrist splinting in a neutral position
C) Corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel
D) Physical therapy focusing on wrist range of motion
E) Immediate MRI of the wrist
questions.answer:
B)
Wrist splinting in a neutral position is the most appropriate initial management for carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) with mild to moderate symptoms. Neutral positioning minimizes pressure within the carpal tunnel and is supported as first-line conservative treatment by AAOS guidelines. Activity modification and nighttime splinting are typically tried before more invasive interventions.

A is incorrect because surgical decompression (carpal tunnel release) is reserved for patients who fail conservative management or who present with severe symptoms such as thenar atrophy or persistent motor/sensory deficits.
C is incorrect because corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel can provide temporary relief and may be considered if splinting fails, but it is not the most appropriate initial intervention.
D is incorrect because physical therapy focusing on wrist range of motion is not a primary evidence-based first-line treatment for CTS; nerve gliding exercises may be adjunctive but splinting takes priority.
E is incorrect because immediate MRI of the wrist is not indicated for the initial workup of typical CTS; the diagnosis is clinical, and electrodiagnostic studies (NCS/EMG) are the confirmatory test of choice if needed, not MRI.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man presents after sustaining a laceration to his wrist while using a power tool. The laceration appears to be deep and extends over the flexor tendons. On examination, he demonstrates flexion loss of his ring and little fingers. What mechanism of injury is most likely to have caused the observed flexion loss? 
A) Complete laceration of the flexor digitorum profundus 
B) Incomplete laceration of the flexor digitorum superficialis 
C) Quadriga effect due to over-tightening 
D) Laceration of the flexor carpi ulnaris
questions.answer:
A)
A deep laceration over the wrist flexor tendons with loss of flexion of the ring and little fingers is most consistent with complete laceration of the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendons to those digits. The FDP tendons to the ring and small fingers share a common muscle belly and travel in close proximity at the wrist, making them vulnerable to simultaneous injury. Complete FDP laceration eliminates DIP flexion and significantly impairs overall finger flexion.

B is incorrect because an incomplete laceration of the FDS would not cause complete loss of flexion — the tendon would retain partial function, and the intact FDP would still allow DIP flexion and contribute to overall finger flexion.
C is incorrect because the quadriga effect occurs after surgical repair or advancement when one FDP tendon is overtightened, limiting excursion of the adjacent FDP tendons; it is not a mechanism seen in acute lacerations.
D is incorrect because the flexor carpi ulnaris is a wrist flexor and ulnar deviator — its laceration would not cause loss of ring and little finger flexion.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old patient with a history of osteoporosis presents with wrist pain after a low-energy fall. X-rays show a distal radius fracture with a dorsal angulation of 25 degrees. What is the next best management strategy?
A) Splinting without reduction
B) Surgical intervention with volar locking plate
C) Closed reduction and casting
D) Immediate external fixation
questions.answer:
C)
In an elderly, low-demand patient with a distal radius fracture and 25 degrees of dorsal angulation, the angulation exceeds the generally accepted threshold (~10–20 degrees depending on functional demand). Closed reduction and casting is the appropriate first-line treatment to restore acceptable alignment before considering surgical options.

A is incorrect because 25 degrees of dorsal angulation exceeds the acceptable range even in elderly patients, so immobilization without reduction would result in malunion and functional impairment.
B is incorrect because surgical fixation with a volar locking plate is generally reserved for unstable fracture patterns, intra-articular involvement, or failure of closed reduction, not as the initial management step.
D is incorrect because external fixation is not the first-line treatment; it may be considered for highly comminuted or unstable fractures that cannot be maintained with casting, but closed reduction and casting should be attempted first.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis is evaluated for pain and swelling at the first tarsometatarsal joint. Physical examination reveals significant pain on palpation and a decreased range of motion. After discussing treatment options, you recommend a surgical procedure. Which procedure is indicated for her condition?
A) Total ankle arthroplasty
B) First TMT joint arthrodesis
C) Ankle arthroscopy
D) Achilles tendon lengthening
questions.answer:
B)
First TMT joint arthrodesis is the indicated procedure for severe arthritis or instability at the first tarsometatarsal joint. In patients with rheumatoid arthritis causing painful, destructive changes at this joint, fusion relieves pain and restores a stable weight-bearing platform. This is a well-established treatment for inflammatory arthropathy of the first TMT joint.

A is incorrect because total ankle arthroplasty addresses end-stage ankle (tibiotalar) joint arthritis, not first TMT joint disease.
C is incorrect because ankle arthroscopy is used for intra-articular ankle pathology (e.g., loose bodies, impingement) and does not address the first TMT joint.
D is incorrect because Achilles tendon lengthening is performed for equinus contracture and has no role in treating first TMT joint arthritis.

questions.question:
A 16-year-old male with idiopathic scoliosis presents with a 35-degree curve and is currently undergoing treatment with a brace. He reports compliance with the bracing regimen but is still concerned about the progression of his curve. What is the most reliable method to evaluate the effectiveness of his current management?
A) Repeat physical examination
B) MRI of the spine
C) X-ray of the spine
D) CT scan of the spine
questions.answer:
C)
Standing posteroanterior (PA) X-rays of the spine are the standard and most reliable method to monitor scoliosis curve magnitude over time. Serial Cobb angle measurements on plain radiographs allow direct comparison to prior studies and objectively determine whether the curve is stable, improving, or progressing despite bracing.

A is incorrect because physical examination (e.g., Adam's forward bend test, scoliometer) provides a screening assessment but does not yield precise, reproducible Cobb angle measurements needed to track curve progression.
B is incorrect because MRI is used to evaluate intraspinal pathology (e.g., syringomyelia, Chiari malformation, tethered cord) rather than to measure curve magnitude; it is not the standard tool for monitoring brace effectiveness.
D is incorrect because CT scanning delivers significantly higher radiation than plain radiographs and is not indicated for routine scoliosis curve monitoring; it may be used for preoperative planning but not for serial follow-up of brace treatment.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old male presents with complaints of clumsiness in his hands and difficulty maintaining balance while walking. Neurological examination reveals a positive Hoffman’s sign and sustained clonus in the lower extremities. An MRI shows cervical spinal cord compression at the C5-C6 level. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Physical therapy
B) Surgical decompression
C) Corticosteroid injection
D) Observation and follow-up
questions.answer:
B)
Surgical decompression is indicated in cases of cervical spinal cord compression, especially when neurological deficits, such as clumsiness of the hands and gait abnormalities, are present. Non-surgical management is less effective in significant cases of compression. A is incorrect because physical therapy does not address the underlying spinal cord compression causing neurological deficits. C is incorrect because corticosteroid injections are not effective for mechanical compression of the spinal cord. D is incorrect because observation and follow-up are inappropriate when there are significant neurological deficits.

questions.question:
A pediatric orthopaedic surgeon is assessing a 10-year-old girl with a progressive scoliosis curve measuring 30 degrees. The child has no significant cardiovascular symptoms. At what degree of curvature is she at increased risk for cardiopulmonary dysfunction?
A) 20 degrees
B) 30 degrees
C) 50 degrees
D) 70 degrees
E) 90 degrees
questions.answer:
E)
Explanation: A scoliotic curve exceeding 90 degrees is associated with significant cardiopulmonary dysfunction due to compression of the thoracic cavity and reduced lung capacity. Monitoring and possible surgical intervention may be warranted as the curve progresses.

questions.question:
A pediatric patient is referred for evaluation of a potentially abnormal hip joint. The physician determines that the left hip is dislocated and decides to use a Pavlik harness for treatment. Which of the following complications is most commonly associated with improper application of this harness?
A) Femoral head avascular necrosis
B) Hip joint contracture
C) Sciatic nerve injury
D) Osteomyelitis
questions.answer:
A)
Avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head is the most commonly cited complication of improper Pavlik harness application. It occurs when the hip is forced into excessive abduction, compressing the lateral epiphyseal vessels. Proper positioning in the "safe zone" of Ramsey (flexion ~100° and gentle abduction) is critical to avoid this complication.

B is incorrect because while hip joint contracture can occur (particularly inferior/posterior dislocation from excessive flexion without adequate abduction), it is less commonly associated with improper Pavlik use than AVN. C is incorrect because sciatic nerve injury is rare; femoral nerve palsy from excessive flexion is the more classically described nerve injury with the Pavlik harness, and even that is less common than AVN. D is incorrect because osteomyelitis is an infectious complication unrelated to harness application.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a painful, swollen right hand after accidentally striking a wall. On examination, there is tenderness and swelling over the second metacarpal. An x-ray reveals a non-displaced metacarpal neck fracture. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this type of fracture?
A) Immediate surgical intervention
B) Splinting and early range of motion exercises
C) Buddy taping with analgesics
D) Immobilization in a cast for 6 weeks
questions.answer:
B)
Non-displaced metacarpal neck fractures of the index finger are typically stable and can be managed conservatively with splinting and early range of motion exercises. The index metacarpal tolerates less angulation than the ring or small finger metacarpals, but a non-displaced fracture does not require surgical fixation. Early motion helps prevent stiffness and promotes functional recovery.

A is incorrect because immediate surgical intervention is reserved for significantly displaced fractures, rotational deformity, or open fractures — none of which are present here.
C is incorrect because buddy taping alone does not provide adequate immobilization for a metacarpal neck fracture; it is more appropriate for stable phalangeal fractures.
D is incorrect because prolonged cast immobilization for 6 weeks is excessive for a non-displaced metacarpal neck fracture and risks significant hand stiffness; a shorter period of splinting with early range of motion is preferred.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old athlete presents with a painful, swollen elbow after falling onto an outstretched arm during a game. Examination reveals tenderness over the anterior aspect of the cubital fossa and limited range of motion. During an anterior surgical approach to the elbow, which structure must the surgeon be cautious of to avoid compromising function?
A) Brachial artery
B) Ulnar nerve
C) Median nerve
D) Musculocutaneous nerve
questions.answer:
C)
During an anterior surgical approach to the elbow (cubital fossa), the median nerve is a critical structure at risk. It courses through the cubital fossa medial to the brachial artery and passes between the two heads of the pronator teres. Injury to the median nerve would result in significant loss of forearm pronation, wrist flexion, and thumb/index finger function, making its identification and preservation essential.

A is incorrect because while the brachial artery is also encountered in the anterior approach and must be protected, the question specifically asks about compromising function, making the median nerve the more critical neural structure to preserve.
B is incorrect because the ulnar nerve runs posterior to the medial epicondyle and is not a structure encountered during the anterior approach to the elbow; it is at risk during medial or posterior approaches.
D is incorrect because the musculocutaneous nerve exits the lateral aspect of the biceps as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm; while it can be encountered laterally, it is a sensory nerve at this level and is less critical to motor function than the median nerve.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male athlete presents with shoulder pain and limited range of motion following a fall onto his outstretched arm. Physical examination reveals significant weakness in abduction and external rotation. X-rays show no fractures. Which of the following muscles is most likely weak due to injury affecting the rotator cuff?
A) Subscapularis
B) Supraspinatus
C) Coracobrachialis
D) Pectoralis major
questions.answer:
B)
The supraspinatus is the rotator cuff muscle most commonly injured and is primarily responsible for initiating shoulder abduction. In a fall on an outstretched hand, the supraspinatus tendon is the most frequently torn rotator cuff structure. The stem also mentions external rotation weakness, which could implicate the infraspinatus; however, among the choices provided, the supraspinatus (B) is the best answer as the most commonly injured rotator cuff muscle causing abduction weakness.

A is incorrect because the subscapularis is an internal rotator of the shoulder; its injury would cause weakness in internal rotation, not abduction or external rotation. C is incorrect because the coracobrachialis assists in shoulder flexion and adduction and is not part of the rotator cuff. D is incorrect because the pectoralis major is a powerful adductor, flexor, and internal rotator of the shoulder and is not a rotator cuff muscle.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old boy presents with recurrent fractures and blue sclera. His mother reports that he has had multiple bone fractures from minimal trauma, with an incident involving a fall while running. On examination, you note short stature and skeletal deformities. What is the most likely underlying condition?
A) Osteosarcoma
B) Osteogenesis Imperfecta
C) Rickets
D) Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome
questions.answer:
B)
Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI) is characterized by defective type I collagen synthesis, leading to markedly fragile bones with recurrent fractures from minimal trauma, blue sclera, short stature, and skeletal deformities. This presentation in a 5-year-old with all of these classic features is essentially pathognomonic for OI.

A is incorrect because osteosarcoma is a malignant bone tumor typically presenting in adolescents with localized bone pain, swelling, and a single destructive lesion — not recurrent fractures with blue sclera.
C is incorrect because rickets (vitamin D deficiency) causes bowing of the long bones, widened growth plates, and rachitic rosary, but does not cause blue sclera or the degree of bone fragility seen here.
D is incorrect because Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome is a connective tissue disorder primarily manifesting with joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility, and tissue fragility — not recurrent fractures or blue sclera.

questions.question:
A 15-year-old female soccer player presents with complaints of knee pain and instability after a twisting injury during a game. Physical examination reveals a positive Lachman test. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) MRI of the knee
B) Referral for orthopedic consultation
C) Initiate physical therapy
D) Rest and ice treatment
questions.answer:
A)
In a 15-year-old athlete with a positive Lachman test suggesting an ACL injury, the most appropriate next step is to obtain an MRI of the knee. MRI is the gold-standard imaging study to confirm the ACL tear, evaluate meniscal and chondral injuries, and identify associated ligamentous damage, all of which are critical for guiding definitive management.

B is incorrect because while orthopedic referral will ultimately be necessary, it should follow confirmatory imaging so the consultant has the information needed to plan treatment. C is incorrect because initiating physical therapy without first confirming the diagnosis and ruling out associated injuries (e.g., meniscal tears, bone bruises) would be premature. D is incorrect because rest and ice alone are insufficient management for a suspected ACL tear; the diagnosis must first be confirmed with imaging to determine whether surgical reconstruction or other definitive treatment is indicated.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old man presents with hip pain and a history of multiple falls. An x-ray reveals a subtrochanteric femur fracture. Which of the following deforming forces is most likely contributing to the patient's fracture?
A) Valgus stress on the hip
B) Varus stress on the hip
C) Adduction forces during ambulation
D) Flexion forces at the knee
questions.answer:
B)
Subtrochanteric femur fractures are characterized by classic deforming forces: the proximal fragment is flexed by the iliopsoas, abducted by the gluteus medius/minimus, and externally rotated by the short external rotators, while the shaft is pulled medially (adducted) by the adductors. The net result is a varus deformity at the fracture site. Varus stress on the hip is therefore the predominant deforming force.

A is incorrect because valgus stress would push the femoral shaft laterally relative to the proximal fragment; the opposite (varus) occurs at a subtrochanteric fracture due to the pull of the adductors on the distal fragment and the abductors on the proximal fragment. C is incorrect because while adductor pull on the distal fragment contributes to the overall deformity, the question asks about the stress on the hip, which is best described as varus; 'adduction forces during ambulation' is not the primary deforming force of the fracture pattern. D is incorrect because flexion forces at the knee do not significantly contribute to the deformity of a subtrochanteric femur fracture; the relevant flexion force acts at the hip (iliopsoas on the proximal fragment), not the knee.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman presents with a humeral shaft fracture resulting from a fall. She is otherwise healthy and has no significant comorbidities. Given her age and the nature of the fracture, what is the most appropriate initial management?
A) Surgical intervention
B) Brace and rest
C) Immediate physical therapy
D) Close monitoring without treatment
questions.answer:
B)
The majority of humeral shaft fractures in otherwise healthy patients can be managed non-operatively. Initial treatment with a coaptation splint followed by transition to a functional brace (e.g., Sarmiento brace) is the standard of care, with high union rates and acceptable functional outcomes. Surgery is reserved for specific indications such as open fractures, vascular injury, polytrauma, or failure of closed management.

A is incorrect because surgical intervention is not the first-line treatment for an isolated, closed humeral shaft fracture without signs of neurovascular compromise, significant shortening, or other operative indications.
C is incorrect because immediate physical therapy is not appropriate in the acute setting; the fracture must first be immobilized to allow early healing before initiating range-of-motion exercises.
D is incorrect because close monitoring without any treatment (no immobilization, no pain management) would be inadequate — a functional brace provides alignment, comfort, and support for fracture healing.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old runner presents with pain along the lateral aspect of the foot, specifically near the base of the fifth metatarsal. Radiographs suggest a fracture in Zone 2. What is the most appropriate initial management for this type of injury?
A) Surgical fixation
B) Non-weight-bearing cast
C) RICE protocol and immediate mobilization
D) Boot immobilization and gradual weight-bearing
E) Physical therapy
questions.answer:
A)
Zone 2 fractures of the fifth metatarsal (Jones fractures) occur at the meta-diaphyseal junction, a watershed area with poor blood supply and high rates of delayed union and non-union. In a young, active runner, early surgical fixation with an intramedullary screw is the recommended initial management to optimize healing and expedite return to activity.

B is incorrect because non-weight-bearing cast immobilization is a described conservative option but carries a high non-union rate (up to 25–50%) and prolonged recovery, making it suboptimal in an athlete. C is incorrect because RICE and immediate mobilization are appropriate for minor soft-tissue injuries, not for a Jones fracture which requires protection from loading. D is incorrect because boot immobilization with gradual weight-bearing is appropriate for Zone 1 (tuberosity avulsion) fractures, which have a reliable blood supply and heal well conservatively; Zone 2 fractures require more aggressive treatment. E is incorrect because physical therapy alone does not address the fracture healing problem and would risk displacement or non-union.

questions.question:
A 67-year-old woman presents with severe neck pain and weakness in her right upper extremity. Neurological examination reveals reduced bicep strength when tested with resisted elbow flexion. Which cervical nerve roots are primarily responsible for this motor function?
A) C5-C6
B) C6-C7
C) C7-T1
D) C8-T1
questions.answer:
A)
The biceps brachii is innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve, which derives primarily from the C5 and C6 nerve roots. Weakness of resisted elbow flexion therefore localizes to C5-C6 radiculopathy.

B is incorrect because C6-C7 primarily innervates the wrist extensors (C6) and triceps/wrist flexors (C7), not the biceps. C is incorrect because C7-T1 supplies the triceps (C7), finger extensors (C7), and intrinsic hand muscles (T1), none of which are primary elbow flexors. D is incorrect because C8-T1 innervates the intrinsic hand muscles and finger flexors, not the biceps.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after a fall, complaining of severe hip pain. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the greater trochanter, and her x-ray shows a displaced fracture at this site. Which of the following imaging modalities would be most beneficial to assess for associated soft tissue injuries and plan her treatment?
A) CT scan
B) MRI
C) Ultrasound
D) Bone scan
questions.answer:
B)
MRI is the most beneficial imaging modality in this scenario because it provides superior soft tissue contrast, allowing evaluation of associated injuries such as gluteus medius and minimus tendon tears, which commonly accompany greater trochanter fractures in elderly patients and significantly influence surgical planning and rehabilitation.

A is incorrect because CT scan excels at bony detail and fracture characterization but provides limited soft tissue assessment compared to MRI, making it less useful for evaluating associated tendon or muscle injuries. C is incorrect because ultrasound can detect superficial tendon pathology but is operator-dependent, has limited ability to assess deep structures around the hip, and cannot evaluate intra-articular or bone marrow pathology as well as MRI. D is incorrect because bone scan is a nuclear medicine study useful for detecting occult fractures or metastatic disease but does not provide the anatomic soft tissue detail needed to plan treatment for associated tendon or muscle injuries.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old female who underwent corrective surgery for a bunion now presents with a painful great toe that is deviated medially. What is the most likely diagnosis for her current condition?
A) Hallux rigidus
B) Hallux varus
C) Morton's neuroma
D) Metatarsalgia
questions.answer:
B)
Hallux varus is a recognized complication of overcorrection during hallux valgus surgery, resulting in medial deviation of the great toe. This patient's history of recent bunion surgery and a medially deviated, painful great toe is classic for this diagnosis.

A is incorrect because hallux rigidus refers to degenerative arthritis of the first MTP joint causing stiffness and pain with limited dorsiflexion, not medial deviation of the toe. C is incorrect because Morton's neuroma involves interdigital nerve compression (typically between the 3rd and 4th metatarsals) causing burning pain and numbness in the toes, not angular deviation of the great toe. D is incorrect because metatarsalgia is a general term for pain under the metatarsal heads, typically related to overload, and does not describe angular malalignment of the hallux.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old male presents with acute pain and swelling in his left foot following a fall. An x-ray shows a fleck sign. What does this finding indicate, and what is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Avulsion fracture at the base of the second metatarsal; Lisfranc injury
B) Fracture of the navicular bone; midfoot fracture
C) Fracture of the lateral malleolus; ankle sprain
D) Fracture of the fifth metatarsal; Jones fracture
questions.answer:
A)
The fleck sign is a small avulsion fragment seen between the base of the first and second metatarsals (or between the medial cuneiform and second metatarsal base), representing an avulsion of the Lisfranc ligament. It is pathognomonic for a Lisfranc (tarsometatarsal) injury. Early recognition is critical because missed Lisfranc injuries lead to midfoot instability, post-traumatic arthritis, and significant long-term disability.

B is incorrect because a navicular fracture does not produce a fleck sign between the first and second metatarsal bases; navicular fractures present with dorsal midfoot tenderness and different imaging findings.
C is incorrect because a lateral malleolus fracture is an ankle injury and would not produce a fleck sign in the midfoot.
D is incorrect because a Jones fracture involves the proximal fifth metatarsal metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction and is unrelated to the fleck sign, which is located in the medial midfoot.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male presents with pain and swelling in his hand after falling on an outstretched hand. X-rays reveal a Bennett's fracture of the base of the first metacarpal. Which of the following complications is he at risk for if the fracture is not properly managed?
A) Ulnar nerve entrapment
B) Stenosing tenosynovitis
C) Scapholunate dissociation
D) Malunion leading to osteoarthritis
E) Flexor tendon rupture
questions.answer:
D)
A Bennett fracture is an intra-articular fracture-dislocation at the base of the first metacarpal involving the trapeziometacarpal (CMC) joint. If not anatomically reduced and stabilized, residual articular incongruity and joint subluxation lead to malunion and progressive post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the thumb CMC joint, causing chronic pain and loss of grip/pinch strength.

A is incorrect because ulnar nerve entrapment is not a recognized complication of a Bennett fracture; the ulnar nerve is anatomically remote from the thumb CMC joint. B is incorrect because stenosing tenosynovitis (trigger finger/de Quervain's) is unrelated to this fracture pattern. C is incorrect because scapholunate dissociation involves the carpal bones of the proximal row and is not a consequence of a first metacarpal base fracture. E is incorrect because flexor tendon rupture is not a typical complication of Bennett fractures; it is more associated with conditions such as distal radius malunion (e.g., Mannerfelt lesion) or rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old female sustains an injury during a soccer match, landing awkwardly after a jump. She reports immediate swelling and instability of her right knee. Upon examination, there is a positive anterior drawer test. An MRI confirms a complete tear of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). Which of the following surgical techniques is most commonly used for ACL reconstruction?
A) Tension band wiring
B) Hamstring autograft
C) Plate and screws fixation
D) Intramedullary nailing
questions.answer:
B)
Hamstring autograft is one of the most commonly used techniques for ACL reconstruction due to its favorable outcomes in terms of graft strength and reduced donor site morbidity. It allows for a minimally invasive approach and good functional results. A is incorrect because tension band wiring is used for patellar or olecranon fractures, not ACL reconstruction. C is incorrect because plate and screws fixation is used for bone fractures, not ligament reconstruction. D is incorrect because intramedullary nailing is used for long bone fractures, not ACL reconstruction.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old woman presents with persistent pain in her thumb and difficulty with gripping activities. On examination, there is a notable weakness in her ability to extend her thumb against resistance. Which of the following muscles is primarily responsible for this motion?
A) Abductor pollicis longus
B) Extensor pollicis longus
C) Flexor pollicis longus
D) Extensor pollicis brevis
questions.answer:
B)
The extensor pollicis longus (EPL) is the primary muscle responsible for extending the thumb, particularly at the interphalangeal (IP) joint, and also contributes to extension at the MCP and CMC joints. Weakness in thumb extension against resistance points to EPL dysfunction, which can occur with tendon rupture (e.g., after distal radius fracture) or posterior interosseous nerve palsy.

A is incorrect because the abductor pollicis longus (APL) primarily abducts the thumb at the CMC joint and only assists with extension; it is not the primary thumb extensor. C is incorrect because the flexor pollicis longus (FPL) flexes the thumb at the IP joint — the opposite motion of extension. D is incorrect because the extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) extends the thumb at the MCP joint but is not the primary muscle tested with resisted thumb extension, which predominantly assesses EPL function at the IP joint.

questions.question:
During a hip replacement procedure, the surgeon notes that the rectus femoris muscle originates from the anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS). Which of the following actions is primarily associated with this muscle during hip movement?
A) Hip adduction
B) Hip extension
C) Hip flexion
D) Hip abduction
questions.answer:
C)
The rectus femoris originates from the anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) and crosses both the hip and knee joints. Its primary actions are hip flexion and knee extension. During hip movement, it is one of the key hip flexors.

A is incorrect because hip adduction is performed by the adductor group (adductor longus, brevis, magnus, gracilis, and pectineus), not the rectus femoris. B is incorrect because hip extension is performed by the gluteus maximus and hamstrings; the rectus femoris is actually an antagonist to hip extension. D is incorrect because hip abduction is performed by the gluteus medius and minimus, not the rectus femoris.

questions.question:
A 15-year-old girl presents with increasing thigh pain, particularly at night, low-grade fever, and localized swelling. Laboratory studies show an elevated ESR. An MRI shows a large soft tissue mass arising from the femoral diaphysis with a permeative, moth-eaten pattern of bone destruction and an associated onion-skin periosteal reaction. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient's condition?
A) Osteosarcoma
B) Ewing's sarcoma
C) Rhabdomyosarcoma
D) Fibrosarcoma
E) Chordoma
questions.answer:
B)
Ewing's sarcoma is a small round blue cell tumor that most commonly affects children and adolescents (peak 5–15 years). It classically presents with diaphyseal bone pain (often worse at night), fever, elevated inflammatory markers, and imaging showing a permeative lytic lesion with onion-skin periosteal reaction and a large associated soft tissue mass.

A is incorrect because osteosarcoma typically arises in the metaphysis (not diaphysis), produces a sunburst periosteal reaction or Codman triangle, and usually presents with a sclerotic/mixed lesion rather than a permeative pattern with onion-skinning.
C is incorrect because rhabdomyosarcoma is a soft tissue sarcoma that does not primarily arise from bone; it originates from skeletal muscle and is more common in the head/neck and genitourinary regions in children.
D is incorrect because fibrosarcoma of bone is rare in adolescents and does not typically present with systemic symptoms (fever, elevated ESR) or the classic onion-skin periosteal reaction.
E is incorrect because chordoma arises from notochordal remnants and occurs in the sacrum or skull base, predominantly in adults aged 40–70; it would not present as a femoral diaphyseal lesion in an adolescent.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old male sustains a complex tibia and fibula fracture from a motorcycle accident. In addition to fracture stabilization, the surgical team is concerned about the neurovascular bundles in the posterior compartment. Which of the following surgical techniques would best protect these structures during external fixation?
A) Anterior placement of fixator pins
B) Lateral placement of fixator pins
C) Proximal placement of screws on the proximal segment
D) Distal placement of screws on the distal segment
questions.answer:
B)
Placing the external fixator pins laterally helps to avoid injury to the neurovascular bundles located posteriorly. This technique minimizes the risk of complications such as nerve palsy or vascular compromise, which are critical considerations in complex injuries.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man is undergoing a posterior approach lumbar spine surgery. During positioning, the surgical team is cautious to avoid damaging the lumbar nerve roots. Which of the following structures is most closely associated with the lumbar pedicles?
A) Dorsal root ganglion
B) Cauda equina
C) Spinal cord
D) Intervertebral disc
questions.answer:
A)
The dorsal root ganglion (DRG) is located in the intervertebral foramen directly inferior to the pedicle at each lumbar level. During pedicle screw placement, a medially or inferiorly misdirected screw can directly injure the DRG or exiting nerve root, making this the structure most closely associated with the lumbar pedicles.

B is incorrect because the cauda equina resides within the central spinal canal (thecal sac) and, while a severely medially breached pedicle screw could injure it, it is not the structure most closely or specifically associated with the pedicle itself. C is incorrect because the spinal cord typically terminates at the L1-L2 level (conus medullaris), so it is not present at most lumbar pedicle levels. D is incorrect because the intervertebral disc is located anterior to the vertebral body and is not in close anatomic proximity to the pedicle.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman with a history of knee arthritis reports severe lateral knee pain after a minor twist while stepping off a curb. Examination reveals tenderness along the joint line, and an MRI shows a tear of the lateral meniscus. Which of the following structures is primarily involved in stabilizing the meniscus?
A) The anterior cruciate ligament
B) The coronary ligaments
C) The medial collateral ligament
D) The popliteus tendon
questions.answer:
B)
The coronary ligaments (meniscotibial ligaments) attach the peripheral rim of each meniscus to the tibial plateau and are the primary structures responsible for stabilizing the meniscus in position. A lateral meniscus tear, especially in a degenerative knee, often involves disruption of these peripheral attachments, contributing to abnormal meniscal mobility and symptoms.

A is incorrect because the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is a primary stabilizer against anterior tibial translation and rotational instability; it does not directly anchor the meniscus to the tibia.
C is incorrect because the medial collateral ligament (MCL) has attachments to the medial meniscus via the deep layer (meniscofemoral portion), but it is not the primary stabilizer of the lateral meniscus described in this stem.
D is incorrect because the popliteus tendon passes through the posterolateral corner and has a fascicle attaching to the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus (popliteomeniscal fascicles), but its primary role is dynamic posterolateral knee stability and femoral internal rotation, not primary meniscal stabilization to the tibia.

questions.question:
A pediatric patient presents with a distal femoral fracture and is noted to have a significant amount of displacement. The surgical team is considering various fixation techniques. Which of the following methods would best ensure stability in an unstable fracture, particularly in a case of suspected slipped capital femoral epiphysis?
A) Intramedullary nailing
B) Cannulated screw fixation
C) External fixation
D) Plate and screw fixation
E) Casting alone
questions.answer:
B)
Explanation: In cases of unstable slipped capital femoral epiphysis, cannulated screw fixation is the preferred method of treatment. This technique provides adequate stabilization and allows for early mobilization while minimizing the risk of avascular necrosis.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old male presents with a painful bunion deformity and is scheduled for a surgical correction. The surgeon plans to perform a bunionectomy using a dorsolateral approach. Which anatomical structure must the surgeon be cautious to avoid during this procedure?
A) Abductor hallucis muscle
B) Deep peroneal nerve
C) Flexor hallucis longus tendon
D) Medial plantar nerve
questions.answer:
A)
The abductor hallucis muscle is located medially and is at risk during a dorsolateral approach for bunion surgery. Careful dissection is required to avoid damaging this structure, which is crucial for toe alignment and function.

questions.question:
A patient who had knee arthroplasty is discharged with a postoperative drainage system in place. The nursing staff is unsure of the protocol for managing the drainage. What is the recommended approach for monitoring and management of the drainage?
A) Remove the drain after 24 hours regardless of output
B) Monitor the output and remove the drain when output is less than 30 mL in a 24-hour period
C) Change the drain every 48 hours
D) Irrigate the drain daily to prevent blockage
questions.answer:
B)
Postoperative drains after knee arthroplasty should be monitored for output volume. The drain is typically removed when output falls below approximately 30 mL in a 24-hour period, indicating that active bleeding or fluid accumulation has subsided and the risk of hematoma or wound complications is low.

A is incorrect because removing the drain at a fixed 24-hour mark regardless of output may lead to premature removal while significant drainage persists, increasing the risk of hematoma formation.
C is incorrect because routinely changing the drain every 48 hours is not standard practice; doing so introduces unnecessary infection risk and disrupts the closed drainage system.
D is incorrect because irrigating a closed suction drain is contraindicated — it breaks the sterile closed system, increases infection risk, and serves no therapeutic purpose in routine postoperative drainage management.

questions.question:
A 66-year-old male is scheduled for hip arthroplasty due to severe osteoarthritis. He expresses concern about the longevity of the prosthesis. Which type of bearing surface has been associated with a lower incidence of wear and improved longevity in hip arthroplasty?
A) Polyethylene-on-polyethylene
B) Metal-on-metal
C) Ceramic-on-ceramic
D) Metal-on-polyethylene
questions.answer:
C)
Ceramic-on-ceramic bearing surfaces have the lowest volumetric wear rates among commonly used bearing couples in total hip arthroplasty. This results in minimal particulate debris, reduced risk of osteolysis, and improved long-term implant survivorship, making it a favorable option for patients concerned about prosthetic longevity.

A is incorrect because polyethylene-on-polyethylene is not a standard bearing combination used in hip arthroplasty; it would not provide the hardness or low-friction articulation needed for a durable hip bearing surface.

B is incorrect because metal-on-metal bearings, while initially promoted for low volumetric wear, have fallen out of favor due to adverse local tissue reactions (ALTR), pseudotumor formation, and elevated serum metal ion levels.

D is incorrect because metal-on-polyethylene (especially with conventional polyethylene) has higher wear rates compared to ceramic-on-ceramic, leading to greater particulate debris generation and a higher risk of osteolysis over time. Highly cross-linked polyethylene has improved this, but ceramic-on-ceramic still demonstrates the lowest wear rates.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old female with osteoporosis falls and is found to have a displaced acetabular fracture on imaging. Which of the following types of imaging views would best help assess the displacement of the fracture?
A) Anteroposterior (AP) view only
B) Lateral view only
C) Inlet and Outlet views
D) Judet oblique views (iliac and obturator obliques) with CT scan
questions.answer:
D)
Judet oblique views (45° iliac and obturator obliques) combined with CT scan are the gold standard for evaluating acetabular fractures. The Judet views profile the anterior and posterior columns and walls, while CT provides detailed assessment of fracture displacement, marginal impaction, intra-articular fragments, and femoral head congruency — all critical for surgical planning.

A is incorrect because an AP pelvis view alone, while useful as an initial screening tool, does not adequately characterize column involvement or subtle displacement patterns of acetabular fractures. B is incorrect because a lateral view of the pelvis provides minimal useful information for acetabular fracture assessment due to overlapping bony structures. C is incorrect because inlet and outlet views are designed to evaluate pelvic ring injuries (sacral fractures, AP compression injuries), not acetabular fractures.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman presents with hip pain and difficulty walking after a fall. Examination reveals tenderness over the ischial tuberosity. An MRI shows a fracture at this site. Which muscle, primarily responsible for external rotation of the hip, originates from this area?
A) Obturator internus
B) Quadratus femoris
C) Gluteus maximus
D) Piriformis
questions.answer:
B)
The quadratus femoris originates from the lateral border of the ischial tuberosity and inserts on the intertrochanteric crest of the femur. It is a short external rotator of the hip. A fracture of the ischial tuberosity can disrupt its origin and impair external rotation strength.

A is incorrect because the obturator internus originates from the internal (pelvic) surface of the obturator membrane and surrounding bone, not from the ischial tuberosity. Although it is an external rotator, its origin does not match the fracture site described.
C is incorrect because the gluteus maximus has a broad origin from the ilium, sacrum, and sacrotuberous ligament; while some fibers are near the ischial tuberosity, it is primarily described as originating from the posterior ilium and sacrum, and it functions mainly as a hip extensor rather than being primarily an external rotator.
D is incorrect because the piriformis originates from the anterior surface of the sacrum, not the ischial tuberosity.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis presents for evaluation of her right hip. She experiences significant pain and stiffness, limiting her daily activities. Upon examination, her hip is found to be in a position of flexion, adduction, and internal rotation. Which of the following findings is most likely to be present in her x-rays?
A) Joint effusion
B) Osteophyte formation
C) Subchondral sclerosis
D) Decreased joint space
questions.answer:
D)
In rheumatoid arthritis, the hallmark plain-film finding is symmetric/uniform decreased joint space (joint-space narrowing) resulting from inflammatory destruction of articular cartilage. In the hip, this typically manifests as axial (medial) migration of the femoral head. The clinical picture of pain, stiffness, and a fixed flexion-adduction-internal rotation posture is consistent with advanced RA-related hip destruction.

A is incorrect because joint effusion is a clinical or ultrasound/MRI finding and is not reliably identified on plain films of the hip.
B is incorrect because osteophyte formation is a hallmark of osteoarthritis (a reparative process), not rheumatoid arthritis, which is characterized by erosive, inflammatory destruction without prominent osteophyte production.
C is incorrect because subchondral sclerosis is a feature of osteoarthritis; in rheumatoid arthritis, periarticular osteopenia and erosions are more characteristic than sclerosis.

questions.question:
A 10-year-old boy falls from his bike and presents with swelling and pain in both forearms. An x-ray shows fractures of the radius and ulna in both forearms, but they appear stable. What is the best initial management for this type of fracture in a pediatric patient?
A) Surgical intervention
B) Closed reduction and casting
C) Immediate splinting only
D) Observation and follow-up
questions.answer:
B)
Closed reduction and casting is the standard initial management for pediatric both-bone forearm fractures. Even when fractures appear stable, closed reduction ensures acceptable alignment, and a well-molded long-arm cast provides immobilization for healing. This is the most widely accepted board-level answer for this clinical scenario.

A is incorrect because surgical intervention (e.g., intramedullary nailing or plate fixation) is reserved for unstable fractures, open fractures, fractures with failed closed reduction, or those with unacceptable alignment after reduction.
C is incorrect because immediate splinting alone does not provide definitive treatment; splinting may be used as a temporizing measure, but both-bone forearm fractures require reduction and circumferential casting for adequate immobilization.
D is incorrect because observation and follow-up without immobilization is insufficient for both-bone forearm fractures, which require active management to maintain alignment and promote healing.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old female gymnast presents with wrist pain after landing awkwardly during a routine. She has tenderness over the lunate fossa and imaging shows a depressed fracture in that area. Which type of fracture does this represent?
A) Colles' fracture
B) Die-punch fracture
C) Barton's fracture
D) Chauffeur's fracture
questions.answer:
B)
A die-punch fracture refers to a depressed fracture of the lunate fossa of the distal radius, typically caused by axial loading such as landing on an outstretched hand. The lunate impacts the lunate fossa, creating a depressed articular fragment that can compromise wrist joint congruity and stability.

A is incorrect because a Colles' fracture is an extra-articular or simple intra-articular fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement/angulation, not a specific depressed lunate fossa fragment. C is incorrect because a Barton's fracture is a shear-type fracture-subluxation of the distal radius involving the dorsal or volar rim, not a depressed lunate fossa injury. D is incorrect because a Chauffeur's (radial styloid) fracture involves the radial styloid process, not the lunate fossa.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male with a history of diabetes presents with sudden onset of numbness and tingling in the first three fingers of his right hand. On physical examination, there is a positive Tinel's sign at the wrist. An MRI shows swelling of the median nerve at the carpal tunnel. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
A) Conservative management with splinting and corticosteroids
B) Immediate surgical release of the carpal tunnel
C) Referral to neurology for further evaluation
D) Obtain an electromyography and nerve conduction study
E) Begin physical therapy for hand strengthening
questions.answer:
A)
Conservative management with splinting (especially nocturnal wrist splinting) and corticosteroid injection is the accepted first-line treatment for carpal tunnel syndrome when there is no evidence of severe denervation (e.g., thenar atrophy, constant numbness, or fibrillations on EMG). This patient has sensory symptoms without motor deficit, making conservative care appropriate initially.

B is incorrect because immediate surgical release is reserved for patients with severe or progressive motor deficits (e.g., thenar atrophy), failed conservative management, or electrodiagnostic evidence of significant axonal loss. This patient has not yet undergone a trial of conservative treatment.

C is incorrect because the clinical and MRI findings are sufficient to diagnose carpal tunnel syndrome; a neurology referral is not necessary before initiating standard first-line treatment.

D is incorrect because while EMG/NCS can confirm the diagnosis and grade severity, the clinical picture (Tinel's sign, classic distribution of symptoms, MRI showing median nerve swelling) is adequate to begin conservative management. EMG/NCS would be more appropriate if the diagnosis were uncertain or if surgical planning were needed after failed conservative care.

E is incorrect because physical therapy for hand strengthening does not address the underlying nerve compression at the carpal tunnel and is not a recognized first-line treatment for carpal tunnel syndrome. Splinting and corticosteroid injection have far stronger evidence.

questions.question:
During an evaluation for chronic ankle instability, a 28-year-old male athlete is found to have a critical angle of Gissane of 150 degrees on imaging. What does this finding suggest about his ankle biomechanics?
A) Increased risk of lateral ankle sprains
B) High likelihood of subtalar joint osteoarthritis
C) Normal ankle biomechanics
D) Increased risk of Achilles tendon rupture
questions.answer:
A)
Explanation: A critical angle of Gissane greater than 145 degrees is indicative of a potential structural abnormality that may predispose to an increased risk of lateral ankle sprains. This angle reflects the relationship between the calcaneal and talar surfaces and helps assess the alignment and load distribution through the subtalar joint.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old male presents with pain at the base of his great toe. On examination, extension of the great toe elicits significant pain. An X-ray shows osteophyte formation at the first metatarsophalangeal joint. What is the most appropriate surgical procedure for this condition?
A) Total joint arthroplasty
B) Cheilectomy
C) Arthrodesis
D) Akin osteotomy
questions.answer:
B)
Cheilectomy is the most appropriate initial surgical procedure for hallux rigidus presenting with dorsal osteophyte formation at the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint. It involves excision of dorsal osteophytes and up to 25-30% of the dorsal metatarsal head, relieving impingement and improving dorsiflexion. It is the standard first-line surgical treatment when conservative measures fail.

A is incorrect because total joint arthroplasty of the first MTP joint has unpredictable long-term results, higher complication rates, and is not considered first-line surgical treatment for hallux rigidus.
C is incorrect because arthrodesis (fusion) of the first MTP joint is reserved for advanced (grade 3-4) hallux rigidus with significant joint space loss or failed cheilectomy; it is not the initial surgical procedure of choice when osteophytes are the primary finding.
D is incorrect because an Akin osteotomy is a medial closing-wedge osteotomy of the proximal phalanx of the great toe used as an adjunct in hallux valgus correction, not for hallux rigidus.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male construction worker presents with severe pain in his shoulder after a fall from a height, landing on his shoulder. X-rays reveal a four-part proximal humeral fracture. Which of the following minimally invasive surgical approaches would be recommended for the management of this type of fracture? 
A) Anterolateral approach 
B) Posterior approach 
C) Lateral approach 
D) Anterior approach to the humerus
questions.answer:
C)
The lateral approach to the proximal humerus is effective for managing four-part fractures. This technique allows for minimal soft tissue disruption and access to the fracture site for stabilization while preserving blood supply to the humeral head.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old male presents with persistent back pain and sciatica after a motor vehicle accident. He has difficulty walking and has lost strength in his right leg. An MRI reveals an extruded disc at the L5-S1 level. Which of the following physical examination findings would you expect to be present in this patient?
A) Patellar reflex hyperactivity
B) Decreased Achilles reflex
C) Increased sensation in the lateral foot
D) Positive Babinski sign
questions.answer:
B)
An extruded disc at L5-S1 most commonly compresses the S1 nerve root. The S1 nerve root mediates the Achilles (ankle jerk) reflex, so compression leads to a decreased or absent Achilles reflex. This is a classic board-tested finding for S1 radiculopathy.

A is incorrect because the patellar reflex tests the L3-L4 nerve roots, not S1. An L5-S1 disc herniation would not cause patellar reflex hyperactivity.
C is incorrect because S1 radiculopathy causes decreased (not increased) sensation along the lateral foot and sole, which is the S1 dermatome.
D is incorrect because a positive Babinski sign indicates an upper motor neuron lesion (e.g., spinal cord compression). An L5-S1 disc herniation causes a lower motor neuron (nerve root) lesion, so a Babinski sign would not be expected.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man undergoes an internal fixation for a humeral fracture but returns six months later with persistent pain and nonunion. Upon examination, the fracture site shows increased motion. What is the primary cause contributing to the atrophic nonunion in this case?
A) Insufficient blood supply
B) Inadequate immobilization
C) Infection at the fracture site
D) Malalignment of the fracture ends
questions.answer:
A)
Atrophic nonunion results from insufficient blood supply to the fracture site, leading to inadequate biologic response and failure of callus formation. This distinguishes it from hypertrophic nonunion, which is caused by mechanical instability but retains adequate vascularity.

B is incorrect because inadequate immobilization (excessive motion) typically produces a hypertrophic nonunion with exuberant callus formation, not an atrophic pattern. C is incorrect because infection at the fracture site leads to septic nonunion, a distinct entity that requires identification and treatment of the causative organism in addition to stabilization. D is incorrect because malalignment of the fracture ends may contribute to malunion or delayed union but is not the primary mechanism underlying atrophic nonunion, which is fundamentally a vascular/biologic problem.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male is brought to the clinic after experiencing sudden-onset severe leg pain following an intense workout. He reports numbness and tingling in his foot, and upon examination, there is marked swelling and tenderness in the anterior compartment of the leg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Achilles tendon rupture
B) Anterior compartment syndrome
C) Lateral ankle sprain
D) Fibular fracture
questions.answer:
B)
Anterior compartment syndrome occurs when increased pressure within the anterior compartment of the leg compromises perfusion and nerve function. The combination of pain, tense swelling localized to the anterior compartment, and neurological symptoms (numbness/tingling from deep peroneal nerve involvement) after intense exercise is classic for acute exertional compartment syndrome.

A is incorrect because Achilles tendon rupture involves the posterior compartment, presents with a palpable gap at the tendon, a positive Thompson test, and weakness of plantarflexion — not anterior compartment swelling or numbness. C is incorrect because a lateral ankle sprain involves injury to the lateral ligament complex (typically the ATFL), presenting with lateral ankle swelling and pain, not anterior compartment findings or neurological symptoms. D is incorrect because a fibular fracture would present with point tenderness over the fibula and would not typically cause diffuse anterior compartment swelling with neurological compromise.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old athlete comes to the clinic with pain and stiffness at the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Examination reveals limited dorsiflexion of the great toe and palpable bony prominence. What is the most appropriate next step in managing this condition?
A) Corticosteroid injection
B) Surgical fusion
C) Joint mobilization exercises
D) Orthotic devices
questions.answer:
D)
The clinical presentation — pain, stiffness, limited dorsiflexion of the great toe, and a palpable dorsal bony prominence at the first MTP joint — is consistent with hallux rigidus. In a young athlete, initial management centers on conservative measures, and orthotic devices (e.g., a rigid-soled shoe or Morton's extension) limit MTP dorsiflexion, reduce joint stress, and relieve pain. This is the most appropriate first-line intervention.
