B is incorrect because the flexor carpi ulnaris lies proximal to Guyon's canal and, while the ulnar nerve passes deep to it in the forearm, it is not the structure primarily responsible for the deep motor branch's location at the wrist.
C is incorrect because the palmaris longus is a midline structure associated with the median nerve and the flexor retinaculum; it has no anatomical relationship to the deep motor branch of the ulnar nerve.
D is incorrect because the abductor digiti minimi is a muscle innervated by the ulnar nerve and forms part of the floor/roof of Guyon's canal, but the canal itself (Guyon's canal) is the named structure primarily responsible for the deep motor branch's anatomical course at the wrist.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male soccer player presents to the emergency department with a swollen knee after twisting his leg during a match. He reports pain localized to the lateral aspect of the knee. Physical examination reveals a positive McMurray's test and tenderness along the joint line. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A) ACL tear
B) Lateral meniscus tear
C) Medial collateral ligament sprain
D) Patellar dislocation
questions.answer:
B)
The combination of a twisting mechanism in a young athlete, pain localized to the lateral joint line, joint-line tenderness, and a positive McMurray's test is classic for a lateral meniscus tear. McMurray's test specifically evaluates for meniscal pathology by reproducing a painful click or catch with combined flexion-extension and rotational stress.

A is incorrect because an ACL tear typically presents with an audible pop, rapid hemarthrosis, a positive Lachman test, and anterior drawer sign rather than isolated lateral joint-line tenderness and a positive McMurray's test. C is incorrect because a medial collateral ligament sprain causes tenderness along the medial joint line and medial knee, with pain on valgus stress testing, not lateral-sided symptoms. D is incorrect because patellar dislocation presents with anterior knee pain, apprehension with lateral patellar translation, possible visible deformity, and a positive patellar apprehension test, not lateral joint-line tenderness or a positive McMurray's test.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old athlete presents with lateral knee pain after a jumping injury. The pain worsens with activity, and x-rays show a subtle line along the lateral tibial plateau suggestive of a stress fracture. Which of the following is the most critical factor in the management of this condition?
A) Immediate surgical fixation
B) Activity modification and rest
C) Corticosteroid injection
D) Physical therapy to strengthen surrounding muscles
questions.answer:
B)
The cornerstone of stress fracture management is activity modification and relative rest to reduce repetitive loading and allow bone healing. In a lateral tibial plateau stress fracture without displacement, protected weight-bearing and avoidance of the inciting activity are the most critical initial steps.

A is incorrect because immediate surgical fixation is reserved for displaced fractures, fractures at high risk of nonunion (e.g., tension-side femoral neck), or those failing prolonged conservative management; an undisplaced tibial plateau stress fracture does not meet these criteria. C is incorrect because corticosteroid injections impair bone healing and are contraindicated in the setting of a stress fracture. D is incorrect because while physical therapy plays a supportive role in rehabilitation, initiating strengthening exercises without first modifying the offending activity and allowing adequate rest would perpetuate the mechanical overload and delay healing.

questions.question:
A 36-year-old female is evaluated for chronic knee pain and instability following an ACL reconstruction. Upon examination, her knee shows an excessive valgus alignment. Which of the following is the most likely underlying issue contributing to her symptoms?
A) Malunion of the ACL graft
B) Patellofemoral pain syndrome
C) Excessive lateral release
D) Abnormal lower extremity alignment
questions.answer:
D)
Abnormal lower extremity alignment is the most likely underlying issue. Excessive valgus alignment alters the mechanical axis of the lower extremity, placing abnormal stress on the lateral compartment and the ACL graft, contributing to chronic pain and recurrent instability even after reconstruction. Correcting alignment (e.g., with osteotomy) is often necessary before or concurrent with revision surgery.

A is incorrect because "malunion of the ACL graft" is not a recognized entity — ACL grafts are soft-tissue structures that can fail by stretching, re-rupture, or tunnel malposition, but they do not undergo malunion.
B is incorrect because patellofemoral pain syndrome causes anterior knee pain, typically with stair climbing and prolonged sitting, and does not explain excessive valgus alignment or instability.
C is incorrect because excessive lateral release can lead to medial patellar subluxation or persistent anterior knee pain, but it does not cause a valgus malalignment of the entire lower extremity.

questions.question:
During a physical examination of a patient with knee pain, you notice that the patellar retinaculum is intact, and the patient is able to actively extend their knee. What does this suggest about the integrity of the extensor mechanism?
A) It is compromised
B) It is intact
C) There is a possibility of a patellar fracture
D) There is a complete ACL tear
questions.answer:
B)
An intact patellar retinaculum combined with the ability to actively extend the knee confirms that the extensor mechanism is functioning properly. The extensor mechanism (quadriceps tendon, patella, patellar tendon, and retinaculum) must be in continuity for active knee extension to occur; disruption of any critical component would impair or abolish active extension.

A is incorrect because a compromised extensor mechanism would manifest as an inability to perform a straight-leg raise or actively extend the knee, which is not the case here.
C is incorrect because while a patellar fracture is possible even with some preserved extension (if the retinaculum is intact), the stem specifically states the retinaculum is intact and active extension is maintained, making a displaced patellar fracture with extensor mechanism disruption unlikely; furthermore, the question asks about extensor mechanism integrity, not fracture diagnosis.
D is incorrect because the ACL is not part of the extensor mechanism; an ACL tear would not affect the ability to actively extend the knee and is assessed with different examination maneuvers (e.g., Lachman test, anterior drawer).

questions.question:
A 55-year-old woman is seen after suffering a fall, resulting in a fracture of the ulnar shaft. She is diagnosed with a Monteggia fracture, which involves a fracture of the ulnar shaft along with an associated injury. According to the Bado classification, which of the following best describes the type of injury that commonly accompanies this fracture?
A) Anterior dislocation of the radial head
B) Radial head fracture
C) Distal biceps tendon rupture
D) Humeral head fracture
questions.answer:
A)
A Monteggia fracture is defined as a fracture of the ulnar shaft with an associated dislocation of the radial head. The Bado classification categorizes these injuries into four types based on the direction of radial head dislocation and the pattern of the ulnar fracture. The most common type (Bado Type I) involves anterior dislocation of the radial head with an apex-anterior ulnar shaft fracture.

B is incorrect because a Monteggia fracture involves dislocation of the radial head, not a fracture of the radial head. A radial head fracture with distal radioulnar joint disruption describes an Essex-Lopresti injury. C is incorrect because distal biceps tendon rupture is a soft-tissue injury unrelated to the Monteggia fracture pattern. D is incorrect because a humeral head fracture is a proximal humerus injury and is not part of the Monteggia fracture complex.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old man presents with persistent pain and limited range of motion in his shoulder after a hemiarthroplasty performed for a humeral head fracture. An MRI shows significant erosion of the glenoid. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
A) Physical therapy
B) Revision to total shoulder arthroplasty
C) Corticosteroid injections
D) Humeral head replacement only
questions.answer:
B)
Significant glenoid erosion following hemiarthroplasty causes painful articulation of the prosthetic humeral head against eroded bone (so-called "glenoid arthritis"). Revision to a total shoulder arthroplasty — adding a glenoid component — addresses the source of pain and restores a congruent articulation, improving both pain and function.

A is incorrect because physical therapy cannot correct the structural problem of glenoid erosion; it will not relieve pain caused by metal-on-eroded-bone articulation.

C is incorrect because corticosteroid injections provide only temporary symptomatic relief and do not address the progressive mechanical problem of glenoid erosion.

D is incorrect because the existing humeral component is a hemiarthroplasty (humeral head replacement); simply replacing the humeral head again without addressing the eroded glenoid would not resolve the underlying pathology.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old female presents with neck pain and increasing difficulty with fine motor tasks. MRI reveals significant compression at the C3-C4 level. During a posterior approach to decompress the spinal cord, which anatomical structure must the surgeon be cautious of to avoid excessive bleeding?
A) Ligamentum flavum
B) Anterior longitudinal ligament
C) Intervertebral disc
D) Thoracic duct
questions.answer:
A)
During a posterior cervical laminectomy, the ligamentum flavum must be carefully managed because it lies immediately dorsal to the epidural space. Incising or removing the ligamentum flavum exposes the epidural venous plexus, which can be a significant source of bleeding, particularly in elderly patients with degenerative hypertrophy of this ligament. Careful dissection of the ligamentum flavum is essential to avoid inadvertent dural tears and epidural hemorrhage.

B is incorrect because the anterior longitudinal ligament is located on the anterior aspect of the vertebral bodies and is not encountered during a posterior approach.
C is incorrect because the intervertebral disc is an anterior structure accessed via an anterior cervical approach, not a posterior decompression.
D is incorrect because the thoracic duct is located in the lower left neck/superior mediastinum and is not relevant to a posterior cervical approach at C3-C4.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman comes to the clinic with complaints of pain and weakness in her right wrist after repetitive motion at work. Physical exam reveals numbness and weakness of thumb opposition. An MRI shows a compression of the median nerve in the carpal tunnel. Which muscle's function is most affected by this condition?
A) Flexor digitorum profundus
B) Abductor pollicis brevis
C) Flexor carpi radialis
D) Extensor pollicis longus
E) Dorsal interossei
questions.answer:
B)
The abductor pollicis brevis (APB) is innervated by the recurrent (motor) branch of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel. It is the key muscle tested clinically in carpal tunnel syndrome and is critical for thumb palmar abduction and assists in opposition. Weakness of thumb opposition in CTS is primarily attributed to denervation of the APB (and opponens pollicis), and APB wasting is a classic late finding.

A is incorrect because the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) to the index and long fingers is innervated by the anterior interosseous nerve (a branch of the median nerve) in the forearm, proximal to the carpal tunnel; it is not affected by carpal tunnel compression.
C is incorrect because the flexor carpi radialis is innervated by the median nerve in the forearm, proximal to the carpal tunnel, and is unaffected by compression at the wrist.
D is incorrect because the extensor pollicis longus is innervated by the posterior interosseous nerve (a branch of the radial nerve) and is not related to median nerve pathology.
E is incorrect because the dorsal interossei are innervated by the ulnar nerve (deep branch) and are not affected by median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman is diagnosed with an acetabular fracture after a low-energy fall. Using the Letournel-Judet classification, which of the following is considered an elementary (simple) fracture pattern?
A) Posterior column with posterior wall fracture
B) Anterior column fracture
C) T-type fracture
D) Both-column fracture
questions.answer:
B)
The Letournel-Judet classification divides acetabular fractures into 5 elementary (simple) patterns and 5 associated (complex) patterns. The anterior column fracture is one of the five elementary patterns, along with posterior wall, posterior column, anterior wall, and transverse fractures. Identifying the fracture pattern is critical for surgical planning and approach selection.

A is incorrect because a posterior column with posterior wall fracture is an associated (complex) pattern in the Letournel-Judet classification, not an elementary one.

C is incorrect because a T-type fracture is an associated pattern consisting of a transverse fracture with an inferior vertical split, making it a complex pattern.

D is incorrect because a both-column fracture is an associated pattern in which both the anterior and posterior columns are fractured and no part of the articular surface remains attached to the intact ilium (the 'spur sign').

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male construction worker presents with severe left arm pain after lifting a heavy object. X-rays reveal a humeral shaft fracture that is minimally displaced. What is the most appropriate initial management for this type of fracture?
A) Immediate surgical intervention
B) Closed reduction and splinting
C) Application of a hanging arm cast
D) Non-operative management with a sling
E) Referral for orthopedic consultation
questions.answer:
D)
A minimally displaced humeral shaft fracture is best managed initially with nonoperative treatment. A sling (or coaptation splint transitioning to a functional brace) allows gravity-assisted alignment and is the standard initial approach when there is no significant displacement, angulation, or neurovascular compromise. Most humeral shaft fractures heal well with conservative management.

A is incorrect because immediate surgical intervention is reserved for open fractures, fractures with vascular injury, pathologic fractures, polytrauma, or fractures that fail nonoperative management — none of which are described here.
B is incorrect because closed reduction is unnecessary when the fracture is already minimally displaced; manipulation adds no benefit and risks further soft-tissue injury.
C is incorrect because a hanging arm cast, while a nonoperative option, relies on the weight of the cast for traction and can cause fracture-site distraction and malunion in a minimally displaced fracture; it is better suited for shortened or significantly displaced fractures.
E is incorrect because while orthopedic follow-up is appropriate, simple referral without initiating treatment (immobilization with a sling) is not the best initial management step.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male presents with chronic wrist pain and limited range of motion after many years of repetitive wrist activities. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the radial styloid and pain with resisted wrist extension. Which muscle is most likely implicated in this condition?
A) Extensor carpi ulnaris
B) Extensor carpi radialis brevis
C) Flexor carpi radialis
D) Flexor digitorum superficialis
questions.answer:
B)
The extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) is the muscle most commonly implicated when there is pain with resisted wrist extension in the setting of chronic repetitive wrist use. ECRB is the primary pathologic muscle in lateral epicondylitis and can also be involved in intersection syndrome, which presents with radial-sided dorsal wrist/forearm pain. Tenderness near the radial styloid with pain on resisted wrist extension in a patient with repetitive activity is consistent with ECRB overuse pathology.

A is incorrect because the extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU) is located on the ulnar side of the wrist; its pathology would cause ulnar-sided wrist pain, not radial styloid tenderness. C is incorrect because the flexor carpi radialis (FCR) is a wrist flexor on the volar side; it would not cause pain with resisted wrist extension. D is incorrect because the flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) is a finger flexor and would not be implicated in pain with resisted wrist extension.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old man sustains a laceration to his palm while working with a sharp tool. After initial assessment, it is noted that he has difficulty abducting his fifth finger. Upon examination of the neurovascular status, you suspect an injury to the ulnar nerve. Which anatomical structure in the wrist is most likely involved in this nerve injury?
A) Hook of the hamate
B) Pisiform
C) Flexor retinaculum
D) Scaphoid tubercle
questions.answer:
A)
The hook of the hamate forms the lateral (radial) wall of Guyon's canal, through which the ulnar nerve passes at the wrist. A laceration in this area can injure the deep motor branch of the ulnar nerve, leading to weakness of the hypothenar muscles including the abductor digiti minimi. This is the most likely anatomical structure involved in ulnar nerve injury from a palmar laceration.

B is incorrect because the pisiform forms the medial (ulnar) wall of Guyon's canal and, while related to the canal, is not the structure most commonly associated with ulnar nerve injury from a palmar laceration in this location.

C is incorrect because the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament) forms the roof of the carpal tunnel and is primarily associated with median nerve compression, not ulnar nerve injury.

D is incorrect because the scaphoid tubercle is located on the radial side of the wrist and is a landmark for the carpal tunnel, not Guyon's canal; it has no direct anatomical relationship to the ulnar nerve.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man presents with chronic back pain and is noted to have a kyphotic deformity. An MRI shows degenerative changes in the thoracic spine. What is the typical normal value for thoracic kyphosis in an adult that would help in assessing the severity of his condition?
A) 10-20 degrees
B) 20-40 degrees
C) 30-50 degrees
D) 40-60 degrees
questions.answer:
B)
The normal thoracic kyphosis in adults typically ranges from 20 to 40 degrees (T2–T12, measured by the Cobb method). Values exceeding this range suggest pathological hyperkyphosis, which can contribute to back pain, sagittal imbalance, and functional limitations.

A is incorrect because 10–20 degrees is below the accepted normal range and would represent a hypokyphotic (flattened) thoracic spine, not the normal value.
C is incorrect because 30–50 degrees extends above the upper limit of normal; while the lower end overlaps, the upper end (50 degrees) is considered pathological hyperkyphosis.
D is incorrect because 40–60 degrees exceeds the normal range and would represent moderate to severe hyperkyphosis requiring further evaluation.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old competitive gymnast presents with lower back pain that has worsened over the past few months. Physical examination reveals a full range of motion, but lumbar extension exacerbates her pain. Oblique lumbar x-rays show a 'scottie dog' sign with a defect at the pars interarticularis (collar on the scottie dog). She is neurologically intact with no evidence of listhesis. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) MRI of the lumbar spine
B) Physical therapy
C) Surgical intervention
D) Bracing
questions.answer:
B)
Spondylolysis (pars interarticularis defect) in a young athlete is most commonly managed conservatively. In a patient with chronic symptoms, no neurological deficits, and no spondylolisthesis, the mainstay of treatment is physical therapy emphasizing core stabilization, hamstring flexibility, and activity modification. This approach is successful in the majority of cases.

A is incorrect because MRI is useful when the diagnosis is uncertain or to evaluate for an acute stress reaction versus a chronic defect, but the diagnosis is already established here with the classic oblique x-ray finding, and the clinical scenario does not suggest a need for further imaging before initiating conservative care.
C is incorrect because surgical intervention (e.g., direct pars repair or fusion) is reserved for patients who fail prolonged conservative management (typically 6+ months) or who have significant spondylolisthesis with instability or neurological compromise.
D is incorrect because bracing (e.g., a thoracolumbosacral orthosis) is sometimes used for acute pars stress reactions to promote healing, but in a chronic established pars defect with months of symptoms, bracing alone is less effective than a structured physical therapy program as the primary intervention.

questions.question:
A 26-year-old athlete undergoes hip arthroscopy for a labral tear and experiences temporary numbness in the thigh postoperatively. This is likely due to traction neurapraxia. Which of the following factors most contributes to the risk of this complication?
A) Duration of traction applied
B) Age of the patient
C) Type of anesthesia used
D) Body mass index
questions.answer:
A)
Traction neurapraxia during hip arthroscopy is most closely related to the duration and magnitude of traction applied. Prolonged traction (generally >2 hours) increases the risk of compressive or stretch injury to the pudendal, sciatic, or lateral femoral cutaneous nerves, causing transient sensory changes. Limiting traction time and force is the most important modifiable factor.

B is incorrect because, while younger patients may tolerate traction better, patient age is not the primary modifiable risk factor for traction neurapraxia; duration and force of traction are far more significant.
C is incorrect because the type of anesthesia (general vs. regional) does not directly contribute to the mechanical nerve stretch/compression caused by traction, though regional anesthesia may mask early warning signs.
D is incorrect because body mass index, while it may influence the amount of traction force needed, is not the most significant or most commonly cited risk factor; traction duration remains the dominant contributor.

questions.question:
A patient undergoes an anterior approach for a shoulder procedure. The surgical team notes that the cephalic vein is located anterior to the humeral shaft. Which structure should be carefully identified to avoid complications during this approach?
A) Axillary nerve
B) Long head of biceps tendon
C) Subscapularis muscle
D) Coracoid process
questions.answer:
A)
During the deltopectoral (anterior) approach to the shoulder, the axillary nerve is the most critical structure to identify and protect. It courses along the inferior border of the subscapularis and passes through the quadrilateral space, placing it at risk during dissection. Injury to the axillary nerve results in loss of deltoid function and lateral shoulder sensation, causing significant functional impairment.

B is incorrect because the long head of the biceps tendon, while encountered during the approach, is an intra-articular landmark rather than a structure whose inadvertent injury causes the most significant complication. C is incorrect because the subscapularis muscle is a structure that is intentionally managed (released or split) during the approach rather than one that must be carefully avoided. D is incorrect because the coracoid process is a bony landmark used for orientation during the approach and is not a structure at risk for iatrogenic injury.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman presents with persistent lateral ankle pain following an inversion injury. An MRI shows a tear of the calcaneofibular ligament. What is the optimal surgical approach to repair this ligament if surgical intervention is warranted?
A) Anterior approach to the ankle
B) Lateral approach to the lateral malleolus
C) Posterior approach to the Achilles tendon
D) Medial approach to the deltoid ligament
questions.answer:
B)
The lateral approach to the lateral malleolus is optimal for accessing and repairing the calcaneofibular ligament (CFL). The CFL runs from the tip of the fibula to the lateral calcaneus, and a direct lateral approach provides excellent visualization for repair or reconstruction while protecting the peroneal tendons that lie deep to the ligament.

A is incorrect because the anterior approach to the ankle exposes the anterior capsule and the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) but does not provide adequate access to the CFL, which lies more posteroinferiorly. C is incorrect because the posterior approach to the Achilles tendon is used for Achilles pathology or posterior ankle structures (e.g., FHL, posterior malleolus) and does not expose the CFL. D is incorrect because the medial approach to the deltoid ligament addresses medial-sided ankle structures and is on the opposite side of the ankle from the CFL.

questions.question:
A 10-year-old girl is brought to the clinic with wrist pain and noticeable prominence on the ulnar side of her wrist. An examination reveals localized tenderness and limited range of motion. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Distal radius fracture
B) Madelung's deformity
C) Ulnar wrist ligament injury
D) Carpal tunnel syndrome
questions.answer:
B)
Madelung's deformity is characterized by a distinctive ulnar prominence at the wrist and is often associated with wrist pain in children. The clinical presentation aligns with this condition rather than the other options. A is incorrect because a distal radius fracture would typically present with more generalized wrist swelling and pain rather than isolated ulnar prominence. C is incorrect because an ulnar wrist ligament injury would not typically cause a noticeable bony prominence. D is incorrect because carpal tunnel syndrome presents with neurological symptoms rather than bony prominence or localized tenderness.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman complains of pain and swelling in her distal tibia after a fall during a hiking trip. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the area, and x-rays show a non-displaced fracture of the tibial shaft. Which of the following is the primary nerve innervating the muscles that control dorsiflexion of the ankle and extension of the toes?
A) Tibial nerve
B) Common peroneal nerve
C) Femoral nerve
D) Saphenous nerve
questions.answer:
B)
The common peroneal (fibular) nerve divides into the deep peroneal nerve and the superficial peroneal nerve. The deep peroneal nerve innervates the anterior compartment muscles—tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus—which are responsible for ankle dorsiflexion and toe extension. Because the deep peroneal nerve is a terminal branch of the common peroneal nerve, injury to the common peroneal nerve (e.g., at the fibular neck) results in foot drop.

A is incorrect because the tibial nerve innervates the posterior compartment muscles (gastrocnemius, soleus, tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus), which control plantarflexion and toe flexion, not dorsiflexion. C is incorrect because the femoral nerve innervates the anterior thigh muscles (quadriceps) and is responsible for knee extension, not ankle dorsiflexion. D is incorrect because the saphenous nerve is a purely sensory branch of the femoral nerve supplying the medial leg and foot; it does not innervate any muscles.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman is undergoing rehabilitation for a knee injury. The physical therapist decides to implement isometric exercises to improve muscle strength without joint movement. Which of the following describes the primary characteristic of isometric contractions?
A) Muscle length changes while tension remains constant
B) Muscle tension increases while length remains constant
C) Muscle length changes with a constant load
D) Muscle fibers undergo eccentric contraction
E) Muscle fibers experience maximal shortening
questions.answer:
B)
Isometric contractions occur when muscle tension increases while the muscle length remains constant. This type of contraction is effective for maintaining or improving muscle strength without stressing the joint, making it ideal for early rehabilitation after knee injury.

A is incorrect because a contraction in which muscle length changes while tension remains constant describes an isotonic contraction, not isometric. C is incorrect because a contraction with changing muscle length under a constant load also describes isotonic (concentric or eccentric) exercise, not isometric. D is incorrect because eccentric contraction involves muscle lengthening under load (e.g., lowering a weight), which is not isometric. E is incorrect because maximal shortening of muscle fibers describes a concentric contraction at its extreme, not an isometric contraction where no length change occurs.

questions.question:
A 10-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a mid-shaft femoral fracture sustained while playing soccer. After discussing treatment options, his parents are concerned about the implications of surgery versus non-operative management. Given the child's age and activity level, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in treatment?
A) Spica casting
B) Flexible nails
C) Intramedullary nailing
D) Observation with weight bearing as tolerated
questions.answer:
B)
Flexible intramedullary nails (titanium elastic nails, TENs) are the preferred treatment for mid-shaft femoral fractures in children approximately 5–11 years of age. They provide adequate stability, allow early mobilization, and avoid the morbidity of prolonged immobilization or the risks of rigid nailing in a skeletally immature patient.

A is incorrect because spica casting is generally reserved for younger children (typically under 5–6 years); in a 10-year-old, it is poorly tolerated, difficult to maintain, and delays mobilization. C is incorrect because rigid intramedullary nailing (antegrade through the piriformis fossa or trochanteric entry) risks avascular necrosis of the femoral head and growth disturbance in skeletally immature patients and is generally reserved for adolescents nearing skeletal maturity. D is incorrect because a mid-shaft femoral fracture is an unstable injury that requires definitive stabilization; observation with weight bearing alone would not provide adequate fracture alignment or healing.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a motorcycle accident resulting in multiple fractures including a comminuted humeral shaft fracture. He is complaining of severe arm pain and there is notable gross motion at the fracture site. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Immediate surgical fixation
B) Apply a sling and refer for outpatient follow-up
C) Perform closed reduction and splint
D) Initiate physical therapy
E) Obtain a CT scan for better visualization
questions.answer:
C)
For a comminuted humeral shaft fracture presenting with gross motion, the most appropriate next step in the emergency department is closed reduction and application of a coaptation (sugar-tong) splint. The vast majority of humeral shaft fractures are successfully managed nonoperatively; initial splinting provides pain relief, provisional stability, and allows time for definitive planning. Surgical fixation may ultimately be indicated (e.g., polytrauma, vascular injury, open fracture), but the immediate ED step is reduction and splinting.

A is incorrect because immediate surgical fixation is not the standard first step; surgery is reserved for specific indications (open fracture, vascular injury, floating elbow, failed nonoperative management) and gross motion alone in a closed fracture does not mandate emergent operative intervention.
B is incorrect because a simple sling without reduction or splinting provides inadequate immobilization for a comminuted fracture with gross instability, and outpatient referral alone is insufficient acute management.
D is incorrect because initiating physical therapy is premature and inappropriate in the acute setting of an unstable fracture; therapy begins after fracture stabilization and early healing.
E is incorrect because a CT scan is not the most appropriate next step; the diagnosis is established clinically and with plain radiographs, and obtaining advanced imaging delays necessary stabilization.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man reports persistent pain and limited range of motion in his right elbow after a workplace injury. During examination, he can flex his elbow to only 90 degrees and extends to 30 degrees. What is the minimum functional range of motion for elbow flexion that would indicate a need for intervention?
A) 100 degrees
B) 130 degrees
C) 90 degrees
D) 150 degrees
questions.answer:
B)
According to Morrey's classic study, the functional arc of elbow motion is approximately 30° to 130° of flexion (a 100° arc). A minimum of 130° of flexion is generally required for essential daily activities such as feeding, personal hygiene, and reaching the head. The patient in this scenario flexes to only 90°, which falls well below this threshold and would warrant intervention.

A is incorrect because 100° of flexion is insufficient for many activities of daily living (e.g., bringing the hand to the mouth typically requires ~130° of flexion); using 100° as the threshold would underestimate the functional deficit.
C is incorrect because 90° of flexion is the patient's current limitation and is clearly below the accepted functional minimum; using this as the threshold would falsely suggest adequate function.
D is incorrect because 150° approaches full elbow flexion and exceeds the minimum functional requirement; setting the bar at 150° would over-indicate intervention in patients who already have adequate functional motion.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old female presents with a twisted knee injury sustained while playing soccer. She reports a popping sensation at the time of injury and now has joint swelling and difficulty bearing weight. Physical examination reveals a positive Lachman test. An MRI confirms a complete tear of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). What is the most appropriate surgical approach for ACL reconstruction in this patient?
A) Anteromedial portal
B) Anterolateral portal
C) Posteromedial approach
D) Posterolateral approach
E) Lateral incision
questions.answer:
A)
The anteromedial (AM) portal technique is the preferred method for femoral tunnel drilling during anatomic ACL reconstruction. It allows independent placement of the femoral tunnel at the anatomic ACL footprint on the lateral femoral condyle, rather than being constrained by the tibial tunnel. This has become the standard approach for achieving anatomic reconstruction.

B is incorrect because the anterolateral portal is typically used as the primary viewing portal during knee arthroscopy; it is not the portal through which the femoral tunnel is drilled in anatomic ACL reconstruction. C is incorrect because a posteromedial approach is used for procedures such as posterior cruciate ligament reconstruction or posteromedial corner repair, not standard ACL reconstruction. D is incorrect because a posterolateral approach is utilized for posterolateral corner reconstruction or repair, not for ACL reconstruction. E is incorrect because a lateral incision is not a standard arthroscopic portal for ACL reconstruction; it may be used for extra-articular lateral tenodesis procedures but is not the primary surgical approach for ACL graft placement.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old man is involved in a high-energy car accident and presents with a severely deformed left leg. On examination, his left hip is flexed and adducted, with an inability to move it. An x-ray confirms a posterior hip dislocation. What is the most appropriate initial management for this injury?
A) Immediate reduction in the emergency department
B) Conservative management with pain control
C) MRI to assess associated injuries
D) Total hip arthroplasty
questions.answer:
A)
Posterior hip dislocation is an orthopaedic emergency. Immediate closed reduction—ideally within 6 hours of injury—is critical to minimize the risk of avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head and sciatic nerve injury. Reduction is typically performed under procedural sedation in the emergency department.

B is incorrect because conservative management with pain control alone does not address the dislocation; prolonged dislocation dramatically increases the risk of AVN and cartilage damage. C is incorrect because obtaining an MRI prior to reduction unnecessarily delays treatment; advanced imaging (CT or MRI) is appropriate after successful reduction to evaluate for associated acetabular fractures, loose bodies, or labral injury. D is incorrect because total hip arthroplasty is not indicated acutely for a traumatic hip dislocation in a young patient; it may be considered only in the setting of late complications such as post-traumatic arthritis or established AVN.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male presents with pain and swelling in his right ankle following a sports injury. He has difficulty standing on his toes and experiences weakness in foot inversion. Physical examination reveals tenderness along the posterior tibial tendon. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Achilles tendon rupture
B) Posterior tibial tendon insufficiency
C) Flexor digitorum longus strain
D) Lateral ankle sprain
questions.answer:
B)
The clinical picture—tenderness along the posterior tibial tendon, weakness of foot inversion, and difficulty performing a single-limb heel rise—is classic for posterior tibial tendon insufficiency (PTTI). The posterior tibial tendon is the primary dynamic stabilizer of the medial longitudinal arch, and its dysfunction leads to progressive adult-acquired flatfoot deformity.

A is incorrect because Achilles tendon rupture presents with a palpable gap at the Achilles, a positive Thompson test, and weakness of plantarflexion rather than inversion. C is incorrect because a flexor digitorum longus strain would cause pain more distally along the plantar foot and weakness of lesser-toe flexion, not inversion weakness or difficulty with heel rise. D is incorrect because a lateral ankle sprain involves the lateral ligament complex (typically the ATFL), producing lateral ankle tenderness and instability, not medial/posterior tibial tendon tenderness or inversion weakness.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old male with a history of chronic steroid use presents with hip pain after a minor fall. X-rays show a subcapital femoral neck fracture. What is the most likely complication this patient faces if the fracture is not appropriately managed?
A) Acute compartment syndrome
B) Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
C) Malunion of the fracture
D) Non-displaced fracture of the acetabulum
questions.answer:
B)
Patients on chronic steroid therapy are at increased risk of avascular necrosis (AVN). Subcapital femoral neck fractures disrupt the tenuous blood supply to the femoral head (medial femoral circumflex artery), and when combined with steroid-induced vascular compromise, the risk of AVN is markedly elevated if the fracture is not appropriately managed.

A is incorrect because acute compartment syndrome is exceedingly rare in the hip/thigh following a simple femoral neck fracture and is not a characteristic complication of this injury pattern.
C is incorrect because malunion is not the primary concern with subcapital femoral neck fractures; the main risks are nonunion and AVN due to the precarious blood supply.
D is incorrect because a non-displaced acetabular fracture is a separate injury entity and is not a complication of a femoral neck fracture.

questions.question:
During a surgical procedure, a surgeon needs to identify the pectineus muscle and its anatomical landmarks. Which of the following accurately describes the origin and insertion of the pectineus?
A) Originates from the inferior pubic ramus and inserts on the linea aspera
B) Originates from the pectineal line of the pubis and inserts on the lesser trochanter
C) Originates from the pectineal line of the pubis and inserts on the pectineal line of the femur
D) Originates from the anterior inferior iliac spine and inserts on the tibial tuberosity
questions.answer:
C)
The pectineus muscle originates from the pectineal line (pecten pubis) of the superior pubic ramus and inserts on the pectineal line of the femur, a ridge running from the lesser trochanter to the linea aspera. This attachment allows it to function as a hip flexor and adductor.

A is incorrect because the pectineus does not originate from the inferior pubic ramus (that is more consistent with adductor brevis/gracilis origins), and it does not insert on the linea aspera itself but rather on the pectineal line of the femur proximal to the linea aspera.

B is incorrect because the pectineus does not insert on the lesser trochanter; the lesser trochanter is the insertion of the iliopsoas.

D is incorrect because the pectineus does not originate from the anterior inferior iliac spine (origin of the rectus femoris straight head) and does not insert on the tibial tuberosity (insertion of the patellar tendon/quadriceps mechanism).

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male presents after falling and landing on his outstretched hand. X-rays reveal an oblique fracture of the metacarpal of his index finger. During the follow-up examination, the physician notes that the metacarpal appears shortened and rotated. What is the mechanism by which this deformity has occurred?
A) Malunion due to improper immobilization
B) Muscle imbalance from denervated intrinsic muscles
C) Apex volar deformity caused by interossei muscle contraction
D) Incomplete reduction at the fracture site
questions.answer:
C)
In oblique metacarpal fractures, the interosseous muscles exert a deforming force that causes shortening (telescoping of the oblique fracture fragments) and rotational malalignment. Additionally, the interossei flex the distal fragment while the extrinsic extensors extend the proximal fragment, producing an apex dorsal angulation. These combined forces account for the shortening and rotation seen on follow-up.

A is incorrect because malunion from improper immobilization is a late complication, not the mechanism of the acute deformity; the question asks about the deforming force, not a treatment failure. B is incorrect because there is no indication of nerve injury or denervation of intrinsic muscles in this scenario; the intrinsic muscles are intact and their normal pull is the deforming force. D is incorrect because incomplete reduction describes a treatment inadequacy rather than the biomechanical mechanism by which the deformity develops.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old boy presents with a painless limp and slight knee pain. His parents report that he has been more sedentary, avoiding activities he once enjoyed. Physical examination reveals a limited range of motion in the left hip. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Perthes disease
B) Osteochondritis Dissecans
C) Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis
D) Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
questions.answer:
A)
Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease is idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head, most commonly affecting boys aged 4–8 years. It classically presents with an insidious limp, referred knee or thigh pain, and limited hip range of motion (especially internal rotation and abduction). This child's age, sex, activity avoidance, and limited hip motion are consistent with Perthes disease. Referred knee pain is a well-recognized presentation.

B is incorrect because osteochondritis dissecans typically affects the knee (medial femoral condyle) and presents with knee-specific symptoms such as locking, catching, and effusion — not a limp with limited hip motion.
C is incorrect because juvenile idiopathic arthritis usually presents with joint swelling, warmth, morning stiffness, and systemic features (e.g., fever, rash in systemic JIA); isolated painless limp with limited hip ROM in a boy of this age is more characteristic of Perthes.
D is incorrect because slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) typically occurs in older, often overweight adolescents (ages 10–16) and presents with hip or knee pain, an externally rotated and shortened limb, and obligate external rotation with hip flexion — this child's age makes SCFE much less likely.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old man presents with elbow pain after a fall. An x-ray shows a displaced olecranon fracture classified as a type III according to the Colton classification. Which of the following findings is most likely to be present in this type of fracture?
A) Non-displaced with intact triceps function
B) Comminuted with associated ulnar nerve injury
C) Fracture with minimal displacement
D) Isolated avulsion of the olecranon
questions.answer:
B)
A displaced olecranon fracture classified as type III is usually comminuted and can lead to complications such as ulnar nerve injury due to the proximity of the nerve to the medial aspect of the elbow. This type of fracture often requires surgical intervention due to instability.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man sustains a mid-shaft tibial fracture due to a motorcycle accident. He is hemodynamically stable and has no associated injuries. Considering the nature of his fracture and his overall health, what is the most appropriate initial management strategy?
A) Immediate surgical fixation
B) Nonoperative management with casting
C) Intramedullary nailing
D) External fixation
questions.answer:
C)
Intramedullary nailing is the gold-standard treatment for displaced mid-shaft tibial fractures in hemodynamically stable patients. It provides excellent axial and rotational stability, allows early weight-bearing, and has lower infection rates compared with plate fixation for diaphyseal tibial fractures.

A is incorrect because 'immediate surgical fixation' is a nonspecific term; while surgery is indeed indicated, the best answer specifies the modality — intramedullary nailing. B is incorrect because nonoperative management with casting is generally reserved for stable, minimally displaced, low-energy tibial shaft fractures; a motorcycle accident typically produces a displaced fracture pattern better treated surgically. D is incorrect because external fixation is primarily used as a temporizing measure in open fractures with significant soft-tissue compromise, polytrauma with hemodynamic instability, or when intramedullary nailing is contraindicated — none of which apply here.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents with chronic pain in her left hip and a history of bisphosphonate use for osteoporosis. An x-ray shows a subtrochanteric femur fracture. Which of the following features is most characteristic of atypical femur fractures due to long-term bisphosphonate therapy?
A) Garden stage II fracture
B) Lateral cortex thickening
C) Comminuted fracture pattern
D) Intramedullary nail fixation requirement
questions.answer:
B)
Lateral cortex thickening is the hallmark radiographic feature of atypical femur fractures (AFFs) associated with prolonged bisphosphonate use. These fractures characteristically present as transverse or short oblique fracture lines originating at the lateral cortex of the subtrochanteric or diaphyseal femur, often with periosteal/endosteal thickening ("beaking") at the fracture site and minimal comminution. They may be preceded by prodromal thigh pain and can occur with low-energy mechanisms.

A is incorrect because Garden staging applies to femoral neck (intracapsular) fractures, not subtrochanteric fractures; it is irrelevant to atypical femur fractures. C is incorrect because atypical femur fractures are characteristically non-comminuted or minimally comminuted; a comminuted pattern is more typical of high-energy injuries or typical osteoporotic fractures. D is incorrect because intramedullary nail fixation is a treatment option, not a characteristic radiographic feature of the fracture itself.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male presents with lower back pain after a fall from a ladder. Imaging reveals a fracture of the sacrum. According to the Denis Classification, which of the following statements is true regarding a Type I sacral fracture?
A) Involves the neural canal
B) Is associated with neurologic deficits
C) Is stable and generally requires conservative treatment
D) Is a comminuted fracture of the sacral body
questions.answer:
C)
A Type I Denis sacral fracture involves the alar region lateral to the neural foramina. Because it does not compromise the sacral neural canal or foramina, it is considered stable and is generally managed conservatively with pain control and progressive mobilization. Neurologic deficits are uncommon with this fracture pattern.

A is incorrect because involvement of the neural canal defines a Type III Denis fracture, not Type I. B is incorrect because neurologic deficits are most commonly associated with Type III fracral fractures (up to 57%) and to a lesser extent Type II; Type I fractures rarely cause neurologic injury (~6%). D is incorrect because a comminuted fracture of the sacral body is not the defining feature of a Type I fracture — Type I fractures occur in the sacral ala, lateral to the foramina.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old woman presents with severe hip pain and decreased mobility due to osteoarthritis. An x-ray reveals advanced degenerative changes in the hip joint. After discussing treatment options, she is interested in hip arthroplasty. Which of the following factors primarily contributes to increased stability in the design of modern hip implants?
A) Decreased head-to-neck ratio
B) Increased head-to-neck ratio
C) Increased surface roughness
D) Smaller femoral head size
questions.answer:
B)
An increased head-to-neck ratio is a key design feature in modern hip implants that enhances stability. A larger femoral head relative to the neck diameter allows a greater arc of motion before impingement occurs between the neck and the acetabular liner, thereby reducing the risk of dislocation.

A is incorrect because a decreased head-to-neck ratio would cause earlier neck-liner impingement, reducing the range of motion before dislocation and thus decreasing stability. C is incorrect because increased surface roughness relates to implant fixation (promoting bony ingrowth on porous-coated surfaces) rather than to joint stability against dislocation. D is incorrect because a smaller femoral head size decreases the jump distance required for dislocation and reduces the head-to-neck ratio, both of which decrease stability.

questions.question:
A patient with a history of chronic ankle sprains is now complaining of pain when walking and during activity. Physical examination reveals pain over the subtalar joint. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
A) Corticosteroid injection into the subtalar joint
B) Ankle arthroscopy
C) MRI of the ankle
D) Custom orthotics
questions.answer:
C)
An MRI is the best next step to evaluate the subtalar joint in a patient with chronic ankle instability and new subtalar pain. MRI can identify sinus tarsi syndrome, subtalar chondral damage, ligamentous injury (e.g., interosseous talocalcaneal ligament), or coalitions that may be driving symptoms.

A is incorrect because a corticosteroid injection may provide temporary relief but is not appropriate as a next step before establishing a diagnosis with advanced imaging.
B is incorrect because ankle arthroscopy is a surgical intervention; it is premature without first obtaining imaging to characterize the pathology.
D is incorrect because custom orthotics may be part of conservative management but should not be prescribed before the underlying pathology is identified with appropriate imaging.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old athlete sustains a knee injury resulting in a knee dislocation. Post-reduction imaging reveals significant soft tissue injury but no apparent fracture. Which imaging modality is most appropriate to assess for potential ligamentous injuries?
A) X-ray
B) MRI
C) CT scan
D) Ultrasound
questions.answer:
B)
MRI is the gold standard for evaluating soft tissue injuries, including ligamentous structures of the knee, especially after a significant trauma such as a knee dislocation. It provides excellent contrast resolution for menisci, cruciate ligaments, collateral ligaments, and posterolateral/posteromedial corner structures. Additionally, vascular injury (popliteal artery) must be ruled out after knee dislocation, but for ligamentous assessment specifically, MRI is the most appropriate modality.

A is incorrect because standard X-rays evaluate bony structures and are useful for ruling out fractures but cannot adequately visualize ligaments, cartilage, or other soft tissue injuries.
C is incorrect because CT scanning excels at bony detail (e.g., fracture characterization, bone loss quantification) but is inferior to MRI for soft tissue and ligamentous evaluation.
D is incorrect because ultrasound has limited utility in evaluating intra-articular and deep ligamentous structures of the knee; it may detect effusions or superficial soft tissue pathology but cannot reliably assess cruciate ligaments or the posterolateral corner.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old athlete has been experiencing groin pain and limited internal rotation of the hip. An MRI shows a cam-type femoroacetabular impingement. Which physical examination maneuver is most likely to reproduce his symptoms?
A) FADIR (anterior impingement) test
B) Trendelenburg test
C) FABER (Patrick's) test
D) Thomas test
E) Log roll test
questions.answer:
A)
The FADIR (Flexion, ADduction, Internal Rotation) test, also called the anterior impingement test, is the most sensitive provocative maneuver for femoroacetabular impingement. It reproduces groin pain by driving the cam lesion into the anterosuperior acetabular labrum, which is the typical site of impingement in cam-type FAI.

B is incorrect because the Trendelenburg test evaluates hip abductor (gluteus medius) strength and does not provoke impingement symptoms.
C is incorrect because the FABER (Patrick's) test places the hip in flexion, abduction, and external rotation, which primarily stresses the sacroiliac joint and posterior hip structures rather than reproducing anterior cam-type impingement.
D is incorrect because the Thomas test assesses for a hip flexion contracture (iliopsoas tightness) and does not specifically provoke FAI.
E is incorrect because the log roll test evaluates for intra-articular hip pathology by gently rotating the hip in extension; it is less specific and less sensitive for reproducing impingement symptoms compared with the FADIR test.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male with persistent back pain undergoes MRI of the lumbar spine, which shows a lesion in the vertebral body with abnormal marrow signal. What is the primary purpose of using MRI in this scenario?
A) To assess for pulmonary metastasis
B) To determine the presence of skip lesions
C) To evaluate the local staging of the tumor with marrow involvement
D) To assess the need for a bone scan
questions.answer:
C)
MRI is the gold standard for local staging of bone tumors because it provides superior soft-tissue contrast and detailed evaluation of marrow involvement, tumor extent, and relationship to adjacent neurovascular structures. This information is critical for surgical planning and margin assessment.

A is incorrect because chest CT, not MRI of the spine, is the primary modality used to assess for pulmonary metastasis.
B is incorrect because while MRI can detect skip lesions, the primary purpose described in this scenario is local staging and evaluation of marrow involvement, not specifically screening for skip lesions.
D is incorrect because a bone scan is a separate nuclear medicine study; MRI is not used to determine whether a bone scan is needed. The two modalities serve different roles in the workup of bone tumors.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old woman with a known history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with swelling and tenderness in her wrist and the palm of her hand. She is unable to fully extend her fingers, and there is marked tenderness over the tendon sheath. On physical examination, the Kanavel signs are positive. What is the most appropriate management? 
A) Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs 
B) Surgical intervention for drainage 
C) Immobilization with a cast 
D) Corticosteroid injection
questions.answer:
B)
Kanavel signs (fusiform swelling, flexed posture of the digit, tenderness along the flexor tendon sheath, and pain with passive extension) are pathognomonic for infectious (pyogenic) flexor tenosynovitis. This is a surgical emergency requiring urgent incision and drainage with irrigation of the tendon sheath to prevent tendon necrosis, adhesions, and potential digit loss.

A is incorrect because NSAIDs alone are insufficient to treat an established pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis; antibiotics and surgical drainage are required. C is incorrect because immobilization with a cast does not address the purulent infection within the tendon sheath and would delay definitive treatment. D is incorrect because corticosteroid injection into an infected tendon sheath can worsen the infection and is contraindicated in the setting of septic tenosynovitis.

questions.question:
A 75-year-old woman is evaluated for her chronic hip pain, and imaging reveals significant acetabular dysplasia. After discussing treatment options, the decision is made to proceed with total hip arthroplasty. What is the optimal anteversion angle for the acetabular component in this patient to enhance stability?
A) 10-15°
B) 20-30°
C) 30-40°
D) 40-50°
questions.answer:
B)
The Lewinnek safe zone for acetabular component anteversion in total hip arthroplasty is 15 ± 10° (5–25°). Among the available choices, 20–30° (B) most closely approximates the ideal range. Placing the cup within this anteversion range helps balance anterior and posterior stability and reduces the risk of postoperative dislocation.

A is incorrect because 10–15° of anteversion, while within the safe zone, is at the lower end and may increase the risk of posterior dislocation, particularly in a dysplastic hip where additional stability is desired. C is incorrect because 30–40° of anteversion is excessive and would predispose to anterior dislocation during extension and external rotation. D is incorrect because 40–50° of anteversion is far beyond the safe zone and would result in significant anterior instability and a high dislocation risk.

questions.question:
A 10-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after falling off his skateboard. He is holding his left arm and is in visible pain. X-rays reveal a mid-shaft fracture of both the radius and ulna. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Splint the arm and schedule for outpatient follow-up
B) Perform open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF)
C) Apply a long arm cast
D) Refer to a pediatric orthopaedic specialist for surgical evaluation
questions.answer:
C)
For a 10-year-old child with a mid-shaft both-bone forearm fracture that is not significantly displaced, the standard initial management is closed reduction (if needed) and application of a long arm cast. Children have significant remodeling potential, though at age 10 this is more limited than in younger children. A well-molded long arm cast maintains alignment and allows fracture healing.

A is incorrect because a splint alone with outpatient follow-up is insufficient for a both-bone forearm fracture; these fractures require circumferential immobilization with a long arm cast after appropriate reduction. B is incorrect because ORIF is generally reserved for open fractures, fractures with significant displacement that cannot be maintained with closed reduction, or fractures in older adolescents near skeletal maturity; it is not the first-line treatment for a typical pediatric both-bone forearm fracture. D is incorrect because while referral may ultimately be appropriate if the fracture is significantly displaced, the most appropriate immediate next step for a non-displaced or reducible fracture is application of a long arm cast.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after a fall from a swing set. He is unable to extend his elbow and has significant swelling over the lateral aspect. X-rays reveal a displaced supracondylar humerus fracture. On examination, he exhibits wrist drop. Which of the following nerves is most likely injured in this scenario?
A) Ulnar nerve
B) Median nerve
C) Radial nerve
D) Musculocutaneous nerve
questions.answer:
C)
The clinical finding of wrist drop (inability to extend the wrist and fingers at the MCP joints) localizes the injury to the radial nerve. In supracondylar humerus fractures, the radial nerve can be injured, particularly in posterolaterally displaced (extension-type) fractures. Although the anterior interosseous nerve (median nerve branch) is the most commonly injured nerve overall in extension-type supracondylar fractures, the specific finding of wrist drop is pathognomonic for radial nerve palsy.

A is incorrect because ulnar nerve injury typically presents with clawing of the ring and small fingers and weakness of intrinsic hand muscles, not wrist drop. Ulnar nerve injury is more commonly associated with flexion-type supracondylar fractures.
B is incorrect because median nerve injury (or its anterior interosseous branch) would present with loss of flexion at the thumb IP joint and index DIP joint (inability to make an "OK" sign), not wrist drop.
D is incorrect because musculocutaneous nerve injury would present with weakness of elbow flexion (biceps, brachialis) and loss of sensation over the lateral forearm, not wrist drop.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old dancer presents with a snapping sensation in the hip, particularly during external rotation. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the iliopsoas tendon, and imaging shows no significant structural abnormalities. What is the most appropriate non-surgical treatment?
A) Corticosteroid injection
B) Surgical release of the iliopsoas tendon
C) Physical therapy focusing on stretching and strengthening
D) Activity modification with complete rest
questions.answer:
C)
The presentation is consistent with internal (iliopsoas) snapping hip syndrome. In the absence of structural abnormalities on imaging, first-line treatment is physical therapy focused on stretching the iliopsoas and strengthening the surrounding hip musculature. This approach addresses the underlying biomechanical cause and is the most effective initial intervention.

A is incorrect because corticosteroid injection may provide temporary symptom relief but does not address the underlying muscular imbalance and is not considered first-line treatment.
B is incorrect because surgical release of the iliopsoas tendon is reserved for refractory cases that fail prolonged conservative management, and the question specifically asks for non-surgical treatment.
D is incorrect because complete rest alone does not correct the biomechanical factors contributing to the snapping and symptoms typically recur upon return to activity without a structured rehabilitation program.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old man complains of persistent wrist pain and limited motion following a fall two months ago. An MRI shows loss of coupled motion between the scaphoid and lunate. What is the potential long-term consequence of this loss?
A) Increased grip strength
B) Carpal instability
C) Decreased risk of arthritis
D) Improved wrist function
E) Enhanced blood supply to the scaphoid
questions.answer:
B)
The loss of coupled motion between the scaphoid and lunate indicates scapholunate dissociation, which leads to carpal instability. If untreated, this progresses through a predictable pattern of degenerative arthritis known as SLAC (scapholunate advanced collapse) wrist.

A is incorrect because scapholunate dissociation disrupts normal carpal kinematics and typically decreases grip strength due to pain and altered mechanics. B is correct. C is incorrect because scapholunate instability increases the risk of progressive degenerative arthritis (SLAC wrist), not decreases it. D is incorrect because loss of coupled scapholunate motion impairs wrist function through pain, reduced range of motion, and abnormal loading patterns. E is incorrect because scapholunate dissociation does not enhance blood supply to the scaphoid; in fact, altered mechanics may compromise the already tenuous retrograde blood supply of the scaphoid.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman with a history of osteoporosis complains of severe back pain after a minor fall. X-rays reveal a compression fracture at L1. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of injury for this type of fracture in patients with osteoporosis?
A) Flexion injury
B) Axial loading
C) Lateral bending
D) Extension injury
questions.answer:
A)
Osteoporotic compression fractures of the lumbar spine most commonly result from a flexion mechanism. Even minor forward bending or a low-energy fall produces a flexion moment across the anterior column, causing the weakened osteoporotic vertebral body to fail in compression and produce the characteristic anterior wedge fracture. This is the classic mechanism described in the Denis classification for compression fractures.

B is incorrect because pure axial loading tends to produce burst fractures, in which both the anterior and middle (or posterior) columns fail, rather than the simple anterior wedge compression fracture described here.
C is incorrect because lateral bending would produce a lateral compression or asymmetric fracture pattern, not the typical anterior wedge compression fracture seen in osteoporotic patients.
D is incorrect because extension injuries cause failure of the anterior column in tension and the posterior column in compression, producing distraction-type injuries (e.g., extension teardrop or posterior element fractures), not anterior compression fractures.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male presents with acute pain and swelling in the ankle after twisting it while running. An x-ray reveals a fracture of the lateral malleolus, and an MRI shows associated soft tissue injury. As part of the surgical planning, the surgeon considers the superficial peroneal nerve. Which of the following statements regarding this nerve is true?
A) It is located medially to the fibula
B) It provides sensation to the plantar aspect of the foot
C) It is typically at risk during anterolateral approaches to the distal fibula
D) It supplies the peroneus longus muscle only
questions.answer:
C)
The superficial peroneal nerve (SPN) courses in the lateral compartment of the leg and pierces the deep fascia approximately 10–12 cm proximal to the tip of the lateral malleolus, becoming subcutaneous. It is therefore at risk during anterolateral approaches to the distal fibula, and meticulous dissection is required to avoid iatrogenic injury.

A is incorrect because the SPN is located laterally, within the lateral compartment of the leg along the fibula, not medially to it.
B is incorrect because the SPN provides sensation to the dorsum of the foot (except the first web space, which is supplied by the deep peroneal nerve); the plantar aspect is innervated by the tibial nerve branches (medial and lateral plantar nerves).
D is incorrect because the SPN supplies both the peroneus longus and peroneus brevis muscles, not the peroneus longus alone.

questions.question:
A 68-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer presents with increasing pain in her left femur. On examination, she has tenderness and a localized swelling. Mirels' criteria indicate a score of 8. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
A) Immediate surgical fixation
B) Bisphosphonate therapy
C) Observation
D) Radiation therapy to the femur
questions.answer:
A)
A Mirels' score of 8 or above indicates a significant risk of pathologic fracture in the setting of metastatic disease. Prophylactic surgical fixation is recommended to prevent an impending fracture and to provide pain relief and maintain function, particularly in a weight-bearing bone such as the femur.

B is incorrect because bisphosphonate therapy (e.g., zoledronic acid) is an adjunctive systemic treatment that reduces skeletal events but does not address the immediate mechanical risk of fracture in a high-risk lesion.
C is incorrect because observation alone is inappropriate when the Mirels' score indicates high fracture risk; delay may result in a completed pathologic fracture, which carries greater morbidity and more complex surgical management.
D is incorrect because while radiation therapy can provide pain relief and local tumor control, it does not restore structural integrity of the bone and is insufficient as sole management when the fracture risk is high (Mirels' ≥ 8).

questions.question:
A 9-year-old boy is being treated for a slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE). His growth plates are evaluated, and a hypertrophic zone is noted. What does this indicate regarding the condition?
A) It is a type of acute fracture
B) The epiphyseal blood supply is compromised
C) The physis is undergoing abnormal growth
D) There is normal healing progression
questions.answer:
C)
In SCFE, histopathologic studies demonstrate that the slip occurs through the hypertrophic zone of the physis. This zone shows abnormal endochondral ossification with disorganized, widened columns of chondrocytes and irregular calcification, indicating the physis is undergoing abnormal growth and is mechanically weakened, predisposing to epiphyseal displacement.

A is incorrect because SCFE is not simply an acute fracture; it is a chronic or acute-on-chronic displacement through a pathologically abnormal physis, specifically at the hypertrophic zone. B is incorrect because the hypertrophic zone abnormality in SCFE reflects a disorder of endochondral ossification within the physis itself, not compromise of the epiphyseal blood supply (which is more relevant to avascular necrosis as a complication). D is incorrect because a widened, disorganized hypertrophic zone is pathologic in SCFE; normal healing progression would show orderly maturation and calcification of chondrocytes, not the structural weakness seen here.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old athlete presents with complaints of groin pain after a fall during a football match. MRI shows a loose body in the hip joint, possibly resulting from an old injury. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Arthroscopic removal
B) Physical therapy
C) Joint injection
D) Observation
questions.answer:
A)
In cases where symptomatic intra-articular loose bodies are present in the hip joint causing groin pain and mechanical symptoms, arthroscopic removal is the most appropriate management. This procedure relieves symptoms, prevents further chondral damage, and restores joint function.

B is incorrect because physical therapy cannot address a mechanical problem caused by a loose body within the joint; it will not resolve locking, catching, or pain from the fragment.
C is incorrect because a joint injection (e.g., corticosteroid) may temporarily reduce inflammation but does not remove the offending loose body and will not provide definitive treatment.
D is incorrect because observation is inappropriate when a loose body is symptomatic; continued mechanical irritation risks progressive cartilage damage and worsening symptoms.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male sustains a coronoid fracture after a fall onto an outstretched hand. The injury is classified according to the Regan-Morrey system. Which of the following factors is most critical in determining the surgical approach for this type of fracture?
A) Age of the patient
B) Mechanism of injury
C) Presence of associated ligamentous injury
D) Location of the fracture
E) Degree of fragment displacement
questions.answer:
C)
The presence of associated ligamentous injuries (e.g., lateral collateral ligament complex disruption in the "terrible triad" or medial collateral ligament injury) is the most critical factor in determining the surgical approach for coronoid fractures. These associated injuries significantly affect elbow stability and often mandate surgical fixation of the coronoid and ligament repair, even for smaller coronoid fragments that might otherwise be treated nonoperatively.

A is incorrect because while age may influence healing potential, it is not the primary determinant of surgical approach for coronoid fractures. B is incorrect because although mechanism of injury helps explain the fracture pattern, it does not directly dictate the surgical approach as much as the resulting ligamentous instability does. D is incorrect because the Regan-Morrey classification already accounts for fracture location (tip, ≤50%, >50% of coronoid height); however, the associated soft-tissue/ligamentous injuries are more critical in guiding surgical decision-making. E is incorrect because while fragment displacement matters, the overall stability of the elbow—determined largely by associated ligamentous injury—is the most important factor driving the need for and type of surgical intervention.

questions.question:
During a surgical procedure to repair a fracture of the distal humerus, the surgeon is concerned about preserving the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve. Which approach should be utilized to minimize the risk of injury to this nerve?
A) Anterior approach to the elbow
B) Posterior approach without olecranon osteotomy
C) Medial approach to the elbow
D) Lateral approach to the distal humerus
questions.answer:
B)
The posterior approach to the elbow without olecranon osteotomy is preferred as it minimizes the risk of transecting the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve, which can occur with certain anterior or lateral approaches.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman presents with unilateral hand pain and swelling after an injury to her wrist during gardening. On examination, her symptoms extend to the volar aspect of her fingers, and she has difficulty flexing her proximal interphalangeal joints. Which structure is likely preventing the reduction of her interphalangeal joint dislocations?
A) Collateral ligaments
B) Volar plate
C) Flexor sheath
D) Extensor hood
questions.answer:
B)
The volar plate is the most common structure that becomes interposed in the joint and prevents closed reduction of a PIP joint dislocation. During dorsal dislocation of the PIP joint, the volar plate can avulse from its proximal attachment and become trapped between the articular surfaces, making the dislocation irreducible by closed means.

A is incorrect because while the collateral ligaments may be injured during a PIP dislocation, they rarely become interposed in the joint to block reduction.
C is incorrect because the flexor sheath surrounds the flexor tendons and, although it can occasionally be involved, it is not the classic structure that blocks PIP joint reduction.
D is incorrect because the extensor hood lies dorsally and is not typically interposed in the joint during a dorsal PIP dislocation; it does not classically prevent reduction.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman presents with a complaint of her ring finger catching during flexion and extension. On examination, there is a palpable nodule at the base of the finger and pain when attempting to fully extend the finger. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
A) Trigger finger due to A2 pulley involvement
B) Flexor tendon rupture
C) Dupuytren's contracture
D) Ganglion cyst
E) Tendonitis
questions.answer:
A)
The symptoms described are characteristic of trigger finger, which commonly involves the A1 pulley. The nodule and catching sensation are due to the inflammation of the flexor tendon as it passes through the constricted pulley, leading to the catching or locking mechanism.

questions.question:
A 12-year-old boy is found to have a nonossifying fibroma (NOF) on imaging after evaluation for a leg length discrepancy. The lesion is asymptomatic and measures 5 cm. What is the most appropriate management decision?
A) Surgical resection
B) Observation with follow-up
C) Intralesional corticosteroid injection
D) Bone grafting
questions.answer:
B)
Nonossifying fibromas are benign developmental cortical defects that are common in children and adolescents. When asymptomatic, observation with periodic follow-up is the standard management, as most NOFs undergo spontaneous resolution through progressive ossification during skeletal maturation. Although larger lesions (>50% of bone diameter or >3.3 cm) may carry increased pathologic fracture risk, the initial approach for an asymptomatic lesion remains observation with clinical and imaging follow-up.

A is incorrect because surgical resection is unnecessarily aggressive for a benign, self-limiting lesion; curettage and grafting are reserved for symptomatic lesions, impending pathologic fracture, or lesions that occupy a significant portion of the bone cross-section.
C is incorrect because intralesional corticosteroid injection has no role in the management of NOFs; it is used for other lesions such as unicameral bone cysts.
D is incorrect because bone grafting is not indicated for an asymptomatic NOF; grafting is considered only after curettage in cases where the lesion is large enough to compromise structural integrity or has caused a pathologic fracture.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old male presents with chronic hip pain after a fall two months ago. An x-ray reveals a non-union of a femoral neck fracture. He is not interested in hip replacement surgery. Which treatment modality is most appropriate at this stage?
A) Repeat fixation of the fracture
B) Bone grafting with internal fixation
C) Observation and analgesics
D) Total hip arthroplasty
questions.answer:
B)
In cases of non-union of a femoral neck fracture, especially when the patient prefers to avoid hip replacement, bone grafting combined with internal fixation can provide a viable option to promote healing and restore function. A is incorrect because repeat fixation without addressing the non-union may not be successful. C is incorrect because observation and analgesics do not address the non-union. D is incorrect because the patient is not interested in hip replacement surgery.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a high-energy motorcycle accident. He complains of severe hip pain and inability to move his leg. On examination, the leg is held in an adducted position. Which of the following structures is most likely affected in this situation?
A) Femoral nerve
B) Adductor longus
C) Rectus femoris
D) Sciatic nerve
questions.answer:
B)
