B is incorrect because while calcium content does decline, this is a consequence of increased osteoclastic resorption rather than a primary decrease in calcium storage; the fundamental mechanism is cellular (osteoclast overactivity), not simply a mineral deficit.
D is incorrect because osteoporosis preferentially affects the axial skeleton (trabecular-rich sites such as vertebral bodies and the proximal femur), not the appendicular skeleton; the stem itself states significant axial bone density loss.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female presents with elbow pain after a fall. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the medial side of the elbow, and imaging shows a stress-related injury. Which structure is most likely involved due to its anatomical location and function in relation to the sublime tubercle?
A) Medial collateral ligament (MCL)
B) Lateral collateral ligament (LCL)
C) Flexor carpi ulnaris tendon
D) Biceps brachii tendon
questions.answer:
A)
The medial collateral ligament (MCL) of the elbow, specifically its anterior bundle, inserts on the sublime tubercle of the ulna. This is the primary stabilizer against valgus stress at the elbow and is commonly injured with medial-sided elbow trauma or repetitive valgus loading. Tenderness over the medial elbow with a stress-related injury localizes to this structure.

B is incorrect because the lateral collateral ligament (LCL) complex is located on the lateral side of the elbow and is not associated with medial-sided tenderness or the sublime tubercle.
C is incorrect because while the flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) originates in part from the medial epicondyle and the olecranon, it does not insert on the sublime tubercle. The sublime tubercle is specifically the attachment site of the anterior bundle of the MCL.
D is incorrect because the biceps brachii tendon inserts on the radial tuberosity on the anterior/lateral aspect of the proximal forearm and is not related to the sublime tubercle or medial elbow pathology.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman experiences severe back pain after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. Neurological examination reveals saddle anesthesia and bladder dysfunction. Which of the following findings is most suggestive of a cauda equina syndrome?
A) Loss of proprioception below the injury
B) Presence of deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities
C) Severe bilateral leg pain
D) Loss of bowel control
questions.answer:
D)
Loss of bowel control is a hallmark of cauda equina syndrome (CES). CES results from compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots and classically presents with saddle anesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, and variable lower extremity weakness with areflexia. Loss of bowel control, combined with the saddle anesthesia and bladder dysfunction already described, is the most specific finding pointing to CES.

A is incorrect because loss of proprioception is mediated by the dorsal columns of the spinal cord, not the cauda equina nerve roots. This finding is more suggestive of a spinal cord (upper motor neuron) lesion such as posterior cord syndrome, not a cauda equina (lower motor neuron) process.

B is incorrect because the cauda equina is composed of peripheral nerve roots (lower motor neurons). Compression of these roots typically causes diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes, not preserved reflexes. Presence of deep tendon reflexes would be more consistent with an upper motor neuron (spinal cord) lesion.

C is incorrect because while bilateral leg pain can occur in CES, it is nonspecific and can be seen in many conditions (e.g., bilateral radiculopathy, spinal stenosis, vascular claudication). It is not as characteristic of CES as bowel/bladder dysfunction and saddle anesthesia.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old male presents to the clinic with persistent heel pain that worsens during activities such as running and jumping. He describes the pain as sharp and located at the back of his heel, especially during the push-off phase. He mentions that the pain is less severe when he is at rest. Based on this presentation, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Plantar fasciitis
B) Achilles tendinitis
C) Calcaneal bursitis
D) Retrocalcaneal exostosis
questions.answer:
B)
Achilles tendinitis is the most likely diagnosis. The patient describes sharp pain at the back of the heel that worsens with running, jumping, and push-off — activities that load the Achilles tendon — and improves with rest. This is the classic presentation of insertional or mid-substance Achilles tendinitis in an active individual.

A is incorrect because plantar fasciitis causes pain at the plantar aspect of the heel (medial calcaneal tubercle), classically worst with the first steps in the morning, not at the posterior heel during push-off. C is incorrect because calcaneal (retrocalcaneal) bursitis presents with pain and swelling deep to the Achilles tendon at its insertion, often aggravated by shoe pressure; the description here of activity-related sharp posterior heel pain during push-off is more consistent with tendinitis. D is incorrect because a retrocalcaneal exostosis (Haglund deformity) typically causes a visible bony prominence at the posterosuperior calcaneus with pain from shoe friction and secondary bursitis, rather than the activity-dependent tendon-loading pain described.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male presents with a laceration of the palm after a knife injury. He has difficulty flexing his fingers and reports numbness in the index and middle fingers. An examination reveals a cut over the carpal tunnel area. Which structure is most likely injured that could explain his symptoms?
A) Flexor digitorum superficialis tendon
B) Median nerve
C) Flexor pollicis longus tendon
D) Flexor digitorum profundus tendon
E) Ulnar nerve
questions.answer:
B)
The median nerve passes through the carpal tunnel and provides sensory innervation to the palmar aspect of the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger. A laceration over the carpal tunnel can injure the median nerve, causing numbness in the index and middle fingers (sensory) and weakness of thenar muscles (motor), which impairs thumb opposition and grip, contributing to difficulty with finger function. The median nerve is the single structure that best accounts for both motor and sensory deficits described.

A is incorrect because the flexor digitorum superficialis tendons flex the PIP joints and could be lacerated here, but their injury would not explain the numbness in the index and middle fingers. C is incorrect because the flexor pollicis longus tendon flexes the thumb IP joint; its injury would not cause numbness in the index and middle fingers. D is incorrect because the flexor digitorum profundus tendons flex the DIP joints and their laceration would not explain the sensory deficit. E is incorrect because the ulnar nerve does not pass through the carpal tunnel (it travels through Guyon's canal) and innervates the small finger and ulnar half of the ring finger, not the index and middle fingers.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman presents with hip pain and difficulty walking following a fall from a height. An x-ray shows a fracture involving more than 40% of the posterior wall of the acetabulum. Which of the following surgical approaches is most appropriate for accessing this fracture?
A) Posterior approach
B) Anterior approach
C) Lateral approach
D) Ilioinguinal approach
questions.answer:
A)
Fractures involving greater than 40% of the acetabular posterior wall typically require a posterior approach for optimal visualization and stabilization. The ilioinguinal approach is useful for anterior fractures, while the lateral approach does not provide adequate access to the posterior structures.

questions.question:
A 12-year-old girl with a family history of scoliosis is referred for evaluation after her mother notices asymmetry in her shoulders and waist. X-rays reveal a 30-degree thoracic curvature. What is the most appropriate treatment option for this child?
A) Observation with regular follow-up
B) Full-time bracing
C) Surgery for spinal fusion
D) Physical therapy only
questions.answer:
B)
For a skeletally immature 12-year-old with a 30-degree thoracic curve, full-time bracing (typically 16–23 hours/day) is the standard of care to prevent curve progression during remaining growth, supported by the BrAIST trial.

A is incorrect because observation alone is generally recommended for curves <25 degrees in skeletally immature patients; a 30-degree curve in a growing child warrants active treatment with bracing.
C is incorrect because surgical spinal fusion is typically reserved for curves exceeding 40–50 degrees or those that progress despite bracing; a 30-degree curve does not meet surgical threshold.
D is incorrect because physical therapy alone has not been shown to reliably prevent curve progression in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis of this magnitude, though Schroth-type exercises may be used as an adjunct to bracing.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old man presents with chronic knee pain and a history of multiple injuries to the knee. On examination, there is tenderness at the patellar tendon insertion site. An x-ray shows mild patellar osteophyte formation. Which area of the patella is most likely to have a vascular supply deficiency, contributing to his symptoms?
A) Inferomedial aspect of the patella
B) Superior pole of the patella
C) Inferolateral aspect of the patella
D) Central region of the patella
questions.answer:
A)
The inferomedial aspect of the patella is known to have a predominant blood supply deficiency, which can lead to avascular necrosis and chronic pain symptoms in patients with knee injuries. Recognizing these anatomical variations is crucial for effective management of patellar-related conditions.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old athlete presents with pain along the anterior aspect of the leg after playing football. Imaging reveals a stress fracture of the tibial shaft. Which of the following muscles is primarily responsible for the action of dorsiflexion at the ankle joint and is most likely affected by this injury?
A) Soleus
B) Gastrocnemius
C) Tibialis anterior
D) Peroneus longus
questions.answer:
C)
The tibialis anterior is the primary dorsiflexor of the ankle. It originates from the lateral condyle and upper two-thirds of the lateral surface of the tibia, so a tibial shaft stress fracture in the anterior cortex can directly affect this muscle's origin and function, producing anterior leg pain exacerbated by dorsiflexion.

A is incorrect because the soleus is a plantar flexor of the ankle (originating from the posterior tibia and fibula), not a dorsiflexor.
B is incorrect because the gastrocnemius is a plantar flexor (originating from the femoral condyles), not a dorsiflexor.
D is incorrect because the peroneus (fibularis) longus primarily everts the foot and assists in plantar flexion; it originates from the fibula, not the tibia, and is not a dorsiflexor.

questions.question:
A CT scan shows a fracture pattern in the sacrum consistent with the Denis Classification. Which of the following is NOT a category in this classification?
A) Zone I - fracture lateral to the sacral foramina
B) Zone II - fracture through the sacral foramina
C) Zone III - fracture medial to the sacral foramina
D) Type IV - fracture involving the sacroiliac joint
questions.answer:
D)
The Denis classification of sacral fractures includes three zones only: Zone I (lateral to the foramina, alar region), Zone II (through the sacral foramina), and Zone III (medial to the foramina, involving the central sacral canal). There is no 'Type IV' in this system; therefore D is not a valid category.

A is incorrect because Zone I (lateral/alar fracture) is a recognized Denis category.
B is incorrect because Zone II (transforaminal fracture) is a recognized Denis category.
C is incorrect because Zone III (medial to foramina/central canal fracture) is a recognized Denis category.

questions.question:
During a surgical procedure using an anterolateral approach to the proximal tibia, which structure is the primary concern for potential injury?
A) Tibialis posterior tendon
B) Anterior tibial artery
C) Common peroneal nerve
D) Peroneus longus tendon
questions.answer:
C)
The common peroneal nerve (also called the common fibular nerve) wraps around the fibular neck and is the structure most at risk during an anterolateral approach to the proximal tibia. Injury can result in foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion and eversion) and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot.

A is incorrect because the tibialis posterior tendon lies in the deep posterior compartment of the leg and is not encountered during an anterolateral approach.
B is incorrect because the anterior tibial artery, while in the anterior compartment, lies deep on the interosseous membrane and is not the primary structure at risk during this approach; the common peroneal nerve is more superficial and vulnerable.
D is incorrect because the peroneus longus tendon lies in the lateral compartment and, while in relative proximity, is not the primary structure at risk — the common peroneal nerve is more vulnerable as it courses around the fibular neck.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old athlete presents with pain at the musculotendinous junction of the shoulder after a sudden overhead throw. Physical examination reveals tenderness and a palpable defect at the site of pain. Which of the following structures is most likely affected by the injury?
A) Muscle belly
B) Tendon
C) Synovial membrane
D) Ligament
E) Cartilage
questions.answer:
B)
The musculotendinous junction (MTJ) is the weakest link in the muscle–tendon unit and is the most common site of strain injuries during explosive movements such as overhead throwing. A palpable defect and localized tenderness at this junction indicate a tendon-side disruption at the MTJ.

A is incorrect because isolated muscle belly injuries typically occur more centrally within the muscle substance, not at the musculotendinous junction. C is incorrect because the synovial membrane lines joint cavities and tendon sheaths; it is not the structure at risk during a musculotendinous junction strain. D is incorrect because ligaments connect bone to bone and are injured in sprains, not in strains at the musculotendinous junction. E is incorrect because cartilage (articular or fibrocartilage) is an intra-articular structure and is not involved in musculotendinous junction injuries.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female presents with persistent pain in her right hip that is worse at night and is relieved by NSAIDs. Imaging shows a small, well-circumscribed lytic lesion in the femoral neck. Considering the diagnosis of osteoid osteoma, what is the most appropriate treatment option?
A) Observation
B) Curettage
C) Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)
D) Total hip arthroplasty
questions.answer:
C)
Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is the preferred treatment for osteoid osteoma, particularly for small, well-circumscribed lesions. It is minimally invasive, targets the nidus directly, and provides excellent pain relief with rapid recovery and high success rates (>90%).

A is incorrect because osteoid osteomas cause significant pain and, while symptoms may occasionally self-resolve over years, observation is not the standard of care when effective definitive treatment is available, especially in a weight-bearing location like the femoral neck.
B is incorrect because curettage (open surgical excision) is a valid but more invasive alternative; RFA is preferred for small, accessible lesions due to lower morbidity and equivalent efficacy.
D is incorrect because total hip arthroplasty is a reconstructive procedure for end-stage arthritis or major bone loss and is not indicated for a benign bone tumor such as osteoid osteoma.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female runner presents with a burning sensation between the third and fourth toes. On examination, there is tenderness in the interspace, and a positive Mulder's sign is noted. Which of the following conservative treatments should be considered first-line for her Morton neuroma?
A) Surgical excision
B) Corticosteroid injection
C) Custom orthotics
D) Physical therapy
questions.answer:
C)
Custom orthotics (including metatarsal pads and accommodative shoe modifications) are the accepted first-line conservative treatment for Morton neuroma. They offload pressure from the affected interdigital nerve and can significantly reduce symptoms without invasive intervention.

A is incorrect because surgical excision is reserved for cases that fail prolonged conservative management and is not a first-line treatment.
B is incorrect because corticosteroid injection, while a useful adjunct, is typically considered a second-line measure after footwear modification and orthotic use have been tried.
D is incorrect because physical therapy alone does not directly address the mechanical compression of the interdigital nerve and is not the standard first-line recommendation for Morton neuroma.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male mechanic presents with pain and numbness in the ring and little fingers of his left hand, especially when he bends his elbow. On examination, the ulnar nerve is found to be tender at the elbow. What anatomical consideration explains the ulnar nerve's vulnerability in this region?
A) The ulnar nerve runs anterior to the medial epicondyle
B) The ulnar nerve passes through the cubital tunnel
C) The ulnar nerve is closely associated with the brachial artery
D) The ulnar nerve is covered by the triceps muscle at the elbow
questions.answer:
B)
The ulnar nerve passes through the cubital tunnel, located posterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus. The tunnel is bounded by the medial epicondyle, the olecranon, and the arcuate (Osborne's) ligament. This superficial, confined location makes the nerve vulnerable to compression and traction, particularly with repetitive or sustained elbow flexion.

A is incorrect because the ulnar nerve runs posterior (not anterior) to the medial epicondyle. It lies in the groove between the medial epicondyle and the olecranon before entering the cubital tunnel.

C is incorrect because the brachial artery is closely associated with the median nerve in the antecubital fossa, not the ulnar nerve at the elbow. The ulnar nerve diverges from the brachial artery proximally in the arm.

D is incorrect because the ulnar nerve is not covered by the triceps muscle at the elbow. It passes posterior to the medial epicondyle in a superficial position; the triceps inserts on the olecranon but does not cover the cubital tunnel.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old man with a history of wrist arthritis presents with pain and limited range of motion in his right wrist. He reports that the pain worsens with activity, and the examination reveals crepitus during wrist motion. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
A) Scaphoid fracture
B) Triangular fibrocartilage complex injury
C) Secondary osteoarthritis of the wrist
D) Scapholunate ligament tear
E) Carpal tunnel syndrome
questions.answer:
C)
A 60-year-old man with a known history of wrist arthritis presenting with activity-related pain, limited range of motion, and crepitus during wrist motion is most consistent with secondary osteoarthritis of the wrist. This condition results from progressive cartilage degeneration and joint surface irregularity, producing the characteristic crepitus and functional decline.

A is incorrect because a scaphoid fracture typically follows acute trauma and presents with anatomical snuffbox tenderness, not chronic crepitus and a history of arthritis.
B is incorrect because a triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) injury usually presents with ulnar-sided wrist pain, often after a rotational or axial load injury, rather than diffuse crepitus.
D is incorrect because a scapholunate ligament tear presents with dorsal wrist pain, a positive Watson (scaphoid shift) test, and may lead to DISI deformity, but crepitus from established arthritis with a known arthritis history points more directly to osteoarthritis.
E is incorrect because carpal tunnel syndrome is a compressive neuropathy of the median nerve presenting with numbness/tingling in the radial 3½ digits and nocturnal symptoms, not crepitus or mechanical joint pain.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old female presents to the clinic with pain and swelling in the web space between her index and middle fingers. On examination, there is a fluctuant mass in this area. A collar button abscess is suspected. What is the most appropriate initial imaging study to assess the extent of the infection?
A) X-ray
B) CT scan
C) MRI
D) Ultrasound
questions.answer:
D)
Ultrasound is the most appropriate initial imaging study for evaluating a suspected collar button abscess. It can delineate the characteristic dumbbell-shaped fluid collection spanning the palmar and dorsal sides of the web space, assess the extent of the abscess, and guide aspiration or drainage — all without radiation exposure.

A is incorrect because plain X-rays are useful for ruling out foreign bodies or osteomyelitis but cannot adequately characterize the soft-tissue extent of an abscess. B is incorrect because CT scan provides good bony detail but exposes the patient to radiation and is not the first-line study for superficial soft-tissue infections when ultrasound is available. C is incorrect because MRI, while excellent for soft-tissue evaluation, is more costly, time-consuming, and not typically the initial study for a clinically suspected superficial abscess when ultrasound can provide the needed information quickly and inexpensively.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old male presents with acute ankle pain after a fall from a height. Physical examination shows significant swelling, tenderness, and bruising around the ankle joint. X-rays reveal a fracture-dislocation of the ankle. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Perform emergent closed reduction and apply a well-padded splint
B) Apply a splint without reduction and schedule for outpatient follow-up
C) Obtain a CT scan prior to any intervention
D) Perform a Thompson test to evaluate for Achilles tendon rupture
questions.answer:
A)
An ankle fracture-dislocation is an orthopaedic emergency. The most important immediate step is emergent closed reduction in the emergency department to restore gross alignment, relieve pressure on the overlying skin, and protect the neurovascular structures. A well-padded posterior splint is then applied. After reduction, advanced imaging (CT) and definitive surgical planning (ORIF) follow in a staged fashion.

B is incorrect because splinting without reduction leaves the ankle dislocated, risking skin necrosis, compartment syndrome, and neurovascular injury.
C is incorrect because obtaining a CT scan before reducing the dislocation delays a time-sensitive intervention; CT is appropriate after reduction to plan definitive fixation.
D is incorrect because the Thompson test evaluates Achilles tendon continuity, which is not relevant to the management of an ankle fracture-dislocation.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male presents with chronic pain at the base of the fifth metatarsal. An MRI reveals a stress fracture at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction. What is the typical zone classification for fractures at this location?
A) Zone 1
B) Zone 2
C) Zone 3
D) Zone 4
questions.answer:
B)
The Lawrence-Botte classification divides proximal fifth metatarsal fractures into three zones. Zone 2 encompasses the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction (the Jones fracture zone), which is the location described in this stem. This area has a tenuous blood supply and is prone to delayed union and nonunion, often warranting surgical fixation in athletes or with chronic/stress presentations.

A is incorrect because Zone 1 refers to the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal, the site of avulsion fractures (pseudo-Jones fractures), which occur more proximally than the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction.
C is incorrect because Zone 3 refers to the proximal diaphysis distal to the Zone 2 region; true diaphyseal stress fractures occur here but are not at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction itself.
D is incorrect because there is no Zone 4 in the standard Lawrence-Botte classification of proximal fifth metatarsal fractures.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man presents with pelvic pain and difficulty walking after sustaining a fall from a height. CT imaging reveals a vertical shear injury pattern. Which of the following describes this injury mechanism?
A) Compression from the front and back of the pelvis
B) A lateral force causing displacement of the hemipelvis
C) Vertical loading leading to fracture at the sacroiliac joint
D) Direct blow to one side of the pelvis with rotational component
questions.answer:
C)
A vertical shear (VS) injury of the pelvis results from axial/vertical loading forces (e.g., fall from height landing on one leg) that drive one hemipelvis cephalad. This produces fractures or dislocations through the posterior ring (sacroiliac joint or sacrum) and anterior ring, creating complete vertical instability. It is the most unstable pattern in the Young-Burgess classification and is frequently associated with significant hemorrhage and soft-tissue disruption.

A is incorrect because compression from front and back describes an anteroposterior compression (APC) mechanism, which disrupts the pelvis from front to back (symphysis, then sacroiliac ligaments) rather than vertically. B is incorrect because a lateral force causing hemipelvic displacement describes a lateral compression (LC) mechanism, which causes internal rotation of the hemipelvis rather than vertical displacement. D is incorrect because a direct blow with a rotational component also fits a lateral compression or combined mechanism pattern, not the purely vertical shear force that characterizes this injury.

questions.question:
A 12-year-old boy is referred for scoliosis evaluation after his pediatrician noted an abnormal spine curvature during a routine physical exam. The curve is primarily located in the thoracic spine and measures 30 degrees on standing AP x-ray. He is Risser 0 and has significant growth remaining. The patient is asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate management strategy at this time?
A) Immediate surgical correction
B) Serial clinical and follow-up imaging only
C) Initiation of a bracing regimen
D) Referral to a physical therapist
questions.answer:
C)
A 30-degree thoracic curve in a Risser 0, skeletally immature 12-year-old meets established criteria for bracing (Cobb angle 25–40 degrees with significant remaining growth). The BrAIST trial demonstrated that bracing significantly reduces the risk of curve progression to the surgical threshold in this population. Bracing should be initiated rather than simply observing.

A is incorrect because surgical correction is reserved for curves that progress beyond 40–50 degrees or fail brace treatment; a 30-degree curve does not warrant immediate surgery. B is incorrect because observation alone is appropriate for curves <25 degrees or for skeletally mature patients; a 30-degree curve in a Risser 0 patient carries high progression risk and warrants active treatment with bracing. D is incorrect because physical therapy alone has not been shown to prevent curve progression in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis and is not a substitute for bracing in this clinical scenario.

questions.question:
An 8-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department after falling off her bike. She has tenderness and swelling over her right forearm and is unable to move her wrist. X-rays confirm a both-bone forearm fracture. Considering the treatment options, what is the most appropriate management for this age group?
A) Long arm cast
B) Short arm cast
C) Surgical intervention with plating
D) Observation only
questions.answer:
A)
In an 8-year-old child with a both-bone forearm fracture, closed reduction and application of a long arm cast is the standard initial management, provided acceptable alignment is achieved. The long arm cast immobilizes both the wrist and elbow, preventing forearm rotation and maintaining reduction during healing. Children in this age group have significant remodeling potential, which favors non-operative treatment when alignment criteria are met.

B is incorrect because a short arm cast does not immobilize the elbow and therefore cannot prevent forearm rotation, leading to a high risk of loss of reduction in a both-bone forearm fracture.

C is incorrect because surgical intervention with plating is generally reserved for adolescents approaching skeletal maturity, open fractures, fractures that fail closed reduction, or those with unacceptable alignment that cannot be maintained in a cast. It is not first-line for a typical pediatric both-bone forearm fracture in an 8-year-old.

D is incorrect because observation alone without immobilization would not provide the stability needed for fracture healing and would risk displacement, malunion, and continued pain.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old male presents with a progressive loss of light touch sensation in his legs. Neurological examination reveals intact deep tendon reflexes. Which sensory pathway is primarily responsible for transmitting light touch sensations?
A) Spinothalamic tract
B) Dorsal columns
C) Corticospinal tract
D) Anterolateral tract
questions.answer:
B)
The dorsal columns (posterior columns / medial lemniscus pathway) are the primary pathway for fine (discriminative) light touch, vibration, and proprioception. Progressive loss of light touch with intact deep tendon reflexes localizes the deficit to the sensory (dorsal column) pathway rather than a motor pathway.

A is incorrect because the spinothalamic tract primarily transmits pain and temperature (and crude touch); while it carries some light touch information, it is not the primary pathway for discriminative light touch. C is incorrect because the corticospinal tract is a descending motor pathway and does not carry sensory information. D is incorrect because the anterolateral tract (which includes the spinothalamic tract) primarily conveys pain, temperature, and crude touch rather than fine light touch.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old male is undergoing a surgical intervention for a posterior dislocation of the hip. The surgeon plans to use a posterior approach. Which nerve is particularly at risk for injury with this approach?
A) Femoral nerve
B) Sciatic nerve
C) Obturator nerve
D) Peroneal nerve
questions.answer:
B)
The sciatic nerve, which runs posteriorly in the thigh, is at significant risk during the posterior approach to the hip. Injury can lead to motor and sensory deficits in the lower limb. A is incorrect because the femoral nerve is located anteriorly and is not at risk with a posterior approach. C is incorrect because the obturator nerve is located medially and is not at risk with a posterior approach. D is incorrect because the peroneal nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve and is not directly at risk during the posterior approach to the hip.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male athlete presents with persistent hip pain following a soccer game. MRI reveals a compression-sided femoral neck stress fracture. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
A) Surgical fixation
B) Activity modification and crutches
C) Corticosteroid injection
D) Physical therapy
questions.answer:
B)
Compression-sided (inferomedial) femoral neck stress fractures are considered lower risk and are managed non-operatively with activity modification, protected weight-bearing with crutches, and close follow-up. These fractures are biomechanically more stable because compressive forces tend to keep the fracture compressed rather than displacing it. Surgical fixation is reserved for tension-sided (superolateral) stress fractures or compression-sided fractures that progress to displacement despite conservative care.

A is incorrect because surgical fixation is indicated for tension-sided (superolateral) femoral neck stress fractures, which carry a higher risk of displacement and completion; compression-sided fractures do not routinely require surgery. C is incorrect because corticosteroid injections have no role in stress fracture management and may actually impair bone healing. D is incorrect because while physical therapy may be part of later rehabilitation, the critical initial treatment is activity modification and protected weight-bearing to allow fracture healing; premature physical therapy with continued loading could worsen the fracture.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman is evaluated for wrist pain after a fall. Physical examination reveals tenderness over Lister's tubercle and limited wrist extension. What is the most appropriate intervention if a fracture is confirmed at this site?
A) Splinting and observation
B) Open reduction and internal fixation
C) Corticosteroid injection
D) Arthroscopy for debridement
E) Physical therapy
questions.answer:
B)
If a fracture at Lister's tubercle is confirmed, especially with associated instability, open reduction and internal fixation may be necessary to ensure proper healing and restore wrist function. This area is critical for wrist mechanics due to its role in tendon attachment.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with a noticeable curvature of his spine. On examination, it is noted that he has rib deformities and a shortened segment of the thoracic spine. Imaging shows a failure of segmentation at T8 and T9. What is the most likely diagnosis? 
A) Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis 
B) Congenital scoliosis 
C) Neuromuscular scoliosis 
D) Scheuermann's disease
questions.answer:
B)
The combination of rib deformities, a shortened thoracic spinal segment, and failure of segmentation (unsegmented bar) at T8–T9 in a young child is characteristic of congenital scoliosis. This condition results from vertebral developmental anomalies during embryogenesis, such as failures of formation or segmentation.

A is incorrect because adolescent idiopathic scoliosis presents in adolescents (typically age 10+) without congenital vertebral anomalies.
C is incorrect because neuromuscular scoliosis is associated with underlying neuromuscular conditions (e.g., cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy) and does not feature primary vertebral segmentation defects.
D is incorrect because Scheuermann's disease is a condition of vertebral endplate irregularity and wedging seen in adolescents, not a failure of segmentation in a 5-year-old.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male presents with chronic lower back pain that worsens with prolonged sitting and improves with movement. MRI shows degenerative changes in the lumbar spine. Which of the following muscles is primarily responsible for adducting the arm and is often involved in compensatory patterns due to lumbar spine issues?
A) Rhomboid major
B) Latissimus dorsi
C) Trapezius
D) Pectoralis major
questions.answer:
B)
The latissimus dorsi is the primary muscle responsible for arm adduction (along with extension and internal rotation). It originates from the thoracolumbar fascia and spinous processes of T7–L5, the sacrum, and the iliac crest, giving it a direct anatomical link to the lumbar spine. In patients with chronic lumbar pathology, altered recruitment of the latissimus dorsi can contribute to compensatory movement patterns affecting both the spine and upper extremity.

A is incorrect because the rhomboid major retracts and stabilizes the scapula; it does not primarily adduct the arm at the glenohumeral joint.
C is incorrect because the trapezius elevates, retracts, and rotates the scapula but is not a primary adductor of the arm.
D is incorrect because the pectoralis major is a powerful adductor and internal rotator of the arm, but it originates from the clavicle, sternum, and upper ribs — it has no direct attachment to the lumbar spine or thoracolumbar fascia and is therefore less likely to be involved in compensatory patterns arising from lumbar pathology.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old competitive runner experiences sudden onset of hip pain during a training run. A subsequent MRI shows a stress fracture of the femoral neck. The fracture is located on the inferior side of the neck. What is the most appropriate non-operative management for this type of fracture?
A) Surgical intervention with a hip screw
B) Immediate full weight-bearing activity
C) Activity modification and non-weight bearing for 6-8 weeks
D) Application of a hip brace
E) Corticosteroid injection
questions.answer:
C)
Compression-side (inferior/medial) femoral neck stress fractures are generally managed non-operatively. The standard approach is activity modification with protected weight bearing (crutch-assisted, toe-touch to partial weight bearing) for approximately 6–8 weeks, with serial imaging to confirm healing before gradual return to activity. This is the best answer among the choices provided.

A is incorrect because surgical intervention (e.g., cannulated screws) is indicated for tension-side (superior) femoral neck stress fractures or displaced fractures, not for non-displaced compression-side fractures.
B is incorrect because immediate full weight-bearing activity risks fracture displacement and is contraindicated in the acute management of a femoral neck stress fracture.
D is incorrect because a hip brace does not effectively immobilize or offload the femoral neck and is not a standard treatment for femoral neck stress fractures.
E is incorrect because corticosteroid injection does not promote fracture healing; in fact, corticosteroids can impair bone healing and increase fracture risk.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old man suffers a fall onto an outstretched hand and is diagnosed with a Galeazzi fracture. What is the characteristic feature of this type of fracture?
A) Fracture of the distal radius with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint
B) Fracture of the distal ulna with fracture of the proximal radius
C) Fracture of the mid-shaft radius with associated ulnar nerve injury
D) Fracture of the scaphoid with lunate dislocation
questions.answer:
A)
A Galeazzi fracture is characterized by a fracture of the distal third of the radius accompanied by dislocation or subluxation of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ). This injury pattern typically results from a fall onto an outstretched hand and almost always requires operative fixation (ORIF of the radius with assessment of DRUJ stability).

B is incorrect because a fracture of the distal ulna with a fracture of the proximal radius does not describe a recognized eponymous fracture pattern; a Monteggia fracture involves a proximal ulna fracture with radial head dislocation, not the combination described here.

C is incorrect because a Galeazzi fracture involves the distal (not mid-shaft) radius and is associated with DRUJ disruption, not ulnar nerve injury.

D is incorrect because a scaphoid fracture with lunate dislocation describes a perilunate or trans-scaphoid perilunate injury pattern, not a Galeazzi fracture.

questions.question:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency room with complaints of back pain that has persisted for 2 weeks. His parents report he has been unusually tired and has lost weight. On examination, he has tenderness to palpation over the lumbar spine. What red flags should prompt further investigation for a serious underlying condition? 
A) Age under 10 years 
B) Recent increase in physical activity 
C) Presence of fever and unintentional weight loss 
D) History of minor trauma
questions.answer:
C)
The combination of fever and unintentional weight loss in a child with persistent back pain are classic constitutional red-flag symptoms that raise suspicion for serious underlying conditions such as infection (e.g., discitis, vertebral osteomyelitis) or malignancy (e.g., leukemia, Ewing sarcoma). These findings should prompt urgent laboratory workup and advanced imaging.

A is incorrect because while young age (<10 years) lowers the threshold for concern, age alone is not a specific red-flag symptom — it is a demographic risk factor, not a clinical finding that independently warrants emergent workup.
B is incorrect because a recent increase in physical activity is a common benign cause of back pain in children and is not a red flag for serious pathology.
D is incorrect because a history of minor trauma is common in children and typically explains mechanical pain; it does not suggest infection or malignancy.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old female soccer player presents with knee pain after a twisting injury during a game. On examination, she has a positive dial test indicating increased external rotation at 30 degrees of knee flexion. MRI findings reveal tears of both the posterior cruciate ligament and the posterolateral corner structures. What is the most likely mechanism of injury?
A) Direct blow to the knee
B) Hyperextension
C) Varus stress with flexion
D) Valgus stress with rotation
questions.answer:
C)
Combined posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) and posterolateral corner (PLC) injuries most commonly result from a varus force applied to the flexed knee, or a combined varus and rotational mechanism. This damages the PLC structures first, and with continued force, the PCL fails as well. A positive dial test at 30 degrees (but not 90 degrees) localizes the rotational instability to the posterolateral corner, consistent with PLC injury.

A is incorrect because a direct blow to the anterior proximal tibia (dashboard injury) is the classic mechanism for an isolated PCL tear, not a combined PCL/PLC injury.
B is incorrect because hyperextension of the knee more typically injures the ACL and/or posterior capsule; while it can contribute to PCL injury, it is not the classic mechanism for combined PCL + PLC disruption.
D is incorrect because a valgus stress with rotation is the typical mechanism for medial collateral ligament (MCL) and ACL injuries, not posterolateral corner injuries.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man who runs regularly experiences sudden pain in the posterior aspect of his ankle after sprinting. He is unable to plantarflex his foot and exhibits a positive Thompson test. An MRI confirms a rupture of the Achilles tendon. Which of the following factors most likely contributed to the rupture?
A) Excessive dorsiflexion of the ankle
B) Avascular watershed area of the tendon
C) Inflammatory changes in the tendon
D) Poor footwear support
questions.answer:
B)
The Achilles tendon has a well-recognized avascular watershed zone located approximately 2–6 cm proximal to its calcaneal insertion, where blood supply is relatively diminished. This hypovascularity predisposes the tendon to degenerative changes and makes it the most common site of rupture. In a middle-aged recreational athlete, this intrinsic vascular deficiency is the factor most strongly associated with rupture.

A is incorrect because while excessive dorsiflexion can mechanically load the tendon, it describes a mechanism of injury rather than a predisposing factor; the stem asks what most likely contributed to the rupture, pointing to an intrinsic tendon vulnerability. C is incorrect because Achilles tendon ruptures are typically associated with degenerative (tendinotic) rather than inflammatory changes; true inflammatory tendinitis of the Achilles is relatively uncommon. D is incorrect because poor footwear support may be a minor contributing factor but is not the primary recognized predisposing factor for Achilles tendon rupture at the classic watershed zone.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old male with a history of osteoporosis presents with acute onset back pain after lifting a heavy object. X-rays reveal a compression fracture of T12. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism for this type of fracture?
A) Flexion-distraction injury
B) Axial loading
C) Hyperextension injury
D) Lateral bending
questions.answer:
B)
Compression fractures of the thoracolumbar spine in osteoporotic patients are most commonly caused by axial loading forces. Activities such as lifting a heavy object transmit compressive force through the vertebral body, and weakened osteoporotic bone fails under this load, resulting in a wedge or compression fracture.

A is incorrect because flexion-distraction (Chance-type) injuries involve failure of the posterior elements under tension, typically seen in high-energy mechanisms such as lap-belt injuries in motor vehicle accidents, not simple lifting.

C is incorrect because hyperextension injuries cause failure of the anterior column under tension and are more commonly associated with cervical spine injuries (e.g., in elderly patients with falls), not thoracolumbar compression fractures from lifting.

D is incorrect because lateral bending mechanisms produce asymmetric lateral compression or transverse process fractures rather than the classic anterior wedge compression fracture pattern described here.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old woman with severe osteoarthritis of the knee is scheduled for total knee arthroplasty (TKA). During preoperative planning, the surgeon discusses the differences between mechanical and kinematic alignment. What is a key characteristic of kinematic alignment?
A) It aims to achieve a neutral mechanical axis.
B) It adjusts the joint line to correlate with the native knee's kinematics.
C) It relies solely on the surgeon's experience and judgment.
D) It requires extensive imaging for each individual knee.
questions.answer:
B)
Kinematic alignment aims to restore the native joint line and the patient's individual constitutional alignment, thereby preserving more natural knee kinematics and ligament balance. Bone cuts are made to resurface—rather than realign—the joint, matching the pre-disease anatomy. This contrasts with mechanical alignment, which targets a neutral hip-knee-ankle axis regardless of individual anatomy.

A is incorrect because achieving a neutral mechanical axis is the goal of mechanical alignment, not kinematic alignment.
C is incorrect because kinematic alignment is a systematic, reproducible technique guided by anatomic landmarks and measured resection principles; it does not rely solely on surgeon judgment.
D is incorrect because, while advanced imaging (e.g., CT-based planning) can be used, kinematic alignment can also be performed with standard instrumentation and intraoperative landmarks and does not inherently require extensive imaging for every patient.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male athlete sustains an ankle injury during a soccer match. He has pain on the medial aspect of the ankle, and physical examination reveals tenderness and swelling. An MRI shows damage to the deltoid ligament. Which of the following tests would best assess the integrity of this ligament?
A) Anterior drawer test
B) Eversion (valgus) stress test
C) External rotation stress test
D) Thompson test
questions.answer:
B)
The eversion (valgus) stress test directly assesses the integrity of the deltoid ligament by applying a valgus force to the ankle, opening the medial clear space. Widening of the medial clear space (>4 mm) under stress indicates deltoid insufficiency. This is the most specific clinical and fluoroscopic test for deltoid ligament competence.

A is incorrect because the anterior drawer test evaluates the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL), a lateral ankle structure, by translating the talus anteriorly in the mortise. C is incorrect because the external rotation stress test primarily assesses the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis (AITFL, interosseous membrane), not the deltoid ligament specifically. D is incorrect because the Thompson test evaluates the continuity of the Achilles tendon (gastrocnemius-soleus complex) and is used to diagnose Achilles tendon rupture.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old female basketball player sustains a knee injury during a game, resulting in a sudden onset of pain and swelling. The MRI reveals a complete ACL tear with associated bone bruises on the femur and tibia. What is the most appropriate management for this patient considering her age and activity level?
A) Brace and rehabilitate with a focus on strengthening
B) Arthroscopic ACL reconstruction
C) Activity modification and observation
D) Corticosteroid injection to manage pain
E) Open ACL reconstruction
questions.answer:
B)
In a 22-year-old competitive basketball player with a complete ACL tear, arthroscopic ACL reconstruction is the standard of care. Young, active athletes who wish to return to cutting and pivoting sports require surgical reconstruction to restore knee stability and reduce the risk of secondary meniscal and chondral injuries. Arthroscopic techniques are preferred due to lower morbidity, better visualization, and faster recovery compared to open approaches.

A is incorrect because nonoperative management with bracing and rehabilitation alone is unlikely to provide sufficient knee stability for return to high-level pivoting sports and carries a high risk of recurrent instability and secondary meniscal tears. C is incorrect because activity modification and observation are appropriate for low-demand patients but not for a young competitive athlete who intends to return to sport. D is incorrect because corticosteroid injection addresses only pain and inflammation temporarily and does nothing to restore the mechanical stability lost with a complete ACL tear. E is incorrect because open ACL reconstruction is rarely performed today; arthroscopic reconstruction is the gold standard, offering equivalent or superior outcomes with less surgical morbidity.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe pain and swelling in his right lower leg after a crush injury from a heavy object. On examination, his leg is tense, and he has diminished sensation in his foot. Which of the following imaging findings is most likely to confirm the diagnosis of compartment syndrome?
A) Increased muscle density on MRI
B) Increased fluid signal on T2-weighted MRI
C) Bone marrow edema on CT
D) Muscle atrophy on x-ray
questions.answer:
B)
Explanation: Increased fluid signal on T2-weighted MRI indicates edema within the muscle compartments, which is consistent with compartment syndrome. Other imaging modalities may show different findings, but the increase in fluid signal is a direct indicator of the condition.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old male presents after a workplace accident where he caught his hand in a machine. He reports pain and swelling in his thumb. Examination reveals tenderness along the ulnar side of the metacarpophalangeal joint and a positive valgus stress test. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) MRI of the thumb
B) Surgical repair of the UCL
C) Buddy taping of the thumb
D) Splinting of the thumb in extension
questions.answer:
B)
Explanation: The positive valgus stress test indicates a potential injury to the ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) of the thumb. Given the mechanism of injury and the presence of instability, surgical repair is often indicated to restore the function of the thumb, especially if there is significant joint instability or if the injury is chronic.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman with a history of osteoporosis presents to the clinic with worsening hip pain and a recent x-ray shows an atypical femur fracture. Which of the following features is most suggestive of this type of fracture?
A) Comminution of the fracture
B) Fracture line perpendicular to the long axis of the bone
C) Fracture located in the proximal third of the femur
D) Presence of a spiral fracture pattern
E) Lack of trauma history
questions.answer:
B)
Atypical femur fractures (AFFs), as defined by the ASBMR task force, characteristically demonstrate a transverse fracture line that is perpendicular (or near-perpendicular) to the long axis of the femoral shaft, often with lateral cortical beaking and periosteal thickening. They are associated with prolonged bisphosphonate use and occur with minimal or no trauma.

A is incorrect because comminution is a feature of high-energy or typical osteoporotic fractures; AFFs are characteristically non-comminuted or minimally comminuted.
C is incorrect because AFFs are located in the subtrochanteric region or femoral shaft (from just distal to the lesser trochanter to just proximal to the supracondylar flare), not the proximal third (e.g., femoral neck or intertrochanteric region).
D is incorrect because a spiral fracture pattern implies a rotational mechanism and is not a feature of AFFs, which show transverse or short oblique configurations.
E is incorrect because while AFFs may occur with minimal trauma, the lack of trauma history alone is not the most distinguishing radiographic feature; the transverse fracture morphology with cortical beaking is the hallmark finding.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old male presents with a fractured femur after a motor vehicle accident. On examination, he has notable pain and swelling in the distal thigh. An x-ray reveals a mid-shaft femoral fracture. What is a potential complication of this type of fracture that might affect his recovery?
A) Avascular necrosis
B) Stiffness and loss of range of motion
C) Non-union
D) Compartment syndrome
questions.answer:
C)
Non-union is a recognized potential complication of femoral shaft fractures, particularly if fixation is inadequate, there is significant comminution, or soft tissue stripping occurs. While femoral shaft fractures generally have high union rates with intramedullary nailing, non-union remains a clinically significant complication that can substantially affect recovery.

A is incorrect because avascular necrosis is primarily associated with femoral neck fractures (disruption of the medial femoral circumflex artery supply to the femoral head), not mid-shaft femoral fractures. B is incorrect because while stiffness and loss of range of motion can occur (particularly at the knee), this is a general rehabilitation concern rather than a complication specific to the fracture biology of mid-shaft femoral fractures. D is incorrect because compartment syndrome of the thigh, although possible, is uncommon with isolated femoral shaft fractures and is more classically associated with tibial fractures; it is less specific to this fracture pattern than non-union.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old male with a history of osteoporosis presents with acute back pain after a fall. Imaging reveals a compression fracture of the thoracic vertebrae. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for managing his pain?
A) Corticosteroids
B) Opioids
C) Bracing
D) Physical therapy
questions.answer:
C)
For an acute osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture, initial management centers on conservative treatment including bracing (e.g., a thoracolumbosacral orthosis), analgesics (acetaminophen/NSAIDs as first-line), and activity modification. Bracing provides mechanical support, limits painful motion, and is a cornerstone of early fracture management.

A is incorrect because corticosteroids are not indicated for compression fracture pain management; they can worsen osteoporosis and impair fracture healing.
B is incorrect because opioids are not first-line therapy for compression fractures; they carry significant risks (sedation, falls, dependence) especially in elderly patients and are reserved for pain refractory to non-opioid measures.
D is incorrect because physical therapy is an important component of rehabilitation but is typically introduced after the acute pain phase has been controlled; it is not the most appropriate initial treatment.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents with weakness in her right hand and difficulty with fine motor tasks. She has a history of repetitive overhead activities and now notes tingling in her thumb, index, and middle fingers. Physical examination reveals a positive Tinel's sign at the elbow. Which structure is likely compressing the median nerve in this patient?
A) Biceps aponeurosis
B) Ligament of Struthers
C) Pronator teres
D) Flexor retinaculum
questions.answer:
C)
The pronator teres is the most common site of median nerve compression at the proximal forearm (pronator syndrome). Repetitive overhead and pronation/supination activities predispose to this condition. Patients present with forearm aching, weakness of fine motor tasks, and paresthesias in the median nerve distribution (thumb, index, and middle fingers). A positive Tinel's sign over the proximal forearm/elbow region supports the diagnosis.

A is incorrect because the biceps aponeurosis (lacertus fibrosus) can compress the median nerve but is a less common site than the pronator teres and typically presents with pain exacerbated by resisted elbow flexion and supination.
B is incorrect because the ligament of Struthers is a rare anatomic variant arising from a supracondylar process; it is an uncommon cause of median nerve compression.
D is incorrect because the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament) compresses the median nerve at the wrist (carpal tunnel syndrome), not at the elbow/proximal forearm.

questions.question:
A 36-year-old female presents with hip pain after a low-energy fall. She has a history of rheumatoid arthritis and is on long-term corticosteroid therapy. X-rays reveal a femoral head fracture. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Conservative management with crutches
B) Surgical repair with internal fixation
C) Total hip arthroplasty
D) Joint aspiration and corticosteroid injection
E) Refer for physical therapy
questions.answer:
B)
Surgical repair with internal fixation is the most appropriate next step in managing a femoral head fracture, especially in a young patient. Total hip arthroplasty is typically reserved for cases with significant displacement or in older patients.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman complains of pain in her foot that worsens with weight-bearing activities. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal joint, and an MRI confirms inflammation of the surrounding soft tissues. Which structure is primarily involved in this area and is responsible for stabilizing the joint during the mid-stance phase of gait?
A) Tibialis posterior
B) Tibialis anterior
C) Lisfranc ligament
D) Flexor hallucis longus
questions.answer:
A)
The tibialis posterior tendon inserts broadly on the navicular, cuneiforms, and metatarsal bases and is the primary dynamic stabilizer of the medial longitudinal arch during the mid-stance phase of gait. Dysfunction of this tendon leads to progressive flatfoot deformity and pain over the medial midfoot, consistent with the clinical scenario described.

B is incorrect because the tibialis anterior inserts on the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal base and functions primarily as a dorsiflexor during the swing phase; it plays a lesser role in mid-stance arch stabilization compared with the tibialis posterior. C is incorrect because the Lisfranc ligament is a static interosseous ligament connecting the medial cuneiform to the base of the second metatarsal; while it stabilizes the tarsometatarsal complex, it does not dynamically stabilize the first metatarsal–cuneiform joint during mid-stance gait. D is incorrect because the flexor hallucis longus acts primarily on the great toe (hallux flexion) and runs along the plantar aspect of the foot; it does not primarily stabilize the medial cuneiform–first metatarsal joint during mid-stance.

questions.question:
A 68-year-old man presents with progressive thigh pain and difficulty bearing weight 3 years after a primary total hip arthroplasty. Imaging demonstrates loosening of the femoral component with periosteal reaction and cortical erosion. Laboratory studies show an elevated ESR (55 mm/hr) and CRP (35 mg/L). Hip aspiration yields a turbid fluid with a WBC count of 28,000 cells/μL (>80% PMNs) and cultures grow coagulase-negative Staphylococcus. What is the most appropriate surgical management?
A) Single-stage revision with immediate re-implantation of a new femoral component
B) Two-stage revision arthroplasty
C) Conservative management with suppressive antibiotics and physical therapy
D) Revision with a cemented femoral component without antibiotic spacer
questions.answer:
B)
In the setting of a confirmed periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) — evidenced by elevated inflammatory markers, positive aspirate cell count, and positive cultures — a two-stage revision arthroplasty is the gold-standard treatment in North America. The first stage involves explantation of all components, thorough debridement, and placement of an antibiotic-impregnated cement spacer, followed by a course of IV antibiotics. The second stage involves re-implantation once infection has been eradicated.

A is incorrect because single-stage (direct) exchange carries a higher reinfection risk for most organisms in the North American practice setting and is not the standard of care when infection is confirmed with a virulent or biofilm-forming organism.
C is incorrect because conservative management with suppressive antibiotics alone does not address the loose, infected implant and is reserved for patients who are not surgical candidates.
D is incorrect because revision without an antibiotic spacer stage fails to adequately treat the infection before re-implantation, leading to a high rate of persistent or recurrent infection.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman comes to the clinic with complaints of numbness and tingling in her thumb, index, and middle fingers, particularly when driving. An EMG study reveals prolonged sensory and motor latencies. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Surgical decompression of the carpal tunnel
B) Corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel
C) Wrist splinting at night
D) Activity modification
questions.answer:
A)
Explanation: Given the prolonged sensory and motor latencies on the EMG, which indicate significant median nerve entrapment, surgical decompression is warranted to relieve symptoms and prevent further nerve damage. Conservative measures may have been appropriate earlier in the process, but the findings suggest a more advanced stage of carpal tunnel syndrome.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old male presents with pain and swelling in his right thigh after a direct blow during football practice. Clinical examination indicates a positive FABER test, and imaging shows a fracture in the femoral neck. Which of the following represents the correct sequence of the FABER test for assessing hip dysfunction?
A) Flexion, Abduction, External Rotation
B) Flexion, Adduction, Internal Rotation
C) Extension, Abduction, Internal Rotation
D) Flexion, Abduction, Internal Rotation
questions.answer:
A)
The FABER test stands for Flexion, Abduction, and External Rotation. It is performed by placing the patient's foot on the opposite knee (creating a figure-of-four position), which combines hip flexion, abduction, and external rotation. Pain reproduced in the hip or sacroiliac region helps differentiate hip joint pathology from lumbar spine issues.

B is incorrect because it lists Adduction and Internal Rotation; the FABER test specifically involves abduction and external rotation, not adduction or internal rotation.
C is incorrect because it begins with Extension; the FABER test begins with Flexion (the 'F' in FABER).
D is incorrect because it lists Internal Rotation; the 'ER' in FABER stands for External Rotation, not Internal Rotation.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a fall from a height. He has neck pain and weakness in his hands. CT imaging reveals a fracture at the C3 level with potential spinal cord involvement. Which of the following is the most critical detail to assess in this patient’s examination?
A) Range of motion of the neck
B) Deep tendon reflexes
C) Sensory level
D) Presence of clonus
questions.answer:
C)
Assessing the sensory level is critical in this scenario to determine the extent of spinal cord injury and potential deficits. This information helps guide immediate management and surgical planning, especially in the context of a traumatic cervical spine injury. A is incorrect because range of motion assessment is contraindicated in acute cervical spine trauma due to risk of exacerbating injury. B is incorrect because while deep tendon reflexes can provide information about neurological function, they are less immediately critical than determining the sensory level. D is incorrect because clonus assessment is less relevant in the acute setting of cervical spine trauma compared to sensory level assessment.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency department with neck pain and difficulty swallowing after a motor vehicle accident. Imaging reveals a fracture of the C6 vertebrae. Upon surgical intervention, which structure must be carefully retracted to avoid injury during an anterior approach to the cervical spine?
A) Longus colli muscle
B) Sympathetic chain
C) Recurrent laryngeal nerve
D) Thyroid cartilage
questions.answer:
C)
During an anterior approach to the cervical spine, the recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) runs in the tracheoesophageal groove and is at significant risk of injury, particularly on the right side where its course is more variable. Injury leads to vocal cord paralysis, hoarseness, and potentially airway compromise. Careful identification and gentle retraction of surrounding soft tissues is essential to protect it.

A is incorrect because the longus colli muscle is a midline prevertebral structure that is routinely elevated subperiosteally off the vertebral body to place retractors; while it is dissected, it is not the critical structure at risk of injury — rather, retractors placed deep to it help protect other structures.

B is incorrect because the sympathetic chain lies on the longus colli laterally and can be injured if dissection extends too far laterally, but it is not a structure that is "retracted" during the approach; injury causes Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), and it is protected by keeping dissection midline.

D is incorrect because the thyroid cartilage is a laryngeal framework structure that serves as an anatomic landmark (e.g., C4-C5 level) but is not a structure that requires retraction during the anterior cervical approach.

questions.question:
A patient presents with severe pain in the sacroiliac region after a fall. Physical examination reveals a positive Patrick's test. An MRI shows a disruption of the posterior sacroiliac complex. Which ligament is the primary stabilizer of the pelvis that might be compromised in this injury?
A) Anterior sacroiliac ligament
B) Sacrotuberous ligament
C) Posterior sacroiliac ligament
D) Iliolumbar ligament
questions.answer:
C)
The posterior sacroiliac ligament complex (including the interosseous sacroiliac ligament) is the strongest and primary stabilizer of the sacroiliac joint, resisting vertical shear and rotational forces. Disruption of this complex, as described on MRI, leads to significant pelvic instability and sacroiliac pain.

A is incorrect because the anterior sacroiliac ligament is a relatively thin structure that provides only minor restraint to external rotation; it is not the primary stabilizer of the pelvis.
B is incorrect because the sacrotuberous ligament is a secondary stabilizer that resists nutation and vertical shear but is not the primary stabilizer of the SI joint.
D is incorrect because the iliolumbar ligament connects L4-L5 to the iliac crest and primarily stabilizes the lumbosacral junction, not the sacroiliac joint itself.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman presents with pain and deformity at the base of the fifth toe. Physical examination reveals a lateral deviation of the fifth toe and tenderness over the metatarsal head. An x-ray confirms a bunionette deformity. Which surgical procedure is most appropriate for the correction of this condition?
A) Lapidus procedure
B) Modified McBride procedure
C) Lateral condylectomy
D) Fifth metatarsal osteotomy
E) Ankle arthrodesis
questions.answer:
D)
A fifth metatarsal osteotomy (e.g., distal chevron, oblique diaphyseal, or proximal osteotomy depending on the deformity) is the most appropriate surgical procedure for bunionette (tailor's bunion) correction. It addresses the underlying bony malalignment by reducing the 4-5 intermetatarsal angle and correcting the lateral prominence of the fifth metatarsal head, thereby relieving pain and correcting the deformity.

A is incorrect because the Lapidus procedure is a first tarsometatarsal arthrodesis used for hallux valgus correction, not for bunionette deformity. B is incorrect because the modified McBride procedure involves soft-tissue correction (adductor hallucis release, medial capsulorrhaphy) for hallux valgus and is not applicable to fifth toe pathology. C is incorrect because lateral condylectomy (shaving the lateral condyle of the fifth metatarsal head) may provide symptomatic relief in mild cases with only a lateral condylar prominence, but it does not correct the underlying angular deformity and is not the most appropriate procedure for a true bunionette with lateral deviation. E is incorrect because ankle arthrodesis is used for end-stage ankle arthritis and has no role in the treatment of bunionette deformity.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old female with a history of fibrous dysplasia presents with an increasing pain in her left femur. Imaging shows a new lytic lesion within the fibrous dysplastic area, raising concern for malignant transformation. Which of the following imaging modalities would be most useful in assessing for malignant transformation?
A) X-ray
B) MRI
C) CT scan
D) PET-CT
questions.answer:
D)
Explanation: A PET-CT scan is useful for evaluating metabolic activity and identifying malignant transformation, which is critical in this case of fibrous dysplasia. The presence of new lytic lesions combined with increased metabolic activity on PET may indicate transformation to osteosarcoma or another malignancy.

questions.question:
During a surgical procedure, you are using a bone graft to enhance healing in a non-union fracture. The graft is expected to provide a scaffold for new bone formation. What property of the graft is primarily responsible for facilitating the growth of new bone?
A) Osteoclast activation
B) Osteoconductivity
C) Osteoinduction
D) Osteogenesis
questions.answer:
B)
Osteoconductivity is the property by which a graft material serves as a scaffold that supports the ingrowth of blood vessels and the migration of osteoblasts, allowing new bone to form along and within its structure. When the stem describes a graft providing a "scaffold for new bone formation," it is defining osteoconductivity.

A is incorrect because osteoclast activation refers to bone resorption, not new bone formation; it is not a recognized graft property that facilitates healing.
C is incorrect because osteoinduction is the ability of a graft to recruit and stimulate undifferentiated mesenchymal stem cells to differentiate into osteoblasts (mediated by growth factors such as BMPs), rather than simply providing a physical scaffold.
D is incorrect because osteogenesis refers to the graft itself containing living osteoprogenitor cells that directly form new bone; the stem specifically describes a scaffold function, not the contribution of living cells.

questions.question:
A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department with a limp and swelling in her right hip following a fall while playing. The physician is concerned about the possibility of septic arthritis. Using the Kocher criteria, which score indicates the highest likelihood of septic arthritis?
A) 0
B) 1
C) 2
D) 3
questions.answer:
D)
The Kocher criteria assign one point each for: (1) fever >38.5°C, (2) non–weight-bearing, (3) ESR >40 mm/hr, and (4) WBC >12,000/mm³. A score of 3 corresponds to a ~93% predicted probability of septic arthritis, and a score of 4 approaches ~99.6%. Among the choices listed, a score of 3 represents the highest likelihood of septic arthritis.

A is incorrect because a Kocher score of 0 corresponds to a <0.2% probability of septic arthritis, indicating very low risk. B is incorrect because a score of 1 corresponds to approximately 3% probability, still low risk. C is incorrect because a score of 2 corresponds to approximately 40% probability, which is moderate but not the highest likelihood among the options listed.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male presents with pain in the medial aspect of the foot after a fall. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the spring ligament. Which of the following is the main function of the spring ligament in the context of foot biomechanics?
A) Support the medial longitudinal arch
B) Stabilize the ankle joint
C) Assist in dorsiflexion of the foot
D) Protect the posterior tibial tendon
questions.answer:
A)
The spring (plantar calcaneonavicular) ligament is the primary static stabilizer of the medial longitudinal arch. It spans from the sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus to the navicular, supporting the head of the talus from below. Injury or attenuation of this ligament contributes to progressive flatfoot deformity.

B is incorrect because the spring ligament does not stabilize the ankle joint; ankle stability is primarily provided by the deltoid ligament medially and the lateral ligament complex (ATFL, CFL, PTFL) laterally.
C is incorrect because the spring ligament has no role in dorsiflexion of the foot; dorsiflexion is performed by the tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, and extensor digitorum longus.
D is incorrect because while the spring ligament and posterior tibial tendon work synergistically to maintain the arch, the spring ligament's primary function is arch support, not protection of the posterior tibial tendon.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male with chronic kidney disease presents with bone pain and deformities. Imaging studies show brown tumors in the pelvis and ribs. Which of the following pathophysiological processes is most likely responsible for these findings?
A) Osteoblastic tumor formation
B) Secondary hyperparathyroidism
C) Primary osteoporosis
D) Paget's disease of bone
questions.answer:
B)
Brown tumors (osteitis fibrosa cystica) result from secondary hyperparathyroidism, which is a well-known complication of chronic kidney disease. Impaired renal phosphate excretion and decreased 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D production lead to hypocalcemia, which stimulates parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion. Chronically elevated PTH causes excessive osteoclastic bone resorption, resulting in lytic lesions filled with fibrous tissue and hemosiderin-laden macrophages — the characteristic brown tumors.

A is incorrect because brown tumors are not true neoplasms and are not formed by osteoblastic tumor activity; they are reactive, reparative lesions resulting from excessive osteoclast-mediated resorption.

C is incorrect because primary osteoporosis causes diffuse bone loss with decreased bone density but does not produce focal lytic lesions or brown tumors.

D is incorrect because Paget's disease of bone is characterized by disorganized bone remodeling with a mosaic pattern of lamellar bone, cortical thickening, and bone enlargement — not brown tumors. Paget's disease is also not associated with chronic kidney disease.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man, a self-described "weekend warrior," presents with acute onset of severe pain in the back of his ankle after playing tennis. He cannot stand on his toes and has a palpable defect in the Achilles tendon. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Achilles tendinitis
B) Achilles tendon rupture
C) Gastrocnemius strain
D) Plantar fasciitis
E) Calcaneal fracture
questions.answer:
B)
The presentation is classic for an acute Achilles tendon rupture: a middle-aged recreational athlete with sudden onset of severe posterior ankle pain, inability to perform a single-leg toe raise, and a palpable gap in the tendon. A positive Thompson test (absence of plantarflexion with calf squeeze) would further confirm the diagnosis.

A is incorrect because Achilles tendinitis is a chronic overuse condition characterized by gradual-onset pain and tendon thickening, not an acute event with a palpable defect and loss of plantarflexion strength.
C is incorrect because a gastrocnemius strain ("tennis leg") typically presents with pain in the mid-calf at the musculotendinous junction, not a palpable defect in the Achilles tendon itself, and toe-raise ability is usually preserved.
D is incorrect because plantar fasciitis causes plantar heel pain, classically worse with the first steps in the morning, and does not produce a posterior ankle defect or loss of push-off strength.
E is incorrect because a calcaneal fracture typically results from an axial-loading mechanism (e.g., fall from height), presents with heel swelling and ecchymosis, and would not produce a palpable gap in the Achilles tendon.

questions.question:
During a research study investigating a new surgical technique for rotator cuff repair, a Type I error occurs. What does this indicate about the study's findings?
A) The study failed to detect an actual effect of the surgery.
B) The study incorrectly concluded that the surgery is effective when it is not.
C) The study showed no difference in outcomes between the new technique and traditional methods.
D) The study's sample size was too small to achieve reliable results.
questions.answer:
B)
A Type I error (false positive, α error) occurs when the null hypothesis is incorrectly rejected, meaning the study falsely concluded that the new rotator cuff repair technique is effective when, in reality, there is no true difference. This underscores the importance of setting an appropriate significance level (typically α = 0.05) and using rigorous statistical methods.

A is incorrect because failing to detect an actual effect describes a Type II error (false negative, β error), not a Type I error.
C is incorrect because finding no difference in outcomes would represent a failure to reject the null hypothesis, which is not an error per se (or could be a Type II error if a real difference exists).
D is incorrect because an inadequate sample size relates to statistical power and increases the risk of a Type II error, but it does not define a Type I error.

questions.question:
A 75-year-old female is seen in the emergency department after a fall. She has significant pain and swelling in her right shoulder, and her arm is held in a position of adduction. X-rays show an acromioclavicular joint dislocation with superior displacement of the distal clavicle and widening of the coracoclavicular distance to 100% compared to the contralateral side. What is the Rockwood classification of her injury?
A) Type I
B) Type II
C) Type III
D) Type IV
questions.answer:
C)
A Rockwood Type III acromioclavicular joint injury involves complete disruption of both the acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular ligaments, resulting in superior displacement of the distal clavicle (up to 100% increase in coracoclavicular distance compared to the normal side). This is the most common high-grade AC joint injury pattern tested on boards.
