A 30-year-old male construction worker presents with shoulder pain following a fall from height. X-rays show a fracture involving the glenoid fossa of the scapula. Given the fracture location, which classification is most applicable to this patient's fracture?
A) Ideberg classification
B) Neer classification
C) AO classification
D) Gustilo classification
questions.answer:
A)
The Ideberg classification is specifically designed to categorize intra-articular glenoid fractures based on fracture pattern and extent of involvement (Types I–V, later expanded by Goss). It is the most commonly referenced classification for glenoid fossa fractures and helps guide surgical versus nonoperative management.

B is incorrect because the Neer classification is used for proximal humerus fractures, categorizing them by the number of displaced parts (greater tuberosity, lesser tuberosity, articular segment, shaft). C is incorrect because while the AO/OTA classification can be applied broadly to many fractures including the scapula, the Ideberg classification is the most specific and widely used system for glenoid fractures on board examinations. D is incorrect because the Gustilo classification is used for open fractures to grade the severity of soft-tissue injury, not for classifying scapular or glenoid fracture patterns.

questions.question:
A 10-year-old boy falls from his bicycle and presents with severe pain in his forearm. Upon examination, his arm is swollen, and he exhibits limited range of motion. X-rays reveal an incomplete fracture of the distal radius with cortical disruption on only one side. Which of the following best describes this type of injury?
A) Greenstick fracture
B) Galeazzi fracture
C) Colles fracture
D) Jersey finger
questions.answer:
A)
A greenstick fracture is an incomplete fracture seen in the pediatric population in which the bone bends and breaks on the tension side while the cortex on the compression side remains intact. This pattern is characteristic of the immature, porous bone of children. The mechanism of a fall from a bicycle in a 10-year-old with an incomplete cortical disruption is classic for a greenstick fracture.

B is incorrect because a Galeazzi fracture is a fracture of the radial shaft with associated dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ), which is not described here. C is incorrect because a Colles fracture is a complete, dorsally displaced fracture of the distal radius typically seen in adults after a fall on an outstretched hand, not an incomplete pediatric fracture. D is incorrect because a jersey finger is an avulsion of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon from the distal phalanx of a finger, which is a soft-tissue injury unrelated to forearm fractures.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman presents with shoulder pain and weakness after a fall. She is unable to raise her arm above shoulder level and has marked atrophy of the supraspinatus muscle. An ultrasound demonstrates a chronic rotator cuff tear. What is the most appropriate surgical approach for repairing this type of tear?
A) Anterior approach
B) Posterior approach
C) Lateral approach
D) Arthroscopic approach
questions.answer:
D)
Arthroscopic rotator cuff repair is the most appropriate surgical approach for rotator cuff tears. It provides superior visualization of the glenohumeral joint and subacromial space, causes less soft tissue disruption than open techniques, and is associated with less postoperative pain and faster rehabilitation.

A is incorrect because the anterior (deltopectoral) approach is used primarily for shoulder arthroplasty, fracture fixation, or subscapularis repairs, not as the standard approach for supraspinatus rotator cuff repair.

B is incorrect because a posterior approach to the shoulder is used for posterior instability procedures or certain fractures, not for rotator cuff repair.

C is incorrect because while a mini-open lateral (deltoid-splitting) approach can be used for rotator cuff repair, arthroscopic repair has become the preferred technique due to less morbidity, better visualization, and the ability to address concomitant intra-articular pathology.

questions.question:
During a surgical procedure on the forearm, the surgeon identifies a fibrous structure that provides stability to the flexor tendons of the wrist. What is this structure called, and what is its clinical significance?
A) Flexor retinaculum; prevents bowstringing of tendons
B) Lacertus fibrosis; protects the median nerve
C) Extensor retinaculum; stabilizes extensor tendons
D) Palmaris longus; acts as a tendon graft
questions.answer:
A)
The flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament) is a thick fibrous band spanning the carpal bones on the palmar side of the wrist. It holds the flexor tendons in place during wrist and finger flexion, preventing bowstringing, and forms the roof of the carpal tunnel.

B is incorrect because the lacertus fibrosus (bicipital aponeurosis) is a fascial expansion of the biceps tendon in the antecubital fossa; it does not stabilize the flexor tendons at the wrist.
C is incorrect because the extensor retinaculum is located on the dorsal side of the wrist and stabilizes the extensor tendons, not the flexor tendons.
D is incorrect because the palmaris longus is a vestigial muscle/tendon commonly harvested as a tendon graft; it is not a retinacular stabilizing structure for the flexor tendons.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman presents with pain and tingling in her ring and little fingers after working long hours at a computer. On examination, you note a positive Tinel's sign at the elbow and decreased sensation in the ulnar nerve distribution. Which of the following best describes the underlying mechanism of her symptoms?
A) Compression of the median nerve at the wrist
B) Entrapment of the ulnar nerve in the cubital tunnel
C) Injury to the radial nerve at the mid-humerus
D) Thoracic outlet syndrome affecting the brachial plexus
questions.answer:
B)
The patient's symptoms — pain and tingling in the ring and little fingers, a positive Tinel's sign at the elbow, and decreased sensation in the ulnar nerve distribution — are classic for cubital tunnel syndrome. This condition results from compression or entrapment of the ulnar nerve as it passes through the cubital tunnel (formed by the medial epicondyle and the olecranon with the overlying Osborne ligament). Prolonged elbow flexion during computer work increases pressure within the tunnel, exacerbating symptoms.

A is incorrect because compression of the median nerve at the wrist (carpal tunnel syndrome) causes numbness in the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger — not the ulnar 1½ digits — and Tinel's sign would be at the wrist, not the elbow.
C is incorrect because radial nerve injury at the mid-humerus causes wrist and finger drop (motor) and sensory loss over the dorsal first web space, not ulnar-sided finger symptoms.
D is incorrect because thoracic outlet syndrome can affect the lower trunk/medial cord of the brachial plexus and mimic ulnar symptoms, but it would not produce a positive Tinel's sign specifically at the elbow; symptoms are typically provoked by overhead arm positioning and may include vascular findings.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old man presents with pain and swelling over the hypothenar eminence after a fall. Physical examination reveals tenderness along the ulnar side of the wrist and an inability to oppose the little finger. An MRI shows an injury to the muscle responsible for this action. Which muscle is primarily involved, and what is its nerve supply?
A) Flexor digiti minimi brevis; median nerve
B) Opponens digiti minimi; ulnar nerve
C) Abductor digiti minimi; radial nerve
D) Flexor digiti minimi longus; ulnar nerve
questions.answer:
B)
The opponens digiti minimi is the hypothenar muscle responsible for opposition of the little finger (cupping the palm). It is innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. Injury to this muscle explains the inability to oppose the little finger along with hypothenar pain and swelling.

A is incorrect because the flexor digiti minimi brevis flexes the MCP joint of the little finger (not opposition) and is innervated by the ulnar nerve, not the median nerve. C is incorrect because the abductor digiti minimi abducts the little finger and is innervated by the ulnar nerve, not the radial nerve. D is incorrect because there is no muscle called 'flexor digiti minimi longus'; this is a fabricated option.

questions.question:
A 16-year-old female athlete presents with increasing back pain and difficulty with certain movements. She has a known diagnosis of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis with a Cobb angle of 50 degrees. After discussing treatment options, she opts for surgical intervention. Which surgical approach is typically utilized for correction of a thoracolumbar scoliosis?
A) Anterior approach
B) Posterior approach
C) Lateral approach
D) Open thoracotomy
questions.answer:
B)
The posterior approach with pedicle screw instrumentation is the most commonly utilized surgical approach for correction of thoracolumbar scoliosis in current practice. Modern pedicle screw constructs provide excellent three-column fixation and powerful correction, and the posterior approach avoids the morbidity associated with thoracotomy or thoracoabdominal exposures. While anterior approaches were historically favored for thoracolumbar curves to spare distal fusion levels, posterior-only surgery has become the predominant technique.

A is incorrect because although the anterior approach was historically used for thoracolumbar curves (offering fewer fused segments), it carries greater morbidity including diaphragm takedown, pulmonary complications, and vascular risks, and has been largely supplanted by posterior techniques. C is incorrect because a lateral-only approach does not provide adequate access for long-segment scoliosis correction and instrumentation. D is incorrect because open thoracotomy is an access approach (used in anterior surgery) rather than a definitive correction strategy, and it carries significant pulmonary morbidity.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male presents with severe pain, swelling, and inability to bear weight on his right foot after an ankle injury during basketball. X-rays show widening of the syndesmosis. What is the most likely mechanism of injury that led to this condition?
A) Dorsiflexion and external rotation
B) Plantarflexion and inversion
C) Direct trauma to the lateral ankle
D) Plantarflexion and external rotation
questions.answer:
A)
Dorsiflexion combined with external rotation is the classic mechanism for syndesmosis (high ankle sprain) injuries. In this position, the wider anterior portion of the talus is forced into the mortise while external rotation torque stresses the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (AITFL), interosseous membrane, and posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (PITFL), leading to syndesmotic widening.

B is incorrect because plantarflexion and inversion is the typical mechanism for a lateral ankle (low ankle) sprain involving the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL), not the syndesmosis.
C is incorrect because direct trauma to the lateral ankle may cause a fibula fracture or lateral ligament injury but does not produce the rotational stress needed to disrupt the syndesmosis.
D is incorrect because plantarflexion and external rotation can contribute to some ankle injuries (e.g., certain Weber B fracture patterns), but the syndesmosis is most vulnerable in dorsiflexion, when the wider anterior talar body wedges the mortise apart; plantarflexion narrows the mortise and relatively unloads the syndesmotic ligaments.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman with a history of diabetes presents with a non-healing ulcer on the plantar aspect of her foot. She reports increasing pain and difficulty walking. X-rays show osteomyelitis in the fifth metatarsal. Considering the anatomy of the foot, which of the following approaches would best facilitate surgical intervention for this condition?
A) Dorsal approach to the midfoot
B) Medial approach to the first metatarsal
C) Direct lateral approach to the fifth metatarsal
D) Posterolateral approach to the ankle
questions.answer:
C)
The direct lateral approach to the fifth metatarsal provides the most appropriate surgical exposure for debridement or resection of the fifth metatarsal in the setting of osteomyelitis. This approach follows the lateral border of the foot directly over the fifth metatarsal, avoids the weight-bearing surface, and allows adequate visualization for thorough debridement of infected bone.

A is incorrect because the dorsal approach to the midfoot is centered over the central metatarsals and tarsometatarsal joints and does not provide direct or adequate exposure of the fifth metatarsal. B is incorrect because the medial approach to the first metatarsal is on the opposite side of the foot and has no relevance to fifth metatarsal pathology. D is incorrect because the posterolateral approach to the ankle is used for posterior malleolus or distal fibula fractures and does not expose the fifth metatarsal.

questions.question:
A 10-year-old boy who plays Little League baseball presents with medial elbow pain after a season of heavy pitching. Examination shows tenderness over the medial epicondyle and limited range of motion. What is the most likely pathophysiological cause of his symptoms?
A) UCL tear
B) Osteochondritis dissecans
C) Growth plate injury
D) Lateral epicondylitis
questions.answer:
C)
In a skeletally immature 10-year-old pitcher, the medial epicondylar apophysis (growth plate) is biomechanically weaker than the UCL. Repetitive valgus stress from throwing preferentially injures the physis, causing medial epicondyle apophysitis or even avulsion fracture — the hallmark of "Little League elbow." This is the most likely pathophysiological cause of his medial elbow pain and tenderness over the medial epicondyle.

A is incorrect because UCL tears occur in skeletally mature athletes whose ligament is weaker than the surrounding bone; in a 10-year-old the apophysis fails before the UCL. B is incorrect because osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) of the elbow affects the lateral compartment (capitellum), not the medial epicondyle, and presents with lateral elbow pain, catching, or locking. D is incorrect because lateral epicondylitis ("tennis elbow") involves the lateral epicondyle and extensor origin, not the medial side, and is exceedingly rare in children.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old male presents with a painful mass on his right foot that has increased in size over the past few months. MRI shows a soft tissue mass with infiltrative margins, and a biopsy reveals synovial sarcoma. Which imaging modality is most useful in evaluating for metastatic disease?
A) X-ray
B) CT scan of the chest
C) Ultrasound
D) PET-CT
questions.answer:
D)
PET-CT is particularly useful for identifying metastatic disease in cases of synovial sarcoma due to its ability to detect metabolically active lesions throughout the body. B is incorrect because while a CT scan of the chest is important for evaluating pulmonary metastases, it does not assess other potential sites of metastasis. A is incorrect because X-rays are not sensitive for detecting metastatic disease. C is incorrect because ultrasound is not typically used for evaluating metastases.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old male presents to the emergency department after falling onto an outstretched hand while playing basketball. He reports pain and swelling in his wrist, particularly on the thumb side. An x-ray reveals a fracture of the scaphoid. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Apply a short arm cast
B) Obtain a CT scan of the wrist
C) Refer for surgical fixation
D) Initiate physical therapy
E) Administer a splint and discharge
questions.answer:
A)
When a scaphoid fracture is confirmed on plain x-rays and is non-displaced, the standard initial management is immobilization in a thumb spica cast (short arm cast) for approximately 8–12 weeks. This allows healing of the fracture while protecting the scaphoid's tenuous blood supply.

B is incorrect because a CT scan is most useful when x-rays are negative but clinical suspicion remains high (occult fracture), or to evaluate displacement in equivocal cases; here the fracture is already confirmed. C is incorrect because surgical fixation is generally reserved for displaced scaphoid fractures (>1 mm displacement), proximal pole fractures, or cases where the patient requires rapid return to activity; it is not the default first step for a confirmed non-displaced fracture. D is incorrect because initiating physical therapy before fracture healing would risk nonunion and further displacement. E is incorrect because simple splinting and discharge without proper immobilization and follow-up is inadequate management for a confirmed scaphoid fracture, which requires prolonged immobilization and close monitoring.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old female patient presents with worsening hip pain and difficulty walking. She underwent a total hip arthroplasty three years ago. On examination, there is tenderness over the greater trochanter, and she reports start-up pain with ambulation. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
A) Acetabular loosening
B) Trochanteric bursitis
C) Femoral neck fracture
D) Infection
questions.answer:
B)
Trochanteric bursitis is a common cause of lateral hip pain after total hip arthroplasty. Point tenderness directly over the greater trochanter and start-up pain with ambulation are classic findings. It is often related to altered gait mechanics or irritation from hardware.

A is incorrect because acetabular loosening typically presents with groin pain (anterior/medial) that worsens with weight-bearing, and imaging would show progressive radiolucent lines around the acetabular component rather than isolated lateral trochanteric tenderness.
C is incorrect because a periprosthetic femoral neck fracture would present acutely with severe pain, inability to bear weight, and limb shortening/rotation — not the insidious, activity-related lateral pain described here.
D is incorrect because periprosthetic joint infection usually presents with constant pain (rest and activity), may include systemic signs (fever, malaise), and laboratory markers (elevated ESR/CRP) would be expected; isolated trochanteric tenderness is not characteristic.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old girl with severe scoliosis is being considered for treatment with growing rods. What is the primary advantage of using early onset growing rods in this patient's management? 
A) They allow for definitive spinal fusion at a young age. 
B) They can accommodate growth without the need for multiple surgeries. 
C) They are less invasive than traditional spinal fusions. 
D) They eliminate the need for bracing entirely.
questions.answer:
B)
The primary advantage of early onset growing rods is that they accommodate continued spinal and thoracic growth while controlling progressive scoliosis, avoiding the detrimental effects of early definitive fusion on trunk height and pulmonary development. Traditional growing rods do require periodic surgical lengthenings, but magnetically controlled growing rods (MCGR) can reduce the number of operative lengthenings. The overarching benefit is growth preservation.

A is incorrect because the goal of growing rods is specifically to delay or avoid definitive spinal fusion at a young age, as early fusion leads to a short trunk and impaired lung development (thoracic insufficiency syndrome).
C is incorrect because growing rod placement is a significant surgical procedure and is not less invasive than a traditional spinal fusion; in fact, traditional growing rods require multiple return trips to the operating room for lengthening.
D is incorrect because growing rods do not eliminate the need for bracing entirely; adjunctive bracing may still be used, and the decision depends on the individual patient's curve characteristics and clinical course.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician for a routine check-up. She mentions feeling more fatigued recently and has had several muscle cramps. Her physician suspects a vitamin D deficiency. What is the preferred laboratory assay to evaluate her vitamin D status?
A) Serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
B) Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D
C) Serum calcium
D) Serum phosphate
questions.answer:
B)
Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol) is the preferred assay for evaluating vitamin D status because it reflects total body vitamin D stores, has a long circulating half-life (~2–3 weeks), and is not tightly regulated by other hormones, making it the most reliable marker.

A is incorrect because serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) is the active hormonal form but has a very short half-life (hours) and is tightly regulated by PTH, calcium, and phosphate levels; it does not accurately reflect overall vitamin D stores and may remain normal even in deficiency states.
C is incorrect because serum calcium can be affected by many factors (albumin, PTH, renal function) and may remain normal in vitamin D deficiency due to compensatory secondary hyperparathyroidism; it is not a direct measure of vitamin D status.
D is incorrect because serum phosphate, while it may decrease in vitamin D deficiency, is influenced by numerous other factors (diet, renal function, PTH) and is neither sensitive nor specific for assessing vitamin D status.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman presents with difficulty using her index finger following a wrist fracture. During the examination, you note that she cannot flex the distal interphalangeal joint of her index finger. Which tendon is most likely injured?
A) Flexor digitorum superficialis
B) Extensor digitorum
C) Flexor digitorum profundus
D) Extensor indicis
questions.answer:
C)
The flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) is the sole flexor of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint. Injury to the FDP tendon, which can occur with displaced distal radius fractures or associated soft-tissue trauma, results in inability to actively flex the DIP joint of the affected finger.

A is incorrect because the flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) flexes the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint; it does not act on the DIP joint. B is incorrect because the extensor digitorum is an extrinsic finger extensor; its injury would impair MCP extension, not DIP flexion. D is incorrect because the extensor indicis is an independent extensor of the index finger; its injury would impair extension, not flexion of the DIP joint.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old male with osteoarthritis undergoes a total hip arthroplasty. During surgery, the surgeon notes that the inferior border of the acetabular cup is aligned with the ilioischial line. What is the primary goal of this alignment during the procedure?
A) To prevent postoperative dislocation
B) To facilitate proper weight distribution
C) To ensure adequate soft tissue coverage
D) To minimize the risk of hip impingement
questions.answer:
A)
Explanation: Aligning the inferior border of the acetabular cup with the ilioischial line is crucial for achieving proper stability and minimizing the risk of postoperative dislocation. Proper positioning helps ensure that the cup is well-seated within the acetabulum, promoting a stable joint.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male presents with persistent hip pain after undergoing hip resurfacing five years ago. He describes gradual onset pain that has become debilitating. Examination reveals a positive Trendelenburg sign. An MRI shows fluid collection around the femoral component. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Aseptic loosening
B) Infection
C) Osteonecrosis
D) Hip impingement
questions.answer:
A)
Aseptic loosening is a common complication after hip resurfacing, especially if fluid is noted around the implant without signs of infection. The presence of a positive Trendelenburg sign indicates weakness in the hip abductors, which can be associated with implant failure or loosening.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old female presents with increasing thoracic kyphosis and back pain. A lateral x-ray shows multiple vertebral body deformities and loss of height. What is the most likely underlying cause of her condition?
A) Osteoporosis
B) Disc herniation
C) Spondylolisthesis
D) Spinal stenosis
questions.answer:
A)
Osteoporosis is the most common cause of multiple vertebral compression fractures in elderly women, leading to progressive thoracic kyphosis, loss of body height, and back pain. A lateral radiograph showing anterior wedging or biconcave deformities of multiple vertebral bodies in this demographic is highly characteristic of osteoporotic compression fractures.

B is incorrect because disc herniation causes focal neural compression with radiculopathy; it does not produce multiple vertebral body deformities or generalized height loss.

C is incorrect because spondylolisthesis involves anterior translation of one vertebra on another (most commonly at L4–L5 or L5–S1) and does not cause diffuse vertebral body deformities or thoracic kyphosis.

D is incorrect because spinal stenosis refers to narrowing of the spinal canal causing neurogenic claudication or myelopathy; it is not associated with multiple vertebral body compression deformities or progressive kyphosis.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old male athlete sustains a direct blow to the knee during a tackle. He presents with acute knee pain, a large effusion, and inability to actively extend the knee. Imaging reveals a severely comminuted patella fracture that is not amenable to internal fixation. The surgeon discusses the option of a complete patellectomy. What is the most common long-term consequence of a complete patellectomy?
A) Increased risk of osteoarthritis
B) Improved quadriceps strength
C) Enhanced range of motion
D) Decreased patellar tracking issues
questions.answer:
A)
Complete patellectomy removes the mechanical advantage (moment arm) of the extensor mechanism, leading to significant quadriceps weakness (up to 30–50% loss of extension strength). The altered tibiofemoral contact mechanics and increased joint contact pressures predispose the knee to accelerated degenerative changes and osteoarthritis over time.

B is incorrect because patellectomy decreases quadriceps strength by eliminating the fulcrum effect of the patella on the extensor mechanism; it does not improve it. C is incorrect because while some flexion may be preserved, overall functional range of motion is often compromised by extensor lag and weakness, not enhanced. D is incorrect because with the patella removed there is no patellar tracking to discuss; furthermore, the question asks about a negative long-term consequence, and 'decreased patellar tracking issues' would imply a benefit, which is misleading — the real problem is the loss of extensor mechanism efficiency and subsequent degenerative disease.

questions.question:
A 10-year-old girl falls from a height during gymnastics practice and presents with knee pain and swelling. X-rays reveal a non-displaced avulsion fracture at the tibial tubercle with an intact extensor mechanism. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
A) Immediate open reduction and internal fixation
B) Rest and ice only
C) Immobilization in a long-leg cast or knee immobilizer in extension
D) Tibial tubercle reattachment with screws
questions.answer:
C)
Non-displaced tibial tubercle avulsion fractures with an intact extensor mechanism are managed with immobilization in extension (long-leg cast or knee immobilizer) for 4–6 weeks, allowing the fracture to heal while maintaining knee extension alignment.

A is incorrect because open reduction and internal fixation is reserved for displaced fractures (Watson-Jones Type II/III) or those with intra-articular extension, not non-displaced injuries.
B is incorrect because rest and ice alone do not provide adequate immobilization for fracture healing; formal immobilization in extension is required.
D is incorrect because screw fixation is indicated for significantly displaced fractures or those with disruption of the extensor mechanism, not for non-displaced avulsions.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old woman who underwent a hip resurfacing arthroplasty three years ago presents with hip pain and swelling. An aspiration of the joint reveals cloudy synovial fluid with elevated white blood cell count. What is the most important next step in management?
A) Start antibiotics immediately
B) Obtain additional imaging studies
C) Schedule for revision surgery
D) Perform a thorough laboratory workup
questions.answer:
D)
Cloudy synovial fluid with an elevated white blood cell count after hip resurfacing is highly suspicious for periprosthetic joint infection (PJI). The most important next step is a thorough laboratory workup including serum ESR, CRP, synovial fluid culture with sensitivities, cell count with differential, and potentially alpha-defensin or leukocyte esterase. Identifying the causative organism is essential before initiating targeted antibiotic therapy and planning definitive surgical management.

A is incorrect because starting empiric antibiotics before obtaining adequate cultures can obscure the infecting organism, making subsequent treatment decisions (antibiotic selection, single- vs. two-stage revision) more difficult. Antibiotics should be withheld until cultures are secured unless the patient is systemically septic. B is incorrect because while additional imaging (e.g., bone scan, CT) may provide supplementary information, the aspiration findings already strongly suggest infection, and confirming the diagnosis with laboratory studies takes priority. C is incorrect because scheduling revision surgery without first confirming the diagnosis, identifying the organism, and planning the appropriate revision strategy (one-stage vs. two-stage exchange) is premature.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman presents with a history of knee instability after suffering an ACL injury. The surgeon plans to perform an ACL reconstruction using a Bone-Patellar Tendon-Bone (BTB) graft. What is a primary advantage of using a BTB graft over a hamstring graft?
A) Faster recovery time
B) Lower risk of re-tear
C) Bone-to-bone healing leading to faster integration
D) Less postoperative pain
questions.answer:
C)
A primary advantage of the Bone-Patellar Tendon-Bone (BTB) graft is bone-to-bone healing at the graft–tunnel interface, which allows faster and more rigid biological fixation compared to the soft-tissue-to-bone healing required by hamstring tendon grafts. This earlier integration can enhance initial graft stability.

A is incorrect because BTB grafts are generally associated with a slower return to full activity due to anterior knee pain and donor-site morbidity, not a faster recovery time.
B is incorrect because while some studies suggest lower re-rupture rates with BTB grafts, the most consistently cited primary advantage on board examinations is bone-to-bone healing, not re-tear rate; furthermore, re-tear risk is multifactorial and study-dependent.
D is incorrect because BTB grafts are well known for causing more postoperative anterior knee pain (e.g., kneeling pain, patellar tendinitis) compared to hamstring grafts, making this the opposite of a BTB advantage.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male presents with persistent right shoulder pain following a dislocation that occurred during a sports activity. He is unable to lift his arm, and physical examination suggests a possible rotator cuff tear. Which imaging modality is crucial for assessing associated injuries after a shoulder dislocation?
A) X-ray of the shoulder
B) MRI of the shoulder
C) CT scan of the shoulder
D) Ultrasound of the shoulder
questions.answer:
B)
MRI is the imaging modality of choice for evaluating soft tissue injuries following shoulder dislocation, including rotator cuff tears, labral tears (Bankart lesions), and capsular injury. In a 30-year-old with inability to lift the arm after dislocation, MRI provides the detailed soft tissue contrast needed to guide surgical decision-making.

A is incorrect because while plain radiographs are important as an initial study to confirm reduction and identify fractures (e.g., Hill-Sachs, greater tuberosity), they cannot adequately assess soft tissue structures such as the rotator cuff or labrum. C is incorrect because CT is superior for bony detail (e.g., glenoid bone loss, Hill-Sachs quantification) but does not provide the soft tissue resolution needed to diagnose rotator cuff or labral tears. D is incorrect because ultrasound can detect rotator cuff tears but is operator-dependent, cannot evaluate intra-articular structures such as the labrum, and is less comprehensive than MRI for the full spectrum of post-dislocation pathology.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old woman presents with progressive knee pain and instability. She has a history of multiple knee surgeries for meniscal tears. Physical examination reveals a varus deformity and tenderness along the lateral joint line. MRI shows damage to the arcuate ligament complex. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Physical therapy
B) Arthroscopic debridement
C) Osteotomy
D) Total knee arthroplasty
questions.answer:
C)
Given the patient's history of multiple surgeries and the presence of a varus deformity, an osteotomy would effectively address the alignment issue and relieve symptoms associated with lateral compartment arthritis, particularly when the arcuate ligament is involved in instability.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman presents with chronic lateral ankle pain after repeated ankle sprains. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) and there is a positive anterior drawer test. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of injury associated with damage to the ATFL?
A) Eversion of the foot
B) Plantarflexion and inversion of the foot
C) Dorsiflexion and external rotation
D) Compression of the ankle joint
questions.answer:
B)
The ATFL is the weakest of the lateral ankle ligaments and is the first to be injured during an inversion sprain. It is most commonly damaged by a mechanism of plantarflexion and inversion, such as landing from a jump or stepping on an uneven surface. The ATFL is taut in plantarflexion and resists anterior translation of the talus, making it vulnerable in this combined position.

A is incorrect because eversion of the foot stresses the medial (deltoid) ligament complex, not the lateral ligaments including the ATFL.
C is incorrect because dorsiflexion and external rotation is the classic mechanism for a syndesmotic (high ankle) sprain or a Maisonneuve-type injury, not an ATFL injury.
D is incorrect because pure axial compression of the ankle joint would be associated with tibial plafond (pilon) fractures or osteochondral lesions, not an isolated ligamentous injury to the ATFL.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male competitive runner experiences persistent pain and swelling on the anterior aspect of his knee. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the patellar tendon, and he experiences pain with resisted knee extension. An MRI does not show any tears or ruptures. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for his condition?
A) Surgical debridement
B) Corticosteroid injection
C) Rest and activity modification
D) Physical therapy focusing on eccentric strengthening
E) Complete immobilization of the knee
questions.answer:
D)
Physical therapy focusing on eccentric strengthening is the most appropriate first-line treatment for patellar tendinopathy (jumper's knee). Eccentric quadriceps exercises (e.g., decline squat protocol) have the strongest evidence for reducing pain and promoting tendon remodeling in chronic patellar tendinopathy, and are considered the cornerstone of initial management.

A is incorrect because surgical debridement is reserved for refractory cases that have failed prolonged (≥6 months) conservative treatment. B is incorrect because corticosteroid injection into or around the patellar tendon is generally avoided due to the risk of tendon weakening and rupture. C is incorrect because while rest and activity modification are components of management, they alone do not address the underlying tendon pathology; eccentric strengthening is the active intervention with the best evidence. E is incorrect because complete immobilization leads to muscle atrophy, joint stiffness, and further tendon deconditioning without promoting tendon healing.

questions.question:
An 8-year-old girl is brought in by her parents due to her feet appearing 'flat' and turning outward. You suspect a calcaneovalgus foot deformity. Which of the following statements best describes this condition?
A) It is characterized by an increased arch and heel varus.
B) It is a common condition that usually resolves spontaneously.
C) It is often associated with neurological disorders.
D) It requires surgical intervention for correction.
questions.answer:
B)
Calcaneovalgus foot is a common positional deformity seen in pediatrics, characterized by a dorsiflexed and everted foot. It is benign and typically resolves spontaneously with growth, rarely requiring any intervention.

A is incorrect because calcaneovalgus foot is characterized by hindfoot valgus and a flattened (not increased) arch; an increased arch with heel varus describes a cavovarus foot deformity.
C is incorrect because calcaneovalgus is a positional deformity, not typically associated with neurological disorders. Neurological associations are more characteristic of conditions such as cavovarus foot (e.g., Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease) or equinovarus deformity.
D is incorrect because the vast majority of calcaneovalgus feet resolve spontaneously and do not require surgical intervention.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female with a history of diabetes presents with a non-healing ulcer on the plantar aspect of her foot, adjacent to the fifth metatarsal head. Physical examination reveals a bony prominence at this location, likely due to mechanical overload. Which of the following structures is most likely contributing to the formation of this ulcer?
A) Intermetatarsal ligament
B) Adductor hallucis tendon
C) Flexor digiti minimi tendon
D) Abductor digiti minimi tendon
questions.answer:
D)
Explanation: The abductor digiti minimi tendon originates from the lateral side of the calcaneus and inserts onto the base of the proximal phalanx of the fifth toe. Its function can contribute to abnormal weight distribution and increased pressure under the fifth metatarsal head, potentially leading to ulcer formation, especially in patients with diabetes.

questions.question:
A 3-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a routine check-up. The physician suspects developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) and decides to perform an ultrasound. Which of the following findings on ultrasound would most likely confirm the diagnosis of DDH?
A) Shallow acetabulum
B) Increased acetabular index
C) Irregular femoral head contour
D) Joint effusion
questions.answer:
A)
On ultrasound evaluation of DDH using the Graf method, a shallow acetabulum — reflected by a decreased alpha angle (< 60°) — is the hallmark finding that confirms the diagnosis. The alpha angle measures the bony acetabular roof coverage of the femoral head; a reduced angle indicates inadequate bony coverage consistent with DDH.

B is incorrect because the acetabular index is measured on an anteroposterior pelvic radiograph (Hilgenreiner's method), not on ultrasound. While an increased acetabular index does suggest DDH, it is not an ultrasound finding.
C is incorrect because an irregular femoral head contour may be seen in conditions such as Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease or avascular necrosis, and is not the characteristic ultrasound finding of DDH.
D is incorrect because joint effusion is a nonspecific finding associated with septic arthritis or transient synovitis, not a diagnostic criterion for DDH.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female presents with symptoms of peroneal tendon instability after an ankle sprain. The physical examination reveals tenderness along the lateral ankle and a positive apprehension test when the foot is positioned in dorsiflexion and eversion. What is the underlying problem likely contributing to her symptoms?
A) Rupture of the peroneus longus tendon
B) Subluxation of the peroneal tendons
C) Injury to the ATFL
D) Chronic lateral ankle instability
questions.answer:
B)
Peroneal tendon subluxation occurs when the superior peroneal retinaculum (SPR) is torn or attenuated, allowing the peroneal tendons to dislocate from the retromalleolar groove. The positive apprehension test with dorsiflexion and eversion is specific for peroneal tendon instability/subluxation, reproducing the sensation of the tendons slipping over the lateral malleolus.

A is incorrect because rupture of the peroneus longus tendon would present with weakness of plantarflexion and eversion and would not produce a positive apprehension test for subluxation. C is incorrect because injury to the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) causes anterolateral ankle instability tested by the anterior drawer test, not an apprehension test for peroneal subluxation. D is incorrect because chronic lateral ankle instability involves incompetence of the lateral ligament complex (ATFL, CFL) and is assessed with anterior drawer and talar tilt tests; while it may coexist with peroneal pathology, the stem specifically describes peroneal tendon instability with a positive peroneal apprehension test, pointing to subluxation rather than ligamentous instability.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male athlete presents with severe left flank pain after being tackled during a football game. Physical examination reveals point tenderness over the left iliac crest. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Lumbar strain
B) Iliac crest fracture
C) Intercostal muscle tear
D) Renal calculi
questions.answer:
B)
Point tenderness directly over the iliac crest following a direct blow (tackle) in a contact sport is most consistent with an iliac crest fracture (or hip pointer injury). This is a common injury mechanism in football where the unpadded iliac crest absorbs a direct impact.

A is incorrect because lumbar strain presents with diffuse paraspinal muscle tenderness and pain with range of motion, not localized point tenderness over the iliac crest. C is incorrect because an intercostal muscle tear typically causes pain with deep inspiration and trunk rotation, localized to the rib cage rather than the iliac crest. D is incorrect because renal calculi present with colicky flank pain often radiating to the groin, are not associated with trauma, and would not produce point tenderness over the iliac crest.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man is diagnosed with adhesive capsulitis after several months of shoulder stiffness and pain. An arthrogram demonstrates decreased capsular volume. Which of the following is the most likely finding on imaging?
A) Increased joint effusion
B) Normal capsular thickness
C) Thickened capsular pattern
D) Decreased capsular distensibility
questions.answer:
D)
In adhesive capsulitis, the hallmark arthrographic finding is decreased capsular distensibility (reduced capsular volume), reflecting fibrosis and contracture of the glenohumeral joint capsule. This correlates with the clinical presentation of global restriction of motion and pain.

A is incorrect because adhesive capsulitis is characterized by a contracted, fibrotic capsule with reduced joint volume, not increased joint effusion. Effusion is more typical of inflammatory arthropathy or infection.
B is incorrect because the capsule in adhesive capsulitis is pathologically thickened and fibrotic, not normal in thickness.
C is incorrect because while capsular thickening does occur in adhesive capsulitis (seen on MRI), the classic arthrographic finding specifically asked about in this stem is decreased capsular distensibility/volume, which is the defining feature on arthrography.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old male collegiate baseball pitcher presents with persistent pain in his throwing arm after increasing his pitch count during the season. On examination, he has tenderness over the medial aspect of the elbow and pain with valgus stress testing. An MRI reveals injury to the ulnar collateral ligament. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of injury?
A) Overhead throwing motion
B) Direct trauma to the elbow
C) Chronic overuse from lifting weights
D) Fall onto an outstretched arm
questions.answer:
A)
The overhead throwing motion places significant valgus stress on the medial elbow, particularly during the late cocking and acceleration phases. Repetitive microtrauma from this mechanism leads to attenuation and eventual tearing of the ulnar collateral ligament, making it the most likely cause in a baseball pitcher with increasing pitch counts.

B is incorrect because direct trauma to the elbow typically causes fractures or contusions rather than isolated UCL injury, and there is no history of a direct blow.
C is incorrect because while weight lifting can stress the elbow, it does not produce the repetitive valgus forces characteristic of UCL injuries; this mechanism is specifically associated with overhead throwing.
D is incorrect because a fall onto an outstretched arm (FOOSH) typically causes injuries such as radial head fractures, distal radius fractures, or elbow dislocations, not isolated UCL tears.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man presents with muscle weakness and bone pain. Laboratory tests reveal a vitamin D deficiency. The physician decides to prescribe a vitamin D supplement. What is the preferred laboratory assay to evaluate his vitamin D status?
A) Serum calcium
B) 25-hydroxyvitamin D
C) 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
D) Parathyroid hormone levels
questions.answer:
B)
25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol) is the preferred laboratory assay to evaluate vitamin D status. It is the major circulating form of vitamin D, has a long half-life (~2–3 weeks), and reflects both dietary intake and cutaneous synthesis, making it the best indicator of overall vitamin D stores.

A is incorrect because serum calcium can be affected by many factors (albumin, PTH, renal function) and may remain normal even in vitamin D deficiency due to compensatory secondary hyperparathyroidism; it does not directly measure vitamin D status.
C is incorrect because 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) is the active hormonal form produced in the kidney, has a very short half-life, is tightly regulated by PTH and phosphate, and may be normal or even elevated in vitamin D deficiency due to compensatory PTH elevation — it does not reliably reflect vitamin D stores.
D is incorrect because parathyroid hormone levels rise secondarily in response to low vitamin D and low calcium (secondary hyperparathyroidism) and thus are an indirect marker; they do not directly measure vitamin D status.

questions.question:
A pediatric patient is evaluated for a suspected physeal injury after a trampoline accident. X-rays show an incomplete fracture through the physis with less than 50% involvement of the growth plate. The child is 10 years old and has 3 years of growth remaining. What is the most appropriate management for this type of injury?
A) Observation and follow-up
B) Surgical intervention to excise the physeal bar
C) Closed reduction and casting
D) Immediate referral for internal fixation
questions.answer:
A)
Explanation: With less than 50% physeal involvement and significant growth remaining, the best approach is observation and follow-up. Most incomplete physeal injuries heal well with conservative management, especially in younger patients.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old man with a history of chronic back pain is evaluated for progressive stiffness in his thoracic spine. Imaging shows flowing ossification along the anterolateral aspect of at least four contiguous vertebral bodies, with preservation of disc height and no sacroiliac joint erosion or fusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Ankylosing spondylitis
B) Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis
C) Osteoarthritis
D) Osteoporosis
questions.answer:
B)
Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) is defined by flowing ossification along the anterolateral aspect of at least four contiguous vertebral bodies (Resnick criteria), with preservation of intervertebral disc height and absence of sacroiliac joint erosion or intra-articular ankylosis. It is a non-inflammatory condition most common in older men.

A is incorrect because ankylosing spondylitis is characterized by thin, marginal (vertical) syndesmophytes, sacroiliac joint erosion/fusion, and inflammatory changes — none of which are described here. C is incorrect because osteoarthritis of the spine involves facet joint degeneration, disc space narrowing, and osteophyte formation at disc margins, not flowing anterolateral ossification across four or more contiguous levels. D is incorrect because osteoporosis causes decreased bone density and compression fractures, not hyperostotic ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male sustains a mid-shaft humeral fracture from a motorcycle accident. The orthopedic surgeon decides to use a coaptation splint as a temporary measure. What is the primary function of this type of splint?
A) Stabilize the elbow joint
B) Provide traction to the humerus
C) Maintain alignment of the humeral shaft
D) Allow for early movement of the shoulder
questions.answer:
C)
A coaptation (sugar-tong) splint for the humerus is a U-shaped plaster slab that extends from the axilla, around the elbow, and up to the deltoid region. Its primary function is to maintain alignment of the humeral shaft by using gravity and the weight of the arm while providing circumferential support to resist angular deformity.

A is incorrect because while the coaptation splint does incorporate the elbow at 90° of flexion, its primary purpose is to maintain humeral shaft alignment, not to stabilize the elbow joint.
B is incorrect because a coaptation splint does not provide traction; traction devices (e.g., hanging arm cast, skeletal traction) are separate methods of fracture management.
D is incorrect because a coaptation splint restricts shoulder movement to protect the fracture; early shoulder motion is not its intended function, though gentle pendulum exercises may be started later.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman who is a competitive runner complains of persistent pain in the front of her knee, which worsens with activity. On examination, she has tenderness at the patellar tendon and limited range of motion due to pain. An x-ray shows a potential avulsion at the inferior pole of the patella. What is the likely diagnosis?
A) Patellar tendinopathy
B) Patellar fracture
C) Quadriceps tendon rupture
D) Osgood-Schlatter disease
E) Patellar dislocation
questions.answer:
A)
Explanation: The clinical presentation is consistent with patellar tendinopathy (jumper's knee), particularly given the patient's activity level as a runner. The x-ray finding of an avulsion at the inferior pole of the patella often correlates with chronic tendinopathy, where the tendon pulls off a small piece of bone.

questions.question:
A 10-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after falling from his bike. He has swelling and tenderness along his forearm, with a noticeable deformity. The x-ray confirms a fracture of the distal radius, and the physician notes that the fracture appears incomplete. Which of the following best describes this type of fracture?
A) Complete fracture
B) Greenstick fracture
C) Comminuted fracture
D) Torus fracture
questions.answer:
B)
A greenstick fracture is an incomplete fracture seen in children in which one cortex breaks and the opposite cortex bends but remains intact. This produces an angular deformity, which is consistent with the noticeable deformity described in this child. The pediatric bone's greater plasticity and thicker periosteum predispose to this pattern.

A is incorrect because a complete fracture disrupts both cortices entirely; the stem specifically states the fracture appears incomplete.
C is incorrect because a comminuted fracture involves fragmentation of bone into three or more pieces, which is a complete fracture pattern and is uncommon in children due to the elasticity of pediatric bone.
D is incorrect because a torus (buckle) fracture is also an incomplete pediatric fracture, but it involves compression buckling of one cortex without a true cortical break on the tension side; it typically presents with mild swelling and tenderness but does not produce a noticeable angular deformity as described in this stem.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a laceration to his palm sustained while working with a power tool. On examination, there is a deep laceration over the base of the small finger, and he has difficulty flexing the finger at the distal joint. Which of the following structures is most likely injured?
A) Flexor digitorum superficialis
B) Flexor digitorum profundus
C) Lumbrical muscle
D) Extensor digitorum tendon
E) A1 pulley
questions.answer:
B)
Difficulty flexing the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint of the small finger indicates injury to the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon, which is the sole flexor of the DIP joint. A deep palmar laceration at the base of the small finger can divide the FDP tendon, requiring surgical repair.

A is incorrect because the flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) flexes the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint; its injury would impair PIP flexion, not DIP flexion.
C is incorrect because the lumbrical muscle flexes the MCP joint and extends the IP joints via the lateral bands; its isolated injury would not present as loss of DIP flexion.
D is incorrect because the extensor digitorum tendon extends the finger; it is located on the dorsum of the hand and would not be injured by a palmar laceration, nor would its injury cause loss of flexion.
E is incorrect because the A1 pulley is a restraint that keeps the flexor tendons close to the bone; its disruption can contribute to bowstringing but would not eliminate active DIP flexion.

questions.question:
A patient presents with forefoot pain and a radiograph is obtained. The medial aspect of the 4th metatarsal should line up with which structure for a normal finding?
A) Medial aspect of the 3rd metatarsal
B) Lateral aspect of the cuboid
C) Medial aspect of the cuboid
D) Lateral aspect of the cuneiform
questions.answer:
C)
On an AP foot radiograph, the medial border of the 4th metatarsal base should align with the medial border of the cuboid. This is one of the key alignment lines used to evaluate the tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc) joint complex; disruption of this alignment suggests a Lisfranc injury or other midfoot malalignment.

A is incorrect because the medial aspect of the 4th metatarsal does not articulate with the 3rd metatarsal; the 3rd metatarsal articulates with the lateral cuneiform, not the cuboid.
B is incorrect because the lateral aspect of the cuboid articulates with the lateral border of the 5th metatarsal base, not the 4th metatarsal medial border.
D is incorrect because the lateral cuneiform articulates with the 3rd metatarsal base; the 4th metatarsal base articulates with the cuboid, not the cuneiform.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old construction worker presents with wrist pain and swelling after a heavy fall. A CT scan reveals an Essex-Lopresti injury. Which of the following findings is most characteristic of this injury?
A) Fracture of the scaphoid
B) Dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint
C) Proximal migration of the radius
D) Tear of the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon
questions.answer:
C)
The Essex-Lopresti injury is a triad consisting of a radial head fracture, disruption of the interosseous membrane (IOM), and dislocation/instability of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ). The most characteristic finding is proximal migration of the radius, which occurs because the IOM — the primary longitudinal stabilizer of the forearm — is torn, allowing the radius to migrate proximally relative to the ulna.

A is incorrect because a scaphoid fracture is not a component of the Essex-Lopresti injury; the fracture in this injury involves the radial head, not the carpus. B is incorrect because while DRUJ disruption is part of the Essex-Lopresti triad, it is not the most characteristic or distinguishing feature — DRUJ instability can occur in many other injuries. Proximal radial migration is the hallmark finding that defines this injury pattern. D is incorrect because the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon is not involved in the Essex-Lopresti injury; the key soft-tissue disruption is of the interosseous membrane.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents with severe pain in the groin and lateral aspect of the hip following a fall. Physical examination reveals a positive Trendelenburg sign. Imaging shows a fracture of the acetabulum. Which structure is most likely to be affected in the context of this injury?
A) Inferior gluteal nerve
B) Superior gluteal nerve
C) Obturator nerve
D) Femoral nerve
questions.answer:
B)
The superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1) innervates the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus, which are the primary hip abductors responsible for maintaining pelvic stability during single-leg stance. An acetabular fracture can injure this nerve as it exits the greater sciatic notch above the piriformis, resulting in hip abductor weakness and a positive Trendelenburg sign.

A is incorrect because the inferior gluteal nerve innervates the gluteus maximus, which is primarily a hip extensor; its injury would cause difficulty with stair climbing and rising from a seated position, not a Trendelenburg sign.
C is incorrect because the obturator nerve innervates the hip adductors (adductor longus, brevis, magnus, gracilis); its injury would cause adductor weakness and medial thigh sensory loss, not a Trendelenburg sign.
D is incorrect because the femoral nerve innervates the quadriceps and hip flexors (iliacus, sartorius); its injury would cause knee extension weakness and anterior thigh sensory loss, not a Trendelenburg sign.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old woman comes to the clinic with pain and weakness in her shoulder after a traumatic dislocation that occurred during a soccer game. She reports that she has had multiple dislocations in the past. On examination, there is apprehension with the arm in an abducted and externally rotated position. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Physical therapy
B) MRI to assess for labral tear
C) Surgical stabilization with Bankart repair
D) Corticosteroid injection
questions.answer:
C)
In a 38-year-old patient with a history of multiple traumatic anterior shoulder dislocations and a positive apprehension test, the clinical diagnosis of recurrent anterior instability is well established. Surgical stabilization with a Bankart repair is the most appropriate next step, as conservative measures have clearly failed and further imaging is unlikely to change management.

A is incorrect because physical therapy alone is insufficient for recurrent traumatic instability with multiple prior dislocations; it may be appropriate after a first-time dislocation but not in this setting.
B is incorrect because while MRI can confirm a labral tear, the clinical history of multiple traumatic dislocations with a positive apprehension test already establishes the diagnosis of recurrent instability, making further imaging unlikely to alter the surgical plan.
D is incorrect because corticosteroid injection does not address the underlying structural pathology (labral/capsular injury) causing recurrent instability and has no role in the management of recurrent shoulder dislocations.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old boy presents to the clinic with a complaint of right knee pain and limping for the past two weeks. He has a history of multiple café-au-lait spots and his mother reports he has had increasing difficulty walking. On examination, there is tenderness over the right tibia, and an x-ray reveals anterior bowing of the tibia with an associated fibular deformity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Osteogenesis imperfecta
B) Neurofibromatosis type 1
C) Congenital pseudoarthrosis of the tibia
D) Blount's disease
questions.answer:
C)
Congenital pseudoarthrosis of the tibia (CPT) is the most likely orthopaedic diagnosis. The combination of café-au-lait spots (suggesting underlying neurofibromatosis type 1) with anterolateral bowing of the tibia and associated fibular deformity is the classic presentation of CPT. Approximately 50% of CPT cases are associated with NF-1, and this tibial dysplasia may progress to pathologic fracture and pseudoarthrosis.

A is incorrect because osteogenesis imperfecta presents with generalized osteopenia, multiple fractures, blue sclerae, and ligamentous laxity — not café-au-lait spots or isolated anterolateral tibial bowing. B is incorrect because while NF-1 is the underlying systemic condition, the specific orthopaedic diagnosis explaining the tibial bowing and fibular deformity is congenital pseudoarthrosis of the tibia; NF-1 alone does not describe the skeletal pathology seen on imaging. D is incorrect because Blount's disease (tibia vara) causes proximal tibial varus deformity due to a growth disturbance of the medial proximal tibial physis, not anterolateral mid-diaphyseal bowing, and is not associated with café-au-lait spots.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old recreational athlete reports a feeling of instability in his shoulder after a fall during a basketball game. Upon physical examination, the anterior drawer test is positive, and an MRI reveals a Bankart lesion. What is the most likely mechanism of injury that led to this injury?
A) Direct blow to the shoulder
B) Forced external rotation with abduction
C) Anterior dislocation of the shoulder
D) Chronic repetitive overhead motions
questions.answer:
B)
Forced external rotation with the arm in abduction is the classic mechanism that leads to anterior shoulder dislocation and subsequent Bankart lesion. During a fall with the arm in this vulnerable position, the humeral head is levered anteriorly over the glenoid rim, avulsing the anteroinferior labrum (Bankart lesion). This is the most commonly tested mechanism on board exams.

A is incorrect because a direct blow to the shoulder more commonly causes acromioclavicular joint injuries or proximal humerus fractures rather than anterior dislocation with a Bankart lesion. C is incorrect because anterior dislocation is the resulting injury/pathological event, not the mechanism of injury; the question specifically asks for the mechanism. D is incorrect because chronic repetitive overhead motions are associated with superior labral (SLAP) tears and internal impingement rather than traumatic Bankart lesions.

questions.question:
A pediatric patient is being evaluated for potential growth-related issues. The physician is particularly interested in determining the Risser stage to assess the patient's skeletal maturity. The patient is currently showing signs of peak growth velocity. At what Risser stage is it expected that the peak growth velocity occurs?
A) Risser Stage 1
B) Risser Stage 2
C) Risser Stage 3
D) Risser Stage 4
questions.answer:
A)
Risser Stage 1 is typically associated with the peak growth velocity in adolescents. Understanding the Risser stages helps in predicting the growth potential and planning for interventions if necessary.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male presents with a puncture wound from a fight. He has redness, swelling, and purulent discharge from the wound. Cultures from the wound show Eikenella corrodens. What is the most likely reason for this organism being isolated?
A) Contamination from the skin flora
B) Its association with human bite injuries
C) Its resistance to antibiotics
D) Its association with animal bites
questions.answer:
B)
Eikenella corrodens is a gram-negative rod that is part of the normal oral flora and is classically associated with human bite wounds, including "fight bite" injuries (clenched-fist injuries). Its isolation from a puncture wound sustained during a fight is characteristic of inoculation from an opponent's teeth.

A is incorrect because Eikenella corrodens is not a typical skin commensal; it is part of the oropharyngeal flora, so its presence indicates oral contamination (bite) rather than simple skin contamination.
C is incorrect because while Eikenella can be resistant to certain antibiotics (e.g., clindamycin, first-generation cephalosporins), antibiotic resistance is not the reason it was isolated — the reason relates to the mechanism of inoculation.
D is incorrect because animal bite infections are classically associated with Pasteurella multocida (dogs and cats) or Capnocytophaga canimorsus, not Eikenella corrodens.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old female runner complains of anterior knee pain that worsens with activity, especially during downhill running. She has tenderness along the lateral aspect of the knee and a positive apprehension test. An MRI shows lateral patellar compression syndrome. Which of the following is a likely contributing factor to her condition?
A) Tight quadriceps muscles
B) Hyperlaxity of the patellar tendon
C) Weakness of the vastus medialis
D) Excessive lateral tracking of the patella
E) Insufficient range of motion of the hip
questions.answer:
D)
Excessive lateral tracking of the patella is the hallmark pathomechanism of lateral patellar compression syndrome. Factors such as VMO weakness, tight lateral retinaculum, increased Q-angle, and iliotibial band tightness all contribute to the patella being pulled laterally, increasing contact pressure on the lateral patellar facet and producing anterior knee pain that worsens with activity.

A is incorrect because while tight quadriceps can contribute to patellofemoral symptoms in general, isolated quadriceps tightness does not specifically cause lateral patellar tracking or compression.
B is incorrect because hyperlaxity of the patellar tendon would not cause lateral compression; it might contribute to patella alta or generalized instability but does not explain lateral tracking.
C is incorrect because VMO weakness is a contributing factor to lateral tracking (and thus is related), but it is a cause rather than the direct mechanism — the question asks for the likely contributing factor, and excessive lateral tracking (D) is the more encompassing and direct pathomechanical description of the condition.
E is incorrect because insufficient hip range of motion is not a recognized primary contributor to lateral patellar compression syndrome; hip weakness (especially abductors) can affect lower-extremity alignment, but limited hip ROM is not the classic association.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents to the clinic with pain and swelling at the base of her great toe. On examination, there is a noticeable bunion deformity, and she reports difficulty wearing shoes. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for her condition?
A) Surgical correction with osteotomy
B) Custom orthotics and padding
C) Corticosteroid injection
D) Physical therapy focused on strengthening
questions.answer:
B)
Custom orthotics and padding are the most appropriate initial management for hallux valgus (bunion). Conservative measures—including wider shoe wear, bunion pads, and custom orthotics—are first-line treatment to reduce pressure over the medial eminence and alleviate symptoms.

A is incorrect because surgical correction with osteotomy is reserved for patients who fail an adequate trial of conservative management and have significant functional impairment or progressive deformity. It is not initial management.
C is incorrect because corticosteroid injection is not a standard treatment for hallux valgus. While it may temporarily reduce inflammation in the bursa overlying the bunion, it does not address the underlying mechanical problem and is not considered first-line therapy.
D is incorrect because physical therapy focused on strengthening does not meaningfully correct or relieve symptoms of hallux valgus; the deformity is structural, and strengthening exercises alone will not reduce the bony prominence or realign the first metatarsal.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female falls from a height and presents with severe pelvic pain and instability. Imaging reveals a pubic diastasis greater than 2.5 cm and an anterior sacroiliac joint injury, but the vertical stability is maintained. What is the most appropriate classification of her injury?
A) Anterior-posterior compression injury
B) Lateral compression injury
C) Vertical shear injury
D) Open book injury
questions.answer:
A)
This patient's presentation with a pubic diastasis greater than 2.5 cm and an anterior sacroiliac injury, while remaining vertically stable, classifies her injury as an anterior-posterior compression injury according to the Young-Burgess classification. Correct classification is crucial for guiding treatment.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman presents with a shoulder dislocation following a fall while playing soccer. During surgical intervention via a posterior approach, the surgeon must navigate the internervous plane to avoid damaging the axillary nerve. Which muscles demarcate this plane?
A) Infraspinatus and supraspinatus
B) Teres major and teres minor
C) Subscapularis and latissimus dorsi
D) Deltoid and supraspinatus
questions.answer:
A)
The posterior approach to the shoulder utilizes the internervous plane between the infraspinatus (suprascapular nerve) and the teres minor (axillary nerve). The axillary nerve runs along the inferior border of the teres minor, so identifying this plane is critical to protecting the nerve during dissection.

B is incorrect because teres major (lower subscapular nerve) and teres minor (axillary nerve) do not define the standard internervous plane of the posterior shoulder approach; teres major lies inferior and is not routinely encountered in this dissection. C is incorrect because subscapularis and latissimus dorsi are anterior/medial structures and are not relevant to the posterior approach internervous plane. D is incorrect because deltoid and supraspinatus are not separated as an internervous plane in the posterior approach; the deltoid is split or retracted but the true internervous interval is between infraspinatus and teres minor.

questions.question:
A 12-year-old boy presents with shoulder pain after a recent baseball season, where he pitched extensively. You suspect little leaguer's shoulder. Which mechanism leads to this condition?
A) Overuse resulting in rotator cuff tears
B) Excessive pitching leading to physeal stress
C) Sudden traumatic injury during a pitch
D) Chronic instability due to shoulder laxity
questions.answer:
B)
Excessive pitching subjects the proximal humeral physis to repetitive rotational stress (torsional shear forces during the cocking and deceleration phases of throwing). This leads to widening and irregularity of the growth plate — a Salter-Harris type I–equivalent stress injury — causing lateral shoulder pain and potential growth disturbance if not addressed with rest.

A is incorrect because rotator cuff tears are exceedingly rare in skeletally immature patients; the physis is the weakest link in the kinetic chain and fails before the rotator cuff tendons. C is incorrect because Little Leaguer's shoulder is an overuse/stress injury to the physis, not an acute traumatic event during a single pitch. D is incorrect because chronic glenohumeral instability from capsular laxity is a separate entity (multidirectional instability); it is not the mechanism underlying physeal stress injury in Little Leaguer's shoulder.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male construction worker presents with severe hip pain and swelling after a fall from a height. A CT scan shows a fracture extending from the iliac crest through the anterior acetabulum and into the superior pubic ramus. Which of the following best describes the injury?
A) Posterior column fracture
B) Anterior column fracture
C) Transverse acetabular fracture
D) Acetabular fracture with central displacement
questions.answer:
B)
A fracture extending from the iliac crest through the anterior acetabulum and into the superior pubic ramus is characteristic of an anterior column fracture in the Judet-Letournel classification. The anterior column encompasses the iliopectineal line, anterior wall, and superior pubic ramus. These injuries can significantly impact hip stability and often require surgical fixation to restore articular congruity.

A is incorrect because a posterior column fracture involves the ischial portion of the acetabulum, extending from the greater sciatic notch through the retroacetabular surface to the ischial tuberosity — not the anterior structures described here. C is incorrect because a transverse acetabular fracture divides the acetabulum into superior (iliac) and inferior (ischiopubic) segments, crossing both columns, which is not the pattern described. D is incorrect because central displacement (protrusio) implies medial migration of the femoral head through the acetabular floor, typically associated with both-column or quadrilateral plate disruption, which is not described in this scenario.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female presents with shoulder pain that has developed gradually over the last six months. Upon examination, she has limited external rotation and abduction of the arm. An MRI reveals a tear of the rotator cuff. Which ligament is primarily responsible for stabilizing the shoulder during abduction?
A) Superior glenohumeral ligament
B) Inferior glenohumeral ligament
C) Middle glenohumeral ligament
D) Coracoacromial ligament
questions.answer:
B)
The inferior glenohumeral ligament (IGHL) is the primary static stabilizer of the glenohumeral joint when the arm is abducted to 90°. Its anterior band resists anterior translation in abduction and external rotation, while its posterior band resists posterior translation in abduction and internal rotation. This makes it the most important ligamentous stabilizer during overhead and abducted positions.

A is incorrect because the superior glenohumeral ligament primarily resists inferior translation of the adducted arm (at rest) and limits external rotation in the adducted position. B is incorrect — skip (correct answer). C is incorrect because the middle glenohumeral ligament is a secondary stabilizer that primarily limits external rotation at 45° of abduction and resists anterior translation at lower degrees of abduction, but it is not the primary stabilizer during full abduction. D is incorrect because the coracoacromial ligament forms part of the coracoacromial arch and acts as a restraint against superior humeral head migration; it is not a glenohumeral stabilizing ligament during abduction.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male construction worker presents with severe calf pain following a work-related knee injury. His pain worsens with passive stretching of the gastrocnemius muscle, and he exhibits signs of compartment syndrome. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management step?
A) Immediate fasciotomy
B) Application of a compression bandage
C) Elevation of the limb
D) Measurement of intracompartmental pressure
questions.answer:
A)
When a patient presents with classic clinical findings of compartment syndrome — severe pain out of proportion to injury, pain with passive stretch of the involved muscles, and other signs of elevated compartment pressure — immediate fasciotomy is the definitive and most appropriate management. Delay for confirmatory pressure measurements in a clinically obvious case risks irreversible muscle necrosis and nerve injury.

B is incorrect because a compression bandage would increase external pressure on the compartment, worsening the syndrome.
C is incorrect because while elevation may modestly reduce swelling, it does not treat established compartment syndrome and can actually decrease arterial perfusion pressure to the compartment.
D is incorrect because intracompartmental pressure measurement is useful when the clinical picture is equivocal or the patient cannot be reliably examined (e.g., intubated, obtunded); in a patient with clear clinical signs, it should not delay definitive surgical treatment.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female runner experiences acute lateral knee pain after a fall while jogging. She has a tenderness over the lateral aspect of her knee and a small effusion. X-rays show a Segond fracture. What is the most likely associated injury?
A) Medial collateral ligament tear
B) Anterior cruciate ligament tear
C) Lateral meniscus tear
D) Patellar tendon rupture
E) Posterior cruciate ligament tear
questions.answer:
B)
A Segond fracture is a small avulsion fracture of the lateral tibial plateau at the attachment of the anterolateral ligament/lateral capsular ligament. It is considered pathognomonic for an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear, occurring via internal rotation and varus stress. Its presence on imaging should prompt a thorough evaluation for ACL injury.

A is incorrect because the medial collateral ligament (MCL) is injured by valgus stress, not the varus/internal rotation mechanism that produces a Segond fracture.
C is incorrect because although lateral meniscus tears can coexist, the strongest and most classic association with a Segond fracture is an ACL tear, not an isolated lateral meniscus tear.
D is incorrect because patellar tendon rupture results from an eccentric quadriceps contraction mechanism and is not associated with a Segond fracture.
E is incorrect because posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) tears result from a posterior-directed force on the proximal tibia (e.g., dashboard injury), which is a different mechanism from that producing a Segond fracture.

questions.question:
A young athlete is diagnosed with a morel-lavallee lesion following a traumatic event. Which of the following best describes this condition?
A) Fracture of the pubic symphysis
B) Closed, internal degloving injury of the skin
C) Lateral compression pelvic fracture
D) Anterior column acetabular fracture
questions.answer:
B)
A Morel-Lavallée lesion is a closed, internal degloving injury in which tangential shear forces separate the skin and subcutaneous fat from the underlying fascia, creating a potential space that fills with blood, lymph, and necrotic fat. It classically occurs over the greater trochanter or lateral thigh in association with pelvic/acetabular trauma. Recognition is important because undiagnosed lesions can become infected and complicate surgical approaches.

A is incorrect because a pubic symphysis fracture is a bony injury of the anterior pelvic ring, not a soft-tissue degloving lesion. C is incorrect because a lateral compression pelvic fracture is a specific bony injury pattern classified in the Young-Burgess system, unrelated to the soft-tissue pathology described.
