A Hawkins type II talar neck fracture is defined by displacement with subtalar subluxation or dislocation, carrying an approximate osteonecrosis (AVN) risk of 20–50%. The blood supply to the talus is tenuous and includes the artery of the tarsal canal (from the posterior tibial artery), the deltoid branch, and the artery of the sinus tarsi. The Hawkins sign—subchondral lucency of the talar dome seen at 6–8 weeks—indicates preserved vascularity and is a favorable prognostic finding.

A is incorrect because a 0% AVN rate corresponds roughly to Hawkins type I (nondisplaced) fractures, not type II. C is incorrect because an AVN risk of less than 10% is too low for a type II injury; this range is more consistent with nondisplaced (type I) fractures. D is incorrect because a 90–100% AVN rate corresponds to Hawkins type III (subtalar and tibiotalar dislocation) or type IV (additional talonavicular dislocation), not type II. E is incorrect because AVN risk is directly related to the degree of fracture displacement and dislocation, which disrupts the talar blood supply; the Hawkins classification is specifically designed to correlate displacement with AVN risk.

questions.question:
An infant treated in a Pavlik harness develops weakness of knee extension and an absent quadriceps contraction. The most appropriate management is:
A) Perform open reduction
B) Discontinue or loosen the harness, as this represents a femoral nerve palsy from excessive hip flexion
C) Obtain electromyography before any change
D) Continue the harness unchanged and observe
E) Convert to a spica cast in maximum abduction
questions.answer:
B)
Femoral nerve palsy in a Pavlik harness results from excessive hip flexion, typically beyond 100–110 degrees, and is recognized by loss of active knee extension and absent quadriceps contraction. It generally resolves within days once the anterior straps are loosened or the harness is discontinued temporarily. Persistent palsy predicts a lower likelihood of successful reduction. Excessive abduction is a separate hazard producing osteonecrosis.

A is incorrect because open reduction is not indicated for a harness complication; the immediate priority is to relieve the nerve compression by adjusting or removing the harness. C is incorrect because the clinical diagnosis of femoral nerve palsy (absent knee extension, no quadriceps contraction) is straightforward in this setting and does not require electromyography before taking action; delaying harness adjustment risks prolonged nerve injury. D is incorrect because continuing the harness unchanged will perpetuate the excessive flexion causing the femoral nerve palsy and may lead to permanent nerve damage. E is incorrect because converting to a spica cast in maximum abduction does not address the femoral nerve palsy and introduces the risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head from forced abduction.

questions.question:
Which examination finding is most specific for cervical myelopathy?
A) Hoffmann sign with hyperreflexia and gait instability
B) Numbness in the small finger
C) Reproducible pain with neck extension
D) Weakness of the deltoid
E) Positive Spurling test
questions.answer:
A)
Cervical myelopathy is an upper motor neuron syndrome caused by spinal cord compression. The combination of a Hoffmann sign, hyperreflexia, and gait instability is the most specific cluster for myelopathy. Other classic findings include inverted radial reflex, sustained clonus, Babinski sign, Lhermitte phenomenon, and loss of hand dexterity. Because myelopathy is generally progressive, surgical decompression is recommended for moderate-to-severe disease.

B is incorrect because small-finger numbness is a dermatomal finding suggesting C8 radiculopathy or ulnar neuropathy, not spinal cord dysfunction. C is incorrect because reproducible pain with neck extension is a nonspecific finding that can occur with facet arthropathy, foraminal stenosis, or radiculopathy and does not indicate upper motor neuron pathology. D is incorrect because deltoid weakness is a lower motor neuron/radiculopathy finding (C5 root) and does not suggest myelopathy. E is incorrect because a positive Spurling test is a provocative maneuver for cervical radiculopathy (nerve root compression), not for spinal cord compression/myelopathy.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old presents with back pain, fever, and an MRI showing destruction of the L2-L3 disc space with adjacent vertebral endplate erosion. The most likely diagnosis and organism are:
A) Metastatic carcinoma
B) Modic type I degenerative change
C) Pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis, Staphylococcus aureus
D) Multiple myeloma
E) Tuberculous spondylitis, Mycobacterium tuberculosis
questions.answer:
C)
Disc space destruction with adjacent vertebral endplate erosion in a febrile patient is the hallmark of pyogenic spondylodiscitis. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common causative organism, accounting for roughly 50% of cases. Blood cultures and/or CT-guided biopsy should be obtained before initiating antibiotics.

A is incorrect because metastatic carcinoma typically involves the vertebral body and pedicles while sparing the disc space; it does not usually present with fever. B is incorrect because Modic type I changes are degenerative endplate signal changes on MRI that are not associated with disc space destruction or systemic signs of infection. D is incorrect because multiple myeloma causes lytic vertebral body lesions but spares the disc space and does not typically present with fever or endplate erosion. E is incorrect because tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) characteristically spares the disc space until late stages, preferentially involves the anterior vertebral body with subligamentous spread across multiple levels, and produces large paraspinal (cold) abscesses; the classic early disc space destruction described here favors pyogenic infection.

questions.question:
A pilon fracture with severe soft tissue swelling and fracture blisters is best managed initially by:
A) Spanning external fixation with delayed definitive fixation once soft tissues permit
B) Casting alone
C) Immediate open reduction internal fixation
D) Primary ankle arthrodesis
E) Below-knee amputation
questions.answer:
A)
Staged management of pilon fractures with severe soft tissue compromise uses ankle-spanning external fixation (with or without fibular plating) followed by definitive ORIF at 7–21 days once swelling resolves and skin wrinkles return. This approach, popularized by Sirkin and Patterson, dramatically reduced the historically catastrophic wound complication rates seen with immediate fixation. Key principles include restoration of length, alignment, and articular congruity while respecting the soft tissue envelope.

B is incorrect because casting alone does not restore articular congruity or maintain length and alignment in a displaced pilon fracture, leading to malunion and post-traumatic arthritis. C is incorrect because immediate ORIF through severely swollen, blistered soft tissues carries unacceptably high rates of wound dehiscence, infection, and flap coverage needs. D is incorrect because primary ankle arthrodesis is not indicated as initial management; the goal is articular reconstruction, and arthrodesis is reserved as a salvage procedure for post-traumatic arthritis. E is incorrect because below-knee amputation is not indicated for a pilon fracture with soft tissue swelling; limb salvage is the standard of care in this setting.

questions.question:
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease in a child most often presents orthopaedically as:
A) Congenital vertical talus
B) Congenital scoliosis
C) Planovalgus foot
D) Progressive cavovarus foot deformity with clawing and frequent ankle sprains
E) Genu recurvatum
questions.answer:
D)
CMT is the most common inherited neuropathy; type 1A, an autosomal dominant PMP22 duplication on chromosome 17, is most frequent. Intrinsic foot muscle weakness with relative preservation of peroneus longus and tibialis posterior drives progressive cavovarus deformity, claw toes, and lateral ankle instability. Any child with a unilateral or progressive cavovarus foot warrants neurologic evaluation and spine MRI to exclude a tethered cord, syrinx, or tumor.

A is incorrect because congenital vertical talus presents as a rigid rocker-bottom flatfoot at birth and is associated with conditions such as arthrogryposis or chromosomal abnormalities, not CMT. B is incorrect because congenital scoliosis results from vertebral formation or segmentation defects and is not a typical presentation of CMT (CMT may cause neuromuscular scoliosis but not congenital scoliosis). C is incorrect because CMT produces cavovarus, not planovalgus; planovalgus feet are seen in conditions such as cerebral palsy or ligamentous laxity syndromes. E is incorrect because genu recurvatum is not a characteristic orthopaedic presentation of CMT; it is more commonly associated with connective tissue disorders or quadriceps over-pull in neuromuscular conditions such as polio.

questions.question:
The lateral pillar (Herring) classification of Perthes disease is based on:
A) Height of the lateral third of the capital femoral epiphysis during the fragmentation phase
B) Extent of epiphyseal involvement on the AP radiograph
C) Presence of metaphyseal cysts
D) MRI perfusion
E) Femoral head extrusion index
questions.answer:
A)
The lateral pillar (Herring) classification is assessed during the fragmentation phase and grades the height of the lateral third (lateral pillar) of the capital femoral epiphysis: Group A shows no loss of height, Group B maintains more than 50% of lateral pillar height, the B/C border has a narrow lateral pillar or exactly 50% maintained, and Group C has less than 50% maintained. It is the most reliable prognostic indicator for Perthes disease and, together with age at onset, guides treatment decisions.

B is incorrect because the extent of overall epiphyseal involvement on the AP radiograph describes the Catterall classification (groups I–IV), not the Herring lateral pillar classification. C is incorrect because metaphyseal cysts are one of the Catterall head-at-risk signs; they are not the basis of the lateral pillar classification. D is incorrect because MRI perfusion can assess femoral head vascularity but is not used in the Herring classification, which is based on plain AP radiograph findings during fragmentation. E is incorrect because the femoral head extrusion index (subluxation percentage) is a separate prognostic measurement and is not part of the lateral pillar classification system.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old woman falls from height and sustains a transverse sacral fracture with bilateral vertical components and neurologic deficit involving bowel and bladder. This U-type pattern is associated with which finding?
A) Stable ligamentous injury treated with bed rest alone
B) No association with a history of a fall from height
C) Exclusive involvement of the L5 nerve root
D) Isolated Denis zone I injury without neurologic risk
E) Spinopelvic dissociation, often requiring lumbopelvic fixation
questions.answer:
E)
The U-shaped (or H-shaped) sacral fracture pattern consists of a transverse sacral fracture with bilateral vertical components, effectively disconnecting the spine and upper sacrum from the pelvis—spinopelvic dissociation. It typically results from an axial load (fall from height) and carries high rates of cauda equina/sacral root injury with bowel, bladder, and sexual dysfunction. Treatment usually requires lumbopelvic (triangular osteosynthesis) fixation, with decompression for neurologic deficits.

A is incorrect because this fracture pattern is highly unstable with complete spinopelvic dissociation; bed rest alone is insufficient. B is incorrect because the U-type sacral fracture is classically associated with falls from height (axial loading mechanism). C is incorrect because the transverse component typically injures multiple sacral nerve roots (S1–S4), not exclusively L5; the stem describes bowel and bladder dysfunction indicating lower sacral root involvement. D is incorrect because the vertical fracture lines in a U-type pattern typically traverse Denis zones II or III (through or medial to the foramina), carrying a high risk of neurologic injury, not an isolated zone I injury.

questions.question:
Bracing for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is most appropriate for:
A) A Risser 0-1 patient with a 30-degree curve who is premenarchal
B) A patient with a 15-degree curve
C) A patient with a 60-degree curve and continued growth
D) A Risser 5 patient with a 30-degree curve
E) A skeletally mature patient with a 55-degree curve
questions.answer:
A)
The BrAIST trial demonstrated that bracing significantly reduces progression to the surgical threshold, with a dose-response relationship to wear time (more than 13 hours per day is most effective). Bracing is indicated for curves of approximately 25-45 degrees in skeletally immature patients (Risser 0-2, premenarchal or within 1 year of menarche). A Risser 0-1, premenarchal patient with a 30-degree curve meets all criteria for bracing.

B is incorrect because a 15-degree curve is below the bracing threshold (typically 25 degrees); curves of this magnitude are observed with serial imaging rather than braced.
C is incorrect because a 60-degree curve in a growing patient exceeds the upper limit for effective bracing (approximately 45-50 degrees) and is a surgical indication.
D is incorrect because a Risser 5 patient is skeletally mature, and bracing has no role in preventing curve progression after skeletal maturity.
E is incorrect because a skeletally mature patient will not benefit from bracing regardless of curve magnitude; a 55-degree curve in a mature patient would be considered for surgical correction if symptomatic.

questions.question:
A patient cannot actively flex the distal interphalangeal joint after grabbing an opponent's jersey. The most likely injury and management is:
A) A1 pulley stenosis, treated with injection
B) Sagittal band rupture, treated with a yoke splint
C) Terminal extensor rupture, treated with a DIP extension splint
D) Flexor digitorum profundus avulsion (jersey finger), requiring prompt surgical repair
E) Central slip rupture, treated with extension splinting
questions.answer:
D)
Jersey finger is FDP avulsion, most often of the ring finger. The mechanism — grabbing an opponent's jersey while the finger is forcibly extended — avulses the FDP from the distal phalanx, resulting in inability to actively flex the DIP joint. Leddy-Packer type I retracts into the palm with disruption of both vincula and should be repaired within 7–10 days; type II retracts to the PIP level where a vinculum tethers it, allowing repair up to a few weeks; type III has a large bony fragment caught at the A4 pulley and is least urgent. Prompt surgical repair is required for all types.

A is incorrect because A1 pulley stenosis (trigger finger) causes catching or locking of the digit in flexion, not loss of active DIP flexion after a jersey-grabbing injury.
B is incorrect because sagittal band rupture causes inability to actively initiate MCP extension (extensor tendon subluxation), not loss of DIP flexion.
C is incorrect because terminal extensor tendon rupture (mallet finger) causes loss of active DIP *extension*, not flexion; it is treated with DIP extension splinting.
E is incorrect because central slip rupture leads to boutonnière deformity (PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension) and does not present as isolated loss of active DIP flexion after a grabbing mechanism.

questions.question:
In total knee arthroplasty, excessive external rotation of the femoral component leads to:
A) Tibial component loosening
B) Stiffness in extension
C) Lateral flexion gap laxity and potential patellar tracking issues
D) Anterior femoral notching
E) Patellar maltracking with lateral subluxation
questions.answer:
C)
Excessive external rotation of the femoral component shifts the posterior femoral condylar resection so that more bone is removed from the lateral posterior condyle and less from the medial, creating asymmetric flexion gap laxity — specifically, the lateral flexion gap becomes loose while the medial flexion gap becomes tight. This can also alter patellar tracking. The normal 3° of external rotation relative to the posterior condylar axis is designed to balance the flexion gap and optimize tracking.

A is incorrect because tibial component loosening is related to malalignment, polyethylene wear, or fixation failure, not specifically to femoral component rotation.
B is incorrect because stiffness in extension relates to issues such as an oversized component, inadequate distal femoral resection, or posterior osteophytes, not femoral rotation.
D is incorrect because anterior femoral notching results from excessive anterior resection of the distal femur (e.g., oversizing or excessive flexion of the cutting guide), not rotational malalignment.
E is incorrect because patellar maltracking with lateral subluxation is the classic consequence of excessive INTERNAL rotation of the femoral component, not external rotation.

questions.question:
Six hours after a lumbar decompression, a patient develops severe back pain, progressive bilateral leg weakness, and urinary retention. The most appropriate next step is:
A) Emergent MRI and return to the operating room for evacuation
B) Lumbar puncture
C) Intravenous corticosteroids and reassessment in the morning
D) Electromyography
E) Observation overnight with serial neurologic checks
questions.answer:
A)
Postoperative epidural hematoma presents within hours of surgery with disproportionate back pain and a progressive neurologic deficit, often including bowel and bladder dysfunction. Time to decompression is the strongest determinant of neurologic recovery, so emergent imaging (MRI or CT myelogram) followed by immediate surgical evacuation is the standard of care. Risk factors include multilevel decompression, coagulopathy, and early resumption of anticoagulation.

B is incorrect because lumbar puncture does not address the compressive hematoma and could worsen the situation or delay definitive treatment. C is incorrect because intravenous corticosteroids do not treat a surgical hematoma, and delaying intervention until morning risks irreversible neurologic damage. D is incorrect because electromyography is a diagnostic tool for chronic denervation and is neither timely nor therapeutic in this acute emergency. E is incorrect because observation alone allows continued spinal cord/cauda equina compression, and delay in evacuation is the primary determinant of poor outcome.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old man arrives after a high-speed collision with a systolic blood pressure of 78 mm Hg, an unstable pelvis, and ongoing hemorrhage. Massive transfusion is initiated. Current evidence supports a component ratio closest to:
A) Packed red cells alone until hemoglobin exceeds 10 g/dL
B) Balanced administration of red cells, plasma, and platelets in approximately equal ratios
C) Platelets alone until the count exceeds 150,000
D) Crystalloid boluses of 4 L before any blood product
E) Plasma alone until the INR normalizes
questions.answer:
B)
Damage control resuscitation for hemorrhagic shock emphasizes early, balanced administration of packed red blood cells, fresh frozen plasma, and platelets in ratios approaching 1:1:1, as supported by the PROPPR trial. This strategy minimizes coagulopathy, acidosis, and hypothermia. Adjuncts include permissive hypotension until surgical hemorrhage control, limited crystalloid use, and early tranexamic acid administration.

A is incorrect because transfusing packed red cells alone without plasma and platelets leads to dilutional coagulopathy and does not address the clotting factor and platelet consumption seen in massive hemorrhage.
C is incorrect because administering platelets alone does not replace lost red cell oxygen-carrying capacity or depleted clotting factors; isolated platelet transfusion is not a resuscitation strategy.
D is incorrect because large-volume crystalloid resuscitation before blood products dilutes clotting factors, worsens acidosis and hypothermia, and increases the risk of ARDS and tissue edema — the opposite of damage control resuscitation principles.
E is incorrect because plasma alone replaces clotting factors but does not restore oxygen-carrying capacity (red cells) or platelet function, making it insufficient as a sole resuscitation product in massive hemorrhage.

questions.question:
Which classification is used for proximal femoral focal deficiency, and what is the key determinant of treatment?
A) Herring classification; lateral pillar height
B) Salter-Harris classification; physeal involvement
C) Loder classification; stability
D) Gartland classification; displacement
E) Aitken classification; presence of an acetabulum and stability of the hip along with predicted limb length discrepancy
questions.answer:
E)
The Aitken classification (Types A through D) categorizes proximal femoral focal deficiency based on the presence of the femoral head, adequacy of the acetabulum, and the osseous connection between the femoral head and shaft. Treatment is determined by hip stability and predicted limb-length discrepancy: limb lengthening is considered for smaller discrepancies with a stable hip (Aitken A), whereas amputation (e.g., Syme or knee disarticulation) or Van Nes rotationplasty with prosthetic fitting is used for severe deficiency (Aitken C/D). Ipsilateral fibular hemimelia coexists in a substantial proportion of cases and should be sought.

A is incorrect because the Herring (lateral pillar) classification is used for Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, not PFFD. B is incorrect because the Salter-Harris classification describes physeal fracture patterns in children and is unrelated to PFFD. C is incorrect because the Loder classification distinguishes stable from unstable slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE), not PFFD. D is incorrect because the Gartland classification grades supracondylar humerus fractures by displacement and is unrelated to PFFD.

questions.question:
A 15-year-old gymnast has activity-related low back pain worsened by extension. Radiographs are equivocal. Which imaging is most appropriate to identify an active pars stress injury while limiting radiation?
A) Bone scan with SPECT alone
B) MRI with fat-suppressed sequences showing pars marrow edema
C) Standing scoliosis films
D) Repeat plain radiographs in 6 months
E) Myelography
questions.answer:
B)
MRI with fat-suppressed (STIR) sequences detects marrow edema in the pars interarticularis, identifying an active stress reaction before a frank defect appears, without ionizing radiation — an important consideration in an adolescent. Early active lesions detected this way have the best healing potential with activity restriction and bracing.

A is incorrect because bone scan with SPECT, while sensitive for pars stress injuries, delivers ionizing radiation and lacks the specificity of MRI; it cannot distinguish stress reaction from other causes of increased uptake.
C is incorrect because standing scoliosis films evaluate coronal-plane deformity and are not designed to identify pars interarticularis stress injuries.
D is incorrect because delaying imaging for 6 months risks progression of a stress reaction to a complete pars defect (spondylolysis); early diagnosis allows timely bracing and activity modification.
E is incorrect because myelography is an invasive study involving intrathecal contrast and ionizing radiation, used to evaluate neural compression — it has no role in diagnosing pars stress injuries.

questions.question:
A 63-year-old woman undergoes primary total knee arthroplasty and is at standard risk for venous thromboembolism. Current guidelines support which approach?
A) Warfarin bridged with heparin in all patients
B) Therapeutic-dose anticoagulation for 6 months
C) No prophylaxis in any patient
D) Inferior vena cava filter placement routinely
E) Risk-stratified prophylaxis, with aspirin an acceptable agent in standard-risk patients alongside early mobilization and mechanical devices
questions.answer:
E)
Current AAOS and ACCP guidelines endorse risk-stratified VTE prophylaxis after total knee arthroplasty. For standard-risk patients, aspirin (alone or combined with early mobilization and mechanical compression devices) is an acceptable agent, offering comparable efficacy to more potent anticoagulants with a lower bleeding profile. Higher-risk patients (prior VTE, active malignancy, known thrombophilia) warrant escalation to agents such as low-molecular-weight heparin or direct oral anticoagulants.

A is incorrect because warfarin bridged with heparin is overly aggressive for standard-risk TKA patients and carries unnecessary bleeding risk; it is not recommended as a universal protocol.
B is incorrect because therapeutic-dose anticoagulation for 6 months far exceeds the recommended duration (typically 2–6 weeks) and intensity of prophylaxis for routine arthroplasty, substantially increasing hemorrhagic complications.
C is incorrect because withholding all prophylaxis is not supported by any major guideline; even low-risk patients benefit from at least mechanical prophylaxis and early mobilization.
D is incorrect because routine inferior vena cava filter placement is not indicated; IVC filters are reserved for patients with contraindications to pharmacologic prophylaxis or documented proximal DVT/PE despite anticoagulation.

questions.question:
Limb salvage rather than amputation is generally contraindicated in which situation?
A) A tumor abutting but not encasing the neurovascular bundle
B) Major neurovascular encasement with an anticipated nonfunctional limb, or inability to achieve negative margins
C) High-grade histology
D) Age under 12 in all cases
E) Pathologic fracture in all cases
questions.answer:
B)
Limb salvage requires the ability to obtain adequate surgical margins and to produce a limb that is more functional than an amputation with a prosthesis. Contraindications include major neurovascular involvement precluding functional reconstruction, extensive soft tissue loss preventing coverage, and inability to achieve negative margins.

A is incorrect because a tumor abutting but not encasing the neurovascular bundle can often be resected with adequate margins while preserving the vessels and nerves, so this is not a contraindication to limb salvage.
C is incorrect because high-grade histology alone is not a contraindication to limb salvage; many high-grade sarcomas are successfully treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by wide resection and limb-sparing reconstruction.
D is incorrect because age under 12 is not an absolute contraindication; expandable endoprostheses and rotationplasty allow limb salvage even in young children.
E is incorrect because pathologic fracture was formerly considered a contraindication but is now often managed with limb salvage after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, provided the fracture hematoma is contained and adequate margins can still be achieved. Studies show comparable survival between limb salvage and amputation when margins are adequate.

questions.question:
Reamed intramedullary nailing compared with unreamed nailing of closed tibial shaft fractures results in:
A) No difference in any outcome
B) Higher nonunion rates
C) Lower rates of reoperation and nonunion
D) Higher infection rates in closed fractures
E) Higher rates of compartment syndrome
questions.answer:
C)
The SPRINT trial demonstrated a benefit of reamed nailing in closed tibial shaft fractures, with fewer reoperations largely driven by lower rates of nonunion and implant failure; no significant benefit was found in open fractures. Reaming disrupts endosteal blood supply temporarily but stimulates periosteal blood flow and deposits osteogenic material at the fracture site, and allows placement of a larger-diameter, mechanically stronger nail.

A is incorrect because the SPRINT trial showed a statistically significant reduction in reoperation for closed fractures with reamed nailing, so outcomes are not equivalent. B is incorrect because reamed nailing is associated with lower, not higher, nonunion rates in closed tibial fractures. D is incorrect because reaming does not increase infection rates in closed fractures; concerns about thermal necrosis and infection are more relevant to open fractures. E is incorrect because reamed nailing has not been shown to increase compartment syndrome rates; while reaming transiently raises intramedullary pressure, this has not translated into a clinically significant increase in compartment syndrome.

questions.question:
An incidental 8-mm round sclerotic focus is found in the femoral neck of a 45-year-old woman with breast cancer. It has spiculated margins blending with surrounding trabeculae and does not take up tracer on bone scan. The most likely diagnosis is:
A) Osteoblastoma
B) Blastic metastasis
C) Enostosis (bone island)
D) Osteoid osteoma
E) Osteosarcoma
questions.answer:
C)
An enostosis (bone island) is a focus of compact lamellar bone within cancellous bone. It is recognized by radiating spicules that blend into surrounding trabeculae ("thorny radiation") and by absent or minimal uptake on bone scan. Serial imaging showing stability provides further reassurance; growth of more than 25% in 6 months warrants further evaluation.

A is incorrect because osteoblastoma is typically >2 cm, expansile, and symptomatic, and would show increased tracer uptake on bone scan.
B is incorrect because blastic metastases are characteristically "hot" on bone scan with avid tracer uptake and lack the spiculated margins blending smoothly with trabeculae seen in an enostosis.
D is incorrect because osteoid osteoma presents with pain (classically nocturnal, relieved by NSAIDs), has a characteristic nidus with surrounding reactive sclerosis, and shows intense uptake on bone scan (double-density sign).
E is incorrect because osteosarcoma is an aggressive lesion with destructive features, periosteal reaction, and soft-tissue extension; it would be intensely hot on bone scan and would not present as a small, incidental, quiescent sclerotic focus.

questions.question:
Which is the most reliable early sign of a septic hip rather than transient synovitis in a limping child?
A) Recent viral illness
B) Normal ESR and CRP
C) Fever above 38.5 C, refusal to bear weight, ESR above 40, WBC above 12,000
D) Pain relieved by NSAIDs
E) Bilateral symptoms
questions.answer:
C)
The Kocher criteria — fever > 38.5 °C, refusal to bear weight, ESR > 40 mm/hr, and WBC > 12,000/μL — are the most reliable clinical predictors for distinguishing septic arthritis from transient synovitis. The presence of all four criteria confers an approximately 99% probability of septic arthritis. CRP > 2.0 mg/dL has been validated as an additional independent predictor. Ultrasound can identify an effusion but cannot differentiate infection from synovitis; aspiration with cell count, Gram stain, and culture remains the definitive diagnostic step.

A is incorrect because a recent viral illness is actually more suggestive of transient synovitis, which commonly follows a viral upper respiratory infection. B is incorrect because normal ESR and CRP argue against septic arthritis and make transient synovitis more likely; they do not help identify a septic hip. D is incorrect because pain relief with NSAIDs is characteristic of transient synovitis and does not reliably distinguish it from early septic arthritis. E is incorrect because bilateral symptoms are more consistent with transient synovitis or other non-infectious conditions; septic arthritis is typically unilateral.

questions.question:
Which physis contributes the most longitudinal growth in the lower extremity?
A) Distal tibia
B) Distal femur
C) Proximal tibia
D) Proximal fibula
E) Proximal femur
questions.answer:
B)
The distal femoral physis contributes approximately 9 mm of growth per year, accounting for roughly 70% of femoral longitudinal growth and about 38% of total lower-extremity growth — making it the single greatest contributor to lower-limb length. This is a classic board fact and explains why injuries to the distal femoral physis carry significant risk of limb-length discrepancy.

A is incorrect because the distal tibial physis contributes only about 5 mm/year (approximately 40% of tibial growth), substantially less than the distal femur. C is incorrect because the proximal tibial physis contributes approximately 6 mm/year (about 55–60% of tibial growth), which is less than the distal femur's contribution. D is incorrect because the proximal fibular physis contributes a relatively small amount of growth and is not a major contributor to overall lower-extremity length. E is incorrect because the proximal femoral physis contributes only about 3–4 mm/year (roughly 30% of femoral growth), far less than the distal femur.

questions.question:
Remodeling potential of a pediatric fracture is greatest when:
A) The physis is closed
B) The child is young, the fracture is near a rapidly growing physis, and the deformity is in the plane of adjacent joint motion
C) The deformity is at the diaphysis in a 15-year-old
D) The fracture is intra-articular
E) The deformity is rotational
questions.answer:
B)
Remodeling is driven by physeal growth and periosteal apposition. It is greatest when the child is young (maximum remaining growth), the fracture is near a rapidly growing physis, and the angular deformity lies in the plane of motion of the adjacent joint.

A is incorrect because a closed physis means no remaining growth, eliminating the primary driver of remodeling. C is incorrect because a diaphyseal fracture in a 15-year-old has minimal remaining growth and is far from the physis, both of which severely limit remodeling capacity. D is incorrect because intra-articular incongruity does not reliably remodel and typically requires anatomic reduction. E is incorrect because rotational malalignment does not correct with growth-mediated remodeling and generally requires intervention if significant.

questions.question:
Which type of bite injury has the highest risk of deep infection and warrants coverage for Eikenella corrodens?
A) Rodent bite to the finger
B) Cat bite to the hand
C) Dog bite to the forearm
D) Human clenched-fist injury over the MCP joint
E) Snake bite to the calf
questions.answer:
D)
Fight bites (clenched-fist injuries) over the MCP joint frequently penetrate the extensor tendon and joint capsule; when the finger extends, the tendon slides proximally and seals contaminated material within the joint space. Eikenella corrodens is the characteristic pathogen of human bite wounds and requires amoxicillin-clavulanate or ampicillin-sulbactam plus thorough irrigation and debridement.

A is incorrect because rodent bites rarely cause deep infection and are not associated with Eikenella; the primary concern with rodent bites is rat-bite fever (Streptobacillus moniliformis). B is incorrect because cat bites, while carrying a high overall infection rate due to deep puncture inoculation, are associated with Pasteurella multocida rather than Eikenella corrodens and less commonly involve joint penetration. C is incorrect because dog bites to the forearm typically cause crush-type wounds with a lower infection rate than cat or human bites and are associated with Pasteurella and Capnocytophaga species, not Eikenella. E is incorrect because snake bites pose risks of envenomation and local tissue necrosis but are not associated with Eikenella corrodens or the same deep joint infection mechanism seen with clenched-fist injuries.

questions.question:
A Salter-Harris type IV fracture is characterized by:
A) Fracture through the physis only
B) Physeal fracture exiting through the metaphysis
C) Physeal fracture exiting through the epiphysis
D) Crush injury to the physis
E) Fracture crossing the metaphysis, physis, and epiphysis
questions.answer:
E)
A Salter-Harris type IV fracture crosses the metaphysis, physis, and epiphysis. Types III and IV are intra-articular and require anatomic reduction (often with internal fixation) because malreduction produces both articular incongruity and physeal bar formation with subsequent growth arrest.

A is incorrect because a fracture through the physis only (transphyseal separation) describes a Salter-Harris type I injury.
B is incorrect because a physeal fracture exiting through the metaphysis (producing a Thurston-Holland fragment) describes a Salter-Harris type II injury, the most common type.
C is incorrect because a physeal fracture exiting through the epiphysis describes a Salter-Harris type III injury.
D is incorrect because a crush injury to the physis describes a Salter-Harris type V injury, which carries a high risk of growth arrest and is often diagnosed retrospectively.

questions.question:
The most common soft tissue sarcoma in adults, historically called malignant fibrous histiocytoma, is now designated:
A) Rhabdomyosarcoma
B) Epithelioid sarcoma
C) Synovial sarcoma
D) Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma
E) Liposarcoma
questions.answer:
D)
Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (UPS) is the current WHO designation for the entity historically known as malignant fibrous histiocytoma (MFH). Along with liposarcoma, it is one of the most common soft tissue sarcomas in adults, typically arising in the extremities of older patients. The reclassification reflects the understanding that MFH lacked a specific line of differentiation.

A is incorrect because rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft tissue sarcoma in children, not adults, and was never termed MFH.

B is incorrect because epithelioid sarcoma is a rare sarcoma that characteristically occurs in the distal upper extremity of young adults and is not the entity formerly called MFH.

C is incorrect because synovial sarcoma typically occurs in young adults near (but rarely within) joints, may show calcification, and has a propensity for lymph node metastasis; it is a distinct entity from MFH.

E is incorrect because liposarcoma, while also among the most common adult soft tissue sarcomas, shows adipocytic differentiation and was never classified as MFH. The stem specifically asks for the tumor formerly called MFH, which is UPS.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman has painful posttraumatic arthritis of the index finger proximal interphalangeal joint. Compared with arthroplasty, arthrodesis of this particular joint is favored because the index PIP joint primarily requires:
A) Rotational mobility
B) Maximum flexion for grip
C) No specific functional demand
D) Lateral stability for pinch
E) Hyperextension for release
questions.answer:
D)
The radial digits (index and long fingers) are used primarily for pinch, which demands lateral stability. Arthrodesis of the index PIP joint is therefore generally preferred over arthroplasty because it provides reliable lateral stability under pinch loads. The ulnar digits (ring and small fingers) are used more for power grip and benefit from a flexion arc, making arthroplasty more attractive there when bone stock and collateral ligaments are adequate. Silicone arthroplasty in an index PIP is prone to lateral instability and deformity under repetitive pinch loads.

A is incorrect because rotational mobility is not a primary functional demand of the PIP joint; rotation occurs minimally at the CMC level and is not a reason to choose arthrodesis over arthroplasty.
B is incorrect because maximum flexion for grip is the primary demand of the ulnar (ring and small finger) PIP joints, not the index finger; this is the rationale for arthroplasty in those digits.
C is incorrect because the index PIP joint has a very specific functional demand — lateral stability for pinch — and is not without functional requirements.
E is incorrect because hyperextension for release is not a recognized primary functional demand of the index PIP joint; normal PIP function does not require hyperextension.

questions.question:
A far lateral (extraforaminal) disc herniation at L4-L5 compresses which nerve root?
A) L3
B) L2
C) S1
D) L5
E) L4
questions.answer:
E)
In the lumbar spine, the exiting nerve root at L4-L5 is L4 and the traversing root is L5. A paracentral (posterolateral) herniation compresses the traversing (L5) root, whereas a far lateral (extraforaminal) herniation lies lateral to the foramen and compresses the exiting (L4) root. Far lateral herniations often cause more severe radicular pain and may be approached through a paraspinal (Wiltse) muscle-splitting exposure.

A is incorrect because L3 is the exiting root at L3-L4, not L4-L5. B is incorrect because L2 exits at the L2-L3 level and is not involved at L4-L5. C is incorrect because S1 is the traversing root at L5-S1, not L4-L5. D is incorrect because L5 is the traversing root at L4-L5 and would be compressed by a paracentral herniation, not a far lateral one.

questions.question:
The single most important principle of biopsy for a suspected musculoskeletal sarcoma is:
A) Avoid tourniquet use in all cases
B) Place the biopsy tract so that it can be completely excised with the definitive resection specimen, ideally performed by the treating surgeon
C) Open the joint for complete visualization
D) Use a transverse incision in the extremity
E) Use the largest incision possible for exposure
questions.answer:
B)
The biopsy tract is considered contaminated and must be excised en bloc with the tumor during definitive resection. Longitudinal incisions in line with the definitive surgical approach, meticulous hemostasis, drains placed in line with and close to the incision, and performance by or in close consultation with the treating oncologic surgeon are all essential. Landmark studies by Mankin demonstrated that biopsies performed at referring institutions had markedly higher rates of error, complications, and changes in treatment plan, including unnecessary amputation.

A is incorrect because tourniquet use is not absolutely contraindicated; a tourniquet may be used judiciously to improve visualization and hemostasis, and its avoidance is not the single most important biopsy principle.
C is incorrect because opening the joint contaminates the entire joint space, potentially converting a limb-salvage case into one requiring amputation or extra-articular resection.
D is incorrect because transverse incisions in the extremity cross multiple tissue compartments and cannot be easily excised with the definitive longitudinal resection incision, increasing the risk of tumor spillage and compromising limb salvage.
E is incorrect because using the largest incision possible increases hematoma formation, tissue contamination, and the volume of tissue that must be excised at definitive surgery; the smallest incision adequate for diagnosis should be used.

questions.question:
A patient with a solitary lytic vertebral lesion causing vertebra plana in a 6-year-old most likely has:
A) Langerhans cell histiocytosis (eosinophilic granuloma)
B) Ewing sarcoma
C) Metastatic neuroblastoma
D) Osteosarcoma
E) Tuberculous spondylitis
questions.answer:
A)
Eosinophilic granuloma (Langerhans cell histiocytosis) is the classic cause of vertebra plana in children. Histology shows Langerhans cells with coffee-bean grooved nuclei, CD1a and S-100 positivity, and Birbeck granules on electron microscopy. Isolated lesions often heal spontaneously with restoration of vertebral height; treatment options include observation, bracing, injection, or low-dose radiation. Multisystem disease (Hand-Schüller-Christian, Letterer-Siwe) requires chemotherapy.

B is incorrect because Ewing sarcoma typically presents as a permeative/moth-eaten lesion with an onion-skin periosteal reaction in the diaphysis or metadiaphysis of long bones; it does not classically cause vertebra plana. C is incorrect because metastatic neuroblastoma in the spine more commonly causes epidural compression or multifocal disease rather than the classic solitary vertebra plana pattern. D is incorrect because osteosarcoma is predominantly a metaphyseal long-bone tumor and is exceedingly rare as a solitary vertebral lesion causing vertebra plana in a 6-year-old. E is incorrect because tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) typically involves two contiguous vertebral bodies and the intervening disc with kyphotic collapse, not the classic solitary vertebra plana seen in eosinophilic granuloma.

questions.question:
Which instrument is used to grade the functional severity of cervical spondylotic myelopathy and guide surgical decision making?
A) modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association score
B) Harris Hip Score
C) American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons score
D) Oswestry Disability Index
E) Constant-Murley score
questions.answer:
A)
The modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) score quantifies upper and lower extremity motor function, sensory function, and bladder function in cervical myelopathy, stratifying severity as mild (≥15), moderate (12–14), or severe (≤11). Surgery is generally recommended for moderate and severe myelopathy given the stepwise progressive natural history. The Nurick grade is an older, gait-focused scale also used in myelopathy but is less comprehensive.

B is incorrect because the Harris Hip Score is used to evaluate hip function (pain, function, range of motion) after hip arthroplasty or fracture, not cervical myelopathy.
C is incorrect because the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) score assesses shoulder pain and function, and is not relevant to cervical myelopathy.
D is incorrect because the Oswestry Disability Index measures functional disability related to low back pain, not cervical myelopathy.
E is incorrect because the Constant-Murley score evaluates shoulder function (pain, activities of daily living, range of motion, strength) and has no role in cervical myelopathy assessment.

questions.question:
A patient with an isolated Weber B fibula fracture has no medial tenderness and a normal medial clear space on weight-bearing radiographs. The most appropriate treatment is:
A) Syndesmotic screw fixation
B) Ankle arthrodesis
C) Open reduction internal fixation
D) Non-weight bearing cast for 12 weeks
E) Functional bracing or a walking boot with weight bearing as tolerated
questions.answer:
E)
A stable Weber B (SER II) fibula fracture with no medial tenderness and a normal medial clear space on weight-bearing films indicates an intact deltoid ligament and a stable ankle. These injuries do well with functional treatment — a walking boot or brace with early weight bearing as tolerated.

A is incorrect because syndesmotic screw fixation is indicated for syndesmotic instability (e.g., Weber C or high fibula fractures with syndesmotic disruption), which is not present here.
B is incorrect because ankle arthrodesis is reserved for end-stage ankle arthritis, not an acute stable fracture.
C is incorrect because open reduction internal fixation is indicated for unstable ankle fractures (e.g., medial clear space widening, talar shift); this fracture pattern is stable and does not require surgical fixation.
D is incorrect because prolonged non-weight-bearing immobilization for 12 weeks is unnecessarily restrictive for a stable Weber B fracture; functional treatment with early weight bearing yields equivalent outcomes with less morbidity.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old man in Connecticut has a large, minimally painful knee effusion with 28,000 WBC/microL, negative Gram stain, and a history of a summer rash. Which is the most appropriate management?
A) Urgent irrigation and debridement of the knee
B) Serologic testing with ELISA and confirmatory Western blot, and oral doxycycline if positive
C) Synovectomy
D) Empiric antifungal therapy
E) Intra-articular corticosteroid injection
questions.answer:
B)
Lyme arthritis typically presents as a large, relatively painless monoarticular knee effusion in an endemic area (Connecticut is highly endemic), with synovial white cell counts that can overlap the septic range but with disproportionately preserved function and absence of systemic toxicity. A history of a summer rash (erythema migrans) is a key clue. Two-tier serologic testing (ELISA followed by confirmatory Western blot) confirms the diagnosis, and oral doxycycline is effective first-line treatment for Lyme arthritis.

A is incorrect because urgent irrigation and debridement is indicated for septic arthritis; here the Gram stain is negative, the joint is only minimally painful, and the clinical picture (endemic area, prior rash, large painless effusion) strongly favors Lyme arthritis over a pyogenic process.
C is incorrect because synovectomy is reserved for refractory Lyme arthritis that fails prolonged antibiotic therapy; it is not appropriate as initial management.
D is incorrect because there is no indication of fungal arthritis; fungal joint infections are rare and typically occur in immunocompromised hosts, not in this clinical scenario.
E is incorrect because intra-articular corticosteroid injection does not address the underlying spirochetal infection and could worsen an undiagnosed infectious process; definitive antibiotic treatment is required.

questions.question:
A 61-year-old man with diabetic peripheral neuropathy sustains an unstable bimalleolar ankle fracture. Compared with a neurologically intact patient, his operative plan should include:
A) Closed treatment in all cases
B) Immediate arthrodesis
C) Standard fixation with early weight bearing at 2 weeks
D) Augmented, rigid fixation with prolonged protected weight bearing and anticipation of higher complication rates
E) Removal of hardware at 6 weeks
questions.answer:
D)
Diabetic patients with peripheral neuropathy have markedly higher rates of wound complications, infection, malunion, Charcot collapse, and hardware failure after ankle fracture surgery. Operative principles include rigid, often augmented fixation (supplemental transarticular or hindfoot fixation, multiple syndesmotic screws, locked plates), meticulous soft-tissue handling, and roughly double the usual period of protected weight bearing and immobilization.

A is incorrect because an unstable bimalleolar fracture in a neuropathic patient treated nonoperatively carries a very high risk of displacement, malunion, and Charcot arthropathy; operative stabilization is generally indicated.
B is incorrect because immediate primary arthrodesis is overly aggressive for an acute fracture; anatomic reduction and rigid fixation should be attempted first, with arthrodesis reserved for cases of established Charcot collapse or failed fixation.
C is incorrect because early weight bearing at 2 weeks with standard fixation invites hardware failure and Charcot breakdown in a neuropathic limb; prolonged non-weight-bearing is essential.
E is incorrect because routine hardware removal at 6 weeks is far too early and would destabilize the fracture before healing; hardware is typically retained longer in neuropathic patients given their delayed healing.

questions.question:
Central cord syndrome is characterized by:
A) Isolated loss of proprioception
B) Greater lower extremity than upper extremity weakness
C) Greater upper extremity than lower extremity weakness with variable sacral sparing
D) Complete loss of all modalities below the level
E) Ipsilateral motor loss with contralateral pain and temperature loss
questions.answer:
C)
Central cord syndrome is the most common incomplete spinal cord syndrome, typically occurring in older patients with preexisting cervical spondylosis after a hyperextension injury. Upper extremities are disproportionately weaker than lower extremities because of the somatotopic (laminar) arrangement of the corticospinal tract, with cervical fibers located centrally. Bladder dysfunction and variable sensory loss with sacral sparing are characteristic. Prognosis for ambulation is generally favorable.

A is incorrect because isolated loss of proprioception describes a posterior column syndrome, not central cord syndrome. B is incorrect because central cord syndrome produces greater upper extremity weakness, not greater lower extremity weakness; the central location of cervical-level fibers makes them more vulnerable. D is incorrect because complete loss of all modalities below the level describes a complete spinal cord injury, not an incomplete syndrome. E is incorrect because ipsilateral motor loss with contralateral pain and temperature loss describes Brown-Séquard syndrome (cord hemisection), which has the best prognosis among incomplete cord syndromes.

questions.question:
Which scaphoid fracture pattern is most likely to require surgical fixation?
A) Nondisplaced waist fracture in a compliant patient
B) Displaced proximal pole fracture
C) Incomplete waist fracture
D) Distal pole avulsion
E) Nondisplaced distal tubercle fracture
questions.answer:
B)
Proximal pole fractures have a tenuous blood supply (retrograde from the distal dorsal ridge) and are prone to avascular necrosis and nonunion. Displacement greater than 1 mm, a scapholunate angle above 60°, an intrascaphoid (humpback) angle above 35°, and associated carpal instability are additional indications for surgical fixation. Among the choices, a displaced proximal pole fracture carries the highest risk of complications and is most likely to require operative treatment.

A is incorrect because nondisplaced waist fractures in compliant patients heal in approximately 90% of cases with thumb spica casting; surgery is an option but not required.
C is incorrect because incomplete (nondisplaced) waist fractures are stable injuries that respond well to cast immobilization.
D is incorrect because distal pole avulsion fractures are extra-articular, have an excellent blood supply, and heal reliably with conservative treatment.
E is incorrect because nondisplaced distal tubercle fractures are low-energy injuries with a robust blood supply and heal predictably with short-term immobilization.

questions.question:
Which imaging modality is most useful for identifying occult distant disease and for selecting the most metabolically active region of a heterogeneous tumor for biopsy?
A) Ultrasound
B) Technetium bone scan alone
C) Non-contrast head CT
D) PET-CT
E) Plain radiography
questions.answer:
D)
PET-CT combines metabolic and anatomic information, detecting nodal and distant metastases and skip lesions that other modalities may miss. It identifies the region of highest metabolic activity (SUV) within a heterogeneous mass, guiding biopsy to the highest-grade component rather than a necrotic or low-grade area. It is also used to assess treatment response.

A is incorrect because ultrasound is useful for superficial soft-tissue mass characterization and guiding needle biopsy but has no role in systemic staging or identifying the most metabolically active region of a tumor.
B is incorrect because technetium bone scan detects osseous metastases via osteoblastic activity but does not provide metabolic information about soft-tissue or nodal disease and cannot guide biopsy to the highest-grade region of a heterogeneous mass.
C is incorrect because non-contrast head CT is limited to evaluating intracranial pathology and has no utility in whole-body staging or metabolic characterization of musculoskeletal tumors.
E is incorrect because plain radiography is the first study obtained for a bone lesion and helps characterize the lesion locally, but it cannot detect occult distant disease or identify the most metabolically active area for biopsy.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old man sustains a low-velocity gunshot wound to the thigh with a transverse femoral shaft fracture, an intact neurovascular examination, and small entry and exit wounds. The most appropriate treatment is:
A) Nonoperative management in skeletal traction
B) Local wound care, a short course of antibiotics, and intramedullary nailing
C) Extensive debridement of the entire missile tract with delayed fixation
D) Immediate amputation because of contamination
E) External fixation for 6 weeks followed by casting
questions.answer:
B)
Low-velocity civilian gunshot wounds cause limited soft-tissue injury, and the fracture is treated according to its pattern rather than as a conventional open fracture. Local wound care, tetanus prophylaxis, a short course of antibiotics (typically a first-generation cephalosporin for 24–48 hours), and standard intramedullary nailing produce good outcomes. High-velocity injuries, close-range shotgun wounds, and wounds traversing the bowel require formal surgical debridement.

A is incorrect because a transverse femoral shaft fracture in a young adult is best treated with intramedullary nailing; prolonged skeletal traction leads to longer hospitalization, knee stiffness, and inferior functional outcomes.
C is incorrect because extensive debridement of the entire missile tract is unnecessary for low-velocity gunshot wounds, which cause minimal soft-tissue devitalization; this approach increases surgical morbidity without benefit.
D is incorrect because amputation is not indicated; low-velocity gunshot fractures have a low infection rate and an intact neurovascular examination confirms a viable limb.
E is incorrect because external fixation is reserved for damage-control situations or severe soft-tissue compromise; a low-velocity injury with small entry/exit wounds and intact soft tissues is best managed with definitive intramedullary nailing.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old man has bowing of the tibia, hearing loss, an alkaline phosphatase of 750 U/L, and radiographs showing coarsened trabeculae and cortical thickening. Histology would most likely show:
A) Fibrous stroma with Chinese-character trabeculae lacking osteoblastic rimming
B) Nests of chondrocytes in a hyaline matrix
C) Mosaic pattern of irregular cement lines
D) Osteoid seams with poor mineralization
E) Sheets of foamy histiocytes with Langerhans cells
questions.answer:
C)
Paget disease of bone is characterized by a chaotic mosaic pattern of irregular cement lines resulting from repeated cycles of osteoclastic resorption and osteoblastic formation. Clinical features include bowing of long bones, hearing loss (skull involvement), and markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium and phosphate. Bisphosphonates are first-line therapy; a sudden destructive lytic lesion raises concern for secondary sarcoma (~1%).

A is incorrect because fibrous stroma with Chinese-character trabeculae lacking osteoblastic rimming describes fibrous dysplasia, not Paget disease. B is incorrect because nests of chondrocytes in a hyaline matrix describes a cartilaginous neoplasm (e.g., enchondroma or chondrosarcoma), not Paget disease. D is incorrect because widened osteoid seams with poor mineralization describes osteomalacia, which presents with low or normal alkaline phosphatase relative to Paget levels and lacks the mosaic cement-line pattern. E is incorrect because sheets of foamy histiocytes with Langerhans cells describes Langerhans cell histiocytosis (eosinophilic granuloma), a different pathologic process entirely.

questions.question:
After closed reduction and spica casting for DDH, which study best confirms concentric reduction while the child remains in the cast?
A) Limited CT or MRI through the cast
B) No confirmation is necessary
C) Fluoroscopy in the clinic
D) Plain radiograph alone
E) Ultrasound through plaster
questions.answer:
A)
Plaster and the largely cartilaginous femoral head make plain radiographs unreliable for confirming concentric reduction after closed reduction and spica casting for DDH. Limited-cut CT (low-dose) or MRI through the cast documents the position of the femoral head within the acetabulum and can identify soft-tissue interposition; MRI additionally assesses femoral head perfusion. Confirmation is essential, since an unrecognized malreduction leads to persistent dysplasia and repeated surgery.

B is incorrect because failure to confirm reduction risks missing a malreduction or interposed soft tissue (e.g., inverted limbus, pulvinar), leading to ongoing dysplasia and the need for further surgery.
C is incorrect because fluoroscopy in the clinic provides limited information through a spica cast, delivers radiation, and does not reliably visualize the cartilaginous femoral head or soft-tissue interposition.
D is incorrect because plain radiographs are unreliable in this setting — the largely unossified femoral head and the overlying plaster cast obscure the relationship between the femoral head and acetabulum.
E is incorrect because ultrasound cannot reliably penetrate plaster/fiberglass spica casts to provide adequate imaging of the hip; it is useful for screening and monitoring before casting but not for post-reduction confirmation through a cast.

questions.question:
During fluoroscopically assisted femoral nailing, which action most reduces radiation exposure to the surgical team?
A) Positioning the image intensifier below the table and the emitter above it
B) Standing on the side of the image intensifier rather than the emitter
C) Removing the lead apron to improve mobility during imaging
D) Using continuous rather than pulsed fluoroscopy
E) Increasing the distance from the beam, since exposure falls with the square of distance
questions.answer:
E)
Scatter radiation follows the inverse square law: doubling the distance from the radiation source reduces exposure approximately fourfold. Maximizing distance from the beam is considered the single most effective method of reducing radiation exposure to the surgical team.

A is incorrect because the image intensifier should be positioned ABOVE the table (closer to the surgeon) with the x-ray emitter BELOW; this arrangement directs scatter radiation downward away from the surgeon. The described configuration (intensifier below, emitter above) is the reverse and would increase scatter exposure to the team. B is incorrect because while standing on the intensifier side is indeed safer than standing on the emitter side (scatter is greatest at the beam entry point), this alone is less impactful than maximizing distance from the source. C is incorrect because removing lead shielding would increase radiation exposure; lead aprons should always be worn during fluoroscopy. D is incorrect because continuous fluoroscopy delivers more radiation than pulsed fluoroscopy; pulsed mode reduces dose by limiting beam-on time.

questions.question:
Which statement about the superficial (tangential) zone of articular cartilage is correct?
A) It has the lowest water content and the highest proteoglycan content
B) It is separated from bone by the tidemark
C) Collagen fibers are oriented perpendicular to the joint surface
D) It contains the largest chondrocytes arranged in columns
E) It has the highest water content and collagen oriented parallel to the surface
questions.answer:
E)
The superficial (tangential) zone of articular cartilage has the highest water content (~80%) and the lowest proteoglycan concentration. Collagen fibers (primarily type II) are oriented parallel (tangential) to the articular surface, which allows this zone to resist shear forces. Chondrocytes here are small and flattened.

A is incorrect because it states the exact opposite — the superficial zone has the highest (not lowest) water content and the lowest (not highest) proteoglycan content. B is incorrect because the tidemark separates the deep (radial) zone from the calcified cartilage zone, not the superficial zone from bone. C is incorrect because collagen fibers in the superficial zone run parallel to the surface; perpendicular orientation is characteristic of the deep (radial) zone. D is incorrect because the largest chondrocytes arranged in columns are found in the deep (radial) zone, not the superficial zone.

questions.question:
After a clean laceration and primary repair of a digital nerve, which finding best indicates functional sensory recovery?
A) Normal radiographs
B) Return of static two-point discrimination to less than 6 mm
C) Restoration of sweating alone
D) Presence of a Tinel sign at the repair site alone
E) Absence of pain at rest
questions.answer:
B)
Static two-point discrimination less than 6 mm indicates recovery of slowly adapting fiber density sufficient for functional sensation and fine object identification. This is the gold-standard clinical measure of useful sensory recovery after digital nerve repair.

A is incorrect because plain radiographs assess bony structures and have no role in evaluating nerve recovery. C is incorrect because restoration of sweating indicates autonomic (sympathetic) fiber regeneration only and does not confirm recovery of discriminative sensory function. D is incorrect because a Tinel sign at the repair site merely documents the presence of regenerating axons at that level; it does not confirm that functional end-organ reinnervation has occurred. E is incorrect because absence of pain at rest is a nonspecific finding that does not indicate meaningful sensory recovery; it simply reflects the lack of a painful neuroma or neuropathic process.

questions.question:
Increasing the working length of a plate or nail has which effect?
A) Decreases construct rigidity and increases interfragmentary motion
B) Increases construct rigidity and decreases interfragmentary strain
C) Increases axial stiffness only
D) Converts relative stability to absolute stability
E) Has no effect on rigidity but increases screw pullout
questions.answer:
A)
Working length is the distance between the points of fixation on either side of the fracture. A longer working length decreases construct stiffness (bending rigidity is inversely proportional to the cube of the working length for a beam, and inversely proportional to the square for a plate in some simplified models) and therefore permits more interfragmentary motion, which promotes secondary (callus) healing in bridge plating. Excessive flexibility, however, can produce strain high enough to cause nonunion.

B is incorrect because increasing working length decreases—not increases—construct rigidity, and interfragmentary strain increases rather than decreases.
C is incorrect because the effect is not limited to axial stiffness; bending and torsional stiffness are also reduced with a longer working length.
D is incorrect because increasing working length moves the construct toward relative stability (more motion), not absolute stability; absolute stability requires rigid fixation with minimal interfragmentary motion.
E is incorrect because increasing working length clearly decreases rigidity; it does not leave rigidity unchanged, nor does it primarily affect screw pullout strength.

questions.question:
Spinal shock is best defined as:
A) Hypotension with bradycardia after cord injury
B) Loss of sympathetic tone lasting 6 weeks
C) Transient loss of all cord function below the level of injury, whose resolution is signaled by return of the bulbocavernosus reflex
D) Permanent complete cord injury
E) Hypovolemia from associated injuries
questions.answer:
C)
Spinal shock is a transient physiologic phenomenon of areflexia and flaccid paralysis below the level of spinal cord injury, typically lasting 24–72 hours. Its resolution is signaled by the return of the bulbocavernosus reflex; only after spinal shock has resolved can a complete injury (ASIA A) be reliably diagnosed.

A is incorrect because hypotension with bradycardia describes neurogenic shock, a hemodynamic condition caused by loss of sympathetic tone (typically with injuries above T6), which is a separate entity from spinal shock.
B is incorrect because loss of sympathetic tone is a feature of neurogenic shock, not spinal shock, and spinal shock itself typically resolves within 24–72 hours, not 6 weeks.
D is incorrect because spinal shock is, by definition, a transient and reversible state of areflexia; it does not equate to a permanent complete cord injury.
E is incorrect because hypovolemia from associated injuries describes hemorrhagic (hypovolemic) shock, which is unrelated to the spinal cord–mediated phenomenon of spinal shock.

questions.question:
What is the significance of a "reactive zone" or pseudocapsule around a sarcoma?
A) It is only present in benign lesions
B) It represents the tumor's blood supply
C) It is a true capsule that safely contains all tumor cells
D) It is avascular and acellular
E) It contains compressed tumor cells and satellite lesions, so dissection through it yields a marginal margin with high recurrence risk
questions.answer:
E)
The pseudocapsule (reactive zone) around a sarcoma consists of compressed tumor cells, reactive inflammatory tissue, and neovascularity, and typically harbors satellite tumor nodules. Dissecting along this plane ("shelling out") constitutes a marginal margin, leaving microscopic disease behind and resulting in high local recurrence rates. This is why an unplanned excision along the pseudocapsule often necessitates re-resection of the entire tumor bed.

A is incorrect because pseudocapsules are characteristically found around malignant soft-tissue tumors (sarcomas), not only benign lesions. B is incorrect because while the reactive zone contains neovascularity, its clinical significance lies in harboring compressed tumor cells and satellite lesions, not merely representing the tumor's blood supply. C is incorrect because the pseudocapsule is not a true capsule; it does not safely contain all tumor cells and is regularly infiltrated by microscopic disease. D is incorrect because the reactive zone is neither avascular nor acellular — it contains inflammatory cells, new blood vessels, and compressed tumor cells.

questions.question:
A child with myelomeningocele at the L4 level is most likely to have:
A) Full plantar flexion strength
B) Quadriceps function with community ambulation using orthoses, and risk of calcaneus foot deformity from unopposed tibialis anterior
C) Hip stability at all levels
D) No ambulatory potential
E) Normal bowel and bladder function
questions.answer:
B)
At the L4 functional level, the quadriceps and medial hamstrings are innervated, allowing active knee extension and community ambulation with AFOs or KAFOs. However, the gastrocnemius-soleus complex (S1-S2) is non-functional, so unopposed tibialis anterior (L4) produces a calcaneus foot deformity. Latex allergy prophylaxis is essential, and any change in neurologic function, spasticity, or scoliosis progression should prompt evaluation for tethered cord, hydrocephalus, or shunt malfunction.

A is incorrect because plantar flexion is powered by the gastrocnemius-soleus (S1-S2), which is denervated at the L4 level; full plantar flexion strength would not be expected. C is incorrect because hip instability is common in myelomeningocele, particularly at higher levels where hip flexors and adductors are unopposed by weak or absent extensors and abductors; hip stability at all levels is not expected. D is incorrect because L4-level patients typically have sufficient quadriceps function for community ambulation with orthoses; wheelchair dependence is characteristic of thoracic-level lesions. E is incorrect because bowel and bladder function is controlled by sacral nerve roots (S2-S4), which are denervated at the L4 level, so neurogenic bowel and bladder are expected.

questions.question:
Which finding on MRI is most indicative of posterior ligamentous complex disruption in a thoracolumbar burst fracture?
A) Endplate fracture
B) Retropulsion of 30% of the canal
C) Anterior vertebral body height loss of 40%
D) Increased signal on fat-suppressed T2 images between the spinous processes with interspinous widening
E) Paraspinal muscle edema alone
questions.answer:
D)
Increased signal on fat-suppressed T2 (STIR) images in the supraspinous/interspinous ligaments and ligamentum flavum, combined with interspinous widening, is the most specific MRI finding for posterior ligamentous complex (PLC) disruption. PLC integrity is a key determinant of thoracolumbar fracture stability and guides surgical decision-making (TLICS classification).

A is incorrect because an endplate fracture is a feature of the vertebral body injury (anterior column) and does not reflect PLC integrity.
B is incorrect because retropulsion and canal compromise correlate poorly with instability or neurologic outcome in isolation; they reflect anterior/middle column injury, not PLC status.
C is incorrect because anterior vertebral body height loss reflects anterior column compression and, while contributing to kyphosis assessment, does not directly indicate PLC disruption.
E is incorrect because paraspinal muscle edema alone is a nonspecific finding seen with many spinal injuries and does not reliably indicate disruption of the PLC ligaments (supraspinous, interspinous, ligamentum flavum).

questions.question:
A 58-year-old woman is enrolled in a trial of an agent that inhibits sclerostin. Compared with a bisphosphonate, this agent is expected to have which primary effect on bone?
A) Direct mineralization of unmineralized osteoid seams
B) Suppression of parathyroid hormone secretion
C) Increased renal calcium excretion
D) Inhibition of osteoclast attachment to the bone surface
E) Activation of Wnt signaling with increased osteoblastic bone formation
questions.answer:
E)
Sclerostin is produced by osteocytes and inhibits the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, restraining bone formation. Antibodies to sclerostin (romosozumab) relieve that inhibition, producing a primarily anabolic response (increased osteoblastic bone formation) with a transient antiresorptive effect. This distinguishes it from bisphosphonates, which are purely antiresorptive.

A is incorrect because direct mineralization of unmineralized osteoid describes the mechanism of vitamin D or phosphate supplementation in osteomalacia, not anti-sclerostin therapy. B is incorrect because suppression of parathyroid hormone secretion describes the action of calcimimetics (e.g., cinacalcet) or calcium/vitamin D supplementation, not romosozumab. C is incorrect because increased renal calcium excretion is not a primary mechanism of anti-sclerostin agents; thiazide diuretics actually decrease renal calcium excretion, and this is unrelated to the Wnt pathway. D is incorrect because inhibition of osteoclast attachment to the bone surface describes the mechanism of bisphosphonates (via the mevalonate pathway in osteoclasts) or denosumab (RANKL inhibition); the primary distinguishing effect of anti-sclerostin therapy is anabolic (bone formation), not antiresorptive.

questions.question:
A grade II medial collateral ligament injury of the knee typically heals without surgery, whereas an anterior cruciate ligament tear does not. The best explanation is:
A) The MCL receives its blood supply from the middle geniculate artery
B) The MCL is composed of elastin rather than collagen
C) The extrasynovial MCL retains a fibrin clot scaffold, whereas the intra-articular ACL is bathed in synovial fluid that lyses the clot
D) The ACL is under continuous compressive rather than tensile load
E) The ACL has no intrinsic healing capacity because it lacks fibroblasts
questions.answer:
C)
The MCL is an extra-articular structure that forms and retains a hematoma, allowing an organized healing response with progression to a fibrous scar. The ACL is intra-articular and intrasynovial, so synovial fluid disperses the clot and plasmin lyses the fibrin scaffold, preventing bridging. This biologic difference underlies both the reliable nonoperative treatment of isolated MCL injuries and the interest in scaffold-augmented ACL repair techniques.

A is incorrect because the MCL receives its blood supply primarily from the superior and inferior medial geniculate arteries, not the middle geniculate artery (which supplies the cruciate ligaments); moreover, blood supply alone does not explain the healing difference.
B is incorrect because the MCL is composed predominantly of type I collagen, not elastin; its composition is similar to other ligaments.
D is incorrect because the ACL is primarily under tensile load, not compressive load; the mechanical environment is not the principal reason it fails to heal.
E is incorrect because the ACL does contain fibroblasts (synoviocyte-like cells) and has some intrinsic healing capacity; the problem is the hostile intra-articular environment that prevents clot retention and organized scar formation.

questions.question:
Which cement mantle finding on postoperative imaging corresponds to the poorest grade using the Barrack classification and predicts early loosening?
A) Radiolucency involving 100% of the bone-cement interface or complete failure to fill the medullary canal
B) A well-centered stem with a uniform mantle
C) Slight radiolucency at less than 50% of the interface
D) A mantle with minor voids
E) Complete filling of the medullary canal with no radiolucency
questions.answer:
A)
The Barrack cement mantle grading system ranges from Grade A (complete "white-out" filling with no radiolucency) to Grade D (radiolucency at 100% of the bone-cement interface or complete failure to fill the medullary canal). Grade D represents the poorest mantle and is strongly associated with early aseptic loosening. Modern cementing techniques—including canal preparation, pulsatile lavage, a distal cement restrictor, retrograde cement filling, and pressurization—are designed to achieve a Grade A mantle.

B is incorrect because a well-centered stem with a uniform mantle describes a Grade A (best) cement mantle. C is incorrect because slight radiolucency at less than 50% of the interface corresponds to Grade B, which is not the poorest grade. D is incorrect because minor voids within the mantle are consistent with a Grade B mantle and do not predict early loosening. E is incorrect because complete filling of the medullary canal with no radiolucency is the definition of a Grade A (best) cement mantle.

questions.question:
The dominant mechanism of polyethylene wear in a well-functioning total hip arthroplasty is:
A) Fatigue (delamination) wear
B) Third-body wear
C) Adhesive wear
D) Abrasive wear
E) Corrosive wear
questions.answer:
C)
Adhesive wear is the dominant mechanism of polyethylene wear in a well-functioning total hip arthroplasty. It occurs when microscopic bonds form between the polyethylene liner and the femoral head surface; as the surfaces slide, fragments of polyethylene are pulled away. This is the primary mode of wear generation in normal THA bearing couples.

A is incorrect because fatigue (delamination) wear involves subsurface crack propagation and is more characteristic of polyethylene failure in total knee arthroplasty (especially with gamma-in-air sterilized components), not the dominant mode in a well-functioning THA.
B is incorrect because third-body wear requires interposed particulate debris (e.g., cement, metal, bone fragments) between the bearing surfaces; while it can accelerate wear, it is not the dominant mechanism in a well-functioning prosthesis without loose debris.
D is incorrect because abrasive wear (hard surface scratching a softer one) contributes to polyethylene wear but is secondary to adhesive wear in a well-functioning THA with a smooth, undamaged femoral head.
E is incorrect because corrosive wear involves chemical or electrochemical degradation and is relevant to metal-on-metal interfaces or modular taper junctions, not the primary polyethylene wear mechanism.

questions.question:
