E is incorrect because myositis ossificans characteristically produces ossification (its defining feature); absence of any ossification would not be consistent with the diagnosis.

questions.question:
According to widely used diagnostic criteria, which synovial fluid finding is most consistent with chronic periprosthetic joint infection of a total knee arthroplasty?
A) WBC 3,000 cells/microL with 80% neutrophils
B) WBC 50,000 cells/microL with 95% neutrophils in the first postoperative week
C) Presence of negatively birefringent crystals
D) WBC 500 cells/microL with negative alpha-defensin
E) WBC 1,000 cells/microL with 40% neutrophils
questions.answer:
A)
For chronic PJI (>90 days from index surgery), the MSIS/ICM diagnostic thresholds for synovial fluid are approximately ≥3,000 WBC/μL and ≥80% polymorphonuclear cells, making this profile most consistent with chronic periprosthetic joint infection of a TKA. Elevated serum ESR and CRP further support the diagnosis.

B is incorrect because although WBC 50,000 with 95% neutrophils is markedly elevated, in the first postoperative week the normal inflammatory response produces high synovial WBC counts; acute postoperative PJI thresholds are ~10,000 WBC/μL and 90% PMN, and this scenario more likely reflects expected postoperative inflammation rather than a finding specific to chronic PJI.

C is incorrect because negatively birefringent crystals (monosodium urate) indicate gout/crystalline arthropathy, not infection. Although crystals and infection can coexist, crystal presence alone does not diagnose PJI.

D is incorrect because WBC 500 cells/μL is well below the chronic PJI threshold (~3,000), and a negative alpha-defensin further argues against infection, making this profile inconsistent with PJI.

E is incorrect because WBC 1,000 cells/μL with only 40% neutrophils falls below both the WBC and PMN percentage thresholds for chronic PJI and is more consistent with a non-infected or inflammatory (non-septic) effusion.

questions.question:
A 31-year-old man has an acromioclavicular joint injury with the distal clavicle displaced posteriorly through the trapezius. This corresponds to which Rockwood type and management?
A) Type I, treated with ice and analgesics
B) Type IV, generally treated operatively
C) Type II, treated with a sling
D) Type III, always treated nonoperatively
E) Type V, treated with closed reduction and casting
questions.answer:
B)
Rockwood type IV describes posterior displacement of the distal clavicle through or into the trapezius muscle. This injury does not reduce with closed means and is typically managed surgically.

A is incorrect because a Type I AC injury involves a sprain of the AC ligaments without displacement; the stem describes posterior displacement through the trapezius, which is far more severe. C is incorrect because a Type II injury involves disruption of the AC ligaments with intact coracoclavicular ligaments and slight superior displacement, not posterior displacement into the trapezius; it is managed nonoperatively. D is incorrect because a Type III injury involves complete disruption of both AC and CC ligaments with superior displacement of the clavicle, not posterior displacement; furthermore, Type III is not "always" treated nonoperatively — management is controversial and surgery may be considered for high-demand patients. E is incorrect because a Type V injury involves marked superior displacement (100–300% increase in CC distance), not posterior displacement; it is treated surgically, not with closed reduction and casting.

questions.question:
Which surgical option is most appropriate for an active 45-year-old with an irreparable posterosuperior cuff tear, preserved passive motion, and no arthritis?
A) Lower trapezius or latissimus dorsi tendon transfer, or superior capsular reconstruction
B) Total shoulder arthroplasty
C) Glenohumeral arthrodesis
D) Isolated biceps tenodesis
E) Reverse total shoulder arthroplasty
questions.answer:
A)
In a young, active patient with an irreparable posterosuperior rotator cuff tear, preserved passive motion, and no arthritis, joint-preserving procedures are preferred. Lower trapezius or latissimus dorsi tendon transfer restores the external rotation force couple, and superior capsular reconstruction restores superior stability — both avoid prosthetic replacement in this age group.

B is incorrect because total shoulder arthroplasty requires an intact or reparable rotator cuff for reliable function; it does not address the irreparable cuff tear and would lead to early failure (rocking-horse loosening). C is incorrect because glenohumeral arthrodesis is a salvage procedure reserved for young patients with combined bone loss, infection, or failed prior reconstructions — not appropriate when passive motion is preserved and no arthritis exists. D is incorrect because isolated biceps tenodesis addresses biceps pathology only and does nothing to restore the lost posterosuperior cuff force couple or superior stability. E is incorrect because reverse total shoulder arthroplasty, while effective for irreparable cuff tears in older patients, carries significant concerns about implant longevity, polyethylene wear, and revision burden in a 45-year-old; it is generally reserved for older or lower-demand patients or those with cuff tear arthropathy/pseudoparalysis.

questions.question:
The most common nerve complication after single-incision anterior distal biceps repair is:
A) Ulnar nerve injury
B) Radial artery injury
C) Median nerve injury
D) Lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve neurapraxia
E) Anterior interosseous nerve palsy
questions.answer:
D)
The lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve (LABCN), the terminal sensory branch of the musculocutaneous nerve, lies just lateral to the biceps tendon and is the most frequently injured nerve during single-incision anterior distal biceps repair, usually as a transient neurapraxia from retraction. The posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) is at risk with excessive forearm pronation or aggressive lateral dissection at the radial tuberosity. Two-incision techniques reduce PIN risk but historically carry a higher rate of proximal radioulnar synostosis.

A is incorrect because the ulnar nerve is located on the medial side of the elbow and is not in the surgical field of an anterior distal biceps repair. B is incorrect because radial artery injury is a vascular complication, not a nerve complication, and while the artery is in proximity, the question specifically asks about nerve complications. C is incorrect because the median nerve, although in the antecubital fossa, is medial to the surgical approach and is much less commonly injured than the LABCN. E is incorrect because the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) is a motor branch of the median nerve that lies deep in the forearm; while theoretically at risk, it is far less commonly injured than the LABCN during this approach.

questions.question:
Regarding perioperative management of antirheumatic medications for elective arthroplasty, current consensus recommends:
A) Continue methotrexate; withhold biologic agents and schedule surgery at the end of the dosing cycle
B) Double the prednisone dose for 1 week postoperatively in all patients
C) Discontinue methotrexate 4 weeks preoperatively
D) Continue biologics uninterrupted to prevent disease flare
E) Discontinue all agents including prednisone 2 weeks preoperatively
questions.answer:
A)
Per ACR/AAHKS guidelines, conventional DMARDs such as methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, and leflunomide are generally continued perioperatively because stopping them increases disease flare risk without clearly reducing surgical infection rates. Biologic DMARDs (TNF inhibitors, IL-6 inhibitors, rituximab, JAK inhibitors) are withheld, and surgery is scheduled at the end of the dosing cycle; they are resumed once the wound shows adequate healing, typically around 14 days postoperatively. Daily glucocorticoids are continued at the patient's usual dose.

B is incorrect because supraphysiologic "stress-dose" steroids are no longer routinely recommended; patients should continue their usual daily glucocorticoid dose without doubling. C is incorrect because methotrexate should be continued, not discontinued; withholding it increases flare risk without proven benefit in reducing infection. D is incorrect because biologics should be withheld perioperatively due to their immunosuppressive effect and associated increased infection risk; continuing them uninterrupted is not recommended. E is incorrect because discontinuing all agents, including prednisone, risks both disease flare and adrenal insufficiency; conventional DMARDs and maintenance glucocorticoids should be continued.

questions.question:
After resection of a proximal humeral sarcoma with sacrifice of the rotator cuff and abductor mechanism, which reconstruction couples an allograft with a prosthesis to permit soft-tissue attachment?
A) Standard hemiarthroplasty
B) Vascularized fibular graft alone
C) Intercalary allograft
D) Arthrodesis with a spanning plate
E) Allograft-prosthetic composite
questions.answer:
E)
An allograft-prosthetic composite (APC) combines a segmental allograft — which provides bone stock and soft-tissue attachments (capsule, tendon) for reattachment of the rotator cuff or abductors — with a prosthetic articular component that offers immediate mechanical stability and predictable joint function. This is particularly useful at the proximal humerus and proximal femur after oncologic resection with loss of the abductor mechanism. Drawbacks include nonunion at the host-allograft junction, infection, and graft resorption.

A is incorrect because a standard hemiarthroplasty does not provide bone stock or soft-tissue attachment sites to reconstruct the sacrificed rotator cuff and abductor mechanism after segmental resection.
B is incorrect because a vascularized fibular graft alone lacks an articular surface and does not provide soft-tissue attachment points for the rotator cuff; it is better suited for intercalary or diaphyseal defects.
C is incorrect because an intercalary allograft reconstructs a mid-diaphyseal (non-articular) segmental defect and does not address the need for a prosthetic joint surface or proximal soft-tissue reattachment.
D is incorrect because arthrodesis with a spanning plate eliminates glenohumeral motion entirely, resulting in significant functional limitation, and does not couple an allograft with a prosthesis as described in the stem.

questions.question:
Anterior femoral notching during total knee arthroplasty is a concern because it:
A) Improves flexion
B) Has no clinical consequence
C) Improves patellar tracking
D) Causes tibial loosening
E) Increases the risk of supracondylar periprosthetic fracture
questions.answer:
E)
Notching of the anterior femoral cortex creates a stress riser that substantially reduces torsional and bending strength of the distal femur, predisposing to supracondylar periprosthetic fracture. It typically results from excessive femoral component flexion, undersizing, or malpositioned anterior referencing. Significant notching (>3 mm) may warrant use of a stemmed femoral component for added protection.

A is incorrect because anterior femoral notching does not improve flexion; it is an iatrogenic cortical defect, not a technique that enhances range of motion.
B is incorrect because notching has a well-documented clinical consequence — it increases fracture risk by up to threefold in biomechanical studies and is not benign.
C is incorrect because anterior femoral notching has no relationship to patellar tracking; patellar tracking is influenced by component rotation, lateral release, and Q-angle.
D is incorrect because notching involves the femoral cortex and predisposes to femoral (supracondylar) fracture, not tibial loosening; tibial loosening is related to tibial component alignment, fixation, and polyethylene wear.

questions.question:
A 10-year-old undergoes distal femoral resection and reconstruction with a magnetically controlled expandable endoprosthesis. Which complication is most characteristic of this reconstruction?
A) Physeal arrest of the contralateral limb
B) Graft-versus-host disease
C) Mechanical failure of the lengthening mechanism and the need for repeated procedures
D) Immediate limb length equalization with no further surgery
E) Nonunion at the host-graft junction
questions.answer:
C)
Expandable endoprostheses allow noninvasive or minimally invasive lengthening to address anticipated limb length discrepancy in growing children, but the lengthening mechanism is a mechanical device subject to failure, and these reconstructions have high cumulative reoperation rates for lengthening failure, infection, aseptic loosening, and soft-tissue contracture. Families should be counseled that multiple procedures are expected.

A is incorrect because physeal arrest of the contralateral limb is not a complication of the patient's own endoprosthetic reconstruction; the contralateral physis is unaffected by the prosthesis. B is incorrect because graft-versus-host disease is an immunologic complication of allogeneic bone marrow or organ transplantation, not of metallic endoprosthetic reconstruction. D is incorrect because expandable prostheses do not provide immediate limb length equalization; serial lengthening procedures are required over the remaining growth period, and further surgery is expected. E is incorrect because nonunion at a host-graft junction is a complication associated with osteoarticular allografts or intercalary allografts, not with endoprosthetic reconstruction where there is no biologic graft-host junction.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old sustains a displaced femoral neck fracture in a motorcycle crash. The most important principle of management is:
A) Hemiarthroplasty
B) Urgent anatomic reduction and stable internal fixation to preserve the femoral head
C) Skeletal traction for 6 weeks
D) Delay surgery until the patient is fully worked up
E) Percutaneous pinning in situ without reduction
questions.answer:
B)
In young patients with displaced femoral neck fractures, the primary goal is femoral head preservation. Urgent anatomic reduction (open if necessary) with stable internal fixation is the standard of care. Varus malreduction and residual displacement are the strongest predictors of osteonecrosis and nonunion. Capsulotomy to decompress the intracapsular hematoma is often performed, and evidence supports minimizing time to surgery.

A is incorrect because hemiarthroplasty sacrifices the native femoral head and is reserved for elderly, low-demand patients. In a 28-year-old, head preservation is paramount to avoid the inevitable need for revision arthroplasty over a long lifespan.

C is incorrect because skeletal traction alone does not provide anatomic reduction or stable fixation and leads to prolonged immobility, increased osteonecrosis risk, nonunion, and systemic complications.

D is incorrect because delaying surgery increases the risk of osteonecrosis by prolonging femoral head ischemia. While the patient should be resuscitated and stabilized, unnecessary delay for a full elective workup is detrimental; urgent surgical treatment is indicated.

E is incorrect because percutaneous pinning without reduction accepts a displaced (often varus) position, which is the strongest predictor of nonunion and osteonecrosis. Anatomic reduction must be achieved before fixation.

questions.question:
A well-defined lucent lesion of the proximal humerus in a 9-year-old, central, with a pathologic fracture and a "fallen leaf" sign, is:
A) Unicameral (simple) bone cyst
B) Fibrous dysplasia
C) Aneurysmal bone cyst
D) Enchondroma
E) Osteosarcoma
questions.answer:
A)
The fallen fragment (or "fallen leaf") sign — a bone fragment settling to the dependent portion of a fluid-filled cavity — is pathognomonic for a unicameral (simple) bone cyst (UBC). UBCs are central, metaphyseal lesions of the proximal humerus or femur in children, and they commonly present with pathologic fracture. Treatment options include aspiration and injection (corticosteroid, bone marrow aspirate, demineralized bone matrix) or decompression with flexible nails; recurrence is more likely in active cysts abutting the physis in young children.

B is incorrect because fibrous dysplasia produces a ground-glass matrix, is typically diaphyseal/metadiaphyseal, and does not produce a fluid-filled cavity or a fallen fragment sign. C is incorrect because aneurysmal bone cysts are eccentric, expansile, "blown-out" lesions with fluid-fluid levels on MRI, not a central lucency with a fallen fragment sign. D is incorrect because enchondromas contain chondroid (ring-and-arc calcification) matrix and are most common in the hands; they do not produce a simple fluid-filled cavity. E is incorrect because osteosarcoma is an aggressive lesion with periosteal reaction (sunburst pattern, Codman triangle) and a soft-tissue mass, not a well-defined lucent cyst with a fallen fragment sign.

questions.question:
A patient with a tibial shaft fracture has severe pain with passive toe extension, a compartment pressure of 42 mm Hg, and a diastolic blood pressure of 70 mm Hg. The most appropriate next step is:
A) Observation with serial examinations
B) Emergent four-compartment fasciotomy
C) Elevate the limb above the heart
D) Doppler assessment of the dorsalis pedis pulse
E) Bivalve the cast and recheck in 2 hours
questions.answer:
B)
The delta pressure (diastolic BP minus compartment pressure) is 70 − 42 = 28 mm Hg, which is below the accepted threshold of 30 mm Hg for fasciotomy. Combined with the classic clinical finding of pain with passive toe extension, emergent four-compartment fasciotomy is indicated. Pain with passive stretch is the earliest and most reliable clinical sign of compartment syndrome; pulselessness and paralysis are late findings.

A is incorrect because observation is inappropriate when both clinical signs (pain with passive stretch) and objective pressure measurements (delta P ≤ 30 mm Hg) confirm compartment syndrome; delay risks irreversible muscle necrosis and Volkmann-type contracture.
C is incorrect because elevating the limb above the heart further reduces arterial perfusion pressure to the compartment, worsening ischemia; the limb should be kept at heart level.
D is incorrect because Doppler assessment of distal pulses is misleading — pulses are typically maintained until very late in compartment syndrome, and their presence does not rule out the diagnosis.
E is incorrect because while bivalving a cast can reduce extrinsic pressure, this patient already has confirmed compartment syndrome by clinical and pressure criteria; temporizing measures are insufficient and surgical fasciotomy is required.

questions.question:
Peroneal tendon subluxation results from injury to which structure?
A) Calcaneofibular ligament
B) Spring ligament
C) Superior peroneal retinaculum
D) Inferior extensor retinaculum
E) Anterior talofibular ligament
questions.answer:
C)
Forced dorsiflexion with reflexive peroneal contraction avulses the superior peroneal retinaculum from the posterolateral fibula, allowing the peroneal tendons to sublux anteriorly. Patients report snapping and lateral ankle pain often misdiagnosed as a chronic sprain. A shallow or convex retromalleolar groove predisposes. Treatment of recurrent subluxation is retinacular repair with groove deepening.

A is incorrect because the calcaneofibular ligament is a lateral ankle stabilizer that resists inversion; its injury causes ankle instability, not peroneal tendon subluxation. B is incorrect because the spring (calcaneonavicular) ligament supports the talar head and maintains the medial longitudinal arch; it is unrelated to peroneal tendon stability. D is incorrect because the inferior extensor retinaculum restrains the extensor tendons on the dorsum of the foot and has no role in maintaining the peroneal tendons in the retromalleolar groove. E is incorrect because the anterior talofibular ligament resists anterior translation of the talus; its disruption causes lateral ankle instability, not peroneal subluxation.

questions.question:
A 14-year-old has fever, elevated ESR, and a diaphyseal lesion with a permeative pattern and onion-skin periosteal reaction. Biopsy shows small round blue cells that stain for CD99. The genetic hallmark is:
A) t(12;16) FUS-DDIT3
B) t(X;18) SYT-SSX
C) t(11;22) EWSR1-FLI1 translocation
D) EXT1 mutation
E) MDM2 amplification
questions.answer:
C)
Ewing sarcoma most often carries the t(11;22)(q24;q12) translocation producing the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion, and cells express CD99 (MIC2). The clinical picture mimics osteomyelitis with fever, leukocytosis, and elevated inflammatory markers. Treatment includes chemotherapy with local control by surgery, radiation, or both, since Ewing sarcoma is radiosensitive.

A is incorrect because t(12;16) FUS-DDIT3 is the hallmark translocation of myxoid liposarcoma, not Ewing sarcoma. B is incorrect because t(X;18) SYT-SSX is characteristic of synovial sarcoma. D is incorrect because EXT1 (or EXT2) mutations are associated with hereditary multiple exostoses (osteochondromatosis), a benign cartilage condition, not Ewing sarcoma. E is incorrect because MDM2 amplification is the genetic hallmark of well-differentiated/dedifferentiated liposarcoma and parosteal osteosarcoma.

questions.question:
A reverse Hill-Sachs (McLaughlin) lesion involving 30% of the articular surface in a locked posterior dislocation is best treated by:
A) Reverse total shoulder arthroplasty
B) Transfer of the subscapularis tendon or lesser tuberosity into the defect
C) Anterior capsular shift
D) Arthroscopic labral repair alone
E) Closed reduction and sling alone
questions.answer:
B)
For anteromedial humeral head defects (reverse Hill-Sachs lesions) involving roughly 20-40% of the articular surface in a locked posterior dislocation, the McLaughlin procedure (subscapularis tendon transfer into the defect) or the modified Neer version (lesser tuberosity transfer with attached subscapularis) fills the defect and prevents re-engagement. Allograft reconstruction is an alternative for similar-sized defects.

A is incorrect because reverse total shoulder arthroplasty is reserved for defects exceeding 40-50% of the articular surface, significant articular cartilage destruction, or elderly patients with poor bone quality. A 30% defect is amenable to joint-preserving reconstruction.

C is incorrect because an anterior capsular shift addresses capsular laxity and does not address the bony humeral head defect. The primary pathology here is a structural defect that allows re-engagement, not capsular redundancy.

D is incorrect because arthroscopic labral repair alone addresses the posterior labral (reverse Bankart) lesion but does not fill the humeral head defect. Without addressing the engaging bony defect, recurrent posterior instability is likely.

E is incorrect because a 30% articular surface defect is too large for nonoperative management. Closed reduction and sling immobilization may suffice for defects less than 20% of the articular surface, but larger defects have a high risk of recurrent posterior dislocation without surgical stabilization.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman has an L5-S1 isthmic spondylolisthesis in which the L5 body has translated 60% over the sacrum. This corresponds to which Meyerding grade?
A) Grade II
B) Grade I
C) Grade IV
D) Spondyloptosis
E) Grade III
questions.answer:
E)
Meyerding grading divides the superior surface of the caudal vertebra into quarters: Grade I is 0–25% translation, Grade II is 26–50%, Grade III is 51–75%, Grade IV is 76–100%, and Grade V (spondyloptosis) is complete translation beyond the sacrum. A 60% slip falls within the 51–75% range, corresponding to Grade III. High-grade slips are also assessed with the slip angle and pelvic incidence, which are more predictive of progression and need for reduction.

A is incorrect because Grade II corresponds to 26–50% translation, which is less than the 60% described. B is incorrect because Grade I corresponds to 0–25% translation, far less than 60%. C is incorrect because Grade IV corresponds to 76–100% translation, which exceeds the 60% described. D is incorrect because spondyloptosis (Grade V) denotes complete translation (>100%) of the vertebral body beyond the sacrum, which is not the case here.

questions.question:
A 68-year-old woman has a displaced, comminuted olecranon fracture with articular involvement extending distal to the coronoid. The most appropriate fixation is:
A) Plate fixation contoured over the proximal ulna
B) Cast immobilization in extension
C) Excision of all fragments with triceps advancement in a young laborer
D) Tension band wiring
E) Percutaneous screws alone
questions.answer:
A)
Comminuted olecranon fractures with articular involvement extending distal to the coronoid require plate fixation contoured over the proximal ulna, which resists axial, bending, and rotational loads across the comminuted segments. Precontoured locking plates are the standard for these complex fracture patterns.

B is incorrect because cast immobilization in extension is not appropriate for displaced, comminuted articular fractures; it would result in malunion, stiffness, and loss of function. C is incorrect because fragment excision with triceps advancement is reserved for low-demand elderly patients with simple, small proximal olecranon fragments—not for a young laborer or for fractures with distal extension and significant articular involvement. D is incorrect because tension band wiring is effective only for simple transverse or short oblique fractures at or proximal to the coronoid with an intact distal cortical buttress; it cannot adequately stabilize comminuted fractures extending distally. E is incorrect because percutaneous screws alone do not provide sufficient stability for comminuted, articular fractures with distal extension and cannot resist the bending and axial forces across the olecranon.

questions.question:
Which imaging modality is preferred to detect a contralateral pre-slip or early SCFE when radiographs are equivocal?
A) CT with contrast
B) Bone scan
C) Fluoroscopy
D) Ultrasound
E) MRI
questions.answer:
E)
MRI demonstrates physeal widening, marrow edema, and effusion before displacement is visible on plain radiographs and involves no ionizing radiation, making it the preferred modality for detecting a contralateral pre-slip or early SCFE when radiographs are equivocal.

A is incorrect because CT with contrast adds ionizing radiation to an adolescent and, while useful for characterizing bony anatomy and surgical planning, is inferior to MRI for detecting early physeal changes and marrow edema.

B is incorrect because bone scan can show increased uptake in the physis but lacks the spatial resolution and soft-tissue detail of MRI and also involves ionizing radiation.

C is incorrect because fluoroscopy is a real-time radiographic technique that provides no advantage over standard radiographs for detecting subtle physeal changes and adds radiation exposure.

D is incorrect because ultrasound can detect a hip effusion but cannot reliably evaluate the physis for widening or marrow edema, limiting its utility in diagnosing a pre-slip.

questions.question:
A 9-year-old has a displaced distal radius metaphyseal fracture that loses reduction at 10 days with 25 degrees of dorsal angulation. The most appropriate management is:
A) Repeated forceful manipulation every week until anatomic
B) Immediate open reduction and plating in all cases
C) Removal of the cast and free mobilization
D) Remanipulation and pinning, or acceptance of the alignment based on remaining growth, avoiding repeat closed manipulation after 7 to 10 days because of physeal injury risk
E) Corrective osteotomy at 3 weeks
questions.answer:
D)
Repeat manipulation more than about a week after injury encounters early callus, requires greater force, and carries a real risk of physeal injury and growth arrest. The decision rests on remaining growth and the plane of deformity: substantial sagittal angulation remodels well in a young child, whereas an older child or a large deformity warrants remanipulation with percutaneous pinning at the initial loss of reduction rather than repeated forceful closed reduction.

A is incorrect because repeated forceful weekly manipulation after early callus formation increases the risk of physeal damage and growth arrest without reliably achieving reduction.
B is incorrect because open reduction and plating is not routinely indicated for pediatric distal radius metaphyseal fractures; percutaneous pinning after closed reduction is preferred when surgical stabilization is needed, and many cases remodel without surgery.
C is incorrect because 25 degrees of dorsal angulation in a 9-year-old cannot simply be left to free mobilization without addressing alignment; some intervention or at least a decision regarding remodeling potential is required.
E is incorrect because corrective osteotomy at 3 weeks is premature; significant remodeling potential exists in a 9-year-old, and osteotomy is reserved for malunions that fail to remodel after a prolonged observation period, not performed at 3 weeks.

questions.question:
In a diabetic patient with a plantar ulcer, which factor most predicts healing potential?
A) Patient age
B) HbA1c alone
C) Adequate perfusion (toe pressure and transcutaneous oxygen) plus effective offloading
D) Duration of diabetes
E) Type of dressing
questions.answer:
C)
Healing of diabetic plantar ulcers depends on adequate perfusion, infection control, offloading, and metabolic optimization. Transcutaneous oxygen pressure (TcPO2) above approximately 30–40 mmHg, toe pressure above 40 mmHg, and an ankle-brachial index (ABI) above 0.45 predict healing; ABI can be falsely elevated by medial arterial calcinosis, making toe pressures more reliable. Total contact casting is the gold standard for offloading neuropathic plantar ulcers. Loss of protective sensation is assessed with a 5.07 (10 g) Semmes-Weinstein monofilament.

A is incorrect because patient age alone is not the most predictive factor for ulcer healing; elderly patients with adequate perfusion and offloading can still heal well. B is incorrect because while HbA1c reflects glycemic control and influences healing, it alone does not predict healing as reliably as direct assessment of tissue perfusion combined with mechanical offloading. D is incorrect because duration of diabetes is a risk factor for developing complications but does not directly predict whether a given ulcer will heal. E is incorrect because the type of dressing used is a secondary consideration; without adequate perfusion and offloading, no dressing will reliably promote healing.

questions.question:
Which deformity pattern is characteristic of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease?
A) Isolated equinus
B) Planovalgus foot with forefoot abduction
C) Vertical talus
D) Cavovarus foot with plantarflexed first ray, hindfoot varus, and claw toes
E) Congenital metatarsus adductus
questions.answer:
D)
In Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, relative weakness of the tibialis anterior and peroneus brevis with preserved peroneus longus and tibialis posterior drives first ray plantarflexion and hindfoot varus, with intrinsic muscle weakness producing claw toes. The Coleman block test determines whether hindfoot varus is flexible and forefoot-driven, guiding whether a dorsiflexion first metatarsal osteotomy alone suffices or a calcaneal osteotomy is also required.

A is incorrect because isolated equinus is not the characteristic pattern of CMT; equinus may be seen in conditions such as cerebral palsy or Achilles contracture but does not capture the cavovarus deformity of CMT. B is incorrect because planovalgus with forefoot abduction is the opposite deformity pattern, more commonly associated with posterior tibial tendon dysfunction or tarsal coalition. C is incorrect because congenital vertical talus is a distinct entity presenting with a rigid rocker-bottom flatfoot deformity in infancy, unrelated to CMT. E is incorrect because congenital metatarsus adductus is a forefoot adduction deformity seen in neonates and is not associated with the progressive cavovarus pattern of CMT.

questions.question:
Which structure limits inferior translation of the adducted shoulder?
A) Posterior capsule
B) Inferior glenohumeral ligament anterior band
C) Coracoacromial ligament
D) Superior glenohumeral ligament and rotator interval
E) Middle glenohumeral ligament
questions.answer:
D)
The superior glenohumeral ligament and coracohumeral ligament in the rotator interval are the primary restraints to inferior translation and external rotation in adduction; a positive sulcus sign that persists in external rotation indicates rotator interval insufficiency. The anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament is the primary restraint to anterior translation with the arm abducted 90 degrees and externally rotated.

questions.question:
A 4-year-old with progressive early-onset scoliosis has a thoracic curve of 65 degrees and restrictive pulmonary function. Growth-friendly instrumentation is recommended primarily to:
A) Avoid all anesthetic exposure
B) Achieve immediate definitive fusion
C) Correct associated intraspinal anomalies
D) Control the curve while permitting continued thoracic and pulmonary growth
E) Eliminate the need for any future surgery
questions.answer:
D)
Early definitive fusion in a young child arrests spinal and thoracic growth, producing thoracic insufficiency syndrome with permanent restrictive lung disease, because alveolar multiplication continues through roughly age 8. Growth-friendly strategies (traditional or magnetically controlled growing rods, vertical expandable prosthetic titanium ribs, guided growth) control deformity while allowing growth, at the cost of repeated procedures and implant-related complications.

A is incorrect because growth-friendly instrumentation (especially traditional growing rods) requires multiple anesthetic exposures for lengthening procedures; it does not avoid anesthetic exposure.
B is incorrect because the entire purpose of growth-friendly surgery is to delay definitive fusion, not achieve it immediately; early fusion would arrest thoracic growth and worsen pulmonary function.
C is incorrect because intraspinal anomalies (e.g., tethered cord, syrinx) are addressed separately with neurosurgical intervention, not by growth-friendly spinal instrumentation.
E is incorrect because most patients with growth-friendly constructs will eventually require a definitive posterior spinal fusion at skeletal maturity, and implant-related complications frequently necessitate additional surgeries during the growth period.

questions.question:
Which benign lesion of the tibia in a child must be distinguished from adamantinoma?
A) Chondromyxoid fibroma
B) Osteofibrous dysplasia
C) Osteoid osteoma
D) Simple bone cyst
E) Nonossifying fibroma
questions.answer:
B)
Osteofibrous dysplasia and adamantinoma both favor the anterior tibial diaphysis and may be indistinguishable on imaging, showing multiloculated anterior cortical lucency with sclerosis and anterior bowing. Adamantinoma is a low-grade malignancy with epithelial elements (keratin-positive) requiring wide resection, whereas osteofibrous dysplasia is benign, generally observed, and often regresses after skeletal maturity. The two may exist on a spectrum ("differentiated" or osteofibrous dysplasia-like adamantinoma), so careful follow-up and biopsy for atypical features are essential.

A is incorrect because chondromyxoid fibroma is a rare benign cartilage tumor typically found in the metaphysis of long bones; it is not specifically confused with adamantinoma and does not share its predilection for the anterior tibial cortex.

C is incorrect because osteoid osteoma presents as a small (<1.5 cm) intracortical nidus with surrounding reactive sclerosis and night pain relieved by NSAIDs; it has a distinct clinical and imaging appearance that is not confused with adamantinoma.

D is incorrect because a simple (unicameral) bone cyst is a central, fluid-filled metaphyseal lesion most common in the proximal humerus and femur of children; it does not mimic the cortically based, multiloculated anterior tibial pattern of adamantinoma.

E is incorrect because nonossifying fibroma is an eccentric metaphyseal lesion with a well-defined sclerotic border, typically found around the knee; it is easily distinguished from adamantinoma by location, imaging characteristics, and histology.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old woman has a comminuted radial head fracture with three articular fragments, an associated coronoid fracture, and elbow instability. The most appropriate treatment of the radial head is:
A) Excision without replacement
B) Nonoperative management with early motion
C) Total elbow arthroplasty
D) Radial head arthroplasty
E) Open reduction with mini-fragment screws in all cases
questions.answer:
D)
A comminuted radial head fracture with three or more articular fragments (Mason type III) in the setting of associated coronoid fracture and elbow instability is best treated with radial head arthroplasty. The radial head is a critical secondary stabilizer against valgus and axial forces; replacing it restores stability when reliable anatomic fixation is not achievable.

A is incorrect because excision without replacement removes an essential stabilizer in an already unstable elbow, leading to valgus instability, proximal radial migration, and potential wrist pain. B is incorrect because nonoperative management cannot restore elbow stability in the presence of a comminuted radial head fracture combined with coronoid fracture and ligamentous injury; persistent instability and arthritis would result. C is incorrect because total elbow arthroplasty is reserved for elderly low-demand patients with unreconstructable distal humerus fractures or end-stage inflammatory arthritis, not for an isolated radial head/coronoid injury pattern in a 38-year-old. E is incorrect because comminuted fractures with three or more articular fragments have poor outcomes with attempted internal fixation due to difficulty achieving stable anatomic reduction; arthroplasty is preferred over ORIF in this scenario.

questions.question:
Which patient with DDH treated in infancy requires ongoing surveillance until skeletal maturity?
A) Only males
B) None; discharge at age 2 is appropriate
C) Only bilateral cases
D) All treated patients, because residual dysplasia may become apparent with growth
E) Only those with failed reduction
questions.answer:
D)
All patients treated for DDH in infancy require surveillance until skeletal maturity. Residual acetabular dysplasia may not become apparent until later childhood or adolescence, and it is a leading cause of early-onset hip osteoarthritis in young adults. Serial imaging permits timely detection of a persistent elevated acetabular index, lateral center-edge angle below 20°, or a broken Shenton line, allowing reconstructive surgery before degenerative changes occur.

A is incorrect because DDH surveillance is not sex-specific; females are in fact more commonly affected, and all treated patients regardless of sex need follow-up. B is incorrect because discharge at age 2 is premature; residual dysplasia can declare itself well beyond that age as the acetabulum continues to develop. C is incorrect because the need for surveillance is not limited to bilateral cases; unilateral DDH carries the same risk of residual dysplasia. E is incorrect because even patients with a successful initial reduction can develop residual acetabular dysplasia during growth, so surveillance is not limited to those with failed reduction.

questions.question:
Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment for a patient with mild to moderate cubital tunnel syndrome?
A) Medial epicondylectomy
B) Activity modification, night extension splinting, and avoidance of prolonged elbow flexion
C) Ulnar nerve decompression at the wrist
D) Corticosteroid injection into the cubital tunnel
E) Anterior submuscular transposition
questions.answer:
B)
Nonoperative treatment with elbow extension splinting at night, padding, and activity modification is the accepted first-line management for mild to moderate cubital tunnel syndrome. It resolves symptoms in many patients with intermittent paresthesias and no fixed motor deficit. Surgery is reserved for persistent symptoms, progressive weakness, or intrinsic atrophy.

A is incorrect because medial epicondylectomy is a surgical option reserved for cases that fail conservative management, and it carries risks of medial elbow instability.
C is incorrect because ulnar nerve decompression at the wrist addresses compression at Guyon canal, not the cubital tunnel at the elbow.
D is incorrect because corticosteroid injection into the cubital tunnel is not a standard or recommended treatment; it risks direct nerve injury and has no proven efficacy for cubital tunnel syndrome.
E is incorrect because anterior submuscular transposition is a surgical procedure indicated for refractory cases, nerve subluxation, or revision surgery, and is not appropriate as first-line treatment for mild to moderate disease.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman has lateral ankle pain and swelling posterior to the fibula with weakness of eversion. MRI shows a longitudinal split tear of the peroneus brevis with less than 50% of the tendon involved. Recommended treatment is:
A) Ankle arthrodesis
B) Complete excision of the peroneus brevis
C) Tubularization (repair) of the tendon with debridement of degenerative tissue
D) Observation with no role for surgery
E) Tenodesis to the peroneus longus regardless of tear size
questions.answer:
C)
Peroneus brevis split tears result from the tendon being compressed against the fibula, commonly associated with a shallow retromalleolar groove, retinacular insufficiency, or hindfoot varus. Tears involving less than approximately 50% of the tendon are debrided and tubularized (repaired); more extensive tears (>50%) are treated with excision of the damaged segment and tenodesis to the peroneus longus. Correcting underlying hindfoot varus is important to prevent recurrence.

A is incorrect because ankle arthrodesis is reserved for end-stage ankle arthritis, not for an isolated peroneal tendon split tear.
B is incorrect because complete excision of the peroneus brevis is not indicated when less than 50% of the tendon is involved; the viable tendon should be preserved by tubularization.
D is incorrect because a symptomatic longitudinal split tear causing pain and eversion weakness warrants surgical intervention when conservative measures fail; observation alone is insufficient.
E is incorrect because tenodesis to the peroneus longus is reserved for tears involving more than 50% of the tendon cross-section; with less than 50% involvement, tubularization and debridement is the preferred treatment.

questions.question:
A patient reports anterolateral thigh numbness after a direct anterior approach total hip arthroplasty. The most likely explanation is:
A) Superior gluteal nerve injury
B) Injury to the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
C) Femoral nerve palsy
D) Sciatic nerve traction
E) Obturator nerve injury
questions.answer:
B)
The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (LFCN) crosses near the interval between sartorius and tensor fasciae latae and is the structure most commonly injured during the direct anterior approach (DAA), producing anterolateral thigh numbness or dysesthesia. Incidence is reported as high as 50–80% in some series, though most cases are not functionally limiting. Placing the incision slightly more lateral and dissecting through the tensor fascia rather than medial to it reduces the risk.

A is incorrect because the superior gluteal nerve innervates the hip abductors and is at risk during lateral or posterolateral approaches, not the DAA; its injury would cause a Trendelenburg gait, not anterolateral thigh numbness.
C is incorrect because femoral nerve palsy would produce quadriceps weakness and anterior thigh/medial leg sensory loss in the femoral nerve distribution, not isolated anterolateral numbness; it is uncommon with the DAA.
D is incorrect because sciatic nerve traction is primarily a risk of the posterior approach and limb lengthening; it would cause posterior thigh, leg, and foot motor/sensory deficits, not anterolateral thigh numbness.
E is incorrect because the obturator nerve lies deep in the pelvis and is not in the surgical field of the DAA; its injury would cause medial thigh sensory loss and adductor weakness.

questions.question:
A patient with ankylosing spondylitis falls from standing and complains of new mid-thoracic pain. Radiographs appear unremarkable. The next step is:
A) Physical therapy
B) Bone scan in 2 weeks
C) Flexion-extension radiographs
D) CT of the entire spine, with MRI if still suspicious
E) Reassurance and outpatient follow-up
questions.answer:
D)
The ankylosed spine behaves like a long bone and fails in extension through all three columns after trivial trauma, with a high rate of epidural hematoma and neurologic injury. Fractures are easily missed on plain radiographs because of osteoporosis and complex ossification, so CT of the entire spine is mandatory, supplemented by MRI to evaluate for epidural hematoma and cord compression. These injuries are highly unstable and usually require long-segment posterior instrumentation; the patient should be positioned in their preinjury deformity rather than flat.

A is incorrect because initiating physical therapy without ruling out an occult fracture in an ankylosed spine risks catastrophic displacement and neurologic deterioration. B is incorrect because a bone scan in 2 weeks unacceptably delays diagnosis of a potentially unstable three-column injury; advanced imaging is needed urgently. C is incorrect because flexion-extension radiographs are dangerous in this setting — the fused spine is at risk for catastrophic displacement, and plain films are unreliable for detecting fractures in ankylosing spondylitis. E is incorrect because reassurance and outpatient follow-up are inappropriate; new-onset spinal pain after a fall in ankylosing spondylitis must be presumed to represent an unstable fracture until proven otherwise.

questions.question:
On a stress-strain curve, the modulus of elasticity is represented by which of the following?
A) The strain at failure
B) The slope of the linear elastic portion of the curve
C) The point at which permanent deformation begins
D) The maximum stress the material can sustain
E) The area under the entire curve
questions.answer:
B)
The elastic modulus (Young's modulus) is defined as the slope of the linear (elastic) portion of the stress-strain curve and represents the material's stiffness. A stiffer material has a steeper slope.

A is incorrect because the strain at failure represents the ductility (or elongation at break) of the material, not its stiffness. C is incorrect because the point at which permanent (plastic) deformation begins is the yield point, not the modulus of elasticity. D is incorrect because the maximum stress a material can sustain is the ultimate tensile strength (the peak of the curve). E is incorrect because the area under the entire stress-strain curve represents toughness (total energy absorbed before fracture), not stiffness.

questions.question:
Which imaging modality best evaluates ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament and its canal occupancy?
A) Standing radiographs alone
B) Myelography without CT
C) Bone scan
D) CT
E) Ultrasound
questions.answer:
D)
CT best defines the morphology (continuous, segmental, mixed, circumscribed), thickness, and canal occupancy ratio of OPLL, and identifies the double-layer sign that predicts dural ossification and CSF leak risk during anterior surgery. MRI complements CT by showing cord signal change. An occupancy ratio above approximately 60% generally favors a posterior or combined approach.

A is incorrect because standing radiographs can suggest OPLL but lack the resolution to accurately quantify canal occupancy, classify morphologic subtype, or detect the double-layer sign. B is incorrect because myelography without CT shows the degree of block but does not directly image the ossified mass or allow precise measurement of occupancy ratio and morphology. C is incorrect because bone scan detects areas of increased metabolic activity and is useful for infection or metastatic screening, but it cannot delineate the detailed anatomy or canal occupancy of OPLL. E is incorrect because ultrasound has no role in evaluating OPLL; it cannot penetrate the bony spinal canal to assess posterior longitudinal ligament ossification or spinal cord compression.

questions.question:
Which imaging feature best distinguishes rheumatoid arthritis from osteoarthritis of the hand?
A) Chondrocalcinosis of the triangular fibrocartilage complex
B) Asymmetric joint space narrowing with osteophytes at the DIP joints
C) Symmetric MCP and PIP joint involvement with periarticular erosions and osteopenia
D) Subchondral sclerosis and subchondral cysts at the thumb CMC joint
E) Pencil-in-cup deformity of the DIP joints
questions.answer:
C)
Rheumatoid arthritis produces symmetric, inflammatory involvement of the MCP, PIP, and wrist joints with marginal erosions, uniform joint space loss, periarticular osteopenia, and soft tissue swelling; DIP joints are characteristically spared. This pattern clearly distinguishes it from the degenerative changes of osteoarthritis.

A is incorrect because chondrocalcinosis of the TFCC is characteristic of calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD/pseudogout), not rheumatoid arthritis. B is incorrect because asymmetric joint space narrowing with osteophytes at the DIP joints is the hallmark of osteoarthritis (Heberden nodes), not RA. D is incorrect because subchondral sclerosis and cysts at the thumb CMC joint are classic findings of osteoarthritis at that location. E is incorrect because pencil-in-cup deformity is the hallmark of psoriatic arthritis (arthritis mutilans), not rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.question:
In a child with brachial plexus birth palsy, persistent internal rotation contracture leads to which secondary bony change?
A) Acromioclavicular arthritis
B) Distal humeral physeal arrest
C) Glenoid anteversion with anterior dislocation
D) Humeral shaft bowing
E) Glenoid retroversion with posterior humeral head subluxation and dysplasia
questions.answer:
E)
Persistent internal rotation and adduction contracture from unopposed subscapularis and pectoralis activity produces posterior subluxation of the humeral head, which in turn causes increasing glenoid retroversion and a biconcave, dysplastic glenoid. Serial examination for loss of passive external rotation is essential, and ultrasound or MRI defines the deformity. Treatment ranges from botulinum toxin and anterior soft-tissue release with tendon transfers (latissimus dorsi and teres major) to humeral derotational osteotomy for established bony deformity.

A is incorrect because acromioclavicular arthritis is a degenerative condition of adulthood and is not a recognized sequela of brachial plexus birth palsy.
B is incorrect because distal humeral physeal arrest is associated with elbow trauma (e.g., supracondylar fractures), not with the internal rotation contracture pattern of brachial plexus palsy.
C is incorrect because the deforming force of persistent internal rotation drives the humeral head posteriorly, producing glenoid retroversion and posterior subluxation — not anteversion with anterior dislocation.
D is incorrect because humeral shaft bowing is not a recognized consequence of the muscle imbalance seen in brachial plexus birth palsy; the pathology is centered at the glenohumeral joint.

questions.question:
A patient with a stiff, fused lumbar spine undergoing total hip arthroplasty is at increased risk of dislocation because:
A) The hip capsule is thickened
B) Leg length is always increased
C) Abductor strength is reduced
D) Loss of pelvic rotation between standing and sitting prevents functional reorientation of the acetabulum
E) The femoral head is larger than normal
questions.answer:
D)
Normally the pelvis rotates posteriorly on sitting, functionally increasing acetabular anteversion and opening anterior clearance. A fused or rigid lumbar spine eliminates this pelvic tilt accommodation, so a cup positioned for standing alignment may impinge when seated, increasing dislocation risk. Preoperative standing and seated lateral films, adjusted cup anteversion targets, larger femoral heads, and dual-mobility or constrained constructs are management strategies.

A is incorrect because a thickened hip capsule would, if anything, add stability rather than increase dislocation risk; capsular thickening is not a recognized consequence of spinal fusion that predisposes to hip dislocation.
B is incorrect because leg length is not "always increased" in patients with a fused spine, and leg-length discrepancy is not the primary mechanism linking spinal stiffness to hip dislocation.
C is incorrect because abductor weakness can contribute to instability in general, but it is not the specific biomechanical reason a fused lumbar spine increases dislocation risk; the key issue is loss of spinopelvic motion.
E is incorrect because femoral head size is unrelated to a fused spine; in fact, a larger head would improve stability, not increase dislocation risk.

questions.question:
A 9-year-old girl of below-average height presents with bilateral slipped capital femoral epiphysis. Which evaluation is most appropriate?
A) Endocrine evaluation, including thyroid function and growth hormone axis
B) Genetic testing for collagen defects
C) No additional workup
D) Muscle biopsy
E) Rheumatologic panel only
questions.answer:
A)
SCFE presenting outside the typical age range (under 10 or over 16), in a child of short stature, or bilaterally at presentation should raise suspicion for an underlying endocrinopathy such as hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, panhypopituitarism, or renal osteodystrophy. An endocrine evaluation including thyroid function tests and growth hormone axis assessment is the most appropriate next step, as identifying and treating the underlying disorder affects contralateral slip risk and overall management.

B is incorrect because genetic testing for collagen defects (e.g., osteogenesis imperfecta) is not the primary concern in a short-statured child with bilateral SCFE; endocrine disorders are far more commonly associated with atypical SCFE. C is incorrect because bilateral SCFE in a young, short-statured child is an atypical presentation that warrants further workup — dismissing it would miss a treatable systemic condition. D is incorrect because muscle biopsy has no role in the evaluation of SCFE. E is incorrect because a rheumatologic panel alone would not address the most likely underlying endocrine etiologies in this clinical scenario.

questions.question:
A surgeon plans to fill a contained metaphyseal defect after curettage of a benign lesion in a 20-year-old. Calcium sulfate is selected. Compared with tricalcium phosphate, calcium sulfate is characterized by:
A) Slower resorption than cortical allograft
B) Rapid resorption over weeks with minimal structural support
C) Permanent incorporation as a load-bearing strut
D) Osteogenic potential from included mesenchymal cells
E) Osteoinductive activity mediated by bone morphogenetic protein
questions.answer:
B)
Calcium sulfate is purely osteoconductive and resorbs rapidly, typically within 6–12 weeks, sometimes producing a sterile serous wound drainage as it dissolves. It provides essentially no structural support. In contrast, tricalcium phosphate resorbs over months and hydroxyapatite persists for years.

A is incorrect because calcium sulfate resorbs much faster than cortical allograft (weeks vs. months to years), not slower. C is incorrect because calcium sulfate is completely resorbed and never permanently incorporates; it cannot serve as a load-bearing strut. D is incorrect because calcium sulfate is a synthetic ceramic and contains no living cells; only autograft is osteogenic. E is incorrect because calcium sulfate has no osteoinductive activity; it contains no bone morphogenetic proteins. Osteoinduction is a property of demineralized bone matrix and BMPs, not synthetic ceramics.

questions.question:
A snowboarder has persistent lateral hindfoot pain and swelling after an "ankle sprain," with tenderness just distal and anterior to the tip of the fibula. Radiographs appear normal. The most likely missed injury is:
A) Peroneal tendon rupture
B) Fifth metatarsal base fracture
C) Anterior process of the calcaneus fracture
D) Os trigonum syndrome
E) Fracture of the lateral process of the talus
questions.answer:
E)
Lateral process talus fractures are strongly associated with snowboarding and are frequently missed on standard radiographs, being mistaken for a lateral ankle sprain. Tenderness is located just anterior and inferior to the fibular tip. CT identifies the fracture and guides treatment: nondisplaced fractures are immobilized, while displaced fragments are fixed or excised if comminuted. Missed injuries lead to subtalar arthritis.

A is incorrect because peroneal tendon rupture typically presents with pain and weakness along the retromalleolar groove posterior to the fibula, not anterior and distal to the fibular tip, and is not the classic missed snowboarding injury.
B is incorrect because a fifth metatarsal base fracture causes tenderness at the proximal fifth metatarsal, not the lateral hindfoot, and is associated with an inversion mechanism but not specifically with snowboarding.
C is incorrect because an anterior process of the calcaneus fracture causes tenderness more plantar and anterior (near the calcaneocuboid joint) and, while also missed on plain films, is not the classic snowboarding-associated fracture.
D is incorrect because os trigonum syndrome causes posterior ankle pain (behind the ankle), exacerbated by plantarflexion, and is not associated with an inversion-type snowboarding mechanism or lateral hindfoot tenderness anterior to the fibula.

questions.question:
Femoral anteversion in a normal newborn is approximately what value, and how does it change with growth?
A) 0 degrees, unchanged
B) 10 degrees, increasing to 40 degrees by maturity
C) 60 degrees, decreasing to 40 degrees
D) 15 degrees, unchanged
E) 30-40 degrees, decreasing to 10-15 degrees by skeletal maturity
questions.answer:
E)
Newborn femoral anteversion averages 30-40 degrees and decreases with growth to approximately 10-15 degrees in adults. Persistent excessive anteversion produces in-toeing with increased internal and decreased external hip rotation, W-sitting, and typically resolves by age 8-10; derotational osteotomy is reserved for severe functional or cosmetic problems persisting past age 8-10. Internal tibial torsion is the most common cause of in-toeing in toddlers, and metatarsus adductus in infants.

A is incorrect because newborn femoral anteversion is not 0 degrees; it averages 30-40 degrees at birth. B is incorrect because neonatal anteversion is not 10 degrees, and it decreases rather than increases with growth. C is incorrect because newborn anteversion is approximately 30-40 degrees (not 60 degrees), and it decreases to 10-15 degrees (not 40 degrees) by maturity. D is incorrect because newborn anteversion is not 15 degrees, and it does not remain unchanged—it progressively decreases with skeletal growth.

questions.question:
Which condition presents in an adolescent or young adult with persistent ankle pain after a sprain, and MRI shows an osteochondral lesion of the talus most commonly located:
A) Anterolateral and posteromedial
B) In the talar neck
C) Centromedial and centrolateral, with medial lesions typically deeper and cup-shaped
D) Only in the lateral process
E) Only anteriorly
questions.answer:
C)
Contemporary mapping shows medial lesions are more common, deeper, and cup-shaped, occurring centromedially, while lateral lesions are shallower and wafer-shaped and more often associated with trauma. Small lesions may be treated with debridement and microfracture; large or cystic lesions may require osteochondral autograft or allograft transplantation or cell-based therapy.

questions.question:
Degenerative spondylolisthesis is most common at which level and in which population?
A) T12-L1 in postmenopausal women
B) L5-S1 in adolescent athletes
C) C5-C6 in the elderly
D) L3-L4 in men under 40
E) L4-L5 in women over 50
questions.answer:
E)
Degenerative spondylolisthesis occurs most often at L4-L5, is several times more common in women, and is associated with age over 50, sagittally oriented facets, and ligamentous laxity. The slip is typically grade I and the pars interarticularis is intact.

A is incorrect because T12-L1 is not a typical level for degenerative spondylolisthesis; the thoracolumbar junction is more associated with fractures or kyphotic deformity than with degenerative listhesis.
B is incorrect because L5-S1 spondylolisthesis in adolescent athletes is characteristic of isthmic (pars defect) spondylolisthesis, not the degenerative type.
C is incorrect because C5-C6 is a common level for cervical spondylosis and myelopathy, not for degenerative spondylolisthesis, which is a lumbar condition.
D is incorrect because L3-L4 is a less common level than L4-L5 for degenerative spondylolisthesis, and the condition predominantly affects women over 50, not men under 40.

questions.question:
A 9-year-old with Legg-Calve-Perthes disease has limited abduction, and arthrography demonstrates the femoral head levering laterally on the acetabular rim with abduction. This finding is:
A) Normal for this stage
B) Hinge abduction, which contraindicates containment by simple abduction bracing and may require a valgus osteotomy or shelf procedure
C) Diagnostic of SCFE
D) Evidence of septic arthritis
E) An indication for immediate arthrodesis
questions.answer:
B)
Hinge abduction occurs when a flattened, extruded femoral head impinges on the lateral acetabular rim so that abduction levers the head out rather than seating it. Containment through abduction is therefore ineffective and can worsen symptoms. Treatment options include a valgus (or valgus-extension) proximal femoral osteotomy to move the hinge point, or a shelf procedure to support the extruded lateral segment.

A is incorrect because hinge abduction is a pathologic finding in Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, not a normal stage of the disease process; it indicates mechanical impingement that requires specific intervention.

C is incorrect because slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) is a distinct diagnosis characterized by displacement of the proximal femoral epiphysis through the physis, typically in adolescents; the arthrographic finding of lateral levering of the femoral head on the acetabular rim is characteristic of hinge abduction in Perthes disease, not SCFE.

D is incorrect because septic arthritis presents with systemic signs of infection (fever, elevated inflammatory markers, joint effusion with purulent aspirate); the arthrographic finding described is mechanical impingement, not an infectious process.

E is incorrect because arthrodesis (joint fusion) of the hip is not indicated in a 9-year-old child with Perthes disease; hip-preserving procedures such as valgus osteotomy or shelf acetabuloplasty are the appropriate surgical options to address hinge abduction.

questions.question:
Laminoplasty is most appropriate for which patient with multilevel cervical myelopathy?
A) A patient with previous posterior cervical fusion
B) A patient with cervical kyphosis of 15 degrees
C) A patient with lordotic alignment and no significant axial neck pain
D) A patient with a single-level soft disc herniation
E) A patient with severe axial neck pain and instability
questions.answer:
C)
Laminoplasty preserves motion and avoids fusion-related complications but requires lordotic or neutral alignment for posterior cord drift, and it does not reliably address axial neck pain or instability. It is the ideal procedure for multilevel cervical myelopathy in a patient with maintained lordosis and no significant axial pain.

A is incorrect because a previous posterior cervical fusion eliminates the motion segments that laminoplasty is designed to preserve, and altered posterior anatomy makes the procedure technically problematic.
B is incorrect because cervical kyphosis of 15 degrees is a contraindication to laminoplasty; posterior decompression relies on the cord drifting away from anterior pathology, which does not occur in a kyphotic spine.
D is incorrect because a single-level soft disc herniation is best treated with anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF), which directly removes the pathology; laminoplasty is reserved for multilevel disease.
E is incorrect because laminoplasty does not address instability (it is a non-fusion, motion-preserving procedure) and does not reliably improve axial neck pain, which may even worsen after laminoplasty.

questions.question:
Which structure is the primary restraint to valgus stress at the elbow between 20 and 120 degrees of flexion?
A) Lateral ulnar collateral ligament
B) Olecranon
C) Anterior bundle of the medial (ulnar) collateral ligament
D) Radial head
E) Annular ligament
questions.answer:
C)
The anterior bundle of the medial (ulnar) collateral ligament, inserting on the sublime tubercle of the ulna, is the primary restraint to valgus stress throughout the functional arc of elbow flexion (20–120°). It is the structure most commonly injured in overhead-throwing athletes.

A is incorrect because the lateral ulnar collateral ligament (LUCL) resists posterolateral rotatory instability, not valgus stress; it is assessed with the lateral pivot-shift test. B is incorrect because the olecranon contributes to valgus stability only in full extension (via its articulation with the trochlea) and is not the primary restraint through the functional arc. D is incorrect because the radial head is the most important secondary restraint to valgus stress; radial head excision in an MCL-deficient elbow leads to gross valgus instability, but it is not the primary restraint. E is incorrect because the annular ligament stabilizes the proximal radioulnar joint (preventing radial head subluxation) and does not primarily resist valgus force at the elbow.

questions.question:
A 13-year-old with a stable moderate SCFE should be treated with:
A) Immediate open reduction with aggressive manipulation
B) Spica casting
C) Observation and non-weight bearing
D) Bilateral prophylactic osteotomy
E) In situ percutaneous screw fixation
questions.answer:
E)
In situ fixation with a single cannulated screw placed perpendicular to the physis and centered in the epiphysis is the standard treatment for stable SCFE; it halts progression and allows remodeling. Screw threads should all cross the physis, and the surgeon must avoid joint penetration, which is checked with a fluoroscopic approach-withdrawal technique.

A is incorrect because aggressive open reduction of a stable (chronic) slip risks avascular necrosis of the femoral head by disrupting the already tenuous retinacular blood supply. B is incorrect because spica casting does not reliably prevent further slippage and is not the standard of care for SCFE. C is incorrect because observation alone allows continued slip progression; surgical stabilization is required to prevent worsening deformity and chondrolysis. D is incorrect because bilateral prophylactic osteotomy is not indicated as initial treatment for a unilateral stable moderate slip; prophylactic fixation of the contralateral hip (with a screw, not osteotomy) is considered only in select high-risk patients.

questions.question:
Hip surveillance in cerebral palsy is important because hip subluxation:
A) Is rare and self-limited
B) Occurs only in ambulatory children
C) Always resolves with bracing
D) Correlates with GMFCS level and, if untreated, progresses to painful dislocation, with migration percentage the key monitoring parameter
E) Requires no radiographic monitoring
questions.answer:
D)
Risk of hip displacement rises steeply with GMFCS level, approaching 90% in level V. The Reimers migration percentage quantifies the proportion of the femoral head lateral to Perkin line; values above 30–40% indicate progressive subluxation requiring intervention. Early management includes adductor and psoas lengthening; established subluxation requires varus derotational osteotomy with or without pelvic osteotomy. Chronic painful dislocation is difficult to salvage.

A is incorrect because hip subluxation in CP is neither rare nor self-limited; it is common, especially in nonambulatory children, and progresses without treatment. B is incorrect because hip displacement occurs predominantly in nonambulatory children (GMFCS IV–V), not only in ambulatory children. C is incorrect because bracing does not reliably prevent or reverse hip subluxation in CP; surgical intervention is typically required for progressive displacement. E is incorrect because serial imaging to monitor the migration percentage is the cornerstone of hip surveillance programs in CP and is essential for timely intervention.

questions.question:
Adult acquired flatfoot deformity stage II is characterized by:
A) Flexible hindfoot valgus deformity that is passively correctable
B) Valgus tilt of the talus within the ankle mortise
C) Tenosynovitis with a normal arch and no deformity
D) Rigid forefoot varus with ankle arthritis
E) Fixed hindfoot valgus deformity
questions.answer:
A)
In the Johnson and Strom classification (modified by Myerson), stage II adult acquired flatfoot deformity is characterized by a flexible hindfoot valgus deformity that remains passively correctable. Patients demonstrate inability to perform a single-limb heel rise and a positive "too many toes" sign. Treatment typically involves flexor digitorum longus transfer combined with a medial displacement calcaneal osteotomy ± lateral column lengthening.

B is incorrect because valgus tilt of the talus within the ankle mortise defines stage IV disease, indicating deltoid ligament insufficiency.
C is incorrect because tenosynovitis with a normal arch and no deformity describes stage I, where the posterior tibial tendon is inflamed but still functional.
D is incorrect because rigid forefoot varus with ankle arthritis is not a recognized single stage; rigid hindfoot deformity characterizes stage III, and ankle involvement defines stage IV.
E is incorrect because a fixed (rigid) hindfoot valgus deformity defines stage III, in which the deformity is no longer passively correctable.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old woman has a type IIIA open tibia fracture. Regarding wound irrigation, current evidence best supports:
A) Antibiotic-containing irrigation to reduce reoperation
B) Low-pressure lavage with normal saline
C) Omitting irrigation if antibiotics are given within 1 hour
D) Irrigation with dilute povidone-iodine as the standard solution
E) High-pressure pulsatile lavage with castile soap
questions.answer:
B)
The FLOW (Fluid Lavage of Open Wounds) trial demonstrated no benefit of high-pressure over low-pressure lavage and found that soap irrigation was associated with a higher reoperation rate compared with normal saline. Low-pressure lavage with normal saline is the current evidence-based standard for open fracture irrigation, with volume generally scaled to injury severity (e.g., 3 L for type I, 6 L for type II, 9 L for type III).

A is incorrect because the FLOW trial showed that adding antibiotic solution (castile soap or bacitracin) to the irrigant did not reduce reoperation rates and soap actually increased them; antibiotic-containing irrigation has not demonstrated consistent benefit. C is incorrect because wound irrigation is a critical component of open fracture management regardless of the timing of systemic antibiotics; irrigation mechanically removes debris and reduces bacterial burden in a way that systemic antibiotics alone cannot. D is incorrect because povidone-iodine is cytotoxic to osteoblasts and soft tissues and has not been shown to improve outcomes compared with normal saline; it is not the standard irrigation solution. E is incorrect because high-pressure pulsatile lavage can drive contaminants deeper into tissues, damage bone and soft tissue, and was not shown to be superior to low-pressure lavage in the FLOW trial; furthermore, castile soap was associated with increased reoperation rates.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old woman has a dense, lobulated mass on the posterior distal femoral cortex with a broad base and a radiolucent cleft separating it from the cortex. Biopsy shows low-grade bone-forming tumor. The diagnosis and treatment are:
A) Myositis ossificans treated with observation
B) Osteochondroma treated with observation
C) Conventional osteosarcoma treated with chemotherapy and resection
D) Periosteal chondroma treated with curettage
E) Parosteal osteosarcoma treated with wide resection
questions.answer:
E)
Parosteal osteosarcoma is a low-grade surface osteosarcoma with a strong predilection for the posterior distal femur, appearing as a heavily ossified, lobulated juxtacortical mass with a characteristic radiolucent cleft between tumor and cortex. Biopsy showing a low-grade bone-forming tumor confirms the diagnosis. Wide resection alone is usually curative; chemotherapy is reserved only if dedifferentiated components are found. MDM2/CDK4 amplification is typical.

A is incorrect because myositis ossificans is a reactive, non-neoplastic process with a characteristic zonal maturation pattern (peripheral mature bone), not a bone-forming tumor arising from the cortical surface with a radiolucent cleft.

B is incorrect because osteochondroma is a cartilage-capped bony exostosis with cortical and medullary continuity with the parent bone; it does not show a radiolucent cleft separating it from the cortex, and biopsy would show a cartilage cap, not a bone-forming tumor.

C is incorrect because conventional (intramedullary) osteosarcoma is a high-grade lesion arising within the medullary canal, not a low-grade surface lesion on the cortex. The stem specifies a low-grade bone-forming tumor on the cortical surface.

D is incorrect because periosteal chondroma is a benign cartilage-forming (not bone-forming) surface lesion that causes cortical saucerization; biopsy would show chondroid matrix rather than a bone-forming tumor.

questions.question:
Which tendon is most commonly involved in insertional versus noninsertional pathology 2 to 6 cm proximal to its calcaneal attachment?
A) Anterior tibial tendon
B) Achilles tendon
C) Posterior tibial tendon
D) Peroneus brevis
E) Flexor hallucis longus
questions.answer:
B)
The Achilles tendon has a relative hypovascular watershed zone 2–6 cm above its calcaneal insertion where noninsertional tendinosis occurs; treatment emphasizes eccentric strengthening, which has strong evidence. Insertional tendinopathy occurs at the calcaneus, often with a Haglund prominence and retrocalcaneal bursitis, responds less well to eccentric protocols, and may require debridement with reattachment. Corticosteroid injection into the tendon is avoided because of rupture risk.

A is incorrect because the anterior tibial tendon is not characterized by a watershed zone 2–6 cm proximal to its insertion; its pathology typically involves insertional tendinopathy or spontaneous rupture at or near its navicular/cuneiform attachment.
C is incorrect because posterior tibial tendon dysfunction most commonly involves degeneration at or just distal to the medial malleolus (zone of hypovascularity behind the malleolus), not 2–6 cm proximal to a calcaneal attachment.
D is incorrect because peroneus brevis pathology (longitudinal splits, tendinosis) occurs at the level of the fibular groove behind the lateral malleolus, not in a watershed zone proximal to the calcaneus.
E is incorrect because flexor hallucis longus tendinopathy typically occurs at the fibro-osseous tunnel posterior to the talus (os trigonum region), not 2–6 cm proximal to a calcaneal insertion.

questions.question:
Adjuvant radiation therapy for a high-grade extremity soft tissue sarcoma primarily:
A) Replaces surgical resection
B) Is never used preoperatively
C) Improves overall survival substantially
D) Improves local control, allowing limb-sparing surgery with more limited margins
E) Prevents pulmonary metastasis
questions.answer:
D)
Randomized data show radiation combined with limb-sparing surgery achieves local control comparable to amputation, without a demonstrated overall survival benefit. Preoperative radiation uses lower doses and smaller fields with better long-term function and less fibrosis, but roughly doubles acute wound complication rates; postoperative radiation reverses that trade-off.

A is incorrect because radiation is an adjunct to surgery, not a replacement; wide surgical resection remains the cornerstone of treatment. B is incorrect because preoperative (neoadjuvant) radiation is well-established and often preferred for its smaller field size, lower dose, and improved long-term limb function. C is incorrect because adjuvant radiation improves local control but has not been shown to substantially improve overall survival. E is incorrect because radiation treats the local disease; pulmonary metastases are driven by hematogenous spread and are not prevented by local radiation therapy.

questions.question:
A core needle biopsy of a soft-tissue sarcoma is planned. Which technique best minimizes the consequences of tract contamination?
A) Entering through an uninvolved adjacent compartment
B) Using multiple separate entry sites to sample widely
C) Approaching through the shortest distance regardless of compartment
D) Placing the needle so the tract lies within the planned resection specimen and marking the skin entry site
E) Avoiding any documentation of the entry point
questions.answer:
D)
The needle tract is considered contaminated and must be excised en bloc with the definitive resection specimen. Therefore, the biopsy tract is placed in direct line with the planned surgical incision, within the same compartment, and the skin entry site is marked (suture, ink, or tattoo) so it can be reliably identified and included in the resection.

A is incorrect because entering through an uninvolved adjacent compartment contaminates a previously clean compartment, potentially expanding the required resection or rendering the tumor unresectable.
B is incorrect because multiple separate entry sites create multiple contaminated tracts, all of which must be excised, increasing tissue loss and surgical complexity.
C is incorrect because the shortest distance may traverse uninvolved compartments or cross neurovascular structures, spreading contamination outside the planned resection field.
E is incorrect because failing to document the entry point makes it impossible to identify and excise the contaminated tract at definitive surgery, risking local recurrence.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old woman with severe osteoporosis and a recent vertebral compression fracture is to begin pharmacologic therapy. Current evidence best supports which sequence?
