Tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT), whether localized (giant cell tumor of tendon sheath) or diffuse (PVNS), contains abundant hemosiderin-laden macrophages that produce characteristic low signal on both T1- and T2-weighted MRI sequences with blooming artifact on gradient echo imaging. It is associated with CSF1 translocations. Joint aspiration classically yields serosanguinous brown fluid. Treatment is synovectomy; diffuse disease has a high recurrence rate, and CSF1R inhibitors (e.g., pexidartinib) are available for refractory cases.

A is incorrect because myxoma is a benign intramuscular lesion that appears homogeneously low on T1 and markedly high on T2 due to its myxoid (water-rich) content — it does not contain hemosiderin and does not bloom on gradient echo. B is incorrect because lipoma follows fat signal on all MRI sequences (high on T1, intermediate on T2, suppresses with fat saturation) and contains no hemosiderin. D is incorrect because hemangioma typically shows intermediate-to-low T1 signal and high T2 signal with serpentine vascular channels and may contain phleboliths; it does not demonstrate diffuse low signal on T2 or hemosiderin blooming. E is incorrect because desmoid tumor (aggressive fibromatosis) shows low-to-intermediate signal on T1 and variable (often heterogeneous) signal on T2 with characteristic bands of low signal representing collagen — it does not contain hemosiderin-laden macrophages and does not bloom on gradient echo.

questions.question:
Which metastatic lesions are classically blastic?
A) Prostate and breast (breast may be mixed)
B) Renal cell and thyroid
C) Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
D) Lung and melanoma
E) Multiple myeloma
questions.answer:
A)
Prostate carcinoma is characteristically blastic and breast is often mixed lytic and blastic. Renal cell and thyroid metastases are lytic and notably hypervascular, so preoperative arterial embolization within 24–48 hours of surgery is recommended to limit catastrophic bleeding. Lung and melanoma are typically lytic.

B is incorrect because renal cell and thyroid metastases are classically lytic (and hypervascular), not blastic. C is incorrect because gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) are not classically associated with blastic osseous metastases. D is incorrect because lung and melanoma metastases are typically lytic. E is incorrect because multiple myeloma produces purely lytic, punched-out lesions with no blastic component.

questions.question:
Which reconstructive option after intercalary diaphyseal resection provides biologic incorporation and preserves the adjacent joints?
A) Amputation
B) Intercalary allograft or vascularized fibular autograft
C) Arthrodesis
D) Rotationplasty
E) Total joint endoprosthesis
questions.answer:
B)
When the tumor spares the epiphysis, intercalary reconstruction with structural allograft, vascularized fibula, or a combination (the "Capanna" technique) preserves native joints on both sides of the defect. Allograft alone risks nonunion and late fracture; the vascularized fibula provides biologic healing and hypertrophies over time under load, making these options ideal for diaphyseal defects.

A is incorrect because amputation sacrifices the limb entirely and does not reconstruct the defect. C is incorrect because arthrodesis fuses an adjacent joint, thereby sacrificing joint motion rather than preserving it. D is incorrect because rotationplasty is used for distal femoral or proximal tibial resections that include the knee joint; it does not preserve native joints and is not an intercalary reconstruction. E is incorrect because a total joint endoprosthesis replaces an adjacent joint rather than preserving it and is indicated for juxta-articular or intra-articular resections, not mid-diaphyseal intercalary defects.

questions.question:
Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis is distinguished from ankylosing spondylitis by:
A) Bilateral sacroiliitis with fusion
B) Onset before age 30
C) Preserved disc height and absent sacroiliac joint erosion
D) Strong HLA-B27 association
E) Marginal syndesmophytes
questions.answer:
C)
DISH is characterized by flowing anterior ossification bridging at least four contiguous vertebrae with preservation of disc height and no sacroiliac or apophyseal joint erosion or fusion. It typically affects older patients and is associated with diabetes and obesity. Like ankylosing spondylitis, the ankylosed spine is at risk for unstable extension-type fractures after low-energy trauma.

A is incorrect because bilateral sacroiliitis with fusion is a hallmark of ankylosing spondylitis, not DISH; DISH specifically lacks sacroiliac joint involvement. B is incorrect because onset before age 30 is characteristic of ankylosing spondylitis; DISH typically presents in patients over 50. D is incorrect because a strong HLA-B27 association is a feature of ankylosing spondylitis (present in ~90% of cases), whereas DISH has no HLA-B27 association. E is incorrect because marginal (thin, vertically oriented) syndesmophytes are characteristic of ankylosing spondylitis; DISH produces bulky, flowing anterior osteophytes that are distinct from true syndesmophytes.

questions.question:
A 76-year-old woman develops an acutely swollen, warm knee on postoperative day 2 following hip arthroplasty. Aspiration shows 22,000 WBC/microL with rhomboid-shaped, positively birefringent crystals and a negative Gram stain. The most appropriate treatment is:
A) Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or corticosteroids with observation
B) Emergent arthroscopic irrigation
C) Immediate revision of the hip arthroplasty
D) Allopurinol as monotherapy for the acute episode
E) Six weeks of intravenous vancomycin
questions.answer:
A)
Positively birefringent, rhomboid-shaped crystals are pathognomonic for calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD/pseudogout). Postoperative pseudogout flares are common in elderly patients, provoked by the physiologic stress and fluid shifts of surgery. Treatment of an acute CPPD flare is anti-inflammatory therapy (NSAIDs or corticosteroids). Cultures should still be sent to exclude coexistent infection, but the crystal-positive, Gram-stain-negative aspirate supports a crystal arthropathy.

B is incorrect because emergent arthroscopic irrigation is indicated for septic arthritis; the aspirate here shows crystals consistent with pseudogout and a negative Gram stain, making infection unlikely as the primary diagnosis.
C is incorrect because the affected joint is the knee, not the replaced hip, and the findings indicate a crystal flare rather than a periprosthetic joint infection; revision surgery is not warranted.
D is incorrect because allopurinol is a urate-lowering agent used for gout prophylaxis, not CPPD, and xanthine oxidase inhibitors should never be initiated during an acute flare as they can paradoxically worsen symptoms.
E is incorrect because six weeks of intravenous vancomycin is the treatment for a confirmed periprosthetic joint infection; the clinical picture here is consistent with pseudogout, not infection.

questions.question:
A patient has anterior shoulder pain with a positive Speed and Yergason test and a "Popeye" deformity after acute onset of a snap. This represents:
A) Distal biceps rupture
B) Subscapularis rupture
C) Long head of biceps rupture at the glenoid origin
D) Pectoralis major rupture
E) Rupture of the long head of biceps tendon
questions.answer:
E)
Rupture of the long head of biceps tendon is characterized by anterior shoulder pain, positive Speed and Yergason tests (which specifically stress the proximal LHB tendon), an audible or palpable snap, and a "Popeye" deformity caused by distal retraction of the muscle belly. This is the classic presentation of a proximal LHB rupture.

A is incorrect because distal biceps rupture causes pain and ecchymosis at the antecubital fossa (elbow), not anterior shoulder pain; the hook test is the key exam finding, and Speed/Yergason tests evaluate the proximal biceps, not the distal insertion. B is incorrect because subscapularis rupture presents with increased passive external rotation, a positive lift-off or belly-press test, and does not produce a Popeye deformity. C is incorrect because while the LHB does originate from the superior glenoid labrum, the most common site of proximal rupture is at the bicipital groove or its exit from the joint; rupture specifically at the glenoid origin is less common and is more associated with a SLAP lesion pattern rather than the acute snap and Popeye deformity described. D is incorrect because pectoralis major rupture presents with ecchymosis and swelling of the anterior chest wall/axilla, loss of the anterior axillary fold, and weakness of adduction and internal rotation — not a Popeye deformity or positive biceps provocation tests.

questions.question:
Which is the most appropriate management of a hemodynamically stable patient with a vertically unstable pelvic ring injury (APC-III/vertical shear) after initial resuscitation?
A) Pelvic binder for 6 weeks
B) Isolated symphyseal plating
C) Protected weight bearing and observation
D) Anterior and posterior surgical stabilization
E) Bed rest for 12 weeks
questions.answer:
D)
Vertically unstable pelvic ring injuries (APC-III or vertical shear) disrupt both the anterior ring and the posterior sacroiliac complex, including the posterior SI ligaments, sacrospinous, and sacrotuberous ligaments. Restoration of stability requires both anterior fixation (symphyseal plating or external fixator) and posterior fixation (percutaneous iliosacral screws, posterior tension-band plating, or triangular osteosynthesis). Careful assessment of sacral dysmorphism is essential before iliosacral screw placement.

A is incorrect because a pelvic binder is a temporizing measure for acute hemorrhage control and does not provide definitive stabilization of a vertically unstable injury; prolonged use risks skin complications and does not address posterior instability. B is incorrect because isolated symphyseal plating addresses only the anterior ring and will fail without posterior stabilization, as the posterior complex is the primary load-bearing structure. C is incorrect because vertically unstable injuries will displace with weight bearing and cannot be managed nonoperatively; observation risks malunion, leg-length discrepancy, and chronic pain. E is incorrect because prolonged bed rest alone does not restore anatomic alignment of the posterior ring, leads to significant morbidity (DVT, deconditioning, pressure ulcers), and is not the standard of care for these injuries.

questions.question:
A 4-year-old has 3 weeks of limp, diffuse bone pain in several limbs, pallor, and night sweats. Radiographs show metaphyseal lucent bands and periosteal reaction in more than one bone. The most appropriate next step is:
A) Bracing
B) Observation
C) Immediate open biopsy of the most painful lesion
D) Antibiotics for presumed multifocal osteomyelitis
E) Complete blood count with differential and peripheral smear, with referral for marrow evaluation
questions.answer:
E)
Acute leukemia commonly presents to the orthopaedic surgeon with limb pain, limp, and refusal to walk. Radiographs may show metaphyseal lucent bands, diffuse osteopenia, permeative change, and periosteal reaction in multiple bones. Constitutional symptoms (pallor, night sweats), multifocal skeletal involvement, and cytopenias are classic clues. A complete blood count with differential and peripheral smear is the appropriate first step; abnormal findings prompt referral for bone marrow biopsy to confirm the diagnosis.

A is incorrect because bracing does not address the underlying systemic disease causing multifocal bone lesions and constitutional symptoms. B is incorrect because observation would dangerously delay diagnosis and treatment of a potentially fatal hematologic malignancy. C is incorrect because immediate open biopsy of a bone lesion is unnecessarily invasive; a simple CBC with smear will suggest leukemia and a subsequent marrow aspirate is far less morbid and more diagnostic than an open bone biopsy. D is incorrect because although multifocal osteomyelitis can cause bone pain and periosteal reaction, the combination of pallor, night sweats, metaphyseal lucent bands in multiple bones, and diffuse constitutional symptoms is far more consistent with leukemia; empiric antibiotics without first obtaining blood work would delay the correct diagnosis.

questions.question:
Ulnar nerve compression at Guyon canal distal to the bifurcation typically produces:
A) Loss of dorsal ulnar hand sensation
B) Weakness of flexor carpi ulnaris
C) Isolated motor weakness of the ulnar-innervated intrinsics with normal sensation
D) Isolated sensory loss with normal strength
E) Motor and sensory loss in the ulnar distribution
questions.answer:
C)
Compression at Guyon canal distal to the bifurcation involves either the deep motor branch (zone 2) or the superficial sensory branch (zone 3). Zone 2 compression produces isolated motor weakness of the ulnar-innervated intrinsics with preserved sensation, making C the best answer for a stem specifying "distal to the bifurcation" with motor findings.

A is incorrect because the dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve arises 5–8 cm proximal to the wrist and does not traverse Guyon canal; dorsal ulnar hand sensation is unaffected by any Guyon canal lesion.
B is incorrect because flexor carpi ulnaris is innervated by the ulnar nerve proximal to the elbow; its weakness localizes a lesion to the cubital tunnel, not Guyon canal.
D is incorrect because isolated sensory loss with normal strength describes zone 3 (superficial sensory branch) compression, which is also distal to the bifurcation but is a pure sensory pattern, not a motor one; the stem asks about the pattern that "typically" results from deep branch involvement.
E is incorrect because combined motor and sensory loss in the ulnar distribution describes zone 1 compression, which is proximal to the bifurcation, not distal to it.

questions.question:
Vertebral osteomyelitis in an intravenous drug user with negative blood cultures and no prior antibiotics is best managed initially by:
A) Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics for 6 weeks without biopsy
B) CT-guided biopsy for culture before initiating antibiotics
C) Observation
D) Corticosteroids
E) Immediate anterior debridement and fusion
questions.answer:
B)
In a hemodynamically stable patient with vertebral osteomyelitis, negative blood cultures, and no prior antibiotics, CT-guided biopsy should be performed before starting antibiotics to identify the causative organism and guide prolonged targeted therapy. Biopsy yield drops significantly once empiric antibiotics are initiated, making pre-antibiotic tissue sampling critical.

A is incorrect because starting empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics without identifying the organism risks inadequate coverage (especially in IV drug users who may harbor unusual organisms such as Pseudomonas or fungi) and reduces the diagnostic yield of any subsequent biopsy.
C is incorrect because vertebral osteomyelitis requires active treatment; observation alone risks progression of infection, vertebral destruction, epidural abscess formation, and neurologic compromise.
D is incorrect because corticosteroids are immunosuppressive and would worsen an active spinal infection; they have no role in the primary management of vertebral osteomyelitis.
E is incorrect because immediate anterior debridement and fusion is reserved for patients with neurologic deficit, spinal instability, epidural abscess with cord compression, or failure of medical therapy; in a stable patient without these indications, a tissue diagnosis should be obtained first via less invasive means.

questions.question:
An 82-year-old woman with Parkinson disease and abductor insufficiency requires total hip arthroplasty. Which bearing option best reduces her dislocation risk while preserving range of motion?
A) A fully constrained tripolar device as the first choice in all such patients
B) A hemiarthroplasty with a unipolar head
C) A dual-mobility construct
D) A 28-mm head on conventional polyethylene
E) Metal-on-metal resurfacing
questions.answer:
C)
Dual-mobility constructs use a small inner head articulating within a mobile polyethylene liner that in turn articulates with the metal shell, producing a large effective head diameter, greater jump distance, and increased impingement-free range of motion. This makes them ideal for patients with neuromuscular disease (e.g., Parkinson disease), cognitive impairment, abductor deficiency, or spinopelvic stiffness, all of which increase dislocation risk.

A is incorrect because fully constrained tripolar devices restrict range of motion and transfer significant stress to the bone-implant interface, increasing the risk of loosening; they are reserved as salvage for recurrent instability, not used as a first-line choice.
B is incorrect because a unipolar hemiarthroplasty does not address the acetabular side, can cause acetabular erosion, and does not provide the enhanced stability of a dual-mobility design; it also does not address the instability risk in a patient with abductor insufficiency and Parkinson disease.
D is incorrect because a 28-mm head on conventional polyethylene provides a small head-to-neck ratio with limited jump distance, resulting in the highest dislocation risk among modern bearing options—particularly inappropriate in a high-risk patient.
E is incorrect because metal-on-metal resurfacing is contraindicated in elderly patients (poor bone quality, femoral neck fracture risk), in women (higher adverse reaction to metal debris risk), and does not address the instability concerns; it also has largely fallen out of favor due to adverse local tissue reactions.

questions.question:
A 33-year-old man has a type IIIB open tibia fracture requiring free flap coverage. With respect to timing, soft-tissue coverage is best achieved:
A) After the wound granulates completely
B) After 4 weeks of dressing changes to allow demarcation
C) Within the first 7 days after injury, following adequate debridement
D) At the same setting as the initial debridement regardless of contamination
E) Only after radiographic evidence of callus
questions.answer:
C)
Early definitive soft-tissue coverage, generally within the first week after thorough debridement, is associated with lower rates of deep infection and improved union compared with delayed coverage. Serial debridements are performed as needed until the wound is clean, and negative-pressure dressings serve as a temporizing bridge rather than a substitute for definitive flap coverage. The coordinated "orthoplastic" team approach optimizes outcomes.

A is incorrect because waiting for complete granulation delays definitive coverage, increases infection risk, and allows colonization of the wound bed. B is incorrect because prolonged dressing changes for 4 weeks significantly raise the risk of deep infection and osteomyelitis; early coverage within the first week is superior. D is incorrect because performing free flap coverage at the initial debridement regardless of contamination risks covering a contaminated wound, leading to deep infection; adequate serial debridement must precede definitive soft-tissue coverage. E is incorrect because waiting for callus formation would delay coverage by many weeks, greatly increasing infection and nonunion rates; soft-tissue coverage should precede, not follow, bony healing.

questions.question:
Which growth arrest pattern results from a peripheral physeal bar?
A) Symmetric growth arrest with pure shortening
B) Angular deformity with progressive deviation toward the bar
C) Overgrowth
D) Joint dislocation
E) No clinical consequence
questions.answer:
B)
A peripheral physeal bar tethers one side of the physis, producing progressive angular deformity toward the bar as the unaffected portion continues to grow. This is in contrast to a central bar, which produces symmetric tenting of the physis and relative shortening without significant angulation. Bars occupying less than approximately 50% of the physis in a child with at least 2 years or 2 cm of growth remaining may be resected with interposition of fat or polymethylmethacrylate; larger bars are managed with completion epiphysiodesis, contralateral epiphysiodesis, osteotomy, or lengthening.

A is incorrect because symmetric growth arrest with pure shortening is the pattern seen with a complete physeal arrest or a central bar, not a peripheral bar. C is incorrect because overgrowth is not a consequence of a physeal bar; bars restrict growth rather than stimulate it. D is incorrect because joint dislocation is not a typical consequence of a peripheral physeal bar; the primary deformity is angular. E is incorrect because a peripheral physeal bar does have significant clinical consequences, namely progressive angular deformity that worsens with remaining growth.

questions.question:
Which of the following is the most appropriate level and consideration for a transtibial amputation?
A) As long as possible regardless of soft tissue coverage
B) Through the knee joint in all vascular patients
C) Approximately 12-15 cm below the knee joint line, preserving the gastrocnemius-soleus myocutaneous flap
D) As short as possible to reduce weight
E) Above the knee for all diabetics
questions.answer:
C)
A residual limb of approximately 12–15 cm below the knee joint line (or roughly 2.5 cm of tibia per 30 cm of patient height) provides an optimal lever arm for prosthetic fitting while allowing adequate space for prosthetic componentry. A long posterior myofasciocutaneous (gastrocnemius-soleus) flap provides durable, well-padded soft tissue coverage over the bone end. Preserving the knee joint dramatically reduces the energy expenditure of ambulation compared with transfemoral amputation (~25% increase vs. ≥65%).

A is incorrect because maximizing length without regard to soft tissue coverage leads to poor wound healing, exposed bone, and revision; adequate soft tissue padding is essential.
B is incorrect because through-knee (knee disarticulation) amputation is not universally indicated in vascular patients; preserving a functional below-knee level is preferred when feasible because it preserves the knee joint and lowers energy cost of gait.
D is incorrect because an excessively short transtibial residual limb provides a poor lever arm, making prosthetic control difficult and increasing energy expenditure.
E is incorrect because above-knee amputation in all diabetics is unnecessarily aggressive; many diabetic patients heal well at the transtibial level, and preserving the knee joint significantly improves functional outcomes.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old sustains a mid-shaft humerus fracture with a radial nerve palsy present on arrival. The most appropriate initial management is:
A) Immediate plate fixation with nerve exploration
B) Immediate open exploration of the nerve
C) Intramedullary nailing
D) Functional bracing with observation and serial examination
E) Electromyography within 48 hours
questions.answer:
D)
Radial nerve palsy accompanies approximately 10–12% of humeral shaft fractures, most commonly with Holstein-Lewis distal-third spiral patterns. More than 85–90% of these palsies are neurapraxias that recover spontaneously. The standard initial management is functional bracing (or splinting) with wrist extension support to prevent contracture, followed by serial clinical examination. EMG/NCS is obtained at 3–4 months if no clinical recovery is observed; surgical exploration is reserved for open fractures, palsy developing after closed reduction or fixation, associated vascular injury, or failure to recover by 3–6 months.

A is incorrect because immediate plate fixation with nerve exploration is not indicated for a closed humeral shaft fracture with a radial nerve palsy present at the time of injury; the vast majority recover without surgery, and operative exploration is reserved for specific indications.
B is incorrect because immediate open exploration of the nerve alone is unnecessary; the palsy is most likely a neurapraxia from the initial injury, and observation is the accepted first-line approach.
C is incorrect because intramedullary nailing is not the standard initial treatment for a mid-shaft humerus fracture with radial nerve palsy; nonoperative management with functional bracing is preferred, and nailing carries its own risk of iatrogenic nerve injury or shoulder complications.
E is incorrect because EMG performed within 48 hours of injury is uninformative, as Wallerian degeneration has not yet occurred; EMG/NCS should be delayed to at least 3–4 weeks (and typically 3–4 months) to provide meaningful prognostic data.

questions.question:
Epidural steroid injections for lumbar radiculopathy are best described as:
A) Providing short-term symptom relief without proven change in long-term surgical rates
B) Curative for the underlying herniation
C) Contraindicated in all patients with disc herniation
D) Indicated as first-line for progressive foot drop
E) More effective than surgery for cauda equina syndrome
questions.answer:
A)
Transforaminal and interlaminar epidural steroid injections provide meaningful short-term relief of radicular pain and can serve a diagnostic role, but evidence for long-term benefit or avoidance of surgery is limited. They are not appropriate substitutes for decompression in progressive neurologic deficit or cauda equina syndrome. Particulate steroid should be avoided in cervical transforaminal injections because of embolic cord infarct risk.

B is incorrect because epidural steroids reduce inflammation around the nerve root but do not cure or reverse the underlying disc herniation.
C is incorrect because epidural steroid injections are commonly used and not contraindicated in disc herniation; they are a standard non-operative treatment option.
D is incorrect because progressive foot drop (motor deficit) is an indication for surgical decompression, not for continued conservative measures such as injections.
E is incorrect because cauda equina syndrome is a surgical emergency requiring urgent decompression; epidural steroids play no role in its management.

questions.question:
Two years after total knee arthroplasty, a patient has an extensor lag of 40 degrees and a palpable defect over the patellar tendon. Regarding management, the best statement is:
A) Bracing alone is definitive
B) Direct primary repair reliably restores function in chronic cases
C) Immediate revision arthroplasty is required regardless of component fixation
D) Chronic extensor mechanism disruption after arthroplasty has high failure rates with direct repair, and reconstruction with allograft or synthetic mesh is generally required
E) Arthrodesis is the first-line option
questions.answer:
D)
Chronic extensor mechanism disruption after knee arthroplasty responds poorly to direct repair because the tissue is attenuated and scarred and the repair is loaded immediately. Reconstruction using an extensor mechanism allograft or synthetic mesh, tensioned in full extension, produces more reliable results, although residual extensor lag is common. Component position, infection, and patellar bone stock must be assessed as contributing factors.

A is incorrect because bracing alone cannot restore active extension in a chronic complete extensor mechanism rupture; it may temporize but is not definitive treatment. B is incorrect because direct primary repair in chronic cases has unacceptably high failure rates due to tissue attenuation, retraction, and poor healing capacity. C is incorrect because revision arthroplasty is not automatically required; it is only indicated if component malposition, loosening, or infection contributed to the disruption. E is incorrect because arthrodesis is a salvage option reserved for cases where reconstruction has failed or is not feasible, not a first-line treatment.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old woman with chronic axial low back pain and multilevel degenerative disc disease asks about gabapentin. The best counsel is that:
A) Evidence for benefit in nonradicular axial back pain is limited, and structured exercise remains the mainstay
B) It is contraindicated in all patients over 50
C) It is first-line therapy and superior to exercise
D) It reliably produces fusion-level pain relief
E) It should be combined with long-term opioids for best effect
questions.answer:
A)
Evidence supporting gabapentinoids for chronic axial (nonradicular) low back pain is weak, and these agents carry sedation, dizziness, and falls risk in older adults, along with recognized misuse potential when combined with opioids. Structured exercise, cognitive-behavioral approaches, weight management, and nonopioid analgesia remain the foundation of care for nonradicular back pain.

B is incorrect because gabapentin is not contraindicated solely based on age over 50; it requires dose adjustment and caution in the elderly but is not absolutely contraindicated. C is incorrect because gabapentin has not been shown to be superior to exercise for axial back pain and is not considered first-line therapy for this indication. D is incorrect because gabapentin does not reliably produce pain relief equivalent to that achieved by surgical fusion, and its efficacy in axial back pain is not well supported. E is incorrect because combining gabapentin with long-term opioids increases the risk of respiratory depression, sedation, and overdose death; guidelines recommend against routine co-prescription.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old man has fusiform swelling and tenderness in the thenar and hypothenar regions with pain on passive extension of the index and small fingers, and a laceration in the web space. The most likely diagnosis is:
A) Herpetic whitlow
B) de Quervain tenosynovitis
C) Carpal tunnel syndrome
D) Isolated cellulitis
E) A collar-button (web space) abscess with spread along fascial planes
questions.answer:
E)
A web space (collar-button) abscess forms on both dorsal and volar sides of the interdigital space connected through the palmar fascia, and infection can track along the lumbrical canals into the thenar and midpalmar deep spaces. The combination of fusiform swelling in both thenar and hypothenar regions, pain on passive extension of the index and small fingers, and a web space laceration is classic for a collar-button abscess with proximal spread along fascial planes. Treatment is prompt surgical drainage through both dorsal and volar incisions, avoiding a longitudinal web-crossing incision that produces contracture.

A is incorrect because herpetic whitlow presents as grouped vesicles on a single digit (usually the fingertip), not fusiform swelling in the thenar and hypothenar eminences with a web space wound.
B is incorrect because de Quervain tenosynovitis involves the first dorsal compartment at the radial styloid (APL and EPB tendons) and does not cause thenar/hypothenar swelling or pain with passive finger extension.
C is incorrect because carpal tunnel syndrome is a compressive neuropathy of the median nerve presenting with numbness and tingling in the radial digits, not with swelling, tenderness, and signs of deep space infection.
D is incorrect because isolated cellulitis would present with diffuse superficial erythema and warmth without the characteristic fusiform deep-space swelling pattern or pain on passive digital extension that indicates deep fascial plane involvement.

questions.question:
Which lesion classically presents with night pain relieved by nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and shows a small radiolucent nidus with surrounding reactive sclerosis?
A) Brodie abscess
B) Chondroblastoma
C) Osteosarcoma
D) Osteoid osteoma
E) Osteoblastoma
questions.answer:
D)
Osteoid osteoma has a nidus smaller than 1.5 cm that produces prostaglandins, explaining the characteristic night pain and dramatic response to NSAIDs. CT best demonstrates the nidus. Many lesions resolve over years with NSAIDs; radiofrequency ablation is highly effective for those requiring treatment, although it is avoided within roughly 1 cm of neurovascular structures or the spinal cord.

A is incorrect because a Brodie abscess is a subacute osteomyelitis that may appear as a lucent lesion with surrounding sclerosis, but it presents with infectious signs (low-grade pain, possible warmth) rather than the classic prostaglandin-mediated night pain relieved by NSAIDs, and it lacks a discrete calcified nidus.
B is incorrect because chondroblastoma is an epiphyseal lesion in skeletally immature patients; it does not produce the classic small sclerotic-rimmed nidus in the cortical diaphysis/metaphysis, nor does it show the dramatic NSAID response characteristic of osteoid osteoma.
C is incorrect because osteosarcoma is a malignant bone-forming tumor that presents with an aggressive, destructive metaphyseal lesion (sunburst periosteal reaction, Codman triangle) rather than a small benign nidus with surrounding reactive sclerosis.
E is incorrect because osteoblastoma is histologically similar to osteoid osteoma but is defined as larger than 1.5–2 cm, tends to be more locally aggressive, favors the posterior spinal elements, and does not reliably respond to NSAIDs.

questions.question:
Which staging system for benign bone lesions describes stage 3 as:
A) Latent, well-defined, asymptomatic
B) Malignant transformation
C) Active, progressive growth with a well-defined margin and cortical expansion
D) Metastatic
E) Aggressive, with cortical destruction and extension beyond the bone
questions.answer:
E)
Enneking's benign staging system designates stage 3 as aggressive, characterized by cortical destruction and soft tissue extension (e.g., aggressive giant cell tumor). Treatment typically requires marginal or wide resection, or extended curettage with adjuvants.

A is incorrect because "latent, well-defined, asymptomatic" describes Enneking stage 1 (e.g., nonossifying fibroma), not stage 3.
B is incorrect because malignant transformation is not a stage in the Enneking benign staging system.
C is incorrect because "active, progressive growth with a well-defined margin and cortical expansion" describes Enneking stage 2 (e.g., aneurysmal bone cyst), not stage 3.
D is incorrect because "metastatic" is not a stage in the Enneking benign staging system; metastatic disease is addressed separately.

questions.question:
Which factor is most strongly associated with recurrent instability after a first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation?
A) Dominant arm involvement
B) Immobilization for 3 weeks
C) Female sex
D) Age under 20 with participation in contact sports
E) Age over 40
questions.answer:
D)
Young age is the single most important risk factor for recurrent anterior shoulder instability, with recurrence rates of 70–90% in patients under 20 years old. This risk is compounded by participation in contact or collision sports, which subject the shoulder to repeated at-risk positions. This is why early surgical stabilization is considered in high-risk young athletes.

A is incorrect because dominant arm involvement has not been shown to be a significant independent predictor of recurrent instability.
B is incorrect because the duration of immobilization (e.g., 1 week vs. 3 weeks) has not been demonstrated to significantly alter recurrence rates after a first-time dislocation.
C is incorrect because female sex is not a strong risk factor; in fact, male sex is associated with higher recurrence rates.
E is incorrect because patients over 40 have lower recurrence rates (approximately 10–15%); their primary risk after dislocation is associated rotator cuff tear rather than recurrent instability.

questions.question:
A patient falls and presents with wrist pain; lateral radiograph shows the capitate displaced dorsally relative to the lunate, with the lunate remaining aligned with the radius. This is:
A) Perilunate dislocation
B) Lunate dislocation
C) Scaphoid fracture
D) Distal radius fracture
E) Midcarpal instability
questions.answer:
A)
In perilunate dislocation the lunate maintains its normal articulation with the radius while the remaining carpus (including the capitate) dislocates dorsally. Mayfield described the progressive sequence of ligamentous failure from radial to ulnar that produces this injury pattern. These injuries require urgent reduction and surgical repair; up to 25% are missed on initial presentation.

B is incorrect because in a lunate dislocation the lunate itself is displaced (typically volarly, producing the "spilled teacup" sign on the lateral view), rather than remaining aligned with the radius as described in this stem.
C is incorrect because a scaphoid fracture is a bony injury of the scaphoid without carpal malalignment; the stem describes dorsal displacement of the capitate relative to the lunate, indicating a ligamentous/dislocation pattern.
D is incorrect because a distal radius fracture involves a fracture of the distal radius, not carpal dislocation; the stem describes carpal malalignment with the radius uninvolved.
E is incorrect because midcarpal instability is a chronic condition characterized by a painful clunk during ulnar deviation, not an acute traumatic dorsal dislocation of the capitate relative to the lunate.

questions.question:
An asymptomatic, well-defined eccentric metaphyseal lesion of the distal femur in a 12-year-old with a sclerotic scalloped border and a bubbly appearance is best managed by:
A) Amputation
B) Chemotherapy
C) Observation, with consideration of curettage and grafting if it exceeds approximately 50% of the bone diameter
D) Radiation therapy
E) Immediate wide resection
questions.answer:
C)
Nonossifying fibroma (NOF) is a common benign developmental lesion of the metaphysis in children and adolescents, typically discovered incidentally. It characteristically appears as a well-defined, eccentric, bubbly lytic lesion with a sclerotic scalloped border. Most NOFs resolve spontaneously with skeletal maturity. Intervention (curettage and bone grafting) is reserved for lesions large enough to risk pathologic fracture, generally when they exceed approximately 50% of the transverse bone diameter or are longer than ~33 mm. Jaffe-Campanacci syndrome combines multiple NOFs with café-au-lait spots.

A is incorrect because amputation is a radical procedure reserved for aggressive or malignant tumors and is never indicated for a benign, asymptomatic NOF.
B is incorrect because NOF is a benign developmental lesion, not a malignancy, and chemotherapy has no role in its management.
D is incorrect because radiation therapy is not used for benign bone lesions such as NOF; it carries risks of radiation-induced sarcoma and is unnecessary here.
E is incorrect because immediate wide resection is reserved for malignant bone tumors; an asymptomatic NOF with classic imaging features requires only observation unless it is large enough to risk pathologic fracture.

questions.question:
A 48-year-old has neck pain radiating to the thumb with weakness of elbow flexion and a diminished brachioradialis reflex. The most likely level of disc herniation is:
A) C5-C6 affecting the C6 root
B) C7-T1 affecting the C8 root
C) C6-C7 affecting the C7 root
D) C3-C4 affecting the C4 root
E) C4-C5 affecting the C5 root
questions.answer:
A)
In the cervical spine each nerve root exits above its numbered pedicle, so a C5-C6 disc herniation compresses the C6 root. The C6 root supplies sensation to the thumb and radial forearm, contributes to elbow flexion (biceps, brachioradialis) and wrist extension, and mediates the brachioradialis reflex. All three findings in the stem — thumb-distribution pain, elbow flexion weakness, and diminished brachioradialis reflex — localize to C6.

B is incorrect because C7-T1 affects the C8 root, which supplies the intrinsic hand muscles and small-finger sensation, not the thumb or brachioradialis reflex. C is incorrect because C6-C7 affects the C7 root, which is associated with the triceps reflex, wrist flexion, finger extension, and middle-finger sensation. D is incorrect because C3-C4 affects the C4 root, which has no specific limb reflex and primarily involves neck/shoulder cape sensation, not the thumb. E is incorrect because C4-C5 affects the C5 root, which primarily weakens the deltoid and biceps and alters the biceps reflex, with sensory changes over the lateral arm/shoulder rather than the thumb.

questions.question:
Which condition is characterized by anterosuperior femoral head-neck junction bony prominence with a crossover sign absent and an alpha angle of 68 degrees?
A) Legg-Calve-Perthes disease
B) Cam-type femoroacetabular impingement
C) Pincer-type femoroacetabular impingement
D) Synovial chondromatosis
E) Developmental dysplasia
questions.answer:
B)
Cam-type femoroacetabular impingement is caused by an aspherical bony prominence at the anterosuperior femoral head-neck junction. An alpha angle above approximately 55 degrees (here 68 degrees) confirms the asphericity. The absence of a crossover sign rules out acetabular overcoverage (pincer morphology). Cam impingement produces shear-type chondrolabral damage, typically anterosuperior cartilage delamination, and is most common in young athletic males.

A is incorrect because Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease is an idiopathic childhood avascular necrosis of the femoral head that may produce secondary head deformity, but the stem describes a focal head-neck junction prominence with a classic cam alpha angle, not the fragmentation/collapse pattern of Perthes. C is incorrect because pincer-type FAI is characterized by acetabular overcoverage with positive crossover sign, posterior wall sign, or coxa profunda; the stem explicitly states the crossover sign is absent. D is incorrect because synovial chondromatosis is a synovial proliferative disorder producing multiple loose bodies within the joint, not a bony head-neck prominence with an elevated alpha angle. E is incorrect because developmental dysplasia of the hip involves acetabular undercoverage (decreased lateral center-edge angle, increased acetabular index), not a femoral head-neck junction bony prominence.

questions.question:
In a 55-year-old with medial compartment osteoarthritis, varus alignment, intact ACL, and full range of motion, which procedure best preserves the lateral and patellofemoral compartments?
A) Knee arthrodesis
B) Arthroscopic debridement
C) Medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty
D) Patellofemoral arthroplasty
E) Total knee arthroplasty
questions.answer:
C)
Medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) is the best option for isolated medial compartment osteoarthritis with varus alignment, an intact ACL, full range of motion, and no significant flexion contracture. It preserves the lateral and patellofemoral compartments, offers faster recovery, better kinematics, and lower morbidity than total knee arthroplasty, though with higher revision rates.

A is incorrect because knee arthrodesis eliminates all motion and is reserved for salvage situations (e.g., failed arthroplasty with infection), not for a patient with isolated medial compartment disease and preserved function.
B is incorrect because arthroscopic debridement has not been shown to provide lasting benefit for established osteoarthritis without discrete mechanical symptoms (e.g., a locked meniscal tear); it does not address the underlying cartilage loss.
D is incorrect because patellofemoral arthroplasty addresses isolated patellofemoral disease, not medial compartment osteoarthritis; the stem specifies the medial compartment is the affected area.
E is incorrect because total knee arthroplasty replaces all three compartments and is unnecessarily aggressive when only the medial compartment is involved and the patient meets UKA criteria (intact ACL, correctable deformity, good ROM).

questions.question:
Avascular necrosis after treatment of DDH is most associated with:
A) Early diagnosis
B) Female sex
C) Excessive abduction and forced positioning of the reduced hip
D) Use of ultrasound
E) Delayed weight bearing
questions.answer:
C)
Forceful or extreme abduction compresses the posterosuperior retinacular vessels (lateral ascending branches of the medial femoral circumflex artery) against the acetabular margin, producing osteonecrosis of the femoral head. The "human position" (flexion with moderate abduction, approximately 100° of flexion and 40–50° of abduction) minimizes this risk. Adductor tenotomy and preliminary traction have been used to reduce the force required for reduction. The Kalamchi and MacEwen classification describes the resulting growth disturbance patterns.

A is incorrect because early diagnosis actually reduces the risk of AVN by allowing gentler, less forceful reduction methods (e.g., Pavlik harness). B is incorrect because female sex is a risk factor for DDH itself but is not the factor most associated with AVN after treatment. D is incorrect because ultrasound monitoring helps guide safe treatment and does not cause AVN; it is protective by allowing early detection of instability and monitoring reduction. E is incorrect because delayed weight bearing has not been identified as a primary risk factor for AVN; it is the position and force applied during reduction that are most critical.

questions.question:
Which imaging modality is best for determining the intramedullary extent of a bone sarcoma and detecting skip lesions?
A) Bone scan
B) Ultrasound
C) Plain radiographs
D) PET-CT alone
E) MRI of the entire involved bone with contrast
questions.answer:
E)
MRI of the entire involved bone with contrast is the best modality for delineating intramedullary tumor extent, detecting skip lesions, and evaluating soft tissue extension and neurovascular involvement. The entire bone including both adjacent joints should be imaged.

A is incorrect because bone scan detects areas of increased skeletal metabolic activity and is useful for screening for distant skeletal metastases, but it lacks the spatial resolution to accurately define intramedullary extent or reliably detect small skip lesions.
B is incorrect because ultrasound has no role in evaluating intramedullary bone pathology; it cannot penetrate cortical bone.
C is incorrect because plain radiographs are the best initial study for characterizing a bone lesion and generating a differential diagnosis, but they cannot adequately assess marrow involvement or skip lesions.
D is incorrect because PET-CT is useful for systemic staging and detecting distant metastases but has inferior spatial resolution compared with MRI for defining local intramedullary extent and skip metastases.

questions.question:
A 14-month-old is diagnosed with a dislocated hip that fails closed reduction because of an inverted limbus and hourglass capsule. The blocking structures typically include:
A) Iliopsoas tendon, transverse acetabular ligament, pulvinar, ligamentum teres, and inverted labrum
B) Rectus femoris and gluteus medius
C) Piriformis and superior gemellus
D) Obturator externus alone
E) Sartorius and tensor fascia lata
questions.answer:
A)
Obstacles to closed reduction in DDH are classified as extra-articular (iliopsoas tendon crossing the capsule creating the hourglass constriction, tight adductors) and intra-articular (inverted limbus/labrum, hypertrophied ligamentum teres, pulvinar, and the transverse acetabular ligament). Open reduction through an anterior (Smith-Petersen) approach addresses all of these; a medial (Ludloff) approach risks injury to the medial femoral circumflex artery.

B is incorrect because the rectus femoris and gluteus medius are not recognized as primary blocking structures to closed reduction of a developmentally dislocated hip. C is incorrect because the piriformis and superior gemellus are posterior structures that do not constitute the classic intra- or extra-articular obstacles to reduction. D is incorrect because the obturator externus alone does not account for the multiple well-described blocking structures (both intra-articular and extra-articular) that prevent concentric reduction. E is incorrect because the sartorius and tensor fascia lata are superficial muscles that are not among the recognized obstacles to closed reduction in DDH.

questions.question:
In a 2-year-old with residual acetabular dysplasia after successful reduction, which procedure redirects the acetabulum by hinging on the flexible triradiate cartilage?
A) Shelf acetabuloplasty
B) Chiari osteotomy
C) Salter innominate osteotomy
D) Ganz periacetabular osteotomy
E) Varus derotational femoral osteotomy
questions.answer:
C)
The Salter innominate osteotomy is a redirectional procedure that makes a single cut from the sciatic notch to the AIIS and hinges on the flexible, open triradiate cartilage (and the symphysis pubis) to rotate the entire acetabulum anterolaterally, improving femoral head coverage. It is the classic choice for residual acetabular dysplasia in young children (18 months–6 years) with an open triradiate cartilage.

A is incorrect because a shelf acetabuloplasty is a salvage (augmentation) procedure that adds bone to the lateral acetabular rim to increase coverage; it does not redirect the native acetabulum.
B is incorrect because the Chiari osteotomy is a salvage medial-displacement osteotomy of the ilium that provides capsular interposition coverage; it does not redirect the true acetabulum and is not a first-line choice in a 2-year-old.
D is incorrect because the Ganz (Bernese) periacetabular osteotomy requires a closed or closing triradiate cartilage and is used in adolescents and adults; it makes multiple periacetabular cuts and does not hinge on the triradiate cartilage.
E is incorrect because a varus derotational femoral osteotomy is a femoral-side procedure that improves containment by redirecting the proximal femur; it does not address acetabular dysplasia directly.

questions.question:
A neurologically intact patient has an L1 burst fracture with 45% canal compromise, 20 degrees of kyphosis, and an intact posterior ligamentous complex. The most appropriate management is:
A) Bed rest for 8 weeks
B) Anterior corpectomy and fusion
C) Posterior long-segment fusion
D) Vertebroplasty
E) Bracing or early mobilization with close follow-up
questions.answer:
E)
In neurologically intact patients with stable burst fractures (intact PLC, kyphosis < ~30°), nonoperative management with bracing or early mobilization yields outcomes equivalent to surgery. Randomized trials (e.g., Wood et al.) demonstrate no significant difference in long-term outcomes between operative and nonoperative treatment in this population. Canal compromise remodels over time and does not predict neurologic deterioration in intact patients.

A is incorrect because prolonged bed rest for 8 weeks is unnecessarily restrictive, promotes deconditioning and complications (DVT, pneumonia, pressure sores), and is not supported by current evidence when early mobilization is safe.
B is incorrect because anterior corpectomy and fusion is an aggressive surgical intervention reserved for unstable fractures with significant anterior column destruction, neurologic deficit, or PLC disruption — none of which mandate surgery here.
C is incorrect because posterior long-segment fusion is indicated for unstable injuries (e.g., PLC disruption, progressive deformity, neurologic compromise); a stable burst fracture with intact PLC does not warrant instrumented fusion.
D is incorrect because vertebroplasty is primarily used for painful osteoporotic compression fractures, not acute traumatic burst fractures; it does not address the fracture morphology and is not standard of care in this setting.

questions.question:
A polyethylene tibial insert is loaded with a constant force and slowly deforms over several hours. This behavior is best described as:
A) Creep
B) Anisotropy
C) Fatigue failure
D) Stress relaxation
E) Hysteresis
questions.answer:
A)
Creep is the progressive, time-dependent deformation of a material under a constant applied load. Polyethylene tibial inserts are particularly susceptible to creep, which contributes to dimensional changes and wear over time.

B is incorrect because anisotropy describes a material whose mechanical properties vary depending on the direction of loading (e.g., cortical bone is stronger along its longitudinal axis); it is not a time-dependent deformation behavior.
C is incorrect because fatigue failure results from repetitive cyclic loading that causes crack initiation and propagation, ultimately leading to fracture — not slow deformation under a single constant load.
D is incorrect because stress relaxation is the decrease in internal stress over time when a material is held at a constant strain (deformation), which is the converse of creep; examples include halo pin loosening and the mechanism behind serial casting.
E is incorrect because hysteresis refers to the energy lost (as heat) during a loading-unloading cycle, represented by the area between the loading and unloading curves on a stress-strain diagram; it does not describe progressive deformation under constant load.

questions.question:
A 74-year-old woman has a painful osteoporotic L1 compression fracture 3 weeks after a fall, with no neurologic deficit. Regarding vertebral augmentation, the best summary of current evidence is:
A) It should be performed on the day of injury in every patient
B) Randomized data are conflicting, with several sham-controlled trials showing no significant benefit, so it is generally reserved for refractory pain after a trial of nonoperative care
C) It restores normal vertebral height in all cases
D) It is clearly superior to nonoperative care in all randomized trials
E) It reliably prevents adjacent-level fracture
questions.answer:
B)
Two influential sham-controlled trials (Buchbinder 2009, Kallmes 2009) found no significant benefit of vertebroplasty over a sham procedure, whereas other trials (e.g., VERTOS II, VAPOUR) and registry data reported meaningful early pain relief, particularly in acute fractures with marrow edema on MRI and severe refractory pain. Consensus practice reserves augmentation for patients who fail a period of analgesia, bracing, and mobilization.

A is incorrect because vertebral augmentation is not indicated on the day of injury in every patient; an initial trial of nonoperative management (analgesia, bracing, mobilization) is standard, and patient selection based on refractory pain and imaging findings is essential.
C is incorrect because vertebral augmentation (vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty) does not reliably restore normal vertebral height in all cases; kyphoplasty may achieve partial height restoration, but complete restoration is uncommon and not guaranteed.
D is incorrect because randomized data are conflicting — several sham-controlled trials showed no significant benefit over placebo, so it cannot be stated that augmentation is clearly superior in all trials.
E is incorrect because vertebral augmentation does not reliably prevent adjacent-level fractures; in fact, cement augmentation may alter load transfer and is a recognized concern for increasing the risk of adjacent-level fractures.

questions.question:
Which nerve is most commonly injured in an extension-type supracondylar humerus fracture with posterolateral displacement?
A) Radial nerve
B) Anterior interosseous nerve
C) Ulnar nerve
D) Median nerve proper
E) Musculocutaneous nerve
questions.answer:
B)
The anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) is the most commonly injured nerve in extension-type supracondylar humerus fractures with posterolateral displacement. The AIN is a pure motor branch of the median nerve; its injury produces inability to make an "OK" sign (weakness of flexor pollicis longus, flexor digitorum profundus to the index finger, and pronator quadratus) without any sensory deficit. This is the most frequently tested nerve injury pattern for this fracture type on board examinations.

A is incorrect because the radial nerve is more commonly injured with posteromedial displacement of the distal fragment, not posterolateral displacement. C is incorrect because the ulnar nerve is most at risk in flexion-type supracondylar fractures, not extension-type. D is incorrect because while the median nerve proper can be injured, the AIN (its branch) is more commonly affected; median nerve proper injury would produce sensory deficits in the hand, which is not the classic presentation described. E is incorrect because the musculocutaneous nerve is not at significant risk in supracondylar fractures.

questions.question:
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity from bupivacaine is best treated with:
A) Intravenous lipid emulsion
B) Flumazenil
C) Sodium bicarbonate alone
D) Naloxone
E) Protamine sulfate
questions.answer:
A)
Intravenous 20% lipid emulsion is the specific treatment for local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), thought to act as a "lipid sink" sequestering lipophilic drug and by improving cardiac metabolism. Bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic common local anesthetic because of its avid sodium channel binding. Management also includes airway support, seizure control with benzodiazepines, and avoidance of high-dose epinephrine and vasopressin.

B is incorrect because flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist and has no role in treating local anesthetic toxicity. C is incorrect because sodium bicarbonate alone does not address the lipophilic sodium-channel blockade central to bupivacaine cardiotoxicity; it may be a temporizing adjunct but is not definitive treatment. D is incorrect because naloxone is an opioid antagonist and does not reverse local anesthetic toxicity. E is incorrect because protamine sulfate is used to reverse heparin anticoagulation and has no role in LAST management.

questions.question:
The most common long-term complication of a massive segmental endoprosthesis after limb salvage is:
A) Heterotopic ossification
B) Infection and aseptic loosening with eventual mechanical failure
C) Dislocation only
D) Nerve palsy
E) Tumor recurrence within the implant
questions.answer:
B)
Endoprostheses provide rapid restoration of function and immediate stability, but long-term survivorship is limited by aseptic loosening, mechanical failure (bushing wear, stem fracture, hinge breakage), and periprosthetic infection. Infection rates are higher than in conventional arthroplasty owing to large implant surface area, extensive soft-tissue dissection, and chemotherapy-related immunosuppression. These mechanical and infectious complications are the leading reasons for revision and are the most common long-term problems.

A is incorrect because heterotopic ossification can occur but is not the most common long-term complication of segmental endoprostheses. C is incorrect because dislocation (particularly of proximal femoral replacements) can occur but is far less frequent than aseptic loosening and infection as a long-term issue. D is incorrect because nerve palsy is an acute perioperative complication, not a characteristic long-term complication. E is incorrect because local tumor recurrence is related to surgical margins and tumor biology, not to the implant itself; it is not the most common long-term implant-related complication.

questions.question:
Ultrasonography of an infant hip demonstrates a Graf alpha angle of 48 degrees. This value indicates:
A) An uninterpretable study
B) A normal, mature hip
C) A dislocated hip by definition
D) A dysplastic acetabulum, since the alpha angle should exceed 60 degrees
E) Acetabular overcoverage
questions.answer:
D)
The Graf alpha angle measures the bony acetabular roof on ultrasound. Values above 60 degrees are considered mature and normal. An alpha angle of 43–49 degrees (Graf Type IIc/IId range) indicates significant dysplasia, confirming that 48 degrees represents a dysplastic acetabulum. Below 43 degrees indicates severe dysplasia or dislocation. Findings must be interpreted with the infant's age because of physiologic immaturity in the first weeks of life.

A is incorrect because the study is interpretable — an alpha angle of 48 degrees is a valid, measurable result that can be classified within the Graf system.
B is incorrect because a normal, mature hip requires an alpha angle of at least 60 degrees; 48 degrees falls well below this threshold.
C is incorrect because dislocation (Graf Type III/IV) is characterized by alpha angles below 43 degrees with severe deficiency of the bony roof and displacement of the femoral head; 48 degrees indicates dysplasia, not frank dislocation by definition.
E is incorrect because acetabular overcoverage (coxa profunda/protrusio) is not a concept assessed by the Graf alpha angle in infant hip ultrasound; moreover, overcoverage would imply excessive bony coverage, the opposite of what a low alpha angle indicates.

questions.question:
On an AP pelvis radiograph of an infant, the femoral head epiphysis should normally lie in which quadrant formed by the Hilgenreiner and Perkin lines?
A) Inferomedial
B) Inferolateral
C) Directly on the intersection
D) Superolateral
E) Superomedial
questions.answer:
A)
Hilgenreiner's line is drawn horizontally through both triradiate cartilages, and Perkin's line is drawn perpendicular to it at the lateral edge of each acetabulum. These two lines divide the area around the hip into four quadrants. In a normal infant hip, the proximal femoral metaphysis (or ossific nucleus, once it appears) should lie in the inferomedial quadrant. Displacement out of this quadrant suggests hip dysplasia or dislocation.

B is incorrect because the inferolateral quadrant indicates lateral subluxation of the femoral head, a sign of developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH). C is incorrect because the femoral head should not sit directly on the intersection; it should be clearly within the inferomedial quadrant. D is incorrect because the superolateral quadrant indicates a frank dislocation of the hip. E is incorrect because the superomedial quadrant would imply abnormal superior migration without lateral displacement, which is not the normal position.

questions.question:
Which injury is characterized by widening between the first and second metatarsal bases with a fleck sign at the base of the second metatarsal?
A) Sesamoid fracture
B) Jones fracture
C) Lisfranc (tarsometatarsal) injury
D) Chopart dislocation
E) Navicular stress fracture
questions.answer:
C)
The Lisfranc ligament runs from the medial cuneiform to the base of the second metatarsal, which is recessed into a mortise between the cuneiforms and serves as the keystone of the arch. A fleck sign represents an avulsion fragment of this ligament at the base of the second metatarsal, and widening of the first–second intermetatarsal interval on weight-bearing views confirms the diagnosis. Displacement greater than 2 mm warrants anatomic reduction with rigid fixation or primary arthrodesis of the medial column.

A is incorrect because a sesamoid fracture involves the hallux sesamoids beneath the first metatarsal head and does not produce widening at the first–second metatarsal bases or a fleck sign at the second metatarsal base. B is incorrect because a Jones fracture occurs at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction of the proximal fifth metatarsal and has no association with first–second intermetatarsal widening or a fleck sign. D is incorrect because a Chopart dislocation involves the midtarsal (talonavicular and calcaneocuboid) joints, not the tarsometatarsal articulation, and does not produce a fleck sign at the second metatarsal base. E is incorrect because a navicular stress fracture presents with dorsal midfoot pain and is located in the navicular body, not at the tarsometatarsal junction, and does not cause first–second metatarsal base widening.

questions.question:
Which finding on radiographs is most predictive of the need for a femoral shortening osteotomy at the time of open reduction in an older child with DDH?
A) High riding dislocation with proximal migration, in a child older than approximately 2-3 years
B) Bilateral involvement
C) Presence of an ossific nucleus
D) Mild acetabular index elevation
E) Age under 12 months
questions.answer:
A)
Femoral shortening osteotomy is indicated when open reduction of a DDH hip would require excessive force to seat the femoral head, risking avascular necrosis. This situation arises most commonly in children older than approximately 2–3 years who have a high-riding, proximally migrated femoral head, because the soft-tissue contracture and distance the head must travel are greatest. Shortening the femur decreases reduction pressure and the risk of osteonecrosis.

B is incorrect because bilateral involvement alone does not predict the need for femoral shortening; it is the degree of proximal migration and the child's age that determine the need. C is incorrect because the presence of an ossific nucleus is a normal developmental finding and does not itself indicate the need for shortening. D is incorrect because mild acetabular index elevation is common in DDH and is addressed by pelvic osteotomy or remodeling, not femoral shortening. E is incorrect because children under 12 months are typically treated with closed reduction and a Pavlik harness or spica cast; femoral shortening is rarely if ever needed at this young age because soft-tissue contracture is minimal.

questions.question:
A 6-year-old has a Gartland type III extension supracondylar humerus fracture. Regarding pin configuration, current evidence best supports:
A) A single lateral pin
B) Crossed medial and lateral pins in every case
C) Medial-entry pins alone
D) Two or three lateral-entry divergent pins, which provide adequate stability while avoiding iatrogenic ulnar nerve injury
E) Closed reduction and casting in hyperflexion without pins
questions.answer:
D)
Biomechanical and clinical studies show that two or three lateral-entry pins, placed divergently with maximal separation at the fracture site, engaging both columns and the far cortex, provide stability comparable to crossed pins for most Gartland type III supracondylar humerus fractures while avoiding the 2–6% risk of iatrogenic ulnar nerve injury associated with medial pin placement. If a medial pin is deemed necessary for very unstable or flexion-type patterns, it should be placed with the elbow extended through a small incision to protect the ulnar nerve.

A is incorrect because a single lateral pin does not provide adequate rotational stability for a completely displaced type III fracture. B is incorrect because, although crossed pins provide excellent biomechanical stability, routine use of a medial pin in every case exposes the patient to unnecessary risk of iatrogenic ulnar nerve injury when lateral-only configurations can achieve comparable fixation. C is incorrect because medial-entry pins alone risk ulnar nerve injury during placement and do not offer a biomechanical advantage over lateral-entry pins. E is incorrect because a displaced Gartland type III fracture is inherently unstable and requires percutaneous pinning after closed reduction; casting in hyperflexion alone risks loss of reduction and may compromise the brachial artery by kinking it in the antecubital fossa.

questions.question:
Ultrasound screening for DDH is most appropriate at which age, and why?
A) At 12 months
B) At birth, since findings are always definitive
C) At 6 months, once the ossific nucleus is present
D) Ultrasound has no role
E) At approximately 4-6 weeks, because physiologic laxity resolves and the femoral head remains largely cartilaginous
questions.answer:
E)
Ultrasound screening for DDH is optimally performed at approximately 4–6 weeks of age. Before this time, physiologic neonatal ligamentous laxity leads to a high false-positive rate. Ultrasound remains the imaging study of choice until the ossific nucleus of the femoral head appears (typically 4–6 months), after which radiographs become more informative. Standard measurements include the Graf alpha angle (bony acetabular roof; normal ≥60°), beta angle, and percent femoral head coverage (normal ≥50%).

A is incorrect because at 12 months the ossific nucleus is well established and radiographs (not ultrasound) are the preferred imaging modality.
B is incorrect because ultrasound at birth has a high false-positive rate due to physiologic ligamentous laxity; findings at birth are not always definitive.
C is incorrect because by 6 months the ossific nucleus is typically present, making radiographs more useful than ultrasound; the optimal ultrasound window is earlier.
D is incorrect because ultrasound plays a critical role in DDH screening and diagnosis, particularly between 4–6 weeks and 4–6 months of age when the femoral head is largely cartilaginous.

questions.question:
Which of the following is the strongest risk factor for developmental dysplasia of the hip?
A) Cesarean delivery
B) Male sex
C) Breech presentation
D) Birth weight under 2,500 g
E) Twin gestation
questions.answer:
C)
The classic risk factors for DDH are breech presentation, female sex, positive family history, and firstborn status, with breech presentation carrying the greatest single risk (roughly 2–20% depending on the series). Associated conditions include torticollis and metatarsus adductus. The left hip is involved more often because the usual left occiput anterior intrauterine position adducts the left hip against the maternal sacrum.

A is incorrect because cesarean delivery is not an established independent risk factor for DDH; vaginal delivery (especially breech vaginal delivery) is more commonly associated. B is incorrect because female sex, not male sex, is a well-recognized risk factor, likely related to greater ligamentous laxity from maternal relaxin. D is incorrect because low birth weight has not been shown to be a strong risk factor for DDH; in fact, macrosomia with intrauterine crowding is more concerning. E is incorrect because while twin gestation may contribute to intrauterine crowding, it is a weaker risk factor than breech presentation.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old woman with metastatic breast carcinoma has extensive acetabular destruction with loss of the medial wall and superior dome, and cannot bear weight. The most appropriate reconstruction is:
A) Standard uncemented acetabular component with screws
B) Harrington-type reconstruction transferring load to intact ilium with antegrade pins or screws and a cemented acetabular component
C) Curettage and cement alone with no fixation
D) Girdlestone resection as first-line treatment
E) Hemiarthroplasty
questions.answer:
B)
The Harrington principle addresses extensive acetabular metastatic destruction by transferring load from the deficient periacetabular bone to intact ilium using antegrade threaded pins or screws augmented with cement, supporting a cemented acetabular component as part of a total hip reconstruction. This technique is specifically designed for Harrington class III defects with loss of the medial wall and superior dome.

A is incorrect because a standard uncemented acetabular component relies on biologic ingrowth, which cannot occur in tumor-involved or irradiated bone, and there is insufficient host bone stock remaining for stable press-fit fixation. C is incorrect because curettage and cement alone without structural fixation cannot restore the load-bearing arc when both the medial wall and superior dome are destroyed; the construct would fail rapidly under physiologic loads. D is incorrect because Girdlestone resection (excision arthroplasty) as a first-line treatment leaves the patient with a flail hip and significant functional impairment; it is reserved as a salvage procedure. E is incorrect because a hemiarthroplasty requires an intact acetabulum to articulate against; with extensive acetabular destruction, there is no socket to support the prosthetic femoral head, and central migration would occur.

questions.question:
When performing a biopsy of a thoracic vertebral body lesion, which approach limits contamination and provides safe access to the vertebral body?
A) Transdural approach
B) Open posterior laminectomy in all cases
C) Anterior transthoracic approach for all lesions
D) Transpedicular approach under CT or fluoroscopic guidance
E) Percutaneous approach through the paraspinal muscles on the contralateral side
questions.answer:
D)
The transpedicular route provides a corridor from posterior to the vertebral body that is contained within bone, limits contamination of the paraspinal soft tissues and epidural space, avoids the great vessels and pleura, and can be performed percutaneously under CT or fluoroscopic guidance. The tract should be planned so that it can be incorporated into a definitive posterior approach if resection becomes necessary.

A is incorrect because a transdural approach violates the dura and risks cerebrospinal fluid leak, neural injury, and tumor seeding of the intradural space.
B is incorrect because open posterior laminectomy is not appropriate for all cases; it does not provide direct access to the vertebral body, risks wide soft-tissue contamination, and may destabilize the spine without addressing the anterior column lesion.
C is incorrect because an anterior transthoracic approach is a major procedure that requires thoracotomy, risks contamination of the thoracic cavity and great vessels, and is not necessary when a less invasive transpedicular route can safely access the vertebral body.
E is incorrect because a percutaneous approach through the contralateral paraspinal muscles does not follow the transpedicular corridor, unnecessarily contaminates additional soft-tissue planes, and creates a biopsy tract on the wrong side that would be difficult to excise during definitive surgery.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman has chronic distal radioulnar joint instability and arthritis after a malunited distal radius fracture, with preserved radiocarpal cartilage. Which salvage procedure preserves forearm rotation by creating a pseudarthrosis of the distal ulna?
A) Ulnar shortening osteotomy
B) Darrach resection
C) Proximal row carpectomy
D) Sauve-Kapandji procedure
E) Total wrist arthrodesis
questions.answer:
D)
The Sauvé-Kapandji procedure fuses the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) and creates a proximal pseudarthrosis of the ulna, thereby preserving forearm rotation while maintaining the ulnar head as a buttress against ulnar translation of the carpus. It is particularly suited for younger, higher-demand patients with DRUJ arthritis and instability.

A is incorrect because ulnar shortening osteotomy addresses ulnar-positive variance and ulnocarpal impaction but does not create a pseudarthrosis and does not directly address DRUJ arthritis. B is incorrect because the Darrach resection excises the distal ulna entirely rather than creating a pseudarthrosis; it can lead to ulnar translation of the carpus and painful radioulnar convergence, especially in active patients. C is incorrect because proximal row carpectomy is a salvage procedure for radiocarpal or midcarpal arthritis (e.g., SLAC/SNAC wrist) and does not address DRUJ pathology. E is incorrect because total wrist arthrodesis eliminates all wrist and forearm motion and does not specifically create a pseudarthrosis to preserve rotation; it is reserved for pan-articular wrist destruction.

questions.question:
A 15-year-old has 6 weeks of increasing tibial pain with night symptoms, a mild fever, and a radiolucent lesion with surrounding sclerosis in the distal tibial metaphysis. Aspiration yields purulent material. The most likely diagnosis is:
A) Osteoid osteoma
B) Brodie abscess
C) Ewing sarcoma
D) Chondroblastoma
E) Osteosarcoma
questions.answer:
B)
A Brodie abscess is a form of subacute osteomyelitis that presents as a well-defined radiolucent lesion with surrounding sclerosis, most commonly in the metaphysis of the tibia in children and adolescents. The clinical picture of weeks of progressive pain, low-grade fever, and aspiration of purulent material confirms an infectious etiology. MRI may show a serpiginous tract extending toward the physis ("penumbra sign"). Treatment consists of surgical debridement and targeted antibiotics.

A is incorrect because osteoid osteoma presents with a small (<1.5 cm) nidus with surrounding sclerosis and dramatic relief with NSAIDs; it would not yield purulent material on aspiration and does not cause fever.
C is incorrect because Ewing sarcoma typically presents in the diaphysis with a permeative/moth-eaten pattern and onion-skin periosteal reaction; aspiration would yield small round blue cells, not pus.
D is incorrect because chondroblastoma is an epiphyseal lesion (not metaphyseal) in skeletally immature patients and would not produce purulent aspirate.
E is incorrect because osteosarcoma typically presents in the metaphysis with an aggressive appearance (Codman triangle, sunburst periosteal reaction) and would yield malignant osteoid-producing cells on biopsy, not purulent material.

questions.question:
Which soft tissue sarcomas are most likely to metastasize to lymph nodes?
A) Desmoid tumor
B) Rhabdomyosarcoma, epithelioid sarcoma, synovial sarcoma, clear cell sarcoma, and angiosarcoma
C) Liposarcoma and undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma
D) Myxoma and lipoma
E) Schwannoma
questions.answer:
B)
Most sarcomas metastasize hematogenously to the lungs, but a small group has a meaningful rate of lymphatic (nodal) spread, remembered by the mnemonic RACES: Rhabdomyosarcoma, Angiosarcoma, Clear cell sarcoma, Epithelioid sarcoma, and Synovial sarcoma. Regional nodal assessment (including sentinel lymph node biopsy consideration) is warranted in these histologies.

A is incorrect because desmoid tumors (aggressive fibromatosis) are locally aggressive but do not metastasize at all — neither hematogenously nor to lymph nodes.
C is incorrect because liposarcoma and undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (UPS/MFH) typically metastasize hematogenously to the lungs; they do not have a significant propensity for lymph node metastasis.
D is incorrect because myxoma and lipoma are benign soft tissue tumors and do not metastasize.
E is incorrect because schwannoma is a benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor and does not metastasize.

questions.question:
Which intervention has the strongest evidence for reducing the incidence of noncontact anterior cruciate ligament injury in female athletes?
A) Restricting participation to noncutting sports
B) Preseason MRI screening
C) Oral supplementation with collagen
D) Neuromuscular training programs emphasizing landing mechanics, core control, and plyometrics
E) Prophylactic bracing
questions.answer:
D)
Structured neuromuscular training programs that combine plyometrics, strengthening, balance, core stability, and feedback on landing and cutting technique have the strongest Level-I evidence for reducing noncontact ACL injury rates in female athletes, with the greatest benefit when performed consistently in both the preseason and in-season.

A is incorrect because restricting sport participation is not a practical or evidence-based preventive strategy; the goal is to modify neuromuscular risk factors, not eliminate athletic activity.
B is incorrect because preseason MRI screening has no role in predicting or preventing noncontact ACL injuries; it does not address the modifiable biomechanical risk factors.
C is incorrect because oral collagen supplementation has no high-quality evidence supporting a reduction in ACL injury incidence.
