D is incorrect because osteoid osteoma presents as a small (<2 cm) painful lesion with a radiolucent nidus and surrounding sclerosis, classically causing night pain relieved by NSAIDs, not a painless pedunculated prominence. E is incorrect because parosteal osteosarcoma is a surface-based low-grade malignancy that appears as a dense, lobulated mass on the posterior distal femur without true medullary continuity (at least early on) and lacks the characteristic cartilage-capped pedunculated morphology of an osteochondroma.

questions.question:
Adjacent segment disease after lumbar fusion is most associated with:
A) Preserved sagittal balance
B) Fusion in kyphosis with iatrogenic facet violation at the adjacent level
C) Shorter fusion constructs with normal alignment
D) Use of autograft rather than allograft
E) Younger patient age
questions.answer:
B)
Risk factors for adjacent segment disease (ASD) after lumbar fusion include malalignment (fusion in relative kyphosis with loss of lumbar lordosis), iatrogenic violation of the adjacent facet joint by screw heads or dissection, longer constructs, preexisting adjacent-level degeneration, and older age with osteoporosis. Careful screw trajectory and preservation of the supra-adjacent facet and posterior ligaments reduce risk.

A is incorrect because preserved sagittal balance is protective against ASD; loss of lordosis and sagittal imbalance are the risk factors. C is incorrect because shorter fusion constructs with normal alignment are associated with lower, not higher, rates of ASD. D is incorrect because the choice of graft material (autograft vs. allograft) is not a recognized major risk factor for ASD; the key biomechanical drivers are alignment, construct length, and facet violation. E is incorrect because younger patient age is not a risk factor for ASD; older age (with associated osteoporosis and preexisting degeneration) is the recognized demographic risk factor.

questions.question:
A patient treated for SCFE develops progressive joint space narrowing to less than 3 mm with painful loss of motion 6 months after fixation. The most likely diagnosis is:
A) Femoroacetabular impingement
B) Septic arthritis
C) Chondrolysis
D) Normal postoperative change
E) Osteonecrosis
questions.answer:
C)
Chondrolysis is acute loss of articular cartilage producing joint space narrowing below 3 mm, pain, and progressive stiffness within months of SCFE treatment. It has classically been linked to unrecognized transient penetration of the joint by hardware, though it also occurs without instrumentation. Treatment includes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medication, physical therapy to preserve motion, and removal of any offending hardware; many cases partially recover.

A is incorrect because femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) can cause pain and limited motion after SCFE but does not produce acute diffuse joint space narrowing to <3 mm at 6 months; it causes gradual labral/cartilage damage at the cam lesion over a longer time course.
B is incorrect because septic arthritis would present with systemic signs of infection (fever, elevated inflammatory markers, joint effusion with purulent aspirate) rather than insidious progressive joint space narrowing and stiffness.
D is incorrect because progressive joint space narrowing to <3 mm with painful loss of motion is not a normal postoperative finding after in-situ pinning of SCFE.
E is incorrect because osteonecrosis (AVN) of the femoral head initially presents with femoral head collapse and subchondral changes (crescent sign, sclerosis) rather than diffuse, uniform joint space narrowing; joint space is typically preserved early in AVN.

questions.question:
An eccentric, lytic, subchondral lesion extending to the articular surface in the distal femur of a 30-year-old with a nonsclerotic border most likely represents:
A) Nonossifying fibroma
B) Enchondroma
C) Osteoid osteoma
D) Chondroblastoma
E) Giant cell tumor of bone
questions.answer:
E)
Giant cell tumor (GCT) of bone arises in the epiphysis/metaphysis of skeletally mature patients (peak age 20–40), most often about the knee and distal radius. It is characteristically eccentric, lytic, and extends to the subchondral bone with a nonsclerotic (poorly defined) border. Histology shows uniformly distributed multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells with mononuclear stromal cells that overexpress RANKL. Treatment is extended curettage with adjuvant (phenol, liquid nitrogen, argon beam) and cement or graft. Denosumab is used for unresectable or complex lesions. Benign pulmonary metastases occur in 2–5%.

A is incorrect because nonossifying fibroma (NOF) is a metaphyseal, eccentric, cortically based lesion with a well-defined sclerotic (scalloped) border, typically found incidentally in children and adolescents — it does not extend to the articular surface or arise in the epiphysis.

B is incorrect because enchondroma is a central (not eccentric) medullary lesion with characteristic stippled or ring-and-arc calcifications (chondroid matrix), most common in the small bones of the hands, and it has a well-defined sclerotic margin.

C is incorrect because osteoid osteoma is a small (<1.5 cm) cortical or medullary lesion with a central nidus surrounded by dense reactive sclerosis, presenting with night pain relieved by NSAIDs — it does not produce a large lytic subchondral lesion.

D is incorrect because chondroblastoma is an epiphyseal lesion but occurs in skeletally immature patients (open physes), has a thin sclerotic rim, and shows characteristic chicken-wire calcification on histology — the nonsclerotic border and age of 30 favor GCT.

questions.question:
Glenoid bone loss exceeding approximately what percentage generally warrants bone augmentation (Latarjet or bone block) rather than isolated soft tissue Bankart repair?
A) 5%
B) 20-25%
C) 40%
D) 50%
E) 10%
questions.answer:
B)
Critical glenoid bone loss has traditionally been set near 20–25%, though some data suggest subcritical loss of 13.5% already compromises outcomes. The glenoid track concept evaluates the combined bipolar (glenoid plus Hill-Sachs) lesion: an off-track Hill-Sachs engages the glenoid rim and typically requires bony augmentation or remplissage. The Latarjet procedure works through bony augmentation, the sling effect (conjoint tendon), and capsular repair.

A is incorrect because 5% glenoid bone loss is minimal and does not compromise the stability provided by an isolated soft-tissue Bankart repair. E is incorrect because 10% bone loss is generally subcritical and can typically be managed with arthroscopic Bankart repair alone. C is incorrect because 40% bone loss far exceeds the threshold; bone augmentation is indicated well before this level of loss. D is incorrect because 50% glenoid bone loss is a massive deficiency far beyond the recognized critical threshold and would represent an extreme scenario rarely encountered in clinical practice.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old restrained passenger has neck pain and cranial nerve deficits after a high-speed collision. CT shows a basion-dental interval of 14 mm. This finding indicates:
A) Atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation
B) A normal measurement in an adult
C) Occipitocervical dissociation requiring halo or occipitocervical fusion and avoidance of traction
D) A type I odontoid fracture
E) A stable ligamentous sprain
questions.answer:
C)
A basion-dental interval (BDI) greater than 10–12 mm in an adult indicates occipitocervical dissociation (OCD), a highly unstable and frequently fatal ligamentous injury. The clinical picture—high-energy mechanism, neck pain, and cranial nerve deficits—is classic. MRI confirms ligamentous disruption. Traction is absolutely contraindicated because it can produce catastrophic brainstem distraction; treatment is halo immobilization or, more commonly, occipitocervical fusion.

A is incorrect because atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation presents with torticollis and rotational malalignment at C1-C2, not with a widened basion-dental interval of 14 mm. B is incorrect because the normal BDI in adults is ≤12 mm; 14 mm is abnormal and pathologic. D is incorrect because a type I odontoid fracture is an avulsion of the dens tip and would not produce a widened BDI of this magnitude or cranial nerve deficits. E is incorrect because a BDI of 14 mm with cranial nerve deficits represents a highly unstable injury (OCD), not a stable ligamentous sprain.

questions.question:
Tranexamic acid reduces perioperative blood loss by which mechanism?
A) Competitive inhibition of plasminogen binding to fibrin
B) Direct activation of factor X
C) Vasoconstriction of arterioles
D) Vitamin K-dependent clotting factor synthesis
E) Platelet aggregation via GP IIb/IIIa
questions.answer:
A)
Tranexamic acid (TXA) is a synthetic lysine analogue that competitively binds the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen, preventing its attachment to fibrin. This inhibits fibrinolysis and stabilizes formed clot, thereby reducing perioperative blood loss and transfusion requirements. In major trauma, TXA is most effective when administered within 3 hours of injury.

B is incorrect because TXA has no direct effect on the coagulation cascade factors; it does not activate factor X. C is incorrect because TXA does not cause vasoconstriction; its mechanism is antifibrinolytic, not vascular. D is incorrect because vitamin K–dependent clotting factor synthesis is the mechanism of vitamin K supplementation (and the target of warfarin reversal), not TXA. E is incorrect because platelet aggregation via the GP IIb/IIIa receptor is the target of antiplatelet agents (e.g., abciximab); TXA does not act on platelet glycoprotein receptors.

questions.question:
Multiple myeloma is best identified by which combination of findings?
A) Sclerotic lesions with elevated PSA
B) Blastic vertebral lesions with normal labs
C) Punched-out lytic lesions that are often bone-scan negative, with monoclonal protein on serum/urine electrophoresis and marrow plasmacytosis
D) Positive bone scan with elevated alkaline phosphatase
E) Positive rheumatoid factor
questions.answer:
C)
Myeloma lesions are purely lytic with little osteoblastic reaction, so technetium bone scans are frequently falsely negative and a skeletal survey or whole-body MRI/PET is preferred. Diagnostic features include a monoclonal spike on SPEP/UPEP, Bence-Jones proteinuria, marrow plasmacytosis, anemia, hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, and elevated ESR. Treatment is systemic therapy with bisphosphonates or denosumab, radiation for symptomatic lesions, and stabilization of impending fractures.

A is incorrect because sclerotic (blastic) lesions with elevated PSA suggest prostate carcinoma metastases, not myeloma, which produces purely lytic lesions. B is incorrect because myeloma does not produce blastic vertebral lesions; its lesions are lytic, and laboratory values are characteristically abnormal (monoclonal protein, elevated ESR, hypercalcemia, anemia). D is incorrect because myeloma lesions lack osteoblastic activity and are frequently bone-scan negative; a positive bone scan with elevated alkaline phosphatase is more typical of blastic metastases (e.g., prostate) or Paget disease. E is incorrect because rheumatoid factor is associated with rheumatoid arthritis and certain autoimmune conditions, not with multiple myeloma.

questions.question:
X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets is caused by a defect that results in:
A) Elevated FGF23 with renal phosphate wasting
B) Deficient 1-alpha-hydroxylation of vitamin D
C) Deficient carbonic anhydrase II
D) Absent vitamin D receptor
E) Defective type I collagen synthesis
questions.answer:
A)
X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets results from a loss-of-function mutation in the PHEX gene, leading to elevated circulating FGF23. Excess FGF23 inhibits renal sodium-phosphate cotransporters (causing phosphate wasting) and suppresses renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, reducing 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D production. Patients present with hypophosphatemia, normal calcium, and normal or low PTH. Treatment includes oral phosphate supplementation with calcitriol, or burosumab (anti-FGF23 monoclonal antibody).

B is incorrect because deficient 1-alpha-hydroxylation of vitamin D describes vitamin D-dependent rickets type I (pseudovitamin D-deficiency rickets), caused by CYP27B1 mutations. C is incorrect because deficient carbonic anhydrase II causes a form of osteopetrosis with renal tubular acidosis, not hypophosphatemic rickets. D is incorrect because an absent or dysfunctional vitamin D receptor describes vitamin D-dependent rickets type II (hereditary vitamin D-resistant rickets). E is incorrect because defective type I collagen synthesis describes osteogenesis imperfecta, not rickets.

questions.question:
A 14-year-old has pain and stiffness at the second metatarsal head with radiographs showing flattening, sclerosis, and joint space widening. This condition is:
A) Kohler disease
B) Morton neuroma
C) Freiberg infraction, an osteonecrosis of the second metatarsal head
D) Iselin disease
E) Sever disease
questions.answer:
C)
Freiberg infraction is osteonecrosis of a lesser metatarsal head, most often the second, occurring predominantly in adolescent girls. It is thought to result from repetitive microtrauma to the subchondral bone. Radiographic findings include flattening, sclerosis, and widening of the metatarsophalangeal joint space. Early treatment is offloading and immobilization; refractory cases may require debridement, dorsiflexion osteotomy of the metatarsal head, or interpositional arthroplasty.

A is incorrect because Köhler disease is osteonecrosis of the tarsal navicular, typically presenting in younger children (ages 3–7) with midfoot pain, not at the metatarsal head.
B is incorrect because Morton neuroma is a compressive neuropathy of the interdigital nerve (most commonly in the third web space) causing burning/tingling pain; it does not cause bony changes such as flattening and sclerosis on radiographs.
D is incorrect because Iselin disease is an apophysitis of the base of the fifth metatarsal (traction injury at the peroneus brevis insertion), not osteonecrosis of the second metatarsal head.
E is incorrect because Sever disease is calcaneal apophysitis affecting the heel in active adolescents, unrelated to the metatarsal head.

questions.question:
A 6-year-old has a temperature of 38.9 C, refuses to bear weight on the right leg, has an ESR of 55 mm/h, and a WBC of 14,000/microL with a painful hip held in flexion, abduction, and external rotation. The probability of septic arthritis based on these predictors is closest to:
A) 40%
B) Less than 5%
C) 93%
D) 99%
E) Cannot be estimated without MRI
questions.answer:
D)
The Kocher criteria are fever above 38.5°C, inability to bear weight, ESR above 40 mm/h, and WBC above 12,000/μL. This child meets all four criteria, giving an approximately 99% predicted probability of septic arthritis. CRP above 2.0 mg/dL is an additional strong independent predictor (Caird modification). Aspiration remains the definitive diagnostic test.

A is incorrect because a 40% probability corresponds to only two of four Kocher predictors, not four. B is incorrect because a probability of less than 5% corresponds to zero or one predictor; this child has all four. C is incorrect because 93% corresponds to three of four predictors; this child meets all four. E is incorrect because the Kocher criteria allow estimation of septic arthritis probability using clinical and laboratory parameters alone; MRI is not required for this prediction model.

questions.question:
Which distal radius fracture parameter, if uncorrected, most reliably predicts poor functional outcome in a young active patient?
A) Ulnar variance of neutral
B) Articular step-off greater than 2 mm
C) Radial inclination of 22 degrees
D) Volar tilt of 8 degrees
E) Radial height of 12 mm
questions.answer:
B)
Articular step-off greater than 2 mm is the parameter most reliably associated with the development of posttraumatic radiocarpal arthritis and poor functional outcomes, particularly in young active patients. Multiple studies have shown that intra-articular incongruity is less well tolerated than extra-articular malalignment. Normal distal radius parameters include radial inclination ~22°, volar tilt ~11°, and radial height ~11 mm.

A is incorrect because neutral ulnar variance is a normal finding and does not represent a deformity requiring correction.
C is incorrect because radial inclination of 22 degrees is within the normal range (~22–23°) and does not constitute malalignment.
D is incorrect because volar tilt of 8 degrees is close to normal (~11°) and within generally accepted limits; mild loss of volar tilt is well tolerated functionally.
E is incorrect because radial height of 12 mm is within the normal range (~11–12 mm) and does not represent pathologic shortening.

questions.question:
A newborn with congenital scoliosis from a hemivertebra should be evaluated for which associated anomalies?
A) Craniosynostosis only
B) Congenital cataracts only
C) No associated anomalies are expected
D) Hypothyroidism only
E) Cardiac and genitourinary anomalies and intraspinal abnormalities
questions.answer:
E)
Congenital vertebral anomalies form during the same embryologic window (weeks 4–8) as the cardiac, renal, and neural structures, so screening echocardiography, renal ultrasound, and spinal MRI are standard. Intraspinal anomalies such as tethered cord, diastematomyelia, and syrinx occur in a substantial minority and must be identified before deformity correction. The association is captured by the VACTERL grouping.

A is incorrect because craniosynostosis (premature fusion of cranial sutures) is not a recognized association with congenital vertebral anomalies.
B is incorrect because congenital cataracts are not part of the embryologic association seen with congenital scoliosis; they are linked to other syndromes (e.g., congenital rubella).
C is incorrect because congenital vertebral anomalies have well-documented associations with cardiac defects (up to 26%), genitourinary anomalies (up to 25%), and intraspinal abnormalities (up to 38%); screening is mandatory.
D is incorrect because hypothyroidism is not an embryologically related anomaly in congenital scoliosis and is not part of the VACTERL spectrum.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old woman has pain beneath the second metatarsal head with a "crossover" deformity in which the second toe drifts medially and dorsally. The underlying lesion is:
A) Stress fracture of the second metatarsal
B) Hammertoe from intrinsic contracture alone
C) Interdigital neuroma
D) Rheumatoid synovitis in all cases
E) Plantar plate attenuation or rupture at the second MTP joint
questions.answer:
E)
Plantar plate attenuation or rupture at the second MTP joint permits dorsal subluxation and medial deviation of the toe, producing the classic "crossover" deformity and submetatarsal pain. A positive dorsal drawer test of the MTP joint confirms instability. Associated hallux valgus contributes by removing the lateral buttress. Treatment includes taping and orthoses early, and plantar plate repair with or without a shortening metatarsal osteotomy for persistent symptoms.

A is incorrect because a stress fracture of the second metatarsal causes localized shaft or neck pain and swelling but does not produce a crossover deformity with medial and dorsal drift of the toe. B is incorrect because hammertoe from intrinsic contracture alone causes a sagittal-plane flexion deformity at the PIP joint; it does not explain the medial deviation and dorsal subluxation at the MTP joint characteristic of crossover toe. C is incorrect because an interdigital (Morton) neuroma causes web-space pain and paresthesias in the adjacent toes but does not produce MTP joint instability or crossover deformity. D is incorrect because although rheumatoid synovitis can cause MTP joint destruction and toe deformities, crossover second toe is most commonly a mechanical/degenerative plantar plate problem and is not attributable to rheumatoid synovitis "in all cases."

questions.question:
In a 65-year-old with a displaced three-part proximal humerus fracture and good bone quality, which factor most strongly predicts avascular necrosis?
A) Greater tuberosity displacement of 3 mm
B) Anatomic neck alignment within 10 degrees
C) Age under 50
D) Isolated surgical neck fracture
E) Metaphyseal head extension less than 8 mm with disrupted medial hinge
questions.answer:
E)
The Hertel criteria identify three key predictors of humeral head avascular necrosis: metaphyseal head extension (calcar length) less than 8 mm, disruption of the medial periosteal hinge (>2 mm displacement), and an anatomic neck fracture component. A short metaphyseal extension with a disrupted medial hinge eliminates the critical posteromedial blood supply to the humeral head, making this combination the strongest predictor of ischemia.

A is incorrect because greater tuberosity displacement of 3 mm is relatively minor and does not significantly compromise the humeral head blood supply; tuberosity displacement alone is not a Hertel criterion for AVN prediction.
B is incorrect because anatomic neck alignment within 10 degrees suggests a relatively well-aligned fracture pattern, which would not increase AVN risk; it is anatomic neck fracture involvement (not alignment) that is a risk factor.
C is incorrect because younger age is not a predictor of AVN in proximal humerus fractures; in fact, older age with osteoporotic bone and comminution is more commonly associated with compromised vascularity.
D is incorrect because an isolated surgical neck fracture preserves the blood supply entering the humeral head through the medial periosteal vessels and the tuberosity attachments, and carries a low risk of AVN compared to anatomic neck or complex fracture patterns.

questions.question:
A randomized trial of two fixation methods reports a statistically significant 2-point difference in a 100-point functional score. The finding is most appropriately interpreted by considering:
A) The impact factor of the publishing journal
B) The minimal clinically important difference for that outcome instrument
C) The number of authors on the study
D) The absolute number of patients screened for eligibility
E) Whether the p value is below 0.10
questions.answer:
B)
Statistical significance indicates only that a difference is unlikely to be due to chance; it says nothing about whether patients would notice or value the difference. The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) defines the smallest change a patient perceives as beneficial. Large trials can detect trivially small differences, which is why effect size and the MCID should be reported alongside p values.

A is incorrect because the impact factor of the publishing journal reflects citation metrics, not the clinical relevance of a reported effect size. B is incorrect — skip (correct answer). C is incorrect because the number of authors has no bearing on the clinical meaningfulness of a treatment effect. D is incorrect because the absolute number of patients screened for eligibility relates to generalizability and enrollment, not to whether a statistically significant difference is clinically important. E is incorrect because a p-value threshold (whether 0.05 or 0.10) addresses the probability of a Type I error, not the magnitude or clinical importance of the observed difference.

questions.question:
Which feature best distinguishes Charcot neuroarthropathy from osteomyelitis in a diabetic patient with a swollen, erythematous midfoot?
A) Warmth of the affected foot
B) Positive bone scan
C) Elevated ESR
D) Erythema that resolves with limb elevation
E) Bone marrow edema on MRI
questions.answer:
D)
The dependent rubor of acute Charcot arthropathy typically diminishes with 5–10 minutes of limb elevation, whereas infectious erythema persists regardless of position. This simple bedside test is one of the most reliable clinical features distinguishing the two conditions. An absent overlying ulcer favors Charcot; a probe-to-bone test through an ulcer strongly favors osteomyelitis. Indium-labeled leukocyte scan with sulfur colloid subtraction or bone biopsy may be required when the diagnosis remains uncertain.

A is incorrect because warmth of the affected foot is present in both acute Charcot neuroarthropathy and osteomyelitis and therefore does not distinguish between them. B is incorrect because a bone scan (technetium-99m) is highly sensitive but nonspecific and will be positive in both Charcot and osteomyelitis. C is incorrect because ESR can be elevated in both conditions, making it a nonspecific marker. E is incorrect because bone marrow edema on MRI is seen in both Charcot neuroarthropathy and osteomyelitis, limiting its discriminatory value.

questions.question:
The Enneking classification of pelvic resections designates a resection of the periacetabular region as which type?
A) Type II (periacetabulum)
B) Type III (pubis and ischium)
C) Type V (femur)
D) Type IV (sacrum)
E) Type I (ilium)
questions.answer:
A)
In the Enneking classification of pelvic resections, Type II designates the periacetabular region. This is the most surgically challenging zone because resection disrupts the weight-bearing arc between the spine and the lower extremity, requiring complex reconstruction or acceptance of a flail hip.

B is incorrect because Type III (obturator region) involves the pubis and ischium, not the periacetabulum. C is incorrect because Type V is not a standard category in the Enneking pelvic resection classification; the system uses Types I–IV (and their combinations). D is incorrect because Type IV designates sacral involvement, not the periacetabular region. E is incorrect because Type I designates the iliac wing (ilium), which is proximal to the acetabulum.

questions.question:
Which muscle is the primary internal rotator tested by the lift-off and belly-press examinations?
A) Teres minor
B) Supraspinatus
C) Infraspinatus
D) Subscapularis
E) Latissimus dorsi
questions.answer:
D)
The subscapularis is the only anterior rotator cuff muscle and the primary internal rotator of the shoulder. The lift-off test (Gerber test) isolates the lower subscapularis, while the belly-press test preferentially assesses the upper subscapularis. Increased passive external rotation compared to the contralateral side is another sign of subscapularis insufficiency.

A is incorrect because the teres minor is an external rotator of the shoulder, not an internal rotator. B is incorrect because the supraspinatus is primarily responsible for initiating abduction and is tested with the Jobe (empty can) test. C is incorrect because the infraspinatus is the primary external rotator of the shoulder, tested with the external rotation lag sign and resisted external rotation. E is incorrect because the latissimus dorsi, while an internal rotator, is not a rotator cuff muscle and is not the muscle specifically tested by the lift-off and belly-press examinations.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old athlete has a symptomatic 2.5-cm full-thickness cartilage defect of the medial femoral condyle with normal alignment and an intact meniscus. Which option provides mature hyaline cartilage from a single-stage procedure?
A) Osteochondral autograft transfer
B) Autologous chondrocyte implantation
C) Debridement alone
D) Lavage
E) Microfracture
questions.answer:
A)
Osteochondral autograft transfer (mosaicplasty) transplants cylindrical plugs of native hyaline cartilage with subchondral bone from a low-weight-bearing donor site to the defect, restoring true hyaline cartilage in a single operation. It is best suited for defects up to approximately 2–2.5 cm²; larger defects may be better served by osteochondral allograft (not listed). Among the given options, it is the only choice that provides mature hyaline cartilage in one stage.

B is incorrect because autologous chondrocyte implantation (ACI) produces hyaline-like cartilage but requires two stages — an initial cartilage biopsy followed by a second implantation procedure after cell expansion. C is incorrect because debridement alone does not restore the articular surface and provides only symptomatic palliation. D is incorrect because lavage does not address the cartilage defect and offers no regenerative benefit. E is incorrect because microfracture stimulates a fibrocartilage repair response (predominantly type I collagen), not true hyaline cartilage, and outcomes tend to deteriorate over time, especially in larger defects.

questions.question:
Which reconstructive procedure directly addresses the proximal femoral deformity of a healed severe SCFE while permitting inspection of the joint and protection of the retinacular blood supply?
A) Salter innominate osteotomy
B) Imhauser osteotomy alone
C) Modified Dunn subcapital realignment via surgical hip dislocation
D) Southwick intertrochanteric osteotomy
E) Arthroscopic osteochondroplasty alone
questions.answer:
C)
The modified Dunn procedure uses a trochanteric flip approach for surgical hip dislocation, developing a retinacular soft-tissue flap that protects the deep branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery. This allows direct subcapital realignment at the site of deformity and intra-articular inspection, uniquely satisfying all criteria in the stem. It is technically demanding with a real risk of osteonecrosis.

A is incorrect because the Salter innominate osteotomy is a pelvic (acetabular-side) procedure that redirects the acetabulum; it does not address the proximal femoral deformity of SCFE.
B is incorrect because the Imhauser osteotomy is an intertrochanteric (extracapsular) procedure that compensates for the deformity distal to its origin; it does not directly correct the subcapital deformity and does not permit joint inspection.
D is incorrect because the Southwick intertrochanteric osteotomy similarly corrects alignment at the intertrochanteric level rather than at the source of the slip, and it does not allow intra-articular visualization.
E is incorrect because arthroscopic osteochondroplasty addresses only the cam-type bump on the femoral head–neck junction; it cannot realign the epiphysis relative to the metaphysis and does not correct the underlying proximal femoral deformity of a severe slip.

questions.question:
Which finding on hand radiographs is most specific for primary hyperparathyroidism?
A) Chondrocalcinosis of the triangular fibrocartilage
B) Marginal erosions with overhanging edges
C) Diffuse osteosclerosis of the phalanges
D) Periarticular osteopenia of the metacarpophalangeal joints
E) Subperiosteal resorption along the radial border of the middle phalanges
questions.answer:
E)
Subperiosteal bone resorption along the radial aspect of the middle phalanges (especially the index and long fingers), along with terminal tuft (acro-osteolysis) resorption, is the most specific hand finding for primary hyperparathyroidism. Brown tumors (osteitis fibrosa cystica) may also be seen. Laboratory findings include elevated PTH, elevated serum calcium, low phosphate, and elevated alkaline phosphatase.

A is incorrect because chondrocalcinosis of the triangular fibrocartilage is associated with calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD/pseudogout), not hyperparathyroidism (though secondary CPPD can occur, it is not the most specific finding). B is incorrect because marginal erosions with overhanging edges are characteristic of tophaceous gout. C is incorrect because diffuse osteosclerosis of the phalanges is not a feature of primary hyperparathyroidism; hyperparathyroidism causes resorption and osteopenia, not sclerosis (osteosclerosis may be seen in renal osteodystrophy but is not specific to primary hyperparathyroidism on hand films). D is incorrect because periarticular osteopenia of the MCP joints is a hallmark of rheumatoid arthritis, not hyperparathyroidism.

questions.question:
Which is the most reliable view for evaluating acromial morphology and the subacromial space?
A) True AP (Grashey)
B) Axillary lateral
C) West Point view
D) Supraspinatus outlet (scapular Y with 10 degrees caudal tilt)
E) Stryker notch view
questions.answer:
D)
The supraspinatus outlet view (scapular Y with ~10° caudal tilt) profiles the acromial arch in the sagittal plane and is the standard view for classifying Bigliani acromial morphology (type I flat, type II curved, type III hooked) and assessing subacromial space narrowing.

A is incorrect because the true AP (Grashey) view evaluates the glenohumeral joint space and is taken in the plane of the scapula; it does not profile the acromion in the sagittal plane. B is incorrect because the axillary lateral view evaluates glenohumeral alignment, os acromiale, and anterior/posterior glenoid bone stock, but does not optimally profile the acromial undersurface. C is incorrect because the West Point view is designed to assess the anteroinferior glenoid rim for bony Bankart lesions, not acromial morphology. E is incorrect because the Stryker notch view is used to identify Hill-Sachs lesions on the posterolateral humeral head and does not visualize the acromion.

questions.question:
Which tendon transfer is most appropriate to restore thumb opposition after a low median nerve palsy?
A) Flexor carpi ulnaris to extensor digitorum communis
B) Pronator teres to extensor carpi radialis brevis
C) Brachioradialis to flexor pollicis longus
D) Extensor carpi radialis longus to flexor digitorum profundus
E) Extensor indicis proprius or flexor digitorum superficialis (ring) to abductor pollicis brevis
questions.answer:
E)
Opponensplasty restores thumb opposition after low median nerve palsy. Classic donor options include the extensor indicis proprius (Burkhalter transfer) and the ring-finger flexor digitorum superficialis (Bunnell transfer), both routed to insert on the abductor pollicis brevis. Other described opponensplasties include the abductor digiti minimi (Huber transfer, favored in congenital thenar hypoplasia) and the palmaris longus with fascial extension (Camitz transfer, often combined with carpal tunnel release).

A is incorrect because FCU to EDC is a tendon transfer used to restore finger extension in radial nerve palsy (part of the classic Brand or Boyes set), not for thumb opposition.
B is incorrect because PT to ECRB is used to restore wrist extension in radial nerve palsy, not to restore thumb opposition.
C is incorrect because BR to FPL is used to restore thumb interphalangeal flexion in high median nerve palsy (or as part of a radial nerve palsy reconstruction); it does not restore opposition.
D is incorrect because ECRL to FDP is used to restore finger flexion in high median or combined median-ulnar nerve palsy, not to restore thumb opposition.

questions.question:
A patient is referred after an "unplanned excision" of what proved to be a high-grade sarcoma at an outside facility. The most appropriate management is:
A) Immediate amputation
B) Radiation alone without further surgery
C) Chemotherapy alone
D) Observation with surveillance imaging
E) Restaging with MRI and chest CT followed by re-resection of the tumor bed and prior incision, with radiation as indicated
questions.answer:
E)
After an unplanned excision of a high-grade sarcoma, residual microscopic tumor is found in 30–70% of re-resection specimens even when postoperative MRI appears negative. Standard management includes complete restaging (MRI of the primary site and chest CT for pulmonary metastases) followed by wide re-excision of the entire prior surgical field — including the scar, drain sites, and any contaminated tissue planes — with adjuvant radiation therapy as indicated. Outcomes after appropriate re-resection approach those of a planned primary wide resection.

A is incorrect because immediate amputation is unnecessarily morbid; limb-salvage re-resection with adjuvant radiation achieves comparable oncologic outcomes in the vast majority of cases. B is incorrect because radiation alone cannot reliably eradicate gross or microscopic residual sarcoma; surgical re-excision of the tumor bed is essential. C is incorrect because chemotherapy alone does not adequately address local disease control; wide re-excision remains the cornerstone of management for residual local disease. D is incorrect because observation risks allowing residual microscopic disease to progress to a clinically apparent local recurrence, significantly worsening prognosis and functional outcomes.

questions.question:
Hip resurfacing arthroplasty is best reserved for which patient?
A) A patient with chronic kidney disease
B) A woman of childbearing age
C) A 62-year-old woman with osteopenia and femoral head cysts
D) A patient with a history of metal hypersensitivity
E) A 38-year-old man with good bone stock, a large femoral head, and no inflammatory arthropathy
questions.answer:
E)
The ideal hip resurfacing candidate is a younger male with good femoral head bone quality, a large native femoral head size, minimal head deformity or cysts, and no inflammatory arthritis or renal impairment. A 38-year-old man with good bone stock and a large femoral head who lacks inflammatory arthropathy fits this profile perfectly. Resurfacing preserves proximal femoral bone stock and allows easier future revision to a standard total hip arthroplasty if needed.

A is incorrect because chronic kidney disease impairs metal ion clearance (cobalt and chromium from the metal-on-metal bearing), increasing the risk of systemic toxicity. B is incorrect because women of childbearing age are generally avoided due to concerns about transplacental transfer of metal ions and because smaller femoral head size in women is associated with higher failure rates. C is incorrect because a 62-year-old woman with osteopenia and femoral head cysts has multiple risk factors for failure—female sex, older age, poor bone quality, and cystic degeneration of the femoral head all increase the risk of femoral neck fracture and adverse metal-related reactions. D is incorrect because metal-on-metal bearings generate cobalt and chromium debris; a known metal hypersensitivity is a contraindication to resurfacing.

questions.question:
A 68-year-old man has persistent pain 3 years after total knee arthroplasty. ESR and CRP are mildly elevated, and aspiration yields 4,200 WBC/microL with 82% neutrophils. Cultures are negative after he received oral antibiotics 1 week ago. Which additional synovial fluid test is least affected by recent antibiotic exposure?
A) Glucose concentration
B) Gram stain
C) Alpha-defensin
D) Crystal analysis
E) Aerobic culture
questions.answer:
C)
Alpha-defensin is an antimicrobial peptide released by activated neutrophils in response to pathogens. Its synovial fluid concentration remains elevated even after recent antibiotic administration, maintaining high sensitivity and specificity for periprosthetic joint infection (PJI). This makes it the most reliable biomarker when antibiotics have not been appropriately withheld. Ideally, antibiotics should be stopped for at least 2 weeks before aspiration to optimize culture yield.

A is incorrect because synovial glucose concentration is a nonspecific marker that can be altered by many factors and is not a validated criterion for PJI diagnosis; it is also not specifically resistant to antibiotic effects. B is incorrect because Gram stain sensitivity is already low (~25–30%) for PJI and is further diminished when antibiotics reduce bacterial load. D is incorrect because crystal analysis evaluates for gout or pseudogout, not infection; it does not help diagnose PJI and is unrelated to antibiotic exposure. E is incorrect because aerobic culture is directly suppressed by recent antibiotic use, which reduces bacterial viability and is the classic test most affected by prior antibiotic administration.

questions.question:
Which finding best distinguishes carpal tunnel syndrome from a C6 radiculopathy?
A) Weak wrist extension
B) Preserved sensation over the thenar eminence in carpal tunnel syndrome
C) Numbness in the thumb
D) Night pain
E) Positive Spurling test in carpal tunnel syndrome
questions.answer:
B)
The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises approximately 5 cm proximal to the wrist and travels superficial to the transverse carpal ligament, so thenar eminence sensation is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome but may be affected in a C6 radiculopathy or proximal median nerve lesion. This distinction is a classic board-tested differentiating feature.

A is incorrect because weak wrist extension is a finding of C6 radiculopathy (radial nerve–innervated extensors), not carpal tunnel syndrome; it does not distinguish CTS from C6 — rather it points toward C6.
C is incorrect because numbness in the thumb can occur in both carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve digital branches) and C6 radiculopathy (C6 dermatome), so it does not reliably distinguish the two.
D is incorrect because night pain (nocturnal paresthesias) is characteristic of carpal tunnel syndrome but is not a distinguishing physical-exam finding that differentiates it from cervical radiculopathy; some radiculopathy patients also have nocturnal symptoms.
E is incorrect because a positive Spurling test is a sign of cervical radiculopathy, not carpal tunnel syndrome; the stem states "positive Spurling test in carpal tunnel syndrome," which is factually wrong and therefore cannot be the correct answer.

questions.question:
The most common indication for revision total knee arthroplasty in contemporary series is:
A) Patellar fracture
B) Polyethylene wear
C) Periprosthetic fracture
D) Infection and aseptic loosening, with instability also prominent
E) Extensor mechanism rupture
questions.answer:
D)
Contemporary registry data show that aseptic loosening and periprosthetic joint infection are the two most common indications for revision TKA, with instability also ranking among the top causes. Early failures (< 2 years) are most often due to infection and instability, while late failures are more commonly from aseptic loosening and polyethylene wear. A thorough infection workup (ESR, CRP, joint aspiration) is mandatory before any revision.

A is incorrect because patellar fracture after TKA is uncommon and accounts for a very small percentage of revision indications.
B is incorrect because polyethylene wear was historically a leading cause of revision but has declined significantly with modern bearing surfaces and is no longer the most common indication.
C is incorrect because periprosthetic fracture, while an important complication, is far less frequent than aseptic loosening, infection, or instability as a reason for revision.
E is incorrect because extensor mechanism rupture (quadriceps or patellar tendon) is a rare but devastating complication and represents only a small fraction of revision TKA cases.

questions.question:
Ankylosing spondylitis is most strongly associated with which of the following?
A) Rheumatoid factor positivity
B) HLA-B27
C) HLA-DR4
D) Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies
E) Antinuclear antibodies
questions.answer:
B)
HLA-B27 is present in roughly 90% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis. Classic features include bilateral symmetric sacroiliitis, syndesmophytes producing a bamboo spine, enthesitis, uveitis, and a rigid osteoporotic spine prone to unstable three-column fractures from minor trauma.

A is incorrect because rheumatoid factor positivity is associated with rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune conditions; ankylosing spondylitis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy by definition. C is incorrect because HLA-DR4 is linked to rheumatoid arthritis, not ankylosing spondylitis. D is incorrect because anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies are highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis. E is incorrect because antinuclear antibodies (ANA) are associated with systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective tissue diseases, not ankylosing spondylitis.

questions.question:
A "ground glass" lucent lesion of the proximal femur with a shepherd's crook deformity in a young adult, with histology showing irregular "Chinese-character" trabeculae lacking osteoblastic rimming, indicates:
A) Adamantinoma
B) Osteofibrous dysplasia
C) Fibrous dysplasia
D) Nonossifying fibroma
E) Paget disease
questions.answer:
C)
Fibrous dysplasia results from an activating GNAS1 mutation and produces ground-glass matrix with woven bone trabeculae in irregular "Chinese-character" patterns lacking osteoblastic rimming. The shepherd's crook deformity of the proximal femur is classic. McCune-Albright syndrome combines polyostotic disease with café-au-lait macules (irregular "coast of Maine" borders) and precocious puberty; Mazabraud syndrome adds intramuscular myxomas. Bisphosphonates help pain; cortical graft or internal fixation is preferred for structural lesions because cancellous autograft tends to resorb.

A is incorrect because adamantinoma is a low-grade malignancy that characteristically involves the anterior tibial diaphysis and contains epithelial elements (keratin-positive); it does not present with ground-glass matrix or shepherd's crook deformity of the femur.

B is incorrect because osteofibrous dysplasia is a cortically based lesion of the anterior tibial diaphysis in children; histologically it shows zonal maturation with osteoblastic rimming of trabeculae, unlike fibrous dysplasia.

D is incorrect because nonossifying fibroma (fibroxanthoma) is an eccentric, well-marginated, sclerotic-bordered metaphyseal lesion composed of spindle cells in a storiform pattern with multinucleated giant cells; it does not produce ground-glass matrix or shepherd's crook deformity.

E is incorrect because Paget disease occurs in older adults (>40 years), shows thickened coarsened trabeculae with a mosaic (cement-line) pattern on histology, and has markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase; it does not produce Chinese-character trabeculae lacking osteoblastic rimming.

questions.question:
When planning a posterior cervical fusion, a high T1 slope with inadequate cervical lordosis restoration most predicts which complication?
A) Cervical sagittal imbalance with postoperative kyphotic deformity and worse patient-reported outcomes
B) Dural tear
C) C5 palsy
D) Dysphagia
E) Vertebral artery injury
questions.answer:
A)
T1 slope reflects the sagittal orientation of the cervicothoracic junction; a high T1 slope requires greater cervical lordosis to keep the head balanced over the pelvis. Failure to restore adequate lordosis relative to T1 slope (a large T1 slope minus cervical lordosis mismatch) produces increased C2–C7 sagittal vertical axis, chin-on-chest posture, and worse disability and neck pain scores.

B is incorrect because dural tears are related to surgical technique and adhesions, not to T1 slope–lordosis mismatch. C is incorrect because C5 palsy is a nerve root traction phenomenon associated with posterior cord drift after decompression, not with sagittal malalignment parameters. D is incorrect because dysphagia is predominantly a complication of anterior cervical approaches (retraction of the esophagus), not a consequence of sagittal imbalance from posterior fusion. E is incorrect because vertebral artery injury is an intraoperative technical complication related to lateral mass or pedicle screw malposition, not to failure of lordosis restoration.

questions.question:
In the Enneking (Musculoskeletal Tumor Society) staging system for malignant bone tumors, stage IIB denotes:
A) High grade, intracompartmental, no metastasis
B) Low grade, extracompartmental, no metastasis
C) High grade, extracompartmental, no metastasis
D) Low grade, intracompartmental, no metastasis
E) Any grade with metastasis
questions.answer:
C)
The Enneking (MSTS) staging system classifies malignant bone tumors by grade (I = low, II = high), compartmental status (A = intracompartmental, B = extracompartmental), and presence of metastasis (stage III). Stage IIB therefore denotes a high-grade, extracompartmental lesion without metastasis — the most common presentation of osteosarcoma. The AJCC system for bone sarcoma instead incorporates tumor size (8 cm cutoff), grade, and the presence of skip metastases and distant disease.

A is incorrect because high grade + intracompartmental + no metastasis defines stage IIA, not IIB. B is incorrect because low grade + extracompartmental + no metastasis defines stage IB. D is incorrect because low grade + intracompartmental + no metastasis defines stage IA. E is incorrect because any grade with metastasis defines stage III in the Enneking system, regardless of compartmental status.

questions.question:
Trendelenburg gait after total hip arthroplasty is most often related to injury or insufficiency of:
A) The sciatic nerve peroneal division
B) The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
C) The obturator nerve
D) The abductor mechanism and superior gluteal nerve
E) The femoral nerve
questions.answer:
D)
The superior gluteal nerve innervates the gluteus medius, minimus, and tensor fascia lata; it exits above the piriformis and courses approximately 3–5 cm proximal to the tip of the greater trochanter, placing it at risk during proximal splitting of the abductors in a direct lateral (Hardinge) approach. Damage to the nerve or direct injury to the abductor tendon insertion results in abductor insufficiency and a Trendelenburg gait (trunk lean over the affected hip during stance phase).

A is incorrect because the peroneal division of the sciatic nerve is the most commonly injured nerve overall in THA (especially with limb lengthening), but its injury causes foot drop, not Trendelenburg gait. B is incorrect because the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is a purely sensory nerve; its injury causes meralgia paresthetica (lateral thigh numbness/dysesthesia), not motor weakness. C is incorrect because the obturator nerve innervates the hip adductors; its injury would cause adductor weakness and medial thigh sensory loss, not an abductor lurch. E is incorrect because the femoral nerve innervates the quadriceps and hip flexors; its injury causes knee extension weakness and anterior thigh numbness, not abductor insufficiency.

questions.question:
Patellar instability with a tibial tubercle-trochlear groove distance of 22 mm and trochlear dysplasia is best addressed by:
A) Immobilization for 12 weeks
B) Tibial tubercle medialization (with MPFL reconstruction as indicated)
C) Patellectomy
D) Total knee arthroplasty
E) Isolated lateral release
questions.answer:
B)
A TT-TG distance of 22 mm exceeds the ~20 mm threshold indicating excessive lateralization of the extensor mechanism, making tibial tubercle medialization the cornerstone procedure. In the setting of trochlear dysplasia and recurrent instability, MPFL reconstruction is added as indicated, since the MPFL is the primary soft-tissue restraint to lateral patellar translation (contributing ~50–60% of restraining force). Anteromedialization (Fulkerson) is preferred when concomitant distal or lateral patellar chondral wear is present.

A is incorrect because prolonged immobilization does not correct the underlying anatomic risk factors (elevated TT-TG, trochlear dysplasia) and leads to stiffness and quadriceps atrophy without reducing recurrence.
C is incorrect because patellectomy is a salvage procedure for severe patellofemoral arthritis or fracture; it eliminates the extensor lever arm and is not appropriate for patellar instability.
D is incorrect because total knee arthroplasty is reserved for end-stage tricompartmental arthritis, not for patellar instability in an otherwise functional knee.
E is incorrect because isolated lateral release does not address the bony malalignment (elevated TT-TG) or the deficient MPFL, and can paradoxically cause iatrogenic medial patellar instability.

questions.question:
Pott disease (tuberculous spondylitis) most characteristically demonstrates:
A) Early disc destruction with endplate erosion
B) Ivory vertebra with sclerosis
C) Anterior vertebral body destruction with relative disc preservation, subligamentous spread, and large paraspinal abscess
D) Diffuse marrow replacement with vertebra plana at a single level in a child
E) Posterior element destruction only
questions.answer:
C)
Mycobacterium tuberculosis lacks proteolytic enzymes, so the intervertebral disc is relatively preserved until late in the disease. The organism spreads beneath the anterior longitudinal ligament, involving multiple contiguous vertebral levels with anterior body destruction, producing cold paraspinal abscesses and progressive kyphosis (gibbus deformity). Treatment is prolonged multidrug chemotherapy, with surgery reserved for neurologic deficit, severe kyphosis, or instability.

A is incorrect because early disc destruction with endplate erosion is characteristic of pyogenic (bacterial) spondylodiscitis, not tuberculosis, which classically preserves the disc early on. B is incorrect because an ivory vertebra with dense sclerosis is seen in Paget disease, lymphoma, or metastatic prostate carcinoma, not TB spondylitis. D is incorrect because diffuse marrow replacement with vertebra plana at a single level in a child is the hallmark of eosinophilic granuloma (Langerhans cell histiocytosis), not Pott disease. E is incorrect because TB spondylitis predominantly affects the anterior vertebral body; isolated posterior element destruction is more typical of metastatic disease.

questions.question:
Which laboratory value best identifies malnutrition as a risk factor for wound complications?
A) Serum albumin less than 3.5 g/dL
B) Platelet count less than 150,000
C) INR greater than 1.2
D) Hemoglobin less than 12 g/dL
E) Serum sodium less than 135 mEq/L
questions.answer:
A)
Serum albumin below 3.5 g/dL is the most widely cited laboratory marker of malnutrition associated with increased wound complications, surgical site infections, and poor healing. Other nutritional markers include total lymphocyte count below 1,500 cells/mm³, transferrin below 200 mg/dL, and prealbumin below 15 mg/dL (prealbumin has a shorter half-life and reflects more acute nutritional changes). Nutritional optimization is recommended before elective surgery, particularly arthroplasty.

B is incorrect because a low platelet count (thrombocytopenia) reflects a hematologic or coagulation issue, not nutritional status relevant to wound healing. C is incorrect because an elevated INR indicates coagulopathy (e.g., warfarin use or liver dysfunction), not malnutrition per se. D is incorrect because low hemoglobin indicates anemia, which has many causes; while it may coexist with malnutrition, it is not the best specific marker for nutritional depletion and wound risk. E is incorrect because hyponatremia reflects fluid/electrolyte imbalance rather than nutritional status and is not a recognized marker for wound complication risk.

questions.question:
A patient develops hypoxemia, bilateral infiltrates, and a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 180 three days after multi-trauma. This is most consistent with:
A) Aspiration pneumonitis with normal radiographs
B) Pulmonary embolism
C) Pneumothorax
D) Cardiogenic pulmonary edema
E) Acute respiratory distress syndrome
questions.answer:
E)
The Berlin definition of ARDS requires onset within 1 week of a known insult, bilateral opacities not fully explained by effusion or collapse, respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload, and impaired oxygenation graded by PaO2/FiO2 (mild 200–300, moderate 100–200, severe <100). This patient's PaO2/FiO2 of 180 classifies as moderate ARDS. Management includes low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg ideal body weight).

A is incorrect because aspiration pneumonitis may cause infiltrates, but the stem already describes bilateral infiltrates (not normal imaging), and the clinical picture with a PaO2/FiO2 of 180 after multi-trauma fits ARDS, not simple aspiration. B is incorrect because pulmonary embolism typically presents with acute hypoxemia and may show a clear lung field or focal atelectasis rather than bilateral infiltrates; the classic triad is dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and tachycardia. C is incorrect because pneumothorax presents with unilateral decreased breath sounds and absent lung markings on one side, not bilateral infiltrates. D is incorrect because cardiogenic pulmonary edema can produce bilateral infiltrates and hypoxemia, but the Berlin definition of ARDS specifically requires that respiratory failure not be fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload; in a young multi-trauma patient without cardiac history, ARDS is the most likely diagnosis.

questions.question:
Periprosthetic osteolysis is mediated principally by macrophage response to polyethylene particles of which size?
A) Greater than 100 microns
B) 0.1 to 1.0 micron
C) 5 to 10 microns
D) 20 to 50 microns
E) Less than 0.1 micron
questions.answer:
B)
Polyethylene wear particles in the 0.1–1.0 micron (submicron) range are the most biologically active size for stimulating macrophage-mediated osteolysis. These particles are readily phagocytosed by macrophages, triggering release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6) and prostaglandin E2, which upregulate RANKL and drive osteoclastogenesis, leading to periprosthetic bone resorption.

A is incorrect because particles greater than 100 microns are too large to be phagocytosed by macrophages; they may elicit a foreign-body giant cell reaction but are not the principal drivers of osteolysis.
C is incorrect because particles of 5–10 microns are at the upper limit of effective phagocytosis and are less efficiently internalized than submicron particles, generating a weaker osteolytic response.
D is incorrect because particles of 20–50 microns are too large for standard macrophage phagocytosis and tend to provoke a giant cell response rather than the cytokine-driven osteolysis seen with submicron debris.
E is incorrect because particles less than 0.1 micron (nanoscale) are generally too small to effectively stimulate the macrophage inflammatory cascade; the peak biologically active range is 0.1–1.0 micron.

questions.question:
Which incomplete spinal cord syndrome has the worst prognosis for neurologic recovery?
A) Brown-Sequard syndrome
B) Central cord syndrome
C) Posterior cord syndrome
D) Anterior cord syndrome
E) Conus medullaris syndrome
questions.answer:
D)
Anterior cord syndrome results from injury or ischemia in the anterior spinal artery territory, causing loss of motor function and pain/temperature sensation below the level of injury while preserving dorsal column (proprioception, vibration, deep pressure) function. It carries the worst prognosis of the incomplete spinal cord syndromes, with only approximately 10–20% of patients achieving meaningful neurologic recovery.

A is incorrect because Brown-Séquard syndrome (cord hemisection) has the best prognosis of all incomplete cord syndromes, with approximately 90% of patients regaining ambulatory function.
B is incorrect because central cord syndrome generally has a favorable prognosis, particularly for lower-extremity and bladder recovery, though residual hand weakness and fine-motor dysfunction often persist.
C is incorrect because posterior cord syndrome (loss of proprioception and vibration with preserved motor and pain/temperature function) is rare but does not carry the worst prognosis; motor function is preserved.
E is incorrect because conus medullaris syndrome affects the sacral cord segments and typically presents with bowel/bladder dysfunction and variable lower-extremity findings; while recovery can be limited, it is not classically cited as the incomplete syndrome with the worst overall prognosis—that distinction belongs to anterior cord syndrome.

questions.question:
A 14-year-old sustains a puncture wound through a rubber-soled sneaker and develops forefoot osteomyelitis. The most likely organism is:
A) Eikenella corrodens
B) Staphylococcus aureus
C) Pseudomonas aeruginosa
D) Pasteurella multocida
E) Salmonella species
questions.answer:
C)
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the classic organism associated with osteomyelitis following a puncture wound through a rubber-soled sneaker. The warm, moist environment inside athletic shoes promotes Pseudomonas colonization, and the puncture inoculates the organism into deep tissues including bone. This is a high-yield board association.

A is incorrect because Eikenella corrodens is associated with human bite wounds (clenched-fist injuries), not sneaker puncture wounds.
B is incorrect because while Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of osteomyelitis in general, the specific scenario of a puncture through a rubber-soled shoe is classically associated with Pseudomonas on orthopaedic board examinations.
D is incorrect because Pasteurella multocida is associated with cat and dog bite wounds, not puncture injuries through footwear.
E is incorrect because Salmonella species are associated with osteomyelitis in patients with sickle cell disease, not with sneaker puncture wounds.

questions.question:
Which structure is released to correct a fixed varus deformity in total knee arthroplasty?
A) Iliotibial band and popliteus
B) Lateral collateral ligament
C) Deep medial collateral ligament, followed by posteromedial structures and semimembranosus as needed
D) Patellar tendon
E) Posterior cruciate ligament only
questions.answer:
C)
Fixed varus deformity in TKA is corrected by sequential medial soft-tissue release. This begins with removal of medial osteophytes and release of the deep medial collateral ligament (dMCL), then progresses to the posteromedial capsule and semimembranosus insertion as needed. If further correction is required, the superficial MCL may be partially elevated.

A is incorrect because the iliotibial band and popliteus are lateral structures released to correct a valgus deformity, not a varus deformity.
B is incorrect because the lateral collateral ligament is a lateral stabilizer; releasing it would worsen valgus laxity and is part of the valgus correction algorithm, not varus.
D is incorrect because the patellar tendon is not part of the medial or lateral release sequence for coronal plane deformity correction; releasing it would compromise the extensor mechanism.
E is incorrect because the posterior cruciate ligament may be sacrificed in certain TKA designs but does not specifically correct a fixed varus deformity; it primarily affects sagittal-plane kinematics.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old presents with a painful pelvic lesion with rings-and-arcs matrix and cortical destruction. The most appropriate treatment for a conventional grade II chondrosarcoma is:
A) Wide surgical resection
B) Chemotherapy alone
C) Observation
D) Intralesional curettage
E) Radiation alone
questions.answer:
A)
Conventional chondrosarcoma is largely chemoresistant and radioresistant, so wide en bloc resection with negative margins is the definitive treatment; margin status is the strongest predictor of local control. A grade II lesion in the pelvis requires wide resection rather than intralesional techniques.

B is incorrect because conventional chondrosarcoma is chemoresistant; chemotherapy alone has no meaningful role (it is considered only for mesenchymal or dedifferentiated variants as an adjunct, not as sole treatment). C is incorrect because a grade II chondrosarcoma with cortical destruction is an intermediate-grade malignancy that will progress and metastasize without surgical treatment. D is incorrect because intralesional curettage (extended or otherwise) is reserved for low-grade (grade I / atypical cartilaginous tumor) lesions in the appendicular skeleton; a grade II pelvic chondrosarcoma requires wide margins to minimize local recurrence. E is incorrect because conventional chondrosarcoma is radioresistant; radiation alone does not provide adequate local control and is used only as an adjunct when margins are compromised or the tumor is unresectable.

questions.question:
Which instrument is used to report functional outcome after limb-salvage surgery for a musculoskeletal tumor?
A) Mirels score
B) Musculoskeletal Tumor Society (MSTS) score
C) Enneking staging system
D) Kocher criteria
E) Oswestry Disability Index
questions.answer:
B)
The Musculoskeletal Tumor Society (MSTS) score (also called the Enneking functional score) is the standard instrument for reporting functional outcome after limb-salvage surgery. It evaluates six domains—pain, function, and emotional acceptance for all patients, plus walking ability, gait, and use of supports for the lower extremity (or hand positioning, manual dexterity, and lifting ability for the upper extremity)—each scored 0–5, with the total expressed as a percentage.

A is incorrect because the Mirels score is a tool for predicting pathologic fracture risk in metastatic bone lesions, not for measuring functional outcome.
C is incorrect because the Enneking staging system classifies musculoskeletal tumors by grade, local extent, and presence of metastases; it does not assess postoperative function.
D is incorrect because the Kocher criteria are used to differentiate septic arthritis from transient synovitis of the hip in children and have no role in functional outcome assessment.
E is incorrect because the Oswestry Disability Index is a patient-reported outcome measure specific to low-back pain and disability, not limb-salvage tumor surgery.

questions.question:
The most appropriate initial management of a patient with a suspected neurogenic shock from a complete cervical spinal cord injury is:
A) Immediate traction reduction before imaging in all patients
B) Fluid resuscitation plus vasopressors to maintain mean arterial pressure of approximately 85-90 mm Hg
C) Aggressive fluid resuscitation alone until normotensive
D) High-dose methylprednisolone as standard of care
E) Beta blockade to control reflex tachycardia
questions.answer:
B)
Neurogenic shock results from loss of sympathetic tone after cervical or high-thoracic spinal cord injury, producing hypotension and bradycardia. Current guidelines recommend judicious fluid resuscitation combined with vasopressors (typically norepinephrine or phenylephrine) to maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of approximately 85–90 mm Hg for the first 5–7 days to optimize spinal cord perfusion.

A is incorrect because immediate traction reduction without advanced imaging (e.g., MRI or CT) risks worsening cord compression from an unrecognized disc herniation or unstable fracture pattern; imaging should precede or guide reduction.
C is incorrect because aggressive crystalloid resuscitation alone risks pulmonary edema and does not adequately restore vascular tone lost from sympathetic denervation; vasopressors are essential.
D is incorrect because high-dose methylprednisolone is no longer recommended as standard of care due to increased risks of infection, sepsis, and gastrointestinal bleeding without proven neurological benefit.
E is incorrect because neurogenic shock produces bradycardia (not tachycardia) from unopposed vagal tone; beta blockade would worsen bradycardia and hypotension.

questions.question:
A "wide" surgical margin as defined by Enneking is:
A) Through the tumor
B) Through the reactive zone (pseudocapsule)
C) Through normal tissue with a cuff of normal tissue around the tumor, within the compartment
D) Amputation only
E) Removal of the entire compartment
questions.answer:
C)
Enneking defined a wide margin as resection through normal tissue with a cuff of normal tissue surrounding the tumor, but remaining within the same compartment. Wide margins with adjuvant chemotherapy are the standard goal for most high-grade sarcomas. Although skip lesions may theoretically be left behind (they lie outside the reactive zone but within the compartment), wide resection is generally considered adequate when combined with appropriate adjuvant therapy.

A is incorrect because resection through the tumor itself defines an intralesional margin, not a wide margin. B is incorrect because resection through the reactive zone (pseudocapsule) defines a marginal margin; satellite lesions within the reactive zone may be left behind. D is incorrect because amputation is a method of achieving a margin (which could be wide or radical depending on the level) but does not itself define a wide margin. E is incorrect because removal of the entire compartment defines a radical margin in the Enneking system.

questions.question:
Necrotizing fasciitis is most commonly caused by which organism in the monomicrobial (type II) form?
A) Staphylococcus epidermidis
B) Bacteroides fragilis
C) Vibrio vulnificus
D) Group A Streptococcus
E) Clostridium perfringens
questions.answer:
D)
Type II (monomicrobial) necrotizing fasciitis is most commonly caused by group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes), alone or occasionally with Staphylococcus aureus. Hallmarks include pain out of proportion to examination, bullae, crepitus, and rapid clinical deterioration. Management requires emergent radical surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin for its antitoxin effect.

A is incorrect because Staphylococcus epidermidis is a coagulase-negative staphylococcus typically associated with indolent prosthetic device infections, not necrotizing fasciitis.
B is incorrect because Bacteroides fragilis is an anaerobe that may participate in type I (polymicrobial) necrotizing fasciitis but is not the classic causative organism of monomicrobial type II disease.
C is incorrect because Vibrio vulnificus can cause a rapidly progressive necrotizing soft-tissue infection but is specifically associated with saltwater exposure or raw shellfish ingestion in patients with liver disease; it is not the most common cause of type II necrotizing fasciitis overall.
E is incorrect because Clostridium perfringens causes gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis), which is a distinct entity from type II necrotizing fasciitis, though clinical overlap can occur.

questions.question:
The most common site of a ganglion cyst of the wrist is:
A) Dorsal, arising from the scapholunate ligament
B) Volar radial at the radiocarpal joint
C) Within the carpal tunnel
D) Ulnar, from the pisotriquetral joint
E) At the first dorsal compartment
questions.answer:
A)
Approximately 60-70% of wrist ganglions are dorsal and originate from the scapholunate interval. Volar cysts most often arise from the radiocarpal or scaphotrapezial joint and lie close to the radial artery, so an Allen test should be performed before excision. Many resolve spontaneously; aspiration has a high recurrence rate, and open or arthroscopic excision must include the stalk and a cuff of capsule to reduce recurrence.

B is incorrect because volar radial ganglions at the radiocarpal joint are the second most common location (approximately 18-20%), not the most common. C is incorrect because intraneural or intra-carpal tunnel ganglions are rare occurrences and not a typical site for wrist ganglions. D is incorrect because ganglions arising from the pisotriquetral joint on the ulnar side are uncommon. E is incorrect because ganglions at the first dorsal compartment (de Quervain's area) can occur but are far less frequent than dorsal scapholunate ganglions.

questions.question:
Which is the most common complication after operative treatment of a distal humerus fracture?
A) Radial nerve palsy
B) Heterotopic ossification requiring excision
C) Nonunion
D) Elbow stiffness with loss of terminal extension
E) Infection
questions.answer:
D)
Elbow stiffness with loss of terminal extension is the most common complication after operative treatment of distal humerus fractures, reported in the majority of patients. This is why stable dual-plate fixation permitting early range-of-motion exercises is emphasized. Loss of 10–15° of terminal extension is typical even with optimal fixation and rehabilitation.

A is incorrect because radial nerve palsy is more commonly associated with humeral shaft fractures (particularly at the spiral groove), not distal humerus fracture surgery. Ulnar neuropathy (not radial) is the more relevant nerve issue at the distal humerus.
B is incorrect because while heterotopic ossification can occur, clinically significant HO requiring surgical excision is relatively uncommon compared to stiffness.
C is incorrect because nonunion after modern dual-plate fixation of the distal humerus occurs in only about 2–5% of cases, making it far less common than stiffness.
E is incorrect because infection rates after operative fixation of distal humerus fractures are low (typically <5%), well below the incidence of postoperative stiffness.

questions.question:
Which laboratory profile is most consistent with nutritional osteomalacia?
A) Normal calcium, normal phosphate, normal alkaline phosphatase
B) Low-normal calcium, low phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase, elevated PTH
C) Low calcium, elevated phosphate, low PTH
D) Elevated calcium, low phosphate, elevated PTH
E) Normal calcium, normal phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase, normal PTH
questions.answer:
B)
Vitamin D deficiency reduces intestinal calcium absorption, triggering secondary hyperparathyroidism that restores serum calcium toward low-normal at the expense of renal phosphate wasting. The classic laboratory profile is therefore low-normal calcium, low phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase (from increased osteoblastic activity at unmineralized osteoid), elevated PTH, and low 25-OH vitamin D. Looser zones (pseudofractures) on imaging are pathognomonic.

A is incorrect because nutritional osteomalacia always produces biochemical abnormalities — at minimum an elevated alkaline phosphatase and low phosphate — so an entirely normal panel excludes the diagnosis.
C is incorrect because low calcium with elevated phosphate and low PTH is the profile of hypoparathyroidism, not osteomalacia; in osteomalacia PTH is elevated (secondary hyperparathyroidism), not low.
D is incorrect because elevated calcium with low phosphate and elevated PTH describes primary hyperparathyroidism, not osteomalacia.
E is incorrect because normal calcium and phosphate with an isolated elevated alkaline phosphatase and normal PTH is characteristic of Paget disease, not osteomalacia.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old sustains an anterior shoulder dislocation. The most likely associated pathology is:
A) Posterior labral tear
B) SLAP tear type II
C) Bankart lesion (anteroinferior labral detachment)
D) Reverse Hill-Sachs lesion
E) Rotator interval tear
questions.answer:
C)
Detachment of the anteroinferior labrum and inferior glenohumeral ligament complex (Bankart lesion) is present in more than 85% of traumatic anterior dislocations, often accompanied by a Hill-Sachs impression on the posterosuperior humeral head. A bony Bankart involves the glenoid rim. In patients over 40, an associated rotator cuff tear becomes increasingly common and should be evaluated.

A is incorrect because a posterior labral tear (reverse Bankart) is associated with posterior shoulder dislocations, not anterior dislocations. B is incorrect because SLAP type II tears involve the superior labrum and biceps anchor; while they can coexist, they are not the most commonly associated pathology with anterior dislocation. D is incorrect because a reverse Hill-Sachs lesion (McLaughlin lesion) is an impaction fracture of the anteromedial humeral head seen with posterior dislocations, not anterior dislocations. E is incorrect because rotator interval tears are not the most common pathology associated with anterior dislocation; the Bankart lesion is far more prevalent.

questions.question:
Which infection presents with Kanavel signs and requires urgent surgical drainage?
A) Cellulitis
B) Felon
C) Pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis
D) Paronychia
E) Herpetic whitlow
questions.answer:
C)
Kanavel's four cardinal signs are fusiform (sausage-shaped) digital swelling, the finger held in slight flexion at rest, tenderness along the flexor tendon sheath, and pain with passive extension of the digit. Pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis requires urgent surgical irrigation of the flexor sheath and intravenous antibiotics to prevent tendon necrosis, adhesions, and proximal spread into the deep palmar spaces.

A is incorrect because cellulitis is a superficial soft-tissue infection that presents with diffuse erythema and warmth but does not produce Kanavel signs and is typically managed with antibiotics alone, not surgical sheath drainage.
B is incorrect because a felon is a closed-space infection of the fingertip pulp that presents with a tense, throbbing distal phalanx; it requires incision and drainage of the pulp but does not involve the flexor sheath or produce Kanavel signs.
D is incorrect because paronychia is an infection of the nail fold (perionychium) that causes localized periungual swelling and erythema; it is treated with warm soaks or incision/drainage of the nail fold, not flexor sheath irrigation.
E is incorrect because herpetic whitlow is a viral (HSV) infection of the fingertip that produces grouped vesicles; it is self-limited, and surgical incision is contraindicated because it risks bacterial superinfection and viral dissemination.

questions.question:
The most common complication after distal radius fracture, occurring even after nondisplaced fractures, is:
A) Median nerve dysfunction/carpal tunnel syndrome
B) Compartment syndrome
C) Nonunion
D) Malunion
E) Extensor pollicis longus rupture
questions.answer:
A)
Median neuropathy is the most common complication of distal radius fracture, resulting from swelling, hematoma, and traction. EPL rupture classically occurs 6-12 weeks after a minimally displaced fracture from attritional damage within the third dorsal compartment and is treated with extensor indicis proprius transfer. Nonunion is rare. Complex regional pain syndrome is another important complication; vitamin C supplementation has been proposed to reduce its incidence.

questions.question:
Which system quantifies the risk of pathologic fracture from a metastatic long bone lesion?
A) Musculoskeletal Tumor Society functional score
B) Karnofsky score
C) TLICS
D) Mirels scoring system
E) Enneking staging
questions.answer:
D)
The Mirels scoring system assigns 1–3 points each for site (upper limb, lower limb, peritrochanteric), pain (mild, moderate, functional/mechanical), lesion type (blastic, mixed, lytic), and size relative to cortical diameter (<1/3, 1/3–2/3, >2/3). A total score ≥9 indicates prophylactic fixation, 8 is borderline, and ≤7 can be managed with radiation. Other classic indications for prophylactic fixation include a lytic lesion >2.5 cm, cortical destruction >50%, and persistent pain after radiation.

A is incorrect because the Musculoskeletal Tumor Society (MSTS) functional score measures post-treatment limb function (pain, function, emotional acceptance, supports, walking, gait), not fracture risk.
B is incorrect because the Karnofsky score rates overall patient performance status and life expectancy, not the mechanical risk of pathologic fracture.
C is incorrect because TLICS (Thoracolumbar Injury Classification and Severity) is used to guide management of thoracolumbar spine trauma, not metastatic long bone lesions.
E is incorrect because the Enneking staging system classifies musculoskeletal tumors by grade, local extent, and presence of metastases to guide surgical margins; it does not quantify pathologic fracture risk.

questions.question:
