A 34-year-old man has an inflammatory arthritis with dactylitis, nail pitting, and asymmetric distal interphalangeal joint involvement. Radiographs of the hand would most likely show:
A) Bilateral sacroiliac ankylosis without peripheral change
B) Chondrocalcinosis of the triangular fibrocartilage
C) Punched-out erosions with overhanging edges
D) Symmetric marginal erosions with periarticular osteopenia
E) Erosive change with adjacent bony proliferation and pencil-in-cup deformity
questions.answer:
E)
Psoriatic arthritis characteristically combines erosion with adjacent new bone formation, producing fluffy periostitis, ankylosis, and the pencil-in-cup deformity, along with DIP involvement and dactylitis; bone density is typically preserved.

A is incorrect because bilateral sacroiliac ankylosis without peripheral joint changes is more characteristic of ankylosing spondylitis, which presents with axial involvement rather than the peripheral DIP disease and dactylitis described here.
B is incorrect because chondrocalcinosis of the triangular fibrocartilage is the hallmark of calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD/pseudogout), not psoriatic arthritis.
C is incorrect because punched-out erosions with overhanging edges (Martel sign) are characteristic of tophaceous gout, not psoriatic arthritis.
D is incorrect because symmetric marginal erosions with periarticular osteopenia are the hallmark of rheumatoid arthritis, which typically involves the MCP and PIP joints symmetrically and spares the DIP joints.

questions.question:
A new screening test for periprosthetic joint infection is applied to a population with low disease prevalence. Compared with a high-prevalence population, which test characteristic will decrease?
A) Likelihood ratio
B) Specificity
C) Negative predictive value
D) Sensitivity
E) Positive predictive value
questions.answer:
E)
Positive predictive value (PPV) depends on disease prevalence. As prevalence decreases, the proportion of true positives among all positive results falls, so PPV decreases. This is why screening tests applied to low-risk populations yield more false-positive results.

A is incorrect because likelihood ratios are derived solely from sensitivity and specificity and are intrinsic to the test; they do not change with prevalence.
B is incorrect because specificity is an intrinsic test property (true-negative rate) determined by the test's performance characteristics, not by prevalence.
C is incorrect because negative predictive value actually increases as prevalence decreases (fewer diseased individuals means fewer false negatives relative to true negatives).
D is incorrect because sensitivity is an intrinsic test property (true-positive rate) and does not vary with prevalence.

questions.question:
Which statement regarding tendon healing is most accurate?
A) Healing is entirely dependent on synovial diffusion with no vascular contribution
B) Immobilization for 12 weeks optimizes final tensile strength
C) Type III collagen predominates early and is replaced by type I during remodeling
D) Tendon regains normal tensile strength by 6 weeks
E) Collagen fibers align randomly and never reorient
questions.answer:
C)
Early tendon repair tissue is rich in type III collagen, which has smaller-diameter fibrils and lower tensile strength. During the remodeling phase, type III collagen is gradually replaced by longitudinally oriented type I collagen, restoring mechanical properties. Both extrinsic (peritendinous vascular) and intrinsic (tenocyte/synovial diffusion) mechanisms contribute to tendon healing, and controlled early motion improves collagen alignment and final strength.

A is incorrect because tendon healing relies on both synovial diffusion (intrinsic) and vascular ingrowth (extrinsic) mechanisms; it is not entirely dependent on diffusion alone.
B is incorrect because prolonged immobilization (12 weeks) leads to adhesion formation, decreased excursion, and inferior tensile strength compared with controlled early motion protocols.
D is incorrect because tendon never fully regains normal tensile strength by 6 weeks; mature remodeling takes months, and repaired tendon typically achieves only a fraction of its original strength at 6 weeks.
E is incorrect because collagen fibers do reorient along lines of stress during the remodeling phase, particularly when early controlled motion is applied; they do not remain randomly oriented.

questions.question:
Which antibiotic is most appropriate for empiric coverage while awaiting cultures in a patient with an acute native joint infection and a history of MRSA colonization?
A) Cefazolin
B) Clindamycin monotherapy
C) Doxycycline
D) Vancomycin
E) Ampicillin
questions.answer:
D)
Vancomycin provides reliable coverage of MRSA and is the empiric agent of choice in patients with known MRSA colonization or in high-prevalence settings. It is typically combined with a gram-negative agent depending on the clinical scenario. Surgical drainage remains essential alongside antibiotic therapy.

A is incorrect because cefazolin is a first-generation cephalosporin that covers methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) but does not provide MRSA coverage.
B is incorrect because clindamycin monotherapy has variable MRSA susceptibility (inducible resistance via erm genes) and is not considered first-line empiric therapy for septic arthritis in a known MRSA-colonized patient; it may be used as an adjunct but not as sole empiric coverage.
C is incorrect because doxycycline has some activity against community-acquired MRSA skin infections but is bacteriostatic, has limited joint penetration data, and is not recommended as empiric monotherapy for acute septic arthritis.
E is incorrect because ampicillin is a penicillin-class antibiotic with no activity against MRSA (or even MSSA due to beta-lactamase production) and would be inappropriate in this setting.

questions.question:
Following total hip arthroplasty, a patient reports the operated leg feels 1 cm longer. Preoperative templating aims to restore both leg length and offset because inadequate femoral offset most directly produces:
A) Sciatic nerve palsy
B) Increased polyethylene wear only
C) Abductor weakness with a limp and increased joint reaction force
D) Femoral stem subsidence
E) Heterotopic ossification
questions.answer:
C)
Femoral offset determines the abductor moment arm. Reduced offset shortens that lever arm, requiring greater abductor force for the same task, which increases the joint reaction force and produces weakness, a Trendelenburg limp, and sometimes instability. Offset can be restored independently of leg length using high-offset stems or by adjusting neck length and stem position, which is why templating addresses both parameters.

A is incorrect because sciatic nerve palsy is related to excessive limb lengthening or direct surgical trauma, not to inadequate femoral offset per se. B is incorrect because while increased joint reaction force from reduced offset can accelerate polyethylene wear, the most direct clinical consequence is abductor dysfunction and limp, not wear alone. D is incorrect because femoral stem subsidence is related to undersizing, poor fixation, or inadequate canal fill rather than to offset restoration. E is incorrect because heterotopic ossification is related to soft-tissue trauma, patient predisposition, and inadequate prophylaxis, not to femoral offset.

questions.question:
An 80-year-old woman with a four-part proximal humerus fracture undergoes reverse total shoulder arthroplasty. Healing of the tuberosities in this setting most affects:
A) Nothing, since the tuberosities are always excised
B) Deltoid strength
C) Glenoid baseplate fixation
D) External rotation and the ability to position the hand in space
E) Prosthetic stability against inferior subluxation
questions.answer:
D)
Reverse arthroplasty restores elevation through the deltoid regardless of cuff status, but external rotation depends on the posterior cuff (infraspinatus and teres minor) attached to a healed greater tuberosity. Tuberosity nonunion or resorption leaves patients unable to rotate the arm externally, limiting the ability to position the hand in space. Techniques that improve healing include a fracture-specific stem, bone grafting, and circumferential suture repair; lateralized glenosphere designs also aid rotation.

A is incorrect because the tuberosities are not routinely excised in fracture reverse shoulder arthroplasty; they are carefully repaired around the prosthesis to restore rotator cuff function, particularly external rotation.
B is incorrect because deltoid strength is determined by axillary nerve integrity and deltoid origin/insertion, not by tuberosity healing; the reverse prosthesis is specifically designed to rely on the deltoid for elevation independent of the tuberosities.
C is incorrect because glenoid baseplate fixation depends on bone quality, screw purchase, and implant design at the glenoid side and is unrelated to tuberosity healing on the humeral side.
E is incorrect because inferior subluxation in reverse arthroplasty is primarily prevented by proper tensioning of the deltoid and appropriate glenosphere/humeral component sizing, not by tuberosity healing.

questions.question:
A 78-year-old becomes acutely confused and agitated on postoperative day 2 after hip fracture surgery, with fluctuating attention. The most appropriate initial approach is:
A) Evaluate for reversible causes including hypoxia, infection, pain, medications, and urinary retention
B) Discharge to home with family supervision
C) Benzodiazepine administration
D) Immediate haloperidol and physical restraints
E) Head CT and neurology consultation for all patients
questions.answer:
A)
Postoperative delirium is common after hip fracture surgery and is associated with increased mortality and institutionalization. Management begins with identifying reversible contributors: hypoxia, sepsis, undertreated pain, anticholinergic and benzodiazepine use, electrolyte abnormalities, urinary retention, and constipation. Nonpharmacologic measures (reorientation, sleep hygiene, early mobilization, glasses and hearing aids) are first-line; low-dose antipsychotics are reserved for dangerous agitation.

B is incorrect because discharging an acutely delirious patient home is unsafe; delirium requires inpatient evaluation and management of its underlying causes. C is incorrect because benzodiazepines worsen delirium (except in alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal) and are contraindicated as initial treatment. D is incorrect because physical restraints increase agitation and injury risk, and haloperidol is reserved only for severe, dangerous agitation after reversible causes have been addressed—not as an immediate first step. E is incorrect because head CT and neurology consultation are not warranted for all patients with postoperative delirium; they should be considered selectively when focal neurologic deficits or other red flags are present, not as a routine initial approach.

questions.question:
Which of the following best describes the organic matrix of mature lamellar bone?
A) Equal proportions of type I and type III collagen
B) Predominantly type X collagen with hydroxyapatite crystals
C) Predominantly type II collagen with proteoglycan aggregates
D) Predominantly type I collagen, approximately 90% of organic matrix
E) Predominantly elastin with interspersed type I collagen
questions.answer:
D)
Bone is roughly 60% mineral, 30% organic, and 10% water by weight. Type I collagen constitutes about 90% of the organic matrix; the remainder is noncollagenous proteins (osteocalcin, osteonectin, osteopontin, proteoglycans). Type II collagen is the dominant collagen of hyaline cartilage, and type X is produced by hypertrophic chondrocytes at the physis and in the calcified zone of articular cartilage.

A is incorrect because mature lamellar bone contains predominantly type I collagen; type III collagen is found mainly in early fracture callus (woven bone) and soft tissues such as skin and blood vessels, and it does not constitute an equal proportion of the bone organic matrix.
B is incorrect because type X collagen is produced by hypertrophic chondrocytes during endochondral ossification and is not a major component of the organic matrix of mature lamellar bone.
C is incorrect because type II collagen with proteoglycan aggregates describes the matrix of hyaline (articular) cartilage, not bone.
E is incorrect because elastin is a structural protein of elastic tissues such as ligaments and arterial walls; it is not a significant component of the bone organic matrix.

questions.question:
Which biopsy technique is generally preferred as the initial approach for a deep soft tissue mass suspicious for sarcoma?
A) Frozen section only
B) Excisional biopsy
C) Incisional biopsy with a transverse incision
D) Fine needle aspiration for all lesions
E) Core needle biopsy, often image-guided
questions.answer:
E)
Core needle biopsy (often image-guided) is the preferred initial approach for a deep soft tissue mass suspicious for sarcoma. It provides tissue architecture sufficient for histologic diagnosis and grading, with high diagnostic accuracy, low complication rates, and minimal contamination of surrounding tissue planes.

A is incorrect because frozen section alone is not a biopsy technique for initial diagnosis; it is an intraoperative adjunct used to confirm tissue adequacy and does not replace permanent histologic analysis needed for definitive diagnosis and grading.
B is incorrect because excisional biopsy of a deep mass contaminates surrounding tissue planes and compromises subsequent limb-salvage surgery; excisional biopsy is acceptable only for small, superficial lesions (generally <3–5 cm and above the fascia).
C is incorrect because incisional biopsy with a transverse incision violates the principle of using a longitudinal incision aligned with the future definitive resection; a transverse incision crosses compartments and cannot be easily excised en bloc, increasing the risk of local contamination.
D is incorrect because fine needle aspiration (FNA) yields cytology without tissue architecture, which is generally insufficient for the initial diagnosis and grading of a new sarcoma; FNA is more appropriate for confirming recurrence or metastasis in a patient with a known diagnosis.

questions.question:
A widened scapholunate interval of 5 mm with a scapholunate angle of 75 degrees and a cortical ring sign indicates:
A) Ulnar impaction syndrome
B) Volar intercalated segment instability
C) Kienbock disease
D) Midcarpal instability
E) Dorsal intercalated segment instability from scapholunate ligament disruption
questions.answer:
E)
Scapholunate ligament rupture allows the scaphoid to flex and the lunate to extend, producing a DISI pattern with a scapholunate angle above 60–70 degrees, the Terry Thomas sign of diastasis (widened SL interval ≥3 mm), and a cortical ring sign from the abnormally flexed scaphoid seen on the PA view. Untreated, SL dissociation progresses to scapholunate advanced collapse (SLAC) wrist in a predictable pattern beginning at the radial styloid.

A is incorrect because ulnar impaction syndrome involves ulnocarpal abutment with ulnar-positive variance causing chondromalacia and lunotriquetral ligament degeneration; it does not produce a widened SL interval or DISI pattern. B is incorrect because volar intercalated segment instability (VISI) is associated with lunotriquetral ligament disruption and a scapholunate angle below 30 degrees, not the increased angle and SL diastasis described here. C is incorrect because Kienböck disease is osteonecrosis of the lunate associated with ulnar-negative variance; it does not cause SL widening or a cortical ring sign. D is incorrect because midcarpal instability involves laxity at the midcarpal joint (capitolunate) and typically presents with a painful clunk during ulnar deviation, not with a widened SL interval and DISI alignment.

questions.question:
A 78-year-old falls and sustains a type II odontoid fracture with 6 mm of displacement. Compared with nonoperative halo treatment, surgical stabilization in this population is associated with:
A) Identical outcomes across all treatments
B) Contraindication to any surgical intervention over age 70
C) Mandatory anterior odontoid screw fixation regardless of fracture obliquity
D) Higher mortality and higher nonunion
E) Lower rates of nonunion, with halo vest use in the elderly carrying significant morbidity
questions.answer:
E)
Type II odontoid fractures have a tenuous blood supply and high nonunion rates, increased by age over 50, displacement greater than 5 mm, angulation greater than 10 degrees, and comminution. Halo vests in the elderly are poorly tolerated with high rates of pneumonia, pin-site complications, and mortality. Posterior C1-C2 fusion is generally more reliable in this population; anterior odontoid screw fixation requires a reducible fracture, an intact transverse ligament, and a fracture line that is not oblique from anterior-inferior to posterior-superior.

A is incorrect because outcomes are not identical — halo treatment in the elderly carries significantly higher morbidity and nonunion rates compared with surgical stabilization. B is incorrect because age over 70 is not an absolute contraindication to surgery; in fact, surgical fixation is often preferred in the elderly to avoid the complications of prolonged halo immobilization. C is incorrect because anterior odontoid screw fixation is not universally applicable — it is contraindicated in fractures with an anterior-inferior to posterior-superior obliquity, transverse ligament disruption, or irreducible fractures. D is incorrect because surgical stabilization is associated with lower (not higher) nonunion rates; it is halo vest treatment in the elderly that carries higher mortality and nonunion.

questions.question:
Scapular notching after reverse total shoulder arthroplasty is reduced by:
A) Increased humeral neck-shaft angle to 155 degrees
B) Superior glenosphere placement with superior tilt
C) Medializing the humeral component
D) Inferior glenosphere positioning with inferior tilt and lateralization
E) A smaller glenosphere
questions.answer:
D)
Inferior glenosphere positioning with inferior tilt and lateralization is the most effective strategy to reduce scapular notching after reverse total shoulder arthroplasty. Placing the baseplate flush with or inferior to the inferior glenoid rim and tilting it inferiorly (~10–15°) increases the impingement-free arc of adduction, reducing mechanical contact between the humeral polyethylene and the scapular neck. Lateralizing the center of rotation further decreases this risk.

A is incorrect because increasing the humeral neck-shaft angle to 155° (more valgus) does not reliably reduce scapular notching and may increase impingement in adduction. B is incorrect because superior glenosphere placement with superior tilt actually increases the risk of scapular notching by reducing the impingement-free arc inferiorly. C is incorrect because medializing the humeral component does not address the glenoid-side impingement that causes notching; in fact, medialization of the overall construct tends to worsen notching. E is incorrect because a smaller glenosphere provides less inferior overhang and a smaller impingement-free arc, thereby increasing the risk of scapular notching (larger glenospheres reduce notching).

questions.question:
Which curve pattern in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is most likely to be associated with an underlying neural axis abnormality requiring MRI?
A) Left thoracic curve with abnormal abdominal reflexes
B) Double major curve with normal reflexes
C) Lumbar curve of 20 degrees in a mature patient
D) Right thoracolumbar curve of 25 degrees
E) Right thoracic curve in a 14-year-old girl with normal neurologic exam
questions.answer:
A)
A left thoracic curve is an atypical curve pattern in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis and, when combined with abnormal (absent or asymmetric) abdominal reflexes, raises significant concern for an underlying neural axis abnormality such as syringomyelia, Chiari malformation, tethered cord, or intraspinal tumor. MRI of the entire spine is indicated in this setting.

B is incorrect because a double major curve with normal reflexes is a recognized typical pattern in AIS and does not independently warrant MRI.
C is incorrect because a small lumbar curve in a skeletally mature patient with no atypical features is a benign presentation unlikely to harbor neural axis pathology.
D is incorrect because a right thoracolumbar curve of moderate magnitude without atypical features (pain, neurologic findings, left-sidedness) does not mandate MRI.
E is incorrect because a right thoracic curve in an adolescent girl with a normal neurologic exam is the classic, most common idiopathic pattern and does not require MRI.

questions.question:
When performing in situ screw fixation for SCFE, correct screw placement is:
A) Started anteriorly on the femoral neck and directed perpendicular to the physis, ending central in the epiphysis, with threads entirely across the physis
B) Placed with threads crossing into the joint space
C) Placed in the inferior epiphysis to maximize purchase
D) Directed along the femoral neck axis without regard to the epiphysis
E) Started posteriorly and directed anteriorly
questions.answer:
A)
Because the epiphysis displaces posteriorly and inferiorly in SCFE, the starting point on the femoral neck moves anteriorly as slip severity increases so that the screw can be directed perpendicular to the physis and end centrally within the epiphysis. Central placement maximizes purchase and minimizes the risk of joint penetration; the approach-withdraw fluoroscopic technique confirms the screw is not intra-articular. All threads must cross the physis to allow compression and prevent slip progression.

B is incorrect because threads crossing into the joint space risks chondrolysis and septic arthritis; the screw must remain entirely within bone, and joint penetration is a recognized serious complication of in situ fixation.

C is incorrect because placing the screw in the inferior epiphysis does not provide optimal central fixation and increases the risk of suboptimal purchase and potential cutout; the goal is central-central placement within the epiphysis on both AP and lateral views.

D is incorrect because directing the screw along the femoral neck axis without regard to the epiphysis would result in the screw missing the epiphysis or being eccentrically placed, especially in moderate-to-severe slips where the epiphysis is posteriorly displaced; the screw must be directed perpendicular to the physis to end centrally in the epiphysis.

E is incorrect because a posterior starting point directed anteriorly would risk posterior cortex penetration and would not achieve the correct trajectory perpendicular to the physis; the anterior starting point is necessary to accommodate the posterior displacement of the epiphysis.

questions.question:
In a child with a painful hip and a history of low-grade fever, MRI shows a subperiosteal collection along the proximal femoral metaphysis with an adjacent joint effusion. The most appropriate management is:
A) Urgent surgical drainage of both the joint and the subperiosteal abscess with culture-directed antibiotics
B) Bracing
C) Observation
D) Aspiration of the hip only
E) Antibiotics alone
questions.answer:
A)
The proximal femoral metaphysis is intracapsular, so metaphyseal osteomyelitis can decompress directly into the hip joint, producing concurrent septic arthritis. Both compartments must be drained. Similar intracapsular metaphyses occur at the proximal humerus, radial neck, and distal fibula. S. aureus is the most common organism; MRSA infections are associated with more severe disease, multifocal involvement, and deep venous thrombosis.

B is incorrect because bracing has no role in the management of an acute bone/joint infection and would allow progression of sepsis.
C is incorrect because observation without intervention risks rapid joint destruction, systemic sepsis, and growth disturbance in a child with a confirmed abscess and effusion.
D is incorrect because aspiration of the hip alone addresses the septic arthritis but leaves the subperiosteal abscess undrained; the ongoing source of infection would persist and recontaminate the joint.
E is incorrect because antibiotics alone, without surgical drainage, are insufficient when a subperiosteal abscess and joint effusion are already present; source control is essential for adequate treatment.

questions.question:
A 6-year-old catches a finger in a door and has a nail plate avulsed from the eponychial fold with an underlying displaced distal phalanx physeal fracture. The most appropriate management is:
A) Radiographs only, with no intervention
B) Irrigation, removal of interposed nail matrix, reduction, and antibiotics, as this represents an open physeal fracture
C) Buddy taping and observation
D) Nail plate replacement alone without exploration
E) Amputation at the DIP joint
questions.answer:
B)
This is a Seymour fracture: an open Salter-Harris type I or II fracture of the distal phalanx with the germinal matrix or nail plate interposed in the fracture site. It is frequently mistaken for a simple mallet injury or nail avulsion. Untreated, it leads to osteomyelitis, physeal arrest, and nail deformity. Treatment requires irrigation and debridement, extraction of interposed tissue, fracture reduction, nail plate (or foil substitute) replacement to splint the eponychial fold, and prophylactic antibiotics.

A is incorrect because this is an open fracture requiring operative intervention; observation alone risks infection and growth disturbance.
C is incorrect because buddy taping does not address the open wound, the interposed soft tissue blocking reduction, or the need for antibiotics.
D is incorrect because simply replacing the nail plate without exploring the fracture site leaves interposed germinal matrix in the physis, preventing reduction and predisposing to osteomyelitis and physeal arrest.
E is incorrect because amputation is not indicated; this injury is reliably treated with irrigation, debridement, reduction, and antibiotics, preserving the digit.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old office worker has 5 months of lateral elbow pain reproduced by resisted wrist extension. Counseling should include which statement about natural history?
A) Symptoms are permanent without surgery
B) The condition reflects acute inflammation of the extensor carpi radialis longus
C) Immediate surgical release is standard of care
D) Corticosteroid injection provides durable long-term cure
E) Most cases resolve within 12 to 18 months with activity modification and therapy, and corticosteroid injection may worsen long-term outcomes
questions.answer:
E)
Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) is an angiofibroblastic tendinosis of the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) origin rather than an acute inflammatory process. The natural history is favorable: most patients improve within 12 to 18 months with activity modification, counterforce bracing, and eccentric strengthening exercises. Corticosteroid injection may provide short-term pain relief but has been associated with higher recurrence rates and worse outcomes at one year compared with observation alone.

A is incorrect because the natural history of lateral epicondylitis is self-limited in the vast majority of cases; symptoms are not permanent, and most patients recover without surgery. B is incorrect because the pathology involves the extensor carpi radialis brevis (not longus) origin, and the process is a degenerative tendinosis rather than an acute inflammation. C is incorrect because surgical release is reserved for refractory cases that fail 6–12 months of conservative treatment; immediate surgery is not the standard of care. D is incorrect because corticosteroid injection provides only short-term symptom relief and randomized trials have shown it is associated with higher recurrence and inferior long-term outcomes compared with physiotherapy or watchful waiting.

questions.question:
A cannulated 7.3-mm screw is compared with a solid screw of the same outer diameter. The cannulated screw demonstrates which biomechanical property?
A) Increased torsional rigidity from the hollow cross-section
B) Substantially reduced bending rigidity because the central core carries most of the load
C) Only a modest reduction in bending rigidity because material near the neutral axis contributes little
D) Increased pullout strength due to greater thread depth
E) No difference in insertional torque
questions.answer:
C)
Bending rigidity depends on the area moment of inertia, which weights material by the square of its distance from the neutral axis. Material at the center contributes very little, so removing it to create a cannulation reduces bending rigidity only modestly while permitting guidewire-directed placement.

A is incorrect because cannulation reduces torsional rigidity (polar moment of inertia decreases when core material is removed); it does not increase it.
B is incorrect because the central core carries the least load in bending (material near the neutral axis contributes minimally to the area moment of inertia), so the reduction in bending rigidity is modest, not substantial.
D is incorrect because pullout strength depends on outer thread diameter and thread purchase in bone, not on the presence of a cannulation; cannulated and solid screws of the same outer diameter and thread design have similar pullout strength.
E is incorrect because cannulated screws typically require higher insertional torque due to the thinner wall and increased friction; there is a measurable difference in insertional torque between cannulated and solid screws.

questions.question:
In adult spinal deformity, which parameter correlates most strongly with patient-reported disability?
A) Sagittal vertical axis, pelvic tilt, and pelvic incidence minus lumbar lordosis mismatch
B) Cobb angle of the thoracic curve
C) Coronal Cobb magnitude alone
D) Apical vertebral rotation
E) Number of levels fused
questions.answer:
A)
Sagittal alignment drives disability in adult deformity far more than coronal magnitude. Thresholds associated with disability include SVA above 5 cm, pelvic tilt above 20-25 degrees, and PI-LL mismatch above 10 degrees. Surgical planning aims to restore these parameters, adjusted for age, since older patients tolerate greater positive sagittal balance.

B is incorrect because the thoracic Cobb angle is a coronal-plane measure and does not correlate as strongly with patient-reported outcomes as sagittal parameters.
C is incorrect because coronal Cobb magnitude alone has a relatively weak correlation with disability; sagittal malalignment is the dominant driver of symptoms.
D is incorrect because apical vertebral rotation is a measure of rotational deformity and has not been shown to correlate most strongly with patient-reported disability scores.
E is incorrect because the number of levels fused is a surgical variable, not a spinal alignment parameter, and does not independently predict patient-reported disability.

questions.question:
A 20-year-old runner has vague midfoot pain with tenderness over the "N spot." Radiographs are normal. Which statement about this injury is most accurate?
A) It is a high-risk stress fracture of the tarsal navicular requiring CT or MRI and non-weight-bearing immobilization or fixation
B) It always heals within 2 weeks
C) It occurs only in patients with rheumatoid arthritis
D) It is a low-risk stress fracture treated with continued running
E) Bone scan is contraindicated
questions.answer:
A)
Navicular stress fractures occur in the relatively avascular central third, are notoriously occult on radiographs, and present with vague dorsal midfoot pain and tenderness at the proximal dorsal navicular (the "N spot"). They are high-risk stress fractures prone to nonunion and require CT or MRI for diagnosis, with non-weight-bearing immobilization for approximately 6 weeks or screw fixation in athletes.

B is incorrect because navicular stress fractures are slow to heal due to the poor vascularity of the central third; they typically require at least 6 weeks of non-weight-bearing treatment and certainly do not resolve in 2 weeks.
C is incorrect because navicular stress fractures are overuse injuries seen in runners and jumping athletes and are not limited to patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
D is incorrect because the tarsal navicular is classified as a high-risk stress fracture site; continued running would risk displacement, nonunion, or complete fracture.
E is incorrect because bone scan is a valid diagnostic tool for detecting stress fractures when radiographs are normal; it is not contraindicated and was historically used before MRI became the preferred advanced imaging modality.

questions.question:
Dupuytren disease is characterized by proliferation of which cell type and involvement of which structure?
A) Chondrocytes in the pulley system
B) Synoviocytes in the flexor sheath
C) Schwann cells in the digital nerve
D) Osteoblasts in the periosteum
E) Myofibroblasts in the palmar fascia, with cords derived from normal bands
questions.answer:
E)
Dupuytren disease is a myofibroblast-driven fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar fascia in which normal anatomic bands become pathologic cords. The spiral cord (formed from the pretendinous band, spiral band, lateral digital sheet, and Grayson ligament) displaces the neurovascular bundle superficially, midline, and proximally, placing it at risk during surgery. Indications for intervention include MCP contracture ≥30°, any PIP contracture, or a positive tabletop test.

A is incorrect because chondrocytes are cartilage-forming cells and the pulley system is not the primary structure involved in Dupuytren disease.
B is incorrect because synoviocytes line the flexor tendon sheath and are involved in conditions such as tenosynovitis or rheumatoid arthritis, not Dupuytren disease.
C is incorrect because Schwann cells are associated with peripheral nerve tumors (e.g., schwannomas) and are not the proliferating cell type in Dupuytren disease.
D is incorrect because osteoblasts are bone-forming cells of the periosteum and play no role in the pathogenesis of Dupuytren disease.

questions.question:
Which patient with a solitary bone lesion should undergo systemic staging before any surgical intervention?
A) A 40-year-old with a destructive lytic humeral lesion of unknown origin
B) A 12-year-old with a classic nonossifying fibroma
C) A 9-year-old with a fallen-fragment simple bone cyst
D) A 20-year-old with a classic osteoid osteoma nidus
E) A 30-year-old with an incidental osteochondroma
questions.answer:
A)
A destructive lytic lesion in a 40-year-old adult is metastatic carcinoma or myeloma until proven otherwise. Intervening surgically without systemic staging risks inadvertently violating a primary bone sarcoma, which contaminates the entire bone and can convert a limb-salvageable situation into an amputation. Appropriate workup includes history and physical examination, laboratory studies (CBC, CMP, SPEP/UPEP, PSA if male, thyroid studies), CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis, and a whole-body bone scan; this identifies the primary tumor in the majority of cases.

B is incorrect because a nonossifying fibroma is a benign, well-characterized developmental lesion with a classic eccentric, cortically based, sclerotic-bordered appearance; it requires no staging workup.
C is incorrect because a simple (unicameral) bone cyst with a fallen-fragment sign is a well-recognized benign lesion that does not require systemic staging.
D is incorrect because an osteoid osteoma with a classic nidus is a benign bone-forming tumor with a characteristic presentation and imaging appearance; systemic staging is unnecessary.
E is incorrect because an incidental osteochondroma is a common benign cartilage-capped exostosis that does not warrant systemic staging in the absence of concerning features (e.g., thick cartilage cap, rapid growth suggesting secondary chondrosarcoma).

questions.question:
The Ortolani maneuver is best described as:
A) Abduction and anterior lifting force reducing a dislocated hip with a palpable clunk
B) Assessment of asymmetric thigh folds
C) Assessment of femoral shortening with hips flexed
D) Measurement of limited abduction
E) Adduction and posterior force reproducing dislocation
questions.answer:
A)
The Ortolani maneuver reduces a dislocated hip: the examiner abducts the flexed hip while applying an anterior lifting force through the greater trochanter, producing a palpable "clunk" as the femoral head reduces over the posterior acetabular rim. It is a test of reducibility, not provocation.

B is incorrect because assessment of asymmetric thigh folds is a general physical examination finding that may suggest DDH but is not a named maneuver and is neither sensitive nor specific.
C is incorrect because assessment of femoral shortening with hips flexed describes the Galeazzi sign (apparent limb-length discrepancy), not the Ortolani maneuver.
D is incorrect because limited abduction is a clinical sign of DDH (most reliable after ~3 months of age) but is not a description of the Ortolani maneuver.
E is incorrect because adduction with a posterior force describes the Barlow maneuver, which is a provocative test that attempts to dislocate or sublux an unstable but currently located hip — the opposite of Ortolani.

questions.question:
A patient with end-stage ankle arthritis and pre-existing adjacent hindfoot joint arthritis is generally best treated with:
A) Bracing indefinitely
B) Ankle arthroscopy
C) Ankle arthrodesis
D) Total ankle arthroplasty
E) Below-knee amputation
questions.answer:
D)
When adjacent hindfoot joints (e.g., subtalar, talonavicular) already have arthritis, total ankle arthroplasty is generally preferred over ankle arthrodesis. Ankle fusion transfers increased stress to these already-compromised adjacent joints, accelerating their degeneration. Arthroplasty preserves ankle motion and reduces adjacent joint loading. Contraindications to total ankle arthroplasty include active infection, Charcot arthropathy, talar avascular necrosis, severe uncorrectable malalignment, and inadequate soft tissue coverage.

A is incorrect because bracing may temporize symptoms but does not definitively address end-stage arthritis and is not a long-term solution.
B is incorrect because ankle arthroscopy (e.g., debridement) is appropriate for early arthritis, not end-stage disease.
C is incorrect because ankle arthrodesis, while durable, transfers stress to adjacent joints; when those joints are already arthritic, fusion accelerates their degeneration, making it a less favorable choice.
E is incorrect because below-knee amputation is a salvage procedure reserved for cases where reconstruction is not feasible and is not first-line treatment for ankle arthritis.

questions.question:
Which patient is at greatest risk for pseudarthrosis after posterolateral lumbar fusion?
A) Nonsmoker with single-level instrumented fusion
B) Patient taking calcium and vitamin D
C) Patient with normal thyroid function
D) Active smoker with multilevel uninstrumented fusion
E) Patient with a BMI of 24
questions.answer:
D)
Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for pseudarthrosis and roughly doubles the nonunion rate. Multilevel fusions have more surfaces that must heal, and uninstrumented constructs lack the rigid fixation that promotes bony union. The combination of active smoking with multilevel uninstrumented fusion therefore carries the greatest pseudarthrosis risk. Other risk factors include NSAID use in the early postoperative period, diabetes, malnutrition, obesity, and osteoporosis.

A is incorrect because a nonsmoker undergoing a single-level instrumented fusion has the lowest-risk profile — single level reduces the number of fusion surfaces and instrumentation provides rigid fixation.
B is incorrect because adequate calcium and vitamin D supplementation supports bone metabolism and healing, reducing rather than increasing pseudarthrosis risk.
C is incorrect because normal thyroid function is a baseline healthy state; hypothyroidism or hyperparathyroidism would impair bone healing, not euthyroidism.
E is incorrect because a BMI of 24 is within the normal range; obesity (BMI ≥ 30) is the risk factor for pseudarthrosis, not a normal BMI.

questions.question:
A newborn has a flaccid arm held in adduction and internal rotation with the elbow extended, forearm pronated, and preserved hand function following a difficult delivery. The most likely lesion and prognosis are:
A) Complete plexus avulsion with no recovery expected
B) Congenital humeral pseudarthrosis
C) Upper trunk (C5-C6) brachial plexus birth palsy, with the majority recovering spontaneously
D) Klumpke palsy affecting C8-T1
E) Isolated radial nerve palsy
questions.answer:
C)
Erb palsy involves the upper trunk (C5-C6, sometimes C7), producing the classic waiter's tip posture — arm adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated — with preserved hand function. The majority recover spontaneously; return of biceps function by 3 months is a favorable prognostic sign, and failure of biceps recovery by 3 to 6 months is a common threshold for microsurgical exploration.

A is incorrect because complete plexus avulsion would produce a totally flaccid arm including loss of hand function; this child has preserved hand function, localizing the injury to the upper trunk.
B is incorrect because congenital humeral pseudarthrosis is an extremely rare condition presenting with abnormal humeral morphology, not a postural pattern of the entire upper extremity following a difficult delivery.
D is incorrect because Klumpke palsy (C8-T1) affects the hand and wrist flexors, presenting with a claw hand deformity and loss of hand function — the opposite of this child's preserved hand function.
E is incorrect because isolated radial nerve palsy would present with wrist and finger drop (loss of extension) rather than the global shoulder and elbow positioning seen in upper trunk palsy.

questions.question:
Morton neuroma most commonly occurs in which interspace and is characterized by:
A) Medial arch with tarsal tunnel signs
B) Third webspace with a positive Mulder click and plantar burning radiating to the toes
C) First interspace with dorsal numbness
D) Second metatarsal head with plantar callus only
E) Fifth interspace with bunionette
questions.answer:
B)
Morton neuroma (interdigital neuroma) is a perineural fibrosis most commonly affecting the third webspace, where the medial and lateral plantar nerve branches converge and where relative motion between the third and fourth rays is greatest. Patients present with plantar burning pain radiating to the toes and a positive Mulder click (palpable/audible click with lateral metatarsal compression). Treatment begins with wide shoes, metatarsal pads, and corticosteroid injection; excision through a dorsal approach with resection proximal to the transverse intermetatarsal ligament is used for refractory cases.

A is incorrect because Morton neuroma is an interdigital pathology, not a medial arch condition; tarsal tunnel signs (Tinel at the medial ankle, diffuse plantar numbness) indicate tarsal tunnel syndrome involving the posterior tibial nerve. C is incorrect because the first interspace is a rare location for Morton neuroma, and dorsal numbness is not a characteristic finding; dorsal foot numbness suggests a superficial peroneal nerve issue. D is incorrect because a plantar callus under the second metatarsal head without neuritic symptoms suggests a mechanical metatarsalgia or transfer lesion, not a neuroma. E is incorrect because the fifth interspace does not exist (there are only four interspaces), and a bunionette is a bony prominence of the fifth metatarsal head unrelated to interdigital neuroma.

questions.question:
The most important classification of SCFE for prognosis is:
A) Pre-slip versus slip
B) Unilateral versus bilateral
C) Acute versus chronic by symptom duration
D) Mild, moderate, severe by slip angle
E) Stable versus unstable, based on ability to bear weight
questions.answer:
E)
The Loder classification defines a stable slip as one in which the patient can bear weight with or without crutches, and unstable as inability to bear weight. Osteonecrosis rates are low in stable slips (~0–10%) but reported from 20% to nearly 50% in unstable slips, making stability the dominant prognostic factor.

A is incorrect because the "pre-slip" designation (widened physis without displacement) is a radiographic observation that does not carry the same prognostic weight as stability status.
B is incorrect because laterality (unilateral vs. bilateral) affects treatment planning but does not predict osteonecrosis or overall prognosis as strongly as stability.
C is incorrect because the acute-versus-chronic distinction by symptom duration (< 3 weeks vs. ≥ 3 weeks) does not reliably predict osteonecrosis; an acute-on-chronic slip can be stable or unstable, and it is the ability to bear weight that determines risk.
D is incorrect because slip severity by the Southwick angle correlates with later femoroacetabular impingement and degenerative arthritis but does not predict acute osteonecrosis risk as reliably as the Loder stability classification.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old woman with single-level C5-C6 radiculopathy, no facet arthropathy, preserved motion, and normal alignment is considering cervical disc arthroplasty rather than fusion. Which factor would contraindicate arthroplasty?
A) Single-level disease
B) Preserved disc height
C) Significant facet arthrosis with segmental instability
D) Age under 50
E) Absence of prior cervical surgery
questions.answer:
C)
Disc arthroplasty aims to preserve segmental motion and potentially reduce adjacent segment degeneration. It requires a mobile, well-aligned segment without instability. Significant facet arthrosis with segmental instability is a contraindication because the arthroplasty relies on intact posterior elements and facet joints to constrain motion; diseased facets cannot provide this, risking abnormal kinematics and poor outcomes.

A is incorrect because single-level disease is actually the ideal indication for cervical disc arthroplasty, not a contraindication.
B is incorrect because preserved disc height is favorable for arthroplasty; it allows proper device sizing and restoration of foraminal height.
D is incorrect because younger age (under 50) is considered favorable for arthroplasty, as these patients benefit most from motion preservation and reduced adjacent segment stress over their remaining lifespan.
E is incorrect because the absence of prior cervical surgery is not a contraindication; in fact, prior cervical fusion at adjacent levels may complicate arthroplasty, so a virgin cervical spine is preferable.

questions.question:
Duchenne muscular dystrophy is characterized by:
A) Anterior horn cell degeneration
B) Peripheral nerve demyelination
C) X-linked recessive absence of dystrophin, with calf pseudohypertrophy, Gower sign, and markedly elevated creatine kinase
D) Autosomal dominant inheritance with distal weakness
E) Reduced but present dystrophin with a milder course
questions.answer:
C)
DMD results from a dystrophin gene mutation on Xp21 with complete absence of the protein. Boys present at 3–6 years with proximal weakness, waddling gait, toe walking, calf pseudohypertrophy (fatty/fibrous replacement), and the Gower maneuver (climbing up the legs to stand). CK is elevated 10–100 fold. Corticosteroids prolong ambulation. Scoliosis progresses rapidly after loss of ambulation, and early posterior spinal fusion is considered before forced vital capacity falls below approximately 35–40% of predicted.

A is incorrect because anterior horn cell degeneration describes spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), not DMD. B is incorrect because peripheral nerve demyelination characterizes hereditary motor-sensory neuropathies (e.g., Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease), not a myopathy like DMD. D is incorrect because DMD is X-linked recessive (not autosomal dominant) and causes proximal (not distal) weakness. E is incorrect because reduced but present dystrophin with a milder course describes Becker muscular dystrophy, not Duchenne.

questions.question:
A trauma patient has a heart rate of 130, blood pressure of 90/70, respiratory rate of 32, and confusion. This corresponds to which class of hemorrhagic shock?
A) Class IV (more than 40%)
B) Class III (30-40%)
C) Class I (up to 15% blood loss)
D) Neurogenic shock
E) Class II (15-30%)
questions.answer:
B)
Class III hemorrhagic shock (30–40% blood volume loss, ~1,500–2,000 mL) is characterized by heart rate >120, systolic hypotension with narrowed pulse pressure, tachypnea (RR 30–40), decreased urine output, and altered mental status (confusion/anxiety). This patient's HR of 130, BP 90/70, RR 32, and confusion match Class III criteria. Blood product transfusion is typically required.

A is incorrect because Class IV shock (>40% loss) presents with markedly depressed consciousness (obtundation/lethargy), heart rate >140, negligible blood pressure, and minimal or absent urine output — more severe than this presentation. C is incorrect because Class I shock (up to 15% loss) produces minimal physiologic changes: normal heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, and mental status. D is incorrect because neurogenic shock results from loss of sympathetic tone (e.g., spinal cord injury) and classically presents with hypotension and bradycardia, not tachycardia. E is incorrect because Class II shock (15–30% loss) causes tachycardia (100–120) and anxiety but maintains systolic blood pressure; the hypotension and confusion seen here exceed Class II parameters.

questions.question:
A 3-year-old treated successfully with closed reduction now has an acetabular index of 32 degrees. The most appropriate management is:
A) Immediate pelvic osteotomy
B) Repeat closed reduction
C) Continued observation with serial radiographs, since acetabular remodeling continues, with osteotomy considered if dysplasia persists
D) Discharge from follow-up
E) Femoral shortening osteotomy
questions.answer:
C)
Acetabular remodeling continues for several years after concentric reduction, with the greatest potential before age 4 and continuing more slowly thereafter. In a 3-year-old with a successful closed reduction and an acetabular index of 32 degrees, serial radiographs should be followed for improvement. Persistent dysplasia beyond roughly age 4–5, or failure to show progressive improvement, prompts consideration of a pelvic osteotomy.

A is incorrect because immediate pelvic osteotomy is premature in a 3-year-old with a concentrically reduced hip; significant acetabular remodeling potential remains and surgery should be reserved for persistent dysplasia. B is incorrect because the hip is already concentrically reduced; repeating the closed reduction is unnecessary and would not address acetabular dysplasia. D is incorrect because premature discharge risks missing residual dysplasia that, if untreated, leads to early degenerative arthritis. E is incorrect because femoral shortening osteotomy is used as an adjunct during open reduction (typically in older children) to facilitate reduction, not to treat acetabular dysplasia in a successfully reduced hip.

questions.question:
Suprascapular nerve entrapment at the spinoglenoid notch produces:
A) Supraspinatus and infraspinatus weakness
B) Isolated infraspinatus weakness and atrophy
C) Trapezius weakness
D) Deltoid weakness
E) Serratus anterior weakness with scapular winging
questions.answer:
B)
At the spinoglenoid notch, the suprascapular nerve has already given off its branch to the supraspinatus, so compression at this site spares the supraspinatus and produces isolated infraspinatus weakness and atrophy with loss of external rotation strength. A common cause is a paralabral (ganglion) cyst associated with a posterosuperior labral tear, treated by cyst decompression and labral repair.

A is incorrect because combined supraspinatus and infraspinatus weakness occurs with entrapment at the suprascapular notch (proximal to the spinoglenoid notch), where the nerve supplies both muscles. B is incorrect — skip (correct answer). C is incorrect because the trapezius is innervated by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), not the suprascapular nerve. D is incorrect because the deltoid is innervated by the axillary nerve (C5–C6), not the suprascapular nerve. E is incorrect because the serratus anterior is innervated by the long thoracic nerve (C5–C7); its palsy causes medial scapular winging, unrelated to suprascapular nerve pathology.

questions.question:
When biopsying a bone lesion with a cortical window, which shape reduces the risk of pathologic fracture?
A) Round or oval window
B) Square window
C) Window shape is irrelevant
D) Triangular window
E) Rectangular window with sharp corners
questions.answer:
A)
Sharp corners act as stress risers; a round or oval cortical window minimizes the reduction in torsional strength. The window should be as small as practical, and the defect can be sealed with bone cement or bone wax to reduce hematoma spread. Protected weight bearing after biopsy of a weight-bearing bone is also prudent.

B is incorrect because a square window has four sharp 90° corners that concentrate stress and significantly increase the risk of pathologic fracture. C is incorrect because window shape is highly relevant — sharp-cornered defects markedly reduce torsional and bending strength compared with rounded ones. D is incorrect because a triangular window has three sharp corners that serve as stress risers, increasing fracture risk. E is incorrect because a rectangular window with sharp corners creates the same stress-riser problem, predisposing to fracture propagation from the corners.

questions.question:
A 13-year-old boy cannot bear weight and has an acute unstable SCFE. Which adjunct at the time of fixation is intended to reduce the risk of osteonecrosis?
A) Capsular decompression of the intracapsular hematoma
B) Aggressive manipulative reduction under anesthesia
C) Placement of three parallel screws
D) Immediate weight bearing postoperatively
E) Delayed treatment for 2 weeks
questions.answer:
A)
In an acute unstable SCFE, elevated intracapsular pressure from the associated hemarthrosis may tamponade the retinacular vessels supplying the femoral head. Capsular decompression — performed percutaneously or via an open approach at the time of fixation — is intended to relieve this pressure and reduce the risk of osteonecrosis. Although osteonecrosis rates remain substantial in unstable slips despite these measures, decompression is a widely recommended adjunct.

B is incorrect because aggressive manipulative reduction under anesthesia increases the risk of osteonecrosis by further damaging the already compromised retinacular blood supply; gentle positional reduction is preferred. C is incorrect because placement of three parallel screws is not standard for SCFE fixation (a single central cannulated screw is the accepted technique) and does not address the vascular tamponade mechanism. D is incorrect because immediate weight bearing is not recommended after fixation of an unstable SCFE and does nothing to reduce osteonecrosis risk. E is incorrect because delaying treatment for 2 weeks would worsen outcomes; urgent surgical stabilization is recommended for unstable SCFE to minimize further slip progression and vascular compromise.

questions.question:
A patient has snuffbox tenderness after a fall but normal radiographs. The most appropriate management is:
A) Immediate surgical fixation
B) Range of motion exercises
C) Thumb spica immobilization with repeat imaging or advanced imaging (MRI or CT)
D) Discharge with reassurance
E) Steroid injection
questions.answer:
C)
Up to 25% of scaphoid fractures are occult on initial radiographs. Standard practice is thumb spica immobilization with repeat radiographs at 10–14 days, or immediate MRI, which is the most sensitive and specific early study and is cost-effective by avoiding unnecessary immobilization. Missed scaphoid fractures progress to nonunion and scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse (SNAC wrist).

A is incorrect because immediate surgical fixation is not indicated when no fracture has been confirmed; the diagnosis must first be established with repeat or advanced imaging.
B is incorrect because range of motion exercises risk displacing an occult scaphoid fracture and are contraindicated until a fracture has been ruled out.
D is incorrect because discharging with reassurance alone risks missing a scaphoid fracture, which can lead to nonunion, avascular necrosis, and SNAC wrist.
E is incorrect because steroid injection has no role in the management of a suspected scaphoid fracture and could mask symptoms, delaying appropriate diagnosis and treatment.

questions.question:
Which sagittal parameter is a fixed, morphologic value that does not change with position?
A) Lumbar lordosis
B) Sagittal vertical axis
C) Sacral slope
D) Pelvic tilt
E) Pelvic incidence
questions.answer:
E)
Pelvic incidence (PI) is an anatomic constant determined by pelvic morphology; it does not change after skeletal maturity regardless of patient position. PI equals the sum of pelvic tilt (PT) and sacral slope (SS). Restoration of lumbar lordosis to within approximately 10 degrees of PI, PT below 20 degrees, and SVA below 5 cm are common sagittal realignment goals correlating with better health-related quality of life.

A is incorrect because lumbar lordosis is a positional parameter that changes with posture, spinal pathology, and compensatory mechanisms.
B is incorrect because the sagittal vertical axis (SVA) is a global balance measure that varies with standing posture and compensatory pelvic or spinal adjustments.
C is incorrect because sacral slope is a positional parameter that changes as the pelvis rotates (tilts) in the sagittal plane.
D is incorrect because pelvic tilt is a positional parameter that changes with pelvic rotation; it increases as a compensatory mechanism for sagittal imbalance.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old man has progressive gait imbalance and lower extremity hyperreflexia with normal cervical imaging. CT of the thoracic spine shows beak-type ossification of the ligamentum flavum at T10-T11. The most appropriate surgical treatment is:
A) Epidural steroid injection
B) Thoracic disc arthroplasty
C) Posterior decompression with laminectomy and en bloc resection of the ossified ligamentum flavum
D) Observation with serial examination
E) Anterior thoracic corpectomy
questions.answer:
C)
Ossification of the ligamentum flavum (OLF) is a posterior compressive pathology that most often affects the lower thoracic spine. When it causes myelopathy (gait imbalance, hyperreflexia), the standard surgical treatment is posterior decompression with laminectomy and en bloc resection of the ossified ligamentum flavum, carefully floating the ossified mass away from the dura. The dura is frequently adherent or ossified, so dural tear and CSF leak are recognized complications.

A is incorrect because epidural steroid injection does not address a structural, progressive compressive myelopathy caused by ossified ligamentum flavum; it is a temporizing measure for radiculopathy, not myelopathy from bony compression. B is incorrect because thoracic disc arthroplasty addresses anterior disc pathology and is not indicated for a posterior compressive lesion; moreover, motion-preserving arthroplasty in the thoracic spine is not a standard procedure. D is incorrect because the patient has progressive myelopathic signs (gait imbalance, hyperreflexia), which constitute a surgical indication; observation risks irreversible spinal cord injury. E is incorrect because anterior thoracic corpectomy is reserved for anterior compressive pathology (e.g., thoracic disc herniation, OPLL); OLF is a posterior pathology best addressed posteriorly.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old man sustains an intra-articular fracture of the base of the thumb metacarpal with a small volar-ulnar fragment held by the anterior oblique ligament while the shaft is displaced proximally and radially by the abductor pollicis longus. This injury is:
A) A Bennett fracture
B) An extra-articular metacarpal base fracture
C) A Rolando fracture
D) A carpometacarpal dislocation without fracture
E) A gamekeeper thumb
questions.answer:
A)
The Bennett fracture is a two-part intra-articular fracture-dislocation of the thumb metacarpal base in which the volar-ulnar fragment remains attached to the trapezium by the anterior oblique (volar beak) ligament while the abductor pollicis longus and adductor pollicis displace the metacarpal shaft proximally and radially. Treatment requires longitudinal traction, extension, pronation, and abduction to reduce the joint, followed by percutaneous pinning or open fixation.

B is incorrect because an extra-articular metacarpal base fracture does not involve the joint surface; the stem explicitly describes an intra-articular fracture. C is incorrect because a Rolando fracture is a comminuted (T- or Y-shaped) intra-articular fracture of the thumb metacarpal base with three or more fragments, whereas the stem describes only two parts. D is incorrect because a carpometacarpal dislocation without fracture involves no fracture fragment; the stem describes a fracture with a volar-ulnar fragment. E is incorrect because gamekeeper's (skier's) thumb refers to an injury of the ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb MCP joint, not a fracture of the metacarpal base.

questions.question:
Which is the most common direction of instability after a seizure or electrocution injury to the shoulder?
A) Anterior
B) Inferior
C) Superior
D) Multidirectional
E) Posterior
questions.answer:
E)
Posterior dislocation is the most common direction of instability after a seizure or electrocution injury. During a seizure or electric shock, violent simultaneous contraction of all shoulder muscles occurs, and the stronger internal rotators (subscapularis, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi) overpower the external rotators, forcing the humeral head posteriorly. The arm is held in adduction and internal rotation, and the AP radiograph may show the classic 'lightbulb sign' (internally rotated humeral head). An axillary lateral or scapular-Y view is essential because posterior dislocations are missed on initial evaluation up to 50% of the time.

A is incorrect because anterior dislocations are typically caused by forced abduction and external rotation (e.g., falls), not by the internal-rotation–dominant muscle forces generated during seizures. B is incorrect because inferior dislocation (luxatio erecta) results from a hyperabduction mechanism, not seizure activity. C is incorrect because superior dislocation is exceedingly rare and requires a massive force directed superiorly. D is incorrect because the mechanism in seizures/electrocution is a specific, reproducible force vector (internal rotation dominance) that produces a unidirectional posterior dislocation, not multidirectional instability.

questions.question:
Which factor most strongly determines screw pullout strength in cancellous bone?
A) Screw material
B) Screw core (root) diameter
C) Bone mineral density and outer thread diameter
D) Thread pitch alone
E) Screw length beyond the far cortex
questions.answer:
C)
Pullout strength in cancellous bone is proportional to the volume of bone captured between threads, which depends on outer thread diameter, thread depth, length of thread engagement, and — most importantly — the density of the bone. Bone mineral density is the single strongest determinant; among screw design variables, outer (major) thread diameter is the most influential. In osteoporotic bone, locking screws, longer threads, and cement augmentation improve fixation.

A is incorrect because screw material (e.g., stainless steel vs. titanium) affects screw strength and biocompatibility but has negligible effect on pullout strength, which is governed by the bone–screw interface. B is incorrect because core (root) diameter determines the screw's resistance to bending and shear failure of the screw itself, not its resistance to pullout from bone. D is incorrect because thread pitch affects the number of threads engaged per unit length but is a secondary factor; it does not independently determine pullout strength as strongly as bone density and outer thread diameter. E is incorrect because screw length beyond the far cortex (i.e., screw protrusion) does not contribute to fixation; only the length of thread engaged within bone matters, and in cancellous bone the quality (density) of that bone is paramount.
